12.s: The 2016 amendment renamed the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 as the
o: Protection of Children from Hazardous Work Act
Child Rights and Bonded Labour Act
12.x: The 2016 amendment renamed the statute as the Child and Adolescent Labour Act and introduced the present age-based restrictions.
12.tq: Test the exact statutory title, a common look-alike wording trap.
xs: The **2016** amendment renamed the **1986** Act the **Child and Adolescent Labour Act** — option **(1)**.
It bars any **child below 14** in any occupation (except **family enterprise/after school**).
xa: Adolescents **14-18** are barred from **hazardous work**.
**Art. 24** — no child below **14** in factories, mines, hazardous work.
**Art. 21A** + **Art. 24** together protect children.

12.s: Which of the following pairs of enabling laws is correctly associated with Article 23?
o: ITPA 1956 and Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976
Maternity Benefit Act and RPwD Act alone
Forest Rights Act 2006 and Arms Act 1959
12.x: The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 and the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 are enabling laws associated with Article 23.
12.tq: Match the constitutional right with laws directly addressing trafficking and bonded labour.
xs: **ITPA 1956** and the **Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976** are the Art. 23 laws — option **(1)**.
ITPA penalises **brothels, pimping**; the 1976 Act abolishes **debt bondage**.
xa: **POCSO Act, 2012** is a linked child-protection law.
Trafficking is now **Sec. 143 BNS** (from **1 July 2024**).
**Art. 23(1):** traffic in human beings, **begar**, forced labour.

12.s: The Child Labour Amendment Act, 2016 provides that:
o: All work by persons below 18 years is prohibited without exception
Children below 14 years may work in any occupation after school hours
Children below 14 years cannot work, except for helping in family work after school, while adolescents aged 14–18 years are barred from hazardous work
Only employment in mines is prohibited for children below 14 years
12.x: The 2016 amendment prohibits work by children below 14 years, subject to the stated family-help exception after school. It also prohibits adolescents aged 14–18 years from hazardous work.
12.tq: Watch for extreme words such as ‘all’ and identify the age-group distinction.
xs: The **2016** amendment: **no child below 14** in any occupation (except **family enterprise/after school**); **adolescents 14-18** barred from **hazardous work** — option **(3)**.
It is not a total bar on all work below **18**, nor limited to mines.
xa: It renamed the law the **Child and Adolescent Labour Act**.
**Art. 24** does not bar **harmless/innocent work**.
DPSP **Art. 39(e)/(f)** protects children's tender age.

12.s: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and the State Commissions (SCPCRs) are constituted under which law?
o: Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
12.x: NCPCR and SCPCRs are set up under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005. POCSO 2012 deals with sexual offences against children, ITPA 1956 with brothels and immoral traffic, and the 1986 Act with child labour; none of them creates the commissions.
12.tq: NCPCR = CPCR Act 2005, not POCSO 2012.
xs: **NCPCR/SCPCR** are set up under the **Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005** — option **(1)**.
**POCSO 2012** — child sexual offences; **ITPA 1956** — brothels; **1986 Act** — child labour.
xa: District **Anti-Human Trafficking Units** are **MHA-funded**.
**Art. 24** bars children **below 14** from hazardous work.
**Art. 21A** gives free education for **6-14 years**.

12.s:
Match List-I (term in Article 25(1)) with List-II (meaning):
List-I
a. Conscience
b. Profess
c. Practise
d. Propagate
List-II
i. Worship, rituals and ceremonies integral to the religion
ii. Spreading one's beliefs to others
iii. Inner freedom to mould one's relation with God, including the freedom to follow no religion
iv. Declaring beliefs openly, verbally or by visible symbols such as a turban, crucifix or kirpan
Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Conscience is the inner freedom (iii), profess is open declaration through words or symbols (iv), practise is worship and rituals (i) and propagate is spreading beliefs (ii), so A is correct. B swaps conscience and profess and also practise and propagate. C swaps profess and practise. D swaps conscience and propagate.
12.tq: Inner = conscience, outward symbol = profess, ritual = practise, spreading = propagate.
xs: **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(1)**.
**Conscience** — inner freedom, incl. following **no religion**; **Profess** — declaring beliefs openly or by symbols (**turban, crucifix, kirpan**).
**Practise** — **worship, rituals, ceremonies**; **Propagate** — **spreading beliefs** to others.
xa: ⚠ Propagation does **NOT** include a right to **convert** another person.
Art. 25(1) is subject to **public order, morality and health** and other Part III provisions.
**Stanislaus v. MP (1977):** no right to convert.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding propagation of religion under Article 25:
1. It includes spreading one's religious beliefs to others.
2. It includes an unrestricted right to convert another person.
3. A right to convert another person would affect that person's freedom of conscience.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Propagation means spreading one's beliefs, but it does not include a right to convert another person because that would impinge on the other person's freedom of conscience.
12.tq: Identify the precise limit concealed by the distinction between propagation and conversion.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **propagate** = **spreading one's beliefs** to others.
Statement 2 wrong: it does **NOT** include a right to **convert** another person.
Statement 3: conversion would **impinge on the other's freedom of conscience**.
xa: **Rev. Stanislaus v. State of MP (1977)** upheld the **Orissa and MP anti-conversion Acts**.
**Orissa Freedom of Religion Act, 1967**; **MP Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam, 1968**.
Limits on Art. 25 include **no forcible conversion**.

12.s:
Freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion under Article 25(1) are subject to which of the following?
1. Public order
2. Morality
3. Health
4. The other provisions of Part III
Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Article 25(1) expressly subjects these freedoms to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III.
12.tq: Read the complete qualifying phrase and avoid omitting the final constitutional condition.
xs: Art. 25(1) is subject to **public order, morality and health** and the **other provisions of Part III** — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
Art. 25 is additionally subject to other **Part III** rights.
xa: Art. 26 rights are subject to **public order, morality, health** only.
**Art. 25(2)** lets the State regulate **secular activity** and provide **social reform**.
The State can intervene to root out **social evils**.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 25(2):
1. Under Article 25(2)(a), the State may regulate or restrict economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religious practice.
2. Under Article 25(2)(b), the State may provide for social welfare and reform or throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.
3. Article 25(2)(a) permits the State to regulate only spiritual beliefs and not the secular activities associated with religion.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: 25(2)(a) covers economic, financial, political or other secular activity. Statement 2 is correct: 25(2)(b) covers social welfare and reform and temple entry for all classes of Hindus. Statement 3 is wrong: 25(2)(a) reaches secular activity, not spiritual belief. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Art. 25(2)(a) = secular activity; 25(2)(b) = reform and temple entry.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **25(2)(a)** — regulate **economic, financial, political or other secular activity** linked to religion.
Statement 2: **25(2)(b)** — **social welfare and reform**, or **throw open Hindu religious institutions** to all Hindus.
Statement 3 wrong: 25(2)(a) reaches **secular activity**, not spiritual belief.
xa: **Explanation II:** "Hindus" includes **Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists**.
Indian secularism allows **positive intervention** for reform, e.g. **temple entry**.
**Church of God (2000):** loudspeakers subject to public order.

12.s:
Consider the following statements about the explanations attached to Article 25:
1. Wearing and carrying kirpans is deemed to be included in the profession of the Sikh religion.
2. For Article 25(2)(b), the expression ‘Hindus’ includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists.
3. The explanation relating to kirpans applies only to the practice and not to the profession of the Sikh religion.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because wearing and carrying kirpans is specifically deemed part of the profession of the Sikh religion.
12.tq: Find the wrong statement by checking the exact constitutional wording of the explanations.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **Explanation I** — wearing and carrying **kirpans** is part of the **profession** of the **Sikh** religion.
Statement 2: **Explanation II** — "Hindus" in **25(2)(b)** includes **Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists**.
Statement 3 wrong: the kirpan explanation is about **profession**, not only practice.
xa: ⚠ **Explanation I = kirpan (Sikh); Explanation II = "Hindus" includes Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists**.
**Profess** includes visible symbols like **turban, crucifix, kirpan**.
Hindu religious institutions are construed accordingly.

12.s: The Supreme Court held in Javed (2003) that polygamy is:
o: Not an essential religious practice protected by Article 25
A practice protected only for religious denominations
An essential religious practice absolutely protected by Article 25
A secular activity regulated exclusively under Article 23
12.x: In Javed (2003), polygamy was held not to be an essential religious practice protected by Article 25.
12.tq: Use the case-law name to discriminate between an essential religious practice and a non-protected practice.
xs: **Javed (2003):** polygamy is **not an essential religious practice** protected by **Art. 25** — option **(1)**.
The **ERP test** decides which practices are integral to a religion.
xa: **Shayara Bano (2017)** invalidated **instant triple talaq**; **polygamy, nikah halala** left open.
The ERP test was formulated by the SC in **1954** (**Shirur Mutt**).
**Karnataka HC 2022:** **hijab** not an ERP.

12.s: A State law seeks to remove a social evil associated with a religious practice. Which constitutional position is most appropriate?
o: The State may intervene to root out social evils, subject to constitutional limitations.
Only Parliament can intervene in every religious practice.
Such intervention is valid only if the practice is followed by foreigners.
The State can never intervene in religious matters.
12.x: Freedom of religion is not absolute. The State can intervene to root out social evils, while respecting the applicable constitutional restrictions.
12.tq: Apply the non-absolute nature of religious freedom to a short constitutional scenario.
xs: The **State can intervene to root out social evils**, subject to constitutional limits — option **(1)**.
**Art. 25(2)(b)** allows **social welfare and reform**; Art. 25 is subject to **public order, morality, health**.
Option 4 is wrong: Indian secularism allows **positive intervention**.
xa: Indian model: **Sarva Dharma Sambhava** = state neutrality + **positive intervention** for reform.
Western model: **strict separation**; religion purely private.
**No forcible conversion** is another limit.

12.s: "All persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion." This text is found in which Article of the Constitution?
12.x: These words are Article 25(1), subject to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III. Article 19(1) lists the six freedoms of citizens. Article 26(1) gives religious denominations the right to manage their own affairs. Article 29(1) protects the language, script and culture of any section of citizens.
12.tq: Conscience + profess, practise, propagate = Art. 25(1). The usual wrong options are 19(1), 26(1) and 29(1).
xs: The quoted text is **Article 25(1)** — option **(2)**.
It is subject to **public order, morality and health** and other Part III provisions.
**Art. 19(1)** has the citizens' freedoms; **Art. 26(1)** is denominations managing affairs.
xa: ⚠ Exam angle: quoted text of 25(1) → identify the Article (asked **2018, 2023**).
Distractors used: **Arts 19(1), 26(1), 29(1)**.
"All persons" — Art. 25 is available to **citizens and non-citizens**.

12.s:
Consider the following pairs regarding the availability of rights:
1. Article 25 — All persons
2. Article 26 — Religious denominations or any section thereof
3. Article 27 — Citizens only
4. Article 28 — All persons
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
12.x: Pairs 1, 2 and 4 are correct: Articles 25 and 28 are available to all persons, and Article 26 to religious denominations or any section of them. Pair 3 is wrong because Article 27 is also available to all persons (citizens and foreigners), not to citizens only.
12.tq: Use the comparison table and identify the swapped eligibility category.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Art. 25** and **Art. 28** — **all persons**; **Art. 26** — **religious denominations** or any section.
Pair 3 wrong: **Art. 27** is also for **all persons**, not citizens only.
xa: **Art. 23** protects **citizens and non-citizens**, against **State and private persons**.
Art. 27 **bars taxes, not fees**.
Art. 28(3): a **minor** needs **guardian's consent** to attend religious instruction.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the neutrality provisions of the Constitution:
1. Article 27 provides that no person shall be compelled to pay a tax for the promotion of one particular religion.
2. Article 28(1) bars religious instruction in educational institutions wholly maintained out of State funds.
3. Article 28(1) bars religious instruction in every educational institution, whether or not it is funded by the State.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: Article 27 bars a tax for one religion. Statement 2 is correct: Article 28(1) applies to institutions wholly maintained out of State funds. Statement 3 is wrong: the bar is limited to wholly State-funded institutions, not every institution. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: 28(1) bites only on 'wholly State-funded' institutions.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **Art. 27** — **no tax for one religion**.
Statement 2: **Art. 28(1)** — **no religious instruction** in institutions **wholly maintained out of State funds**.
Statement 3 wrong: the bar is only for **wholly State-funded** institutions.
xa: State-administered **trust/endowment** institutions: instruction **allowed** if the trust requires.
**Recognised** or **aided** institutions: **voluntary**; minor needs **guardian's consent**.
Secularism means **equal respect for all religions**; **no state religion**.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 26:
1. A religious denomination may establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes.
2. It may own and acquire movable and immovable property.
3. It may administer its property in accordance with law.
4. These rights are subject to public order, morality and health.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Article 26 includes all four rights and expressly subjects them to public order, morality and health.
12.tq: Test the complete set of clauses and the common constitutional limitations together.
xs: All four — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**Art. 26:** (a) **establish and maintain institutions**; (b) manage own affairs; (c) **own and acquire property**; (d) **administer property in accordance with law**.
These are subject to **public order, morality, health**.
xa: Holder: every **religious denomination** or section of it.
**Shirur Mutt (1954)** defined "religious denomination".
**Sabarimala (2018):** Ayyappa devotees **not a separate denomination**.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 27:
1. No person can be compelled to pay taxes whose proceeds are used to promote a particular religion.
2. A fee charged for the secular administration of religious institutions is also barred by Article 27.
3. Taxes may be used to support all religions equally.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: Article 27 bars taxes for promoting a particular religion. Statement 2 is wrong: Article 27 bars taxes, not fees, so a fee for secular administration is allowed. Statement 3 is correct: taxes may support all religions equally. So A (misses 3), C and D (include 2) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Art. 27 bars a tax for one religion; fees and equal support are fine.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **Art. 27** — no one compelled to pay **taxes** that **promote a particular religion**.
Statement 2 wrong: Art. 27 **bars taxes, not fees** — a **fee** for secular administration is allowed.
Statement 3: taxes may support **all religions equally**.
xa: Indian secularism permits **aid** (e.g. **Amarnath Yatra, Haj** support).
Western secularism allows **no state aid** to religious institutions.
**Art. 28(1)** is the other neutrality provision.

12.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
(a) Article 26
(b) Article 27
(c) Article 28(1)
(d) Article 28(3)

List-II (Subject)
(i) No person compelled to attend religious instruction without consent
(ii) Religious denomination’s right to manage religious affairs
(iii) No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
(iv) No compulsory tax for promotion of a particular religion

Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Article 26 concerns denominational religious affairs; Article 27 concerns taxes; Article 28(1) concerns State-funded religious instruction; and Article 28(3) protects freedom from compulsory attendance.
12.tq: Start with the sure Article 27 pair and then complete the Article 28 distinctions.
xs: **a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 26** — denominations **manage religious affairs**; **Art. 27** — **no tax** for a particular religion.
**Art. 28(1)** — no religious instruction in **wholly State-funded** institutions; **Art. 28(3)** — no one compelled to attend **without consent**.
xa: **Art. 28(2):** State-administered **trust/endowment** institutions may give instruction if the trust requires.
A **minor** needs the **guardian's consent**.
Art. 28 is an **individual right**.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding religious instruction under Article 28:
1. In an institution established under a trust or endowment but administered by the State, religious instruction is allowed if the trust requires it.
2. In a State-aided institution, a minor can attend religious instruction only with the guardian's consent.
3. In a State-recognised institution, attendance at religious instruction can be made compulsory.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: Article 28(2) exempts State-administered trust institutions where the trust requires instruction. Statement 2 is correct: under 28(3) attendance is voluntary and a minor needs the guardian's consent. Statement 3 is wrong: in recognised or aided institutions no one can be compelled to attend. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Art. 28: wholly State-funded = prohibited; trust-run by State = allowed; recognised/aided = voluntary.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **trust/endowment** institution **administered by the State** — instruction **allowed** if the trust requires (**28(2)**).
Statement 2: **State-aided** institution — **voluntary**; a minor needs **guardian's consent** (**28(3)**).
Statement 3 wrong: in **recognised** institutions attendance is also **voluntary**.
xa: **Wholly State-funded** institutions: religious instruction **prohibited** (**28(1)**).
**Bijoe Emmanuel (1986):** children cannot be compelled to sing the **National Anthem**.
SC (**12 May 2026**) left religious schools' status to the **Ministry of Education**.

12.s: With reference to the current debate on religious instruction in educational institutions, which one of the following is correct?
o: The Supreme Court has held that all religious instruction is governed exclusively by Article 25.
The Ministry of Home Affairs has been directed to classify every school as a religious denomination.
The Supreme Court has left to the Ministry of Education whether schools imparting religious instruction fall under Article 26(a) rather than Articles 19(1)(g) or 30(1).
The issue concerns only the official language under Article 343.
12.x: The issue left to the Ministry of Education concerns whether schools imparting religious instruction fall under Article 26(a), rather than under Articles 19(1)(g) or 30(1).
12.tq: Compare the constitutional provisions specifically placed against one another instead of substituting Article 25.
xs: The SC left it to the **Ministry of Education** whether schools imparting religious instruction fall under **Art. 26(a)** rather than **Art. 19(1)(g)/30(1)** — option **(3)**.
The Bench was led by **Justice Dipankar Datta** (**12 May 2026**).
xa: **Art. 26(a):** denominations may **establish and maintain institutions** for religious and charitable purposes.
**Art. 28(1):** no religious instruction in **wholly State-funded** institutions.
**Art. 343** is about the **official language** — Hindi — unrelated.

12.s:
With reference to the Essential Religious Practice test, consider the following statements:
1. It was formulated by the Supreme Court in 1954.
2. The Constitution expressly defines the term “essential” in relation to religious practices.
3. It is used to identify practices integral to a religion.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: The doctrine was formulated by the Supreme Court in 1954 and concerns practices integral to a religion. The Constitution does not define “essential”; statement 2 is false.
12.tq: Use a precise constitutional-versus-judicial distinction to reject the false statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: the **ERP test** was formulated by the SC in **1954** (**Shirur Mutt**).
Statement 3: it decides which practices are **integral to a religion** and so protected.
Statement 2 wrong: the **Constitution does not define "essential"**.
xa: Criticism: the ERP test makes **courts arbiters of religion** (e.g. **Sastri Yagnapurushadji, 1966**).
**Nine-judge Bench** under **CJI Surya Kant** heard ERP across faiths (**2026**).
Centre (SG **Tushar Mehta**): protection **not limited to ERP**.

12.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Case)
a. Shirur Mutt case
b. Rev. Stanislaus case
c. Bijoe Emmanuel case
 d. Shayara Bano case

List-II (Issue or holding)
i. Jehovah’s Witness children and the National Anthem
 ii. Instant triple talaq
 iii. Essential Religious Practice doctrine
 iv. Right to propagate does not include right to convert

Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Shirur Mutt is associated with the ERP doctrine; Rev. Stanislaus with propagation and conversion; Bijoe Emmanuel with the National Anthem; and Shayara Bano with instant triple talaq.
12.tq: Start from the sure case-issue pairs and eliminate codes that reverse the landmark holdings.
xs: **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(1)**.
**Shirur Mutt (1954)** — origin of the **ERP doctrine**; **Rev. Stanislaus (1977)** — **propagate ≠ convert**.
**Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)** — **Jehovah's Witness** children and the **National Anthem**; **Shayara Bano (2017)** — **instant triple talaq**.
xa: **Ratilal (1954):** State cannot touch essential practices.
**Javed (2003):** **polygamy** not an ERP.
**Ramji Lal Modi** upheld **Sec. 295A IPC** (now **Sec. 299 BNS**).

12.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Shayara Bano v. Union of India
B. Shirur Mutt case
C. Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala
D. Rev. Stanislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh
12.x: The cases were decided in the order Shirur Mutt (1954), Rev. Stanislaus (1977), Bijoe Emmanuel (1986), and Shayara Bano (2017).
12.tq: Place the earliest and latest cases first, then distinguish the two middle dates.
xs: Order: **Shirur Mutt (1954)** → **Rev. Stanislaus (1977)** → **Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)** → **Shayara Bano (2017)** — **B, D, C, A**, option **(1)**.
Shirur Mutt — **ERP**; Stanislaus — **conversion**; Bijoe — **National Anthem**; Shayara Bano — **triple talaq**.
xa: **St. Stephen's (1992)** — minority-institution autonomy.
**Church of God (2000)** — loudspeakers subject to public order.
**Sabarimala** (**2018**) — **4:1**, age-based bar on women struck down.

12.s: In Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986), the Supreme Court held that Jehovah’s Witness children:
o: Were exempt from attending educational institutions.
Could refuse to stand during the National Anthem as an absolute religious right.
Could be compelled to sing the National Anthem if they stood in the assembly.
Could not be compelled to sing the National Anthem and that standing respectfully was sufficient.
12.x: The Court held that the children could not be compelled to sing the National Anthem; standing respectfully was considered sufficient.
12.tq: Test the precise distinction between non-singing and disrespectful conduct.
xs: **Bijoe Emmanuel (1986):** **Jehovah's Witness** children **cannot be compelled to sing the National Anthem**; **standing respectfully** is enough — option **(4)**.
They were not exempt from school, nor allowed to refuse to stand.
xa: **Art. 28(3):** no one compelled to attend religious instruction without consent.
Freedom of **conscience** includes the freedom to follow **no religion**.
**Shirur Mutt (1954)** — origin of the **ERP** test.

12.s:
With reference to the Sabarimala judgment, consider the following statements:
1. Women of all ages were allowed entry.
2. The Court held that devotion cannot be subjected to gender discrimination.
3. The exclusion of women was accepted as an Essential Religious Practice.
4. Secularism was reaffirmed as part of the Basic Structure.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: The Sabarimala judgment allowed women of all ages, rejected gender discrimination in devotion and reaffirmed secularism as part of the Basic Structure. The exclusion was not accepted as an ERP, making statement 3 false.
12.tq: Identify the single reversed holding in a group of closely related case propositions.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **women of all ages** were allowed entry; the **age-based bar** was struck down.
Statement 2: "**Devotion cannot be subjected to gender discrimination**".
Statement 3 wrong: the exclusion was held **not an ERP**.
Statement 4: **secularism** was reaffirmed as **basic structure**.
xa: Case name: **Indian Young Lawyers Assn. v. State of Kerala** (**28 Sep 2018**), **5-judge** bench, **4:1**.
Ayyappa devotees are **not a separate denomination**.
First women of the barred age group to enter: **Bindu Ammini and Kanaka Durga** (Jan **2019**).

12.s:
With reference to the Sabarimala judgment (Indian Young Lawyers Association, 28 September 2018), consider the following statements:
1. It was delivered by a five-judge Bench by a 4:1 majority.
2. Ayyappa devotees were held to be a separate religious denomination.
3. The exclusion of women of a certain age group was held not to be an Essential Religious Practice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: a 5-judge Bench decided 4:1. Statement 2 is wrong: Ayyappa devotees were held not to be a separate denomination. Statement 3 is correct: the exclusion was not an ERP. So A, C and D (which include 2) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Sabarimala 2018: 5 judges, 4:1, not a denomination, not an ERP.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: a **5-judge bench** decided **4:1**.
Statement 2 wrong: Ayyappa devotees are **not a separate denomination**.
Statement 3: the exclusion was **not an ERP**.
xa: An ERP claim **cannot restrict participation rights** of others; the **state cannot endorse a practice**.
⚠ **Sabarimala 2018 = 5-judge, 4:1; review reference = 9-judge Bench under CJI Surya Kant**.
Principle: "**Devotion cannot be subjected to gender discrimination**".

12.s: Who were the first women of the barred age group reported to have entered the Sabarimala temple in January 2019?
o: Kanaka Durga and Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar
12.x: Bindu Ammini and Kanaka Durga were reported as the first women of the barred age group to enter Sabarimala in January 2019.
12.tq: Recall the paired names associated with the immediate aftermath of a landmark judgment.
xs: **Bindu Ammini and Kanaka Durga** were the first women of the barred age group to enter (**Jan 2019**) — option **(4)** (PYQ G2 2025).
**Bijoe Emmanuel** is the National Anthem case; **Shayara Bano** the triple talaq case; **Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar** the Shirur Mutt case.
xa: The Sabarimala judgment came on **28 Sep 2018** (5-judge bench, **4:1**).
Women of **all ages** were allowed entry.
The review reference went to a **Nine-judge Bench** headed by **CJI Surya Kant** (**2026**).

12.s:
With reference to the 2026 Sabarimala review reference on the Essential Religious Practice (ERP) doctrine, consider the following statements:
1. It was heard by a nine-judge Constitution Bench headed by CJI Surya Kant.
2. The Centre argued that constitutional protection is limited only to essential religious practices.
3. The Centre argued that the burden lies on the person challenging a practice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: a 9-judge Bench headed by CJI Surya Kant heard it. Statement 2 is wrong: the Centre (SG Tushar Mehta) argued protection is NOT limited to ERP; every practice is protected unless it breaches public order, morality or health. Statement 3 is correct: the burden is on the challenger. So A, C and D (which include 2) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Centre's 2026 stand: not limited to ERP, burden on challenger.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: a **9-judge Constitution Bench** headed by **CJI Surya Kant** heard ERP across faiths.
Statement 2 wrong: the Centre (**SG Tushar Mehta**) argued protection is **not limited to ERP**.
Statement 3: every practice is protected unless it breaches **public order, morality, health**; the **burden is on the challenger**.
xa: The Centre's argument was made on **14 May 2026**.
Criticism: the ERP test makes **courts arbiters of religion**; critics seek a **new test**.
The ERP test was formulated by the SC in **1954** (**Shirur Mutt**).

12.s: Which one of the following correctly states the Karnataka High Court position on the hijab in 2022?
o: Hijab was held to be an Essential Religious Practice.
Hijab was declared part of the Basic Structure.
Hijab was held not to be an Essential Religious Practice.
Hijab was held identical to carrying a kirpan under Article 25.
12.x: The Karnataka High Court held in 2022 that hijab was not an Essential Religious Practice. The Allahabad High Court relied on this position in August 2026 while rejecting a schoolgirl’s plea.
12.tq: Test the exact court and holding without confusing hijab with the kirpan explanation.
xs: **Karnataka HC 2022:** **hijab not an ERP** — option **(3)**.
The **Allahabad HC** relied on it to reject a schoolgirl's plea (**26 Aug 2026**).
Kirpan is covered by **Explanation I** to Art. 25 (Sikh profession) — not hijab.
xa: **Javed (2003):** **polygamy** is not an ERP.
The **Constitution does not define "essential"**.
ERP origin: **Shirur Mutt (1954)**.

12.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Church of God — Loudspeakers are subject to public order
Ratilal — State cannot touch essential religious practices
Stanislaus — Propagation does not include a right to convert
St. Stephen's — State may completely abolish minority-institution autonomy
12.x: St. Stephen's is associated with minority-institution autonomy; it did not hold that the State may completely abolish such autonomy.
12.tq: Identify the option that converts a protection of minority autonomy into its opposite.
xs: **St. Stephen's — "State may completely abolish minority-institution autonomy"** is NOT correct — option **(4)**.
**St. Stephen's (1992)** upheld **minority-institution autonomy**.
The others are correct: **Church of God (2000)** — loudspeakers subject to public order; **Ratilal (1954)** — essential practices untouchable; **Stanislaus (1977)** — no right to convert.
xa: **Shirur Mutt (1954)** — origin of the ERP doctrine.
**Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)** — National Anthem.
**Shayara Bano (2017)** — instant **triple talaq** invalidated.

12.s: Which one of the following statements correctly reflects the Sabarimala decision as described?
o: The issue was finally removed from consideration by every Constitution Bench.
An essential-practice claim cannot be used to bar the participation of others, and the State cannot endorse a practice.
Only minority institutions may challenge religious practices.
The State may endorse any religious practice claimed to be essential.
12.x: The Sabarimala ruling stated that the State cannot endorse a practice and that a claim of essential practice cannot be used to bar others' participation. The issue remains before a larger Constitution Bench.
12.tq: Apply the limits on State endorsement and essential-practice claims to the facts of the case.
xs: Sabarimala held an **ERP claim cannot restrict participation rights of others** and the **state cannot endorse a practice** — option **(2)**.
The issue is not closed: it is before a **larger Constitution Bench** (**2026**), so option 1 is wrong.
xa: Exclusion of women was **not an ERP**; women of all ages allowed entry.
**Secularism** reaffirmed as **basic structure**.
Ayyappa devotees **not a separate denomination**.

12.s:
Which of the following pairs of anti-conversion laws and years is correctly matched?
1. Orissa Freedom of Religion Act — 1967
2. Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam — 1968
12.x: The Orissa Freedom of Religion Act was enacted in 1967, while the Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam was enacted in 1968.
12.tq: Use the year-pair method to distinguish two similarly named State anti-conversion laws.
xs: **Both 1 and 2** are correct — option **(3)**.
**Orissa Freedom of Religion Act, 1967**; **MP Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam, 1968**.
xa: They came from concern over **missionary activity**.
Upheld in **Stanislaus v. MP (1977)**.
Later amendments widened scope to **conversions to Islam** (**6 Apr 2026**).

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding State anti-conversion laws:
1. The Orissa Freedom of Religion Act, 1967 and the Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam, 1968 arose from concern over missionary activity.
2. Later amendments by several States widened their scope from Christian missionary activity to conversions to Islam.
3. In Stanislaus v. State of MP (1977), the Supreme Court struck down these laws.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: the early laws came from concern over missionary activity. Statement 2 is correct: later amendments widened them to conversions to Islam. Statement 3 is wrong: Stanislaus upheld these laws, holding that propagation does not include forcible conversion. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Stanislaus UPHELD the Orissa and MP Acts.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: the **Orissa (1967)** and **MP (1968)** Acts came from concern over **missionary activity**.
Statement 2: later amendments widened scope from **Christian missionary activity** to **conversions to Islam**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Stanislaus v. MP (1977)** **upheld** these laws.
xa: Stanislaus held that **propagate** does not include a right to **convert**.
Debate: **anti-conversion laws vs freedom of conscience**.
Limits on Art. 25 include **no forcible conversion**.

12.s: Which one of the following best describes the significance of the Stanislaus v. Madhya Pradesh decision, 1977?
o: It prohibited every form of religious propagation.
It declared all State conversion laws unconstitutional.
It held that propagation necessarily includes a right to convert another person by force.
It upheld State conversion laws and held that propagation does not include forcible conversion.
12.x: In Stanislaus v. Madhya Pradesh, 1977, such State laws were upheld and propagation was held not to include forcible conversion.
12.tq: Separate propagation from forcible conversion, the central conceptual distinction in the case.
xs: **Stanislaus v. MP (1977)** **upheld** the Orissa and MP anti-conversion Acts — propagation does **not include forcible conversion** — option **(4)**.
It did not ban propagation or strike down the State conversion laws.
xa: **Propagate** = spreading one's beliefs; a right to convert would **impinge on the other's freedom of conscience**.
**Orissa Freedom of Religion Act, 1967**; **MP Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam, 1968**.
Anti-conversion laws came from concern over **missionary activity**.

12.s: Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code, concerning deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings, was upheld in
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Ramji Lal Modi v. State of Uttar Pradesh
12.x: Ramji Lal Modi v. State of Uttar Pradesh upheld Section 295A on public-order grounds. The corresponding provision is now Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
12.tq: Match the case with the statutory provision and its constitutional ground.
xs: **Sec. 295A IPC** was upheld on **public-order** grounds in **Ramji Lal Modi v. State of UP** — option **(4)**.
It is now **Sec. 299 of the BNS**.
**Kesavananda Bharati** — basic structure; **Stanislaus** — conversion; **Shirur Mutt** — ERP.
xa: Sec. 295A punishes **deliberate outrage of religious feelings**.
**Punjab's sacrilege Act** (assent **April 2026**) revived the debate.
Trafficking is **Sec. 143 BNS** — don't confuse.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Punjab's Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act:
1. It received assent in April 2026.
2. It provides for punishment up to life imprisonment for sacrilege.
3. It has been challenged directly in the Supreme Court on the ground that it protects only one faith.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: assent came in April 2026. Statement 2 is correct: the punishment goes up to life imprisonment. Statement 3 is wrong: the challenge is in the Punjab and Haryana High Court, not the Supreme Court. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Punjab sacrilege Act: April 2026, life term, challenged in the P&H HC.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **Punjab's sacrilege Act** got assent in **April 2026**.
Statement 2: up to **life imprisonment** for sacrilege.
Statement 3 wrong: it was challenged in the **Punjab & Haryana HC**, not the SC.
xa: Ground of challenge: it **protects only one faith** (**19-20 Aug 2026**).
It reopened the debate on **secularism vs faith protection**.
**Sec. 295A IPC** = now **Sec. 299 BNS** (upheld in **Ramji Lal Modi**).

12.s: Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code, which punished deliberate acts meant to outrage religious feelings, now corresponds to which provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?
12.x: Section 295A IPC is now Section 299 of the BNS, and Ramji Lal Modi v. State of UP had upheld it on public-order grounds. Section 143 of the BNS deals with trafficking and Section 197 with imputations prejudicial to national integration. Section 370 is the old IPC trafficking section.
12.tq: 295A IPC = 299 BNS; trafficking 370 IPC = 143 BNS.
xs: **Sec. 295A IPC** is now **Section 299** of the BNS — option **(3)**.
It was upheld in **Ramji Lal Modi** on **public-order** grounds.
**Section 143 BNS** is trafficking; **Section 370** was the old IPC trafficking section.
xa: BNS in force from **1 July 2024**.
**Punjab's sacrilege Act** gives up to **life imprisonment**.
Trafficking: victim's **consent immaterial**.

12.s: Which one of the following is a characteristic of a theocratic state?
o: The Constitution prohibits any relationship between religion and public policy
Religious practices are entirely outside constitutional regulation
The State has no religion and treats all religions equally
An official religion guides law and State policy
12.x: A theocratic or religious state has an official religion that guides its law and State policy. Such a system is not a feature of the Indian Constitution.
12.tq: Identify the defining feature of a theocratic state.
xs: A **theocratic state** is one where an **official religion guides law and state policy** — option **(4)**.
Option 3 describes India: **no state religion** and **equal respect for all religions**.
xa: ⚠ **Trap:** "**Religious state**" is **not** a feature of the Indian Constitution (APPSC 2018).
Indian model: **Sarva Dharma Sambhava** — state neutrality + positive intervention.
The Constituent Assembly rejected adding **'God'** to the Preamble (**1949**).

12.s: Which one of the following most appropriately describes the constitutional meaning of secularism in India?
o: Complete exclusion of religion from public life
Preference to the religion followed by the majority
Establishment of one official religion by the State
Equal respect for all religions and absence of discrimination on religious grounds
12.x: Indian secularism requires equal respect for all religions and prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion. It does not establish a state religion or demand complete exclusion of religion from public life.
12.tq: Distinguish the Indian model of secularism from strict separation and majoritarian preference.
xs: Secularism means **equal respect for all religions** + **no discrimination on grounds of religion** — option **(4)** (APPSC 2019).
India has **no state religion** (UPPSC 2005) and does not exclude religion from public life.
xa: Indian model: **principled distance and equal respect**; Western: **strict separation**.
Components: freedom of religion, equality of all religions, state neutrality, **no religious tax**, **minority rights**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994):** secularism part of the **basic structure**.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding secularism in India:
1. India has no state religion.
2. The State may intervene positively for social and religious reform.
3. Secularism necessarily prohibits all forms of state aid to religious institutions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: India has no state religion and follows a model allowing positive state intervention for reform. The State is not necessarily prohibited from providing aid to religious institutions.
12.tq: Identify the false absolute statement about state aid and distinguish Indian secularism from the Western model.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: India has **no state religion**.
Statement 2: the Indian model allows **positive intervention** for reform (e.g. **temple entry**).
Statement 3 wrong: **aid is allowed** (e.g. **Amarnath Yatra, Haj** support).
xa: **Western (negative) secularism**: **no state aid** to religious institutions.
Indian model = **Sarva Dharma Sambhava**.
The State may aid **minority institutions**.

12.s: Which of the following is NOT a component of Indian secularism?
o: Non-applicability of secular principles to irreligious persons
12.x: Secularism includes freedom of conscience, which protects believers as well as non-believers. Non-applicability to irreligious persons is not a component of secularism.
12.tq: Find the option that reverses the inclusive scope of freedom of conscience.
xs: "**Not applicable to irreligious persons**" is NOT a component — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 2018).
**Freedom of conscience** covers **non-believers** too.
Components: **freedom of religion**, **equality of all religions**, state neutrality, **no religious tax**, **minority rights**.
xa: **Conscience** includes the freedom to follow **no religion**.
**Religious pluralism** = freedom to practise any religion **or none**.
Related Articles include **25, 26, 27** and **325**.

12.s: The Constituent Assembly, in 1949, rejected the proposal to include which word in the Preamble?
12.x: The Constituent Assembly rejected the proposal to add the word “God” to the Preamble in 1949.
12.tq: Test a specific rejected constitutional proposal rather than a word already present in the Preamble.
xs: The Constituent Assembly rejected adding **'God'** to the Preamble (**1949**) — option **(3)**.
This reflects India having **no state religion**.
xa: Roots of secularism: **Ashoka's Dhamma**, **Nehru Report (1928)**, **Karachi Resolution (1931)**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994):** secularism inherent **even before 1976**.
⚠ "Religious state" is **not** a feature of the Constitution.

12.s:
Which of the following pairs correctly represents sources associated with the roots of Indian secular thought?
1. Ashoka's Dhamma
2. Nehru Report, 1928
3. Karachi Resolution, 1931
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
12.x: Ashoka's Dhamma, the Nehru Report of 1928 and the Karachi Resolution of 1931 are all identified as roots associated with Indian secular thought.
12.tq: Recognise a complete list where all three historically associated sources are correct.
xs: All three — **1, 2 and 3** — are roots — option **(4)**.
**Ashoka's Dhamma** (RE 7, RE 12), **Nehru Report (1928)**, **Karachi Resolution (1931)**.
xa: The Constituent Assembly rejected **'God'** in the Preamble (**1949**).
**Mughal Akbar** promoted tolerance and dialogue.
**Bhakti (6th-18th c.)** rejected ritualism and caste.

12.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Western and Indian models of secularism?
o: The Indian model treats religion as purely private, whereas the Western model promotes public religious dialogue.
The Western model permits state reform of religious practices, whereas the Indian model requires strict separation.
The Western model follows strict separation, whereas the Indian model follows principled distance and equal respect.
Both models prohibit state aid to religious institutions in all circumstances.
12.x: The Western model is generally based on strict separation and mutual exclusion. The Indian model adopts principled distance, equal respect and scope for reform.
12.tq: Compare the defining features of both models instead of matching isolated examples.
xs: **Western** = **strict separation, mutual exclusion**; **Indian** = **principled distance and equal respect** — option **(3)**.
Options 1 and 2 reverse the models; option 4 is wrong as India **allows aid**.
xa: India: state may reform religious practice under **Art. 25(2)**, e.g. **temple entry**.
West: religion **purely private**; **no state aid**.
India: aid like **Amarnath Yatra, Haj** support.

12.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 14 is related to equality before law.
2. Articles 15 and 16 address equality and non-discrimination in specified contexts.
3. Articles 29 and 30 are connected with cultural and educational rights.
4. Article 325 excludes persons from electoral rolls on the ground of religion.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Articles 14, 15, 16, 29 and 30 are related to equality and cultural or educational rights. Article 325 prevents exclusion from electoral rolls on grounds including religion; it does not authorise such exclusion.
12.tq: Locate the single reversed constitutional effect in an otherwise familiar list of related Articles.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Arts. 14, 15, 16** (equality) and **29, 30** (cultural and educational rights) are listed with secularism.
Statement 4 wrong: **Art. 325** says **no exclusion from electoral rolls on religion**.
xa: **Art. 25** — freedom of conscience; **26** — denominations; **27** — no tax for a religion.
**S.R. Bommai (1994):** a State government acting against secularism can be dismissed (**Art. 356**).
India has **no state religion**.

12.s:
With reference to Supreme Court decisions on secularism, consider the following statements:
1. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) set out the basic structure doctrine.
2. S.R. Bommai (1994) held secularism to be part of the basic structure.
3. S.R. Bommai held that secularism was inherent only after the 42nd Amendment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Kesavananda Bharati set out the basic structure doctrine, and S.R. Bommai recognised secularism as part of the basic structure. Bommai also held that secularism was inherent even before 1976, making statement 3 false.
12.tq: Use the distinction between constitutional recognition and the date of textual insertion to reject statement 3.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** set out the **basic structure** doctrine.
Statement 2: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** held secularism part of the **basic structure**.
Statement 3 wrong: Bommai held it inherent **even before 1976**.
xa: Kesavananda counted secularism a **basic feature**.
The **Sabarimala case, 2026** reaffirmed secularism as **Basic Structure**.
Bommai: a State government acting against secularism can be dismissed (**Art. 356**).

12.s: If a State government acts against the secular character of the Constitution, the principle recognised in S.R. Bommai permits its dismissal under:
12.x: S.R. Bommai recognised that a State government acting against secularism may be dismissed under Article 356.
12.tq: Identify the constitutional emergency provision applicable to failure of constitutional machinery in a State.
xs: **S.R. Bommai (1994):** a State government acting against secularism can be dismissed under **Article 356** — option **(1)**.
Bommai also held secularism part of the **basic structure**, inherent **even before 1976**.
xa: **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — basic structure doctrine.
Secularism means **equal respect for all religions**.
India has **no state religion**.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding religious pluralism:
1. It means the freedom and security to practise any religion or none.
2. It requires freedom of religion and mutual respect.
3. Exclusivism strengthens religious pluralism.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: pluralism is freedom and security to practise any religion or none. Statement 2 is correct: it needs freedom of religion and mutual respect. Statement 3 is wrong: exclusivism hinders pluralism. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Exclusivism is the enemy of pluralism.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **religious pluralism** = freedom and security to practise **any religion or none**.
Statement 2: it needs **freedom of religion + mutual respect**.
Statement 3 wrong: pluralism is **hindered by exclusivism**.
xa: **S.R. Bhatt:** pluralism leads to secularism through the **unification of many religions**.
**Fundamentalism** rejects modern and plural readings.
**Bhakti-Sufi** interaction built communal harmony.

12.s: According to S.R. Bhatt, religious pluralism leads to secularism through:
o: The establishment of a state religion
The separation of all communities from public life
12.x: S.R. Bhatt associated the movement from pluralism to secularism with the unification of many religions.
12.tq: Recall the specific relationship proposed between pluralism and secularism.
xs: **S.R. Bhatt:** pluralism leads to secularism through the **unification of many religions** — option **(2)**.
Pluralism needs **freedom of religion + mutual respect**, not suppression or a state religion.
xa: Religious pluralism is **hindered by exclusivism**.
**Revivalism** = restoring a golden past (Arya Samaj's "**Back to the Vedas**").
India has **no state religion**.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Bhakti movement:
1. It rejected ritualism and caste.
2. Its interaction with Sufi traditions built communal harmony and regional literatures.
3. It was confined to the period between the 1st and the 5th centuries.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: Bhakti rejected ritualism and caste. Statement 2 is correct: Bhakti-Sufi interaction built communal harmony and regional literatures. Statement 3 is wrong: Bhakti spans the 6th to the 18th century. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Bhakti = 6th-18th century, anti-ritual, anti-caste.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **Bhakti** rejected **ritualism and caste**.
Statement 2: **Bhakti-Sufi interaction** built **communal harmony** and **regional literatures**.
Statement 3 wrong: Bhakti spans the **6th-18th c.**
xa: Andhra: **Vijayanagara** employed **Muslim officers** and protected **Jains**.
**Bammera Potana** offered the **Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu** to **Lord Rama**.
**Akbar** promoted tolerance and dialogue.

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding religious coexistence in Andhra history:
1. The Vijayanagara rulers employed Muslim officers and protected Jains.
2. Bammera Potana offered the Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu to Krishnadevaraya.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: Vijayanagara employed Muslim officers and protected Jains. Statement 2 is wrong: Potana offered the work to Lord Rama, not to Krishnadevaraya. So B, C and D are wrong; A is correct.
12.tq: Potana dedicated his Bhagavatamu to Rama, not to a king.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **Vijayanagara** employed **Muslim officers** and protected **Jains**.
Statement 2 wrong: **Bammera Potana** offered the **Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu** to **Lord Rama**, not to **Krishnadevaraya**.
xa: **Bhakti (6th-18th c.)** rejected ritualism and caste.
**Mughal Akbar** promoted tolerance and dialogue.
AP angle: **AP Endowments Act, 1987** regulates Hindu temples and mutts.

12.s: Which Mughal ruler is associated with promoting religious tolerance and dialogue?
12.x: Mughal emperor Akbar promoted religious tolerance and dialogue.
12.tq: Match the policy of tolerance and dialogue with the appropriate ruler.
xs: **Akbar** promoted **tolerance and dialogue** — option **(1)** (UPSC).
He is cited as a historical example of **pluralism**.
xa: **Bhakti-Sufi interaction** built communal harmony.
**Vijayanagara** employed **Muslim officers** and protected Jains.
Pluralism is hindered by **exclusivism**.

12.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Fundamentalism means a return to the literal 'fundamentals' of scripture and a rejection of modern and plural readings.
2. Revivalism seeks to restore a golden past, as in the Arya Samaj's call 'Back to the Vedas'.
3. Fundamentalism accepts modern and plural readings of scripture as equally valid.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: this is the meaning of fundamentalism. Statement 2 is correct: revivalism restores a golden past, e.g. 'Back to the Vedas'. Statement 3 is wrong: fundamentalism rejects modern and plural readings. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Fundamentalism = literal scripture; revivalism = golden past.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **fundamentalism** = return to the literal "**fundamentals**" of scripture + **rejection of modern and plural readings**.
Statement 2: **revivalism** = restoring a **golden past** (Arya Samaj's "**Back to the Vedas**").
Statement 3 wrong: fundamentalism **rejects** modern and plural readings.
xa: Forms in India (since the **1970s**): **communalism**, separatism, fanaticism.
Threats: **hate speech** on social media + **illegal conversions**.
**Asghar Ali Engineer** wrote on communalism.

12.s:
Which of the following are identified as forms of religious fundamentalism in India?
1. Communalism
2. Separatism
3. Fanaticism
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
12.x: Communalism, separatism and fanaticism are identified as forms of religious fundamentalism in India, particularly in the context of religion becoming fused with politics since the 1970s.
12.tq: Select the complete list of forms rather than treating the political dimension as a separate form.
xs: **Communalism**, **separatism** and **fanaticism** — all three — option **(4)**.
Since the **1970s**, religion has been **fused into politics** in India.
xa: Riots cited: **1984** anti-Sikh, **1992** Babri Masjid, **2002** Gujarat, **2023** Haryana.
Threats: **hate speech** on social media + **illegal conversions** eroding the "**Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb**".
**Fundamentalism** = return to literal fundamentals of scripture.

12.s: Which of the following pairs of events is correctly matched with the year cited in relation to communal conflict?
12.x: The cited examples are the 1984 anti-Sikh violence, the 1992 Babri Masjid episode, the 2002 Gujarat riots and the 2023 Haryana violence.
12.tq: Match each event with its year and reject the shifted-year distractors.
xs: **Anti-Sikh violence — 1984** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Babri Masjid** was **1992**, **Gujarat** **2002**, **Haryana** **2023** — so options 2-4 are mismatched.
xa: These are cited as forms of **communalism** since the **1970s**.
**Asghar Ali Engineer** wrote on communalism.
Threats named: **hate speech** and **illegal conversions**.

12.s: Which of the following has been identified as a threat to the Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb?
o: Hate speech on social media and illegal conversions
Protection of Jains and employment of Muslim officers
Freedom of conscience and mutual respect
12.x: Hate speech on social media and illegal conversions have been identified as threats that erode the Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb.
12.tq: Distinguish threats to syncretic culture from examples of pluralistic coexistence.
xs: **Hate speech on social media** and **illegal conversions** are the threats eroding the "**Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb**" — option **(1)**.
The other options (Bhakti-Sufi interaction, mutual respect, protecting Jains) build harmony, not threaten it.
xa: Fundamentalism forms: **communalism**, separatism, fanaticism.
**Bhakti-Sufi** interaction built **communal harmony**.
Pluralism is hindered by **exclusivism**.

12.s: Who among the following regarded religion as a form of collective worship of society and examined the distinction between the sacred and the profane?
12.x: Emile Durkheim associated religion with collective worship of society and distinguished the sacred from the profane.
12.tq: Match the distinctive conceptual pair—sacred and profane—with its sociologist.
xs: **Emile Durkheim**: **sacred vs profane**; religion as **collective worship of society** — option **(3)**.
**Tylor** — animism; **Weber** — The Religion of India; **Marx** — "opium of the people".
xa: Durkheim also studied **totemism** (**Elementary Forms of Religious Life, 1912**).
**Malinowski**: personal attachments and **death** are sources of religion.
**Frazer**: **magic → religion → science**.

12.s: Which thinker linked karma, dharma and caste with the shaping of economic life in *The Religion of India*?
12.x: Max Weber examined the relationship of karma, dharma and caste to economic life in *The Religion of India*.
12.tq: Identify the thinker through the specific work and its analytical themes.
xs: **Max Weber** — **The Religion of India**: **karma, dharma, caste** shape economic life — option **(2)**.
He also wrote the **Protestant Ethic**.
xa: **Durkheim** — sacred vs profane.
**Marx** — "**opium of the people**".
⚠ **Tylor = animism; Frazer = magic → religion → science; Malinowski = death**.

12.s: The statement “Religion is the opium of the people” is associated with:
12.x: Karl Marx described religion as “the opium of the people.”
12.tq: Test a famous formulation with the correct author rather than a related theorist.
xs: **Karl Marx** called religion "the **opium of the people**" — option **(2)**.
**Malinowski** — **death** and personal attachments; **Weber** — Religion of India; **Frazer** — **The Golden Bough**.
xa: **Durkheim** — **sacred vs profane**; totemism.
**E.B. Tylor** — **animism**.
**T.N. Madan** criticised the Western **secularisation thesis**.

12.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: J.G. Frazer — Religion as the opium of the people
Karl Marx — Magic, religion and science
12.x: E.B. Tylor associated the origin of religion with animism, or belief in spirits. Marx is associated with the opium formulation, Frazer with magic-religion-science, and Weber with the Protestant Ethic.
12.tq: Find the correctly matched thinker by separating closely related theories and works.
xs: **E.B. Tylor — Animism** (belief in spirits) is correct — option **(1)**.
"Opium of the people" is **Marx**; magic-religion-science is **Frazer**; **Protestant Ethic** is **Weber**.
xa: **Louis Dumont** — caste through **purity-pollution** (**Homo Hierarchicus**).
**Malinowski** — **death** as a source of religion (APPSC-G2 2023).
**Durkheim** — **sacred vs profane**.

12.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Asghar Ali Engineer — Writings on communalism
T.N. Madan — Critique of the Western secularisation thesis
12.x: *Homo Hierarchicus* and the analysis of caste through purity-pollution are associated with Louis Dumont, not B. Malinowski.
12.tq: Use the author-work trap to identify the wrongly attributed work.
xs: **Malinowski — Homo Hierarchicus** is NOT correct — option **(4)**.
**Homo Hierarchicus** is **Louis Dumont**'s (caste through **purity-pollution**).
**Malinowski** held **personal attachments** and **death** are the main sources of religion.
xa: **Asghar Ali Engineer** — communalism; **T.N. Madan** — critique of the **Western secularisation thesis**.
**Tylor** — **animism**; **Frazer** — **The Golden Bough**.
**Weber** — **Protestant Ethic**.

12.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

Term — Meaning

1. Ahura Mazda — Supreme god of good
2. Angra Mainyu — Destructive or evil spirit
3. Tirthankara — Eternal Guru of Sikhism
4. Guru Granth Sahib — Twenty-four teachers of Jainism
12.x: Ahura Mazda means the supreme god of good and Angra Mainyu refers to the destructive or evil spirit. Tirthankara is associated with Jain teachers, while Guru Granth Sahib is the scripture and eternal Guru of Sikhism.
12.tq: Match each term with its exact religious meaning and eliminate swapped descriptions.
xs: Pairs **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Ahura Mazda** — **supreme god of good**; **Angra Mainyu** — **destructive/evil spirit** (both **Zoroastrian**).
Pair 3 wrong: **Tirthankara** = Jain "**Ford-maker**"; the eternal Guru of Sikhism is the **Guru Granth Sahib**.
Pair 4 wrong: the **24** teachers are the Jain **Tirthankaras**.
xa: Guru Granth Sahib was compiled as the **Adi Granth** by **Guru Arjan**.
**Rishabhanatha** was the first Tirthankara, **Mahavira** the last.
Zoroastrianism is followed by the **Parsis**.

12.s: Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu are associated with which religious tradition, respectively?
12.x: Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of good, and Angra Mainyu, the destructive or evil spirit, belong to Zoroastrianism, followed by Parsis in India.
12.tq: Use the confusable-pair method by linking both opposing concepts to the same religious tradition.
xs: **Ahura Mazda** and **Angra Mainyu** both belong to **Zoroastrianism** (Parsis) — option **(4)**.
⚠ **Ahura Mazda = good; Angra Mainyu = evil**.
xa: **Tirthankara** — Jainism (**24** teachers).
**Guru Granth Sahib** — Sikhism (scripture and **eternal Guru**).
The Adi Granth was compiled by **Guru Arjan**.

12.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Tirthankara literally means ‘Ford-maker’.
2. Jainism recognises 24 Tirthankaras.
3. Rishabhanatha was the first and Mahavira was the last Tirthankara.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: All three statements are correct. Tirthankara means ‘Ford-maker’, and Jain tradition identifies 24 Tirthankaras, beginning with Rishabhanatha and ending with Mahavira.
12.tq: Check the definition, numerical count and first-last sequence separately.
xs: All three — **1, 2 and 3** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**Tirthankara** = "**Ford-maker**"; Jainism has **24** teachers; **Rishabhanatha** first, **Mahavira** last.
xa: **Guru Granth Sahib** — Sikh scripture and eternal Guru.
**Ahura Mazda** / **Angra Mainyu** — Zoroastrian good/evil.
Art. 25 Explanation II: "Hindus" includes **Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists**.

12.s: Which thinker held that strong personal attachments and the fact of death are the main sources of religious belief?
12.x: Malinowski traced religious belief mainly to strong personal attachments and to death; this was asked in APPSC Group 2, 2023. Tylor traced religion to animism, or belief in spirits. Durkheim saw religion as the collective worship of society, built on the sacred-profane divide. Frazer described a sequence of magic, then religion, then science.
12.tq: Death and attachments = Malinowski; animism = Tylor; sacred-profane = Durkheim.
xs: **B. Malinowski**: **strong personal attachments** and **death** are the main sources of religious belief — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 2023).
**Tylor** — **animism**; **Durkheim** — **collective worship of society**, sacred vs profane; **Frazer** — **magic → religion → science**.
xa: ⚠ **Tylor = animism; Frazer = magic → religion → science; Malinowski = death**.
**Marx** — "**opium of the people**".
**Weber** — **The Religion of India** and the **Protestant Ethic**.

12.s: The Supreme Court’s nine-judge reference concerning the scope of the Essential Religious Practices test is associated with which of the following issues?
o: Whether Hindi should replace all regional languages as the national language
Whether all temples must be administered by the Union Government
Whether religious practices may be examined by courts in determining constitutional protection
Whether Tirthankaras should be recognised under the Constitution
12.x: The Sabarimala nine-judge reference is examining the scope of the Essential Religious Practices test and the extent to which courts may determine what constitutes an essential religious practice.
12.tq: Identify the constitutional controversy directly connected with the judicial test.
xs: The **9-judge** reference tests how far **courts may examine religious practices** — the scope of the **ERP** test — option **(3)**.
It is headed by **CJI Surya Kant**; hearing on **14 May 2026**.
xa: Centre (**SG Tushar Mehta**): protection **not limited to ERP**; **burden on the challenger**.
Criticism: ERP makes **courts arbiters of religion** (e.g. **Sastri Yagnapurushadji, 1966**).
India has **no national language**; **Art. 343** makes **Hindi** the official language of the Union.

12.s: Which one of the following correctly represents a criticism of the Essential Religious Practices test?
o: It applies exclusively to economic activities connected with religion.
It removes all constitutional protection for religious denominations.
It prevents courts from examining any religious practice.
It allows judges to decide questions of theology and makes courts arbiters of religion.
12.x: A major criticism is that the Essential Religious Practices test permits courts to decide theological questions and thereby makes them arbiters of religion. Critics have sought a new test, including in the context of the Sabarimala reference.
12.tq: Recognise the criticism rather than confusing judicial review with complete non-intervention.
xs: Criticism: the **ERP test** **lets judges decide theology** and makes **courts arbiters of religion** — option **(4)**.
Example: **Sastri Yagnapurushadji (1966)**; critics seek a **new test** (**26 Feb 2026**).
xa: The ERP test was formulated by the SC in **1954**.
The **Sabarimala reference** is testing it.
Other debates: **anti-conversion laws vs freedom of conscience**; **Uniform Civil Code** vs **Art. 25**.

12.s: Which of the following debates is most directly connected with freedom of conscience?
o: Anti-conversion laws and the individual’s freedom of conscience
The classification of temples under the AP Endowments Act
The official compilation of the Adi Granth
The number of Tirthankaras in Jainism
12.x: The relationship between anti-conversion laws and the freedom of conscience is a major constitutional debate concerning religious freedom.
12.tq: Link the constitutional expression ‘freedom of conscience’ with the issue that directly affects individual belief and conversion.
xs: **Anti-conversion laws vs freedom of conscience** is the listed debate — option **(1)**.
**Conscience** = inner freedom to mould one's relation with God, incl. following **no religion**.
xa: **Stanislaus v. MP (1977)** upheld the **Orissa and MP** anti-conversion Acts.
**Uniform Civil Code** is argued to clash with **Art. 25**.
**Ravidassias** renewed demand for a separate **religion code in the Census** (**15 Jul 2026**).

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Andhra Pradesh religious-endowment context:
1. The Sri Swamy Hathiramji Mutt at Tirupati is the hereditary Dharmakarta of the TTD.
2. The AP Endowments Act, 1987 regulates Hindu temples and mutts.
3. The Sri Swamy Hathiramji Mutt is located at Srisailam.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Mutt at Tirupati is the hereditary Dharmakarta of the TTD. Statement 2 is correct: the 1987 Act regulates Hindu temples and mutts. Statement 3 is wrong: the Mutt is at Tirupati. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
12.tq: Hathiramji Mutt = Tirupati, TTD's hereditary Dharmakarta.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **Sri Swamy Hathiramji Mutt**, **Tirupati**, is the **hereditary Dharmakarta of TTD**.
Statement 2: the **AP Endowments Act, 1987** regulates **Hindu temples and mutts**.
Statement 3 wrong: the Mutt is at **Tirupati**, not Srisailam.
xa: The AP Endowments Department administers **42,000+** temples (May **2026**).
AP HC/SC dealt with the Mutt's **interim management**.
**Art. 26** lets denominations **administer property in accordance with law**.

12.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The debate on the Uniform Civil Code is argued by some to have implications for Article 25.
2. The Essential Religious Practices test was discussed in Sastri Yagnapurushadji in 1966.
3. Critics of the Essential Religious Practices test argue that courts should continue deciding theological questions without modification.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because critics argue for a new or different test precisely because the existing test makes courts arbiters of religious theology.
12.tq: Find the statement that reverses the criticism: critics seek change, not continuation of judicial theological control.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: the **Uniform Civil Code** is argued to clash with **Art. 25**.
Statement 2: the ERP test lets judges decide theology, e.g. **Sastri Yagnapurushadji, 1966**.
Statement 3 wrong: critics say the test makes **courts arbiters of religion** and seek a **new test** (**26 Feb 2026**).
xa: The **Sabarimala reference** (**9-judge** Bench) is testing the ERP test.
The ERP test was formulated by the SC in **1954** (**Shirur Mutt**).
Other debate: **anti-conversion laws vs freedom of conscience**.

12.s: Which one of the following statements regarding language and secularism in India is correct?
o: India has no official language of the Union because secularism excludes language from constitutional protection.
Article 343 makes all Indian languages equally official languages of the Union.
Article 343 declares Hindi to be the national language of India.
Article 343 makes Hindi the official language of the Union, but India has no national language.
12.x: Article 343 makes Hindi the official language of the Union, while India has no national language. Indian secularism also treats language as an identity deserving protection.
12.tq: Separate the constitutional terms ‘official language’ and ‘national language’ rather than treating them as synonyms.
xs: **Article 343** makes **Hindi** the **official language of the Union**, but India has **no national language** — option **(4)**.
Indian secularism also protects **language** as an identity.
So option 3 is wrong (Hindi is not "national"), and option 2 is wrong (only Hindi is named).
xa: The "no national language" point was noted in **Jul 2025**.
India has **no state religion**; secularism = **equal respect for all religions**.
**Art. 325**: no exclusion from electoral rolls on religion.

12.s: In July 2026, which community renewed its demand for a separate religion code in the Census?
12.x: The Ravidassias renewed their demand for a separate religion code in the Census in July 2026. Jains, Parsis and Buddhists are already counted as separate religions in the Census, and all three are among the six notified minorities, so they have no such demand.
12.tq: Ravidassias = separate Census religion code demand (Jul 2026).
xs: The **Ravidassias** renewed the demand for a separate **religion code in the Census** (**15 Jul 2026**) — option **(2)**.
**Jains**, **Parsis** and **Buddhists** are already among the **six notified minorities**, so they make no such demand.
xa: The six notified minorities: **Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains**.
Explanation II to Art. 25: "Hindus" includes **Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists** for **25(2)(b)**.
Other current issues: **Allahabad HC hijab ruling** (**26 Aug 2026**); Sabarimala **9-judge** reference.

13.s:
Consider the following statements regarding linguistic minorities in India:
1. The Constitution expressly defines the expression “linguistic minority”.
2. The State is the unit for determining a linguistic minority.
3. Numerical inferiority and non-dominant status are relevant considerations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
13.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. The Constitution does not expressly define “linguistic minority”; therefore, statement 1 is false.
13.tq: Reject the statement carrying an incorrect constitutional definition while retaining the two substantive tests.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 wrong: "**Linguistic minority**" is **not defined** in the Constitution.
Statements 2 and 3: the test is **numerical inferiority**, **non-dominant status in the State** and distinct identity; the unit is the **State** (**T.M.A. Pai**).
xa: Linguistic minorities are determined **State-wise**; religious minorities via the **NCM**, **Ministry of Minority Affairs**.
**Art. 350A:** **mother-tongue instruction** at the **primary stage** for linguistic minority children.
"Minority" appears in **Arts 29, 30, 350A, 350B** but is **not defined**.

13.s: The National Commission for Minorities is best described as a:
o: Judicial body established under the Protection of Civil Rights Act
Statutory body established under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992
Non-statutory advisory body created by executive resolution
13.x: The National Commission for Minorities is a statutory body established under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992.
13.tq: Distinguish a statutory commission from a constitutional office and an executive body.
xs: The **NCM** is a **statutory** body under the **NCM Act, 1992** — option **(2)**.
It is not constitutional — **Art. 350B** is a separate provision using "minority".
xa: The NCM Act does **not define "minority"** — a minority is any community **notified by the Centre**.
**Six notified minorities:** **Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains**.
Notification brings a group within the NCM + central schemes (**scholarships, PMJVK, PM VIKAS**).

13.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the six religious minorities notified for the purposes of the National Commission for Minorities?
o: Linguistic minorities as a general category
13.x: The six notified religious minorities are Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains. “Linguistic minorities” is not one of the six notified religious categories.
13.tq: Find the category that does not belong to the notified religious-minority list.
xs: "**Linguistic minorities as a general category**" is NOT one of the six — option **(3)**.
The **six notified minorities** are **Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains** (Apr **2026**).
xa: Linguistic minorities are determined **State-wise**.
The NCM's definition is **mainly religious**.
Notified under the **NCM Act, 1992**.

13.s: The constitutional provision relating to instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children belonging to linguistic minority groups is:
13.x: Article 350A deals with facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children belonging to linguistic minority groups.
13.tq: Discriminate between the closely numbered Articles 350, 350A and 350B by their functions.
xs: **Article 350A** — **mother-tongue instruction** at the **primary stage** for **linguistic minority** children — option **(2)**.
**Art. 350B** is another Article using "minority", but the mother-tongue clause is 350A.
xa: ⚠ **Trap:** **IYB 2026** (p.**290**) prints it as "**Article 360A**" — a misprint.
"Minority" is used in **Arts 29, 30, 350A, 350B** but **not defined**.
Kerala's **Malayalam Bhasha Bill** was contested for harming the **Kannada linguistic minority** in **Kasaragod**.

13.s: National notification of a community as a minority primarily enables it to:
o: Obtain automatic reservation in every State legislature
Come within the National Commission for Minorities and central minority schemes
Avoid all regulation by State authorities
13.x: National notification brings a community within the National Commission for Minorities and makes it eligible under central minority schemes such as scholarships, PMJVK and PM VIKAS.
13.tq: Apply the practical consequences of notification instead of assuming it creates unrestricted rights.
xs: National notification brings a group **within the NCM** and **central minority schemes** — option **(3)**.
Schemes named: **scholarships, PMJVK, PM VIKAS**.
xa: **Six notified minorities:** Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains.
A minority = any community **notified by the Centre** (Jul **2026**).
