**NCM** is statutory, under the **NCM Act, 1992**.

13.s:
With reference to the term 'minority' in the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. The term is used in Articles 29, 30, 350A and 350B.
2. The Constitution defines 'minority' in Article 366.
3. The National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992 also does not define the term; a minority is any community notified by the Centre.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
13.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Constitution uses the word 'minority' in Articles 29, 30, 350A and 350B. Statement 2 is wrong: the Constitution does not define the word anywhere. Statement 3 is correct: the NCM Act does not define it either, and a minority is any community the Centre notifies. So 1 and 3 only is the answer, and every option containing statement 2 is wrong.
13.tq: 'Minority' is used but never defined, in the Constitution or in the NCM Act.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: "minority" is used in **Arts 29, 30, 350A, 350B**.
Statement 2 wrong: the Constitution **does not define** it anywhere.
Statement 3: the **NCM Act** does not define it either — a minority is any community **notified by the Centre**.
xa: Test: **numerical inferiority**, non-dominant status, distinct identity; unit = **State** (**T.M.A. Pai**).
Types: **religious** (NCM) vs **linguistic** (State-wise).
The NCM's definition is **mainly religious**.

13.s: Article 30(1A), inserted by the 44th Amendment, deals primarily with—
o: Exemption of minority institutions from all State regulation
Compulsory acquisition of property of minority educational institutions
Appointment of teachers in minority institutions
Reservation of seats in minority institutions
13.x: Article 30(1A) concerns compulsory acquisition of the property of a minority educational institution. The amount fixed must not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed by Article 30.
13.tq: Link the sub-clause number with its specific subject instead of the general right under Article 30(1).
xs: **Art. 30(1A)** (**44th Amendment, 1978**) deals with **compulsory acquisition** of a **minority institution's property** — option **(2)**.
The amount fixed must **not restrict or abrogate** the Art. 30 right.
It does not exempt minority institutions from all regulation: the State may **regulate standards**.
xa: **30(1):** all minorities, **religious or linguistic**, may establish and administer institutions of their choice.
30(1) is called the **"Charter of Education Rights"**; **madrasas** run under it.
The same **44th Amendment** deleted the FR to property.

13.s: The 25 per cent quota under the Right to Education Act does not apply to minority schools in view of the decision in—
o: St. Stephen's College v. University of Delhi
T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India
P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra
13.x: In Pramati, decided in 2014, the Supreme Court held that the RTE Act's 25 per cent quota does not apply to minority schools.
13.tq: Distinguish the case concerning RTE exemption from cases concerning autonomy, preference or reservation.
xs: The RTE Act's **25% quota** does not apply to minority schools — **Pramati, 2014** — option **(3)**.
**T.M.A. Pai** made the **State** the unit for deciding a minority.
xa: Critics: only **8.76%** disadvantaged enrolments in minority schools (**NCPCR, Sep 2025**).
Criticism: **misuse of minority status** to escape RTE obligations.
**Art. 30(1)** — the "**Charter of Education Rights**".

13.s:
With reference to Article 30(1), consider the following statements:
1. It gives all minorities, whether based on religion or language, the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
2. It is available only to religious minorities.
3. The State may regulate standards in such institutions but may not take away their minority character.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
13.x: Statement 1 is correct: Article 30(1) covers all minorities, religious or linguistic. Statement 2 is wrong because linguistic minorities are covered too. Statement 3 is correct: the right is not absolute, so the State may regulate standards but may not destroy the minority character. So 1 and 3 only is the answer.
13.tq: Art. 30(1) = religious AND linguistic minorities. The State may regulate standards but not the minority character.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **Art. 30(1)** covers all minorities, **religious or linguistic**.
Statement 2 wrong: **linguistic** minorities are covered too.
Statement 3: not absolute — the State may **regulate standards**, but **not the minority character**.
xa: **30(1A)** (**44th Amendment, 1978**): compensation must **not restrict or abrogate** the right.
**Madrasas** run under Art. 30(1).
**Pramati (2014):** RTE **25% quota** not for minority schools.

13.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the position of the Right to Property under the Constitution as it stood in 1950?
o: It was guaranteed only under Article 31 as a legal right
It was a DPSP under Article 39
It was a statutory right under the Representation of the People Act, 1951
It was a Fundamental Right under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31
13.x: In 1950, the Right to Property was a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(f), relating to acquiring, holding and disposing of property, and Article 31, relating to deprivation and acquisition of property.
13.tq: Use the historical position of the right rather than its present constitutional status.
xs: In **1950** property was a **Fundamental Right** under **Art. 19(1)(f)** and **Art. 31** — option **(4)**.
19(1)(f) — **acquire, hold, dispose** of property; Art. 31 — no deprivation save by **authority of law**, acquisition for **public purpose with compensation**.
xa: **1st Amendment, 1951** inserted **Arts. 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule**.
**44th Amendment, 1978** made it a legal right under **Art. 300A**.
FRs: originally **seven**, now **six**.

13.s:
Consider the following statements regarding amendments affecting the Right to Property:
1. The 4th (1955), 17th (1964) and 25th (1971) Amendments narrowed compensation.
2. The 17th Amendment provided that land under personal cultivation could be acquired only on paying market value.
3. The 1st Amendment, 1951 deleted Article 31 from Part III.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
13.x: Statement 1 is correct: these amendments narrowed compensation. Statement 2 is correct: the 17th Amendment required market value for land under personal cultivation. Statement 3 is wrong: the 1st Amendment inserted Arts. 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule; Art. 31 was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
13.tq: 1st inserted 31A/31B/Ninth Schedule; 44th deleted 31 and 19(1)(f).
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: the **4th (1955), 17th (1964), 25th (1971)** Amendments **narrowed compensation**.
Statement 2: the **17th** — land under **personal cultivation** acquired only on paying **market value**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **1st Amendment, 1951** inserted **Arts. 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule**; Art. 31 was deleted by the **44th (1978)**.
xa: The 1st Amendment shielded **land reform laws**.
After 1978, property is in **Art. 300A**, **Part XII, Chapter IV**.
⚠ A-R pairs: "legal right under **300A** in **Part XII**" + "**44th Amendment, 1978**".

13.s: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 brought about which one of the following changes?
o: It shifted Article 21A from Part IV to Part III
It inserted Articles 31A and 31B in Part III
It converted the Right to Property into a Fundamental Right available only to citizens
It deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 from Part III and placed the Right to Property under Article 300A
13.x: The 44th Amendment deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 from Part III and made property a constitutional legal right under Article 300A in Part XII, Chapter IV.
13.tq: Distinguish the deleting amendment from the earlier amendments that protected land reforms.
xs: The **44th Amendment, 1978** deleted **Art. 19(1)(f)** and **Art. 31** from Part III and placed property under **Art. 300A** — option **(4)**.
**Arts. 31A, 31B** were inserted by the **1st Amendment, 1951**, not the 44th.
It made property a **legal (constitutional) right**, not an FR.
xa: Art. 300A sits in **Part XII, Chapter IV**.
The 44th also inserted **Art. 30(1A)** on minority institutions' property.
FR count: **six** now, **seven** originally.

13.s: Article 300A provides that—
o: No citizen shall be deprived of property except by executive order
No company shall be deprived of property under any circumstances
No person shall be deprived of property except with the consent of Parliament
No person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law
13.x: Article 300A states that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
13.tq: Recall the exact constitutional wording and avoid replacing 'authority of law' with executive action.
xs: **Art. 300A:** "No person shall be deprived of his property save by **authority of law**" — option **(4)**.
It covers **all persons**, not only citizens, and requires **law**, not an executive order or Parliament's consent.
xa: Protects against **executive action**, not legislation.
Enforced via **Art. 226**/ordinary suit, **not Art. 32**.
⚠ **PYQ G1 2019** key said "Article 300"; the correct provision is **Art. 300A**.

13.s: Which one of the following correctly explains the present constitutional status of the Right to Property?
o: It is a constitutional legal right under Article 300A, available to all persons
It is a constitutional legal right enforceable against legislation under Article 32
It is only a statutory right available to citizens under the RPA, 1951
It is a Fundamental Right enforceable under Article 32
13.x: The Right to Property is a constitutional legal right under Article 300A. It is available to all persons, including citizens, non-citizens and companies, but is not a Fundamental Right enforceable under Article 32.
13.tq: Separate Fundamental Rights from constitutional legal rights by status, beneficiaries and remedy.
xs: Property is now a **constitutional legal right** under **Art. 300A**, available to **all persons** — option **(1)**.
It is **not** an FR and is **not enforceable under Art. 32** — options 2 and 4 are wrong.
It is not limited to citizens: it covers **citizens, non-citizens, companies**.
xa: It protects against **executive action**, not legislation.
⚠ **Property = Art. 300A legal right; Vote = Art. 326 constitutional right; neither is an FR**.
AP angle: **GGR Housing v. State** — strict due process under Art. 300A.

13.s: A person is dispossessed of property by an executive order without any authority of law. Which constitutional provision is most directly attracted?
o: Article 31 as a continuing Fundamental Right
13.x: Article 300A protects against deprivation of property without authority of law and operates against executive action. Article 301 and the deleted Articles 31 and 19(1)(f) do not provide the applicable present remedy.
13.tq: Ask which constitutional provision governs the action of the authority actually dispossessing the person.
xs: Dispossession without **authority of law** attracts **Article 300A** — option **(1)**.
Art. 300A protects against **executive action**.
**Art. 31** and **Art. 19(1)(f)** were **deleted** by the **44th Amendment, 1978**.
xa: Remedy: **Art. 226**/ordinary suit, not Art. 32.
⚠ PYQ G1 **2019** key wrongly gave "Article 300".
**LARR Act, 2013** replaced the **Land Acquisition Act, 1894**.

13.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the LARR Act, 2013:
1. It replaced the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
2. It requires 80% consent for PPP projects and 70% consent for private projects.
3. Compensation may be up to four times the market value in rural areas and twice in urban areas.
4. Social Impact Assessment is mandatory.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
13.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct as per the Act. Statement 2 is wrong: the figures are reversed; consent is 70% for PPP and 80% for private projects. So A (misses 4), C and D (include 2) are wrong; B is correct.
13.tq: Private needs more consent (80%) than PPP (70%); rural 4x, urban 2x.
xs: Statements **1, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **LARR Act, 2013** replaced the **Land Acquisition Act, 1894**.
Statement 2 wrong (reversed): consent is **70% (PPP)** / **80% (private)**.
Statements 3 and 4: compensation up to **4x** (rural), **2x** (urban); **SIA mandatory**.
xa: Unused land is **returned after 5 years** (May **2026**).
**Art. 300A** — no deprivation save by authority of law.
AP HC (**GGR Housing**) insisted on strict statutory due process in land acquisition.

13.s: After the 44th Amendment, 1978 removed the Right to Property from Part III, how many Fundamental Rights does the Constitution now contain, and how many did it originally contain?
o: Six now; six originally, since property was never a Fundamental Right
13.x: The Constitution originally had seven Fundamental Rights, and the right to property under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 was one of them. The 44th Amendment, 1978 deleted it and made property a legal right under Article 300A, which leaves six. The other options get the count wrong or deny that property was ever a Fundamental Right.
13.tq: Seven to six: property moved out of Part III into Art. 300A.
xs: **Six** FRs now, **seven** originally — option **(1)**.
The **44th Amendment, 1978** deleted property (**Art. 19(1)(f)** and **Art. 31**) from Part III.
xa: Property is now a legal right under **Art. 300A**, **Part XII, Chapter IV**.
In **1950** property was an FR under 19(1)(f) and 31.
**1st Amendment, 1951** inserted **Arts. 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule**.

13.s: Which one of the following correctly matches the right with its constitutional position?
o: Right to Vote — Article 326 and statutory provisions under the Representation of the People Acts
Education for children aged 6–14 — Article 45 alone
13.x: The right to vote rests on adult suffrage under Article 326 and on statutory provisions (Section 62 of the RPA, 1951; registration under Section 19 of the RPA, 1950). B, C and D are wrong: the right to work is Article 41 (DPSP), information is part of Article 19(1)(a), and education for 6-14 is the Fundamental Right under Article 21A, not Article 45.
13.tq: Trace each right to its precise Article and statutory mechanism rather than relying on its general name.
xs: **Right to Vote — Art. 326** (adult suffrage, **18+**) and the RPA (**Sec. 62, RPA 1951**) — option **(1)**.
**Work** is **Art. 41** (DPSP), not 21A.
**Information** is part of **Art. 19(1)(a)**, not Art. 41.
**Education 6-14** is the FR in **Art. 21A**; **Art. 45** is the DPSP for **under-6**.
xa: Voter **registration**: **Sec. 19, RPA 1950**.
⚠ **Vote = Art. 326 constitutional right**, not an FR.
**RTI Act, 2005** gives the statutory machinery for information.

13.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Right to Information — Fundamental Right as part of Article 19(1)(a)
2. Right to Work — Fundamental Right under Article 41
3. Right to Education for children aged 6-14 — Fundamental Right under Article 21A
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
13.x: Pair 1 is correct: the right to information is read into Article 19(1)(a), and the RTI Act, 2005 provides the machinery. Pair 2 is wrong because Article 41 is a Directive Principle, not a Fundamental Right. Pair 3 is correct because Article 21A makes education for children aged 6-14 a Fundamental Right. Every Fundamental Right is a constitutional right, but not every constitutional right is a Fundamental Right.
13.tq: Information = 19(1)(a), an FR. Work = Art. 41, a DPSP. Education 6-14 = 21A, an FR. Vote = Art. 326, not an FR.
xs: Pairs **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Pair 1: **Information** is an FR — part of **Art. 19(1)(a)** (**RTI Act, 2005** gives machinery).
Pair 2 wrong: **Work** is a **DPSP** under **Art. 41**.
Pair 3: **Education (6-14)** is an FR under **Art. 21A**.
xa: Rule: every **FR is a constitutional right**, but not every constitutional right is an FR.
**Art. 51A(k)** — parents' duty on education.
**Vote**: **Art. 326** — constitutional, not FR.

13.s: The right to vote in India is classified as:
o: A Fundamental Right under Part III
A statutory right under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act
A Directive Principle of State Policy
A natural right beyond statutory regulation
13.x: The right to vote is a statutory right under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act, not a Fundamental Right.
13.tq: Distinguish statutory rights from Fundamental Rights by identifying the governing provision.
xs: Voting is a **statutory right** under **Section 62 of the RPA 1951** — option **(2)**; it is **not an FR**.
It is also constitutional via **Art. 326** (adult suffrage, **18+**), but not in Part III.
xa: Registration: **Sec. 19, RPA 1950**.
**Voting paradox**: right to know candidates, **NOTA**, **ballot secrecy** recognised under **19(1)(a)**.
The Opposition sought **FR status** for the right to vote (**7 Jul 2026**).

13.s: Under Article 326, the right to vote in elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies is based on:
13.x: Article 326 provides for elections based on universal adult suffrage, with the voting age being 18 years.
13.tq: Separate the constitutional voting principle from outdated age and qualification conditions.
xs: **Art. 326** provides **universal adult suffrage** at **18** years — option **(4)**.
It is not based on education or property, and the age is not 21.
xa: Voting is a **constitutional/statutory** right, **not an FR**.
Statutory basis: **Sec. 62, RPA 1951**.
⚠ **Property = Art. 300A legal right; Vote = Art. 326** — neither is an FR.

13.s: Which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Every constitutional right is a Fundamental Right.
Every Fundamental Right is a constitutional right, but not every constitutional right is a Fundamental Right.
No Fundamental Right is a constitutional right.
Constitutional rights and Fundamental Rights are identical in scope.
13.x: Every Fundamental Right is a constitutional right, but not every constitutional right is a Fundamental Right; for example, adult suffrage under Article 326 is constitutional but not a Fundamental Right.
13.tq: FRs are a subset of constitutional rights.
xs: **Every FR is a constitutional right, but not every constitutional right is an FR** — option **(2)**.
Example: voting under **Art. 326** and property under **Art. 300A** are constitutional rights but **not FRs**.
xa: **Work** (**Art. 41**) is a **DPSP**.
**Education (6-14)** under **Art. 21A** is an FR.
**Information** is an FR as part of **Art. 19(1)(a)**.

13.s:
Although the right to vote is statutory, which of the following have been recognised under Article 19(1)(a)?
1. Right to know the details of candidates
2. NOTA option
3. Secrecy of the ballot
Select the correct answer using the code below.
13.x: All three - the right to know candidate details, NOTA and ballot secrecy - have been recognised under Article 19(1)(a), even though voting itself is a statutory right. This is the 'voting paradox'.
13.tq: Vote is statutory, but how you express it is 19(1)(a).
xs: All three — **1, 2 and 3** — are recognised under **Art. 19(1)(a)** — option **(4)**.
Voting is **statutory**, yet the right to know **candidate details**, **NOTA** and **ballot secrecy** fall under 19(1)(a) — the "**voting paradox**".
xa: The Opposition sought **FR status** for the right to vote (**7 Jul 2026**).
Voting: **Art. 326** (adult suffrage, **18+**); **Sec. 62, RPA 1951**.
**Information** itself is an FR as part of 19(1)(a).

13.s: Which recent development was reported as creating concern regarding the Kannada linguistic minority in Kasaragod?
o: A central notification replacing all State languages with Hindi
A Malayalam language Bill in Kerala receiving assent in March 2026
A judicial decision removing the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
13.x: The Kerala Malayalam Bhasha Bill received assent in March 2026 and was contested on the ground that it could harm the Kannada linguistic minority in Kasaragod.
13.tq: Connect the current-affairs development with the precise linguistic-minority issue involved.
xs: Kerala's **Malayalam Bhasha Bill** (assented **Mar 2026**) was contested as harming the **Kannada linguistic minority in Kasaragod** — option **(3)**.
Linguistic minorities are determined **State-wise**.
xa: **Art. 350A:** **mother-tongue instruction** at the primary stage for linguistic minority children.
"**Linguistic minority**" is **not defined** in the Constitution.
**Art. 30(1)** covers **linguistic** minorities too.

13.s: Which one of the following concerns has been raised in debates relating to minority educational institutions?
o: The abolition of the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992
A constitutional prohibition on minority-run schools receiving any public assistance
A complete prohibition on mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage
Misuse of minority status to avoid obligations under the Right to Education framework
13.x: A criticism in the debate is that minority status may sometimes be misused to escape obligations under the Right to Education framework.
13.tq: Identify the stated criticism without converting it into an absolute constitutional prohibition.
xs: A criticism is the **misuse of minority status to escape RTE obligations** — option **(4)**.
The RTE **25% quota** does not apply to minority schools (**Pramati, 2014**).
xa: Only **8.76%** disadvantaged enrolments in minority schools (**NCPCR, Sep 2025**).
**FCRA amendments** are seen as a threat to **minority-run civil society** (**12 Jun 2026**).
The State may **regulate standards** but **not the minority character**.

13.s: In GGR Housing v. State, the Andhra Pradesh High Court emphasised:
o: Strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Article 300A
The abolition of Article 300A as a legal right
The conversion of the right to property into a Fundamental Right
The exclusion of land acquisition from judicial review
13.x: The Andhra Pradesh High Court insisted on strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Article 300A. Article 300A protects the right to property as a legal constitutional right.
13.tq: Apply the case principle to the constitutional protection governing deprivation of property.
xs: **AP HC (GGR Housing v. State)** insisted on **strict statutory due process in land acquisition** under **Art. 300A** — option **(1)** (May **2026**).
Art. 300A: no deprivation of property **save by authority of law**.
xa: Art. 300A is a **legal (constitutional) right**, not an FR, after the **44th Amendment, 1978**.
It protects against **executive action**; enforced via **Art. 226**.
**LARR Act, 2013:** **SIA** mandatory; consent **70%** (PPP) / **80%** (private).

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 32:
1. Clause (1) makes the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcing Part III rights itself a Fundamental Right.
2. Under clause (2), the Supreme Court may issue directions, orders or writs, including the five named writs.
3. Under clause (4), the right under Article 32 may be suspended by an ordinary law of Parliament.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
14.x: Statement 1 is correct: 32(1) is itself a Fundamental Right. Statement 2 is correct: 32(2) empowers directions, orders and writs. Statement 3 is wrong: 32(4) says the right shall not be suspended except as the Constitution provides, not by an ordinary law. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
14.tq: 32(1) right, 32(2) writs, 32(3) other courts, 32(4) no suspension except as the Constitution provides.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **32(1)** — the right to move the **Supreme Court** is itself a **Fundamental Right**.
Statement 2: **32(2)** — SC may issue directions, orders or **writs** incl. the five named.
Statement 3 wrong: **32(4)** — the right is **not suspended except as the Constitution provides**, not by ordinary law.
xa: **32(3):** Parliament may empower **any other court** to issue writs — no such law made so far.
Art. 32 is part of the **basic structure**.
Art. 32 can be suspended under **Art. 359**.

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 32(3) of the Constitution:
1. Parliament may empower any other court to exercise some of the powers of the Supreme Court under Article 32.
2. Parliament has so far enacted a law empowering subordinate courts to issue writs under Article 32.
3. High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Article 32(3) permits Parliament to empower other courts, but no such law has been made so far. High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
14.tq: Watch for the trap that changes a constitutional enabling provision into an enacted law.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1: **32(3)** — Parliament may empower **any other court** to issue writs.
Statement 2 wrong: **no such law** has been made so far — only the **SC and HCs** issue writs.
Statement 3: HCs issue writs under **Art. 226**.
xa: Before **1950**, only the **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** HCs could issue writs.
HC writ power is **wider in scope**; SC's is **wider in territory**.
IYB counts **25 High Courts** (sanctioned strength **1,122**).

14.s: Which of the following statements best expresses the constitutional position of Article 32?
o: It is a statutory remedy created by Parliament and may be withdrawn by Parliament
It can be completely repealed by a constitutional amendment because it is procedural
It forms part of the basic structure and cannot be abridged even by a constitutional amendment
It applies only to legal rights created by ordinary legislation
14.x: Article 32 is part of the basic structure of the Constitution. Its essential guarantee cannot be abridged even through a constitutional amendment.
14.tq: Use the basic-structure doctrine to reject options treating a Fundamental Right as an ordinary statutory remedy.
xs: Art. 32 is part of the **basic structure** — it **cannot be abridged even by amendment** — option **(3)**.
It is a **Fundamental Right**, not a statutory remedy, and covers **only FRs**, not ordinary legal rights.
xa: Rationale: **a right without a remedy is worthless**.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** made **Art. 226** HC writ power basic structure too.
Dr. **Ambedkar** called Art. 32 "the **very soul**... and the **very heart**" of the Constitution.

14.s: The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32 is best described as
14.x: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights, but this jurisdiction is not exclusive because High Courts also exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
14.tq: Split the paired descriptions—original and exclusive—instead of assuming that direct jurisdiction is exclusive.
xs: Art. 32 jurisdiction is **original but not exclusive** — option **(3)**.
It is **concurrent** with the HCs for FRs; the aggrieved person may choose either.
xa: HCs issue writs under **Art. 226**, which is **wider** — FRs and "**any other purpose**".
**Res judicata:** an HC dismissal **on merits** bars a fresh Art. 32 petition on the same plea.
The **Judiciary** is the **guardian of Fundamental Rights** (APPSC 2021).

14.s: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar described which constitutional provision as the ‘heart and soul’ of the Constitution?
14.x: Dr. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the heart and soul of the Constitution because it provides the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
14.tq: Associate the famous description with the exact Article, not merely with Part III generally.
xs: **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** called **Article 32** "the **very soul** of the Constitution and the **very heart** of it" — option **(2)**.
⚠ **Trap:** the **PYQ G2 2025** key gave **Art. 14**; the correct answer is **Art. 32**.
xa: **32(1)** — the right to move the SC — is itself a **Fundamental Right** (APPSC GS 2025).
Art. 32 is part of the **basic structure**.
**PIL** was developed by Justices **P.N. Bhagwati** and **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.

14.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the writ of Prohibition?
o: Issued against a private person to compel performance of a contract
Issued by a higher court to stop a lower judicial or quasi-judicial body from exceeding its jurisdiction
Issued to test the legality of a person’s claim to a public office
Issued to release a person from every form of lawful detention
14.x: Prohibition is issued by a higher court to prevent a lower court or tribunal with judicial or quasi-judicial functions from exceeding its jurisdiction.
14.tq: Match the writ with the body against which it operates and the stage at which it acts.
xs: **Prohibition** ("**to forbid**"): a higher court stops a lower court/tribunal from **exceeding jurisdiction** — option **(2)**.
Claim to **public office** is tested by **quo warranto**; it does not lie against **private persons**; habeas corpus does not lie against **lawful detention**.
xa: Prohibition lies only against **judicial and quasi-judicial** bodies.
It is issued while proceedings are **pending** — **preventive** only.
⚠ **Prohibition** = pending, preventive; **Certiorari** = after order, preventive and curative.

14.s: A writ of Prohibition does NOT ordinarily lie against which of the following?
o: A lower court exceeding its jurisdiction
14.x: Prohibition lies against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies, but not against administrative authorities acting in an administrative capacity. It also does not lie against legislative bodies or private persons.
14.tq: Find the body outside the judicial or quasi-judicial field.
xs: Prohibition does **not** lie against an **administrative authority** — option **(3)**.
It lies only against **judicial and quasi-judicial** bodies — so options 1, 2 and 4 are where it lies.
xa: It also does not lie against **legislative bodies** or **private persons**.
**Certiorari**, since **1991**, lies against certain **administrative** bodies affecting rights.
Prohibition directs **inactivity** — stops the lower body from continuing.

14.s: Which statement regarding Certiorari is correct?
o: It is confined exclusively to private disputes between individuals
It can be issued only before a lower court begins proceedings
It may transfer a case or quash an order of a lower court or authority
It is available only against a legislative body
14.x: Certiorari may be used to transfer a case from, or quash an order of, a lower court or authority. It operates against judicial, quasi-judicial and certain administrative bodies affecting rights.
14.tq: Distinguish the corrective function of Certiorari from the preventive function of Prohibition.
xs: **Certiorari** ("**to be certified**") lets a higher court **transfer a case** or **quash an order** of a lower court/authority — option **(3)**.
It does not lie against **private persons** or **legislative bodies**, and it is not confined to the pre-proceeding stage.
xa: It lies against **judicial, quasi-judicial** and (since **1991**) certain **administrative** bodies.
It is **preventive and curative**; **curative** when issued after the order.
**Prohibition** is issued while proceedings are **pending**.

14.s: Since 1991, the writ of Certiorari may also lie against
o: Certain administrative bodies when their actions affect rights
The President and Governor for their official acts
14.x: The scope of Certiorari has been extended to certain administrative bodies whose decisions affect rights. It does not ordinarily lie against private persons or legislative bodies.
14.tq: Use the date-linked expansion of jurisdiction to identify the precise category added.
xs: Since **1991**, certiorari also lies against **certain administrative bodies** affecting rights — option **(1)**.
It does not lie against **legislative bodies** or **private persons**.
**Art. 361** shields the **President and Governors** from courts for official acts.
xa: Certiorari = "**to be certified**" / to be informed.
It **quashes an order** already passed or transfers a case.
Prohibition still lies only against **judicial and quasi-judicial** bodies.

14.s: Mandamus does NOT ordinarily lie against which of the following?
o: The President or Governor for official acts
An inferior court failing to perform a public legal duty
14.x: Mandamus may lie against public officials, public corporations, inferior courts, tribunals and government authorities, but not against the President or Governor for their official acts. Article 361 protects them from being answerable to any court for official acts.
14.tq: Apply the question ‘who would perform this public duty?’ and remember the constitutional protection of the President and Governors.
xs: Mandamus does not lie against the **President or Governors** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 361:** they are **not answerable to any court** for official acts.
It does lie against **public officials, public corporations, inferior courts**, tribunals.
xa: Mandamus = "**we command**" — to perform a **public legal duty**.
Not against **private individuals/bodies**, **discretionary** duty, **legislative functions**.
Not against the **Chief Justice of a HC** acting judicially.

14.s:
With reference to Habeas Corpus, consider the following statements:
1. It may be directed against public authorities.
2. It may also be directed against a private individual who unlawfully detains another person.
3. It necessarily results in release even when the detention is lawful.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Habeas Corpus may be issued against public authorities and private individuals for unlawful detention. It does not require release where the detention is lawful.
14.tq: Separate the persons against whom the writ lies from the condition that makes detention unlawful.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Habeas corpus** lies against **public authorities and private individuals**.
Statement 3 wrong: it does not lie against **lawful detention**.
xa: Habeas corpus = "**to have the body of**" — produce a detained person before court.
It is the "**bulwark of individual liberty**" against arbitrary detention.
Also not for **contempt of court/legislature** or detention **outside jurisdiction**.

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the writ of Quo Warranto:
1. It may be sought by any interested person, not only by the aggrieved person.
2. It lies against the holder of a substantive public office created by a statute or the Constitution.
3. It lies against a ministerial or private office.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
14.x: Statement 1 is correct: any interested person may seek it. Statement 2 is correct: it tests a claim to a substantive public office created by statute or the Constitution. Statement 3 is wrong: it does not lie against a ministerial or private office. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
14.tq: Quo warranto: substantive public office only; any interested person may ask.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **quo warranto** may be sought by **any interested person**, not only the aggrieved.
Statement 2: it lies against the holder of a **substantive public office** created by statute/Constitution.
Statement 3 wrong: not against a **ministerial or private office**.
xa: Quo warranto = "**by what authority**".
It tests the **legality of a claim** to a **public office**.
**PYQ G2 2025** matched the literal meanings of writs.

14.s: The writ jurisdiction of Indian constitutional courts is historically derived from the
o: English law of prerogative writs issued in the name of the King
United States doctrine of judicial review alone
14.x: The writs were borrowed from English law, where they were known as prerogative writs of the King, regarded as the fountain of justice.
14.tq: Identify the constitutional borrowing by linking the writs with their historical institutional source.
xs: Writs come from **English law** — the **"prerogative writs"** of the **King**, the "**fountain of justice**" — option **(1)**.
They are not from Roman, US or French law in the notes.
xa: Before **1950**, only the **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** HCs could issue writs.
**Five** writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto.
**Art. 226** now empowers all HCs.

14.s:
Which of the following statements regarding writ jurisdiction in India is correct?
1. Before 1950, the High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras could issue writs.
2. Article 226 now empowers all High Courts to issue writs.
3. Article 226 confines High Court writ jurisdiction exclusively to Fundamental Rights.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Before 1950, the Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts had writ jurisdiction. Article 226 now empowers all High Courts, and their jurisdiction extends beyond Fundamental Rights to other purposes as well.
14.tq: Reject the extreme word ‘exclusively’ by comparing the wider scope of Article 226 with Article 32.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: before **1950**, only **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** HCs could issue writs.
Statement 2: **Art. 226** now empowers **all HCs**.
Statement 3 wrong: Art. 226 covers FRs **and "any other purpose"** — wider.
xa: HCs can issue writs beyond their territory if the **cause of action** arises within (**15th Amendment, 1963**).
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997):** Art. 226 is **basic structure**.
Art. 226 is **not suspendable as such**.

14.s: How many writs are specifically recognised for enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32(2)?
14.x: Article 32(2) refers to five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto.
14.tq: Count the constitutionally named writs rather than adding other judicial remedies.
xs: **Five** writs — option **(4)**.
**Habeas corpus**, **mandamus**, **prohibition**, **certiorari**, **quo warranto**.
xa: Both the **SC** (Art. 32) and **HCs** (Art. 226) issue all **five**.
Writs come from **English** prerogative writs.
**Habeas corpus** is the only writ against **private persons**.

14.s: Which writ is traditionally regarded as the bulwark of individual liberty?
14.x: Habeas Corpus is regarded as the bulwark of individual liberty because it provides a prompt judicial remedy against unlawful detention.
14.tq: Associate the liberty-protection function with the writ directed against unlawful detention.
xs: **Habeas corpus** is the "**bulwark of individual liberty** against arbitrary detention" — option **(3)**.
It means "**to have the body of**" — the detained person is produced before court and released if detention is illegal.
xa: It is the **only writ against private persons**.
Producing a person before court = habeas corpus (**APPSC 2021**).
Not for **lawful detention**.

14.s: Which writ can, in appropriate circumstances, run against a private person?
14.x: Habeas corpus may be issued even against a private person who unlawfully detains another. The other writs are ordinarily directed against public, judicial or quasi-judicial authorities.
14.tq: Use the exceptional private-person feature to distinguish habeas corpus from the other writs.
xs: **Habeas corpus** is the **only writ against private persons** — option **(3)**.
**Mandamus** is **not** against private persons; **prohibition** and **certiorari** lie only against judicial/quasi-judicial (and, for certiorari, some administrative) bodies.
xa: Habeas corpus lies against **public authorities and private individuals**.
It safeguards **personal liberty**.
It does not lie against **lawful detention**.

14.s:
With reference to prohibition and certiorari, consider the following statements:
1. Both may check excess of jurisdiction.
2. Traditionally, both are directed against judicial or quasi-judicial bodies.
3. Prohibition quashes an order already passed, whereas certiorari merely prevents future proceedings.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Both writs check jurisdictional excess, and traditionally both operate against judicial or quasi-judicial bodies. Statement 3 reverses their normal functions: prohibition prevents continuation, while certiorari quashes an order.
14.tq: Identify the reversed comparison in the third statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: both **check excess of jurisdiction** and both lie against **judicial/quasi-judicial** bodies (traditionally).
Statement 3 wrong (reversed): **prohibition** stops pending proceedings; **certiorari quashes the order** already passed.
xa: Prohibition is **preventive only**; certiorari **preventive and curative**.
Certiorari can also **transfer a pending case**.
Since **1991** certiorari reaches certain **administrative** bodies.

14.s:
Match List-I (Writ) with List-II (Literal meaning):
List-I
a. Quo warranto
b. Mandamus
c. Habeas corpus
d. Certiorari
List-II
i. We command
ii. To have the body of
iii. To be certified
iv. By what authority
Select the correct answer using the code below.
14.x: Quo warranto means 'by what authority' (iv), mandamus 'we command' (i), habeas corpus 'to have the body of' (ii) and certiorari 'to be certified' (iii), so the first code is right. The second swaps quo warranto and mandamus. The third swaps habeas corpus and certiorari. The fourth swaps quo warranto and certiorari.
14.tq: This match was asked in Group 2, 2025. Prohibition, the fifth writ, means 'to forbid'.
xs: **a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii** — option **(1)** (PYQ G2 2025).
**Quo warranto** — "**by what authority**"; **Mandamus** — "**we command**".
**Habeas corpus** — "**to have the body of**"; **Certiorari** — "**to be certified**".
xa: **Prohibition** — "**to forbid**".
Habeas corpus is the **bulwark of individual liberty**.
Quo warranto may be sought by **any interested person**.

14.s: Which of the following statements regarding a writ of mandamus is correct?
o: It can be issued even when no governmental policy exists, to compel formulation of a policy.
It is issued exclusively against private individuals for performance of personal duties.
It may be issued to the Government to enact a law whenever a court considers the existing law inadequate.
It cannot compel the Government to make a law, but once a policy is laid down, its terms may be enforced through mandamus.
14.x: Mandamus cannot be used to compel the Government to make a law or formulate a policy. However, after a policy is laid down, its enforceable terms may be implemented through mandamus.
14.tq: Test the precise limit of a constitutional remedy rather than accepting an expansive power.
xs: Mandamus is **not issued to the Government to make a law**, but **once a policy is laid down its terms can be enforced** — option **(4)**.
It **cannot lie in the absence of a policy**, so option 1 is wrong; it is **not against private persons**, so option 2 is wrong.
xa: PYQ A-R **G2 2025**: both true, **R explains A**.
Mandamus = "**we command**" — perform a **public legal duty**.
Not against the **President or Governors**.

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding mandamus:
1. It may be issued against a private individual or body as a general rule.
2. It is not issued to enforce a discretionary duty.
3. It is not issued to enforce a legislative function.
4. It may be issued to enforce a non-statutory departmental instruction in every case.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Mandamus is not ordinarily issued against private bodies, for discretionary functions, legislative functions or non-statutory departmental instructions. Statements 2 and 3 correctly state its limitations.
14.tq: Split the options by identifying the statements that describe limits on mandamus.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 2 and 3: mandamus is not issued for a **discretionary duty** or **legislative functions**.
Statement 1 wrong: **not against private individuals/bodies**.
Statement 4 wrong: not for a **non-statutory departmental instruction**.
xa: Also not for a **contractual obligation**.
Not against the **President, Governors** or a **HC Chief Justice** acting judicially.
Lies against **public officials**, **public corporations**, **inferior courts**, **tribunals**.

14.s: Mandamus may NOT ordinarily be issued against which one of the following?
o: A public authority for failure to perform a statutory duty
A government department for breach of an enforceable policy
A private individual for enforcement of a purely private obligation
A public authority for failure to perform a mandatory public duty
14.x: Mandamus is generally directed against public authorities for public or statutory duties. It is not ordinarily available against private individuals or bodies for purely private obligations.
14.tq: Find the option involving a private obligation, which falls outside mandamus.
xs: Mandamus does not lie against a **private individual** for a **private obligation** — option **(3)**.
It commands public officials/bodies to perform a **public legal duty**; it also does not enforce a **contractual obligation**.
xa: Once a **policy** is laid down, its terms can be enforced by mandamus.
Not against the **President or Governors** (**Art. 361**).
⚠ Only **habeas corpus** lies against private persons.

14.s: A writ of mandamus cannot be issued against which of the following?
14.x: Mandamus does not lie against the President or the Governors of States. It can be issued to public authorities, corporations and tribunals that fail to perform public duties.
14.tq: Mandamus spares the heads: President and Governors.
xs: Mandamus cannot be issued against **the President or a Governor** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 361:** they are **not answerable to any court** for official acts.
It does lie against **public corporations** and **tribunals**.
xa: Mandamus = "**we command**".
Not issued to the Government **to make a law**.
Not for a **discretionary duty** or **legislative functions**.

14.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes prohibition from certiorari?
o: Prohibition is curative only, whereas certiorari is preventive only.
Prohibition is issued after final decision, whereas certiorari is issued only before proceedings begin.
Prohibition prevents continuation of proceedings, whereas certiorari generally quashes an order already passed.
Both writs are issued exclusively against private bodies.
14.x: Prohibition is primarily preventive and stops a judicial or quasi-judicial body from continuing proceedings without or in excess of jurisdiction. Certiorari is generally curative and quashes an order already passed.
14.tq: Compare the stage and effect of the two writs instead of their common jurisdictional basis.
xs: **Prohibition prevents continuation** of proceedings; **certiorari quashes an order already passed** — option **(3)**.
Option 1 reverses them: prohibition is **preventive only**; certiorari is **preventive and curative**.
Neither lies against **private persons**.
xa: Prohibition: while proceedings are **pending**; certiorari: **after** an order is **passed**.
Both check **excess of jurisdiction**.
Certiorari can also **transfer a pending case**.

14.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Prohibition is issued while proceedings are pending.
2. Certiorari is generally issued after an order or decision has been passed.
3. Prohibition directs the lower body to stop continuing the proceedings.
4. Certiorari can never be used in relation to a pending proceeding.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Certiorari is generally post-decision, but it may also be used to transfer a pending case; therefore statement 4 is incorrect.
14.tq: Watch for the absolute word 'never' in a comparison of writ stages.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 3: **prohibition** is issued while proceedings are **pending** and stops the lower body from continuing.
Statement 2: **certiorari** is generally issued **after an order is passed**.
Statement 4 wrong: certiorari can also **transfer a pending case**.
xa: Prohibition directs **inactivity**; certiorari is **curative** after the order.
Both traditionally lie against **judicial/quasi-judicial** bodies.
Certiorari reaches certain **administrative** bodies since **1991**.

14.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Prohibition — curative writ quashing an order already passed
Certiorari — preventive writ directing inactivity only
Prohibition — writ issued while proceedings are pending
Certiorari — writ available only against private individuals
14.x: Prohibition is a preventive writ issued during the pendency of proceedings. Certiorari is principally curative, and neither writ is ordinarily directed against private individuals.
14.tq: Start with the sure stage-writ pair and reject reversed descriptions.
xs: **Prohibition — issued while proceedings are pending** — option **(3)**.
Option 1 wrong: **certiorari**, not prohibition, quashes an order; option 2 wrong: prohibition, not certiorari, is **preventive only**.
Option 4 wrong: certiorari does not lie against **private persons**.
xa: Certiorari is **preventive and curative**.
Both check **excess of jurisdiction**.
Prohibition = "**to forbid**".

14.s: Since 1991, certiorari may also be issued against certain bodies performing which kind of function?
14.x: The scope of certiorari has extended, since 1991, to certain administrative bodies in addition to judicial and quasi-judicial bodies.
14.tq: Test the dated expansion of the range of bodies subject to certiorari.
xs: Since **1991**, certiorari also lies against certain **administrative** bodies affecting rights — option **(1)**.
It does not lie against **legislative bodies** or **private persons**.
xa: Traditionally it lay against **judicial and quasi-judicial** bodies.
Prohibition does **not** lie against administrative authorities.
Certiorari = "**to be certified**".

14.s: Which of the following is a feature common to the writs of prohibition and certiorari?
o: Both are issued only after a final order has been passed
Both check excess of jurisdiction by judicial or quasi-judicial bodies
Both are purely curative in nature
Both are available mainly against private individuals
14.x: Both prohibition and certiorari are traditionally issued against judicial or quasi-judicial bodies and both check excess of jurisdiction. Prohibition is preventive and issued while proceedings are pending, so it is not issued after a final order.
14.tq: Prohibition and certiorari: two writs, one target - excess of jurisdiction.
xs: Both **check excess of jurisdiction** by **judicial or quasi-judicial bodies** — option **(2)**.
Prohibition is issued while proceedings are **pending**, so option 1 is wrong; prohibition is **preventive only**, so option 3 is wrong.
xa: Certiorari is **preventive and curative**.
Neither lies against **private persons**.
Certiorari quashes the order already passed; prohibition stops the lower body from continuing.

14.s: A High Court dismisses a writ petition on merits. The petitioner then approaches the Supreme Court under Article 32 on the same plea. What is the correct legal position?
o: The petition is automatically converted into a petition under Article 226.
The Supreme Court must hear the petition because Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.
The petition is maintainable because res judicata applies only to civil suits.
The petition under Article 32 is barred by res judicata and the remedy lies only by way of appeal.
14.x: When a High Court dismisses a writ petition on merits, the same plea cannot ordinarily be raised before the Supreme Court under Article 32; the appropriate course is an appeal. If the dismissal was not on merits, a petition under Article 32 may be moved.
14.tq: Apply the res judicata distinction between dismissal on merits and dismissal on a technical ground.
xs: An HC dismissal **on merits** bars the same plea under Art. 32 by **res judicata**; the remedy lies **only in appeal** — option **(4)**.
If dismissed **not on merits**, the SC can be moved.
xa: Art. 32 jurisdiction is **original but not exclusive** — concurrent with HCs.
Art. 32 is itself a **Fundamental Right**; Art. 226 is a **discretionary** remedy.
Art. 226 is **wider** — FRs and "**any other purpose**".

14.s: Which one of the following statements about Article 32 is correct?
o: It is itself a Fundamental Right and enables enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
It is merely a discretionary statutory remedy available before the Supreme Court.
It can be exercised only after the High Court refuses relief under Article 226.
It enables enforcement of every legal right, whether or not it is a Fundamental Right.
14.x: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and provides a remedy before the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. It does not generally cover every statutory or legal right.
14.tq: Distinguish the constitutional status and narrower scope of Article 32 from Article 226.
xs: Art. 32 is **itself a Fundamental Right** and enables **enforcement of Fundamental Rights** — option **(1)**.
It is not statutory, does not need the HC to refuse first (**original but not exclusive**), and covers **only FRs**, not statutory rights.
xa: HCs under **Art. 226** can enforce FRs and "**any other purpose**".
Art. 32 can be suspended under **Art. 359**.
The **Judiciary** is the guardian of FRs.

14.s: A High Court may issue a writ beyond its territorial limits under Article 226 when—
o: the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises within its territory
the Union Government transfers the proceeding to it
the Supreme Court authorises it in every individual case
the respondent is located anywhere in India, irrespective of cause of action
14.x: A High Court ordinarily exercises Article 226 jurisdiction within its territory, but may do so beyond that territory where the cause of action wholly or partly arises within its territorial jurisdiction. This position followed the Fifteenth Amendment of 1963.
14.tq: Apply the territorial-jurisdiction rule by focusing on the cause of action.
xs: An HC may issue writs beyond its territory if the **cause of action** arises within it — option **(1)**.
This came with the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
xa: The SC's Art. 32 power covers the **whole of India**.
HC writ power is **wider in scope**; SC's **wider in territory**.
Both issue all **five** writs.

14.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Article 32A, which barred challenges to State laws under Article 32.
2. The 43rd Amendment (1977) omitted Articles 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A and 228A.
3. The 42nd Amendment widened the writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
14.x: Statement 1 is correct: the 42nd Amendment inserted Art. 32A. Statement 2 is correct: the 43rd Amendment omitted these Articles. Statement 3 is wrong: the 42nd Amendment curbed Art. 226; the 43rd and 44th restored it. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
14.tq: 42nd curbed, 43rd and 44th restored.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: the **42nd Amendment (1976)** inserted **Art. 32A** (no challenge to State laws under Art. 32).
Statement 2: the **43rd Amendment (1977)** omitted **Arts 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A, 228A**.
Statement 3 wrong: the 42nd **curbed Art. 226**.
xa: The **44th** also restored Art. 226.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997):** Art. 226 HC writ power is **basic structure**.
Art. 32 is also **basic structure**.

14.s: The writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 was held to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution in—
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997
14.x: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review under Articles 226 and 227 forms part of the basic structure.
14.tq: Match the landmark case with the constitutional principle it established.
xs: **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** held **Art. 226** HC writ power part of the **basic structure** — option **(4)**.
**Sunil Batra** — **epistolary jurisdiction**; **S.P. Gupta (1981)** — **PIL**.
xa: The **42nd Amendment** had curbed Art. 226; the **43rd** and **44th** restored it.
Art. 32 is also part of the **basic structure**.
HCs share the role of **guardian of FRs** under Art. 226.

14.s: Which institution is regarded as the guardian of Fundamental Rights, with the Supreme Court acting as their protector and guarantor?
14.x: The Judiciary is regarded as the guardian of Fundamental Rights, and the Supreme Court has the constitutional role of protecting and guaranteeing those rights.
14.tq: Identify the constitutional institution associated with protection and enforcement of rights.
xs: The **Judiciary** is the **guardian of Fundamental Rights**, with the SC as "**protector and guarantor**" — option **(3)** (APPSC 2021).
**HCs share the role** under **Art. 226**.
xa: Art. 32 is itself a **Fundamental Right**.
Art. 32 jurisdiction is **original but not exclusive**.
Art. 32 is part of the **basic structure**.

14.s:
Consider the following statements comparing Article 32 and Article 226:
1. Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, whereas Article 226 is a discretionary constitutional remedy.
2. A High Court under Article 226 can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose'.
3. The right under Article 32 can be suspended under Article 359, while Article 226 is not suspendable as such.
4. The Supreme Court can issue five writs, whereas High Courts can issue only three.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: Article 32 is a Fundamental Right, Article 226 also covers 'any other purpose', and Article 32 can be suspended under Article 359. Statement 4 is wrong because both the Supreme Court and the High Courts issue all five writs. So the first option misses statement 3, and every option containing statement 4 is wrong.
14.tq: In writ jurisdiction, HCs are wider in scope and the SC is wider in territory. Art. 32 can be suspended under Art. 359.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: Art. 32 is a **Fundamental Right**; Art. 226 a **discretionary** constitutional remedy.
Statement 2: Art. 226 covers FRs **and "any other purpose"**.
Statement 3: Art. 32 can be suspended under **Art. 359**; Art. 226 is **not suspendable as such**.
Statement 4 wrong: both SC and HCs issue all **five** writs.
xa: Territory: SC — **whole of India**; HC — own territory (beyond it if cause of action arises within).
Extra-territorial reach came with the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
Jurisdiction is **concurrent** for FRs.

14.s: Public Interest Litigation primarily relaxes which traditional rule?
o: The rule that courts cannot issue writs against public authorities
The rule that Fundamental Rights are enforceable only by Parliament
The rule that judicial review is unavailable against administrative action
The rule that only the directly aggrieved person may approach the court
14.x: PIL relaxes the traditional rule of locus standi by permitting a public-spirited person to approach the court on behalf of persons unable to do so themselves or for a larger public interest.
14.tq: Identify the procedural rule changed by PIL rather than confusing it with a substantive right.
xs: **PIL** relaxes the rule that **only the aggrieved may sue** (**locus standi**) — option **(4)**.
**Any public-spirited person** can move the court for larger public interest or for those unable to.
xa: Pioneered by Justices **P.N. Bhagwati** and **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.
Key case: **S.P. Gupta, 1981**.
PIL is **not itself a Fundamental Right**.

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Public Interest Litigation (PIL):
1. S.P. Gupta (1981) is associated with the development of PIL.
2. Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer are associated with PIL.
3. PIL is itself a Fundamental Right.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
14.x: Statement 1 is correct: S.P. Gupta (1981) is a key PIL case. Statement 2 is correct: Justices Bhagwati and Krishna Iyer pioneered PIL. Statement 3 is wrong: PIL is not itself a Fundamental Right; it is a tool to make the judiciary accessible. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
14.tq: PIL = relaxed locus standi, a tool, not an FR.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **S.P. Gupta, 1981** — PIL.
Statement 2: Justices **P.N. Bhagwati**, **V.R. Krishna Iyer** — relaxed **locus standi**.
Statement 3 wrong: PIL is **not itself a Fundamental Right**; it is a tool to make the judiciary accessible.
xa: **Epistolary jurisdiction:** letters/postcards treated as writ petitions.
**Sunil Batra** — a prisoner's letter.
Quo warranto also may be sought by **any interested person**.

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding epistolary jurisdiction:
1. Under it, letters or postcards are treated as writ petitions.
2. Sunil Batra, where a prisoner's letter was acted upon, is an example of it.
3. It requires a formal petition filed only by the directly aggrieved person.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
14.x: Statement 1 is correct: letters and postcards are treated as writ petitions. Statement 2 is correct: Sunil Batra (prisoner's letter) is the example. Statement 3 is wrong: the whole point is that no formal petition is needed and locus standi is relaxed. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
14.tq: Epistolary = letter becomes a petition (Sunil Batra).
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **epistolary jurisdiction** treats **letters/postcards** as writ petitions.
Statement 2: **Sunil Batra** — a **prisoner's letter**.
Statement 3 wrong: PIL relaxed the rule that **only the aggrieved may sue**.
xa: PIL pioneers: **P.N. Bhagwati**, **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.
**S.P. Gupta, 1981** — PIL.
PIL is **not itself a Fundamental Right**.

14.s: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the comparative scope of writ jurisdiction in India?
o: High Courts can issue writs only for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, whereas the Supreme Court can issue them for any legal right.
The Supreme Court and High Courts have identical writ jurisdiction in both territory and subject matter.
The Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction is wider in territorial scope than that of High Courts.

High Courts have a wider subject-matter scope because they may issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for other purposes, while the Supreme Court's Article 32 jurisdiction is for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
14.x: D is the answer: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose', so their subject-matter scope is wider, while Article 32 is confined to Fundamental Rights. A reverses this and B is wrong. C states a true fact (the Supreme Court is wider in territory, covering the whole of India), but D gives the full scope comparison the question asks for.
14.tq: Split the comparison into territorial reach and subject-matter scope.
xs: **HC writ power is wider in scope** (FRs and "**any other purpose**"); Art. 32 is for **FRs only** — option **(4)**.
Option 1 reverses it; option 2 is wrong as scope and territory differ.
Option 3 is true but partial: the SC is **wider in territory** — option 4 states the scope comparison asked.
xa: Both issue **five** writs.
Art. 32 can be suspended under **Art. 359**.
Jurisdiction is **concurrent** for FRs.

14.s: The statement that “a right without a remedy is a worthless declaration” most directly explains the constitutional significance of
o: Article 30 providing aid to minority institutions
Article 32 making Part III rights judicially enforceable
Article 29 protecting admission to aided institutions
14.x: Article 32 provides a direct constitutional remedy for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, thereby making the rights in Part III effective rather than merely declaratory.
14.tq: Connect the general principle of remedy with the constitutional mechanism that enforces rights.
xs: "**A right without a remedy is a worthless declaration**" — **Article 32 makes Part III real** (judicially enforceable) — option **(3)**.
Art. 32 gives the right to move the **Supreme Court directly** to enforce Part III rights.
xa: Ambedkar: "the **very soul**... and the **very heart**" of the Constitution.
Art. 32 is part of the **basic structure**.
**32(4):** not suspended except as the Constitution provides.

14.s: Which one of the following current developments concerns the Supreme Court's examination of urgent constitutional remedies for threats to life and liberty?
o: A uniform reservation policy for all minority institutions under Article 30
An SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings under Articles 32 and 226
A constitutional amendment replacing Articles 32 and 226 with Article 131
A proposal to abolish High Court writ jurisdiction
14.x: The Supreme Court was examining an SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings in matters involving threats to life and liberty, strengthening practical access to remedies under Articles 32 and 226.
14.tq: Identify the practical remedy being examined rather than confusing it with a change in constitutional text.
xs: The SC is examining an **SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings** in threats to life and liberty, strengthening **Arts 32 and 226** — option **(2)** (**16 Jul 2026**).
No amendment replacing Arts 32 and 226 or abolishing HC writs is in the notes.
xa: **Habeas corpus** is the bulwark of liberty against arbitrary detention.
SC agreed (**20 Jan 2026**) to examine whether the **ED can invoke writ jurisdiction**.
ED-West Bengal: **Art. 32** petition vs **Art. 131** suit.

14.s: A proposal to treat religious-instruction schools under Article 26(a), instead of Article 30(1), was left for consideration to the
14.x: The plea concerning treatment of religious-instruction schools under Article 26(a) rather than Article 30(1) was left to the Ministry of Education.
14.tq: Apply the “which authority handles the matter?” test to distinguish the concerned ministry.
xs: The plea on religious-instruction schools (**Art. 26(a)** vs **Art. 30(1)**) was left to the **Ministry of Education** — option **(3)** (**12 May 2026**).
The NCM and other ministries are not named in the notes for this.
xa: Writs are the remedy under **Art. 32** (SC) and **Art. 226** (HC).
SC examining an **SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings** (**16 Jul 2026**).
ED-West Bengal: Centre defended an **Art. 32** petition (**24 Apr 2026**).

14.s: In the ED-West Bengal matter, the constitutional issue involved a contest between
o: an Article 136 appeal by the Centre and an Article 368 reference by the State
an Article 226 petition by the Centre and an Article 143 reference by the State
an Article 32 petition defended by the Centre and an Article 131 suit claimed by the State
an Article 30 petition by the Centre and an Article 29 claim by the State
14.x: The Centre defended an Article 32 petition, while the State argued that the dispute should proceed as an original suit under Article 131.
14.tq: Distinguish enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32 from intergovernmental original jurisdiction under Article 131.
xs: The Centre defended an **Article 32 petition**, against the State's plea for an **Article 131 suit** — option **(3)** (**24 Apr 2026**).
The other Article pairs are not part of the matter.
xa: Art. 32 is itself a **Fundamental Right**.
SC also examining whether the **Enforcement Directorate** can invoke writ jurisdiction (**20 Jan 2026**).
Art. 32 jurisdiction is **original but not exclusive**.

14.s: In January 2026, the Supreme Court agreed to examine which question in appeals by Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling?
o: Whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction
Whether High Courts can issue writs of quo warranto against Ministers
Whether Article 32 can be suspended during a financial emergency
Whether Parliament can empower district courts to issue writs under Article 32(3)
14.x: On 20 January 2026, a Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and S.C. Sharma agreed to examine whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction. The appeals came from Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling. The other three options are not what was referred.
14.tq: ED itself filing a writ petition = Jan 2026 SC reference.
xs: The SC agreed to examine whether the **Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction** — option **(1)** (**20 Jan 2026**).
Bench: Justices **Dipankar Datta** and **S.C. Sharma**; appeals by **Kerala and Tamil Nadu** against a **Kerala HC** ruling.
xa: **32(3):** Parliament may empower other courts, but **no such law** has been made.
Art. 32 can be suspended under **Art. 359**.
ED-West Bengal matter: **Art. 32** vs **Art. 131**.

15.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the origins of the Directive Principles of State Policy:
1. Their immediate constitutional model was the Irish Constitution of 1937.
2. The Irish Constitution had drawn the idea from the Spanish Constitution.
3. The Directive Principles were borrowed directly from the Spanish Constitution by the Constituent Assembly.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. India borrowed the idea through the Irish Constitution of 1937, which had itself copied it from the Spanish Constitution; it was not borrowed directly from Spain.
15.tq: Distinguish the immediate source from the ultimate antecedent.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: DPSPs were borrowed from the **Irish Constitution of 1937**.
Statement 2 — correct: **Ireland** copied the idea from the **Spanish Constitution**.
Statement 3 — wrong: India took them from **Ireland**, not directly from Spain.
xa: Irish name: **Directive Principles of Social Policy**.
Indian antecedents: **Karachi Resolution (1931)**, **Nehru Report (1928)**, **Sapru Committee (1945)**.
**Ambedkar** called DPSPs a "**novel feature**" of the Constitution.

15.s: Which one of the following was an Indian antecedent of the Directive Principles of State Policy?
o: The Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 only
The Government of India Act of 1919 only
15.x: The Karachi Resolution of 1931 was an important Indian antecedent of the Directive Principles. Socialist-nationalist ideas of the freedom struggle also influenced their development.
15.tq: Identify the constitution-making antecedent rather than a general constitutional enactment.
xs: The **Karachi Resolution (1931)** was an Indian antecedent of the DPSPs — option **(4)**.
It carried the **socialist-nationalist** ideas of the freedom struggle (APPSC GS **2023**).
xa: Other antecedents: **Nehru Report (1928)**, **Gandhian ideals**, **Instrument of Instructions** (GoI Act **1935**).
**Sapru Committee (1945)** split rights into **justiciable** and **non-justiciable**.
Foreign source: **Irish Constitution of 1937**.

15.s: The Sapru Committee of 1945 is significant in the development of constitutional rights because it proposed a division between:
15.x: The Sapru Committee suggested dividing rights into justiciable and non-justiciable categories, an idea reflected later in the distinction between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.
15.tq: Match the committee with its specific constitutional contribution.
xs: The **Sapru Committee (1945)** split rights into **justiciable and non-justiciable** — option **(4)**.
This foreshadowed the **FR (Part III)** vs **DPSP (Part IV)** split.
xa: **Art. 37**: Part IV "**shall not be enforceable by any court**".
Antecedents also include the **Karachi Resolution (1931)** and **Nehru Report (1928)**.
**Instrument of Instructions** under the GoI Act **1935**.

15.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Directive Principles of State Policy:
1. They are contained in Part IV of the Constitution.
2. They extend from Article 36 to Article 51.
3. They are enforceable in a court of law in the same manner as Fundamental Rights.
4. They are fundamental in the governance of the country.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: The DPSPs are in Part IV, Articles 36–51, and are fundamental in governance. They cannot be enforced by courts, so statement 3 is false.
15.tq: Use the constitutional distinction between governance principles and enforceable rights.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 4 only**.
Statements 1 and 2 — correct: DPSPs are in **Part IV**, **Art. 36-51**.
Statement 3 — wrong: under **Art. 37** they are **not enforceable by any court**.
Statement 4 — correct: they are "**fundamental in the governance of the country**".
xa: It is the **duty of the State** to apply them in making laws.
Welfare state: "**The State is everywhere: it leaves hardly a gap**" (JPSC **2016**).

15.s: The Directive Principles of State Policy are often compared to which instrument issued under the Government of India Act, 1935, one of their Indian antecedents?
15.x: The Instrument of Instructions under the Government of India Act, 1935 is listed as an Indian antecedent of the DPSPs, along with the Karachi Resolution (1931), the Nehru Report (1928), Gandhian ideals and the Sapru Committee (1945). The Instrument of Accession joined princely states to the Dominion. The Objectives Resolution (1946) led to the Preamble. The Communal Award (1932) dealt with separate electorates.
15.tq: Instrument of Instructions (GoI Act 1935) leads to the DPSPs; the Objectives Resolution leads to the Preamble.
xs: DPSPs are compared to the **Instrument of Instructions** under the **GoI Act 1935** — option **(1)**.
The **Objectives Resolution** led to the **Preamble**, not the DPSPs — option (3) wrong.
xa: Other antecedents: **Karachi Resolution (1931)**, **Nehru Report (1928)**, **Gandhian ideals**.
**Sapru Committee (1945)**: justiciable vs non-justiciable rights.
**K.T. Shah**: a "**cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank**".

15.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Fundamental Rights from Directive Principles of State Policy?
o: Directive Principles are applicable only to private individuals, whereas Fundamental Rights apply only to the State.
Fundamental Rights are generally negative obligations, whereas Directive Principles are generally positive obligations on the State.
Fundamental Rights are positive obligations, whereas Directive Principles are enforceable by courts.
Both are negative obligations and both are directly enforceable by courts.
15.x: Fundamental Rights mostly restrain the State from certain actions, while Directive Principles generally require the State to undertake measures for social and economic welfare.
15.tq: Split the paired concepts by asking what each requires the State to do or not do.
xs: FRs are mostly **negative** obligations on the State; DPSPs are **positive** obligations — option **(2)**.
DPSPs are **not enforceable by any court** (**Art. 37**) — options (3) and (4) wrong.
xa: FRs and DPSPs are **complementary**.
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: balance between Part III and Part IV is **basic structure**.
**Granville Austin**: together they are the "**conscience of the Constitution**".

15.s:
Assertion (A): Directive Principles of State Policy cannot be independently enforced in a court of law.
Reason (R): Directive Principles are intended to guide the State in making laws.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
15.x: Both statements are true. However, non-enforceability arises from the express provision in Article 37; their role as a legislative guide does not explain the legal bar on enforcement.
15.tq: Separate the constitutional source of non-enforceability from the practical function of the Principles.
xs: Both A and R are true but R is **not the correct explanation** of A — option **(2)** (APPSC G2 **2025**).
A — true: DPSPs are **not independently enforceable**.
R — true: they act as a **guidepost for legislation**.
⚠ Non-enforceability flows from **Art. 37**'s **express bar**, not from their guiding role.
xa: Art. 37 still calls them "**fundamental in the governance of the country**".
Critical remarks (K.T. Shah, T.T. Krishnamachari, Nasiruddin) target the **non-justiciable** nature.

15.s: Courts have generally used the Directive Principles of State Policy in which of the following ways?
o: As independently enforceable rights replacing Fundamental Rights
As provisions applicable exclusively to local governments
As limitations that prevent all legislative action under Part III
As interpretive aids, including in reading certain principles into Article 21
15.x: Although DPSPs are not independently enforceable, courts use them as interpretive aids and have read several welfare-oriented principles into the scope of Article 21.
15.tq: Apply the distinction between non-justiciability and interpretive constitutional relevance.
xs: Courts use DPSPs as **interpretive aids**, reading many into **Art. 21** — option **(4)**.
Courts apply **harmonious construction** of Parts III and IV.
DPSPs are **not enforceable** by courts (**Art. 37**), so option (1) is wrong.
xa: **Minerva Mills (1980)**: the balance between Parts III and IV is **basic structure**.
FRs and DPSPs are **complementary**.

15.s: Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles after the judicial interpretation associated with Minerva Mills (1980)?
o: Part IV has absolute superiority over Part III in every circumstance.
A balance and harmonious relationship between Part III and Part IV is part of the Basic Structure.
Part III has absolute superiority over Part IV in every circumstance.
Both Part III and Part IV are excluded from judicial review.
15.x: The balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is treated as part of the Basic Structure. Neither Part III nor Part IV has unlimited supremacy over the other.
15.tq: Reject absolute-supremacy statements and identify the constitutional-balance principle.
xs: **Minerva Mills (1980)**: a **balance** between **Part III and Part IV** is part of the **Basic Structure** — option **(2)**.
So neither Part has absolute superiority — options (1) and (3) wrong.
xa: Courts use **harmonious construction**.
FRs = **negative** obligations; DPSPs = **positive** obligations.
Granville Austin: FRs and DPSPs together are the "**conscience of the Constitution**".

15.s: Article 36 of the Constitution of India provides that, for the purposes of Part IV, the expression ‘State’ shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in which Part?
15.x: Article 36 states that ‘the State’ in Part IV has the same meaning as in Part III of the Constitution.
15.tq: Use the exact constitutional cross-reference rather than the neighbouring Part numbers.
xs: **Art. 36**: "State" in Part IV has the same meaning as in **Part III** — option **(2)**.
Part III holds the **Fundamental Rights**; Part IV borrows its definition of State.
