xa: **Art. 37**: DPSPs not enforceable but **fundamental in governance**.
DPSPs span **Art. 36-51** in **Part IV**.
**Art. 38**: welfare through social, economic, political justice.

15.s: The Directive Principle relating to a social order based on social, economic and political justice and the minimisation of inequalities is contained in:
15.x: Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order informed by justice and to minimise inequalities of income, status, facilities and opportunities.
15.tq: Distinguish the general welfare-and-inequality provision from the specific objectives listed in Article 39.
xs: **Article 38**: social order of **social, economic, political justice** and **minimising inequalities** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 39** is livelihood, resources, equal pay; **Art. 41** is right to work; **Art. 46** is SC/ST/weaker sections.
xa: **38(2)** (minimise inequalities) was added by the **44th Amendment, 1978**.
Art. 38 is grouped as a **Socialist** principle.

15.s: Which of the following Directive Principles is specifically concerned with workers’ participation in the management of industries?
15.x: Article 43A directs the State to secure workers’ participation in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in industry.
15.tq: Use the lettered Article sequence to distinguish 43A from the adjacent Articles 43 and 43B.
xs: **Article 43A** = **workers' participation in management** of industries — option **(2)**.
**43B** = **co-operative societies**; **43** = **living wage**, **cottage industries**; **42** = **maternity relief**.
xa: 43A was added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
43B was added by the **97th Amendment, 2011**.
43A is a **Socialist** principle; 43B is **Gandhian**.

15.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 43B deals with the promotion of co-operative societies.
2. Article 44 deals with a Uniform Civil Code for citizens.
3. Article 45 presently relates to free and compulsory education for all children up to fourteen years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. After the 86th Amendment, Article 45 concerns early childhood care and education for children until they complete six years; education for children aged six to fourteen is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.
15.tq: Use the amendment-based distinction between the original Article 45 and its present text.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: **43B** = **co-operative societies**.
Statement 2 — correct: **44** = **Uniform Civil Code**.
Statement 3 — wrong: since the **86th Amendment (2002)**, **Art. 45** = **early childhood care till 6**; 6-14 is an FR under **Art. 21A**.
xa: ⚠ IYB **2026** still gives the original Art. 45 ("free and compulsory education up to **14**").
First State UCC: **Uttarakhand**; second: **Gujarat**.

15.s:
Match List-I (Directive) with List-II (Article):
List-I
a. Agriculture and animal husbandry on scientific lines; ban on slaughter of cows and calves
b. Protection of monuments and places of national importance
c. Separation of the judiciary from the executive
d. International peace and security, respect for international law
List-II
i. Article 49
ii. Article 51
iii. Article 48
iv. Article 50
Select the correct answer using the code below.
15.x: Agriculture and cow slaughter = Art. 48 (iii), monuments = Art. 49 (i), separation of judiciary = Art. 50 (iv), international peace = Art. 51 (ii), so A is correct. B swaps 48 with 49 and 50 with 51. C swaps 49 and 50. D swaps 48 and 50.
15.tq: 48 farm, 49 monuments, 50 judiciary, 51 world peace - in order.
xs: **48** — scientific agriculture, cow slaughter; **49** — monuments; **50** — **separation of judiciary**; **51** — international peace: option **(1) a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii**.
Arts. **49, 50, 51** and **48** are all in the **Liberal-intellectual** group.
xa: ⚠ **48** is both **Gandhian** and **Liberal-intellectual**.
**48A** (environment) added by the **42nd, 1976**.
Heritage link: **Art. 49** and FD **51A(f)**.

15.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 39(d) — equal pay; Article 41 — right to work and public assistance
Article 39(d) — prevention of concentration of wealth; Article 41 — distribution of material resources
Article 39(d) — social order based on justice; Article 41 — equal pay
Article 39(d) — public assistance; Article 41 — protection of community resources
15.x: Article 39(d) concerns equal pay for equal work, while Article 41 concerns the right to work and public assistance in specified circumstances.
15.tq: Start from the familiar equal-pay provision and pair it with the correct allied Article.
xs: **39(d)** = **equal pay for equal work**; **41** = **right to work**, education, **public assistance** — option **(1)**.
**Concentration of wealth** is **39(c)**; **material resources** is **39(b)**; a **social order based on justice** is **Art. 38**.
xa: Art. 41's public assistance covers **unemployment, old age, sickness, disablement**.
**MGNREGA (2005)** made right to work a legal right; now replaced by the **VB-G RAM G Act**.
**K.T. Shah** wanted the right to work as an FR.

15.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Article)
 a. Article 41
 b. Article 43
 c. Article 45
 d. Article 47

List-II (Directive)
 i. Nutrition, public health and prohibition of intoxicating drinks
 ii. Living wage and decent standard of life
 iii. Right to work, education and public assistance
 iv. Early childhood care and education up to six years
15.x: Article 41 concerns work, education and public assistance; Article 43 concerns living wage and decent living standards; Article 45 concerns early childhood care up to six years; and Article 47 concerns nutrition, public health and prohibition.
15.tq: Start with the sure pair Article 45–early childhood care and eliminate codes around it.
xs: **41** — right to work; **43** — **living wage**; **45** — **early childhood care up to 6**; **47** — **nutrition, public health, prohibition**: option **(1) a–iii, b–ii, c–iv, d–i**.
Art. 41 also covers **public assistance** in unemployment, old age, sickness, disablement.
xa: Art. 45 was substituted by the **86th Amendment (2002)**.
Art. 47 is in both **Socialist** and **Gandhian** groups.
Art. 47 → **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** and prohibition laws.

15.s:
Match List-I (Directive) with List-II (Article):
List-I
a. Equal justice and free legal aid
b. Organisation of village panchayats
c. Living wage and promotion of cottage industries
d. Uniform Civil Code for citizens
List-II
i. Article 40
ii. Article 44
iii. Article 39A
iv. Article 43
Select the correct answer using the code below.
15.x: Free legal aid is Article 39A (iii), village panchayats Article 40 (i), living wage and cottage industries Article 43 (iv), and the UCC Article 44 (ii), so the first code is right. The second swaps 39A and 40. The third swaps 40 and 43. The fourth swaps 39A and 44.
15.tq: 39A (free legal aid) was tested in APPSC GS 2024, and it was added by the 42nd Amendment.
xs: **39A** — free legal aid; **40** — **village panchayats**; **43** — living wage, **cottage industries**; **44** — **UCC**: option **(1) a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii**.
Art. 43 is **Gandhian** and **Socialist**; Art. 44 is **Liberal-intellectual**.
xa: **39A** was added by the **42nd, 1976**; APPSC GS **2024** tested it.
Art. 40 → **73rd Amendment, 1992** (Panchayati Raj).
Art. 39A → **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.

15.s: Article 39(a) of the Constitution directs the State to secure:
o: The right to work in every circumstance
Free legal aid to economically weaker citizens
Equal pay for equal work for men and women
Adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally
15.x: Article 39(a) directs the State to secure adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally. Equal pay for equal work is contained in Article 39(d).
15.tq: Discriminate between neighbouring clauses of the same Article.
xs: **39(a)**: **adequate means of livelihood** for men and women **equally** — option **(4)**.
**Equal pay** is **39(d)**; **free legal aid** is **39A**; **right to work** is **Art. 41**.
xa: **39(b)**: material resources for the **common good**; **39(c)**: no **concentration of wealth**.
Dignity of women links **39(a), (d), (e), 42** with FD **51A(e)**.

15.s: The protection of children against exploitation and moral or material abandonment, along with development in freedom and dignity, is provided under:
15.x: Article 39(f) directs that children should develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity, and be protected against exploitation and abandonment. The present wording was introduced through the 42nd Amendment.
15.tq: Identify the exact sub-clause by its distinctive subject matter.
xs: **Article 39(f)**: children to develop in **freedom and dignity**, protected from **exploitation** and **moral/material abandonment** — option **(4)**.
39(f) was added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
**39(d)** = equal pay; **39(e)** = health of workers and children; **39(c)** = concentration of wealth.
xa: The 42nd also added **39A, 43A, 48A**.
Education of children: **Art. 45** (below 6), FR **21A**, FD **51A(k)**.

15.s:
With reference to Article 39, consider the following statements:
1. Clause (d) deals with equal pay for equal work for men and women.
2. Clause (e) seeks to protect the health and strength of workers.
3. Clause (e) permits employment of children in unsuitable work when economic necessity exists.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 39(e) seeks to prevent persons from being forced by economic necessity into work unsuited to their age or strength; it does not permit such employment.
15.tq: Find the statement that reverses the protective purpose of a constitutional clause.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: **39(d)** = **equal pay for equal work**.
Statement 2 — correct: **39(e)** protects the **health and strength of workers**.
Statement 3 — wrong: 39(e) says **no one forced by economic necessity** into unsuited work.
xa: 39(e) also protects the **tender age of children** from abuse.
**39(f)**: children's development in freedom and dignity.

15.s: Which one of the following correctly states the subject matter of Articles 39(b) and 39(c)?
o: 39(b): distribution of community resources for the common good; 39(c): prevention of concentration of wealth and means of production
39(b): protection of monuments; 39(c): promotion of international peace
39(b): right to work; 39(c): free legal aid
15.x: Article 39(b) concerns distribution of material resources of the community to subserve the common good, while Article 39(c) seeks to prevent concentration of wealth and means of production.
15.tq: Discriminate between neighbouring Directive Principles by their exact constitutional wording.
xs: **39(b)**: **material resources** distributed for the **common good**; **39(c)**: no **concentration of wealth** and means of production — option **(1)**.
APPSC G2 **2025**: both statements are in the Constitution.
xa: Implemented by **land reforms**, **zamindari abolition**, **ceiling laws**.
**Monuments** = **Art. 49**; **international peace** = **Art. 51**; **equal pay** = **39(d)**.

15.s: Which one of the following correctly matches the constitutional provision with its nature?
o: Article 24 — Directive Principle of State Policy
Article 39(f) — Directive Principle of State Policy
Article 21A — Directive Principle of State Policy
15.x: Article 39(f) is a Directive Principle of State Policy. Articles 24 and 21A are Fundamental Rights, while Article 39(e) is also a Directive Principle.
15.tq: Use the Fundamental Right–DPSP distinction to eliminate swapped classifications.
xs: **Art. 39(f)** is a **Directive Principle of State Policy** — option **(3)**.
**39(e)** is also a DPSP, not a Fundamental Right — option (2) wrong.
**Art. 21A** (education 6-14) is a **Fundamental Right** — option (4) wrong.
xa: 39(f) was added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
**Art. 21A** came with the **86th Amendment (2002)**.

15.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the classification of Directive Principles is correct?
o: The Constitution expressly divides them into Socialist, Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual categories.
The classification was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment.
The classification into Socialist, Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual principles is an academic arrangement.
The Supreme Court alone has classified them into three categories in Part IV.
15.x: The Constitution does not itself classify the Directive Principles. The classification into Socialist, Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual categories is an academic arrangement used for study.
15.tq: Distinguish constitutional text from an academic classification.
xs: The **Socialist, Gandhian, Liberal-intellectual** classification is an **academic** grouping — option **(3)**.
The **Constitution itself does not classify** them — options (1), (2), (4) wrong.
xa: ⚠ **43** and **47** are both Socialist and Gandhian; **48** both Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual.
**43B** is classed as **Gandhian**.

15.s:
Which of the following Articles are generally grouped under the Socialist principles of the Directive Principles?
1. Article 38
2. Article 39A
3. Article 43B
4. Article 47
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
15.x: Articles 38, 39A and 47 are generally grouped under the Socialist principles. Article 43B, relating to co-operative societies, is grouped under the Gandhian category.
15.tq: Use a nearby-category swap as the principal trap.
xs: **38, 39A, 47** are Socialist — option **(1) 1, 2 and 4 only**.
**43B** (co-operatives) is **Gandhian**, not Socialist.
xa: Liberal-intellectual: **44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51**.

15.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of Articles generally classified as Gandhian principles?
15.x: Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46 are generally included among Gandhian principles. The other sets contain Socialist or Liberal-intellectual principles.
15.tq: Classify by the group as a whole and eliminate mixed sets.
xs: **Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46** are all **Gandhian** — option **(1)**.
**44, 45, 48A, 50** and **49, 50, 51** are **Liberal-intellectual**; **38, 39, 41, 42** are **Socialist**.
xa: 40 = panchayats; 43 = **cottage industries**; 43B = co-operatives; 46 = **SC/ST/weaker sections**.
47 (prohibition) and 48 (cow slaughter) are also Gandhian.

15.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 43B — Separation of judiciary from executive
15.x: Article 43B concerns the promotion of co-operative societies and is generally classified as a Gandhian principle. Separation of the judiciary from the executive is provided in Article 50.
15.tq: Find the wrong person-or-provision pairing among closely related entries.
xs: **Art. 43B — Separation of judiciary** is wrong: **43B** = **co-operative societies**; separation is **Art. 50** — option **(1)**.
**49** monuments, **48A** environment, **44** UCC are correct.
xa: 43B came by the **97th Amendment, 2011**.
Art. 50 is **Liberal-intellectual**; 43B is **Gandhian**.

15.s:
Arrange the following Gandhian Directive Principle subjects in ascending order of their constitutional Articles:
A. Prohibition of intoxicating drinks
B. Village panchayats
C. Ban on slaughter of cows and milch cattle
D. Interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections
15.x: The relevant order is Article 40 (village panchayats), Article 46 (weaker sections), Article 47 (prohibition) and Article 48 (cattle protection).
15.tq: Convert the Article numbers into an ascending sequence.
xs: Ascending order: **40** panchayats → **46** SC/ST → **47** prohibition → **48** cow slaughter — option **(1) B, D, A, C**.
All four are in the **Gandhian** group (**40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48**).
xa: **43** (cottage industries) and **43B** (co-operatives) are also Gandhian.
Art. 40 → **73rd Amendment, 1992**.

15.s:
Arrange the following constitutional amendments in chronological order according to their changes relating to the Directive Principles:
A. Addition of Article 43B concerning co-operative societies
B. Substitution of Article 45 concerning early childhood care and education
C. Addition of Article 39A, Article 43A and Article 48A
D. Addition of Article 38(2) concerning minimisation of inequalities
15.x: The 42nd Amendment made the changes in C in 1976, the 44th Amendment made the change in D in 1978, the 86th Amendment changed Article 45 in 2002, and the 97th Amendment added Article 43B in 2011.
15.tq: Fix the 42nd Amendment as the starting point and then place the later amendments by year.
xs: Order to remember: **42nd → 44th → 86th → 97th**.
xa: APPSC G1 **2024** asked two chronology questions on these four.
The 42nd also added **39(f)**.

15.s:
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 added which of the following to the Directive Principles?
1. Article 39A relating to equal justice and free legal aid
2. Article 43A relating to workers’ participation in management
3. Article 48A relating to environment, forests and wildlife
4. Article 38(2) relating to minimisation of inequalities
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
15.x: The 42nd Amendment added Articles 39A, 43A and 48A, as well as Article 39(f). Article 38(2) was added by the 44th Amendment in 1978.
15.tq: Separate the major cluster of additions made by the 42nd Amendment from the later 44th Amendment change.
xs: The **42nd (1976)** added **39A, 43A, 48A** — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**38(2)** came by the **44th Amendment, 1978**.
xa: The 42nd also added **39(f)** (children's development).
**43B** came by the **97th (2011)**; Art. 45 substituted by the **86th (2002)**.

15.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with the amendment that introduced or changed the Directive Principle?
1. Article 38(2) — 44th Amendment
2. Article 43B — 97th Amendment
3. Article 45 in its present early-childhood-care form — 86th Amendment
15.x: All three pairs are correct: Article 38(2) was added in 1978, Article 43B in 2011, and the present Article 45 was substituted in 2002.
15.tq: Verify each amendment–provision pair independently before selecting the combined code.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
xa: 86th also linked to **Art. 21A** and **51A(k)**.

15.s: Which of the following correctly describes Article 45 after the constitutional changes relating to education?
o: It provides for mother-tongue instruction to linguistic minorities.
It makes education from six to fourteen years a Fundamental Duty of the State.
It directs the State to provide early childhood care and education for children below six years of age.
It deals with free legal aid for all citizens.
15.x: Article 45 directs the State to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years of age. Article 21A deals with the Fundamental Right to education for children aged six to fourteen years, while Article 51A(k) is the related Fundamental Duty.
15.tq: Separate the age groups and distinguish DPSP, Fundamental Right and Fundamental Duty provisions.
xs: **Art. 45** now directs **early childhood care and education** for children **below six** — option **(3)**.
Since the **86th Amendment (2002)**, education for **6-14** is an FR under **Art. 21A**.
**Free legal aid** is **Art. 39A** — option (4) wrong.
xa: Education link: Art. 45, FR **21A**, FD **51A(k)**.
**RTE Act, 2009** Sec. **3**: free education **6-14** in a neighbourhood school.

15.s: Which Directive Principle is specifically concerned with maternity relief?
15.x: Article 42 directs the State to make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief.
15.tq: Match the welfare measure with its exact Article.
xs: **Article 42** deals with **maternity relief** — option **(1)**.
**40** = panchayats; **43B** = co-operatives; **39A** = free legal aid.
xa: Art. 42 links to **labour laws**.
Art. 42 is also part of the **dignity of women** theme with FD **51A(e)**.
Art. 42 is a **Socialist** principle.

15.s:
Consider the following statements regarding directives outside Part IV:
1. Article 335 deals with the claims of SCs and STs to services, consistent with the efficiency of administration.
2. Article 351 deals with the development of Hindi as a medium for the composite culture of India.
3. Being outside Part IV, these directives are enforceable by courts.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: Statement 1 is correct: Art. 335 covers SC/ST claims to services. Statement 2 is correct: Art. 351 covers development of Hindi. Statement 3 is wrong: these directives are non-justiciable like Part IV, though outside it. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
15.tq: Outside Part IV but still non-justiciable: 335, 351.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: **Art. 335** — SC/ST claims to services, consistent with **efficiency of administration**.
Statement 2 — correct: **Art. 351** — development of **Hindi** for the **composite culture**.
Statement 3 — wrong: they are **non-justiciable** like Part IV.
xa: DPSPs in Part IV span **Art. 36-51**.
**Art. 37** bars courts from enforcing Part IV.

15.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the relationship between Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties?
o: Fundamental Duties are enforceable in the same manner as Fundamental Rights.
Environmental protection, heritage, education and women’s dignity are themes reflected in both sets of provisions.
The common themes are confined to Articles 39(b) and 39(c).
Every Directive Principle has an identical Fundamental Duty corresponding to it.
15.x: Several themes, including environmental protection, heritage, education and women’s dignity, appear in both the Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties, though the corresponding provisions are not always identical.
15.tq: Reject absolute wording and identify the carefully stated comparison.
xs: **Environment, heritage, education** and **women's dignity** appear in both DPSPs and Fundamental Duties — option **(2)**.
xa: Fraternity: Preamble and duty **51A(e)**.
Free legal aid **39A** links to FR **Art. 14, 22(1)**.

15.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Heritage and monuments — Article 49 and Article 51A(f)
2. Education of children — Article 45 and Article 51A(k)
3. Dignity of women — Article 39 and Article 51A(e)
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
15.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. Article 49 corresponds to heritage and monuments, Article 45 to early childhood care and education, and Article 39 along with Article 42 to women’s dignity and protection, complemented by Article 51A(e).
15.tq: Test parallel coverage of a subject under DPSP and Fundamental Duties.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Heritage — **49** & **51A(f)**; education — **45** & **51A(k)**; dignity of women — **39** & **51A(e)**.
xa: Environment — **48A** & FD **51A(g)**.
Education also links to FR **Art. 21A**.
Maternity relief — **Art. 42**.

15.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding constitutional directives and their implementation:

List-I (Directive)
a. Articles 39(b) and 39(c)
b. Article 40
c. Article 39A
d. Article 41

List-II (Implementation)
i. MGNREGA, 2005
 ii. Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
 iii. Land reforms and ceiling laws
 iv. 73rd Constitutional Amendment, 1992

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
15.x: Articles 39(b) and 39(c) are implemented through land reforms and related laws; Article 40 through the 73rd Amendment; Article 39A through the Legal Services Authorities Act; and Article 41 through MGNREGA.
15.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes with mismatched implementation measures.
xs: **39(b),(c)** — land reforms; **40** — **73rd Amendment, 1992**; **39A** — **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**; **41** — **MGNREGA, 2005**: option **(1) a–iii, b–iv, c–ii, d–i**.
The **73rd Amendment** gave panchayats **constitutional status** (Part IX).
xa: Legal Services Act in force **9 Nov 1995** (National Legal Services Day).
MGNREGA is now replaced by the **VB-G RAM G Act**.

15.s:
Consider the following pairs:

1. Articles 45 and 21A — Right to Education Act, 2009
2. Article 47 — Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 and public health schemes
3. Article 48A — Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
15.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. The Right to Education Act implements the educational guarantee, Article 47 is reflected in public health measures including mental healthcare, and Article 48A is supported by wildlife and environmental legislation.
15.tq: Check each directive against the implementing legislation before selecting the combined code.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**45/21A** — **RTE Act, 2009**; **47** — **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017**; **48A** — **Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972**, **Environment (Protection) Act 1986**.
xa: **44** → State UCCs: **Uttarakhand** (first), **Gujarat** (second).
**Art. 47** → prohibition laws.

15.s:
With reference to land reforms and Directive Principles, consider the following statements:

1. The First Constitutional Amendment, 1951, introduced the Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A and 31B.
2. The constitutional amendments associated with Article 39 included the 4th, 17th, 25th, 42nd and 44th Amendments.
3. The Ninth Schedule was created by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Ninth Schedule was introduced by the First Amendment, not the 73rd Amendment; the 73rd Amendment dealt with Panchayati Raj.
15.tq: Spot the swapped amendment by matching each amendment with its constitutional subject.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: the **1st Amendment (1951)** gave the **Ninth Schedule, Arts 31A, 31B**.
Statement 2 — correct: then the **4th, 17th, 25th, 42nd, 44th** Amendments.
Statement 3 — wrong: the **73rd (1992)** gave **Panchayati Raj** (Art. 40), not the Ninth Schedule.
xa: Land reforms implement **39(b), (c)**: zamindari abolition, ceiling laws.
The 73rd gave panchayats **constitutional status** under **Art. 40**.

15.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987:
1. It implements Article 39A.
2. It came into force on 9 November 1995, observed as National Legal Services Day.
3. Under it, DLSAs function at the national level and NALSA at the district level.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Act implements Art. 39A (free legal aid). Statement 2 is correct: it came into force on 9 November 1995. Statement 3 is wrong: the structure is NALSA (national), SLSAs (State) and DLSAs (district). So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
15.tq: Act 1987, in force 9 Nov 1995; NALSA-SLSA-DLSA from top down.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: it implements **Art. 39A**.
Statement 2 — correct: in force **9 Nov 1995** — **National Legal Services Day**.
Statement 3 — wrong: the chain is **NALSA → SLSAs → DLSAs** (national → state → district).
xa: Legal aid under 39A remains **underfunded** (Aug **2025**).
39A links to FR **Art. 14** and **22(1)** (right to counsel).

15.s:
With reference to the present position concerning employment under Article 41, consider the following statements:

1. MGNREGA, 2005, has since been replaced by the VB-GRAM G Act.
2. A sharp fall in employment under the VB-GRAM G Act has revived the debate on the right to work.
3. The replacement of MGNREGA has converted the right to work into a Fundamental Right.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: the right to work remains associated with Article 41, a Directive Principle, and has not thereby become a Fundamental Right.
15.tq: Reject the overstatement that changes a legal right under a programme into a Fundamental Right.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: **MGNREGA (2005)** has been replaced by the **VB-G RAM G Act**.
Statement 2 — correct: employment fell sharply, reviving the **right-to-work** debate (**1 Sep 2026**).
Statement 3 — wrong: right to work stays under **Art. 41** (DPSP); MGNREGA had made it only a **legal right**.
xa: **K.T. Shah** wanted the right to work as an FR; debate with **Ambedkar** in the CA.
Art. 41 also covers education and **public assistance**.

15.s: Under Section 3 of the Right to Education Act, 2009, free education is provided to children in which age group?
15.x: Section 3 of the Right to Education Act, 2009, provides free education for children from six to fourteen years of age in a neighbourhood school.
15.tq: Focus on the exact statutory age range rather than the broader constitutional education objective.
xs: **RTE Act, 2009**, Sec. **3**: free education for **six to fourteen** years in a neighbourhood school — option **(4)**.
6-14 is an FR under **Art. 21A**; below 6 falls under **Art. 45**.
xa: Art. 45 was substituted by the **86th Amendment (2002)**.
FD **51A(k)** concerns education of children.

15.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 47 — Prohibition laws and public health measures
Article 43 — Labour laws concerning living conditions and wages
Article 42 — Labour laws and maternity-related provisions
15.x: Article 48A is implemented through environmental and forest-protection laws. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, is associated with Article 39A.
15.tq: Find the pair whose implementing legislation belongs to a different Directive Principle.
xs: **Art. 48A — Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** is wrong — option **(1)**.
The Legal Services Act implements **Art. 39A**; **48A** is implemented by **Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972** and **Environment (Protection) Act 1986**.
Correct: **47** → prohibition laws; **42/43** → labour laws.
xa: 48A (environment) was added by the **42nd, 1976**.
Environment duty: FD **51A(g)**.

15.s: Which State was the first in India to adopt a State-level Uniform Civil Code?
15.x: Uttarakhand was the first State identified as adopting a State-level Uniform Civil Code. Gujarat was identified as the second State in this context.
15.tq: Distinguish the first State from the later State associated with the same reform.
xs: **Uttarakhand** was the first State with a State UCC — option **(2)**.
**Gujarat** is the second (**UCC Bill 2026**).
**Goa** follows the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867** — not a State-adopted UCC.
xa: **Art. 44** = UCC for citizens.
**Pavini Shukla (2026)**: SC suggested a UCC to end gender discrimination in personal laws.

15.s: Goa’s civil-law system is based on which of the following?
o: The Uniform Civil Code enacted by Parliament
15.x: Goa follows the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867, making it a distinctive example in discussions concerning a Uniform Civil Code under Article 44.
15.tq: Use the jurisdiction–legal code association to distinguish Goa from proposed State UCCs.
xs: Goa follows the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867** — option **(2)**.
⚠ Goa's code dates from **1867**; the first State UCC was **Uttarakhand**, then **Gujarat**.
xa: **Art. 44** directs a **Uniform Civil Code**.
⚠ State UCC: **Uttarakhand** first, **Gujarat** second.
**22nd Law Commission** sought views (**2022**).

15.s:
With reference to the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code Bill, 2026, consider the following statements:
1. Gujarat is the second State, after Uttarakhand, to move a State-level UCC.
2. It provides for monogamy and equal inheritance.
3. Scheduled Tribes are brought fully within its scope.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: Statement 1 is correct: Uttarakhand was the first State and Gujarat the second. Statement 2 is correct: the Bill provides for monogamy, equal inheritance, marriage registration within 60 days and live-in registration within 30 days. Statement 3 is wrong because Scheduled Tribes are exempted. So 1 and 2 only is the answer.
15.tq: State UCCs: Uttarakhand first, Gujarat second; STs exempted.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: **Gujarat** is second after **Uttarakhand**.
Statement 2 — correct: **monogamy** and **equal inheritance**.
Statement 3 — wrong: **STs are exempted**.
xa: Marriage registration in **60** days; live-in in **30** days.
SC (**11 Mar 2026**): asked whether to defer to Parliament on **Art. 44**.

15.s: Which one of the following observations about the Directive Principles was made as an approving assessment rather than a criticism of their non-justiciable character?
o: They are no better than New Year's resolutions broken on the second of January.
They are a veritable dustbin of sentiments.
They constitute a novel feature of the Indian Constitution.
15.x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the Directive Principles as a “novel feature” of the Indian Constitution. The other observations are critical descriptions of their non-justiciable character.
15.tq: Separate the approving description from the cluster of critical remarks.
xs: Calling the DPSPs a **novel feature** of the Indian Constitution was an approving remark, made by **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**New Year's resolutions** broken on the **second of January** was **Nasiruddin**'s jibe, a criticism.
**Pious aspirations** (**Ivor Jennings**) and a **veritable dustbin of sentiments** (**T.T. Krishnamachari**) are also critical remarks.
Most critical remarks target the **non-justiciable** nature of DPSPs under **Art. 37**; Ambedkar's is the approving one.
xa: **K.T. Shah**: a **cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank**.
**K.C. Wheare**: a **manifesto of aims and aspirations**.
**Granville Austin**: FRs and DPSPs together are the **conscience of the Constitution**.
**Art. 37**: Part IV **shall not be enforceable by any court**, yet the principles are **fundamental in the governance of the country**.

15.s: The description of the Directive Principles as a “manifesto of aims and aspirations” is attributed to:
15.x: K.C. Wheare described the Directive Principles as a “manifesto of aims and aspirations.”
15.tq: Use a direct quotation-to-person attribution question.
xs: **K.C. Wheare** called the DPSPs a **manifesto of aims and aspirations** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**T.T. Krishnamachari** called them a **veritable dustbin of sentiments**.
**Granville Austin** called FRs and DPSPs together the **conscience of the Constitution**.
**Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** called them a **novel feature** — the approving remark.
xa: **Ivor Jennings**: **pious aspirations**.
**Nasiruddin**: no better than **New Year's resolutions** broken on **2 January**.
**K.T. Shah**: a **cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank**; he also wanted the **right to work** as an FR.
⚠ Critical remarks attack the **non-justiciable** character (**Art. 37**); Ambedkar's alone is praise.

15.s: Who characterised the Directive Principles as “pious aspirations”?
15.x: Ivor Jennings referred to the Directive Principles as “pious aspirations.”
15.tq: Discriminate between closely related critical descriptions and their speakers.
xs: **Ivor Jennings** characterised the DPSPs as **pious aspirations** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Nasiruddin** compared them to **New Year's resolutions** broken on the second of January.
**K.C. Wheare** called them a **manifesto of aims and aspirations**.
**Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** called them a **novel feature** of the Constitution.
xa: **T.T. Krishnamachari**: a **veritable dustbin of sentiments**.
**K.T. Shah**: a **cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank**.
**Granville Austin**: FRs + DPSPs = **conscience of the Constitution**.
DPSPs are borrowed from the **Irish Constitution of 1937**, which itself copied the idea from the **Spanish Constitution**.

15.s:
Match List-I (Person) with List-II (Description of the Directive Principles):
List-I
a. K.T. Shah
b. T.T. Krishnamachari
c. Nasiruddin
d. Granville Austin
List-II
i. A veritable dustbin of sentiments
ii. Conscience of the Constitution (with Fundamental Rights)
iii. A cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank
iv. New Year's resolutions broken on the second of January
Select the correct answer using the code below.
15.x: K.T. Shah called the DPSPs a cheque payable at the bank's convenience (iii). T.T. Krishnamachari called them a veritable dustbin of sentiments (i). Nasiruddin compared them to New Year's resolutions broken on 2 January (iv). Granville Austin called FRs and DPSPs together the conscience of the Constitution (ii). So the first code is right; the second swaps Shah and Krishnamachari, the third swaps Krishnamachari and Nasiruddin, and the fourth swaps Shah and Austin.
15.tq: Cheque = Shah, dustbin = TTK, New Year = Nasiruddin, conscience = Austin. Ambedkar's 'novel feature' is the only approving remark.
xs: The correct code is **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — option **(1)**.
**K.T. Shah** → **cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank** (iii); **T.T. Krishnamachari** → **veritable dustbin of sentiments** (i).
**Nasiruddin** → **New Year's resolutions** broken on the second of January (iv); **Granville Austin** → **conscience of the Constitution** (ii).
Option (2) swaps Shah and Krishnamachari; (3) swaps Krishnamachari and Nasiruddin; (4) swaps Shah and Austin.
xa: **K.C. Wheare**: a **manifesto of aims and aspirations**.
**Ivor Jennings**: **pious aspirations**.
**Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**: a **novel feature** — the only approving remark.
K.T. Shah also wanted the **right to work** as an FR — debated against **Ambedkar** in the Constituent Assembly.

15.s:
Consider the following statements regarding recent Supreme Court developments on Article 44:
1. In Pavini Shukla v. Union of India (2026), the Supreme Court suggested a Uniform Civil Code to end gender discrimination in personal laws.
2. In March 2026, hearing a plea against Muslim inheritance law, a three-judge Bench considered deferring to Parliament on Article 44.
3. Article 44 is enforceable in court in the same way as a Fundamental Right.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: Statement 1 is correct: Pavini Shukla suggested a UCC to end gender discrimination. Statement 2 is correct: the March 2026 Bench considered deferring to Parliament on Art. 44. Statement 3 is wrong: Art. 44 is a DPSP with no legal force and is not enforceable like an FR. So A (misses 2), C and D (include 3) are wrong; B is correct.
15.tq: UCC = Art. 44, a DPSP; courts suggest, Parliament decides.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: in **Pavini Shukla v. Union of India (2026)** the SC suggested a **UCC** to end **gender discrimination** in personal laws (**Jun 2026**).
Statement 2 correct: a **3-judge** Bench (**11 Mar 2026**), hearing a plea against **Muslim inheritance law**, considered deferring to **Parliament** on Art. 44.
Statement 3 wrong: Art. 44 is a DPSP, and under **Art. 37** Part IV **shall not be enforceable by any court**.
xa: **Art. 44** directs a **Uniform Civil Code** for citizens; it is classed as **liberal-intellectual**.
State UCCs: **Uttarakhand** first, **Gujarat** second (**UCC Bill 2026**).
Gujarat UCC Bill 2026: monogamy, equal inheritance, marriage registration in **60 days**, live-in in **30 days**, **STs exempted**.
**Goa** follows the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867**; the **22nd Law Commission** sought views in **2022**.

15.s:
Which of the following is identified as a criticism or continuing concern regarding the Directive Principles of State Policy?

1. They have no direct legal force.
2. Their arrangement has been criticised as illogical.
3. Legal aid under Article 39A remains underfunded.
4. They have completely displaced Fundamental Rights.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
15.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 reflect identified criticisms or concerns. Statement 4 is false: the Directive Principles have not completely displaced Fundamental Rights.
15.tq: Reject the extreme claim in statement 4 and retain the specific criticisms supported by constitutional practice.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are criticisms or continuing concerns — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: DPSPs have **no legal force** (**Art. 37**).
Statement 2 correct: their **illogical arrangement** is a standard criticism, along with **conflict with FRs**.
Statement 3 correct: legal aid under **Art. 39A** remains **underfunded** (**Aug 2025**).
Statement 4 wrong: FRs and DPSPs are **complementary**, and their **balance** is part of the **Basic Structure** (**Minerva Mills, 1980**).
xa: Critics: **T.T. Krishnamachari** (**veritable dustbin of sentiments**), **K.T. Shah** (**cheque payable at the convenience of the bank**).
**Art. 39A** (equal justice and **free legal aid**) was added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.
Art. 39A is implemented through the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**, in force **9 Nov 1995** (**National Legal Services Day**).
Courts use **harmonious construction** and read many DPSPs into **Art. 21**.

15.s: The Directive Principles are significant primarily because they provide the constitutional basis for which of the following objectives?
o: Exclusive judicial control over public policy
A state without legislative responsibility for social welfare
A purely unitary system of government
A welfare state and social and economic democracy
15.x: The Directive Principles set the goal of a welfare state and provide a framework for social and economic democracy. They also form the basis of summaries of Part IV in the India Year Book.
15.tq: Choose the option that states the broad constitutional purpose without introducing an unrelated structural claim.
xs: DPSPs set the goal of a **welfare state** — **social and economic democracy** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They are a **positive** obligation on the State: it has a **duty** to apply them in making laws, so (2) is wrong.
Being **non-justiciable** (**Art. 37**), they give courts no exclusive control over policy, so (1) is wrong.
xa: Welfare state: "**The State is everywhere: it leaves hardly a gap**" (**JPSC 2016** key).
Art. 38 directs a social order of **social, economic, political justice** and to **minimise inequalities**.
**38(2)** (minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities, opportunities) was added by the **44th Amendment (1978)**.
Indian roots: **Karachi Resolution (1931)**, **Nehru Report (1928)**, **Gandhian ideals**, **Instrument of Instructions** (**GoI Act 1935**), **Sapru Committee (1945)**.

15.s: The debate over the right to work as a Fundamental Right versus a Directive Principle was associated in the Constituent Assembly with which pair?
o: K. T. Shah and B. R. Ambedkar
Rajendra Prasad and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar
N. Rau and K. M. Munshi
15.x: The Constituent Assembly debate on whether the right to work should be a Fundamental Right or remain a Directive Principle involved K. T. Shah and B. R. Ambedkar.
15.tq: Match the constitutional debate with the specific participants named in it.
xs: The right-to-work debate (FR vs DPSP) in the Constituent Assembly was between **K.T. Shah** and **B.R. Ambedkar** — option **(1)**.
**K.T. Shah** wanted the **right to work** as an FR; it stayed a directive under **Art. 41**.
K.T. Shah also called the DPSPs a **cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank**.
xa: **Art. 41**: right to **work**, education, public assistance (unemployment, old age, sickness, disablement).
**MGNREGA (2005)** made the right to work a legal right; since replaced by the **VB-G RAM G Act**.
The fall in rural work under the **VB-GRAM G Act** revived the right-to-work debate (**1 Sep 2026**).
⚠ Ambedkar called the DPSPs a **novel feature**; Shah's remark was critical.

16.s:
Consider the following statements comparing Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles:
1. Fundamental Rights are mostly negative, restraining the State, whereas Directive Principles are positive directions to the State.
2. Fundamental Rights aim mainly at social and economic democracy, whereas Directive Principles aim mainly at political democracy.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 1 is correct: FRs are mostly negative (restrain the State) and DPSPs positive (direct the State). Statement 2 is wrong because it reverses the aims: FRs aim at political democracy and individual welfare, DPSPs at social and economic democracy and community welfare. So only 1 is correct; 'both' and '2 only' accept the reversed statement, and 'neither' rejects a true one.
16.tq: FR = negative, political democracy; DPSP = positive, social-economic democracy.
xs: Only **statement 1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: FRs are mostly **negative** (restrain the State); DPSPs are **positive** (direct the State).
Statement 2 wrong — it reverses the aims: FRs aim at **political democracy** (individual welfare), DPSPs at **social and economic democracy** (community welfare).
xa: Justiciability: FRs (**Part III**, Arts **12-35**) are **justiciable**; DPSPs (**Part IV**, Arts **36-51**) are **non-justiciable** (**Art. 37**).
Main difference (**UPSC 2009**): DPSPs are **not enforceable** in courts, FRs are.
Sources: FRs from the **USA**, DPSPs from **Ireland**.
Legal status: FRs are **superior**, but DPSPs are **fundamental in governance**.

16.s: A law violating a Fundamental Right and a law violating a Directive Principle have which respective legal consequences?
o: The former may be void under Article 13, while the latter cannot be struck down merely for violating a Directive Principle
The former cannot be examined by courts, while the latter is void under Article 37
Both laws are automatically void under Article 13
Both laws are immune from judicial review
16.x: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void to the extent of inconsistency. Courts cannot strike down a law solely because it violates a Directive Principle.
16.tq: Apply the constitutional consequence separately to an enforceable right and a non-justiciable directive.
xs: A law violating an FR may be **void under Article 13**, but a law **cannot be struck down** merely for violating a DPSP — option **(1)**.
DPSPs are **non-justiciable** under **Art. 37**, so (2) is wrong: Art. 37 does not make laws void.
(3) and (4) are wrong: only FR-violating laws are void; such laws are open to **judicial review**.
xa: FRs are mostly **negative** obligations; DPSPs **positive** directions to the State.
FRs aim at **political democracy**; DPSPs at **social and economic democracy**.
**Harmonious construction**: read Part III and Part IV **together** so both operate (**Kerala Education Bill, 1958**; **Minerva Mills, 1980**).

16.s: With reference to the constitutional status of Directive Principles, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: They are legally superior to all Fundamental Rights in every circumstance
They are enforceable only during a national emergency
They have no constitutional significance because Article 37 excludes them from governance
They are not enforceable in courts but are fundamental in the governance of the country
16.x: Directive Principles are non-justiciable, but Article 37 declares them fundamental in the governance of the country and makes it the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.
16.tq: Avoid the trap of equating non-enforceability with lack of constitutional importance.
xs: DPSPs are **not enforceable in courts** but are **fundamental in the governance** of the country — option **(4)**.
**Art. 37** bars court enforcement, yet declares them fundamental in governance, so (3) is wrong.
(1) is wrong: FRs are legally **superior**; DPSPs are **non-justiciable**.
xa: Main difference (**UPSC 2009**): DPSPs are **not enforceable** in courts, FRs are.
Relationship: **complementary, not competing** — an **integrated scheme**.
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: **balance** between Parts III and IV is part of the **Basic Structure**.

16.s: The statement “Fundamental Rights are the means and Directive Principles are the ends” signifies that
o: Fundamental Rights provide the framework through which the social and economic objectives of Directive Principles may be pursued
Directive Principles have no relationship with Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights may be suspended whenever a Directive Principle is invoked
Directive Principles are enforceable through the same remedies as Fundamental Rights
16.x: Fundamental Rights provide rights-based means, while Directive Principles express broader social and economic goals. The two are therefore to be understood together, not as competing constitutional compartments.
16.tq: Translate a constitutional maxim into its practical relationship between rights and goals.
xs: FRs provide the **framework (means)** through which the social and economic **objectives (ends)** of DPSPs are pursued — option **(1)**.
The notes describe FRs and DPSPs as **complementary, not competing** — an **integrated scheme** — so (2) is wrong.
DPSPs are **non-justiciable** (**Art. 37**), so they are not enforced through FR remedies — (4) is wrong.
xa: **Justice Chandrachud**: FRs and DPSPs together = the **conscience of the Constitution**.
**Harmonious construction**: give effect to both as far as possible (**Kerala Education Bill, 1958**).
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: absolute primacy to either Part destroys the **balance**, which is part of the **Basic Structure**.

16.s:
Which of the following illustrates the use of a Directive Principle as an interpretive aid to expand the content of a Fundamental Right?
1. Article 45 read with Article 21 contributed to the recognition of the Right to Education under Article 21A.
2. Article 48A read with Article 21 supports the right to a healthy environment.
3. Directive Principles are entirely excluded from constitutional interpretation because they are non-justiciable.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
16.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Courts have used Directive Principles to interpret and enrich Fundamental Rights; non-justiciability does not exclude them from constitutional interpretation.
16.tq: Distinguish non-enforceability from non-relevance in constitutional interpretation.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** illustrate DPSPs as interpretive aids — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Art. 45** led to **Art. 21A** — **Right to Education** (**86th Amendment, 2002**).
Statement 2 correct: **Art. 48A + Art. 21** = right to a **healthy environment**.
Statement 3 wrong: courts read Parts III and IV **together** (**harmonious construction**); non-justiciability does not exclude DPSPs from interpretation.
xa: Validity test for a DPSP law abridging FRs: the **basic structure** + **golden triangle** (Arts **14, 19, 21**).
FRs and DPSPs: **FRs are means, DPSPs are the ends**.
**Justice Chandrachud**: together they are the **conscience of the Constitution**.

16.s: In testing the validity of a law based on a Directive Principle but alleged to abridge Fundamental Rights, the relevant constitutional standard includes
o: the non-justiciability of Directive Principles alone
only Article 37, without reference to Fundamental Rights
only Article 32 and the Ninth Schedule
the basic structure doctrine and the golden triangle of Articles 14, 19 and 21
16.x: The validity of such a law is examined against the basic structure doctrine and, in particular, the constitutional guarantees represented by Articles 14, 19 and 21, known as the golden triangle.
16.tq: Apply the controlling constitutional test rather than treating a DPSP objective as conclusive.
xs: A DPSP law abridging FRs is tested against the **basic structure** and the **golden triangle** of Arts **14, 19 and 21** — option **(4)**.
DPSP non-justiciability or **Art. 37** alone is not the test, so (1) and (2) are wrong.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: even Ninth Schedule entries after **1973** fall if they damage the basic structure or the essence of Arts 14, 19, 21 — so (3) is wrong.
xa: **Minerva Mills (1980)**: **FR-DPSP balance** is part of the **Basic Structure**.
**Art. 31C** protects only **39(b)-(c)** laws against **Arts. 14 and 19** — narrow, not blanket, primacy.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: Ninth Schedule entries after **24 April 1973** are open to challenge.

16.s: Justice Chandrachud described Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles together as constituting the
16.x: Justice Chandrachud described Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles together as making up the conscience of the Constitution.
16.tq: Recall the distinctive judicial phrase attached to the combined constitutional role of Parts III and IV.
xs: **Justice Chandrachud** called FRs and DPSPs together the **conscience of the Constitution** — option **(3)**.
The two are **complementary, not competing** — "**FRs are means, DPSPs are the ends**".
xa: **Harmonious construction**: read Part III and Part IV **together** so both operate.
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: **harmony and balance** between Parts III and IV is part of the **Basic Structure**.
DPSPs as interpretive aids: **Art. 45 → Art. 21A** (**86th Amendment, 2002**); **Art. 48A + Art. 21** → healthy environment.

16.s: The right to a clean and pollution-free environment has been read by the Supreme Court into:
16.x: The Supreme Court has interpreted the right to life under Article 21 to include the right to a healthy, clean and pollution-free environment.
16.tq: Identify the constitutional article through the judicially expanded right rather than its literal wording alone.
xs: The right to a clean, healthy environment has been read into **Article 21** — option **(2)**.
It comes from reading the DPSP **Art. 48A** with **Art. 21** — a DPSP used as an **interpretive aid**.
xa: Likewise **Art. 45 → Art. 21A**: **Right to Education** (**86th Amendment, 2002**).
Art. 21 is part of the **golden triangle** (Arts **14, 19, 21**) used to test DPSP laws.
Courts use **harmonious construction** to read Parts III and IV together.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951):
1. It held that Fundamental Rights prevail and that DPSPs must conform to and run subsidiary to them.
2. It struck down a Madras communal order on admissions for violating Article 29(2).
3. It adopted harmonious construction under which DPSPs prevail over Fundamental Rights in case of conflict.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Champakam held FRs prevail with DPSPs subsidiary, and struck down the communal admissions order under Art. 29(2) (leading to Art. 15(4)). Statement 3 is wrong: harmonious construction came in In re Kerala Education Bill (1958), and even there FRs still prevail. So '1 only' misses a true statement, and the options containing 3 are wrong.
16.tq: Champakam = FRs prevail + communal G.O. + Art. 29(2); harmonious construction = Kerala Education Bill.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Champakam Dorairajan (1951)** held **FRs prevail**; DPSPs must conform to and run **subsidiary** to FRs.
Statement 2 correct: it struck down a **Madras communal order** on admissions for violating **Art. 29(2)**.
Statement 3 wrong: **harmonious construction** came in **In re Kerala Education Bill (1958)** — and even there FRs still prevailed.
xa: Champakam led to the **1st Amendment, 1951**, which inserted **Art. 15(4)**.
Champakam was the **first conflict case**; asked as "FR over DPSP in conflict" (**MPPSC 2024**).
Chronology: **Gopalan (1950) → Champakam (1951) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda (1973) → Minerva (1980)**.

16.s: In re Kerala Education Bill, 1958 is associated with which of the following approaches?
o: Harmonious construction, giving effect to both Fundamental Rights and DPSPs as far as possible
Parliament's inability to amend any Fundamental Right
Complete supremacy of DPSPs over Fundamental Rights
16.x: In re Kerala Education Bill adopted harmonious construction, requiring both Parts III and IV to be given effect as far as possible, while Fundamental Rights continued to prevail in case of direct conflict.
16.tq: Distinguish harmonious construction from either absolute rights supremacy or DPSP supremacy.
xs: **In re Kerala Education Bill (1958)** adopted **harmonious construction** — giving effect to both FRs and DPSPs as far as possible — option **(1)**.
FRs **still prevailed** in a conflict, so (4) is wrong.
"Parliament cannot amend FRs" (3) is **Golaknath (1967)**.
xa: **Champakam (1951)**, before it, held DPSPs **subsidiary** to FRs.
**Minerva Mills (1980)** later made **harmony and balance** part of the **Basic Structure**.
Harmonious construction treats FRs and DPSPs as **complementary, not competing**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967):
1. It held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights.
2. It applied the doctrine of prospective overruling.
3. It held that Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights but cannot alter the Basic Structure.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Golaknath gave FRs a 'transcendental' position, denied Parliament the power to amend them, and applied prospective overruling. Statement 3 is wrong: 'amendable but not the Basic Structure' is Kesavananda Bharati (1973). Hence '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' leaves out a true statement and the other options include statement 3.
16.tq: Golaknath = no amendment of FRs + prospective overruling; Basic Structure = Kesavananda.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Golaknath (1967)** held Parliament **cannot amend FRs**, giving them a **transcendental** position.
Statement 2 correct: it applied **prospective overruling**.
Statement 3 wrong: "amendable but not the **Basic Structure**" is **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.
xa: The **24th Amendment (1971)** answered Golaknath: Parliament can amend any part incl. FRs; added Art. **13(4)** and **368(3)**.
The 24th also made the **President's assent** mandatory.
Chronology: **Champakam (1951) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda (1973)**.

16.s:
With reference to Kesavananda Bharati, consider the following statements:
1. Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights.
2. Parliament cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution.
3. The judgment upheld the second provision of Article 31C excluding judicial review.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: Kesavananda Bharati held that Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights but could not destroy the basic structure. It struck down, rather than upheld, the second provision of Article 31C.
16.tq: Combine the basic-structure holding with the specific Article 31C ruling and identify the reversed statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2 correct: **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — Parliament **can amend FRs** but not the **Basic Structure**.
Statement 3 wrong: Kesavananda **struck down** the **second provision** of Art. 31C (bar on judicial review); it upheld the first.
xa: ⚠ Trap (**APPSC G1 2024**): "the first provision of 31C was invalidated in Kesavananda" is **wrong**.
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** responded to Kesavananda by extending 31C to **all DPSPs**.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: Ninth Schedule entries after **24 April 1973** (date of Kesavananda) are open to challenge.

16.s: The central constitutional principle laid down in Minerva Mills was that:
o: DPSPs have absolute primacy over Fundamental Rights.
Fundamental Rights have absolute primacy over DPSPs in every circumstance.
Harmony and balance between Parts III and IV form part of the basic structure.
Parliament has unlimited power to amend the Constitution.
16.x: Minerva Mills held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights in Part III and DPSPs in Part IV are part of the basic structure; absolute primacy to either would destroy that balance.
16.tq: Choose the balanced constitutional principle over extreme claims of absolute supremacy.
xs: **Minerva Mills (1980)** held that **harmony and balance** between Parts III and IV form part of the **basic structure** — option **(3)**.
Absolute primacy to **either** FRs or DPSPs destroys that balance — so (1) and (2) are wrong.
It struck down the **42nd Amendment**'s claim of **unlimited amending power** — so (4) is wrong.
xa: It also struck down the extension of **31C** to all DPSPs, restoring its **pre-1976** position (**39(b), (c)** only).
It held an **Emergency proclamation** is subject to **judicial review**.
**Sanjeev Coke (1983)** doubted Minerva's 31C ruling in **obiter**.

16.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Sanjeev Coke v. Bharat Coking Coal is correct?
o: It held that Parliament could never amend Fundamental Rights.
It struck down the nationalisation of coking coal under Article 39(b).
It upheld coking coal nationalisation under Article 39(b) and read material resources as including privately owned resources.
16.x: Sanjeev Coke upheld the coking coal nationalisation law under Article 39(b) and interpreted material resources as including privately owned resources. It also doubted the Minerva Mills Article 31C ruling in obiter.
16.tq: Match the case with its sector-specific ruling and its interpretation of material resources.
xs: **Sanjeev Coke v. Bharat Coking Coal (1983)** upheld **coking coal nationalisation** under **39(b)** / 31C and read **material resources** to include **privately owned resources** — option **(4)**.
It upheld (did not strike down) the nationalisation law, so (2) is wrong.
"Parliament can never amend FRs" (1) is **Golaknath (1967)**.
xa: It followed **Justice Krishna Iyer**'s minority view in **Ranganatha Reddy (1977)**.
It doubted **Minerva Mills**' 31C ruling (**obiter**).
⚠ **Property Owners Association (2024)**, **7:2**, held **not every** privately owned resource is a 39(b) material resource.

16.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Minerva Mills
B. A.K. Gopalan
C. Sanjeev Coke
D. Golaknath
E. State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
F. Kesavananda Bharati
o: B, E, D, F, A, C
E, B, D, F, C, A
B, D, E, F, A, C
B, E, F, D, A, C
16.x: The correct sequence is A.K. Gopalan (1950), Champakam Dorairajan (1951), Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), and Sanjeev Coke (1983).
16.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the intervening judgments by year.
xs: The order is **B, E, D, F, A, C** — option **(1)**.
**A.K. Gopalan (1950)** → **Champakam Dorairajan (1951)** → **Golaknath (1967)**.
→ **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** → **Minerva Mills (1980)** → **Sanjeev Coke (1983)**.
xa: **Gopalan**: narrow reading of FRs; court checks only procedure.
**Champakam**: FRs prevail; **Golaknath**: Parliament cannot amend FRs.
**Kesavananda**: Basic Structure; **Minerva**: FR-DPSP **balance** is Basic Structure.
**RPSC 2018** asked this chronology.

16.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in A.K. Gopalan (1950)?
o: It established harmony between Parts III and IV as basic structure.
It adopted a narrow reading of Fundamental Rights and examined only procedure.
It held that Fundamental Rights could never be amended.
16.x: A.K. Gopalan adopted a narrow reading of Fundamental Rights, with the Court examining only the prescribed procedure.
16.tq: Identify the earliest case's limited procedural approach before considering later doctrines.
xs: **A.K. Gopalan (1950)** took a **narrow reading of FRs**; the court checked **only procedure** — option **(2)**.
Harmony of Parts III and IV as basic structure (1) is **Minerva Mills (1980)**.
Upholding nationalisation under 39(b) (3) is **Sanjeev Coke (1983)**; FRs not amendable (4) is **Golaknath (1967)**.
xa: Gopalan heads the chronology: **Gopalan → Champakam → Golaknath → Kesavananda → Minerva Mills → Sanjeev Coke**.
**Champakam (1951)** followed a year later: **FRs prevail** over DPSPs.

16.s: Which one of the following Articles was inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, in response to the constitutional issue highlighted by the Champakam Dorairajan case?
16.x: In Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Supreme Court struck down a Madras communal order on admissions for violating Article 29(2). The First Amendment, 1951 responded by inserting Article 15(4), enabling special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs.
16.tq: Identify the precise constitutional provision associated with the judicial controversy.
xs: The **1st Amendment, 1951** inserted **Article 15(4)** in response to **Champakam Dorairajan** — option **(2)**.
Champakam struck down a **Madras communal order** on admissions for violating **Art. 29(2)**.
**Art. 31C** (4) came by the **25th Amendment (1971)**.
xa: Art. 15(4): special provisions for **socially and educationally backward classes**, **SCs**, **STs**.
The right changed was **Art. 15** (equality/non-discrimination), which overrode the Art. 29(2) bar.
The 1st Amendment also added **Arts 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule** — for land-reform laws.

16.s: The First Amendment inserted Article 15(4) primarily to enable special provisions for:
o: Government servants belonging to SCs only
16.x: Article 15(4), inserted by the First Amendment, permits special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes and for SCs and STs.
16.tq: Identify the beneficiary group rather than confusing Article 15(4) with political reservation.
xs: **Art. 15(4)** enables special provisions for **socially and educationally backward classes** (and **SCs, STs**) — option **(4)**.
It was inserted by the **1st Amendment, 1951** after **Champakam Dorairajan**.
It is not limited to religious minorities, SC government servants, or women and children.
xa: Champakam struck down a **Madras communal order** in admissions for violating **Art. 29(2)**.
Champakam = **first conflict case** → led to the **First Amendment**.
The **1st Amendment** was the first amendment responding to a court.

16.s:
With reference to the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, consider the following statements:
1. It inserted Article 15(4) in response to the Champakam Dorairajan judgment.
2. It added Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule.
3. Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule were the direct response to Champakam Dorairajan.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: Statement 1 is correct: Article 15(4) answered Champakam Dorairajan. Statement 2 is correct: the same Amendment added Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule. Statement 3 is wrong because those provisions shielded land-reform laws and answered the land-reform judgments, not Champakam. So 1 and 2 only is the answer.
16.tq: Champakam led to 15(4). Land-reform cases led to 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule. All were in the 1st Amendment.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Art. 15(4)** answered **Champakam Dorairajan**.
Statement 2 correct: the same Amendment added **Arts 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule**.
Statement 3 wrong: those protected **land-reform laws** and answered the **land-reform judgments**, not Champakam.
xa: ⚠ Some notes wrongly link 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule to Champakam.
The Ninth Schedule grew to **over 280 entries**.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: no blanket immunity — post-1973 entries fall if they damage the **Basic Structure**.

16.s: The Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1955 made which aspect non-justiciable?
o: The classification of privately owned material resources
The President's assent to constitutional amendments
16.x: The Fourth Amendment made the adequacy of compensation non-justiciable.
16.tq: Distinguish the subject of compensation adequacy from later changes replacing compensation with amount.
xs: The **4th Amendment (1955)** made the **adequacy of compensation** non-justiciable — option **(2)**.
The **24th Amendment (1971)** made the **President's assent** to amendments mandatory — not the 4th.
xa: **17th (1964)**: widened **estate** in 31A; land under personal cultivation acquired only at **market value**.
**25th (1971)**: **compensation** replaced by **amount**; inserted **Art. 31C**.
Land-reform amendments ran **1st → 4th → 17th → 25th → 42nd**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the Seventeenth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1964:
1. It widened the meaning of ‘estate’ under Article 31A.
2. It provided that land under personal cultivation could be acquired only at market value.
3. It inserted Article 31C.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: The Seventeenth Amendment widened ‘estate’ in Article 31A and dealt with land under personal cultivation. Article 31C was inserted later by the Twenty-fifth Amendment.
16.tq: Separate the land-reform changes of the Seventeenth Amendment from the later Article 31C amendment.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2 correct: the **17th Amendment (1964)** widened **estate** in **Art. 31A** and allowed land under **personal cultivation** to be acquired only at **market value**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Art. 31C** was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)**.
xa: **4th (1955)**: adequacy of compensation made **non-justiciable**.
**Art. 31A** came with the **1st Amendment (1951)**.
**26th (1971)**: abolished **privy purses**.

16.s: The Twenty-fourth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 was enacted in response to Golaknath and provided that:
o: The adequacy of compensation could be examined by courts.
Parliament could amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
Only DPSPs could be amended by Parliament.
16.x: The Twenty-fourth Amendment responded to Golaknath by affirming Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. It added Article 13(4) and Article 368(3), and made presidential assent mandatory.
16.tq: Link the amendment to the judgment it was intended to overcome and identify its broad power.
xs: The **24th Amendment (1971)** answered **Golaknath**: Parliament **can amend any part** of the Constitution, **including FRs** — option **(3)**.
It added Art. **13(4)** and **368(3)** and made the **President's assent** mandatory.
**Privy purses** (1) were abolished by the **26th Amendment (1971)**.
xa: **Golaknath (1967)** had held Parliament **cannot amend FRs** and applied **prospective overruling**.
**25th (1971)** answered **R.C. Cooper (1970)**: **amount** for compensation; **Art. 31C**.
**Kesavananda (1973)** then allowed amendment of FRs but not the **Basic Structure**.

16.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Twenty-fifth Amendment — inserted Article 31C and replaced ‘compensation’ by ‘amount’
Twenty-sixth Amendment — extended Article 31C to all DPSPs
16.x: The Twenty-fifth Amendment replaced ‘compensation’ by ‘amount’ and inserted Article 31C. The Twenty-fourth Amendment dealt with Parliament's amending power, the Twenty-sixth abolished privy purses, and the Forty-second extended Article 31C to all DPSPs.
16.tq: Start from the sure amendment-provision pair and reject swapped amendment responses.
xs: The **25th Amendment** inserted **Art. 31C** and replaced **compensation** by **amount** — option **(1)**.
The **24th** dealt with Parliament's power to amend FRs; the **26th** abolished **privy purses**.
The **42nd** extended 31C to all DPSPs; **Art. 15(4)** came by the **1st Amendment (1951)**.
xa: The 25th responded to the **Bank Nationalisation** case (**R.C. Cooper, 1970**).
Original 31C protected **39(b) and (c)** laws from **Arts 14, 19** (and 31).
**Kesavananda (1973)** struck down the **second provision** of 31C (bar on judicial review).

16.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched in relation to the Twenty-sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971?
o: Champakam case — extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs
Privy Purses case — abolition of privy purses and privileges of former rulers
Bank Nationalisation case — creation of the Ninth Schedule
16.x: The Twenty-sixth Amendment responded to the Privy Purses case associated with Madhav Rao Scindia and abolished privy purses and the privileges of former rulers.
16.tq: Match the case, amendment and constitutional consequence without swapping neighbouring historical responses.
xs: The **26th Amendment (1971)** answered the **Privy Purses** case (**Madhav Rao Scindia, 1970**) by abolishing **privy purses and privileges of former rulers** — option **(3)**.
31C extension to all DPSPs was the **42nd**; **Art. 15(4)** answered **Champakam**, not Golaknath.
The **Ninth Schedule** came with the **1st Amendment (1951)**; the **Bank Nationalisation** case (**R.C. Cooper, 1970**) led to the **25th**.
xa: **24th (1971)** answered **Golaknath**: Arts **13(4)** and **368(3)**.
The 24th, 25th and 26th Amendments all date to **1971**.

16.s:
With reference to the original Article 31C inserted by the Twenty-fifth Amendment, consider the following statements:
1. Laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) were protected from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
2. The protection also extended to Article 31.
3. A declaration by the law-making authority that the law gave effect to the relevant policy could not be questioned in court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: The original Article 31C contained both protections: specified laws were protected from Articles 14, 19 and 31 challenges, and the declaration that they implemented the policy was placed beyond judicial questioning.
16.tq: Separate the two limbs of Article 31C and check the additional protection against Article 31.
xs: All **three** statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statements 1 and 2: the original **Art. 31C** (**25th Amendment, 1971**) protected **39(b) and (c)** laws from **Arts 14, 19** (and **31**).
Statement 3: a law **declaring** it gives effect to that policy **could not be questioned** in court.
xa: **Kesavananda (1973)** upheld the first provision and struck down the **second** (the declaration / bar on judicial review).
**42nd (1976)** extended 31C to **any DPSP**; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck that down.
**Property Owners Association (2024)**: original 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda, **continues in force**.

16.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in Kesavananda Bharati relating to Article 31C?
o: The first provision was upheld and the second provision was struck down.
The first provision was struck down and the second provision was upheld.
Both provisions of Article 31C were struck down.
Both provisions were upheld without limitation.
16.x: Kesavananda Bharati upheld the first part of Article 31C but struck down the second part, which excluded judicial review.
16.tq: Distinguish the first and second provisions rather than treating Article 31C as a single indivisible rule.
xs: **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** upheld the **first provision** of Art. 31C and struck down the **second provision** — option **(1)**.
The second provision was the **bar on judicial review** — a law's **declaration** that it served 39(b)-(c) could not be questioned.
xa: ⚠ Trap (**APPSC G1 2024**): "first provision of 31C was invalidated in Kesavananda" is **wrong**.
Art. 31C was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)**.
The **42nd (1976)** extended 31C to **all DPSPs**; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck it down.

16.s: Which one of the following was the effect of the judgment in Minerva Mills on Article 31C?
o: The extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs was struck down, restoring its application to Articles 39(b) and 39(c).
Article 31C was extended to Fundamental Duties.
The bar on judicial review in the original Article 31C was restored.
16.x: Minerva Mills struck down the Forty-second Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs. Its protection consequently remained confined to laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c).
16.tq: Track what was struck down and what remained after the later judgment.
xs: **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down the **extension of 31C to all DPSPs**, restoring it to **39(b) and (c)** — option **(1)**.
31C returned to its **pre-1976** position; it was not repealed, so (2) is wrong.
The **bar on judicial review** had been struck down in **Kesavananda (1973)** and was not restored — (4) is wrong.
xa: The extension was made by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.
Minerva also held an **Emergency proclamation** is subject to **judicial review**.
Scope today: only **narrow** DPSP primacy — for **39(b)-(c)** laws.

16.s: The continued operation of the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, was reaffirmed in which of the following decisions in 2024?
16.x: The Property Owners Association decision of 2024 affirmed that the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, continues in force.
16.tq: Match the recent decision with the specific constitutional proposition it reaffirmed.
xs: **Property Owners Association (2024)** held the original **Art. 31C**, as upheld in Kesavananda, **continues in force** — option **(3)**.
**R.C. Cooper (1970)** was the **Bank Nationalisation** case; **Madhav Rao Scindia (1970)** the **Privy Purses** case.
**Sanjeev Coke (1983)** upheld coking coal nationalisation under **39(b)**.
xa: It was a **9-judge** Bench, **7:2**, majority by CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud** (**5 Nov 2024**).
It held **not every** privately owned resource is a 39(b) material resource.
It rejected **Justice Krishna Iyer**'s broad view (**Ranganatha Reddy, 1977**).

16.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Forty-Second Amendment attempted to extend Article 31C protection to laws implementing all Directive Principles.
2. The Forty-Fourth Amendment gave all Directive Principles precedence over Articles 14 and 19.
3. The attempt to give all Directive Principles such precedence was struck down by the Supreme Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Forty-Second Amendment, not the Forty-Fourth, attempted to extend Article 31C to all Directive Principles, and that extension was struck down.
16.tq: Catch the amendment-year swap by identifying which amendment made the attempt and which did not.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **42nd Amendment (1976)** tried to extend **31C** to **all DPSPs**.
Statement 2 wrong: the **44th** did **not** give DPSPs precedence — that attempt was the 42nd.
Statement 3 correct: **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck the extension down.
xa: ⚠ Trap (**RPSC 2013**): "the 44th Amendment gave all DPSPs primacy over 14 and 19" is **false**.
Only **39(b)-(c)** laws enjoy primacy, via the **25th (1971)**.
The 42nd also claimed **unlimited amending power** under **Art. 368**.

16.s:
The Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 was associated with which of the following measures?
1. Extending Article 31C protection to laws implementing all Directive Principles
2. Claiming unlimited amending power under Article 368
3. Giving precedence to all Directive Principles over Articles 14 and 19
Which of the above is/are correct?
