16.x: The Forty-Second Amendment attempted all three measures. The extension of Article 31C and the claim of unlimited amending power were subsequently invalidated in the relevant constitutional litigation.
16.tq: Recognise a cluster of provisions associated with one amendment instead of isolating only its best-known feature.
xs: All **three** measures belong to the **42nd Amendment (1976)** — option **(4)**.
Statements 1 and 3: it extended **31C** to give **all DPSPs** precedence over **Arts 14, 19**.
Statement 2: it claimed **unlimited amending power** under **Art. 368**.
xa: **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck both down.
⚠ The **44th** Amendment did **not** give DPSPs precedence (**RPSC 2013** trap).
After Minerva, 31C was restored to **39(b)-(c)**.

16.s: Which one of the following additional propositions was recognised in Minerva Mills in relation to an Emergency proclamation?
o: It is subject only to review by the Election Commission
It can be reviewed only by a joint sitting of Parliament
It is permanently beyond judicial review
It is subject to judicial review
16.x: Minerva Mills recognised that an Emergency proclamation is not wholly immune from judicial review.
16.tq: Identify the constitutional authority involved in reviewing an executive emergency action.
xs: **Minerva Mills** held an **Emergency proclamation** is **subject to judicial review** — option **(4)**.
So "permanently beyond judicial review" (3) is wrong.
xa: Minerva's main ruling: **harmony and balance** between Parts III and IV is part of the **Basic Structure**.
It struck down the **42nd Amendment**'s extension of **31C** and its claim of unlimited amending power.

16.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 31C — Protection of laws relating to acquisition of estates from Articles 14 and 19
Article 350B — Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
Article 350A — Mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage
Article 347 — Recognition of a language spoken by a substantial part of a State
16.x: Article 31C protects laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19. Protection for laws relating to acquisition of estates and agrarian reform is associated with Article 31A.
16.tq: Find the swapped subject between the neighbouring provisions of Articles 31A and 31C.
xs: The wrong pair is **Article 31C — acquisition of estates** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 31C** protects laws implementing **39(b) and (c)** from **Arts 14 and 19**.
Laws on **estates** fall under **Art. 31A** (widened by the **17th Amendment, 1964**).
xa: Art. 31C was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)**.
**Arts 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule** came with the **1st Amendment (1951)** to protect **land-reform laws**.
31C gives only **narrow**, not blanket, DPSP primacy.

16.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 31C:
1. It was introduced by the 25th Constitutional Amendment in 1971.
2. It protects laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c).
3. These are the only two Directive Principles that override Fundamental Rights under Article 31C.
4. Minerva Mills upheld the extension of Article 31C to all Directive Principles made by the 42nd Amendment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false: Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C protection to all Directive Principles.
16.tq: Use the constitutional-amendment and judicial-review distinction to identify the reversed statement.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 2 correct: **Art. 31C** came by the **25th Amendment (1971)** and protects **39(b) and 39(c)** laws.
Statement 3 correct: only these **two** DPSPs get primacy under 31C.
Statement 4 wrong: **Minerva Mills (1980)** **struck down** the 42nd Amendment's extension to all DPSPs.
xa: **PYQ (UPPSC 2009)**: amendment protecting 39(b)-(c) laws from Arts 14/19 = **25th**.
**Kesavananda (1973)** struck down 31C's **second provision**.
**Property Owners Association (2024)**: unamended 31C **continues in force**.

16.s: Which of the following correctly states the latest Supreme Court position on the expression “material resources of the community” in Article 39(b)?
o: No privately owned resource can ever be a material resource of the community
Only resources owned by the Union Government can be covered
Whether a privately owned resource is covered depends on factors such as its nature, scarcity, effect on community well-being and the consequences of concentration in private hands
Every privately owned resource is automatically a material resource of the community
16.x: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court held that private ownership alone does not automatically bring a resource within Article 39(b). The determination depends on the resource and its effects on the community and concentration of wealth.
16.tq: Apply the latest multi-factor judicial test instead of choosing an absolute public-versus-private rule.
xs: Whether a private resource is covered depends on its **nature, scarcity, effect on community well-being** and **consequences of concentration** in private hands — option **(3)**.
**Property Owners Association (2024)**: **not every** privately owned resource is a "material resource of the community", so (4) is wrong.
Private resources are not excluded either — the test decides — so (1) is wrong.
xa: It was a **9-judge** Bench, **7:2**, majority by CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**.
⚠ **Krishna Iyer** (**1977**, minority) = all private resources; Property Owners Association = not every private resource.
The broad view had been followed in **Sanjeev Coke (1983)**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (5 November 2024):
1. It was decided by a nine-judge Bench by a 7:2 majority.
2. The majority opinion was delivered by Justice Krishna Iyer.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 1 is correct: a nine-judge Bench decided it 7:2. Statement 2 is wrong: the majority was written by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud; Justice Krishna Iyer wrote the 1977 Ranganatha Reddy minority view that this judgment rejected. So '1 only'; the other options accept statement 2 or reject statement 1.
16.tq: 2024 = 9 judges, 7:2, CJI D.Y. Chandrachud; Krishna Iyer = 1977 broad view it rejected.
xs: Only **statement 1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: a **nine-judge** Bench decided it **7:2**.
Statement 2 wrong: the majority was by CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**; **Justice Krishna Iyer** wrote the **1977** minority view that it rejected.
xa: It held **not every** privately owned resource falls under **39(b)**.
It held unamended **31C** survives for 39(b)-(c) laws.
Krishna Iyer's view came in **State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977)**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the judicial history of Article 39(b):
1. In State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977), Justice Krishna Iyer's minority view included privately owned resources within “material resources of the community”.
2. The broad view was followed in Sanjeev Coke (1983).
3. Property Owners Association rejected the proposition that every privately owned resource automatically falls within Article 39(b).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: All three statements are correct. The broad interpretation associated with Justice Krishna Iyer in Ranganatha Reddy was followed in Sanjeev Coke, while the 2024 Property Owners Association decision rejected its automatic application to every privately owned resource.
16.tq: Track the evolution of a legal proposition from an earlier minority view to its later qualification.
xs: All **three** statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **Justice Krishna Iyer** (minority) in **Ranganatha Reddy (1977)** included **privately owned** resources.
Statement 2: that broad view was followed in **Sanjeev Coke (1983)**.
Statement 3: **Property Owners Association (2024)** held **not every** private resource is covered.
xa: The 2024 test: the resource's **nature, scarcity**, effect on community well-being, consequences of **concentration**.
It was a **9-judge** Bench, **7:2**, majority by CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**.
Sanjeev Coke upheld **coking coal nationalisation** under 39(b) / 31C.

16.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Ninth Schedule is NOT correct?
o: Article 31B was inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951
The Ninth Schedule has remained confined to land reform laws and never expanded beyond them
The number of entries in it grew to more than 280
The Ninth Schedule was initially associated with protection for land reform laws from Fundamental Rights challenges
16.x: Option B is the incorrect statement: the Ninth Schedule, though created by the 1st Amendment, 1951 (Art. 31B) to shield land-reform laws, later grew to over 280 entries and did not stay confined to land reforms. Options A, C and D are correct statements.
16.tq: Reject the absolute claim that an initially limited constitutional device never expanded.
xs: The incorrect statement is that the Ninth Schedule **stayed confined to land reform** — option **(2)**.
It was meant for **land reforms**, but grew to **over 280 entries**.
**Art. 31B** and the Ninth Schedule came with the **1st Amendment, 1951** — (1), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: **Waman Rao (1981)**: entries after **24 April 1973** open to challenge.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: **no blanket immunity**; the **last word** on the Ninth Schedule.
**Reservation acts** placed in the Ninth Schedule are open to **judicial review**.

16.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
16.x: Waman Rao was decided in 1981, not 2007. I.R. Coelho was the 2007 decision concerning the absence of blanket immunity for Ninth Schedule entries.
16.tq: Use the year mismatch to distinguish closely related constitutional cases.
xs: **Waman Rao — 2007** is wrong; Waman Rao was **1981** — option **(3)**.
The **2007** case is **I.R. Coelho**: no blanket immunity for Ninth Schedule laws.
**Sanjeev Coke (1983)**, **Property Owners Association (2024)** and **Ranganatha Reddy (1977)** are correctly matched.
xa: Waman Rao: post-**24 April 1973** Ninth Schedule entries are open to challenge.
Coelho: post-1973 entries invalid if they damage the **Basic Structure** or the **golden triangle** (Arts **14, 19, 21**).

16.s:
With reference to the Ninth Schedule, consider the following statements:
1. In Waman Rao (1981), the Supreme Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to challenge.
2. In I.R. Coelho (2007), the Court held that Ninth Schedule laws enjoy blanket immunity from judicial review.
3. Under I.R. Coelho, post-1973 entries may be struck down if they damage the basic structure or the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: Statement 1 is correct: Waman Rao used 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda judgment, as the cut-off. Statement 2 is wrong because I.R. Coelho rejected blanket immunity. Statement 3 is correct: post-1973 entries fall if they damage the basic structure or the 'golden triangle' of Articles 14, 19 and 21. So 1 and 3 only is the answer.
16.tq: Cut-off 24 April 1973 (Waman Rao). No blanket immunity (Coelho, 2007).
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Waman Rao (1981)** — entries after **24 April 1973** are open to challenge.
Statement 2 wrong: **I.R. Coelho (2007)** held there is **no blanket immunity**.
Statement 3 correct: post-1973 entries fall if they damage the **Basic Structure** or the essence of Arts **14, 19, 21**.
xa: Arts 14, 19, 21 are the **golden triangle**.
**Art. 31B** (**1st Amendment, 1951**) shields Ninth Schedule laws; entries grew to **over 280**.
I.R. Coelho is the **last word** on the Ninth Schedule.

16.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. I.R. Coelho judgment as the last word on the Ninth Schedule
B. First Constitutional Amendment Act
C. Champakam Dorairajan case
D. Minerva Mills judgment
16.x: Champakam Dorairajan and the First Amendment belong to 1951, followed later by Minerva Mills and then I.R. Coelho in 2007. The stated sequence is therefore C, B, D, A.
16.tq: Anchor the sequence with the two 1951 events and place I.R. Coelho last.
xs: The order is **C, B, D, A** — option **(1)**.
**Champakam Dorairajan (1951)** came first and **led to** the **1st Amendment (1951)**.
Then **Minerva Mills (1980)**, then **I.R. Coelho (2007)**.
xa: Champakam = **first conflict case**; 1st Amendment = first amendment responding to a court.
Coelho = **last word** on the Ninth Schedule.
Minerva made FR-DPSP balance part of the **Basic Structure** — the settled position.

16.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The conflict between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles contributed to the development of the basic structure doctrine.
2. The conflict raised questions concerning the limits of Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution.
3. The conflict has no connection with debates on judicial and parliamentary supremacy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect because the conflict also generated debates over judicial supremacy and parliamentary supremacy.
16.tq: Reject the absolute negative statement and retain the two stated constitutional consequences.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2 correct: the FR-DPSP conflict shaped the **basic structure** doctrine and the **limits of Parliament's amending power**.
Statement 3 wrong: it fed the debate on **judicial vs parliamentary supremacy**.
xa: Another debate: whether **31C** cover for **39(b)-(c)** laws weakens **Art. 14**.
**Minerva Mills** made FR-DPSP **balance** part of the Basic Structure.
**Golaknath (1967)** → **24th Amendment (1971)** → **Kesavananda (1973)** traced the amending-power fight.

16.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Source or development)
 a. Fundamental Rights
 b. Directive Principles of State Policy
 c. First conflict case
 d. Last word on the Ninth Schedule

List-II (Associated reference)
 i. Ireland
 ii. United States of America
 iii. Champakam Dorairajan, 1951
 iv. I.R. Coelho, 2007
16.x: Fundamental Rights were drawn from the United States, while the Directive Principles were inspired by Ireland. Champakam Dorairajan was the first conflict case, and I.R. Coelho in 2007 was the last word on the Ninth Schedule.
16.tq: Start from the sure source pair and then verify the first-case and last-word associations.
xs: The correct code is **a–ii, b–i, c–iii, d–iv** — option **(1)**.
FRs from the **USA** (ii); DPSPs from **Ireland** (i).
First conflict case = **Champakam Dorairajan, 1951** (iii); last word on the Ninth Schedule = **I.R. Coelho, 2007** (iv).
xa: Champakam led to the **First Amendment** — the first amendment responding to a court.
Coelho: no blanket immunity for post-1973 Ninth Schedule entries.
FRs are **justiciable**; DPSPs **non-justiciable** (**Art. 37**).

17.s:
Consider the following statements about the Swaran Singh Committee on Fundamental Duties:
1. It was set up by the Congress party in 1976 and chaired by Sardar Swaran Singh.
2. The need for it was felt during the National Emergency of 1962.
3. It suggested eight Fundamental Duties, while the 42nd Amendment added ten.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the Congress party set it up in 1976 under Sardar Swaran Singh; it suggested 8 duties and the 42nd Amendment (1976) added 10. Statement 2 is wrong: the need was felt during the Internal Emergency of 1975-77, not 1962. So every option containing statement 2 is wrong.
17.tq: Swaran Singh: 1976, Internal Emergency, suggested 8, added 10.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **Congress party** set it up in **1976**, chaired by **Sardar Swaran Singh**.
Statement 2 wrong: the need was felt during the **Internal Emergency (1975-77)**, not 1962.
Statement 3 correct: it suggested **8** duties; the **42nd Amendment, 1976** added **10**.
xa: ⚠ **8 – 10 – 11**: suggested by Swaran Singh – added in 1976 – total after **2002**.
Not accepted: **penalty** for non-observance, bar on court challenge to such penalty laws, and **duty to pay taxes**.
⚠ **Swaran Singh** = 1976, suggested duties; **J.S. Verma** = **1999**, operationalising duties.

17.s: Which one of the following was NOT accepted as a recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee?
o: The broad idea of incorporating duties of citizens
The formulation of a constitutional list of duties
The inclusion of Fundamental Duties in the Constitution
Parliament’s power to prescribe punishment for non-compliance with duties
17.x: The proposal that Parliament could prescribe penalties for non-compliance was not accepted. The constitutional list of Fundamental Duties was incorporated in a modified form.
17.tq: Identify the rejected enforcement proposal rather than the accepted constitutional idea.
xs: **Parliament's power to prescribe punishment** for non-compliance with duties was **not accepted** — option **(4)**.
The idea of a list of duties was accepted: the **42nd Amendment, 1976** inserted **Part IVA** (**Art. 51A**) — so (1), (2), (3) were accepted.
Also rejected: that such penalty laws **not be challenged in court** for violating FRs.
xa: Also rejected: the **duty to pay taxes** as a Fundamental Duty.
The Committee suggested **8** duties; **10** were added.
FDs today are **non-justiciable** — no legal sanction or penalty in the Constitution.

17.s: Which of the following was proposed by the Swaran Singh Committee as a Fundamental Duty but was not ultimately included in the constitutional list?
17.x: The committee suggested that payment of taxes should be a Fundamental Duty, but this proposal was not accepted.
17.tq: Separate a committee proposal from the final constitutional text.
xs: The Committee proposed the **duty to pay taxes**, but it was **not included** — option **(2)**.
**Natural environment** is **51A(g)**, **scientific temper** is **51A(h)**, **safeguarding public property** is **51A(i)** — all in the list.
xa: Paying taxes, **casting a vote** and **family planning** are common "not a duty" distractors.
Criticism: the list is **not exhaustive** — omits voting, paying taxes, family planning.
The penalty proposal for non-observance was also rejected.

17.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment
B. Internal Emergency, 1975-1977
C. Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment
D. Constitution originally came into force
17.x: The Constitution came into force first, followed by the Internal Emergency, the Forty-Second Amendment in 1976 and the Eighty-Sixth Amendment in 2002.
17.tq: Fix the first and last events, then place the Emergency and amendments between them.
xs: The order is **D, B, A, C** — option **(1)**.
Constitution in force (**1950**) → **Internal Emergency (1975-77)** → **42nd Amendment (1976)** → **86th Amendment (2002)**.
xa: The **Swaran Singh Committee** was set up in **1976**, the need felt during the Emergency.
The 42nd added **10** duties; the 86th added the **11th**, **51A(k)**.

17.s: The Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 inserted which of the following?
o: Part IVB containing Article 51B and clauses (a) to (k)
Part IVA containing Article 51A and clauses (a) to (j)
17.x: The Forty-Second Amendment inserted Part IVA, containing the single Article 51A with clauses (a) to (j).
17.tq: Match the amendment with the exact Part, Article and initial clause range.
xs: The **42nd Amendment, 1976** inserted **Part IVA** with **Art. 51A**, clauses **(a)-(j)** — option **(4)**.
Part IVA has a **single Article, 51A**, placed after Part IV (DPSP).
Clause **(k)** was added later by the **86th Amendment (2002)**, so (3) is wrong.
xa: The 42nd is called the "**Mini Constitution**".
Part IVA is one of the **4 Parts added** since 1950 — with **IXA, IXB, XIVA**.
Count: **10 in 1976 → 11 now**.

17.s: The number of Fundamental Duties immediately after the Forty-Second Amendment and the number at present are, respectively:
17.x: The Forty-Second Amendment introduced ten Fundamental Duties. The Eighty-Sixth Amendment later added clause (k), taking the total to eleven.
17.tq: Track the numerical change caused by the later amendment.
xs: **10** duties after the 42nd Amendment and **11** now — option **(2)**.
The **42nd (1976)** added clauses **(a)-(j)**; the **86th (2002)** added **(k)**.
**8** was the number suggested by the **Swaran Singh Committee**, so (1) is a trap.
xa: ⚠ **8 – 10 – 11** = suggested – added in 1976 – total after 2002.
**51A(k)**: parent/guardian to provide education to a child aged **6-14**.

17.s: Which amendment added Article 51A(k) to the Constitution?
17.x: The Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 added Article 51A(k), relating to educational opportunities for children or wards aged six to fourteen.
17.tq: Reject the close-number and close-year distractors by linking the duty to education.
xs: **Art. 51A(k)** was added by the **86th Amendment Act, 2002** — option **(1)**.
The **42nd (1976)** added only clauses **(a)-(j)**.
xa: The same Act inserted **Art. 21A** and substituted **Art. 45**.
51A(k) is addressed to **parents or guardians** — education for a child or ward aged **6-14**.
Total duties after it: **11**.

17.s: The Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 is associated with which combination?
o: Insertion of Article 21A, substitution of Article 45 and addition of Article 51A(k)
Insertion of Article 32A, substitution of Article 44 and deletion of Article 51A
Insertion of Part IXA and addition of Article 51A(a)
Substitution of Article 48A and insertion of Article 51A(j)
17.x: The Eighty-Sixth Amendment inserted Article 21A, substituted Article 45 and added the eleventh Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k).
17.tq: Use the common education theme to match the amendment’s three provisions.
xs: The **86th Amendment (2002)** — **insertion** of **Article 21A**, **substitution** of Art. 45 and **addition** of 51A(k) — option **(1)**.
The **86th** is the Act that added the **11th** duty; the **42nd (1976)** had added **10**.
**51A(a)** and **(j)** came with the **42nd (1976)**, so (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: 51A(k): parent/guardian to provide **opportunities for education** to a child aged **6-14**.
51A(k) is the only duty addressed specifically to **parents or guardians**; it is a **civic** duty.
⚠ Answer is **86th, 2002** — options often mix 86th/96th and 2001/2002.

17.s: Which one of the following Parts was NOT among the four Parts added to the Constitution after 1950 along with Part IVA?
17.x: Part IVA, Part IXA, Part IXB and Part XIVA are identified as four Parts added after 1950. Part VIIIA is not part of that group.
17.tq: Identify the outsider from a list of constitutional Parts.
xs: **Part VIIIA** is not in the group — option **(4)**.
The **4 Parts added** since 1950 are **IVA, IXA, IXB, XIVA**.
**Part IVA** (Art. 51A) was inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
xa: Part IVA is a **single Article, 51A**, placed after Part IV (DPSP).
Criticism: FDs are an **appendage to Part IV** instead of after Part III.

17.s: Under Article 51A, which clause requires citizens to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem?
17.x: Article 51A(a) requires citizens to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
17.tq: Match the exact duty with its clause number.
xs: **Article 51A(a)**: abide by the Constitution; respect its ideals and institutions, the **National Flag** and **National Anthem** — option **(3)**.
**51A(c)** = sovereignty, unity, integrity; **51A(e)** = harmony and common brotherhood; **51A(i)** = public property.
xa: 51A(a) is a **civic** duty.
The **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971** gives effect to 51A(a).
**Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)**: respect for national symbols needs only **respectful conduct**, not compelled participation.

17.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Article 51A(j) — Protect and improve the natural environment
Article 51A(b) — Cherish and follow the noble ideals of the national struggle for freedom
Article 51A(f) — Develop scientific temper and humanism
Article 51A(h) — Safeguard public property and abjure violence
17.x: Article 51A(b) concerns cherishing and following the noble ideals of the national struggle for freedom. Scientific temper, public property and the natural environment are covered by clauses (h), (i) and (g), respectively.
17.tq: Use exact clause-duty matching and reject swapped provisions.
xs: **51A(b)** — cherish and follow the **noble ideals of the national struggle** for freedom — option **(2)**.
Natural environment is **51A(g)**, not (j); **51A(j)** is striving towards **excellence**.
Scientific temper is **51A(h)**, not (f); public property is **51A(i)**, not (h).
xa: **51A(f)**: value and preserve the heritage of our **composite culture**.
Moral duties: **(b), (f), (h), (j)**; civic: **(a), (c), (d), (g), (i)**.
Critics call "**noble ideals**" vague.

17.s: The Fundamental Duty relating to sovereignty, unity and integrity of India is contained in:
17.x: Article 51A(c) requires every citizen to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
17.tq: Test a precise constitutional phrase against nearby clause numbers.
xs: **Article 51A(c)**: uphold and protect the **sovereignty, unity and integrity** of India — option **(2)**.
**51A(b)** = noble ideals of the freedom struggle; **51A(d)** = **defend the country**; **51A(e)** = harmony and brotherhood.
xa: Freedom of speech (**Art. 19(1)(a)**) ↔ duty under **51A(c)** — rights and duties are correlative.
Look-alike: the Preamble's "**unity and integrity of the Nation**".
The **Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967** serves 51A(c).

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 51A(d) relates to defending the country and rendering national service when called upon.
2. Article 51A(e) requires promotion of harmony and common brotherhood transcending religious, linguistic, regional and sectional diversities.
3. Article 51A(e) also requires renunciation of practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: All three statements correctly describe clauses 51A(d) and 51A(e).
17.tq: Verify each component of a closely related pair of civic duties.
xs: All **three** statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **51A(d)** — **defend the country** and render national service when called upon.
Statements 2 and 3: **51A(e)** — **harmony and common brotherhood** transcending diversities; **renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women**.
xa: The Preamble look-alike for 51A(e) is **Fraternity**.
The **Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955** serves 51A(e).
Both (d) and (e) are classed as **civic** duties.

17.s: Which of the following is associated with Article 51A(f)?
o: Providing educational opportunities to children aged 6-14
Striving towards excellence in all spheres
Preservation of the rich heritage of composite culture
Development of scientific temper and humanism
17.x: Article 51A(f) requires citizens to value and preserve the rich heritage of India’s composite culture.
17.tq: Discriminate among similar moral and educational duties.
xs: **Art. 51A(f)**: value and preserve the rich heritage of our **composite culture** — option **(3)**.
Education for 6-14 is **51A(k)**; **excellence** is **51A(j)**; **scientific temper** is **51A(h)**.
xa: ⚠ DPSP **Art. 49** protects **monuments** — not an FD.
51A(f) is a **moral** duty.
"**Composite culture**" is criticised as a vague term.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about the constitutional basis of environmental protection:
1. Article 51A(g) asks citizens to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures.
2. Article 48A is a Fundamental Duty requiring every citizen to protect the environment.
3. Article 21 has been judicially read to include the right to a clean, healthy, pollution-free environment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statement 1 is correct: it is the content of the Fundamental Duty in 51A(g). Statement 2 is wrong: Article 48A is a Directive Principle addressed to the State, not a Fundamental Duty of citizens. Statement 3 is correct: Article 21 has been read to include a clean, healthy environment (Subhash Kumar, 1991). Hence '1 and 3 only'; '1 only' misses statement 3, and the options with statement 2 are wrong.
17.tq: 48A = DPSP (State); 51A(g) = FD (citizen); 21 = judicial right to environment.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **51A(g)** — protect and improve the **natural environment** (forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife); **compassion for living creatures**.
Statement 2 wrong: **Art. 48A** is a **DPSP** directing the **State**, not a citizen's duty.
Statement 3 correct: **Art. 21** has been read to include a clean, healthy environment (**Subhash Kumar, 1991**).
xa: Environmental FD = **51A(g)** (**APPSC 2025**), not 48A.
Both 51A(g) and 48A came with the **42nd Amendment, 1976**, after the **1972 Stockholm Conference**.
**Art. 253** is the basis of the **Environment Protection Act, 1986**.

17.s: Which one of the following is NOT a component of the Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(h)?
o: Protection of monuments of national importance
17.x: Article 51A(h) covers scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform. Protection of monuments is associated with Article 49, a Directive Principle.
17.tq: Find the look-alike provision placed outside the Fundamental Duties.
xs: **Protection of monuments** is not part of 51A(h) — option **(2)**.
**51A(h)** covers **scientific temper, humanism** and the **spirit of inquiry and reform**.
Protection of **monuments** is DPSP **Art. 49**.
xa: Scientific temper is **only an FD** — no look-alike elsewhere.
51A(h) is a **moral** duty.
Critics call "**scientific temper**" vague.

17.s: A citizen deliberately damages a public bus during a violent protest. Which Fundamental Duty is most directly attracted by this conduct?
17.x: Article 51A(i) requires citizens to safeguard public property and abjure violence.
17.tq: Apply the wording of a civic duty to a practical situation.
xs: Damaging a public bus in a violent protest offends **Article 51A(i)** — **safeguard public property** and **abjure violence** — option **(1)**.
**51A(e)** = harmony and brotherhood; **51A(j)** = excellence; **51A(g)** = environment.
xa: 51A(i) is **only an FD** — no look-alike elsewhere.
It is a **civic** duty.

17.s: The duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child or ward between six and fourteen years of age is contained in:
17.x: Article 51A(k) places this duty on a parent or guardian in respect of a child or ward aged six to fourteen years.
17.tq: Use the age range to identify the specific educational duty.
xs: **Article 51A(k)**: parent or guardian to provide **opportunities for education** to a child or ward aged **6-14** — option **(2)**.
Added by the **86th Amendment, 2002** — the **11th** duty.
**51A(g)** = environment; **(h)** = scientific temper; **(j)** = excellence.
xa: The same Act inserted **Art. 21A** and substituted **Art. 45**.
51A(k) is the only duty addressed specifically to **parents or guardians**.

17.s: Which one of the following is NOT enumerated as a Fundamental Duty?
o: To preserve the rich heritage of composite culture
To pay taxes to the government
To renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women
To defend the country when called upon
17.x: Payment of taxes is not enumerated as a Fundamental Duty. The other three duties are covered by Articles 51A(f), 51A(e) and 51A(d), respectively.
17.tq: Check the option word-for-word against the constitutional list.
xs: **Paying taxes** is not a Fundamental Duty — option **(2)**.
Composite culture = **51A(f)**; dignity of women = **51A(e)**; defend the country = **51A(d)**.
xa: The **Swaran Singh Committee** proposed a **duty to pay taxes**, but it was not accepted.
Other "not a duty" distractors: **casting a vote**, **family planning**, protecting the **elderly, differently abled and children**.
Criticism: FDs are **not exhaustive**.

17.s: Which of the following pairs is incorrectly matched?
o: Protection of public property by citizens — Article 48A
Protection of environment by the State — Article 48A
17.x: Protection of public property by citizens is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(i), not Article 48A. Article 48A concerns protection and improvement of the environment by the State.
17.tq: Expose an Article swap between a Fundamental Duty and a DPSP.
xs: **Public property — Article 48A** is wrong — option **(2)**.
Safeguarding public property is FD **51A(i)**; **Art. 48A** is the DPSP on the State protecting the **environment**.
**Art. 49** (monuments), **Art. 46** (SCs, STs, weaker sections) and **Art. 48A** (environment by the State) are correct.
xa: Protection of weaker sections is **not an FD** — only DPSP Art. 46.
Environmental FD for citizens = **51A(g)**.

17.s: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes the Fundamental Duty relating to brotherhood from the Preamble?
o: Article 51A(e) refers to fraternity, while the Preamble refers to common brotherhood.
Article 51A(e) refers to harmony and common brotherhood, while the Preamble refers to fraternity.
Both provisions use only the expression 'common brotherhood'.
Neither provision contains an idea relating to brotherhood or fraternity.
17.x: Article 51A(e) expressly refers to harmony and common brotherhood, whereas the Preamble uses the term fraternity.
17.tq: Distinguish similar constitutional expressions instead of treating them as identical.
xs: **51A(e)** speaks of **harmony and common brotherhood**; the **Preamble** speaks of **Fraternity** — option **(2)**.
51A(e) also asks citizens to **renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women**.
xa: Similarly **51A(c)** (sovereignty, unity, integrity) ↔ Preamble "**unity and integrity of the Nation**".
51A(e) is served by the **Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955**.

17.s: Article 51A(k) specifically casts a duty upon which of the following?
o: The Union Government and State Governments
17.x: Article 51A(k) specifically addresses parents or guardians, requiring them to provide opportunities for education to children or wards within the constitutionally prescribed age group.
17.tq: Identify the specific person or class to whom a constitutional duty is addressed.
xs: **Art. 51A(k)** is addressed to **parents or guardians** — option **(4)**.
It requires them to provide **opportunities for education** to a child or ward aged **6-14**.
xa: Added by the **86th Amendment, 2002**, with **Art. 21A** and a new **Art. 45**.
All other duties apply to **every citizen** of India — not foreigners.

17.s:
With reference to the nature of Fundamental Duties, consider the following statements:
1. Duties under clauses (b), (f), (h) and (j) are generally regarded as moral duties.
2. Duties under clauses (a), (c), (d), (g) and (i) are generally regarded as civic duties.
3. Every Fundamental Duty is addressed specifically to parents or guardians.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 2 correctly describe the broad classification of Fundamental Duties. Statement 3 is false because only Article 51A(k) specifically addresses parents or guardians.
17.tq: Separate a valid classification from an overbroad statement using the word 'every'.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **(b), (f), (h), (j)** are **moral** duties.
Statement 2: **(a), (c), (d), (g), (i)** are **civic** duties.
Statement 3 wrong: only **51A(k)** is addressed to **parents or guardians**.
xa: Example: civic duty **(a)** (respect Flag, Anthem), moral duty **(b)** (ideals of the freedom struggle).
Count: **10 in 1976 → 11 now**.

17.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections — Article 46
17.x: C is correct: Article 46 protects the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections. The others are mismatched: village panchayats are Art. 40 (not 43), cottage industries are Art. 43 (not 40), and prohibition of intoxicating drinks is Art. 47 (not 48).
17.tq: Start from the sure Article–subject pair and eliminate the shifted numbers.
xs: **Art. 46** — interests of **SCs, STs and weaker sections** — option **(3)**.
Protection of weaker sections is a DPSP only — **not an FD**.
xa: DPSP **Art. 48A** = State to protect the environment; **Art. 49** = **monuments**.
FD look-alikes: environment **51A(g)**, composite culture **51A(f)**.

17.s:
Which of the following correctly matches an ideal with its location in the Constitution?

1. Environment — Article 48A and Article 51A(g)
2. Education — Article 45, Article 21A and Article 51A(k)
3. Heritage and monuments — Article 49 and Article 51A(f)
4. Fraternity — Article 39 and Article 51A(e)

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
17.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correctly matched. Statement 4 is false: fraternity appears in the Preamble and is reflected in Article 51A(e), whereas Article 39 is not the listed DPSP location for fraternity.
17.tq: Compare the same ideal across the Preamble, DPSPs and Fundamental Duties without accepting a substituted Article.
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3** are correctly matched — option **(1)**.
Environment: DPSP **48A** + FD **51A(g)**; education: **Art. 45**, **Art. 21A**, **51A(k)**.
Heritage: **Art. 49** (monuments) + **51A(f)** (composite culture).
Item 4 wrong: **Fraternity** is in the **Preamble**; 51A(e) speaks of **common brotherhood**.
xa: Sovereignty: **51A(c)** ↔ Preamble "**unity and integrity of the Nation**".
Scientific temper (**51A(h)**) and public property (**51A(i)**) are **only FDs**.

17.s: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A?
o: To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform
To protect the elderly, the differently abled and children
To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity
To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
17.x: Protecting the elderly, the differently abled and children is not in Article 51A; APPSC Group 2, 2025 used it twice as the distractor. Scientific temper is 51A(h), striving towards excellence is 51A(j), and safeguarding public property is 51A(i).
17.tq: Check the 51A list word for word. Elderly/children, paying taxes, voting and family planning are NOT duties.
xs: Protecting the **elderly, the differently abled and children** is not in Art. 51A — option **(2)**.
**APPSC G2 2025** used this distractor **twice**.
Scientific temper = **51A(h)**; excellence = **51A(j)**; public property = **51A(i)**.
xa: Other distractors: **pay taxes**, **cast a vote**, **family planning**.
Exam tip: "which is not a Fundamental Duty" — check the list **word for word**.

17.s: Which of the following categories is covered by the Fundamental Duties under Article 51A?
o: Only public servants and elected representatives
Citizens and all foreign nationals residing in India
All persons, whether citizens or foreigners
17.x: Fundamental Duties are addressed to every citizen of India and do not extend to foreigners. This differs from certain Fundamental Rights, such as those under Articles 14, 20, 21 and 25, which are available to non-citizens as well.
17.tq: Discriminate between citizens-only duties and rights available to all persons.
xs: FDs apply to **citizens of India only** — option **(3)**.
Art. 51A says "it shall be the duty of **every citizen** of India" — not foreigners.
Unlike several FRs (Arts **14, 20, 21, 25**) that cover non-citizens.
xa: **51A(k)** is addressed specifically to **parents or guardians**.
Source: the former **USSR**; **Japan** is the only major democracy with a comparable list.

17.s: The constitutional provision on Fundamental Duties was inspired primarily by the Constitution of which country?
o: Former Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
17.x: The Fundamental Duties were inspired by the Constitution of the former USSR. The provisions on Fundamental Rights, in contrast, drew inspiration substantially from the United States Constitution.
17.tq: Distinguish the foreign source of one constitutional feature from sources of other features.
xs: FDs were inspired by the Constitution of the former **USSR** — option **(4)**.
**Socialist States** give FRs and duties equal weight.
xa: Among major democracies only **Japan** has a comparable list of citizens' duties.
Inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976** on the **Swaran Singh Committee**'s advice.

17.s: Among the major democratic constitutions, which country is noted for having a comparable list of citizens' duties?
17.x: Japan's Constitution is identified as the only major democratic Constitution with a comparable list of citizens' duties. Socialist States generally give Fundamental Rights and duties relatively equal weight.
17.tq: Use a country-comparison fact rather than confusing democratic and socialist constitutional models.
xs: **Japan** is the only major democracy with a comparable list of citizens' duties — option **(4)**.
The FD idea itself came from the former **USSR**.
xa: **Socialist States** give FRs and duties **equal weight**.
India's FDs apply to **every citizen** — not foreigners.

17.s: The Supreme Court has recognised that corporations, as legal persons, may also carry which duty under Article 51A(g)?
o: To protect and improve the natural environment
To provide free and compulsory education
To preserve the composite culture of India
To promote international peace and security
17.x: Corporations, being legal persons, have also been held capable of carrying the duty under Article 51A(g) to protect and improve the natural environment.
17.tq: Apply the constitutional duty to a non-natural legal person in a practical situation.
xs: Corporations, as **legal persons**, carry the **51A(g)** duty to **protect and improve the natural environment** — option **(1)**.
SC (**Mar 2026**) linked this to **CSR** — at least **2%** of average net profit, **Sec. 135 Companies Act, 2013**.
Education is **51A(k)**; composite culture is **51A(f)**.
xa: **M.K. Ranjitsinh v. UoI**: **CSR includes environmental protection**, linked to 51A(g).
SC (**Aug 2025**) linked **PCB enforcement** to 51A(g).
The **NGT** was formed to secure the environmental right.

17.s: Which amendment simultaneously inserted Article 51A(g), added Article 48A and transferred forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List?
17.x: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted the environmental duty in Article 51A(g), added DPSP Article 48A and moved forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List through Entries 17A and 17B.
17.tq: Recognise a cluster of linked constitutional changes instead of relying on the amendment number alone.
xs: The **42nd Amendment, 1976** did all three — option **(1)**.
It inserted **51A(g)**, added DPSP **Art. 48A**, and moved **Entry 17A/17B** (forests; wild animals and birds) to the **Concurrent List**.
The **86th (2002)** added **51A(k)**, not (g).
xa: These changes followed the **1972 Stockholm Conference**.
Environmental FD = **51A(g)**; 48A is a DPSP for the State.

17.s: The environmental changes associated with Article 51A(g) were introduced after which international development?
17.x: The insertion of Article 51A(g), Article 48A and the related legislative-list changes followed the 1972 Stockholm Conference.
17.tq: Use the date and causal sequence linking an international conference with constitutional change.
xs: The changes followed the **1972 Stockholm Conference** — option **(1)**.
**51A(g)** and **Art. 48A** came through the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
xa: **Entry 17A/17B** (forests; wild animals and birds) moved to the **Concurrent List**.
**Art. 253** lets Parliament implement international agreements → **Environment Protection Act, 1986**.

17.s: Article 253 provides the constitutional basis for Parliament to implement international agreements. Which legislation is identified as having this basis in the environmental field?
o: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
17.x: Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws for implementing international agreements, and this power forms the constitutional basis for the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
17.tq: Match a constitutional enabling provision with the legislation enacted under it.
xs: **Art. 253** is the basis of the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** — option **(3)**.
The **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971** serves **51A(a)** (Flag, Anthem, Constitution).
The **Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972** and **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980** serve **51A(g)**.
xa: **Art. 21** includes a clean, healthy, pollution-free environment (**Subhash Kumar, 1991**).
Changes followed the **1972 Stockholm Conference**.

17.s:
With reference to M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, consider the following statements:
1. Corporate Social Responsibility includes environmental protection.
2. The principle was linked to Article 51A(g).
3. The judgment treated environmental protection as unrelated to constitutional duties.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the case linked environmental protection with Article 51A(g), rather than treating it as unrelated to constitutional duties.
17.tq: Identify the statement that reverses the constitutional link established in the case.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 2: **M.K. Ranjitsinh v. UoI** held **CSR includes environmental protection**, linked to **51A(g)**.
Statement 3 wrong: the case **tied** environmental protection to a constitutional duty.
xa: CSR: at least **2%** of average net profit (**Sec. 135, Companies Act, 2013**).
SC (**Mar 2026**): corporations, as **legal persons**, carry the 51A(g) duty.

17.s: Which constitutional provision has been linked by the Supreme Court with enforcement action by Pollution Control Boards?
17.x: The Supreme Court has linked Pollution Control Board enforcement to the citizen’s environmental duty under Article 51A(g).
17.tq: Use the specific constitutional linkage instead of selecting a generally environment-related provision.
xs: The SC (**Aug 2025**) linked **PCB enforcement** to **Article 51A(g)** — option **(4)**.
Environmental FD = **51A(g)** (**APPSC 2025**), not **48A** (DPSP).
xa: 51A(g): protect and improve the **natural environment**; **compassion for living creatures**.
The **NGT** was formed to secure it.

17.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the enforceability of Fundamental Duties:
1. They are directly enforceable by a constitutional court even in the absence of legislation.
2. Parliament may give effect to them through legislation.
3. Courts may use them while interpreting laws.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable: the Constitution provides no direct court enforcement or penalty, although legislation may enforce them and courts may refer to them in interpretation.
17.tq: Distinguish non-justiciability from the possibility of legislative and interpretive effect.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 wrong: FDs are **non-justiciable** — no direct court enforcement, no penalty in the Constitution.
Statement 2 correct: **Parliament may enforce them by law**.
Statement 3 correct: courts use them to **interpret laws** and judge **reasonableness**.
xa: **Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999)** found existing laws already give effect to some duties.
The **Swaran Singh** idea of penalties for non-observance was **not accepted**.

17.s: Which one of the following laws is most directly associated with giving effect to the duty to respect the National Flag, the National Anthem and the Constitution?
o: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
17.x: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 gives statutory effect to aspects of Article 51A(a), concerning respect for the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem.
17.tq: Match a duty with the legislation that operationalises it.
xs: The **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971** gives effect to **51A(a)** — option **(1)**.
**Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955** → **51A(e)**; **UAPA 1967** → **51A(c)**; **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980** → **51A(g)**.
xa: These links were noted by the **Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999)**.
**Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)**: respect for national symbols needs only respectful conduct.

17.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Law)
a. Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955
b. Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967
c. Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
d. Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980

List-II (Fundamental Duty)
i. Protection of forests
 ii. Promotion of harmony and prevention of caste or religious offences
 iii. Protection of sovereignty and integrity
 iv. Protection of wildlife and compassion for living creatures

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
17.x: The Protection of Civil Rights Act relates to harmony and prevention of caste or religious offences; the UAPA relates to sovereignty and integrity; the Wildlife (Protection) Act protects wildlife and the Forest (Conservation) Act protects forests.
17.tq: Start from the sure law–duty pairs and eliminate codes containing a swapped association.
xs: The correct code is **a–ii, b–iii, c–iv, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955** → harmony (**51A(e)**); **UAPA 1967** → sovereignty and integrity (**51A(c)**).
**Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972** → wildlife; **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980** → forests (both **51A(g)**).
xa: **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971** → **51A(a)**.
Imputations prejudicial to national integration: **Sec. 197, BNS 2023** (earlier IPC Sec. **153B**).

17.s: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee of 1999 was primarily concerned with which of the following?
o: Drafting a new Preamble to the Constitution
Operationalising Fundamental Duties by identifying existing legal provisions
Reviewing the federal distribution of legislative powers
Recommending the abolition of Fundamental Rights
17.x: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee examined ways to operationalise Fundamental Duties and identified existing laws that already gave effect to several of them.
17.tq: Identify the precise mandate of a committee instead of its broad constitutional context.
xs: The **Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999)** worked on **operationalising Fundamental Duties** — option **(2)**.
It found **existing laws** already give effect to some duties.
xa: ⚠ **Swaran Singh** = **1976**, suggested duties; **J.S. Verma** = 1999, operationalising them.
Example: **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971** → **51A(a)**.

17.s: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is associated with imputations prejudicial to national integration?
17.x: Imputations prejudicial to national integration are now dealt with under Section 197 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; the corresponding earlier reference was Section 153B of the Indian Penal Code.
17.tq: Discriminate between the current statutory provision and its earlier IPC counterpart.
xs: Imputations prejudicial to national integration fall under **Section 197**, **BNS 2023** — option **(4)**.
**Sec. 153B** was the earlier **IPC** provision.
xa: Other laws serving FDs: **UAPA 1967** → **51A(c)**; **Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955** → **51A(e)**.
The **J.S. Verma Committee (1999)** listed such laws.

17.s: Which case established that Fundamental Duties cannot override Fundamental Rights and that respect for national symbols does not necessarily mean compelled participation?
o: Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
17.x: In Bijoe Emmanuel (1986), the Supreme Court held that Fundamental Duties cannot override Part III rights and that respectful conduct towards national symbols does not require compelled participation.
17.tq: Match a landmark case with its specific constitutional principle.
xs: **Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)** held FDs **cannot override FRs** and that respect for national symbols needs only **respectful conduct**, not compelled participation — option **(2)**.
**Minerva Mills** is about the **FR-DPSP balance**, not duties.
xa: **Vande Mataram** recitation debate: 51A duties cannot cut down **Arts. 25-26** rights (**24 Aug 2026**).
**AIIMS Students' Union (2002)**: rights and duties are **correlative**.

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Fundamental Duties may be considered by courts in assessing the reasonableness of a law restricting a Fundamental Right.
2. Fundamental Duties are regarded as the counterpart or correlative of Fundamental Rights.
3. Fundamental Duties automatically prevail whenever they conflict with a Fundamental Right.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Fundamental Duties cannot override Fundamental Rights; courts may use them as an aid in judging the reasonableness of restrictions.
17.tq: Reject the absolute-priority trap while retaining the limited interpretive role of duties.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: courts may look to FDs when judging the **reasonableness** of a law restricting an FR.
Statement 2 correct: **AIIMS Students' Union (2002)** — rights and duties are **correlative**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)** — duties **cannot override FRs**.
xa: Example: **Art. 19(1)(a)** ↔ duty under **51A(c)**.
Aim of FDs: a **code of conduct** — civic virtue and patriotism.

17.s: Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is presented as being correlative with which Fundamental Duty?
o: The duty to develop scientific temper
The duty to provide educational opportunities to children
The duty to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
The duty to preserve the rich heritage of composite culture
17.x: Rights and duties are treated as complementary. Freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) is linked with the duty under Article 51A(c) to uphold and protect India's sovereignty, unity and integrity.
17.tq: Apply the idea of reciprocal rights and duties to a constitutional freedom.
xs: **Art. 19(1)(a)** is correlative with **51A(c)** — uphold and protect the **sovereignty, unity and integrity** of India — option **(3)**.
Scientific temper is **51A(h)**; education is **51A(k)**; composite culture is **51A(f)**.
xa: **AIIMS Students' Union (2002)**: rights and duties are **correlative**.
Rights are to be exercised with **restraint** and respect for others' rights.

17.s:
Assertion (A): Fundamental Duties are described as the counterpart of Fundamental Rights.
Reason (R): The exercise of rights is expected to be accompanied by restraint and respect for the rights of others.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
17.x: Both statements are true, and the expectation that rights be exercised with restraint and respect for others explains why duties are regarded as the counterpart of rights.
17.tq: Test whether the reason supplies the constitutional logic behind the assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true** and **R is the correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
A: FDs are the **counterpart of rights** (**AIIMS Students' Union, 2002**).
R: rights are to be exercised with **restraint and respect** for others' rights — which is why duties pair with rights.
xa: ⚠ **Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)**: duties still **cannot override FRs**.

17.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that rights and duties are correlative and that Fundamental Duties are as important as Fundamental Rights?
o: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India
17.x: In AIIMS Students' Union (2002), the Court held that rights and duties are correlative and that duties are as important as rights. Bijoe Emmanuel held that duties cannot override Fundamental Rights. Minerva Mills concerns the FR-DPSP balance. M.K. Ranjitsinh linked CSR to the environmental duty in 51A(g).
17.tq: Correlative = AIIMS Students' Union, 2002. Duties cannot override rights = Bijoe Emmanuel.
xs: **AIIMS Students' Union (2002)** held rights and duties are **correlative** — FDs as important as FRs — option **(1)**.
**Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)**: duties **cannot override FRs**.
**Minerva Mills** concerns FR-DPSP balance; **M.K. Ranjitsinh** linked **CSR** to **51A(g)**.
xa: Courts use FDs to judge the **reasonableness** of laws.
FDs aim at a **code of conduct** for citizens.

17.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a criticism of the Fundamental Duties?
o: They are directly enforceable by courts without legislation
They are not exhaustive and omit matters such as voting and payment of taxes
Their placement as an appendage to Part IV is said to reduce their value
They are vague and ambiguous in several expressions
17.x: A is the odd one out: direct court enforcement without legislation is not a criticism, and it is not even true, because Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable. Being not exhaustive (voting, taxes left out), placed as an appendage to Part IV, and vague are all recognised criticisms.
17.tq: Separate criticism of content and placement from the actual constitutional status of duties.
xs: Being **directly enforceable by courts** is not a criticism — and is untrue, since FDs are **non-justiciable** — option **(1)**.
Real criticisms: **not exhaustive** (omits **voting**, **paying taxes**, family planning).
**Placement** as an **appendage to Part IV** instead of after Part III reduces their value.
**Vague and ambiguous** terms: "noble ideals", "scientific temper", "composite culture".
xa: FDs are also called a "**code of moral precepts**" and **superfluous**.
**Parliament may enforce them by law**; courts use them to interpret laws.
The **Swaran Singh Committee** had proposed a **duty to pay taxes**, which was not accepted.

17.s: The description of Fundamental Duties as a ‘code of moral precepts’ is primarily related to their being:
o: Enforceable only during a National Emergency
Placed within Part III as enforceable rights
Non-justiciable and lacking direct constitutional sanctions
17.x: Because Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable and do not carry direct constitutional sanctions, they have been described as a code of moral precepts and, by critics, as superfluous.
17.tq: Connect a descriptive criticism with the constitutional feature that produces it.
xs: The "**code of moral precepts**" label stems from FDs being **non-justiciable**, with **no direct constitutional sanction** — option **(4)**.
FDs sit in **Part IVA** (**Art. 51A**), not Part III, and bind **every citizen** — so (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: Critics also call them **superfluous**.
There is **no legal sanction or penalty** in the Constitution; the Swaran Singh idea of penalties was **not accepted**.
Still, courts may look to FDs when judging the **reasonableness** of a law restricting an FR.

17.s: Which of the following subjects is omitted from the present list of Fundamental Duties, despite being suggested as a criticism of its non-exhaustive character?
17.x: The list is criticised as non-exhaustive because it does not expressly include duties such as voting, paying taxes and family planning. Respect for the National Flag, environmental protection and scientific temper are already covered.
17.tq: Identify the omitted civic obligation rather than a duty expressly listed in Article 51A.
xs: **Voting** is left out of the list — option **(1)**.
The list is criticised as **not exhaustive**: it omits **voting**, **paying taxes**, family planning.
Respect for the **National Flag** is **51A(a)**; environment is **51A(g)**; scientific temper is **51A(h)**.
xa: Other "not a duty" distractor: protecting the **elderly, differently abled and children** (**APPSC G2 2025**, asked twice).
Exam tip: "which is not a Fundamental Duty" — check the list **word for word**.

17.s:
With reference to the debate over compulsory recitation of ‘Vande Mataram’, consider the following statements:
1. The Fundamental Duties under Article 51A cannot curtail the rights guaranteed under Articles 25 and 26.
2. Articles 25 and 26 relate to freedom of religion.
3. A Fundamental Duty automatically overrides a Fundamental Right in case of conflict.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Fundamental Duties cannot be used to curtail the freedom of religion guaranteed under Articles 25 and 26; Statement 3 is incorrect because a Fundamental Duty does not automatically override a Fundamental Right.
17.tq: Test the constitutional relationship between duties and rights while rejecting the absolute claim that one automatically overrides the other.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: in the **Vande Mataram** recitation debate, Art. 51A duties **cannot cut down Arts. 25-26** rights (**24 Aug 2026**).
Statement 2 correct: **Arts 25 and 26** are the freedom-of-religion rights at stake.
Statement 3 wrong: **Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)** — duties under 51A **cannot override FRs**.
xa: Bijoe Emmanuel: respect for national symbols needs only **respectful conduct**, not compelled participation.
**AIIMS Students' Union (2002)**: rights and duties are **correlative**.
Respect for the **National Flag** and **National Anthem** is duty **51A(a)**.

17.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised significance of the Fundamental Duties?
o: They help in promoting action against anti-national activities.
They provide an independent constitutional basis for suspending all Fundamental Rights.
They help courts assess the reasonableness of laws.
They remind citizens of their obligations towards the nation.
17.x: Fundamental Duties remind citizens of their obligations, assist courts in judging the reasonableness of laws and support action against anti-national activities. They do not provide an independent basis for suspending all Fundamental Rights.
17.tq: Find the option that exaggerates the legal effect of Fundamental Duties by using an absolute constitutional claim.
xs: FDs do **not** provide a basis for **suspending all Fundamental Rights** — option **(2)**.
Their recognised significance: they **remind citizens** of obligations, help courts judge **reasonableness** of laws, and act against **anti-national activity**.
Duties **cannot override FRs** (**Bijoe Emmanuel, 1986**).
xa: Aim: a **code of conduct** for citizens, civic virtue and patriotism.
**Parliament may enforce them by law**.
Example: **UAPA 1967** serves **51A(c)** (sovereignty and integrity).

17.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Introduction of the first ten Fundamental Duties
B. Enactment of the Companies Act containing Section 135
C. Addition of the eleventh Fundamental Duty
D. Supreme Court linkage of corporate responsibility with Article 51A(g)
17.x: The first ten duties were introduced in 1976, the eleventh in 2002, Section 135 of the Companies Act came in 2013, and the cited Supreme Court development is from 2026.
17.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the two intervening developments by year.
xs: The order is **A, C, B, D** — option **(1)**.
→ **Sec. 135, Companies Act, 2013** → SC linking corporate duty to **51A(g)** (**Mar 2026**).
xa: CSR under Sec. 135: at least **2%** of average net profit.
**M.K. Ranjitsinh v. UoI**: **CSR includes environmental protection**.
The 11th duty, **51A(k)**, covers education of a child aged **6-14**.

17.s: Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, the corporate social responsibility expenditure referred to in connection with Article 51A(g) is at least
17.x: The prescribed corporate social responsibility expenditure is at least 2% of the average net profit, as referred to under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013.
17.tq: Distinguish the precise statutory percentage from nearby but incorrect percentage figures.
xs: CSR spending under **Sec. 135, Companies Act, 2013** is at least **2% of the average net profit** — option **(4)**.
The SC (**Mar 2026**) linked corporations' duty under **51A(g)** to **CSR**.
xa: Corporations, as **legal persons**, carry the 51A(g) duty to protect the environment.
**M.K. Ranjitsinh v. UoI**: **CSR includes environmental protection**.
SC (**Aug 2025**) linked **PCB enforcement** to 51A(g).

18.s: The procedure for amendment of the Constitution is contained in:
18.x: The constitutional amendment procedure is contained in Part XX. Article 368 is the sole Article in that Part.
18.tq: Identify the Part rather than repeating the commonly tested Article number.
xs: The amendment procedure is in **Part XX** — option **(4)**.
**Article 368** is the **sole Article** of Part XX.
xa: Art. 368: Parliament "may, in exercise of its **constituent power**, amend **by way of addition, variation or repeal** any provision".
The procedure was borrowed from **South Africa**.
Nature: **neither rigid nor flexible but a synthesis of both**.

18.s: The constitutional amendment procedure in India was borrowed from which country?
18.x: India borrowed the amendment procedure from South Africa. The method of electing members of the Rajya Sabha was also borrowed from South Africa.
18.tq: Test the source of a constitutional feature while avoiding confusion with countries associated with other federal provisions.
xs: The amendment procedure was borrowed from **South Africa** — option **(2)**.
South Africa also gave the **election of Rajya Sabha members**.
⚠ Not the **US**, whose Constitution is **very rigid**.
xa: India's procedure is partly rigid, partly flexible — unlike the flexible **British** one.
**Granville Austin**: "one of the **most ably conceived aspects**" of the Constitution.
Location: **Part XX, Article 368**.

18.s: Which of the following expressions is used in Article 368 to describe Parliament’s constituent power to amend the Constitution?
o: May, in exercise of its judicial power, interpret or repeal any provision
Shall, in exercise of its constituent power, amend every provision by referendum
May, in exercise of its constituent power, amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision
May, in exercise of its legislative power, repeal only those provisions approved by the States
18.x: Article 368 states that Parliament may, in exercise of its constituent power, amend the Constitution by way of addition, variation or repeal of any provision, subject to the basic-structure limitation.
18.tq: Select the precise constitutional wording and reject substitutions of legislative or judicial power.
xs: Art. 368: Parliament "**may, in exercise of its constituent power, amend by way of addition, variation or repeal** any provision" — option **(3)**.
The power lies with **Parliament** alone — no referendum and no prior State approval, so (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: Limit: Parliament **cannot alter the basic structure** (**Kesavananda Bharati, 1973**).
The amending power includes **Fundamental Rights**, by special majority.
Art. 368 is the **sole Article** of **Part XX**.

18.s: Which one of the following best characterises the nature of the Indian constitutional amendment procedure?
o: It is entirely flexible because every provision can be changed by ordinary law.
It is rigid only in matters relating to Fundamental Rights.
It is a synthesis of rigidity and flexibility.
It is entirely rigid because every provision requires State ratification.
18.x: The Indian Constitution combines different methods of amendment and is therefore neither purely rigid nor purely flexible; it is a synthesis of both.
18.tq: Compare the constitutional system as a whole instead of applying one amendment method to every provision.
xs: The procedure is a **synthesis of rigidity and flexibility** — option **(3)**.
It is **neither purely rigid nor purely flexible**: some provisions change by **simple majority**, others by **special majority**, some also need **State ratification**.
Only **federal provisions** need ratification by **half the States** — so (4) is wrong.
xa: Unlike the **very rigid US** Constitution and the **flexible British** one.
**Granville Austin**: the process "**appears complicated**" but "**is merely diverse**".
Source of the procedure: **South Africa**.

18.s: Who described the constitutional amendment process as appearing ‘complicated’ but being ‘merely diverse’?
18.x: Granville Austin described the process as appearing complicated but being merely diverse. He also called it one of the most ably conceived aspects of the Constitution.
18.tq: Distinguish the constitutional scholar associated with the exact evaluative description.
xs: **Granville Austin** said the process "**appears complicated**" but "**is merely diverse**" — option **(3)**.
He also called it "one of the **most ably conceived aspects**" of the Constitution.
xa: The procedure is a **synthesis** of rigidity and flexibility.
Three routes: **simple majority**, **special majority**, **special majority + State ratification**.

18.s: A special majority for amending the Constitution means:
o: Three-fourths of the members present and voting in each House
Two-thirds of the total membership of each House
A majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting
A majority of members present and voting in a joint sitting
18.x: Special majority combines two requirements in each House: a majority of the total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
18.tq: Do not substitute two-thirds of total membership or a joint sitting for the two-part constitutional formula.
xs: Special majority = a **majority of the total membership** of each House + **two-thirds of members present and voting** — option **(3)**.
It applies in **each House separately**; there is **no joint sitting** — so (4) is wrong.
**Two-thirds of total membership** (2) is the **Art. 61** type — impeachment of the President.
xa: Art. 368 type also used for removal of **SC/HC judges** (**124, 217**), **CAG (148)**, **CEC (324)**, **SEC (243K)**, approval of **National Emergency (352)**.
**Art. 249/312** type: two-thirds present and voting in the **Rajya Sabha only**.

18.s: A constitutional amendment bill received 298 votes in favour and 230 against out of 528 members present and voting. What is the correct conclusion, assuming the other requirement of special majority is satisfied?
o: It failed because two-thirds of 528 is 352.
It passed because it secured more than half of the votes cast.
It must be referred to a joint sitting for final approval.
It passed because 298 is more than two-thirds of the total membership.
18.x: Two-thirds of 528 is 352. Since the bill received only 298 votes in favour, it did not secure the required two-thirds majority of members present and voting and therefore failed.
18.tq: Calculate two-thirds of members present and voting; a simple majority is insufficient for a constitutional amendment.
xs: The bill **failed** because two-thirds of **528** is **352** — option **(1)**.
It got only **298** votes — short of two-thirds of members **present and voting**.
A simple majority is not enough, so (2) is wrong; there is **no joint sitting** for amendment bills, so (3) is wrong.
xa: This was the **131st Amendment Bill, 2026** (Lok Sabha **550 → 850**), **negatived** on **17 April 2026**.
⚠ **298** for vs **352** needed = two-thirds of **528** present and voting.
The **129th Bill, 2024** (simultaneous elections, **Art. 82A**) was referred to a **Joint Committee**.

18.s: With reference to the initiation of a constitutional amendment bill in India, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It can be introduced by a State Legislature and thereafter transmitted to Parliament.
It can be introduced in either House of Parliament by a Minister or a private member.
It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha by a Minister.
It can be introduced in either House of Parliament only after the President's prior permission.
18.x: A constitutional amendment bill may be introduced in either House of Parliament by either a Minister or a private member. It cannot be initiated in a State Legislature and does not require prior Presidential permission.
18.tq: Who can initiate the bill? Eliminate the options assigning the power to a State Legislature or imposing prior sanction.
xs: An amendment bill can be introduced in **either House of Parliament** by a **Minister or a private member** — option **(2)**.
It can **never** be introduced in a **State Legislature**, so (1) is wrong.
**No prior permission of the President** is needed, so (4) is wrong.
xa: It must pass each House **separately** by **special majority**.
⚠ Trap (**PYQ 2024**): "prior presidential sanction" is **false** for amendment bills.
States **cannot initiate** amendments.

18.s:
Consider the following statements regarding a Bill for amendment of the Constitution:
1. It may be introduced without the prior permission of the President.
2. It may be introduced by a private member.
3. It can be passed through a joint sitting if the two Houses disagree.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
18.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Article 108 does not apply to constitutional amendment bills and no joint sitting can resolve a disagreement between the Houses.
18.tq: Split the options using the joint-sitting trap; constitutional amendment bills follow a separate procedure.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **no prior permission of the President** is needed.
Statement 2 correct: the mover may be a **Minister or private member**.
Statement 3 wrong: **no joint sitting** — **Art. 108** does not apply; failure in either House makes the bill **lapse**.
xa: Exam angle: "prior permission", "joint sitting" and "President may return" are all **false** for amendment bills.
The President's assent is **obligatory** (**24th Amendment, 1971**).

18.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the President's role after a constitutional amendment bill has been duly passed?
o: The President must give assent and can neither withhold nor return the bill.
The President may refer the bill to a joint sitting of Parliament.
The President may return the bill once for reconsideration.
The President may withhold assent on grounds of public interest.
18.x: The President's assent to a duly passed constitutional amendment bill is obligatory. The President can neither withhold assent nor return the bill for reconsideration; this position was made mandatory by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971.
18.tq: Use the constitutional-assent distinction: amendment bills are not subject to the ordinary return or withholding choice.
xs: The President **must give assent** and can **neither withhold nor return** the bill — option **(1)**.
Assent was made obligatory by the **24th Amendment, 1971**.
There is **no joint sitting** for amendment bills — so (2) is wrong.
xa: No **prior presidential sanction** is needed to introduce the bill either.
The bill passes each House **separately** by **special majority**.
Federal provisions also need ratification by **half the States**.

18.s: The requirement that the President must give assent to a constitutional amendment bill was made obligatory by the:
18.x: The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 made the President's assent to a constitutional amendment bill obligatory.
18.tq: Match the precise amendment with the specific procedural change rather than the more famous 42nd or 44th Amendments.
xs: The **24th Amendment Act, 1971** made the President's **assent** to amendment bills obligatory — option **(1)**.
The 24th answered **Golaknath (1967)** and restored Parliament's power to amend FRs.
xa: It amended **Arts. 13 and 368** and inserted **Art. 13(4)**: an Art. 368 amendment is not "law" under Art. 13.
The **42nd (1976)** later inserted **368(4) and (5)**, struck down in **Minerva Mills (1980)**.

18.s:
With reference to a Constitutional Amendment Bill, consider the following statements:
1. A joint sitting may be summoned if the two Houses disagree.
2. The Bill fails if either House rejects it.
3. The President is constitutionally required to give assent after the Bill is duly passed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
18.x: There is no provision for a joint sitting in respect of a Constitutional Amendment Bill; therefore, rejection by either House causes failure. Under the 24th Amendment, 1971, the President must give assent to a duly passed Constitutional Amendment Bill.
18.tq: Identify the constitutional exception to the ordinary deadlock procedure and the mandatory presidential assent.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 wrong: **no joint sitting** — **Art. 108** does not apply.
Statement 2 correct: failure in **either House** makes the bill **fall**.
Statement 3 correct: the President **must give assent** (**24th Amendment, 1971**).
xa: Criticism: there is no mechanism to resolve a **deadlock** between Houses on an amendment.
The President can neither **withhold** nor **return** the bill.

18.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched regarding Constitutional Amendment Bills and ordinary Bills?
o: Constitutional Amendment Bill — joint sitting possible in case of deadlock
Ordinary Bill — special majority in each House separately
Constitutional Amendment Bill — federal provisions may require ratification by half the States
Ordinary Bill — President must assent in every case
18.x: Certain Constitutional Amendments affecting federal provisions require ratification by at least half the States. Ordinary Bills generally require a simple majority, may be subject to joint sitting, and are not covered by mandatory assent in the same manner.
18.tq: Compare the deadlock, majority, ratification and assent columns before selecting the correctly matched pair.
xs: **Constitutional Amendment Bill — federal provisions may need ratification by half the States** — option **(3)**.
Ratification is by **simple majority** of each State Legislature, with **no time limit**.
An amendment bill has **no joint sitting** (1 wrong); **special majority** is for amendment bills, ordinary bills need a **simple majority** (2 wrong).
xa: Neither type needs the President's **prior sanction** (ordinary bills except **Arts. 3, 117** types).
Assent to amendment bills is **obligatory** (**24th Amendment, 1971**).

18.s:
Which of the following subjects requires a special majority of Parliament along with ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures?
1. Election of the President
2. The Seventh Schedule
