Statement 1: the 42nd's delimitation freeze was extended to **2026** by the **84th**.
Statement 2: it is now tied to the **2027 Census**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **131st Bill** **failed in Lok Sabha (298-230)** in Apr 2026.
xa: The 42nd froze delimitation on the **1971 Census**.
The 131st Bill also aimed to **fast-track** the 106th's women's quota.

19.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the constitutional debate on secularism is correct?
o: The words ‘socialist’ and ‘secular’ were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment, while the Supreme Court has held that secularism is part of the basic structure.
The 103rd Amendment added both words to the Preamble.
The words ‘socialist’ and ‘secular’ were added by the 44th Amendment and secularism is not a basic feature.
Both words were present in the original Preamble and have never been judicially examined.
19.x: The 42nd Amendment added the words ‘socialist’ and ‘secular’ to the Preamble. The Supreme Court has also held that secularism was inherent in the constitutional scheme and forms part of the basic structure.
19.tq: Separate the date of textual insertion from the judicial understanding of a basic feature.
xs: The **42nd** added "**socialist**" and "**secular**", and the SC holds **secularism** is part of the **basic structure** — option **(1)**.
The words were added by the 42nd, not the **44th** or **103rd**, and are still contested.
The SC holds **secularism was always basic** (**Jul 2025**).
xa: The 42nd also added "**Integrity**".
The **103rd (2019)** is **10% EWS** reservation.

19.s: Which group of Constitutional Amendments has been described as the most controversial in the cited constitutional debates?
19.x: The 38th, 39th and 42nd Amendments are identified as the most controversial group in the cited debates.
19.tq: Identify the exact grouped classification instead of selecting amendments by subject similarity.
xs: The **38th, 39th and 42nd Amendments** are called the **most controversial** — option **(3)**.
The **44th (1978)** was the corrective to these three.
xa: The 44th reversed the 39th's bar on courts hearing election disputes of the **President, VP, PM, Speaker**.
The 42nd is the "**Mini-Constitution**".

19.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the proposed 131st Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2026:
1. It sought to fast-track implementation of the women’s reservation associated with the 106th Amendment.
2. It was passed by the Lok Sabha with a vote of 298–230.
3. It failed in the Lok Sabha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
19.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the Bill was meant to lift the delimitation freeze and fast-track the 106th Amendment's women's quota, and it failed in the Lok Sabha. Statement 2 is wrong: 298 voted for and 230 against out of 528 present and voting, short of the 352 (two-thirds) needed, so it was not passed.
19.tq: Catch the false statement that changes failure into passage.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: the **131st Bill** aimed to lift the freeze and **fast-track** the **106th**'s women's quota.
Statement 2 wrong: **298-230** was not enough — it fell short of **two-thirds**.
Statement 3 correct: it **failed in Lok Sabha** in Apr 2026.
xa: The **84th** had extended the delimitation freeze to **2026**; now tied to the **2027 Census**.
The 106th is the **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam** (**2023**).

19.s: The constitutional provisions relating to the Six-Point Formula and the proposed Central University in Andhra Pradesh were inserted by which amendment, as identified in the AP-specific reference?
19.x: The AP-specific reference identifies the 32nd Amendment Act of 1973 as having inserted Articles 371D and 371E relating to the Six-Point Formula and the Central University. A conflicting reference to the 33rd Amendment is ambiguous and is not the applicable identification here.
19.tq: Match the amendment number with the Articles and the regional constitutional subject.
xs: The **32nd Amendment (1973)** inserted **Arts. 371D and 371E** — option **(1)**.
371D: **Six-Point Formula**; 371E: **Central University**.
⚠ Trap: CDX AP History says "**33rd**" — some notes follow it.
xa: The **36th (1975)** dealt with **Sikkim**.
The **35th (1974)** gave Sikkim **associate status**.

20.s: Which one of the following amendments is correctly matched with its principal subject?
o: 100th Amendment — National Commission for Backward Classes
20.x: The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014, provided for the National Judicial Appointments Commission, which was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015. The 97th, 100th and 102nd Amendments dealt respectively with co-operative societies, the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement and the constitutional status of the NCBC.
20.tq: Use the amendment-subject pair and eliminate swapped subjects from neighbouring amendments.
xs: The **99th Amendment (2014)** set up the **National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC)** — option **(2)**.
**GST** came by the **101st (2016)**, not the 97th; the **97th (2011)** is **co-operative societies**.
**One-third seats for women** came by the **106th (2023)**, not the 102nd.
xa: The NJAC was **struck down in 2015**.
**103rd (2019)**: **10% EWS** reservation.
**104th (2019)**: SC/ST seats to **2030**; Anglo-Indian nomination ended.

20.s: Which of the following is the latest enacted Constitutional Amendment referred to in the current constitutional amendment sequence?
20.x: The 106th Constitutional Amendment, enacted in 2023, is the latest enacted amendment in the sequence. The 105th Amendment of 2021 is therefore not the latest.
20.tq: Avoid the stale-current-affairs trap by identifying the highest enacted amendment number and year.
xs: The **106th Amendment, 2023** is the **latest enacted** amendment — option **(4)**.
⚠ UPSC notes calling the **105th** "the most recent" are **stale**.
xa: The 106th gives **one-third seats for women**.
⚠ **103rd and 104th** are both **2019** — EWS and SC/ST seats to **2030**.
Pending: **129th** (ONOE), **130th** (detained ministers); the **131st** was **defeated**.

20.s: Which Constitutional Amendment extended the reservation of seats under Article 334 up to 2030 and also ended the nomination of Anglo-Indians to legislatures?
20.x: The 104th Constitutional Amendment, 2019, extended the reservation of seats for SCs and STs up to 2030 and ended Anglo-Indian nomination.
20.tq: Use the paired consequence—extension plus ending Anglo-Indian nomination—to identify the amendment.
xs: The **104th Amendment (2019)** extended **SC/ST seats to 2030** and **ended Anglo-Indian nomination** — option **(1)**.
The **101st** was **GST** — option (4) wrong.
xa: ⚠ The **103rd** (also **2019**) gave **10% EWS** reservation.
The **106th (2023)**: **one-third seats for women**.

20.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. 97th Amendment (2011) — Co-operative societies
2. 101st Amendment (2016) — Goods and Services Tax
3. 103rd Amendment (2019) — 10 per cent EWS reservation
4. 106th Amendment (2023) — One-third seats for women
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
20.x: All four pairs are correct as per the amendment table: 97th co-operatives, 101st GST, 103rd EWS reservation and 106th women's reservation. Each other code leaves out a correct pair.
20.tq: 97 co-op, 99 NJAC, 101 GST, 103 EWS, 104 SC/ST to 2030, 106 women.
xs: All four pairs are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
xa: The 106th is the **latest enacted** amendment.

20.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act:
1. It inserted Part IXB in the Constitution.
2. Part IXB contains Articles 243ZH to 243ZT.
3. Part IXB was upheld in its entirety by the Supreme Court in 2021.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court struck down Part IXB insofar as it applied to State cooperative societies because the required State ratification was absent.
20.tq: Find the one statement that reverses the judicial outcome.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: the **97th** inserted **Part IXB**.
Statement 2 — correct: Part IXB = **Arts. 243ZH-243ZT**.
Statement 3 — wrong: **Rajendra N. Shah (2021)** struck Part IXB down for **State** co-operatives; it survives only for **multi-State** ones.
xa: The 97th also amended **Art. 19(1)(c)** and added **Art. 43B**.
India has **8.5 lakh+** registered co-operatives (**2026**).

20.s: Which Article was inserted into the Directive Principles of State Policy by the 97th Constitutional Amendment?
20.x: Article 43B was inserted to promote the voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies.
20.tq: Use the exact Article number rather than confusing it with the adjacent Article 43A.
xs: The **97th** inserted **Article 43B** into the DPSPs — option **(2)**.
43B: **voluntary formation, autonomy, democratic control, professional management** of co-operatives.
xa: The 97th also made forming **co-operative societies** a Fundamental Right under **Art. 19(1)(c)**.
New **Part IXB** (**Arts. 243ZH-243ZT**).
Board: **maximum 21** directors; **5-year** term.

20.s: Elections to the board of a co-operative society under Part IXB are to be held
o: Before the expiry of the board's term
Only after the board's term has expired
At the beginning of every financial year
20.x: The election is required to be conducted before the expiry of the board's five-year term.
20.tq: Apply the constitutional time-sequence rule to a board whose term is approaching expiry.
xs: Elections must be held **before the expiry** of the board's term — option **(1)**.
The board has a **5-year** term.
xa: Board of **maximum 21** directors, with **one SC/ST** and **two women** seats.
Audit within **six months** of close of the financial year.

20.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly associated with the constitutional provisions on co-operative societies?
o: Maximum of 21 directors on the board
One seat for an SC or ST member and two seats for women
Audit within six months of the close of the financial year
A six-year fixed term for the board
20.x: The board has a five-year term, not a six-year term. The provisions also mention a maximum of 21 directors, one SC/ST seat, two women seats and audit within six months of the close of the financial year.
20.tq: Find the single altered numerical or time-limit detail among otherwise correct provisions.
xs: **A six-year fixed term** is wrong — the board's term is **5-year** — option **(4)**.
Correct provisions: **maximum 21** directors; **one SC/ST** + **two women** seats; audit within **six months**.
xa: Elections must be held **before the term expires**.
**Rajendra N. Shah (2021)**: Part IXB survives only for **multi-State** co-operatives.

20.s: In Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India (2021), Part IXB was held inapplicable to State co-operative societies mainly because
o: It dealt exclusively with municipal bodies
It had been repealed by the 105th Amendment
It had not been ratified by the States as required
20.x: The Supreme Court struck down Part IXB in its application to State co-operative societies because the required ratification by the States had not been obtained. It continues to operate for multi-State co-operative societies.
20.tq: Connect the judicial outcome with the precise constitutional procedural defect.
xs: Part IXB fell for **State** co-operatives as it had **not been ratified by the States** as required — option **(4)** (**Rajendra N. Shah, 2021**).
It **survives** for **multi-State** co-operatives.
xa: Part IXB came by the **97th Amendment, 2011**.
The 97th also amended **Art. 19(1)(c)** and added **Art. 43B**.
India has **8.5 lakh+** registered co-operatives.

20.s: The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011 made the right to form co-operative societies a Fundamental Right by amending which provision?
20.x: The 97th Amendment added co-operative societies to Article 19(1)(c), which already protected the right to form associations or unions. Article 43B is the new Directive Principle it added, not a Fundamental Right; Art. 19(1)(g) is the freedom of profession and trade; Art. 21A is the right to education (86th).
xs: The **97th (2011)** amended **Article 19(1)(c)** to cover **co-operative societies** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 43B** is the new **DPSP**, not the Fundamental Right — option (4) wrong.
xa: New **Part IXB** (**Arts. 243ZH-243ZT**).
Board seats: **one SC/ST** and **two women**.

20.s: The Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty-Ninth Amendment) Bill, 2024, primarily concerns
o: The constitutional status of the NCBC
20.x: The 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, concerns simultaneous elections under the One Nation, One Election proposal.
20.tq: Match the pending Bill number with its stated constitutional subject.
xs: The **129th Bill, 2024** concerns **One Nation, One Election** — option **(4)**.
It inserts **Art. 82A** and amends Arts. **83, 172, 327**.
xa: Introduced **17 Dec 2024**; with a **JPC** (chair **P.P. Chaudhary**) as of **Aug 2026**.
⚠ **130th** = **30 consecutive days** detention; **131st** = Lok Sabha **850** (defeated).
**EWS** was the **103rd**; women's reservation the **106th**.

20.s: Which of the following Articles is proposed to be inserted by the 129th Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2024?
20.x: The 129th Amendment Bill proposes insertion of Article 82A and amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327 in connection with simultaneous elections.
20.tq: Identify the newly proposed Article while separating it from Articles inserted by enacted amendments.
xs: The **129th Bill, 2024** proposes **Article 82A** (One Nation, One Election) — option **(2)**.
It also amends Arts. **83, 172, 327**.
xa: It came with a **UT Laws Bill**; introduced **17 Dec 2024**.
JPC chair: **P.P. Chaudhary**.

20.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2025?
o: It provides one-third reservation for women in the Rajya Sabha.
It implements the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement.
It concerns removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers detained for 30 consecutive days on serious charges.
It increases the Lok Sabha strength to 850 members.
20.x: The 130th Amendment Bill proposes provisions concerning the removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers detained for 30 consecutive days on serious charges. It also involves Articles 75, 164 and 239AA, including Delhi.
20.tq: Identify the Bill by its distinctive consequence and detention-duration condition.
xs: The **130th Bill, 2025** concerns removal of the **PM, CMs and Ministers** detained **30 consecutive days** on serious charges — option **(3)**.
It amends **Arts. 75, 164, 239AA** (CMs incl. **Delhi**).
Lok Sabha **850** is the **131st** (defeated **17 Apr 2026**) — option (4) wrong.
xa: The 130th is **with a JPC**; deadline extended (**1 Aug 2026**).
Women's **one-third** seats came by the **106th (2023)**.

20.s: With reference to the expected legislative developments concerning women's reservation, which one of the following is correct?
o: A Bill extending reservation only to the Rajya Sabha is expected.
A Bill introducing a BC sub-quota has already been enacted.
A revised delimitation Bill is expected.
A Bill abolishing reservation in local bodies is expected.
20.x: A revised delimitation Bill is expected in the context of implementing the women's reservation law.
20.tq: Use the exact legislative development and reject options that alter the subject or scope of the expected Bill.
xs: A **revised delimitation bill** is expected (Aug **2026**) — option **(3)**.
The **women's quota** remains **unimplemented**, being tied to delimitation.
xa: **No BC sub-quota** for women in the **106th** — a criticism, not an enacted change.
**131st Bill** (Lok Sabha **850**; delimitation) was **defeated** on **17 Apr 2026**.
Local bodies have had **one-third** reservation for women since **1992**.

20.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the debates surrounding the 106th Constitutional Amendment:
1. The amendment has been criticised for not providing a separate sub-quota for BC women.
2. Southern States have expressed apprehension that their share may decline after delimitation.
3. The amendment has already been implemented in all State Legislative Assemblies.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the women's quota remains unimplemented.
20.tq: Find the one false implementation statement; the criticism and regional apprehension are both supported.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: **no BC sub-quota** for women in the **106th**.
Statement 2 — correct: **Southern States** fear a **smaller share after delimitation**.
Statement 3 — wrong: the women's quota is **still unimplemented**.
xa: The LoP asked why the **2023** law was tied to **delimitation** (Aug **2026**).
Local bodies: one-third for women since **1992** (**Arts. 243D, 243T**).

20.s:
Assertion (A): The women's reservation provided by the 2023 law remains unimplemented.
Reason (R): Its implementation has been linked to the completion of delimitation.
Choose the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
20.x: Both the assertion and the reason are true. The linkage of implementation to delimitation explains why the reservation has not yet been operationalised.
20.tq: Test the cause-effect link between a constitutional condition and the present implementation status.
xs: Both A and R are true and R is the correct **explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
A — true: the **2023** women's quota is **still unimplemented**.
R — true: the law was **tied to delimitation**; the LoP questioned this (Aug **2026**).
xa: A **revised delimitation bill** is expected.
The **131st Bill, 2026** on delimitation was **defeated** (**17 Apr 2026**).
Southern States fear a **smaller share** after delimitation.

20.s: With reference to reservation for women in India, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Women have had one-third reservation in local bodies since 1992 under Articles 243D and 243T.
Women have had one-half reservation in local bodies since 1992 under Articles 243D and 243T.
Women have had one-third reservation in Parliament since 1992 under Articles 243D and 243T.
Women have had one-third reservation in local bodies since 2005 under Articles 243G and 243W.
20.x: Local bodies have had one-third reservation for women since 1992. Articles 243D and 243T deal with reservation in Panchayats and Municipalities, respectively.
20.tq: Distinguish the existing local-body reservation framework from the separate and still-unimplemented reservation for Parliament and Assemblies.
xs: Women have had **one-third** reservation in **local bodies** since **1992** under **Arts. 243D, 243T** — option **(1)**.
It is **one-third**, not one-half; and in **local bodies**, not Parliament — options (2), (3) wrong.
xa: The **106th (2023)** extends **one-third seats for women** to legislatures — still **unimplemented**.
Criticism: **no BC sub-quota** in the 106th.

21.s: Which one of the following most accurately describes the basic structure doctrine?
o: The Supreme Court alone may amend the Constitution when required
Only the Preamble can be amended subject to judicial approval
Parliament may amend every constitutional provision without limitation
Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot damage or destroy its core features
21.x: The doctrine permits amendment of any part of the Constitution under Article 368, but prohibits alteration, damage or destruction of features that give the Constitution its identity.
21.tq: Choose the precise statement distinguishing the amending power from its constitutional limitation.
xs: Under the basic structure doctrine, **Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot damage or destroy its core features** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 368** lets Parliament amend any part, including **Fundamental Rights** and the **Preamble**, so "every provision without limitation" (option 3) ignores the limit.
The power to amend lies with **Parliament**, not the Supreme Court; and the doctrine is not about "the Preamble alone".
xa: Basic structure = what **cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Art. 368** (APPSC-G1 2018 key).
The idea was borrowed from **Germany** (Basic Law) and propounded in **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)**.
⚠ PYQ 2024 key: "**core features cannot be amended or altered by Parliament**".

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the basic structure doctrine:
1. It is expressly defined in a separate provision of the Constitution.
2. It was developed by the Supreme Court through judicial decisions.
3. Its content has evolved case by case.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: The doctrine is not expressly defined in the Constitution. It is judge-made and its elements have emerged progressively through case law.
21.tq: Identify the false statement carrying the textual-definition trap.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 is wrong: the doctrine is **judge-made and nowhere defined** in the text of the Constitution.
Statement 2 is correct: it was propounded by the **Supreme Court** in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.
Statement 3 is correct: the SC has **never exhaustively defined** it; the list **grows case by case**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "incorporated by an **Act of Parliament**" is false (PYQ **APPSC-G1 2024**, statement I false).
Origin of the idea: jurist **Dietrich Conrad** (1965) argued that the amending power has **implied limits**.
Critics say the **list is open-ended**, so its content is uncertain.

21.s: With reference to the present position on constitutional amendments, which one of the following is correct?
o: Fundamental Rights may be amended only by an executive order
Fundamental Rights may be amended, provided the basic structure is not damaged
Fundamental Rights cannot be amended under any circumstances
Fundamental Rights are outside the scope of Article 368
21.x: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368, but the amendment remains subject to the basic structure limitation.
21.tq: Apply the rule to a specific constitutional component rather than recalling an isolated case name.
xs: Today, **Fundamental Rights may be amended, provided the basic structure is not damaged** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 368** lets Parliament amend any part, **including FRs and the Preamble**; the only limit is the **basic structure**.
So FRs are neither outside Art. 368 nor unamendable; and amendment is by **Parliament**, never by executive order.
xa: **Golaknath (1967)** once held Parliament **cannot abridge FRs**; **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** overruled it.
**Shankari Prasad (1951)**: Art. 368 **includes the power to amend FRs**.
Exam angle: "can Parliament amend FRs today" — **yes, subject to basic structure**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Preamble is a part of the Constitution.
2. The Preamble may be amended, subject to the basic structure limitation.
3. The basic structure doctrine means that only the Preamble cannot be amended.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: The Preamble is part of the Constitution and is amendable subject to the basic structure doctrine. Basic structure is not confined to the Preamble alone.
21.tq: Separate the true constitutional position from the restrictive ‘only’ formulation.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: **Kesavananda** held the **Preamble is part of the Constitution** and **amendable, subject to the basic structure**.
Statement 3 is wrong: basic structure is what **cannot be amended under Art. 368** — ⚠ it is **not "the Preamble alone"**.
xa: **PYQ G1 2018**: the Preamble's objectives embody the basic structure, so they "**cannot be amended**" under Art. 368.
The word **'secular'** entered the Preamble by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**, yet secularism was basic even before.
Basic structure is **judge-made**, first propounded in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.

21.s: The basic structure doctrine primarily rests on which constitutional principle?
o: Supremacy of Parliament over the Constitution
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
Supremacy of conventions over written provisions
Supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts
21.x: The doctrine rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the power of courts to review constitutional amendments against its basic features.
21.tq: Test the underlying constitutional principle rather than the name of the doctrine.
xs: The doctrine rests on the **supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts** — option **(4)**.
The judicial review principle **accepts the theory of supremacy of Courts** = supremacy of the **Constitution and the courts** over Parliament (APPSC-G2 2017 key).
As a limit, basic structure means supremacy of the **Constitution**, not of **Parliament** — so option 1 is the reverse.
xa: Indian Parliament is **not sovereign in the British sense**.
**Judicial review** is itself basic, so it **cannot be removed even by amendment**.
The doctrine keeps **Art. 368** limited.

21.s: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the Indian Parliament is not sovereign in the British sense?
o: Parliament possesses an unlimited amending power
The Constitution is written and supreme
21.x: Parliament does not possess an unlimited amending power. The written Constitution, Fundamental Rights, judicial review, federal division of powers and limited amending power restrict parliamentary sovereignty.
21.tq: Find the option that reverses a feature of the limited constitutional system.
xs: The odd one out is "**Parliament possesses an unlimited amending power**" — option **(1)**; its amending power is in fact **limited**.
Real reasons Parliament is **not sovereign in the British sense**: **written supreme Constitution**, **FRs**, **judicial review**, **federal division** and **limited amending power**.
So options 2, 3 and 4 are genuine reasons, not exceptions.
xa: **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)**, which tried to make the amending power unlimited and non-justiciable.
Basic structure means supremacy of the **Constitution**, not of courts or Parliament.
The **42nd Amendment** gave Parliament "unlimited amending power" — it was struck down in **Minerva Mills**.

21.s:
Assertion (A): The basic structure doctrine has been criticised as judicial rewriting of the Constitution.
Reason (R): The doctrine has no explicit textual definition and its content is developed by unelected judges case by case.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
21.x: Both statements are true. The absence of a textual definition and the open-ended judicial development of the doctrine form the basis of this criticism.
21.tq: Check whether the reason directly explains the criticism stated in the assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
A is true: critics call the doctrine a "**rewriting of the Constitution**" by **unelected judges**.
R is true and explains A: it has **no textual basis** and its **list is open-ended**, so its content is uncertain.
xa: Critics also call it "**judicial supremacy**"; it is described as **vague and unlisted**.
Defence: it is among the **biggest contributions of the Indian judiciary** to constitutionalism.
Supporters call it the Constitution's **shield against majorities**.

21.s: Which of the following is regarded as a defence of the basic structure doctrine?
o: It checks majoritarian misuse of Article 368 and strengthens constitutionalism
It makes Parliament sovereign in the British sense
It permits majoritarian misuse of Article 368
21.x: The doctrine is defended as a major contribution of the judiciary to constitutionalism because it checks the misuse of the amending power by a temporary majority.
21.tq: Distinguish the stated defence of a doctrine from its criticisms and legal effects.
xs: The defence is that it **checks majoritarian misuse of Article 368** and strengthens **constitutionalism** — option **(1)**.
It is called one of the **biggest contributions of the Indian judiciary** to constitutionalism.
It does not prevent all amendments — Parliament may amend any part, short of the **basic structure** — and it makes Parliament **not sovereign in the British sense**.
xa: Criticism: **no textual basis**; "rewriting of the Constitution" by **unelected judges**.
Support: Constitution's **shield against majorities**; keeps **Art. 368** limited.
**Judicial review** itself is basic and cannot be removed even by amendment.

21.s: Who argued in India in 1965 that the amending power has implied limitations, drawing upon Germany's Basic Law?
21.x: German jurist Dietrich Conrad argued in India in 1965 that constitutional amending power is subject to implied limitations, drawing on the experience of Germany's Basic Law.
21.tq: Pair the jurist with both the year and the country from which the idea was drawn.
xs: **Dietrich Conrad** argued in India in **1965** that the amending power has **implied limits** — option **(3)**.
His argument drew on **Germany**'s **Basic Law** and is treated as the **origin of the idea** of basic structure.
xa: **Justice Mudholkar**'s dissent in **Sajjan Singh (1965)** first spoke of "**basic features**".
CJI **S.M. Sikri** headed the **13-judge bench** in Kesavananda Bharati.
The doctrine was **first propounded** in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.

21.s: The restriction imposed by the 42nd Amendment on High Courts’ power to review central laws was removed by the:
21.x: The 42nd Amendment attempted to bar High Courts from reviewing central laws, and the 43rd Amendment Act, 1977 removed that restriction.
21.tq: Use the amendment sequence to identify the restoring constitutional change.
xs: The **43rd Amendment Act, 1977** removed the bar — option **(2)**.
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** had barred High Courts from declaring central laws invalid; after the 43rd, **High Courts can** do so.
xa: **Constitutional amendments can** also be challenged on **basic structure** grounds.
⚠ Trap: both "cannot" statements are false (**UPSC 2019**).
The **42nd Amendment**'s Art. 368(4), (5) and widened Art. 31C were struck down in **Minerva Mills (1980)**.

21.s: The Supreme Court held in Shankari Prasad (1951) that:
o: The basic structure doctrine applies to all Ninth Schedule laws
Article 368 includes the power to amend Fundamental Rights and an amendment is not law under Article 13
An amendment is law under Article 13 and cannot abridge Fundamental Rights
21.x: Shankari Prasad held that Article 368 covers amendments to Fundamental Rights and that a constitutional amendment is not ‘law’ within the meaning of Article 13.
21.tq: Match the earliest case with its specific holding and avoid later-case attributes.
xs: **Shankari Prasad (1951)** held that **Art. 368 includes the power to amend FRs** and an amendment is **not "law" under Art. 13** — option **(2)**.
Option 4 is the **Golaknath (1967)** view: an amendment **is** "law" and Parliament cannot abridge FRs.
The **42nd Amendment** provisions were struck down later, in **Minerva Mills (1980)**.
xa: **Sajjan Singh (1965)** upheld the **17th Amendment** and reaffirmed Shankari Prasad.
**Golaknath** overruled both, by **11 judges, 6:5**.
Ninth Schedule laws are tested by the **Waman Rao (1981)** cut-off of **24 April 1973**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Golaknath case (1967):
1. It held that Fundamental Rights are "transcendental and immutable".
2. It held that a constitutional amendment is not "law" under Article 13.
3. It was decided by an 11-judge bench by a 6:5 majority.
4. It arose from a challenge to the 24th Amendment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: Golaknath called FRs transcendental and immutable and was decided 6:5 by 11 judges. Statement 2 is wrong: Golaknath held an amendment IS law under Art. 13 (it was Shankari Prasad that said it is not). Statement 4 is wrong: Golaknath challenged the 17th Amendment; the 24th Amendment (1971) was Parliament's reply to Golaknath. Hence options B, C and D, which include 2 or 4, are wrong.
21.tq: Golaknath = 17th Amdt challenged, amendment is 'law', 6:5 of 11; the 24th came after it as the reply.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: Golaknath called FRs **"transcendental and immutable"**.
Statement 2 is wrong: Golaknath held an amendment **is** "law" under **Art. 13** (Shankari Prasad said it is not).
Statement 3 is correct: **11 judges, 6:5**. Statement 4 is wrong: it challenged the **17th Amendment**; the **24th Amendment (1971)** was Parliament's reply.
xa: ⚠ Bench splits: **Golaknath 11 judges, 6:5**; **Kesavananda 13 judges, 7:6**; **NJAC 4:1**.
**Prospective overruling** originated in **Golaknath (1967)**.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** overruled Golaknath.

21.s: The dissent of Justice Mudholkar in which case first referred to the idea of ‘basic features’ of the Constitution?
21.x: Justice Mudholkar’s dissent in Sajjan Singh (1965) is noted as the first judicial reference to the idea of basic features.
21.tq: Test the precursor observation rather than the later case that formally propounded the doctrine.
xs: Justice **Mudholkar**'s dissent in **Sajjan Singh (1965)** first spoke of "**basic features**" — option **(3)**.
**Sajjan Singh** upheld the **17th Amendment** and reaffirmed **Shankari Prasad**.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** came later and **first propounded** the doctrine itself.
xa: Jurist **Dietrich Conrad** argued in India (**1965**) that the amending power has **implied limits**.
**Golaknath (1967)** overruled both Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh.
First application of the doctrine: **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**.

21.s: The constitutional response to the Golaknath judgment was provided through which amendment, which amended Articles 13 and 368?
21.x: The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1971 was Parliament’s response to Golaknath and amended Articles 13 and 368.
21.tq: Match the amendment number and year with the constitutional response to the judgment.
xs: The **24th Amendment, 1971** was Parliament's reply to Golaknath — option **(4)**.
It **amended Arts. 13 and 368**, and **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** **upheld** it.
The **17th Amendment** was what Golaknath challenged; the **39th** was struck in Raj Narain; the **42nd** in Minerva Mills.
xa: **Golaknath (1967)**: an amendment **is** "law" under Art. 13; FRs **"transcendental and immutable"**.
The **25th Amendment, 1971** inserted **Art. 31C**.
⚠ Golaknath **11 judges, 6:5**; Kesavananda **13 judges, 7:6**.

21.s: Which one of the following statements about Kesavananda Bharati is correct?
o: It was decided on 26 January 1975 by a 13-judge bench by a 6:7 majority
It was decided by a 7-judge bench by a 6:5 majority in 1971
It was decided on 24 April 1973 by a 13-judge bench by a 7:6 majority
It was decided by an 11-judge bench by a unanimous decision in 1973
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati was decided on 24 April 1973 by a 13-judge bench with a 7:6 majority.
21.tq: Discriminate among closely related dates, bench sizes and majority figures.
xs: **Kesavananda Bharati** was decided on **24 April 1973** by a **13-judge bench**, **7:6** — option **(3)**.
The **13-judge bench** is the **largest bench ever**, headed by CJI **S.M. Sikri**.
The **11-judge bench** (6:5) belongs to **Golaknath (1967)**, not Kesavananda.
xa: **24 April 1973** became the **Waman Rao** cut-off for Ninth Schedule laws.
Kesavananda **overruled Golaknath** and **upheld the 24th Amendment**.
It held the **Preamble is part of the Constitution**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Kesavananda Bharati:
1. It first propounded the basic structure doctrine.
2. It overruled Golaknath.
3. It upheld the 24th Constitutional Amendment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: All three statements are correct. The judgment propounded the basic structure doctrine, overruled Golaknath and upheld the 24th Amendment.
21.tq: Combine the case’s principal doctrinal contribution with its treatment of the earlier judgment and amendment.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
Statement 1: Kesavananda **first propounded** the **basic structure doctrine**.
Statement 2: it **overruled Golaknath**. Statement 3: it **upheld the 24th Amendment**.
xa: Bench: **13 judges** (largest ever), CJI **S.M. Sikri**, **7:6**, on **24 Apr 1973**.
⚠ Exam angle: first propounded in **Kesavananda Bharati**, not Golaknath or Shankari Prasad (**MPPSC 2025**).
Elements held basic: **secularism**, **federalism**, **separation of powers**, **supremacy of Constitution**.

21.s: In which case was the basic structure doctrine applied for the first time, with free and fair elections treated as a basic feature?
21.x: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) marked the first application of the basic structure doctrine, and the relevant clause of the 39th Amendment was struck down; free and fair elections were recognised as a basic feature.
21.tq: Distinguish the formal propounding of a doctrine from its first subsequent application.
xs: The doctrine was first applied in **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)** — option **(2)**.
The **39th Amendment** clause putting the PM's election disputes beyond courts (**Art. 329A(4)**) was struck down; **free and fair elections** held basic.
**Minerva Mills (1980)** concerned the **42nd Amendment**; **Waman Rao (1981)** the cut-off date; **Golaknath (1967)** predates the doctrine.
xa: The case also held **democracy, rule of law, judicial review** basic.
**Kuldip Nayar (2006)** also tied **free and fair elections, democracy** to basic structure.
In **2026**, free and fair elections as basic structure were cited in the debate on making **voting** a fundamental right.

21.s: Which of the following provisions introduced or widened by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment was struck down in Minerva Mills?
o: Articles 368(4) and 368(5), and the widened Article 31C
21.x: Minerva Mills struck down Articles 368(4) and 368(5), which sought to make Parliament's amending power unlimited and amendments non-justiciable, along with the widened form of Article 31C.
21.tq: Use the specific amendment-provision pairing rather than identifying the case by name alone.
xs: **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)** and the **widened Art. 31C** — option **(2)**.
These **42nd Amendment (1976)** clauses excluded **judicial review** and claimed unlimited amending power.
**Art. 329A(4)** fell in **Raj Narain (1975)**; the **NJAC** fell in **2015**; the Ninth Schedule was never struck down as a whole.
xa: Minerva Mills held **judicial review**, **limited amending power** and **FR-DPSP harmony** basic.
**Art. 31C** was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)** and widened by the **42nd**.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: no blanket immunity for Ninth Schedule laws.

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the NJAC case:
1. The 99th Constitutional Amendment was challenged in the case.
2. The National Judicial Appointments Commission Act was struck down.
3. The decision was delivered by a majority of 4:1.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: All three statements are correct. The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act in 2015 by a 4:1 majority, treating judicial independence as part of the basic structure.
21.tq: Check the amendment, the associated law and the numerical majority together.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
In the **NJAC case (SC Advocates-on-Record Assn., 2015)**, the **99th Amendment (2014)** and the **NJAC Act** were struck down.
The majority was **4:1**, on the ground of **judicial independence**.
xa: ⚠ Bench splits: **Golaknath 6:5**, **Kesavananda 7:6**, **NJAC 4:1**.
**Independent judiciary** was earlier held basic in **All India Judges Association (2002)**.
**Judicial review** is basic — **Raj Narain (1975)**, **Minerva Mills (1980)**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the 39th Constitutional Amendment:
1. It placed election disputes concerning the Prime Minister, President, Vice-President and Speaker beyond judicial scrutiny.
2. The relevant provision was struck down in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain.
3. It was upheld because Parliament’s amending power is unlimited.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: The 39th Amendment attempted to place specified election disputes beyond the courts, and the relevant clause was struck down in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975). Statement 3 is false because Parliament’s amending power is limited by the Basic Structure doctrine.
21.tq: Find the legally significant consequence while rejecting the absolute claim about Parliament’s power.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: the **39th Amendment** put election disputes of the **PM (and President, VP, Speaker)** beyond courts (**Art. 329A(4)**).
Statement 2: that clause was **struck down** in **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the amending power is **limited** — it cannot damage the basic structure.
xa: Raj Narain was the **first application** of the doctrine.
**Free and fair elections** were held a basic feature in that case.
**Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down the **42nd Amendment**'s bid for unlimited amending power.

21.s: Which of the following was held to be part of the basic structure in Minerva Mills?
o: Judicial review, limited amending power and harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP
Only the power of judicial review of High Courts
The absolute supremacy of Parliament over the Constitution
21.x: Minerva Mills (1980) affirmed judicial review, the limited nature of the amending power, and the balance or harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.
21.tq: Use the three-part association of Minerva Mills instead of confusing it with Kesavananda or Golaknath.
xs: **Minerva Mills (1980)** held **judicial review**, **limited amending power** and **harmony between FRs and DPSP** basic — option **(1)**.
It struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)** and the **widened Art. 31C** of the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.
Option 4 is the opposite: the doctrine means supremacy of the **Constitution**, not of Parliament.
xa: **Welfare state** was linked with **Bhim Singhji (1981)**.
**HC powers under Arts. 226, 227**: **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**.
**Waman Rao (1981)** followed a year later, fixing the **24 April 1973** cut-off.

21.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 31B — Laws concerning acquisition of estates and agrarian reform
Article 31A — Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule
Article 31C — Laws implementing Article 39(b) and Article 39(c)
Article 350A — Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
21.x: Article 31C protects laws implementing Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, subject to the constitutional and judicial limitations. Article 31A concerns estate acquisition and agrarian reform, Article 31B concerns Ninth Schedule laws, and Article 350B creates the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
21.tq: Check each Article against its precise subject and identify the only correctly matched pair.
xs: **Art. 31C — laws implementing Art. 39(b), (c)** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Art. 31C** saves such laws from **Arts. 14, 19**; it was inserted by the **25th Amendment, 1971**.
Option 1 is wrong: estates and agrarian reform belong to **Art. 31A**. Option 2 is wrong: the **Ninth Schedule** goes with **Art. 31B**.
xa: **Art. 31A** saves laws on acquisition of estates, agrarian reform from **Arts. 14, 19** — inserted by the **1st Amendment, 1951**.
The **Ninth Schedule** was created by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Art. 31B**.
⚠ Kesavananda struck down the part of **Art. 31C** that barred courts from questioning a law declared to give effect to DPSP.

21.s: Article 31C was inserted by the:
21.x: Article 31C was inserted by the Twenty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1971 to protect laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
21.tq: Separate the amendment associated with Article 31C from the First Amendment associated with Articles 31A and 31B.
xs: **Art. 31C** was inserted by the **Twenty-Fifth Amendment, 1971** — option **(1)**.
It saves laws implementing **Art. 39(b), (c)** from **Arts. 14, 19**.
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** only **widened** it; the **1st Amendment (1951)** inserted **Arts. 31A, 31B**.
xa: The widened Art. 31C was **struck down** in **Minerva Mills (1980)**.
Art. 31C = DPSP primacy over Arts. 14, 19 — a rule from **Parliament**, not a judge-made doctrine.
**Kesavananda** struck down the part of Art. 31C barring judicial review — **judicial review is basic**.

21.s: Which one of the following statements about the Ninth Schedule is correct?
o: It contains only laws implementing Article 39(b) and Article 39(c).
It contains fewer than 50 entries and enjoys complete immunity from judicial review.
It has grown to more than 280 entries, but inclusion does not confer blanket immunity from judicial review.
It has grown to more than 280 entries, and its contents have no constitutional relationship with Fundamental Rights.
21.x: The Ninth Schedule has grown to more than 280 entries, but inclusion does not provide blanket immunity from judicial review, particularly after the decisions in Waman Rao and I.R. Coelho.
21.tq: Reject the absolute claim of complete immunity and combine the numerical fact with the judicial limitation.
xs: The Ninth Schedule has grown to **more than 280** entries, but inclusion **does not confer blanket immunity** — option **(3)**.
It started with **13** Acts and now has **282**.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: **no blanket immunity**, because **judicial review is basic**; it covers land-reform laws, not only Art. 39(b), (c) laws.
xa: Its purpose: protect **land-reform/zamindari-abolition** laws from challenge for violating **Fundamental Rights**.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: entries after **24 April 1973** are open to basic-structure challenge.
Laws enter it **only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment**.

21.s:
Which of the following were associated with the First Amendment Act, 1951?
1. Insertion of Article 15(4)
2. Insertion of Articles 31A and 31B
3. Addition of public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement as grounds under Article 19(2)
4. Insertion of Article 31C
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
21.x: The First Amendment added Article 15(4), Articles 31A and 31B, and the stated grounds under Article 19(2). Article 31C was inserted by the Twenty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1971.
21.tq: Separate provisions belonging to the First Amendment from the closely related provision inserted by the Twenty-Fifth Amendment.
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3** go with the 1st Amendment — option **(1)**.
The **1st Amendment (1951)** created **Arts. 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule**, added **Art. 15(4)**, and added **public order, friendly relations, incitement** to **Art. 19(2)**.
Item 4 is wrong: **Art. 31C** came by the **25th Amendment, 1971**.
xa: **2026 = 75 years** of the 1st Amendment (18 June 2026); assent by President **Rajendra Prasad**.
The Ninth Schedule began with **13** Acts; now **282**.
**I.R. Coelho** limit was restated on the 1st Amendment's **75th** year.

21.s: The Ninth Schedule was introduced into the Constitution by which Amendment and along with which Article?
o: The First Amendment Act, 1951 and Article 31B
The Twenty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1971 and Article 31C
The Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 and Article 31A
The Forty-Second Amendment Act, 1976 and Article 32
21.x: The Ninth Schedule was created by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, along with Article 31B. Article 31A was also inserted by the same Amendment, but Article 31B specifically provides protection to laws placed in the Ninth Schedule.
21.tq: Use the amendment–Article pair rather than identifying the amendment alone.
xs: The Ninth Schedule came by the **First Amendment Act, 1951**, with **Article 31B** — option **(1)**.
The same amendment also inserted **Art. 31A**.
**Art. 31C** came by the **25th Amendment (1971)**, and the **24th (1971)** amended Arts. 13 and 368 — not the Ninth Schedule.
xa: Purpose: shield **land-reform/zamindari-abolition** laws from **FR** challenges.
Covers **both Central and State laws**; entry **only through a constitutional amendment**.
Example: **76th Amendment, 1994** placed Tamil Nadu's **69% reservation** Act.

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Ninth Schedule:
1. It protects both Central and State laws.
2. A law can be placed in it only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment.
3. It was originally created mainly to protect laws relating to land reforms.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: All three statements are correct. The Ninth Schedule covers Central and State laws, inclusion requires a constitutional amendment by Parliament, and its original focus was land-reform legislation.
21.tq: Check the institutional requirement and the original purpose before selecting the combined option.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
Statement 1: it covers **both Central and State laws**.
Statement 2: laws enter **only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment**.
Statement 3: purpose was to protect **land-reform/zamindari-abolition** laws (PYQ G1 2024).
xa: Created by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Art. 31B**.
Size: **13** Acts at start → **282** now.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: post-1973 entries can be tested on basic structure.

21.s: The Ninth Schedule initially contained how many Acts?
21.x: The Ninth Schedule began with 13 Acts, primarily relating to land reforms.
21.tq: Retain the initial numerical value separately from the present number of entries.
xs: The Ninth Schedule began with **13** Acts — option **(1)**.
It has since grown to **282** Acts.
xa: Created by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Art. 31B**, mainly for **land-reform** laws.
⚠ **13** Acts at start → **282** now; cut-off **24 April 1973** = date of Kesavananda.
Example entry: Tamil Nadu's **69% reservation** Act, by the **76th Amendment, 1994**.

21.s: Tamil Nadu's law providing 69 per cent reservation was placed in the Ninth Schedule by which Constitutional Amendment?
21.x: The Tamil Nadu 69 per cent reservation law was placed in the Ninth Schedule through the 76th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1994.
21.tq: Link the famous law with its specific amendment number and year.
xs: The **76th Amendment Act, 1994** placed Tamil Nadu's **69%** reservation Act in the Ninth Schedule — option **(1)**.
It shows that laws enter the Ninth Schedule **only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment**.
xa: Since such an entry came after **24 April 1973**, it is open to basic-structure review (**Waman Rao**, **I.R. Coelho**).
**I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)**: post-1973 laws invalid if they abrogate the essence of **Arts. 14, 19, 21**.
The Schedule covers **both Central and State laws**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Waman Rao treated 24 April 1973 as a significant cut-off date.
2. Ninth Schedule laws added after the cut-off date are completely immune from judicial review.
3. The basic-structure doctrine is relevant to examining post-cut-off Ninth Schedule entries.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because post-24 April 1973 entries are open to basic-structure review rather than enjoying complete immunity.
21.tq: Reject the absolute expression “completely immune” and apply the cut-off rule.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **Waman Rao (1981)** fixed the **cut-off date 24 April 1973**.
Statement 2 is wrong: entries after it are **open to challenge**, not immune.
Statement 3: post-cut-off entries are tested on **basic structure**.
xa: **24 April 1973** is the date of the **Kesavananda Bharati** judgment.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**, a **nine-judge bench**, rejected **blanket immunity**.
Waman Rao applied the cut-off to **Ninth Schedule/Art. 31A** laws.

21.s: The decision in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu is associated with which of the following propositions?
o: Post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws may be invalidated if they damage the basic structure.
Only pre-1973 laws can be tested for violation of Fundamental Rights.
Parliament may place laws in the Ninth Schedule without a constitutional amendment.
Ninth Schedule laws have blanket immunity from judicial review.
21.x: I.R. Coelho rejected blanket immunity and held that post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws can be examined to determine whether they damage the basic structure.
21.tq: Identify the case by its rejection of blanket immunity.
xs: **I.R. Coelho (2007)** held that **post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws** may be invalid if they **damage the basic structure** — option **(1)**.
There is **no blanket immunity**, because **judicial review is basic** — so option 4 is wrong.
Laws enter the Schedule **only through a constitutional amendment** — so option 3 is wrong.
xa: Bench: **nine judges**.
**Rights / direct-impact test**: invalid if they abrogate the essence of **Arts. 14, 19, 21**.
It builds on the **Waman Rao (1981)** cut-off of **24 April 1973**.

21.s: The I.R. Coelho case applied the ‘rights test’ or ‘direct impact test’ primarily with reference to the essence of which Articles?
21.x: Under the rights or direct-impact test, a post-1973 Ninth Schedule law may be invalid if it abrogates the essence of the rights protected under Articles 14, 19 and 21.
21.tq: Separate the three Articles in the direct-impact test from other Fundamental Rights provisions.
xs: The **rights / direct-impact test** looks at the essence of **Arts. 14, 19 and 21** — option **(1)**.
Under **I.R. Coelho (2007)**, post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws are invalid if they damage the basic structure or abrogate the essence of these Articles.
xa: Coelho was decided by a **nine-judge bench**.
**Arts. 31A, 31C** save certain laws from **Arts. 14, 19**.
**No blanket immunity**, because **judicial review is basic**.

21.s: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu was decided by a bench comprising:
21.x: I.R. Coelho was decided by a nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court.
21.tq: Associate the case with its bench strength, a frequently tested numerical detail.
xs: **I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)** was decided by **nine judges** — option **(3)**.
**Eleven** judges sat in **Golaknath (1967)**; **13** in Kesavananda.
xa: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** was also a **nine-judge bench**.
Coelho: **no blanket immunity** for Ninth Schedule laws after **24 Apr 1973**.
Test: essence of **Arts. 14, 19, 21**.

21.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. First Constitutional Amendment introducing Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule
B. Kesavananda Bharati judgment
C. Waman Rao judgment
D. I.R. Coelho judgment

Select the correct sequence.
21.x: The First Amendment was enacted in 1951, Kesavananda Bharati was decided in 1973, Waman Rao in 1981, and I.R. Coelho in 2007.
21.tq: Fix the earliest amendment and latest case first, then place the two Basic Structure decisions between them.
xs: Correct order **A, B, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**1st Amendment (1951)** → **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** → **Waman Rao (1981)** → **I.R. Coelho (2007)**.
xa: Waman Rao's cut-off date (**24 April 1973**) is the date of Kesavananda.
In between: **Golaknath (1967)**, **24th Amendment (1971)**, **Raj Narain (1975)**, **Minerva Mills (1980)**.
Later: **S.R. Bommai (1994)**; **NJAC case (2015)**.

21.s: Which one of the following sets was associated with the basic structure in Kesavananda Bharati?
o: Secularism, federalism and separation of powers
Preventive detention, reservation and emergency powers
Property taxation, trade regulation and local government
Official language, citizenship and electoral rolls
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati associated secularism, federalism and separation of powers, among other constitutional principles, with the basic structure.
21.tq: Recognise the cluster of foundational constitutional principles rather than isolated ordinary provisions.
xs: **Secularism, federalism and separation of powers** were linked to basic structure in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — option **(1)**.
Kesavananda's list also includes **supremacy of Constitution**, **sovereign democratic republic**, **parliamentary system**, **welfare state**, **individual dignity**.
xa: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** **reaffirmed secularism** and federalism.
**Free and fair elections**: **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**.
⚠ Secularism was basic **even before** the **42nd Amendment (1976)** put the word in the Preamble.

21.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Welfare state — Bhim Singhji case
2. Rule of law — P. Sambamurthy case
3. Arts. 32, 136, 141 and 142 — Delhi Judicial Service Association case
4. Independence of judiciary — NJAC case
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
21.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Bhim Singhji is associated with the welfare state, P. Sambamurthy with rule of law, Delhi Judicial Service Association with the specified Supreme Court powers, and the NJAC case with judicial independence.
21.tq: Verify each case against its specific basic-structure element before choosing the cumulative option.
xs: All four pairs are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2, 3 and 4**).
**Welfare state — Bhim Singhji (1981)**; **Rule of law — P. Sambamurthy (1987)**.
**Arts. 32, 136, 141, 142 — Delhi Judicial Service Assn. (1991)**; **Independent judiciary — NJAC case (2015)**.
xa: **Rule of law** was also held in **Indra Sawhney (1992)**.
**Independent judiciary** also: **All India Judges Association (2002)**.
**Principle of equality**: **Indra Sawhney**; **HC powers under Arts. 226, 227**: **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**.

21.s: The principle of secularism was reaffirmed as part of the basic structure in which case?
o: Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Indira Sawhney v. Union of India
21.x: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), decided by a nine-judge Bench, reaffirmed secularism and federalism as basic-structure principles.
21.tq: Link secularism and federalism with S.R. Bommai rather than with the earlier Kesavananda ruling.
xs: **Secularism** was reaffirmed in **S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)** — option **(3)**.
Bommai, a **nine-judge bench**, also held **federalism** basic in the context of **Art. 356**.
**All India Judges Association (2002)** = independent judiciary; **Kuldip Nayar (2006)** = free and fair elections; **Indra Sawhney** = equality.
xa: Secularism was basic even before the **42nd Amendment (1976)** added the word to the Preamble.
Bommai is an **APPSC-G2 2008** key.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** first listed secularism and federalism.

21.s: Which case is associated with the basic-structure status of the powers of the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227?
o: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
P. Sambamurthy v. Union of India
Bhim Singhji v. Union of India
21.x: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) is associated with the basic-structure status of the High Courts’ powers under Articles 226 and 227.
21.tq: Match the specific constitutional Articles with the case dealing with judicial review powers.
xs: **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** made the **HC powers under Arts. 226, 227** basic — option **(1)**.
**Indra Sawhney** = equality and rule of law; **P. Sambamurthy (1987)** = rule of law; **Bhim Singhji (1981)** = welfare state.
xa: SC powers under **Arts. 32, 136, 141, 142**: **Delhi Judicial Service Assn. (1991)**.
**High Courts can** declare central laws invalid: the **42nd Amendment** bar was removed by the **43rd (1977)**.
**Judicial review** is basic: **Raj Narain**, **Minerva Mills**.

21.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Free and fair elections — Minerva Mills
High Court powers under Articles 226 and 227 — S.R. Bommai
21.x: B is correct: Indra Sawhney (1992) is listed for the principle of equality. Free and fair elections go with Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (and Kuldip Nayar), not Minerva Mills; HC powers under Arts. 226-227 with L. Chandra Kumar (1997), not S.R. Bommai; independent judiciary with All India Judges Association and the NJAC case, not Waman Rao.
21.tq: Use the case-specific association and watch for swapped case names.
xs: **Principle of equality — Indra Sawhney** is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
**Free and fair elections** go with **Raj Narain (1975)** and **Kuldip Nayar (2006)**, not Minerva Mills.
**HC powers under Arts. 226, 227** go with **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**, not S.R. Bommai; **independent judiciary** with **All India Judges Association** and **NJAC**, not Waman Rao.
xa: **Indra Sawhney (1992)** is also cited for **rule of law**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: **secularism** and **federalism**.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: Ninth Schedule cut-off **24 April 1973**.

21.s: The expression that the Preamble’s objectives embody the basic structure implies that those objectives:
o: May be altered without constitutional limitation by Parliament
Can be removed by an ordinary parliamentary law
Cannot be amended in a manner that destroys the basic structure under Article 368
Have no relevance to constitutional interpretation
21.x: The objectives embodied in the Preamble form part of the Constitution’s basic structure. They cannot be amended under Article 368 in a manner that destroys that structure.
21.tq: Apply the basic-structure limitation to a proposed constitutional amendment rather than treating amendment power as unlimited.
xs: The Preamble's objectives **cannot be amended in a manner that destroys the basic structure** under **Art. 368** — option **(3)**.
**PYQ G1 2018**: Preamble's objectives embody the basic structure → "**cannot be amended**" under Art. 368.
An ordinary law cannot touch them, and Parliament's amending power is **limited**.
xa: **Kesavananda** held the **Preamble is part of the Constitution** and amendable, subject to the basic structure.
⚠ Basic structure is **not "the Preamble alone"**.
Kesavananda's list includes **sovereign democratic republic**, **secularism**, **welfare state**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Secularism was recognised as a basic feature even before the word was inserted into the Preamble.
2. The word ‘secular’ was inserted into the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
3. Secularism became a basic feature only because of its textual insertion in 1976.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because secularism was treated as a basic feature even before the word ‘secular’ was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment.
21.tq: Separate constitutional text from the underlying basic-structure principle.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **secularism** was basic even before the word entered the Preamble.
Statement 2: the **42nd Amendment (1976)** put 'secular' into the Preamble.
Statement 3 is wrong: it was already basic from **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.
xa: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** reaffirmed **secularism**, with **federalism**.
The **42nd Amendment** also widened **Art. 31C** and added **Art. 368(4), (5)**.
Bommai was a **nine-judge bench** (APPSC-G2 2008 key).

21.s:
Which of the following are recognised as elements of the Basic Structure of the Constitution?
1. Judicial review
2. Independence of the judiciary
3. Powers of the Supreme Court under Articles 32, 136, 141 and 142
4. Power of Parliament to destroy Fundamental Rights without limitation

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
21.x: Judicial review, judicial independence and the specified constitutional powers of the Supreme Court form part of the Basic Structure. Parliament has no unlimited power to destroy Fundamental Rights.
21.tq: Identify the one proposition that contradicts the limitation imposed by the Basic Structure doctrine.
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3** are basic structure — option **(1)**.
**Judicial review** (Raj Narain, Minerva Mills), **independent judiciary** (All India Judges Association, NJAC) and SC powers under **Arts. 32, 136, 141, 142** (Delhi Judicial Service Assn.).
Item 4 is wrong: Parliament's amending power is **limited**; it **cannot damage or destroy the basic structure**.
xa: Other elements: **republican nature**, **unity and integrity**, **effective access to justice**, **principle of reasonableness**.
**HC powers under Arts. 226, 227**: **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**.
SC has **never exhaustively defined** the list.

21.s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court?
o: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance
Article 31C primacy, prospective overruling and colourable legislation
Unlimited amending power, territorial nexus and harmonious construction
21.x: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance are all Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrines. Article 31C primacy, Article 13(4) and unlimited amending power were created through constitutional amendments, while prospective overruling originated in Golaknath.
21.tq: Eliminate sets containing a Parliament-created amendment rule or a separately identified doctrine.
xs: **Eclipse, severability and pith and substance** are all Supreme Court-made doctrines — option **(1)**.
**Art. 31C primacy** came from Parliament's **25th Amendment (1971)**; **unlimited amending power** from the **42nd Amendment**.
So options 2, 3 and 4 each mix in a **Parliament**-made rule.
xa: Other judge-made doctrines: **colourable legislation**, **harmonious construction**, **territorial nexus**.
**Prospective overruling**: Supreme Court — **Golaknath (1967)**.
**Basic structure**: Supreme Court — **Kesavananda (1973)**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 25th Amendment gave primacy to the Directive Principles over Articles 14 and 19 through Article 31C.
2. The 42nd Amendment widened the scope of Article 31C.
3. The widened form of Article 31C was fully upheld in Minerva Mills.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The widened Article 31C was struck down in Minerva Mills; therefore, statement 3 is false.
21.tq: Use the amendment sequence and the later judicial response to identify the false concluding statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: the **25th Amendment (1971)** gave **DPSP primacy over Arts. 14, 19** via **Art. 31C**.
Statement 2: the **42nd** widened it. Statement 3 is wrong: the widened Art. 31C was **struck down in Minerva Mills (1980)**.
xa: Art. 31C originally saved laws implementing **Art. 39(b), (c)**.
Minerva Mills held **FR-DPSP harmony** basic.
**Kesavananda** struck down the part of Art. 31C barring judicial review.

21.s: In Kesavananda Bharati, which part of Article 31C was struck down as violating the basic structure?
o: The provision giving effect to any Directive Principle an absolute priority over the Constitution
The provision creating the Ninth Schedule
The provision enabling Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights
The provision barring courts from questioning whether a law gives effect to the Directive Principles
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati struck down the part of Article 31C that barred courts from examining whether a law actually gave effect to a Directive Principle. Judicial review was held to be part of the basic structure.
21.tq: Identify the precise judicial-review restriction rather than confusing it with the general objective of Article 31C.
xs: Kesavananda struck down the part **barring courts from questioning** whether a law gives effect to the **Directive Principles** — option **(4)**.
Reason: **judicial review is basic**.
The **Ninth Schedule** came from the **1st Amendment** with **Art. 31B**, not Art. 31C; the power to amend FRs was **upheld** (24th Amendment).
xa: **Art. 31C** was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)** for **Art. 39(b), (c)** laws.
The **42nd** widened it; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck the widened form down.
Art. 31C = DPSP primacy — a **Parliament**-made rule, not a judge-made doctrine.

21.s: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court of India in which case?
21.x: Prospective overruling is a judge-made doctrine that the Supreme Court first applied in Golaknath (1967). Kesavananda (1973) propounded the basic structure; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Art. 368(4),(5); Shankari Prasad (1951) upheld Parliament's power to amend FRs.
21.tq: Golaknath = prospective overruling + FRs transcendental.
xs: **Prospective overruling** was first applied by the Supreme Court in **Golaknath (1967)** — option **(2)**.
It is a **judge-made** doctrine, like eclipse, severability and pith and substance.
**Kesavananda (1973)** propounded the **basic structure**; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)**; **Shankari Prasad (1951)** held Art. 368 includes power to amend FRs.
xa: Golaknath: FRs **"transcendental and immutable"**; an amendment **is** "law" under **Art. 13**.
Bench: **11 judges, 6:5**; it challenged the **17th Amendment**.
Parliament's reply: the **24th Amendment (1971)**, amending **Arts. 13 and 368**.

21.s: Which of the following best expresses the constitutional significance of judicial review under the basic-structure doctrine?
o: Judicial review is available only when the President refers a question to the Supreme Court.
Judicial review may be removed by an ordinary law of Parliament.
Judicial review applies only to Fundamental Rights and never to amendments.
Judicial review is basic and cannot be removed even by a constitutional amendment.
21.x: Judicial review is itself regarded as a basic feature of the Constitution. Consequently, even a constitutional amendment cannot abolish it.
21.tq: Test the consequence of recognising a constitutional feature as part of the basic structure.
xs: **Judicial review is basic and cannot be removed even by a constitutional amendment** — option **(4)**.
That is why **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)** and the widened **Art. 31C**, which excluded judicial review.
**Constitutional amendments can** be challenged on basic structure — so option 3 is wrong; an ordinary law cannot remove it either.
xa: **Kesavananda** struck down the part of **Art. 31C** barring courts from questioning DPSP laws.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: no blanket immunity for Ninth Schedule laws, because **judicial review is basic**.
The doctrine **keeps Art. 368 limited**.

21.s: The argument that voting should be elevated beyond a statutory right is linked in the contemporary basic-structure debate primarily with:
o: Democracy and free and fair elections as basic features
The primacy of Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights
The basic feature of judicial independence alone
The immunity of all election disputes from judicial review
21.x: The argument is based on the view that democracy and free and fair elections are basic features of the Constitution, and therefore voting deserves stronger constitutional protection.
21.tq: Connect the proposed legal change with the basic constitutional features invoked to support it.
xs: The argument rests on **democracy and free and fair elections as basic features** — option **(1)**.
In the **2026** debate on making **voting a fundamental right**, it was argued voting should be **more than a statutory right**.
xa: **Free and fair elections** were held basic in **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**, the **first application** of the doctrine.
**Kuldip Nayar (2006)** also linked **free and fair elections, democracy** to basic structure.
Raj Narain struck down the **39th Amendment** clause (**Art. 329A(4)**) putting the PM's election disputes beyond courts.

21.s: Which of the following statements regarding the debate on the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, is correct?
o: The Supreme Court struck down the Bill for violating judicial independence.
Former CJI B.R. Gavai stated before the JPC that the Bill did not violate the basic structure, while U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised doubts.
Former CJI B.R. Gavai stated that simultaneous polls necessarily violate the basic structure.
Former CJIs U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna rejected all basic-structure concerns about simultaneous polls.
21.x: B.R. Gavai told the Joint Parliamentary Committee that the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, did not violate the basic structure, whereas former Chief Justices U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised basic-structure doubts.
21.tq: Match each public position with the correct constitutional office-holder.
xs: Ex-CJI **B.R. Gavai** told the **JPC** the **129th Amendment Bill, 2024** does **not** violate basic structure, while **U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna** raised doubts — option **(2)**.
The Bill concerns **simultaneous polls**; it has not been struck down by the Supreme Court.
Options 3 and 4 reverse the views of Gavai and of Lalit and Khanna.
xa: Basic structure = what **cannot be amended** under **Art. 368**.
**Free and fair elections** and **federalism** are among the listed basic features.
Critics call the doctrine **vague and unlisted**, even "**judicial supremacy**".

22.s: The Supreme Court judgment in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) primarily concerned which of the following?
o: Recognition of privacy as a fundamental right
Imposition of President's Rule in a State
22.x: The Maneka Gandhi case concerned the impounding of her passport. It also expanded the interpretation of Article 21 by requiring procedure to be fair, just and reasonable.
22.tq: Identify the specific issue associated with the landmark case.
xs: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** concerned the **impounding of a passport** — option **(2)**.
**Privacy** as an FR came in **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)**; **President's Rule** in **S.R. Bommai (1994)**; **instant triple talaq** in **Shayara Bano (2017)**.
xa: It held that Art. 21 procedure must be **fair, just and reasonable**, and this **binds the legislature** too.
Art. 21 covers the **right to travel abroad** and a life **with human dignity**, not mere existence.
Bench: **7 judges**.

22.s: Which one of the following propositions was laid down in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India?
o: Procedure established by law need not satisfy standards of fairness.
The right to life includes a life with dignity and the procedure under Article 21 must be just, fair and reasonable.
The right to travel abroad is exclusively a statutory right.
22.x: Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 protects more than mere existence, includes dignity and travel abroad, and requires a procedure that is just, fair and reasonable. This interpretation also binds the legislature.
22.tq: Distinguish the expanded constitutional meaning from the narrow pre-Maneka interpretation of Article 21.
xs: Maneka Gandhi held the right to life includes a life **with dignity** and Art. 21 procedure must be **just, fair and reasonable** — option **(3)**.
Art. 21 is **not mere existence** (option 1 wrong), and it covers the **right to travel abroad** (option 4 wrong).
The fairness standard **now binds the legislature too** — so option 2 is wrong.
xa: The case arose from **passport impounding** in **1978**.
Decided by a **7-judge** bench.
⚠ **ADM Jabalpur (1976)**: FRs incl. Art. 21 **unenforceable in Emergency** — the "darkest day", effectively overruled.

22.s:
With reference to S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, consider the following statements:
1. The exercise of power under Article 356 is subject to judicial review.
2. A floor test is relevant for determining whether a government enjoys majority support.
3. Secularism was recognised as a basic feature of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: All three statements are correct. The nine-judge S.R. Bommai judgment made President's Rule reviewable, emphasised the floor test and recognised secularism as part of the basic structure.
22.tq: Use the three linked holdings of a single landmark constitutional judgment.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
Statement 1: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** made **Art. 356** (President's Rule) subject to **judicial review**.
Statement 2: majority is tested by a **floor test**. Statement 3: **secularism** is a **basic feature**.
xa: Bench: **9 judges** (PYQ G2 2008; **APPSC-G2 2008** key).
Bommai was revived by **Tamil Nadu** government formation **2026** — majority tested on the **floor of the House**.
Other nine-judge cases: **Indra Sawhney (1992)**, **Puttaswamy (2017)**.

22.s: The Vishaka Guidelines were issued primarily because workplace sexual harassment was held to violate which combination of constitutional guarantees?
o: Freedom of religion and cultural rights
Rights against exploitation and freedom of conscience
22.x: The Vishaka judgment treated workplace sexual harassment as a violation of the constitutional guarantees of equality and life. The Guidelines operated until Parliament enacted a law on the subject.
22.tq: Test the rights affected rather than merely recalling the name of the case.
xs: **Vishaka (1997)** held workplace sexual harassment violates **equality and life** — option **(1)**.
So the Court issued binding **Vishaka Guidelines** on sexual harassment at the workplace, to last **till Parliament's law**.
xa: The Guidelines were replaced by the **POSH Act, 2013**.
Bench: **3 judges**, CJI **J.S. Verma**.
⚠ **Vishaka** and **D.K. Basu** are both **1997** — workplace harassment vs arrest/custody.

22.s: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21.
Article 21 does not include decisional autonomy.
Privacy is a statutory right but not a fundamental right.
Privacy is available only to citizens during an Emergency.
22.x: The Puttaswamy judgment recognised the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21. It also rejected the reasoning adopted in ADM Jabalpur.
22.tq: Test the exact constitutional status and Article attached to the right.
xs: **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)** held **privacy is a fundamental right under Art. 21** — option **(1)**.
It rejected the **ADM Jabalpur** reasoning that Art. 21 is unenforceable in Emergency.
xa: Bench: **nine judges**, CJI **J.S. Khehar**.
⚠ **Shreya Singhal** = **Sec. 66A IT Act** (speech); **Puttaswamy** = privacy under **Art. 21**.
**Puttaswamy II (2018)** upheld the **Aadhaar Act 4:1** with limits; Puttaswamy has also been applied to **DNA paternity tests**.

22.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code.
2. Consensual same-sex acts between adults were decriminalised by the judgment.
3. The judgment was delivered by a five-judge Bench.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
