22.x: All three statements are correct. The five-judge Bench in Navtej Singh Johar read down Section 377 and decriminalised consensual same-sex acts between adults.
22.tq: Combine the case year, statutory provision, legal effect and Bench strength.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
**Navtej Singh Johar (2018)** **read down Sec. 377 IPC** and **decriminalised consensual same-sex acts between adults**.
It was a **five-judge bench** (CJI **Dipak Misra**).
xa: It overruled **Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013)**.
**Naz Foundation (Delhi HC, 2009)** first read down Sec. 377.
The **BNS, 2023** (from **1 July 2024**) has **no Sec. 377 equivalent**.

22.s: Which case was the first to read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code?
22.x: The Naz Foundation case before the Delhi High Court in 2009 was the first to read down Section 377. Navtej Singh Johar subsequently gave the Supreme Court ruling in 2018.
22.tq: Separate the earlier initiating judgment from the later Supreme Court judgment.
xs: **Naz Foundation (Delhi HC, 2009)** first read down **Sec. 377** — option **(2)**.
The Supreme Court's **Navtej Singh Johar (2018)** came later, overruling **Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013)**.
**Shreya Singhal (2015)** was about **Sec. 66A IT Act**; **Puttaswamy (2017)** about **privacy**.
xa: ⚠ **Sec. 377** = Navtej (read down); **Sec. 497** = Joseph Shine (struck down); both **2018**.
Navtej was a **five-judge bench**.
**Supriyo (Oct 2023)**: no fundamental right to marry; same-sex marriage left to **Parliament**.

22.s: The Supreme Court in Shayara Bano v. Union of India held that:
o: Instant triple talaq was valid as an essential religious practice.
Article 25 completely excludes personal law from judicial review.
Polygamy and halala were both declared unconstitutional in the same judgment.
Instant triple talaq was invalid and was not an essential religious practice.
22.x: Shayara Bano declared instant triple talaq invalid and held that it was not an essential religious practice under Articles 25 and 26. The questions of polygamy and halala were left open.
22.tq: Find the precisely limited holding and reject the overbroad extension of the judgment.
xs: **Shayara Bano (2017)** held **instant triple talaq invalid** and **not an essential religious practice** — option **(4)**.
**Polygamy and nikah halala were left open** — so option 3 is wrong.
It examined **Arts. 25-26** — personal law was not kept out of review.
xa: Instant triple talaq = **Talaq-e-biddat**.
Bench: **five judges**, split **3:2**.
⚠ SC issued notice (**Aug 2026**) on a PIL to **ban polygamy**; **Javed (2003)**: polygamy not an essential religious practice.

22.s:
Arrange the following judgments in chronological order:
A. Vishaka
B. Shreya Singhal
C. S.R. Bommai
D. K.S. Puttaswamy
22.x: S.R. Bommai was decided in 1994, Vishaka in 1997, Shreya Singhal in 2015 and K.S. Puttaswamy in 2017.
22.tq: Anchor the earliest and latest years, then arrange the middle judgments.
xs: Order **C, A, B, D** — option **(1)**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** → **Vishaka (1997)** → **Shreya Singhal (2015)** → **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)**.
xa: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** and **Minerva Mills (1980)** come before all four.
**Indra Sawhney (1992)** precedes Bommai.
**Shayara Bano** is also **2017**; **Navtej** and **Joseph Shine** are **2018**.

22.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Indra Sawhney — 50 per cent ceiling and creamy layer exclusion
Minerva Mills — Fundamental Rights and DPSP are complementary
22.x: S.R. Bommai concerned Article 356, judicial review, floor tests and secularism as a basic feature; it did not concern abolition of untouchability. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
22.tq: Find the judgment whose subject is unrelated to the constitutional principle in the pair.
xs: **S.R. Bommai — Abolition of untouchability** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
Bommai dealt with **Art. 356**, judicial review of President's Rule, the **floor test** and **secularism**.
**Indra Sawhney** — **50% ceiling, creamy layer**; **Minerva Mills** — FRs and DPSP **complementary**: both correct.
xa: Minerva Mills also struck down the **42nd Amendment**'s unlimited-power clauses.
Indra Sawhney also held **no reservation in promotion** under **Art. 16(4)**.
Bommai: **9 judges** (APPSC-G2 2008 key).

22.s: Which one of the following was NOT a holding associated with Indra Sawhney?
o: A 50 per cent ceiling on reservation in ordinary circumstances
No reservation in promotion under Article 16(4)
Recognition of secularism as a basic feature
22.x: Recognition of secularism as a basic feature was associated with S.R. Bommai, not Indra Sawhney. Indra Sawhney dealt with the reservation ceiling, creamy layer exclusion and reservation in promotion under Article 16(4).
22.tq: Use a nearby landmark judgment as the distractor while isolating the actual subject of the case.
xs: **Recognition of secularism as a basic feature** was not an Indra Sawhney holding — option **(4)**; that was **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
**Indra Sawhney (1992)** held: **50% ceiling**, **creamy layer** excluded, **no reservation in promotion under Art. 16(4)**.
xa: Indra Sawhney was a **nine-judge** bench.
**Davinder Singh (Aug 2024)**: States may **sub-classify SCs**.
Bommai: **Art. 356** reviewable; **floor test**.

22.s: Which statement correctly describes ADM Jabalpur (1976)?
o: It struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act.
It held that Fundamental Rights, including Article 21, were unenforceable during Emergency.
It held that Article 21 remained fully enforceable during Emergency.
It established privacy as a fundamental right.
22.x: ADM Jabalpur held that Fundamental Rights, including Article 21, could not be enforced during the Emergency. The reasoning was later effectively overruled and rejected in Puttaswamy.
22.tq: Discriminate between a discredited earlier ruling and the later judgment that rejected it.
xs: **ADM Jabalpur (1976)** held **FRs incl. Art. 21 unenforceable in Emergency** — option **(2)**.
It is called the "**darkest day**" and has been **effectively overruled**; **Puttaswamy** rejected its reasoning.
**Sec. 66A** fell in **Shreya Singhal (2015)**; privacy came in **Puttaswamy (2017)**.
xa: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: Art. 21 procedure must be **fair, just and reasonable**.
**Andrabi v NIA (18 May 2026)**: **bail is the rule** even under the **UAPA**.
Puttaswamy: **nine judges**, CJI **J.S. Khehar**.

22.s: Which of the following was struck down in the Joseph Shine judgment?
o: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act
22.x: Joseph Shine struck down Section 497 IPC, which dealt with adultery.
22.tq: Associate the judgment with the exact statutory provision rather than the broad subject.
xs: **Joseph Shine (2018)** struck down **Section 497 IPC (adultery)** — option **(4)**.
**Sec. 377** was read down in **Navtej (2018)**; **Talaq-e-biddat** set aside in **Shayara Bano (2017)**; **Sec. 66A** struck in **Shreya Singhal (2015)**.
xa: ⚠ **Sec. 377** = Navtej (read down); **Sec. 497** = Joseph Shine (struck down); both **2018**.
Joseph Shine was a **five-judge** bench under CJI **Dipak Misra**.
The **BNS, 2023** has **no adultery offence**.

22.s: With effect from 1 July 2024, which of the following correctly describes the position under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
o: The IPC continues unchanged and adultery remains an offence under Section 497.
The BNS replaced the IPC, contains no adultery offence and has no equivalent of Section 377 IPC.
The BNS replaced the IPC but retains Section 377 as a separate provision.
The BNS replaced the IPC and abolished the offence of bigamy.
22.x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024. It contains no adultery offence and has no equivalent of Section 377 IPC; bigamy is dealt with under Section 82 BNS.
22.tq: Separate the current statutory position from the earlier IPC provisions.
xs: The **BNS replaced the IPC**, has **no adultery offence** and **no Sec. 377 equivalent** — option **(2)**.
The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** applies from **1 July 2024**.
Bigamy is not abolished: it is **Sec. 82 BNS** — so option 4 is wrong.
xa: Shah Bano's **Sec. 125 CrPC** is now **Sec. 144 BNSS, 2023**.
FIR provision **CrPC 154** is now **Sec. 173 BNSS**.
**Sec. 497 IPC** was struck down in **Joseph Shine (2018)**.

22.s:
With reference to the legal position after the Supriyo v. Union of India judgment, consider the following statements:
1. There is no fundamental right to marry.
2. The issue of same-sex marriage was left to Parliament.
3. Transgender persons in heterosexual relationships can marry under existing law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: All three statements correctly state the position described in Supriyo v. Union of India (October 2023).
22.tq: Test the distinction between decriminalisation, marriage rights and legislative competence.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
**Supriyo v. Union of India (Oct 2023)**: **no fundamental right to marry**; **same-sex marriage left to Parliament**.
**Transgender persons in heterosexual relationships can marry under existing law**.
xa: **Navtej Singh Johar (2018)** decriminalised consensual same-sex acts between adults.
**Naz Foundation (Delhi HC, 2009)** first read down **Sec. 377**.
**Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)**: **compulsory registration of marriages**.

22.s:
Arrange the following judgments in chronological order:
A. Supriyo v. Union of India
B. K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
C. Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
22.x: K.S. Puttaswamy was decided in 2017, Navtej Singh Johar in September 2018, and Supriyo in October 2023.
22.tq: Place the judgments using their stated years and months.
xs: Order **B, C, A** — option **(1)**.
**K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)** → **Navtej Singh Johar (2018)** → **Supriyo (Oct 2023)**.
xa: **Joseph Shine** is also **2018**; **Shayara Bano** is **2017**.
**Puttaswamy II** (Aadhaar) followed in **2018**.
Same-sex marriage was **left to Parliament** in Supriyo.

22.s: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court struck down which provision as violating Article 19(1)(a)?
o: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000
Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code
Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code
Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act
22.x: Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Sec. 66A of the IT Act, 2000 under the freedom of speech, Art. 19(1)(a). Sec. 377 was read down in Navtej Johar (2018); Sec. 497 was struck down in Joseph Shine (2018); Sec. 8(4) RPA was struck down in Lily Thomas (2013).
22.tq: Shreya Singhal = 66A IT Act = free speech.
xs: **Shreya Singhal (2015)** struck down **Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000** under **Art. 19(1)(a)** — option **(1)**.
**Sec. 377** was read down in **Navtej (2018)**; **Sec. 497** struck in **Joseph Shine (2018)**; **Sec. 8(4) RPA** struck in **Lily Thomas (2013)**.
xa: ⚠ **Shreya Singhal** = Sec. 66A (speech); **Puttaswamy** = privacy under Art. 21.
Shreya Singhal came between **Vishaka (1997)** and **Puttaswamy (2017)**.
**Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024)** rested on **voters' right to information**.

22.s: Under the Aadhaar judgment, authentication records could be retained for a maximum period of:
22.x: The Aadhaar ruling limited retention of authentication records to a maximum of six months. A three-month retention period was not the applicable ruling.
22.tq: Distinguish the correct retention period from the close numerical distractor.
xs: Authentication records may be kept **6 months** at most — option **(4)**.
⚠ The **3-month** retention statement is a known trap (UPSC 2020 key).
xa: **Aadhaar (Puttaswamy II, 2018)**: Bench of **5 judges**; Act upheld **4:1** with limits.
**Sec. 57 struck down** → private entities cannot demand Aadhaar.
Aadhaar does **not prove citizenship, domicile or date of birth** (**Sec. 9**).

22.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of striking down Section 57 of the Aadhaar Act?
o: Private entities could not demand Aadhaar merely under the authority of Section 57.
Aadhaar became unavailable for all government subsidies.
Private entities could freely demand Aadhaar for every contract.
Aadhaar was declared invalid for income-tax purposes.
22.x: The Supreme Court struck down Section 57, preventing private entities from demanding or using Aadhaar on that statutory basis. Aadhaar remained relevant for specified public purposes.
22.tq: Ask which authority or legal provision can support the claimed demand for identification.
xs: With **Sec. 57 struck down**, **private entities cannot demand Aadhaar** on that basis — option **(1)**.
**Private entities cannot use Aadhaar data**.
Aadhaar stayed **mandatory** for **Consolidated Fund subsidies** and **PAN/ITR** — so options 2 and 4 are wrong.
xa: UPSC 2020 key: "**no contract with private corporations to share data**" is correct.
**Not mandatory** for bank accounts, SIMs, school admissions, exams.
Records kept **6 months** at most.

22.s: Aadhaar was held mandatory for which of the following purposes?
o: Subsidies or benefits charged to the Consolidated Fund and PAN or income-tax returns
Private insurance contracts and employment applications
Opening every bank account and obtaining every SIM card
22.x: Aadhaar was held mandatory for specified subsidies and benefits funded from the Consolidated Fund, and for PAN and income-tax return requirements. It was not made mandatory for bank accounts, SIMs, school admissions or examinations.
22.tq: Separate constitutionally permitted mandatory uses from services for which Aadhaar was not compulsory.
xs: Aadhaar is mandatory for **subsidies from the Consolidated Fund** and **PAN/ITR** — option **(1)**.
It is **not** mandatory for **bank accounts**, **SIMs / mobiles**, **school admissions**, **exams** — options 3 and 4 wrong.
**Private entities** cannot demand it (**Sec. 57** struck down) — option 2 wrong.
xa: ⚠ UPSC 2020 key: statements 2 and 4 correct; the **3-month retention** and **insurance** statements are wrong.
Act upheld **4:1** by a bench of **5 judges**.
Aadhaar does **not prove citizenship, domicile or date of birth**.

22.s:
With reference to the Aadhaar judgment, consider the following statements:
1. Aadhaar was not mandatory for bank accounts.
2. Aadhaar was not mandatory for SIM cards.
3. Aadhaar was not mandatory for school admissions or examinations.
4. The judgment authorised contracts with private corporations to share Aadhaar data without restriction.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the judgment did not permit unrestricted contracts with private corporations for sharing Aadhaar data.
22.tq: Use the service-by-service distinction and reject the overbroad data-sharing claim.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Aadhaar is **not mandatory** for **bank accounts**, **SIMs**, **school admissions, exams**.
Statement 4 is wrong: **Sec. 57 was struck down**; **no contract with private corporations to share data**.
xa: Mandatory only for **Consolidated Fund** benefits and **PAN/ITR**.
Records kept **6 months** at most.
Bench: **5 judges**, **4:1**.

22.s: Aadhaar, by itself, does NOT establish which of the following?
o: Eligibility for a specified benefit when legally required
Citizenship, domicile or date of birth
22.x: Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act provides that Aadhaar does not by itself prove citizenship, domicile or date of birth.
22.tq: Identify the legal limitation that prevents an identity document from becoming proof of unrelated status.
xs: Aadhaar does **not prove citizenship, domicile or date of birth** — option **(3)**.
This is stated in **Sec. 9, Aadhaar Act**.
xa: Aadhaar is **mandatory** for **Consolidated Fund** subsidies and **PAN/ITR**.
**Private entities cannot use Aadhaar data** (Sec. 57 struck down).
**Puttaswamy II (2018)** upheld the Act **4:1** with limits.

22.s: Which of the following was NOT associated with the guidelines in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal?
o: Informing a relative or friend of the arrested person
Constitution of a State Security Commission
22.x: D.K. Basu dealt with safeguards relating to arrest and custody, including an arrest memo, informing kin and medical checks. A State Security Commission was associated with police reforms in Prakash Singh.
22.tq: Find the guideline belonging to a neighbouring case rather than the arrest-and-custody case.
xs: **Constitution of a State Security Commission** was not part of **D.K. Basu** — option **(4)**.
**D.K. Basu (1997)** laid down arrest and custody safeguards: **arrest memo**, **informing kin**, **medical checks**.
xa: ⚠ **Vishaka** and **D.K. Basu** both **1997** — workplace harassment vs arrest/custody.
**Handcuffing** only in exceptional cases: **Prem Shankar Shukla (1980)**.
Guideline-making (**Vishaka, Prakash Singh**) is criticised as **judicial legislation**; police reforms poorly implemented.

22.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Lalita Kumari (2013) made registration of an FIR mandatory for cognizable offences.
2. The FIR provision, Section 154 CrPC, now corresponds to Section 173 of the BNSS.
3. Lalita Kumari laid down guidelines on arrest memos and medical checks of persons in custody.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
22.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Lalita Kumari made FIR registration mandatory for cognizable offences under Sec. 154 CrPC, now Sec. 173 BNSS. Statement 3 is wrong: arrest memo, informing kin and medical checks are the D.K. Basu (1997) guidelines. So only option A (1 and 2 only) fits.
22.tq: Lalita Kumari = FIR; D.K. Basu = arrest and custody.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **Lalita Kumari (2013)** made an **FIR mandatory** for cognizable offences.
Statement 2: **CrPC 154** is now **Sec. 173 BNSS**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **arrest memo** and **medical checks** are the **D.K. Basu (1997)** guidelines.
xa: **Handcuffing** only in exceptional cases: **Prem Shankar Shukla (1980)**.
**Compulsory registration of marriages**: **Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)**.
Shah Bano's **Sec. 125 CrPC** = **Sec. 144 BNSS**.

22.s: Which one of the following cases is associated with the compulsory registration of marriages?
o: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
22.x: In Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006), the Supreme Court directed compulsory registration of marriages.
22.tq: Match the social reform direction with the correct judgment.
xs: **Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)** directed **compulsory registration of marriages** — option **(1)**.
**Vishaka** = workplace harassment; **Shayara Bano** = triple talaq; **Prem Shankar Shukla** = handcuffing.
xa: **Arts. 32, 141, 142** let judgments like **Vishaka, Seema** fill legislative gaps until Parliament acts.
**D.K. Basu (1997)**: arrest memo, informing kin, medical checks.
**Lalita Kumari (2013)**: **FIR mandatory** for cognizable offences.

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Vishaka judgment:
1. It concerned sexual harassment at the workplace.
2. Its guidelines were later replaced by the POSH Act, 2013.
3. It declared instant triple talaq invalid.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 relates to Shayara Bano, not Vishaka.
22.tq: Separate closely related social-reform judgments by their subject matter.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **Vishaka (1997)** concerned **workplace sexual harassment**.
Statement 2: its guidelines were replaced by the **POSH Act, 2013**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **instant triple talaq** was set aside in **Shayara Bano (2017)**.
xa: Harassment was held to violate **equality and life**.
Bench: **3 judges**, CJI **J.S. Verma**.
Guidelines required **harassment committees**.

22.s: The Supreme Court judgment concerning handcuffing only in exceptional cases is associated with:
o: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab
Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
22.x: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration (1980) held that handcuffing should be confined to exceptional cases.
22.tq: Recall the specific liberty-related holding attached to the case.
xs: **Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration (1980)** — **handcuffing only in exceptional cases** — option **(2)**.
**Andrabi v NIA (18 May 2026)** is about **bail** being the rule under the **UAPA**.
xa: **D.K. Basu (1997)**: arrest memo, informing kin, medical checks.
**Lalita Kumari (2013)**: FIR mandatory (**Sec. 173 BNSS**).
**Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)**: compulsory registration of marriages.

22.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in Shah Bano (1985)?
o: It held that instant triple talaq was constitutionally valid.
It struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act.
It prescribed the composition of the Election Commission.
It concerned maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC and called for a Uniform Civil Code.
22.x: The Shah Bano case concerned maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC and called for a Uniform Civil Code. Section 125 CrPC is now reflected in Section 144 of the BNSS, 2023.
22.tq: Use the provision-and-principle combination to identify the correct case.
xs: **Shah Bano (1985)** concerned **maintenance under Sec. 125 CrPC** and **called for a UCC** — option **(4)**.
**Sec. 125 CrPC** is now **Sec. 144 BNSS, 2023**.
**Sec. 8(4) RPA** fell in **Lily Thomas (2013)**; the EC selection committee came in **Anoop Baranwal (2023)**.
xa: **Sarla Mudgal (1995)** + **Lily Thomas (2000)**: conversion to Islam cannot evade **bigamy** law.
**Shayara Bano (2017)**: instant triple talaq invalid.
Bigamy = **Sec. 82 BNS**.

22.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Sarla Mudgal — Conversion to Islam cannot be used to evade bigamy law
2. Lily Thomas (2000) — Conversion to Islam cannot be used to evade bigamy law
3. Lily Thomas (2013) — Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act struck down
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
22.x: All three pairs are correct. Sarla Mudgal (1995) and Lily Thomas (2000) addressed conversion and bigamy, while Lily Thomas (2013) concerned disqualification of convicted legislators.
22.tq: Separate judgments with the same litigant name by year and legal subject.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
**Sarla Mudgal (1995)** and **Lily Thomas (2000)**: **conversion to Islam cannot be used to evade bigamy law**.
**Lily Thomas (2013)**: **Sec. 8(4) RPA** struck down — convicted MPs/MLAs disqualified at once.
xa: ⚠ The two Lily Thomas cases are distinct: **2000** (bigamy) vs **2013** (Sec. 8(4) RPA).
⚠ **PUCL** and **Lily Thomas** both **2013** = **NOTA** vs Sec. 8(4) RPA.
Bigamy = **Sec. 82 BNS**.

22.s:
In Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002), the Supreme Court held that election candidates must disclose which of the following?
1. Criminal record
2. Assets
3. Educational qualifications
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
22.x: The ADR judgment required candidates to disclose their criminal record, assets and educational qualifications.
22.tq: Identify the complete set of disclosure requirements rather than a partial list.
xs: Candidates must disclose **criminal record, assets and education** — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
This was held in **Union of India v. ADR (2002)**.
xa: **PUCL (2013)**: **NOTA** option on EVMs.
**Lily Thomas (2013)**: **Sec. 8(4) RPA** struck down.
**Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024)**: scheme struck down on **voters' right to information**.

22.s: The introduction of the NOTA option on Electronic Voting Machines was associated with which judgment?
22.x: The PUCL judgment of 2013 directed the provision of the None of the Above option on EVMs.
22.tq: Recall the electoral reform linked to the named judgment.
xs: **NOTA** on EVMs came from **PUCL (2013)** — option **(2)**.
**ADR (2002)** = candidate disclosure; **Lily Thomas (2013)** = **Sec. 8(4) RPA**; **Anoop Baranwal (2023)** = CEC/EC selection.
xa: ⚠ **PUCL** and **Lily Thomas** are both **2013**.
Anoop Baranwal: CEC/ECs chosen by **PM, LoP, CJI** till a law is made.
ADR disclosure covers **criminal record, assets, education**.

22.s: Which one of the following was the effect of Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013)?
o: Candidates were exempted from disclosing their assets.
Convicted MPs and MLAs could continue in office until their appeals were finally decided.
Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act was struck down and convicted MPs and MLAs were disqualified at once.
22.x: The Supreme Court struck down Section 8(4) of the RPA, resulting in immediate disqualification of convicted MPs and MLAs, subject to the applicable legal position.
22.tq: Reject the reversed consequence and identify the precise effect of striking down a provision.
xs: **Lily Thomas (2013)** struck down **Sec. 8(4) RPA**: **convicted MPs/MLAs disqualified at once** — option **(4)**.
So option 3 (continuing till appeal) is the opposite; **NOTA** came from **PUCL (2013)**; disclosure from **ADR (2002)**.
xa: Distinct from **Lily Thomas (2000)** on **bigamy**.
⚠ **PUCL** and **Lily Thomas** both **2013**.
**Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024)**: struck down unanimously.

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the selection of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners:
1. Anoop Baranwal (2023) provided for selection by a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition and the Chief Justice of India.
2. The arrangement in Anoop Baranwal was permanent and could not be changed by a law of Parliament.
3. Parliament's 2023 Act replaced the Chief Justice of India with a Union Minister in the committee.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the Court's committee was PM, LoP and CJI, and the 2023 Act replaced the CJI with a Union Minister. Statement 2 is wrong: the Court's committee was to operate only till Parliament made a law, which Parliament then did. Options B, C and D all include statement 2.
22.tq: Court arrangement = stop-gap 'till a law is made'; the law swapped CJI for a Union Minister.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **Anoop Baranwal (2023)**: CEC/ECs chosen by **PM, LoP, CJI**.
Statement 2 is wrong: that applied only **till a law is made**.
Statement 3: Parliament's **2023 Act** replaced the **CJI** with a **Union Minister**.
xa: **ADR (2002)**: disclosure of criminal record, assets, education.
**Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024)**: voters' **right to information**.

22.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Aadhaar judgment — Five judges, 4:1 majority
2. In re Article 370 — Five judges, unanimous
3. State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh — Seven judges, 6:1 majority
4. In re Article 370 — States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
22.x: Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Pair 4 is false because sub-classification of Scheduled Castes was held in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, not in the Article 370 case.
22.tq: Start with Bench-strength pairs and identify the swapped holding in the final pair.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Aadhaar**: **5 judges**, **4:1**; **Art. 370 (Dec 2023)**: **5 judges, unanimous**; **Davinder Singh (Aug 2024)**: **7 judges, 6:1**.
Pair 4 is wrong: **sub-classification of SCs** was held in **Davinder Singh**, not the Art. 370 case.
xa: **Demonetisation (Jan 2023)**: upheld **4:1** under **Sec. 26(2) RBI Act**.
**Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024)**: **5 judges**, scheme struck down unanimously.
Art. 370 and Electoral Bonds benches were headed by CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**.

22.s: The judgment in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (August 2024) held that:
o: States cannot classify Scheduled Castes internally under any circumstances.
Sub-classification applies only to Other Backward Classes.
Only Parliament may sub-classify Scheduled Castes, and E.V. Chinnaiah was reaffirmed.
States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes, and it overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004).
22.x: The seven-judge Bench in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, by a 6:1 majority, held that States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes and overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004).
22.tq: Test the precise direction of the later judgment and the precedent it overruled.
xs: **Davinder Singh (Aug 2024)**: **States may sub-classify SCs**, overruling **E.V. Chinnaiah (2004)** — option **(4)**.
Bench: **7 judges**, **6:1**.
So options 1 and 3 (no State sub-classification, Chinnaiah reaffirmed) are wrong.
xa: **E.V. Chinnaiah v State of AP (2004)** had struck down AP's **SC sub-categorisation Act, 2000**.
**Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020)**: struck down **100% ST quota** for teachers in Scheduled Areas.
**Indra Sawhney (1992)**: **50% ceiling**, creamy layer excluded.

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Constitution Bench decision on Article 370:
1. The Court held that Article 370 was temporary.
2. The Court held that the President could make Article 370 inoperative.
3. The Court directed that elections be held.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: The December 2023 Article 370 judgment treated Article 370 as temporary, upheld the power of the President to make it inoperative and directed elections.
22.tq: Retain all three holdings of a Constitution Bench decision rather than selecting only the headline issue.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
**In re Article 370 (Dec 2023)**: Art. 370 **temporary**; **President could make it inoperative**; **elections directed**.
xa: Bench: **5 judges, unanimous**, CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**; abrogation **upheld**.
J&K **statehood to be restored**; Assembly polls by **30 Sep 2024**.
Also in **Dec 2023**'s year: **Demonetisation (Jan 2023)** upheld **4:1**.

22.s: The Supreme Court upheld demonetisation in January 2023 by what majority and under which provision?
o: 3:2 under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act
4:1 under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act
22.x: The demonetisation decision was upheld by a 4:1 majority under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act.
22.tq: Combine the majority figure with the exact statutory provision.
xs: Demonetisation was upheld **4:1** under **Section 26(2) of the RBI Act** — option **(4)**.
**Sec. 173 BNSS** is the FIR provision; **3:2** was **Shayara Bano**; **Art. 370** was a separate case.
xa: Decided in **Jan 2023**.
The **Aadhaar Act** was also upheld **4:1** (Puttaswamy II, **2018**).
**Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024)**: struck down unanimously by **5 judges**.

22.s: The Supreme Court struck down the electoral bonds scheme primarily in relation to which constitutional right?
22.x: In February 2024, the Court unanimously struck down the electoral bonds scheme in the context of voters’ right to information.
22.tq: Connect the scheme with the constitutional transparency right identified in the judgment.
xs: The **Electoral Bonds** scheme was struck down on **voters' right to information** — option **(4)**.
Decided **Feb 2024** by **5 judges**, **unanimously** (ADR (Electoral Bonds)).
xa: **Union of India v. ADR (2002)**: candidates must disclose criminal record, assets, education.
**PUCL (2013)**: **NOTA** on EVMs.
Bench headed by CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**.

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding judgments on Andhra Pradesh reservation matters:
1. E.V. Chinnaiah (2004) struck down Andhra Pradesh's SC sub-categorisation Act, 2000.
2. E.V. Chinnaiah was overruled by State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024).
3. Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020) upheld a 100% ST quota for teachers in Scheduled Areas.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
22.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: E.V. Chinnaiah struck down AP's 2000 sub-categorisation Act and was overruled by Davinder Singh (2024). Statement 3 is wrong: Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao struck down (not upheld) the 100% ST quota for teachers in Scheduled Areas. So only option A fits.
22.tq: Both AP reservation cases struck something down; Chinnaiah was later overruled.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **E.V. Chinnaiah (2004)** struck down AP's **SC sub-categorisation Act, 2000**.
Statement 2: it was **overruled by Davinder Singh (2024)**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020)** **struck down** the **100% ST quota**.
xa: Davinder Singh: **7 judges, 6:1**; States may **sub-classify SCs**.
**AP HC (2022)** ruled against **three capitals**.
**Amaravati** = **sole capital w.e.f. 2 June 2024**.

22.s: Which of the following correctly describes the recent legal position regarding the capital of Andhra Pradesh?
o: Kurnool became the sole capital under the 2022 Andhra Pradesh High Court judgment.
Visakhapatnam became the sole capital with effect from 2 June 2024, and the Supreme Court approved three capitals.
Amaravati became the sole capital with effect from 2 June 2024, and Parliament passed the AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026.
The Andhra Pradesh High Court upheld the three-capital proposal in 2022 without legislative action thereafter.
22.x: After the Andhra Pradesh High Court’s 2022 ruling against three capitals, Amaravati became the sole capital from 2 June 2024. Parliament passed the AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026, in April 2026.
22.tq: Track the sequence of court ruling, effective date and subsequent parliamentary action.
xs: **Amaravati** became the **sole capital w.e.f. 2 June 2024**, and Parliament passed the **AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026** — option **(3)**.
The **AP HC (2022)** ruled **against three capitals** — so options 1, 2 and 4 are wrong.
xa: The Bill passed **LS on 1 Apr** and **RS on 2 Apr 2026**.
**E.V. Chinnaiah (2004)**: AP's **SC sub-categorisation Act, 2000** struck down.
**Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020)**: **100% ST quota** struck down.

22.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. E.V. Chinnaiah judgment
B. Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao judgment
C. Davinder Singh judgment
D. AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026
22.x: E.V. Chinnaiah was decided in 2004, Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao in 2020, Davinder Singh in 2024 and the amendment Bill in 2026.
22.tq: Use the years as the first filter and then check the sequence of the AP developments.
xs: Order **A, B, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**E.V. Chinnaiah (2004)** → **Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020)** → **Davinder Singh (2024)** → **AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026**.
xa: Davinder Singh **overruled** E.V. Chinnaiah.
**AP HC (2022)** ruled against three capitals — between Chebrolu and Davinder Singh.
Bill passed **LS 1 Apr, RS 2 Apr 2026**.

22.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the bench size and Chief Justice associated with the case?
o: Vishaka — three judges, CJI J.S. Verma
Maneka Gandhi — five judges, CJI D.Y. Chandrachud
Electoral Bonds — nine judges, CJI J.S. Khehar
Shayara Bano — seven judges, CJI Dipak Misra
22.x: Vishaka was decided by a three-judge Bench headed by CJI J.S. Verma. Maneka Gandhi had seven judges, Electoral Bonds had five judges headed by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, and Shayara Bano had five judges headed by CJI Dipak Misra.
22.tq: Start with the distinctive three-judge Vishaka combination and eliminate swapped bench details.
xs: **Vishaka — three judges, CJI J.S. Verma** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Maneka Gandhi** had **7 judges**; **Electoral Bonds** **5 judges** under CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**; **Shayara Bano** **5 judges** (**3:2**).
xa: **9 judges**: Bommai; Puttaswamy (CJI **J.S. Khehar**).
**5 judges** under CJI **Dipak Misra**: Navtej, Joseph Shine, Aadhaar.
**7 judges**: Maneka Gandhi; Davinder Singh.

22.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Bommai — nine judges
2. Puttaswamy — nine judges, CJI J.S. Khehar
3. Maneka Gandhi — seven judges
4. Davinder Singh — seven judges
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
22.x: Bommai and Puttaswamy were nine-judge cases; Puttaswamy was associated with CJI J.S. Khehar. Maneka Gandhi and Davinder Singh were decided by seven-judge Benches.
22.tq: Verify bench-size clusters before considering the Chief Justice detail.
xs: All four pairs are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2, 3 and 4**).
**9 judges**: **Bommai**; **Puttaswamy** (CJI **J.S. Khehar**).
**7 judges**: **Maneka Gandhi**; **Davinder Singh**.
xa: **5 judges**: Shayara Bano (**3:2**); Navtej, Joseph Shine, Aadhaar (CJI **Dipak Misra**).
**3 judges**: Vishaka (CJI **J.S. Verma**).
**Indra Sawhney** was also a **nine-judge** bench.

22.s: Which group of cases was associated with a five-judge Bench headed by CJI Dipak Misra?
o: Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Aadhaar
Bommai, Maneka Gandhi and Davinder Singh
Vishaka, Shayara Bano and D.K. Basu
22.x: Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Aadhaar were five-judge Bench cases associated with CJI Dipak Misra.
22.tq: Recognise the correct case cluster instead of matching a single isolated case.
xs: **Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Aadhaar** — **5 judges** under CJI **Dipak Misra** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 370** and **Electoral Bonds** were under CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**; **Puttaswamy** and **Bommai** had **9 judges**.
xa: **Vishaka**: **3 judges**, CJI **J.S. Verma**.
**Maneka Gandhi**, **Davinder Singh**: **7 judges**.
**Shayara Bano**: **5 judges**, **3:2**.

22.s:
Which of the following developments has been identified as a current relevance of the Shayara Bano and related personal-law debate?
1. The Supreme Court issued notice on a PIL seeking a ban on polygamy.
2. Javed (2003) held that polygamy is not an essential religious practice.
3. Bigamy is an offence under Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
22.x: All three are correct: the SC issued notice (Aug 2026) on a PIL to ban polygamy among Muslims; Javed (2003) held that polygamy is not an essential religious practice; and bigamy is an offence under Sec. 82 BNS.
22.tq: Combine the judicial precedent, current development and statutory provision without confusing their roles.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
Statement 1: SC issued notice (**Aug 2026**) on a PIL to **ban polygamy** among Muslims.
Statement 2: **Javed (2003)**: polygamy **not an essential religious practice**. Statement 3: bigamy = **Sec. 82 BNS**.
xa: **Shayara Bano (2017)** left **polygamy and nikah halala** open.
**Sarla Mudgal (1995)** + **Lily Thomas (2000)**: conversion cannot evade bigamy law.
**Shah Bano (1985)** called for a **UCC**.

22.s: Which one of the following developments is associated with the application of the privacy principle in Puttaswamy?
o: Selection of Election Commissioners by a committee
22.x: Puttaswamy's privacy principle was reported as having been applied to DNA paternity tests.
22.tq: Apply a broad constitutional right to the specific modern factual context.
xs: The **Puttaswamy** privacy principle has been **applied to DNA paternity tests** — option **(3)**.
**NOTA** came from **PUCL (2013)**; EC selection by committee from **Anoop Baranwal (2023)**; **compulsory registration of marriages** from **Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)**.
xa: **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)**: **privacy** is a fundamental right under **Art. 21**; **nine-judge** bench.
It **rejected the ADM Jabalpur** reasoning.
**Puttaswamy II (2018)** upheld the **Aadhaar Act 4:1** with limits.

22.s: The proposition that “bail is the rule even under the UAPA” was associated with:
o: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab
22.x: Andrabi v. NIA, reported on 18 May 2026, was associated with the proposition that bail is the rule even under the UAPA.
22.tq: Identify the case from the precise bail principle attributed to it.
xs: **Andrabi v NIA (18 May 2026)** held that **bail is the rule even under the UAPA** — option **(1)**.
**S.R. Bommai** concerned **Art. 356** and the floor test; **Vishaka** concerned workplace sexual harassment.
xa: **ADM Jabalpur (1976)**: FRs incl. **Art. 21** unenforceable in Emergency — the "darkest day".
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: Art. 21 procedure must be **fair, just and reasonable**.
**D.K. Basu (1997)**: arrest memo, informing kin, medical checks.

22.s: Which one of the following is cited as a criticism of the Vishaka and Prakash Singh judgments?
o: They avoided issuing any guidelines in the absence of legislation.
Their guideline-making has been criticised as judicial legislation, and police reforms remain poorly implemented.
They transferred all legislative power to the Governors.
They invalidated the power of judicial review.
22.x: Guideline-making in Vishaka and Prakash Singh has been criticised as judicial legislation, while implementation of police reforms remains poor.
22.tq: Identify the criticism rather than confusing judicial guidelines with legislative enactment.
xs: Their **guideline-making** is criticised as **judicial legislation**, and **police reforms are poorly implemented** — option **(2)**.
They did issue guidelines (option 1 wrong) — **Vishaka** guidelines stood till the **POSH Act, 2013**.
xa: **Significance**: **Arts. 32, 141, 142** let judgments fill legislative gaps (**Vishaka, Seema**) until Parliament acts.
Concern also at "**fading**" environmental jurisprudence as clearances pass easily.
Vishaka: **3 judges**, CJI **J.S. Verma**, **1997**.

22.s: The Supreme Court's proposed guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence concerned the conduct of:
22.x: The proposed guidelines concerned the use of artificial intelligence by the bar and the bench.
22.tq: Identify the professional institutions directly covered by the proposed guidelines.
xs: The SC proposed guidelines on **AI use by bar and bench** — option **(4)**.
They concern lawyers and judges, not Election Commissioners, police or legislatures.
xa: Other current items: **Andrabi v NIA (18 May 2026)** — bail is the rule under the **UAPA**.
**Puttaswamy** applied to **DNA paternity tests**.
SC issued notice (**Aug 2026**) on a PIL to **ban polygamy**.

22.s: Articles 32, 141 and 142 are significant in the context of Vishaka and Seema because they enable the Supreme Court to:
o: Fill legislative gaps temporarily until Parliament acts
Dissolve State Legislatures whenever legislation is absent
Exercise only advisory jurisdiction in social matters
22.x: Articles 32, 141 and 142 provide the constitutional basis through which judicial decisions can fill legislative gaps until Parliament acts, as illustrated by Vishaka and Seema.
22.tq: Connect constitutional provisions with the institutional function they collectively support.
xs: **Arts. 32, 141, 142** let judgments **fill legislative gaps until Parliament acts** — option **(1)**.
Examples: **Vishaka (1997)** guidelines and **Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)** on **compulsory registration of marriages**.
xa: Vishaka's guidelines were replaced by the **POSH Act, 2013**.
Criticism: such **guideline-making** is seen as **judicial legislation**.
**Lalita Kumari (2013)**: **FIR mandatory** for cognizable offences.

23.s: The doctrine of parens patriae is primarily associated with which of the following?
o: The State acting as guardian of persons unable to protect themselves
The Union’s power over residuary subjects
The reconciliation of conflicting constitutional provisions
The invalidation of laws enacted by a State legislature
23.x: Parens patriae means that the State acts as guardian of persons who cannot protect themselves. It is generally invoked in welfare and rights cases.
23.tq: Identify the doctrine from its precise meaning and field of application.
xs: **Parens patriae** = **State as guardian of those who cannot protect themselves** — option **(1)**.
Its field is **welfare / rights cases**.
Reconciling conflicting provisions is **harmonious construction**; residuary power rests with Parliament under **Art. 248**.
xa: **Pith and substance**: judge a law by its **true nature**.
**Colourable legislation**: **cannot do indirectly what cannot be done directly**.
**Territorial nexus**: State law valid outside the State if there is a **sufficient nexus**.

23.s: Which one of the following best describes the doctrine of colourable legislation?
o: A law operating outside a State is always unconstitutional
A State law automatically prevails over a Parliamentary law
A law may be invalidated because its political motive is improper
A legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly
23.x: Colourable legislation embodies the principle that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. It is concerned with legislative competence, not with the motive of the legislature.
23.tq: Distinguish legislative competence from legislative motive.
xs: **Colourable legislation**: a legislature **cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly** — option **(4)**.
It is called a "**fraud on the Constitution**" and concerns **competence, not motive** — so option 3 is wrong.
Laws operating outside a State can be valid under **territorial nexus** — so option 1 is wrong.
xa: Field: **legislative competence**.
**Pith and substance**: incidental trespass is fine if the law's **true nature** is within the list.
Entries get the **widest meaning**.

23.s: A State law having operation outside the State may nevertheless be valid when there is a sufficient connection between the State and the subject matter. This principle is known as:
23.x: The doctrine of territorial nexus permits a State law to operate beyond the State when a sufficient nexus exists between the State and the subject matter of the law.
23.tq: Apply the doctrine to an extra-territorial operation scenario.
xs: This is the **doctrine of territorial nexus** — option **(1)**.
A State law is valid outside the State if there is a **sufficient nexus**; field: **extra-territorial operation**.
xa: Case: **State of Bombay v R.M.D.C. (1957)** — tax on **prize competitions run from outside**.
⚠ **1957** = **R.M.D.C.** (territorial nexus) and **A.S. Krishna** (true character).
**Pith and substance** is the doctrine for Union-State lists.

23.s: The doctrine of harmonious construction requires courts to:
o: Prefer Fundamental Rights over every Directive Principle in all cases
Read apparently conflicting provisions so that both can operate
Treat all constitutional provisions as legally unenforceable
23.x: Harmonious construction seeks an interpretation under which apparently conflicting provisions, including Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, can operate together.
23.tq: Select the interpretation that preserves both apparently conflicting provisions.
xs: **Harmonious construction**: read conflicting provisions so **both operate** — option **(2)**.
Its field: **FR vs DPSP**; provision vs provision — so it does not make one side automatically win.
xa: Case: **Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958)** — temple entry (**Art. 25(2)(b)**) reconciled with **Art. 26(b)**.
**Minerva Mills**: **FR-DPSP harmony** — "FRs are means, DPSPs the ends".
**Incidental and ancillary**: power over an entry covers matters incidental to it.

23.s: Which doctrine was identified in an APPSC question as reconciling Central and Provincial laws?
23.x: The doctrine of pith and substance is used to reconcile Central and Provincial, or Union and State, legislative powers by examining the true nature of the law.
23.tq: Recall the doctrine associated with Union-State legislative reconciliation.
xs: **Pith and substance** reconciles **Central & Provincial laws** — option **(4)** (PYQ G2 2017).
It judges a law by its **true nature**; incidental trespass is fine.
**Territorial nexus** is about extra-territorial operation; **colourable legislation** about competence.
xa: Origin: **Canada**.
Case: **State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara (1951)** — Prohibition Act upheld as **public health** despite touching imports.
**A.S. Krishna (1957)**: true character read from the **whole Act, its object and its effect**.

23.s: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) is associated with which doctrine?
23.x: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, the Prohibition Act was upheld as a public-health measure even though it incidentally touched imports. The case illustrates pith and substance.
23.tq: Link the leading case to the doctrine rather than to the incidental subject involved.
xs: **F.N. Balsara (1951)** applied **pith and substance** — option **(1)**.
The **Prohibition Act** was upheld as **public health** despite touching imports.
**Prospective overruling** belongs to **Golaknath (1967)**; **stare decisis** to **Art. 141**.
xa: ⚠ **1951** = **Balsara** (pith and substance); **1957** = **R.M.D.C.** and **A.S. Krishna**.
Pith and substance is borrowed from **Canada**.
It is the APPSC answer for reconciling **Central & Provincial laws** (PYQ G2 2017).

23.s: Which case is associated with the doctrine of territorial nexus in relation to tax on prize competitions conducted from outside the State?
o: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)
23.x: State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. (1957) concerned taxation of prize competitions run from outside the State and is associated with territorial nexus.
23.tq: Distinguish similarly named cases by the doctrine and factual setting.
xs: **State of Bombay v R.M.D.C. (1957)** — **territorial nexus** — option **(4)**.
It upheld a **tax on prize competitions run from outside** the State.
**F.N. Balsara (1951)** is pith and substance; **A.S. Krishna (1957)** is true character.
xa: ⚠ **1957** = **R.M.D.C.** (territorial nexus) and **A.S. Krishna** (true character).
Territorial nexus: State law valid outside the State if there is a **sufficient nexus**.
Field: **extra-territorial operation**.

23.s: Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) is associated with harmonious construction in the context of reconciling:
23.x: Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) reconciled temple-entry provisions under Article 25(2)(b) with the rights of religious denominations under Article 26(b).
23.tq: Start from the sure case-article pairing.
xs: **Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958)** reconciled **Articles 25(2)(b) and 26(b)** — option **(1)**.
Temple entry under **Art. 25(2)(b)** was read with **Art. 26(b)** by **harmonious construction**.
xa: Harmonious construction: read conflicting provisions so **both operate**.
**Minerva Mills** applied it to **FR-DPSP harmony**.
Order of lists: **Union > Concurrent > State**.

23.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The true character of a law is determined by examining the whole Act, its object and its effect.
2. A.S. Krishna (1957) is associated with this approach.
3. The doctrine examines only the title given to the legislation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
23.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the true character is not determined merely by the title; the whole Act, its object and its effect are considered.
23.tq: Reject the narrow title-only formulation and retain the whole-Act test.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **true character** is read from the **whole Act, its object and its effect**.
Statement 2: this is **A.S. Krishna (1957)**. Statement 3 is wrong: the doctrine looks at the whole Act, not the title alone.
xa: This is part of **pith and substance**, borrowed from **Canada**.
**F.N. Balsara (1951)** is the classic pith and substance case.
⚠ **A.S. Krishna** and **R.M.D.C.** are both **1957**.

23.s: The doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers implies that:
o: An incidental matter must always be placed in the Residuary List
Parliament has no power over matters not expressly listed
A legislative entry covers matters incidental to the subject expressly assigned to it
A State legislature can legislate on every subject connected with public order
23.x: A legislative power over a subject includes powers over matters incidental and ancillary to that subject. Legislative entries are given a wide meaning for this purpose.
23.tq: Apply the main-entry rule to an ancillary matter.
xs: **Incidental and ancillary**: power over an entry **covers matters incidental to it** — option **(3)**.
Entries get the **widest meaning**.
xa: Cases: **R.D. Joshi v Ajit Mills**; **Calcutta Gas**.
Residuary power is with Parliament (**Art. 248**).
**Pith and substance**: incidental trespass is fine.

23.s: Which cases are associated with the doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers?
o: R.D. Joshi v. Ajit Mills and Calcutta Gas
23.x: R.D. Joshi v. Ajit Mills and the Calcutta Gas case are associated with the principle that an entry includes matters incidental and ancillary to it.
23.tq: Identify the cases by the doctrine they illustrate, not by their subject alone.
xs: **R.D. Joshi v Ajit Mills** and **Calcutta Gas** — **incidental and ancillary** — option **(1)**.
They hold that entries get the **widest meaning**.
**Golaknath** = prospective overruling; **Navtej Johar**, **Joseph Shine** = transformative constitutionalism.
xa: Doctrine: power over an entry covers matters **incidental** to it.
**F.N. Balsara (1951)**: pith and substance.
**R.M.D.C. (1957)**: territorial nexus.

23.s: Under Article 254, in the event of repugnancy between a Parliamentary law and a State law on a Concurrent List subject, the general rule is that:
o: The Governor decides which law will operate
The State law prevails throughout India
The Parliamentary law prevails over the repugnant State law
23.x: Article 254 provides that, in case of repugnancy in the Concurrent List, the Parliamentary law prevails over the inconsistent State law.
23.tq: Ask which law prevails in a direct repugnancy conflict.
xs: Under **Art. 254**, **Parliament's law prevails** over a repugnant State law in the **Concurrent List** — option **(3)**.
The Governor does not decide; and the State law does not prevail throughout India.
xa: **Art. 254(2)**: a State law with **President's assent** prevails in that State unless Parliament later overrides it.
Order: **Union > Concurrent > State**.
Residuary power with Parliament (**Art. 248**).

23.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 254(2):
1. A State law on a Concurrent List matter may prevail in that State if it has received the President’s assent.
2. Parliament may subsequently override such a State law.
3. President’s assent makes the State law permanently immune from Parliamentary legislation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
23.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Parliament may later override a State law that has received the President’s assent.
23.tq: Watch for the absolute word “permanently” in the false statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: under **Art. 254(2)**, a State law with **President's assent** prevails in that State.
Statement 2: **Parliament** may later override it. So statement 3 (permanent immunity) is wrong.
xa: General rule (**Art. 254**): Parliament's law **prevails** over a repugnant State law.
Order: **Union > Concurrent > State**.
Residuary power: **Art. 248**.

23.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the order of legislative fields from the Union to the State level, followed by the residuary position?
o: Union, State, Concurrent; residuary power with the Supreme Court
Concurrent, Union, State; residuary power with the President
Union, Concurrent, State; residuary power with Parliament
State, Concurrent, Union; residuary power with States
23.x: The order is Union List, Concurrent List and State List. Residuary legislative power belongs to Parliament under Article 248.
23.tq: Recall both the list hierarchy and the authority holding residuary power.
xs: **Union, Concurrent, State; residuary power with Parliament** — option **(3)**.
Order: **Union > Concurrent > State**; residuary power with Parliament under **Art. 248**.
xa: In India, residuary powers lie with the **Centre (Parliament)**.
**Art. 254**: Parliament's law prevails in the Concurrent List.
Entries get the **widest meaning** (incidental and ancillary).

23.s: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied in India in:
23.x: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court in Golaknath (1967).
23.tq: Use the chronology of leading constitutional cases to identify the anchor case.
xs: **Prospective overruling** was first applied in **Golaknath (1967)** — option **(3)**.
**Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)** concerns **separation of powers**; **Kesavananda** the basic structure.
xa: Origin: **USA**.
**Stare decisis**: **Art. 141** — SC's law binds all courts.
**Pleasure**: **Art. 310**, with **Art. 311** safeguards.

23.s: Article 141 embodies the principle of stare decisis by providing that:
o: The law declared by every High Court binds all courts in India
Only advisory opinions of the Supreme Court are binding
Parliament must approve every Supreme Court judgment
The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within India
23.x: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts within India, reflecting the principle of stare decisis.
23.tq: Link the doctrine to the exact constitutional effect of Article 141.
xs: **Art. 141**: the **law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts** — option **(4)**.
This is **stare decisis**; it is the SC's law, not a High Court's.
xa: **Prospective overruling**: first in **Golaknath (1967)**, origin **USA**.
**Pleasure**: **Art. 310**, with **Art. 311** safeguards.
**Separation of powers**: functional, not rigid (**Ram Jawaya Kapur, 1955**).

23.s: The doctrine of pleasure in relation to civil services is primarily contained in:
o: Article 310, subject to safeguards under Article 311
23.x: Article 310 embodies the pleasure doctrine, while Article 311 provides safeguards for civil servants against arbitrary dismissal, removal or reduction in rank.
23.tq: Pair the principal Article with its constitutional safeguard.
xs: The **pleasure** doctrine is in **Art. 310**, with **Art. 311** safeguards — option **(1)**.
Art. 311 protects **civil servants**.
xa: Origin of the pleasure doctrine: **England**.
**Stare decisis** = **Art. 141**.
**Prospective overruling** = **Golaknath (1967)**, origin **USA**.

23.s: Which statement correctly describes the doctrine of separation of powers as understood in Indian constitutional law?
o: It is completely rigid and excludes all overlap among organs
It is functional rather than rigid
It applies only to the executive and judiciary
It is not connected with the basic structure doctrine
23.x: Indian separation of powers is functional rather than rigid. Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) illustrates this approach, while separation of powers is also regarded as part of the basic structure in Kesavananda Bharati.
23.tq: Reject the absolute “rigid” formulation and identify the Indian adaptation.
xs: Indian **separation of powers** is **functional, not rigid** — option **(2)**.
Case: **Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**.
It is also part of the **basic structure** (**Kesavananda**) — so option 4 is wrong.
xa: Origin: **Montesquieu (France)**.
**Pleasure**: **Art. 310**; **stare decisis**: **Art. 141**.
**Basic structure** origin: **Germany**.

23.s: Constitutional morality is best understood as:
o: Following the opinion of the numerical majority in every case
Giving priority to customary morality over constitutional text
Fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality
Applying only the personal morality of judges
23.x: Constitutional morality requires fidelity to constitutional values, even where those values conflict with prevailing or popular morality. The phrase is associated with Ambedkar, drawing on Grote.
23.tq: Distinguish constitutional values from popular or customary morality.
xs: **Constitutional morality** = **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality** — option **(3)**.
It is not the majority's opinion or customary morality.
xa: The phrase is **Ambedkar's, after Grote**.
Applied in **Navtej Johar (2018)**, **Sabarimala (2018)**, **NCT Delhi (2018)**.
Criticism: attacked as **subjective** → route to **judicial overreach**.

23.s: The phrase “constitutional morality” is associated with B.R. Ambedkar’s reference to:
23.x: Ambedkar used the phrase constitutional morality after Grote.
23.tq: Recall the thinker linked to the phrase through Ambedkar.
xs: Ambedkar used "**constitutional morality**" **after Grote** — option **(4)**.
**Montesquieu** is linked with **separation of powers**, not this phrase.
xa: Meaning: **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality**.
Cases: **Navtej Johar**, **Sabarimala**, **NCT Delhi** (all **2018**).
⚠ Criticised as **subjective**.

23.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Constitutional morality was applied in Navtej Johar, Sabarimala and NCT Delhi (all 2018).
2. Transformative constitutionalism was applied in Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Sabarimala.
3. Navtej Johar applied constitutional morality but not transformative constitutionalism.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
23.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct as per the case lists for each tool. Statement 3 is wrong: Navtej Johar appears in both lists - it applied constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism. So only option A fits.
23.tq: Navtej and Sabarimala sit in both lists; NCT Delhi only under morality, Joseph Shine only under transformative.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **constitutional morality** — **Navtej Johar, Sabarimala, NCT Delhi** (**2018**).
Statement 2: **transformative constitutionalism** — **Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine, Sabarimala**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Navtej Johar** applied **both** doctrines.
xa: ⚠ **NCT Delhi** = constitutional morality only; **Joseph Shine** = transformative constitutionalism only.
Transformative constitutionalism: Constitution as a **tool to change an unequal society**.
Constitutional morality phrase: **Ambedkar**, after **Grote**.

23.s: Transformative constitutionalism views the Constitution primarily as:
o: A document concerned only with administrative procedure
A tool for changing an unequal society
A mechanism for preserving all pre-Constitution social practices
A code that excludes judicial interpretation
23.x: Transformative constitutionalism treats the Constitution as an instrument for transforming an unequal society and advancing substantive constitutional values.
23.tq: Identify the purpose-based meaning of the doctrine.
xs: **Transformative constitutionalism** sees the Constitution as a **tool to change an unequal society** — option **(2)**.
It is the opposite of preserving old social practices.
xa: Applied in **Navtej Johar**, **Sabarimala** and **Joseph Shine**.
⚠ **Joseph Shine** = transformative constitutionalism only.
**Constitutional morality**: fidelity to constitutional values over **popular morality**.

23.s: After Minerva Mills, the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles was understood as:
o: Directive Principles being enforceable in preference to Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights being wholly superior and Directive Principles being irrelevant
Both being read harmoniously, with Fundamental Rights as means and Directive Principles as ends
Both being excluded from constitutional interpretation
23.x: After Minerva Mills, Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are read harmoniously. Fundamental Rights are described as the means and Directive Principles as the ends.
23.tq: Use the means-versus-ends comparison to identify the integrated interpretation.
xs: After **Minerva Mills**, FRs and DPSPs are **read harmoniously** — "**FRs are means, DPSPs the ends**" — option **(3)**.
Neither is wholly superior; this is **harmonious construction** applied to **FR vs DPSP**.
xa: Harmonious construction: read conflicting provisions so **both operate**.
**Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958)**: **Art. 25(2)(b)** reconciled with **Art. 26(b)**.
Doctrines set how **FRs operate against laws**.

23.s: Which of the following doctrines is correctly matched with its foreign origin?
23.x: The doctrine of pith and substance was borrowed from Canada. Prospective overruling is associated with the United States, pleasure with England, and public trust with Roman law.
23.tq: Start with the sure foreign-origin pairing and eliminate the swapped origins.
xs: **Pith and substance — Canada** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Prospective overruling** = **USA**; **pleasure** = **England**; **public trust** = **Roman law**.
xa: **Separation of powers** = **Montesquieu (France)**.
**Basic structure** = **Germany**.
"**Procedure established by law**" = **Japan**.

23.s: The doctrine of public trust is stated to have its origin in:
23.x: The doctrine of public trust has its origin in Roman law.
23.tq: Directly identify the origin of the less commonly tested doctrine.
xs: **Public trust** comes from **Roman law** — option **(1)**.
**Germany** = basic structure; **Canada** = pith and substance; **Japan** = "procedure established by law".
xa: **Pleasure** = **England**.
**Prospective overruling** = **USA**.
**Separation of powers** = **Montesquieu (France)**.

23.s: The basic structure doctrine is identified in the material with which foreign origin?
23.x: The basic structure doctrine is identified with Germany as its foreign origin in the given constitutional comparison.
23.tq: Distinguish the origin of basic structure from the origin of separation of powers.
xs: **Basic structure** = **Germany** — option **(2)**.
**Japan** = "procedure established by law"; **Canada** = pith and substance; **France** = separation of powers.
xa: **Separation of powers** is part of the basic structure (**Kesavananda**).
**Public trust** = **Roman law**.
**Pleasure** = **England**; **prospective overruling** = **USA**.

23.s:
Consider the following pairs of a doctrine or expression and its foreign origin:
1. 'Procedure established by law' — Japan
2. Separation of powers — Montesquieu (France)
3. Prospective overruling — England
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
23.x: Pairs 1 and 2 are correct: 'procedure established by law' comes from Japan and separation of powers from Montesquieu (France). Pair 3 is wrong: prospective overruling comes from the USA; the pleasure doctrine is the one from England.
23.tq: Japan = procedure established by law; USA = prospective overruling; England = pleasure.
xs: Pairs **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
"**Procedure established by law**" = **Japan**; **separation of powers** = **Montesquieu (France)**.
Pair 3 is wrong: **prospective overruling** = **USA**; it is **pleasure** that comes from **England**.
xa: **Pith and substance** = **Canada**.
**Basic structure** = **Germany**; **public trust** = **Roman law**.
Prospective overruling was first applied in **Golaknath (1967)**.

23.s: Which one of the following is a criticism of constitutional morality?
o: It is considered subjective and a possible route to judicial overreach
It makes all Directive Principles directly enforceable
It gives unlimited legislative power to State governments
It prevents courts from referring to constitutional values
23.x: Critics argue that constitutional morality may be subjective and may provide a route to judicial overreach.
23.tq: Identify the recognised criticism rather than a consequence not stated.
xs: "Constitutional morality" is attacked as **subjective** → a route to **judicial overreach** — option **(1)**.
It does not make DPSPs enforceable or prevent reference to constitutional values.
xa: Meaning: **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality**.
Applied in **Navtej Johar**, **Sabarimala**, **NCT Delhi**.
No **2025-26** ruling applies these doctrines by name.

23.s: The broader significance of constitutional interpretation doctrines is that they:
o: Replace the Constitution with conventions of foreign countries
Make every legislative dispute a matter of executive privilege
Keep federal lawmaking workable and determine how Fundamental Rights operate against laws
Remove the distinction between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
23.x: These doctrines make federal lawmaking workable and establish the manner in which Fundamental Rights operate in relation to legislation.
23.tq: Select the option covering both stated dimensions of significance.
xs: These doctrines **keep federal lawmaking workable** and set **how FRs operate against laws** — option **(3)**.
They neither replace the Constitution nor remove the FR-DPSP distinction.
xa: Union-State lists: **pith and substance**; extra-territorial operation: **territorial nexus**.
Legislative competence: **colourable legislation**.
No **2025-26** ruling applies these doctrines by name.

24.s: A constitutional government is best described as a government that
o: places no restriction on executive discretion
is limited by the terms of the Constitution
is controlled exclusively by the judiciary
allows the legislature to exercise unlimited power
24.x: Constitutional government is limited government: governmental power operates within the terms and limits of the Constitution.
24.tq: Select the definition that states the governing principle without an absolute institutional claim.
xs: A constitutional government is **limited government** — **limited by the terms of the Constitution** — option **(2)** (UPSC 2020, 2021 keys).
So it cannot mean unlimited executive or legislative power, nor control by the judiciary alone.
xa: **Constitutionalism**: powers within constitutional limits + **rule of law** + **checks and balances** + **judicial review** + protection of **FRs**.
Best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy = **separation of powers** (UPSC 2021 key).
SC: **majoritarianism cannot override constitutionalism**.

24.s: Montesquieu regarded which arrangement as the most effective means of protecting liberty?
24.x: Montesquieu held that division of powers was the most effective way to protect liberty.
24.tq: Test the thinker-principle association directly.
xs: **Montesquieu** saw **division of powers** as the most effective way to **protect liberty** — option **(2)**.
Fusion of all powers or executive supremacy is what he warned against.
xa: His work: **"The Spirit of Laws" (1748)**; he drew on the **British constitution**.
UPSC 2021 key: best safeguard of liberty = **separation of powers**.
Separation of powers is a **presidential (USA)** principle; India and the UK follow **fusion**.

24.s:
Which of the following are elements of constitutionalism?
1. Operation of powers within constitutional limits
2. Rule of law
3. Checks and balances
4. Judicial review and protection of Fundamental Rights
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: Constitutionalism includes constitutional limits on power, rule of law, checks and balances, judicial review and protection of Fundamental Rights.
24.tq: Use the inclusive option when every listed safeguard forms part of the concept.
xs: All four are elements of **constitutionalism** — option **(4)** (**1, 2, 3 and 4**).
Constitutionalism = **powers within constitutional limits** + **rule of law** + **checks and balances** + **judicial review** + **protection of FRs**.
xa: **Constitutional government** = **limited government** (UPSC 2020, 2021 keys).
**Judicial review** covers laws and executive action (Arts. **13, 32, 226**).
SC: **majoritarianism cannot override constitutionalism**.

24.s: Montesquieu’s discussion of the separation of powers is principally associated with which work and year?
24.x: Montesquieu discussed the separation of powers in The Spirit of Laws, published in 1748. His analysis drew substantially on the British Constitution.
24.tq: Discriminate between a thinker’s exact work and nearby political-philosophy titles by checking both the work and year.
xs: Montesquieu's work is **"The Spirit of Laws" (1748)** — option **(1)**.
He drew on the **British constitution** and held **division of powers** the best way to protect **liberty**.
xa: Presidential (USA) = **separation of powers**; parliamentary (India, UK) = **fusion**.
In India separation is **implicit**, not absolute.
Separation of powers is a **basic feature** (**Kesavananda Bharati, 1973**).

24.s:
Consider the following statements comparing the parliamentary and presidential systems:
1. The parliamentary system rests on fusion of powers, with cooperation and coordination between executive and legislature.
2. In the presidential system of the USA, the executive is drawn from and accountable to the legislature.
3. The principal checks in the US presidential system are checks and balances among the three organs.
4. In India the President is the real executive and the Council of Ministers the nominal executive.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: in the USA the President is independent of Congress; being drawn from and accountable to the legislature is the parliamentary feature. Statement 4 is wrong: in India the President is the nominal head and the Council of Ministers the real executive. Options B, C and D include 2 or 4.
24.tq: Parliamentary = fusion + nominal/real heads; presidential = separation + single real executive.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: parliamentary = **fusion** — **cooperation and coordination**. Statement 3: USA = **checks and balances among three organs**.
Statement 2 is wrong: in the USA the **President is independent of Congress**; an executive drawn from the legislature is parliamentary.
Statement 4 is wrong: in India the **President** is the **nominal** head and the **Council of Ministers** the **real** executive.
xa: Parliamentary checks: **questions**, **confidence/no-confidence votes**.
The USA has a **single real executive**.
⚠ Ambedkar preferred **responsibility over stability**.

24.s:
The choice of the parliamentary system by the framers of the Indian Constitution was influenced by which of the following considerations?
1. Familiarity with parliamentary institutions under the Acts of 1919 and 1935
2. The need to accommodate India’s diversity
3. The desire to avoid American-style conflict between the executive and legislature
4. The constitutional preference for stability over responsibility expressed by Ambedkar
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct reasons for choosing the parliamentary system. Statement 4 is false: Ambedkar preferred responsibility over stability.
24.tq: Spot the reversed constitutional preference in the final statement while retaining the three stated reasons for the framers’ choice.
xs: Reasons **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
India chose the parliamentary system for **familiarity (1919/1935 Acts)**, **diversity**, and to **avoid American-style executive-legislature conflict**.
Statement 4 is wrong: **Ambedkar** preferred **responsibility over stability**.
xa: Parliamentary system = **fusion** of legislature and executive; ministers must be legislators.
Council of Ministers stays only while it has **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.
Collective responsibility: **Art. 75(3)** (Union), **Art. 164(2)** (States).

24.s: Article 50 of the Constitution directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in
o: the public services of the State
24.x: Article 50, a Directive Principle, directs separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
24.tq: Read the exact constitutional scope of Article 50 instead of expanding it to all institutions.
xs: **Art. 50 (DPSP)**: State shall **separate the judiciary from the executive** in the **public services of the State** — option **(1)**.
It is a Directive Principle, not about Governors, elections or Parliament.
xa: **Judiciary insulated**: Arts. **50, 121, 211, 235** (control of subordinate courts).
**AP angle**: Madras Presidency separated the **Collector's judicial powers** in **1816**.
India has **no rigid separation**; it is **implicit**, not absolute.

24.s:
Consider the following statements about separation of powers in India:
1. India follows a completely rigid separation of powers.
2. Separation of powers is implicit rather than absolute.
3. Functions of organs overlap to create checks and balances.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: India does not follow a completely rigid separation. Separation is implicit, and overlapping functions help create checks and balances.
24.tq: Reject the absolute formulation and retain the two qualified statements.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is wrong: India has **no rigid separation**.
Statement 2: separation is **implicit**, not absolute. Statement 3: **overlapping functions** → **checks and balances**.
xa: **Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: the Constitution does **not** recognise a rigid separation of powers.
**Legislature-executive fusion** under the parliamentary system; **judiciary insulated**.
**Kesavananda (1973)**: separation of powers among the **basic features**.

24.s: Which one of the following best describes the institutional arrangement adopted in India?
o: Rigid separation between legislature and executive with no overlap
Executive supremacy over the legislature and judiciary
Judicial supremacy over every legislative and executive function
Legislature-executive fusion under a parliamentary system, with an insulated judiciary
24.x: India has legislature-executive fusion in the parliamentary system, while the judiciary is insulated through constitutional safeguards.
24.tq: Compare the parliamentary fusion of legislature and executive with judicial insulation.
xs: India has **legislature-executive fusion under a parliamentary system**, with an **insulated judiciary** — option **(4)**.
Ministers must be **legislators**; the judiciary is insulated by Arts. **50, 121, 211, 235**.
There is **no rigid separation**, and the **executive is subordinate to the legislature** — so options 1 and 2 are wrong.
xa: BPSC 2001 key: in India the **executive is subordinate to the legislature**.
Council of Ministers lasts only with the **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.
Judicial review of laws and executive action: Arts. **13, 32, 226**.

24.s:
Which of the following provisions contribute to the insulation of the judiciary or the control of subordinate courts?
1. Article 50
2. Article 121
3. Article 211
4. Article 235
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: Articles 50, 121, 211 and 235 collectively reflect safeguards relating to judicial separation, discussion of judges and control of subordinate courts.
24.tq: Use the complete Article cluster rather than treating judicial insulation as a single-provision rule.
xs: All four contribute — option **(4)** (**1, 2, 3 and 4**).
**Art. 50** separates judiciary from executive; **Art. 121** and **Art. 211** bar legislatures from discussing judges' conduct; **Art. 235** gives control of subordinate courts.
xa: ⚠ **121 / 211** = legislature cannot discuss judges; **122 / 212** = courts cannot question legislative procedure.
Art. 121 allows discussion only **on a motion for removal**.
**Art. 142** "complete justice" lets the SC fill gaps.

24.s: Which one of the following correctly reflects the ruling in Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)?
o: The executive can exercise power only after receiving prior approval from the judiciary.
The Indian Constitution does not recognise a rigid separation of powers, and executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws.
The Indian Constitution establishes a rigid separation of powers among the three organs of government.
