Statement 1 correct: the **suspensive veto** returns a Bill **for reconsideration once**.
Statement 2 correct: if re-passed, with or without amendment, he **must** assent.
Statement 3 wrong: it applies to **Ordinary Bills** only — **not Money Bills**.
xa: ⚠ "Suspensive veto on Money Bills" is a **trap** (**APPSC-G1 2024**).
The President's veto is under **Article 111**.

25.s: With reference to the pocket veto of the President of India, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It can be exercised only for a period of six months.
It permits the President to return a Money Bill for reconsideration.
It keeps an Ordinary Bill pending without any constitutional time limit for decision.
It is a veto that can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Parliament.
25.x: Pocket veto means keeping a Bill pending without taking a decision. The Constitution prescribes no time limit for the President to act in this manner, and it applies to Ordinary Bills.
25.tq: Separate pocket veto from suspensive veto by focusing on the absence of a constitutional time limit.
xs: The **pocket veto** keeps an **Ordinary Bill pending** with **no time limit in the Constitution** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It has no six-month limit, is not a return of a Money Bill, and cannot be overridden by a higher majority.
xa: An overridable veto (e.g. by **2/3**) is the **qualified veto** — **US practice**, not available in India.
**Money Bill:** only **assent or withhold**.

25.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of the qualified veto in the Indian constitutional system?
o: It involves the possibility of overriding the veto through a specified stronger majority.
It can be overridden by a higher majority.
It is recognised as a veto available to the President of India.
It is conceptually different from an absolute veto.
25.x: Qualified veto is an overridable veto by a higher majority, but it is not available to the President of India. Therefore, its recognition as an Indian presidential power is incorrect.
25.tq: Identify the exception by separating a general constitutional concept from the power actually available in India.
xs: Being "**available to the President of India**" is NOT true of the **qualified veto** — so option **(3)** is correct.
A **qualified veto** can be **overridden by a higher (e.g. 2/3) majority** — **US practice**.
That overridability is what distinguishes it from the **absolute veto** (simply withholding assent).
xa: The Indian President holds the **suspensive** veto (not for money bills).
**Absolute** veto: **private members' Bills**, or Government Bills when the Cabinet resigns before assent.

25.s:
The absolute veto of the President may ordinarily operate in respect of which of the following situations?
1. A private member's Bill
2. A Government Bill when the Council of Ministers has resigned before assent
3. A Constitutional Amendment Bill
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
25.x: Absolute veto may apply to a private member's Bill and to a Government Bill when the Cabinet resigns before assent. A Constitutional Amendment Bill must receive assent.
25.tq: Apply the veto type to the special categories of Bills rather than to ordinary Bills generally.
xs: Items **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Absolute veto** applies to **private members' Bills** and **Government Bills when the Cabinet resigns before assent**.
Item 3 wrong: on a **Constitutional Amendment Bill** he **must assent** (**24th Amdt**).
xa: **Pocket veto**: Bill kept pending — **no time limit** in the Constitution.
**Suspensive veto**: return **once**; then must assent.

25.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. In the case of a Money Bill, the President may either give assent or withhold assent.
2. The President may return a Money Bill for reconsideration under the suspensive veto.
3. The President is constitutionally bound to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: The President may assent to or withhold assent to a Money Bill but cannot return it for reconsideration. Under the Twenty-Fourth Amendment, assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill is mandatory.
25.tq: Use the Bill-type distinction: Money Bills cannot be returned, whereas Constitutional Amendment Bills require assent.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: for a **Money Bill**, he can only **assent or withhold**.
Statement 2 wrong: the **suspensive veto** applies to Ordinary Bills — **not Money Bills**.
Statement 3 correct: **Constitutional Amendment Bill** → **must assent** (**24th Amdt**).
xa: ⚠ "Suspensive veto on Money Bills" = false (**APPSC-G1 2024**; key: **Only III valid**).
The **qualified veto** is **not available** to the Indian President.

25.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Zakir Husain — First President from South India
Rajendra Prasad — Only President elected twice
S. Radhakrishnan — First President to die in office
M. Hidayatullah — Only President elected unopposed
25.x: Rajendra Prasad was the only President elected twice, in 1952 and 1957. Radhakrishnan was the first President from South India, Zakir Husain was the first to die in office, and Hidayatullah acted as President.
25.tq: Use the wrong-person-with-deed trap by matching each President with the correct distinction.
xs: **Rajendra Prasad — only President elected twice** (**1952, 1957**) is correct — option **(2)**.
**Zakir Husain** was the first to **die in office**; **S. Radhakrishnan** the first from **South India**.
**M. Hidayatullah** was the only **CJI** to act as President; the only one elected **unopposed** was **N. Sanjiva Reddy**.
xa: ⚠ Died in office: **Zakir Husain** and **Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed**; acted: **M. Hidayatullah** and **B.D. Jatti**.
**S. Radhakrishnan** was earlier the **first VP**.

25.s: M. Hidayatullah is remembered in the constitutional history of India as the:
o: Only Chief Justice of India to act as President
25.x: M. Hidayatullah was the only Chief Justice of India to act as President.
25.tq: Identify the unique institutional combination rather than confusing an acting President with an elected President.
xs: **M. Hidayatullah** (**1969**, acting) was the **only Chief Justice of India to act as President** — so option **(1)** is correct.
First from South India = **S. Radhakrishnan**; elected twice = **Rajendra Prasad**; first tribal = **Droupadi Murmu**.
xa: He acted after **Zakir Husain** became the first President to **die in office**.
When both President and VP offices are vacant, the **CJI** acts (**President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969**).

25.s: V.V. Giri became President after winning on the basis of:
o: A nomination by the Supreme Court
25.x: V.V. Giri won the 1969 Presidential election on second-preference votes.
25.tq: Test the distinctive election feature attached to the individual President.
xs: **V.V. Giri** (**1969-74**) won on **second-preference votes** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The President is elected indirectly by **single transferable vote**, which is why preferences count; there is no direct popular election.
xa: The method of **STV** with **secret ballot** is from **Ireland**.
**V.V. Giri** was the **4th** President, after **Zakir Husain** died in office.

25.s:
Consider the following statements about N. Sanjiva Reddy:
1. He was the only President elected unopposed.
2. He was from Andhra Pradesh.
3. He had earlier served as Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
4. He was the first Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: All four statements correctly describe N. Sanjiva Reddy, who served as President from 1977 to 1982.
25.tq: Use the all-inclusive option only after verifying each biographical identifier separately.
xs: All four statements, **1, 2, 3 and 4**, are correct — option **(4)**.
**N. Sanjiva Reddy** (**1977-82**): only President elected **unopposed**, from **AP**, earlier **LS Speaker** and **first CM of AP** (**1956**).
xa: He came from **Anantapur / Nandyala**.
⚠ Elected President in **1977** (some notes say **1978**).
He was the **6th** President.

25.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
25.x: Rajendra Prasad was the first President of India and the only President elected twice; Pratibha Patil was the first woman President.
25.tq: Find the biography attached to the wrong President, a standard wrong-person-with-deed trap.
xs: **Rajendra Prasad — First woman President** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
The **first woman** President was **Pratibha Patil** (**2007-12**); **Rajendra Prasad** was the only one **elected twice**.
Correct pairs: **Droupadi Murmu** — first **tribal**; **K.R. Narayanan** — first **Dalit**.
xa: **Droupadi Murmu** took office on **25 July 2022** as the **15th** President.
**K.R. Narayanan** served **1997-2002**.

25.s:
Arrange the following Presidents of India in chronological order of assuming office:
A. K.R. Narayanan
B. Pratibha Patil
C. N. Sanjiva Reddy
D. Droupadi Murmu
25.x: N. Sanjiva Reddy assumed office in 1977, K.R. Narayanan in 1997, Pratibha Patil in 2007 and Droupadi Murmu in 2022.
25.tq: Place the earliest and latest office-holders first, then resolve the two middle dates.
xs: The order is **C, A, B, D** — option **(1)**.
**N. Sanjiva Reddy** (**1977**) → **K.R. Narayanan** (**1997**) → **Pratibha Patil** (**2007**) → **Droupadi Murmu** (**2022**).
xa: Serial numbers: Reddy **6**, Narayanan **10**, Patil **12**, Murmu **15**.
Firsts: Narayanan — **Dalit**; Patil — **woman**; Murmu — **tribal**.

25.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Article)
A. Article 52
B. Article 54
C. Article 60
D. Article 71

List-II (Subject)
1. Oath or affirmation of the President
2. Election disputes
3. There shall be a President of India
4. Electoral college for election of the President
25.x: Article 52 provides for the office of the President, Article 54 concerns the electoral college, Article 60 concerns the oath or affirmation, and Article 71 concerns election disputes.
25.tq: Start with the sure article-subject pairs and eliminate codes with a misplaced constitutional provision.
xs: **Art. 52** = there shall be a President; **Art. 54** = electoral college; **Art. 60** = oath (by **CJI**); **Art. 71** = election disputes.
xa: **Art. 55** = manner of election (value of votes, **STV**).
**Art. 61** = impeachment; **Art. 62** = time of election to fill a vacancy.

25.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President.
2. Article 56 deals with the term of office of the President and resignation to the Vice-President.
3. Article 58 lays down the qualifications for election as President.
4. Article 60 deals with the President's eligibility for re-election.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false: Article 60 concerns the oath or affirmation, while eligibility for re-election is dealt with by Article 57.
25.tq: Catch the adjacent-article substitution between re-election and oath provisions.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Art. 53** = executive power vested in the President; **Art. 56** = term (**5 years**; resignation to VP); **Art. 58** = qualifications.
Statement 4 wrong: **Art. 60** is the **oath**; re-election is **Art. 57**.
xa: **Art. 59** = conditions of office (no office of profit, emoluments).
**Art. 65** = VP to act as President.

25.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 65 — Vice-President to act as President
Article 72 — Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
25.x: Article 65 provides for the Vice-President acting as President in specified circumstances. Article 72 concerns pardon, Article 74 concerns aid and advice by the Council of Ministers, and Article 76 concerns the Attorney General.
25.tq: Use neighbouring constitutional provisions as distractors and identify the exact article-subject pairing.
xs: **Article 65 — Vice-President to act as President** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Art. 72** = **pardon**; **Art. 74** = Council of Ministers to **aid and advise**.
**Art. 78** = PM's duty to **inform the President**; the **Attorney General** is **Art. 76**.
xa: While acting, the VP **stops functioning as Rajya Sabha Chairman**.
**Art. 71** = election disputes.

25.s: Articles 52 to 78 of the Constitution of India constitute
o: Part V, Chapter I dealing with the Union Executive
Part VI, Chapter I dealing with the State Executive
Part III dealing with Fundamental Rights
Part V, Chapter II dealing with Parliament
25.x: Articles 52 to 78 fall under Part V, Chapter I, which deals with the Union Executive.
25.tq: Distinguish the Part and Chapter classification from the adjacent chapter on Parliament.
xs: **Arts. 52-78** form **Part V, Chapter I** — **The Executive** (Union) — so option **(1)** is correct.
It opens with **Art. 52** (there shall be a President) and ends with **Art. 78** (PM's duty to inform the President).
xa: **Art. 74** = Council of Ministers to aid and advise; **Art. 76** = Attorney General.
**Art. 53**: executive power of the Union vested in the President.

25.s: The Eleventh Constitutional Amendment of 1961 is associated with which of the following changes?
o: Removal of nominated members from the Vice-Presidential electoral college
Providing for election of the Vice-President by State Legislatures
Ending the joint-meeting method for the election of the Vice-President
Introduction of direct election to the office of Vice-President
25.x: The Eleventh Amendment ended the earlier joint-meeting method and provided for election of the Vice-President by the members of both Houses of Parliament.
25.tq: Test the amendment by identifying the precise institutional procedure it altered, not the broader office concerned.
xs: The **11th Amendment, 1961** **ended the joint-meeting method** of electing the Vice-President — so option **(3)** is correct.
The VP's electoral college is **all MPs, elected and nominated**, with **no MLAs** — so nominated members were not removed and States play no part.
xa: ⚠ The President's electoral college **excludes nominated MPs** but includes **elected MLAs**.
A **VP vacancy** (**Art. 68**) has **no** 6-month deadline.

25.s: Jagdeep Dhankhar’s resignation as Vice-President in July 2025 and the subsequent election of C. P. Radhakrishnan are relevant primarily to which constitutional provisions?
25.x: Articles 65 and 68 deal respectively with the Vice-President acting as President and the filling of a vacancy in the office of Vice-President. The July 2025 resignation therefore invoked these provisions.
25.tq: Use the office-function pairing: identify the Articles dealing with acting arrangements and a Vice-Presidential vacancy.
xs: The resignation tested the arrangements of **Articles 65 and 68** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned (July 2025)** → **C.P. Radhakrishnan** elected — the **third** mid-term VP vacancy.
**Art. 61** = impeachment, **Art. 72** = pardon, **Art. 74** = aid and advice, **Arts. 52-53** = the President and executive power.
xa: **Art. 65:** VP acts as President; meanwhile the **Deputy Chairman** presides over the Rajya Sabha.
⚠ Unlike a Presidential vacancy, **Art. 68** has **no** 6-month deadline.

25.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the tenure of the President of India:
1. The Constitution prescribes no limit on the number of terms that a person may serve as President.
2. Rajendra Prasad is the only President to have served two full terms.
3. The two-term limit is expressly imposed by a constitutional amendment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Constitution (Art. 57) allows re-election with no limit on terms, and Rajendra Prasad (1950-62) is the only President to have served two full terms. Statement 3 is false: no constitutional amendment imposes a two-term limit.
25.tq: Distinguish a constitutional rule from historical practice and reject the amendment trap.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **no constitutional term limit** — **Art. 57** allows re-election.
Statement 2 correct: only **Rajendra Prasad** has served **two full terms**.
Statement 3 wrong: no Indian amendment imposes a two-term limit; that is the **US 22nd Amendment**.
xa: Term: **5 years** (**Art. 56**).
**Rajendra Prasad** was elected in **1952** and **1957**.

25.s: Which of the following correctly states the comparison concerning presidential term limits?
o: The United States permits only one presidential term, whereas South Korea permits two five-year terms.
The United States limits a President to two terms, whereas South Korea provides for a single five-year term.
Both the United States and South Korea prescribe two presidential terms.
Both the United States and South Korea prescribe a single five-year presidential term.
25.x: The Twenty-Second Amendment of the United States limits a President to two terms. South Korea follows a single five-year presidential term.
25.tq: Handle comparison questions by checking both parts of the pair rather than recognising only one correct country.
xs: The **US** limits a President to **two terms** and **South Korea** has a **single 5-year term** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The US limit comes from its **22nd Amendment**.
xa: India has **no term limit** (**Art. 57**: re-election allowed).
India borrowed **impeachment** from the **USA**.

25.s: President Droupadi Murmu promulgated the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026. What change did the Ordinance provide?
o: Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, excluding the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 37 to 40, excluding the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, including the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 31 to 33, excluding the CJI
25.x: The 2026 Ordinance increased the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, with the Chief Justice of India excluded from this count.
25.tq: Separate the numerical change from the counting exception relating to the Chief Justice of India.
xs: The Ordinance raised SC judges from **33 to 37, excluding the CJI** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Promulgated by **Droupadi Murmu**; gazette dated **16 May 2026**.
xa: It was **criticised as ordinance misuse**.
Ordinances are issued under **Art. 123**.

25.s: Epuru Sudhakar is associated with which constitutional issue?
25.x: The 2006 Epuru Sudhakar case concerned judicial review of the exercise of the pardoning power. It is associated with the constitutional limits on clemency decisions.
25.tq: Link the case name with its distinctive constitutional power instead of the office or emergency provisions.
xs: **Epuru Sudhakar v. Govt of AP (2006)** is about **review of the pardoning power** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It held judicial review of pardons is **limited** — only for **mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant** grounds.
xa: The case **arose from AP**.
**Kehar Singh (1989)**: no right of oral hearing; **Maru Ram (1980)**: advice of the Council of Ministers.

25.s: The procedure of impeachment of the President and the method of electing the President in the Indian Constitution were borrowed respectively from
25.x: Impeachment of the President is modelled on the USA, while election by proportional representation through the single transferable vote is taken from Ireland. 'Ireland and USA' reverses them; the UK has no elected President to impeach; Canada is the source of a strong Centre and residuary powers, not impeachment.
25.tq: Impeachment = USA; PR-STV election = Ireland.
xs: **Impeachment** was borrowed from the **USA** and the **election method** from **Ireland** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses them.
xa: Election: **proportional representation by STV**, **secret ballot** (**Art. 55(3)**).
Impeachment ground: **"violation of the Constitution"** (**Art. 61**).

26.s: Which of the following correctly describes the President's power over a Money Bill passed by Parliament?
o: The President must reject it if it was introduced on prior recommendation.
The President may return it for reconsideration but cannot reject it.
The President has no role after passage by Parliament.
The President may ratify or reject it, but cannot return it for reconsideration.
26.x: In relation to a Money Bill, the President may assent or withhold assent but cannot return it for reconsideration. Such Bills are generally introduced with prior recommendation.
26.tq: Use the Money Bill exception to the general return power under Article 111.
xs: On a **Money Bill** the President may **ratify or reject** it but **cannot return** it for reconsideration — so option **(4)** is correct.
He usually **assents**, since a Money Bill is introduced with his **prior recommendation** — he is not bound to reject it.
Returning a Bill is possible only for **Ordinary Bills** (and Financial Bills I and II).
xa: ⚠ **Money Bill** = cannot return; **Constitutional Amendment Bill** = must assent; **Ordinary Bill** = return once.
The same applies at the State level: Money Bill — **ratify or reject; cannot return**.

26.s: With reference to a Constitutional Amendment Bill passed by Parliament, which one of the following is correct?
o: The President may reject it by absolute veto.
The President may return it once for reconsideration.
The President must give assent under the 24th Amendment, 1971.
The President may refer it to the Governor for advice.
26.x: The 24th Amendment, 1971 made presidential assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill mandatory; the President cannot reject or return it.
26.tq: Remember the special constitutional-amendment exception to presidential veto powers.
xs: The President **must assent** to a **Constitutional Amendment Bill** under the **24th Amendment, 1971** — so option **(3)** is correct.
He **cannot reject or return** it, so absolute veto and return for reconsideration are both ruled out.
xa: For **Ordinary Bills** he may **ratify, reject or return**.
The Constitutional Amendment Bill row is **not applicable** to State legislation.

26.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Returning a Bill for reconsideration is a one-time power of the President.
2. Financial Bills of Category I and Category II may be returned for reconsideration.
3. The President may return a Constitutional Amendment Bill for reconsideration.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: The return power is one-time and may apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II. A Constitutional Amendment Bill cannot be returned because assent is mandatory.
26.tq: Spot the special exception for Constitutional Amendment Bills among otherwise returnable Bills.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: return for reconsideration is a **one-time** power.
Statement 2 correct: **Financial Bills (I) and (II)** can be returned.
Statement 3 wrong: a **Constitutional Amendment Bill** must get assent — it **cannot be returned** (**24th Amendment, 1971**).
xa: A **Money Bill** also **cannot be returned**.
**Pocket veto** is possible because **Art. 111** prescribes **no time limit**.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about the pocket veto of the President of India:
1. Under it, the President neither assents to, nor rejects, nor returns the Bill.
2. It is possible because Article 111 prescribes no time limit for the President's decision on a Bill.
3. As in the USA, the President must decide within 10 days, failing which the Bill becomes law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statement 1 is correct: pocket veto means keeping the Bill pending without assent, rejection or return. Statement 2 is correct: Art. 111 sets no time limit. Statement 3 is wrong: the 10-day limit is a US feature; India has none. Hence '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
26.tq: No time limit in Art 111 (unlike the US 10 days) makes the pocket veto possible.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: under **pocket veto** the President **neither assents, rejects nor returns**.
Statement 2 correct: **Art. 111** prescribes **no time limit**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **10 days** limit is the **US** rule; India has none.
xa: Only Union instance: **Zail Singh (1986)**, **Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill**.
The **Governor** has **no** pocket veto.

26.s: The only instance of a pocket veto at the Union level is associated with which President and which Bill?
o: Dr. Rajendra Prasad — Indian Telegraph Bill
Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed — Indian Post Office Bill
A.P.J. Abdul Kalam — Prevention of Terrorism Bill
Zail Singh — Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill
26.x: President Zail Singh used the pocket veto in 1986 in relation to the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill.
26.tq: Combine the office-holder, year and Bill to defeat near-name distractors.
xs: The only Union pocket veto: **Zail Singh (1986)** on the **Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill** — so option **(4)** is correct.
He kept the Bill pending, using the absence of any time limit in **Art. 111**.
xa: Pocket veto = **neither assents, rejects nor returns**.
⚠ The **US** President must act within **10 days**; India has no such limit.

26.s: Which statement correctly reflects the present constitutional position concerning a Governor's alleged pocket veto?
o: The Governor has the same indefinite pocket veto as the President.
The Governor has no pocket veto; indefinite inaction under Article 200 is justiciable.
The Governor may keep a Bill pending indefinitely without judicial scrutiny.
The Governor can exercise a pocket veto only over Money Bills.
26.x: The Supreme Court held in 2025 that indefinite inaction by the Governor under Article 200 is justiciable; therefore, the Governor does not possess a presidential-style pocket veto.
26.tq: Discriminate between the President's textual time-gap and the Governor's reviewable inaction.
xs: The **Governor has no pocket veto**; **indefinite inaction under Art. 200** is **justiciable** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This was held by the **SC (2025)**, ruling out an indefinite, unreviewable pocket veto for Governors.
xa: The President's pocket veto rests on **Art. 111**'s lack of a time limit.
The Governor's ordinance power is under **Art. 213**.

26.s: An Ordinance under Article 123 may be promulgated by the President only when:
o: Either House of Parliament is not in session and immediate action is considered necessary
The Lok Sabha alone has been dissolved permanently
The Supreme Court directs the President to promulgate it
Both Houses of Parliament are in session and urgent legislation is required
26.x: Article 123 permits an Ordinance when Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied that immediate action is necessary. The expression includes a situation in which either House is not in session.
26.tq: Focus on the exact constitutional condition and avoid the trap that both Houses must be absent simultaneously.
xs: An Ordinance needs **either House not in session** and the President **satisfied immediate action is needed** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is issued **on ministerial advice**, not on a Supreme Court direction, and not while both Houses sit.
xa: It has the **force of an Act**; can be **retrospective**.
Lapses **6 weeks after reassembly**; maximum life **6 months + 6 weeks**.

26.s: Which one of the following statements about the legislative scope of a Presidential Ordinance is correct?
o: It may amend the Constitution because it has the force of an Act
Its scope is co-extensive with Parliament’s legislative power and it cannot amend the Constitution
It may legislate on any matter, including matters beyond Parliament’s competence
It can be issued only on State List subjects
26.x: An Ordinance can cover matters within Parliament’s legislative competence, but it cannot be used to amend the Constitution.
26.tq: Separate the scope of ordinary legislation from the higher power of constitutional amendment.
xs: An Ordinance's scope is **co-extensive with Parliament's power** and it **cannot amend the Constitution** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is **void** if **beyond Parliament's competence** or if it **violates Fundamental Rights**.
xa: It can **amend or repeal an Act** and be **retrospective**.
The power is a relic of the **GoI Act, 1935**.

26.s: The Governor’s power corresponding to the President’s power to promulgate Ordinances under Article 123 is provided under:
26.x: Article 213 confers the parallel Ordinance-making power on the Governor of a State.
26.tq: Discriminate between the Governor’s pardoning provision and the Governor’s Ordinance provision.
xs: The Governor's parallel ordinance power is in **Article 213** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 161** is the Governor's **pardoning** power, not ordinances.
xa: **AP** used an **Art. 213** ordinance on **organ-transplant committees**.
The **38th Amendment (1975)** made satisfaction under **Arts. 123, 213, 352** non-justiciable.

26.s: Which of the following statements regarding an Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 is correct?
o: It remains valid even if it violates Fundamental Rights.
It cannot amend or repeal an existing Act.
It has the force of an Act of Parliament while it remains operative.
26.x: An Ordinance has the force of an Act and may be retrospective or amend or repeal an Act, subject to constitutional limitations. It becomes void if beyond Parliament's competence or inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
26.tq: Reject absolute limitations and identify the legal effect of an Ordinance.
xs: An Ordinance has the **force of an Act** of Parliament while it operates — so option **(3)** is correct.
It **can** be **retrospective** and **can amend or repeal an Act**.
It is **void** if it **violates Fundamental Rights** or is beyond Parliament's competence.
xa: It **cannot amend the Constitution**.
The President may **withdraw** it **at any time**.

26.s: The ordinance-making power of the President under Article 123 is regarded as a relic of which earlier enactment?
26.x: The President's ordinance-making power under Article 123 is a relic of the Government of India Act, 1935, which gave the Governor-General power to issue ordinances. The 1909 Act brought Morley-Minto reforms, the 1919 Act introduced dyarchy, and the 1947 Act ended British rule; none is the stated source of Article 123.
26.tq: Ordinance = 1935 Act legacy, like the Governor-General's ordinances.
xs: The ordinance power is a **relic of the Government of India Act, 1935** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The notes trace **Art. 123** to this Act, not to the 1909, 1919 or 1947 Acts.
xa: Governor's parallel power: **Art. 213**.
Criticism: frequent ordinances **bypass parliamentary deliberation**.

26.s: What is the maximum possible life of a Presidential Ordinance, assuming the constitutional conditions for its promulgation and continuation are met?
26.x: The maximum possible life of an Ordinance is six months plus six weeks, linked to the interval between parliamentary sessions and the post-reassembly period.
26.tq: Do not confuse the six-week post-reassembly period with the total maximum life.
xs: Maximum life of an Ordinance is **six months and six weeks** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It lapses **six weeks after Parliament reassembles**, counted from the later date.
xa: It ends **earlier** if **both Houses disapprove** it.
The President may **withdraw** it **at any time**.

26.s: Which Constitutional Amendment made the President’s satisfaction in promulgating an Ordinance final, and which Amendment reversed that position?
o: 38th Amendment made it final; 44th Amendment reversed it
39th Amendment made it final; 42nd Amendment reversed it
42nd Amendment made it final; 44th Amendment reversed it
44th Amendment made it final; 38th Amendment reversed it
26.x: The 38th Amendment of 1975 made the President’s satisfaction final, while the 44th Amendment reversed that position.
26.tq: Pair the two Amendments with opposite effects and check their chronological order.
xs: The **38th Amendment made it final** (**1975**) and the **44th Amendment reversed it** (**1978**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
The 38th made satisfaction under **Arts. 123, 213, 352** **non-justiciable**.
xa: ⚠ **38th** = non-justiciable; **44th** = reversed; **Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)** = **justiciable**.
**IYB 2026** p.**699** prints "would be called in question" — read "**would not**".

26.s: The Supreme Court in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) held that:
o: Every Ordinance automatically becomes a constitutional amendment
Routine re-promulgation of Ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution
The President’s satisfaction is never subject to review
An Ordinance must remain in force for at least six months
26.x: D.C. Wadhwa held that routine re-promulgation without placing the Ordinance before the legislature amounts to a fraud on the Constitution.
26.tq: Match the case with its distinctive holding and avoid importing the later case’s broader formulation.
xs: **D.C. Wadhwa (1987)**: **repeated re-promulgation** without placing before the legislature is a **fraud on the Constitution** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The case is about re-promulgation; it did not make satisfaction unreviewable or fix a minimum life.
xa: **Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017)**, a **7-judge** bench: **laying before the legislature is mandatory**.
Satisfaction is **open to judicial review** (Krishna Kumar Singh).

26.s: An Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 ordinarily ceases to operate:
o: six months after promulgation in every case
only when the President expressly withdraws it
six weeks after the earlier date of reassembly of Parliament
six weeks after the later date of reassembly of Parliament
26.x: An Ordinance ceases six weeks after the later date on which the two Houses reassemble. It may end earlier if disapproved or withdrawn.
26.tq: Focus on the later reassembly date and distinguish the ordinary period from the maximum possible life.
xs: An Ordinance lapses **six weeks after the later date of reassembly of Parliament** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is not a flat six months, and withdrawal by the President is only one way it ends.
xa: It ends **earlier** if **both Houses disapprove**.
Maximum life: **6 months + 6 weeks**.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about Krishna Kumar Singh (2017):
1. Re-promulgation of an Ordinance may constitute a fraud on the Constitution.
2. Laying the Ordinance before the legislature is mandatory.
3. The President's satisfaction is completely beyond judicial review.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Krishna Kumar Singh held that re-promulgation can be a fraud on the Constitution and that laying before the legislature is mandatory. It also recognised that the satisfaction is open to judicial review, making statement 3 false.
26.tq: Use the judicial-review statement as the discriminator among otherwise correct holdings.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **re-promulgation** is unconstitutional — a **fraud on the Constitution**.
Statement 2 correct: **laying before the legislature is mandatory**.
Statement 3 wrong: the President's satisfaction is **open to judicial review** (justiciable).
xa: It was a **7-judge** bench, **Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017)**.
**D.C. Wadhwa (1987)** first called repeated re-promulgation a fraud on the Constitution.

26.s: Which recent development revived the debate on the possible misuse of the ordinance-making power and executive overreach?
o: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026
The Inter-State Water Disputes Amendment Ordinance, 2026
26.x: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 revived the debate on ordinance misuse and executive overreach.
26.tq: Identify the precise recent development instead of being misled by similarly worded legislative titles.
xs: The **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026** revived the debate on **ordinance misuse** and **executive overreach** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Ordinances are issued under **Art. 123** while Parliament is **not in session**.
xa: Criticism: frequent ordinances **bypass parliamentary deliberation**.
**Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)**: **re-promulgation** is a fraud on the Constitution.

26.s: What is the principal criticism of the frequent promulgation of ordinances?
o: They can be issued only during a financial emergency.
They require prior approval from the Supreme Court.
They transfer all legislative powers to the States.
26.x: Frequent ordinances are criticised because they bypass parliamentary deliberation.
26.tq: Link the institutional criticism to the constitutional function being bypassed.
xs: Frequent ordinances **bypass parliamentary deliberation** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They need no Supreme Court approval, are not limited to emergencies, and do not shift power to the States.
xa: **D.C. Wadhwa (1987)**: repeated **re-promulgation** = fraud on the Constitution.
The **2026** Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Ordinance revived this debate.

26.s: With reference to the veto power of the President of the United States, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It is a pocket veto that can be overridden by a simple majority of Congress.
It is a suspensive veto that automatically becomes ineffective after thirty days.
It is a qualified veto that can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Congress.
It is an absolute veto that cannot be overridden by Congress.
26.x: The US President has only a qualified veto, which can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Congress.
26.tq: Discriminate between absolute, qualified, suspensive and pocket vetoes by focusing on the override condition.
xs: The **US President** has only a **qualified veto**, overridable by **2/3 of Congress** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is neither absolute nor a pocket veto overridable by a simple majority.
xa: The US President must act within **10 days**; India's **Art. 111** has **no time limit**.
The Indian President's **pocket veto** was used only once — **Zail Singh (1986)**.

26.s: The State ordinance concerning organ-transplant committees in Andhra Pradesh was issued under which Article of the Constitution?
26.x: A Governor's ordinance-making power for a State is exercised under Article 213; the Andhra Pradesh ordinance concerned organ-transplant committees.
26.tq: Use the Union ordinance–State ordinance distinction to identify the correct constitutional Article.
xs: **AP**'s ordinance on **organ-transplant committees** was a State ordinance under **Article 213** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 123** is the **President's** ordinance power, not the Governor's.
xa: Satisfaction under **Art. 213** was made non-justiciable by the **38th Amendment (1975)**, reversed by the **44th (1978)**.
The Governor has **no pocket veto** (**SC 2025**).

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the election of the Vice-President of India:
1. The electoral college consists of all members of both Houses of Parliament, elected as well as nominated.
2. Elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies are also part of the electoral college.
3. The election is held by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and secret ballot.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: all MPs, elected and nominated, vote (788 when both Houses are full). Statement 2 is wrong: State legislatures have no role in the Vice-President's election. Statement 3 is correct: PR-STV with secret ballot. Hence '1 and 3 only'; '1 only' misses 3, and options with 2 are wrong.
27.tq: VP: all MPs incl. nominated, no MLAs. President: elected MPs + elected MLAs.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the electoral college is **members of both Houses**, **elected and nominated** (Art 66).
Statement 2 is wrong: **State legislatures have no role** — **State MLAs are NOT** in the VP's electoral college.
Statement 3 is correct: voting is by **PR by single transferable vote** with **secret ballot** — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Size of the electoral college = all MPs, **788** (**543 LS + 245 RS**) when both Houses are full.
The election is conducted by the **ECI** under the **Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952**.
⚠ Nominated MPs **vote** for the VP; State MLAs do **not**.
A removal resolution against the VP can first be moved **only in the Rajya Sabha**.

27.s: Which one of the following is NOT a qualification for election as Vice-President of India?
o: Qualification for election as a member of the Lok Sabha
Qualification for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha
27.x: The Vice-President must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old and qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha. Qualification for election to the Lok Sabha is not the prescribed condition.
27.tq: Find the one swapped constitutional qualification among closely related House requirements.
xs: Qualification for election to the **Lok Sabha** is NOT a VP qualification — so option **(2)** is correct.
The VP must be a **citizen**, aged **35 years**, and eligible for election to the **Rajya Sabha** — options (1), (3), (4) are real qualifications.
⚠ Lok Sabha eligibility is the **President's** qualification; the VP's is **Rajya Sabha** eligibility.
xa: **Art. 64:** the VP is **ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** but is **not a member** of the RS.
The VP holds **no other office of profit**.
**Art. 63** simply says there shall be a Vice-President.

27.s: As Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Vice-President ordinarily exercises
o: A casting vote in the event of an equality of votes
A vote only on Money Bills
27.x: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote when the votes are equally divided.
27.tq: Distinguish an ordinary vote from a casting vote in a presiding-officer question.
xs: As RS Chairman, the VP has only a **casting vote** in the event of a **tie** — so option **(1)** is correct.
He is **not a member** of the Rajya Sabha, so he does not vote in the first instance.
xa: **Art. 64:** VP = **ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**.
While **acting as President** (Art 65), the VP ceases to be RS Chairman and the **Deputy Chairman** presides.
The VP is also ex officio **President of ICWA**.

27.s: The Vice-President of India is ex officio President of which of the following bodies?
27.x: The Vice-President is also the ex-officio President of the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA).
27.tq: Use the exact institutional title to distinguish ICWA from other national bodies.
xs: The VP is ex officio **President of the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
His other ex-officio role is **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** (**Art. 64**).
xa: VP qualifications: **citizen**, **35 years**, eligible for election to the **Rajya Sabha**.
Electoral college: **members of both Houses**, elected **and nominated**, by **PR-STV**.
⚠ The VP holds **no other office of profit**, but ex-officio posts like these are part of the office.

27.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 64 — Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
Article 67 — Oath or affirmation of the Vice-President
Article 71 — Election procedure by single transferable vote
27.x: Article 64 provides that the Vice-President shall be the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Article 67 concerns term and removal, Article 69 concerns oath, and Article 71 concerns election disputes.
27.tq: Match each constitutional Article with its exact subject and reject neighbouring Article swaps.
xs: **Article 64** makes the VP the **ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Art 63** only creates the office; removal is under **Art 67(b)**.
The VP's **oath** is under **Art 69**, not Art 67; **Art 71** deals with **election disputes**, not PR-STV procedure (that is **Art 66**).
xa: **Art 65:** VP acts as President on a vacancy or the President's absence/illness.
**Art 67(a):** resignation to the **President**; **Art 67(c)**: continues till successor takes charge.
**Art 68:** vacancy filled "as soon as possible", **no deadline**.

27.s: All doubts and disputes relating to the election of the President or Vice-President are decided by:
27.x: Article 71 vests the Supreme Court with exclusive authority to decide doubts and disputes concerning Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections.
27.tq: Use the authority-identification method: distinguish the body conducting an election from the body deciding its disputes.
xs: Election disputes of the President and VP are decided by the **Supreme Court** under **Art 71** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Parliament only **regulates other matters** through the **Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952**; the **ECI** conducts the election but does not decide disputes.
xa: **39th Amendment (1975)** removed the SC's power over these disputes; **44th Amendment (1978)** restored it.
If the election is declared **void**, **acts done before** the SC's decision remain **valid**.
The 39th Amendment covered elections of the **President, VP, PM and Speaker**.

27.s: The 39th Constitutional Amendment and the 44th Constitutional Amendment had what effect on Presidential election disputes?
o: The 39th Amendment vested the disputes in Parliament and the 44th retained that arrangement
The 39th Amendment removed the Supreme Court’s power and the 44th Amendment restored it
The 39th Amendment created the power and the 44th Amendment abolished it
Both Amendments transferred the power to the Election Commission
27.x: The 39th Amendment of 1975 took away the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction over these disputes, while the 44th Amendment of 1978 restored it.
27.tq: Link each Amendment to its opposite constitutional effect instead of relying on the later amendment alone.
xs: The **39th Amendment (1975)** removed the **Supreme Court's** power over these election disputes and the **44th Amendment (1978)** restored it — so option **(2)** is correct.
The power was never vested in the **Election Commission**, and the 44th did not abolish or retain a parliamentary forum.
xa: The 39th Amendment covered disputes on elections of the **President, VP, PM and Speaker**.
Today the forum is the **Supreme Court** under **Art 71**.
**Acts done before** the SC voids an election remain valid.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the Vice-President of India:
1. The Vice-President holds office for five years and continues until the successor enters office.
2. The oath of office of the Vice-President is administered by the Chief Justice of India.
3. A resolution for the removal of the Vice-President can be moved only after at least 14 days' notice.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: a five-year term, continuing till the successor takes charge (Art. 67(c)). Statement 2 is wrong: the President administers the Vice-President's oath (Art. 69); the CJI administers the President's oath. Statement 3 is correct: 14 days' notice is needed. Hence '1 and 3 only'; options with 2 are wrong.
27.tq: VP oath by the President; President's oath by the CJI. Removal: 14 days' notice, RS resolution.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **term 5 years**, continuing **till the successor takes charge** (**Art 67(c)**).
Statement 2 is wrong: the VP's oath is administered by the **President** (**Art 69**).
Statement 3 is correct: removal needs **14 days' notice** — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: The VP is **re-eligible any number of times**.
Removal resolution: **only in the RS**, by **effective majority**; LS agrees by **simple majority**; **no grounds** stated.
Resignation is addressed to the **President** (**Art 67(a)**), effective immediately.

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Vice-President while acting as President:
1. The Deputy Chairman presides over the Rajya Sabha during that period.
2. The Vice-President continues to draw the salary of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Vice-President stops functioning as Chairman and the Deputy Chairman presides. Statement 2 is wrong: while acting as President he draws the President's salary, not the Chairman's. Hence '1 only'; '2 only', 'Both' and 'Neither' are wrong.
27.tq: Acting President: stops being RS Chairman, draws the President's salary.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: while acting as President, the VP ceases to be RS Chairman and the **Deputy Chairman** presides.
Statement 2 is wrong: he draws the **President's salary**, not the Chairman's — so option **(1) 1 only** is correct.
xa: **Art 65:** VP acts on a **vacancy** (death, resignation, removal) or the President's **absence/illness**.
He acts until a new President is elected **within six months** of the vacancy.
⚠ Presidential vacancy: **6 months** (Art 62); VP vacancy: **no deadline** (Art 68).

27.s: A vacancy in the office of the Vice-President of India is to be filled
o: Within six months of the vacancy in every case
As soon as possible, without a constitutionally prescribed six-month deadline
Within one year, after approval by the Supreme Court
Only at the next general election to the Lok Sabha
27.x: Article 68 requires an election to fill a vacancy in the office of Vice-President as soon as possible. Unlike the vacancy in the office of President, no six-month deadline is prescribed for this election.
27.tq: Compare the vacancy rules for President and Vice-President, especially the presence or absence of a fixed deadline.
xs: A VP vacancy is filled **"as soon as possible"**, with **no deadline** (**Art 68**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **six-month** limit applies to a **President's** vacancy (**Art 62**), not the VP's.
xa: **Jagdeep Dhankhar** resigned in **July 2025** — the **third mid-term vacancy** after **V.V. Giri (1969)** and **Krishan Kant (2002)**.
**C.P. Radhakrishnan** was elected after that vacancy (**September 2025**).
The VP continues in office till the successor takes charge (**Art 67(c)**).

27.s: When the office of the President falls vacant, the Vice-President acts as President until
o: The Council of Ministers elects a successor
The next session of Parliament begins
A new President is elected, which must take place within six months of the vacancy
The remaining term of the previous President expires
27.x: The Vice-President acts as President until a new President is elected. The election to fill the presidential vacancy must be held within six months of the vacancy.
27.tq: Identify the event that ends the acting arrangement and distinguish it from the former President’s remaining term.
xs: The VP acts as President until **a new President is elected**, which must happen **within six months** of the vacancy — so option **(3)** is correct.
The successor is elected, not chosen by the **Council of Ministers**; there is no link to a **Parliament session** or the predecessor's unexpired term.
xa: **Art 65:** applies on death, resignation, removal or the President's absence/illness.
While acting, the VP draws the **President's salary**; the **Deputy Chairman** presides over the RS.
⚠ VP vacancy (Art 68) has **no deadline**; President's vacancy (Art 62) has **6 months**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the removal of the Vice-President of India:
1. The resolution must originate in the Rajya Sabha.
2. The resolution requires an effective majority of the Rajya Sabha.
3. The Lok Sabha must agree to the resolution by a simple majority.
4. The Constitution specifies grounds on which the Vice-President may be removed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Removal is initiated in the Rajya Sabha, requires a majority of all the then members of that House, and must be agreed to by the Lok Sabha by simple majority. The Constitution does not state grounds for this removal.
27.tq: Break the removal procedure into origin, majority, second-House approval and grounds.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the removal resolution is moved **only in the RS** by a **majority of all its then members (effective majority)** (**Art 67(b)**).
Statement 3 is correct: the **Lok Sabha agrees** by **simple majority**.
Statement 4 is wrong: **no grounds** are stated for the VP's removal — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: **14 days' notice** is needed before the resolution is moved.
⚠ The President is removed by **impeachment** (**Art 61**), in **either House**, by **2/3**.
"Where can the removal resolution first be moved" → **Rajya Sabha** is a stock exam angle.

27.s: The Vice-President of India may resign his office by writing under his hand addressed to the
27.x: Under Article 67(a) the Vice-President resigns by writing to the President, and the resignation takes effect immediately. The President resigns to the Vice-President; the CJI administers the President's oath; the Speaker is informed of the President's resignation; the Prime Minister receives no constitutional resignation of either office.
27.tq: President resigns to VP; VP resigns to President.
xs: The VP resigns by writing to the **President of India** (**Art 67(a)**), effective immediately — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ The **President** resigns to the **Vice-President** — the reverse pair is a common trap.
xa: The VP's **oath** is administered by the **President** (**Art 69**).
**Jagdeep Dhankhar** resigned on health grounds under **Art 67(a)** in **July 2025**.
Term: **5 years**, re-eligible **any number of times**.

27.s: Which one of the following Vice-Presidents also served two full terms?
27.x: Hamid Ansari served two full terms as Vice-President from 2007 to 2017. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was the other Vice-President associated with two terms.
27.tq: Distinguish the two-term office-holders from Vice-Presidents who served only one term.
xs: **Hamid Ansari** served **two full terms** as VP (**2007-17**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**R. Venkataraman** (1987), **K.R. Narayanan** (1997) and **V.V. Giri** (1969) are remembered as VPs who **became President**.
xa: **S. Radhakrishnan**, the **first VP**, also held **two terms** (**1952-62**).
**M. Venkaiah Naidu** (Nellore) was VP **2017-22**.
⚠ **S. Radhakrishnan** = first VP; **C.P. Radhakrishnan** = present VP (2025).

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding Vice-Presidents who later became Presidents of India:

List-I
A. S. Radhakrishnan
B. Zakir Husain
C. V.V. Giri
D. K.R. Narayanan

List-II
i. 1962
ii. 1967
iii. 1969
iv. 1997

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
27.x: S. Radhakrishnan became President in 1962, Zakir Husain in 1967, V.V. Giri in 1969 and K.R. Narayanan in 1997.
27.tq: Start with the secure year-office pair and eliminate codes containing a mismatched pair.
xs: **S. Radhakrishnan – 1962**, **Zakir Husain – 1967**, **V.V. Giri – 1969**, **K.R. Narayanan – 1997** — so option **(1) A-i, B-ii, C-iii, D-iv** is correct.
These are the years in which each VP **became President**.
xa: Other VPs who became President: **R. Venkataraman (1987)** and **S.D. Sharma (1992)**.
**V.V. Giri** also created a **mid-term vacancy** by resigning as VP in **1969**.
**S. Radhakrishnan** was the **first VP** (**1952-62**).

27.s: Who is the Vice-President of India elected after the mid-term vacancy created by the resignation of Jagdeep Dhankhar in July 2025?
27.x: C.P. Radhakrishnan was elected Vice-President after the mid-term vacancy caused by Jagdeep Dhankhar’s resignation in July 2025.
27.tq: Use the vacancy event as the identifying clue for the current office-holder.
xs: **C.P. Radhakrishnan** was elected VP in **September 2025** after **Jagdeep Dhankhar's** resignation — so option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ **S. Radhakrishnan** was the **first VP**; **Hamid Ansari** (2007-17) and **M. Venkaiah Naidu** (2017-22) are past VPs.
xa: Dhankhar resigned on **health grounds** under **Art 67(a)** (**July 2025**).
It was the **third mid-term vacancy** after **V.V. Giri (1969, resigned)** and **Krishan Kant (2002, died)**.
A VP vacancy is filled **"as soon as possible"** (**Art 68**).

27.s: Who was the first Vice-President of India?
27.x: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was the first Vice-President (two terms, 1952-62) and later became President in 1962. Zakir Husain (VP 1962-67) and V.V. Giri (VP 1967-69) came after him, and Hamid Ansari held two full terms from 2007 to 2017.
27.tq: Radhakrishnan = first VP and first President from South India.
xs: The first VP was **S. Radhakrishnan**, who served **two terms (1952-62)** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Zakir Husain** and **V.V. Giri** became President in **1967** and **1969**; **Hamid Ansari** served **2007-17**.
xa: S. Radhakrishnan himself became **President in 1962**.
⚠ **C.P. Radhakrishnan** is the **present VP** (2025) — do not confuse the two.
**Hamid Ansari** is the other VP with **two full terms**.

27.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the tenure of the Prime Minister?
o: The Prime Minister can be removed only by the Supreme Court.
The Prime Minister holds office for life unless removed by impeachment.
The Prime Minister continues in office while commanding the confidence of the Lok Sabha, subject to the President's pleasure in the constitutional sense.
The Prime Minister has a fixed tenure of five years irrespective of legislative support.
27.x: The Prime Minister has no fixed tenure and ordinarily continues while enjoying the confidence of the Lok Sabha. The Constitution formally states that Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure.
27.tq: Reject the fixed-term trap and connect tenure with legislative confidence.
xs: The PM has **no fixed tenure**: he holds office during the **President's pleasure**, in practice while he commands a **Lok Sabha** majority — so option **(3)** is correct.
There is **no five-year fixed term**, no **impeachment**, and no removal by the **Supreme Court** for the PM.
xa: **Art. 75(2):** ministers hold office **during the pleasure of the President**, who removes a minister only **on the PM's advice**.
**No term limit for the PM:** **Ambedkar** preferred daily parliamentary accountability to fixed terms.
PM = **de facto** head of government; President = **de jure** head of State.

27.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the President and the Prime Minister in the Indian parliamentary system?
o: The President is the de facto head of government and the Prime Minister is the de jure head of State.
The President is the de jure head of State and the Prime Minister is the de facto head of government.
The Prime Minister is the de jure head of State and the President is only a ceremonial officer of Parliament.
Both the President and the Prime Minister are de facto heads of government.
27.x: The President is the de jure head of the State, while the Prime Minister functions as the de facto head of government.
27.tq: Discriminate the paired constitutional and political roles rather than treating them as identical.
xs: The **President** is the **de jure head of State** and the **PM** is the **de facto head of government** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Options (1) and (3) reverse the roles; both are not de facto heads.
xa: The PM is appointed by the President under **Art 75(1)** — by convention the leader of the **Lok Sabha majority**.
**Art 74(1):** the CoM headed by the PM **aids and advises** the President; advice is **binding after one reconsideration**.
**Art 77(1):** all executive action is taken **in the President's name**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the Prime Minister of India:
1. He is appointed by the President under Article 75(1).
2. He must be a member of the Lok Sabha at the time of appointment.
3. His oath of office is administered by the President.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: the President appoints the PM under Article 75(1), by convention the leader of the Lok Sabha majority. Statement 2 is wrong: the PM may belong to either House, and a non-member can be PM for six months. Statement 3 is correct: the President administers the oath. Hence '1 and 3 only'; options with 2 are wrong.
27.tq: PM: either House, or none for 6 months.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **President** appoints the PM under **Art 75(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the PM **may belong to either House**, and a non-member can be PM for **six months**.
Statement 3 is correct: the PM's **oath** is administered by the **President** — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: By convention the PM is the leader of the **Lok Sabha majority**.
**P.V. Narasimha Rao** became PM in **1991** without being an MP and later won **Nandyal**.
⚠ The **UK PM** must belong to the **House of Commons**; the Indian PM may come from either House.

27.s: Under Article 75(5) of the Constitution of India, a person appointed as a Minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament must become a member within
27.x: Article 75(5) requires a non-member Minister to become a member of either House of Parliament within six consecutive months; otherwise, the person ceases to be a Minister.
27.tq: Use the precise constitutional time limit and distinguish it from other parliamentary periods.
xs: A non-member minister must become a member of either House within **six months** (**six consecutive months**) under **Art 75(5)** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Otherwise he **ceases to be a minister**; the rule **applies to the PM too**.
xa: **S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001):** a non-member **cannot be re-appointed** repeatedly without getting elected.
**P.V. Narasimha Rao** became PM in **1991** without being an MP.
**Art 75(1B):** a member disqualified for **defection** cannot be a minister until **re-elected**.

27.s: Which one of the following correctly states the ruling in S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001)?
o: A non-member cannot be repeatedly reappointed as Minister without getting elected.
Only a member of the Lok Sabha can be appointed as a Minister.
A non-member may be reappointed as Minister indefinitely without election.
A non-member cannot be appointed as Prime Minister under any circumstances.
27.x: The Supreme Court held that the constitutional provision for a non-member Minister cannot be used for repeated reappointments without the person securing election to the legislature.
27.tq: Discriminate the judicial limitation from the general six-month rule.
xs: In **S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001)**, a non-member **cannot be re-appointed** repeatedly as minister **without getting elected** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Art 75(5)** lets **any person** be a minister for **six months**, so options (2), (3) and (4) are wrong — a non-member can even be **PM** for six months.
xa: The six-month rule is **six consecutive months** and **applies to the PM** too.
UPSC notes spell the case name **"S.R. Chauhan"**.
The PM **may belong to either House** of Parliament.

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding appointment of Ministers:
1. Any person may be appointed as a Minister, subject to the constitutional six-month rule.
2. A non-member Minister must become a member of either House of Parliament within six months.
3. The six-month rule does not apply to a person appointed as Prime Minister.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the six-month rule applies to the Prime Minister as well.
27.tq: Find the exception that improperly excludes the Prime Minister from a general constitutional rule.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: under **Art 75(5)** **any person** may be a minister, but a non-MP must become a member within **six months** — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: the six-month rule **applies to the PM too**.
xa: **S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001):** no repeated **re-appointment** without election.
**P.V. Narasimha Rao (1991)** became PM without being an MP and later entered the LS from **Nandyal**.
Ministers are appointed by the President on the **PM's advice**.

27.s: Article 75(2) was referred to in the acceptance of a Minister's resignation because that Article relates to
o: collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha
the President's pleasure regarding the tenure of Ministers
the Prime Minister's duty to furnish information
27.x: Article 75(2) provides that Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, which operates in practice on the advice of the Prime Minister.
27.tq: Link a constitutional clause to its operative subject instead of to a neighbouring Article.
xs: **Art 75(2)** says ministers hold office **during the pleasure of the President** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The President removes a minister only **on the PM's advice**; collective responsibility, authentication (**Art 77(2)**) and the PM's duty to inform (**Art 78**) are other provisions.
xa: MoS **Ravneet Singh Bittu**'s resignation was accepted "under clause (2) of Article 75" (**Jul 2026**).
**George Kurian** resigned on **23 Jun 2026**; both left after their **Rajya Sabha** terms ended on **21 Jun 2026**.
The PM has **no fixed tenure** — he too holds office during the President's pleasure.

27.s: According to Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, the total number of Union Ministers including the Prime Minister shall not exceed
o: 15 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
12 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
10 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
20 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
27.x: The 91st Amendment inserted Article 75(1A), limiting the Union Council of Ministers including the Prime Minister to 15 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
27.tq: Match the amendment with its exact percentage limit and constitutional Article.
xs: **Art 75(1A)** caps ministers **including the PM** at **15 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was inserted by the **91st Amendment Act, 2003** (asked in **APPSC G2 2025**).
xa: At **543** seats the cap is **81** ministers.
**Art 75(1B):** a member disqualified for **defection** cannot be a minister until **re-elected**.
States: **Art 164(1A)** — not over **15%** of the Assembly and **not less than 12**.

27.s: If the total strength of the Lok Sabha is 543, the maximum permissible strength of the Union Council of Ministers including the Prime Minister is
27.x: Fifteen per cent of 543 is 81.45; the applicable maximum whole-number limit is 81 ministers, including the Prime Minister.
27.tq: Calculate the constitutional percentage cap and apply the whole-number limit.
xs: At **543** Lok Sabha seats, the **15%** cap under **Art 75(1A)** gives a maximum of **eighty-one (81)** ministers including the PM — so option **(2)** is correct.
The cap counts ministers **including the PM**, measured against the **total strength of the Lok Sabha**.
xa: The cap came with the **91st Amendment Act, 2003**.
State example: **West Bengal** Assembly of **294** → max **44** ministers (**Art 164(1A)**).
⚠ States also have a floor: **not less than 12** ministers.

27.s: A member of Parliament disqualified for defection under the Tenth Schedule is, by virtue of Article 75(1B),
o: eligible only after approval by the Election Commission
permanently barred from becoming a Union Minister
ineligible to be appointed Union Minister until re-elected to Parliament
eligible to be appointed Union Minister immediately after disqualification
27.x: Article 75(1B), inserted by the 91st Amendment, prevents a member disqualified for defection from being appointed a minister until re-elected to Parliament.
27.tq: Test the duration and condition of disqualification instead of treating it as a permanent bar.
xs: Under **Art 75(1B)**, a member disqualified for **defection** cannot be a minister **until re-elected** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is not a **permanent** bar, not immediate eligibility, and needs no **Election Commission** approval.
xa: Both **Art 75(1A)** and **75(1B)** came with the **91st Amendment Act, 2003**.
**Art 75(1A):** total ministers including the PM ≤ **15%** of the Lok Sabha.
At **543** seats the cap is **81**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the size of a State Council of Ministers under Article 164(1A):
1. The total number of ministers, including the Chief Minister, shall not exceed 15% of the strength of the Legislative Assembly and shall not be less than 12.
2. This limit was inserted by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.
3. In a State with an Assembly of 294 members, the maximum number of ministers including the Chief Minister is 45.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: ceiling 15% of the Assembly, floor 12. Statement 2 is correct: the 91st Amendment, 2003 brought in these limits. Statement 3 is wrong: 15% of 294 is 44.1, so the maximum is 44 (e.g. West Bengal), not 45. Hence '1 and 2 only'; options with 3 are wrong and '1 only' misses 2.
27.tq: State: max 15%, min 12 (Art 164(1A), 91st Amdt). 294 seats -> 44.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: under **Art 164(1A)**, ministers incl. the CM must **not exceed 15%** of the Assembly and be **not less than 12**.
Statement 2 is correct: the limit came with the **91st Amendment Act, 2003**.
Statement 3 is wrong: an Assembly of **294** (**West Bengal**) allows max **44**, not 45 — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: Union equivalent: **Art 75(1A)** — **15%** of the **Lok Sabha**, i.e. **81** at **543** seats.
The State limit was asked in **APPSC-G2 2017**; the Union limit in **APPSC G2 2025**.
⚠ The Union has **no minimum** like the State floor of **12**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the classification of Union Ministers:
1. The Constitution itself classifies ministers into Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers.
2. The classification into ranks is based on convention and the choice of the Prime Minister.
3. Deputy Ministers form one of the conventionally recognised ministerial ranks.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: The Constitution does not itself classify ministers into ranks. The classification is based on convention and the Prime Minister’s choice, and Deputy Minister is one of the recognised ranks.
27.tq: Separate what the Constitution expressly provides from what operates through convention.
xs: Statement 1 is wrong: the **Constitution does not classify ministers** into ranks.
Statement 2 is correct: ranking is **by convention**, decided by the **PM's choice**.
Statement 3 is correct: **Deputy Ministers** are one of the four conventional ranks — so option **(3) 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: The four ranks: **Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (Independent Charge), Ministers of State, Deputy Ministers**.
**Deputy Ministers** assist Cabinet Ministers/MoS.
**Deputy PM** is **not mentioned in the Constitution** and takes oath as an ordinary minister.

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding categories of Ministers:

List-I
A. Cabinet Minister
B. Minister of State with independent charge
C. Minister of State
D. Deputy Minister

List-II
i. Assists a Cabinet Minister or Minister of State
ii. Heads an important ministry and attends Cabinet meetings
iii. Holds a ministry or department on his or her own
iv. Is attached to a Cabinet Minister

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
27.x: A Cabinet Minister heads an important ministry and attends Cabinet meetings; a Minister of State with independent charge heads a ministry independently; a Minister of State is attached to a Cabinet Minister; and a Deputy Minister assists a senior Minister.
27.tq: Start from the distinctive phrase ‘independent charge’ and then complete the remaining role pairs.
xs: **Cabinet Minister** – heads important ministries and attends Cabinet meetings (A-ii); **MoS (independent charge)** – holds a ministry on his own (B-iii).
**MoS** – attached to Cabinet Ministers (C-iv); **Deputy Minister** – assists Cabinet Ministers/MoS (D-i) — so option **(1) A-ii, B-iii, C-iv, D-i** is correct.
xa: The **Constitution does not classify ministers** into ranks — the ranking is **by convention**, by the PM's choice.
Total ministers incl. the PM ≤ **15%** of the **Lok Sabha** (**Art 75(1A)**).
**Deputy PM** is not a rank in the Constitution; first Deputy PM: **Sardar Patel**.

27.s: Under Article 74(1), the advice of the Council of Ministers becomes binding on the President after the President
o: secures approval from the Election Commission
refers the matter to the Supreme Court
obtains the consent of the Rajya Sabha
27.x: The President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice once, but must act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.
27.tq: Focus on the one permitted reconsideration rather than an unlimited presidential discretion.
xs: Under **Art 74(1)**, the CoM's advice is **binding after one reconsideration** — so option **(4) has it reconsidered once** is correct.
No **Election Commission**, **Supreme Court** or **Rajya Sabha** step is involved.
xa: **Art 74(2):** the advice is **not inquired into** by any court.
⚠ Even in a **National Emergency**, the President gets **no discretionary powers** — advice stays binding (PYQ).
The CoM is **headed by the PM**.

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
 a. Article 74(2)
 b. Article 77(1)
 c. Article 77(2)
 d. Article 77(3)

List-II (Provision)
 i. Authentication of orders
 ii. Executive action expressed in the President's name
 iii. Advice not subject to inquiry by any court
 iv. Rules for convenient transaction and allocation of government business

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
27.x: Article 74(2) concerns non-inquiry into ministerial advice; Article 77(1) concerns expression in the President's name; Article 77(2) concerns authentication; and Article 77(3) concerns transaction and allocation of business rules.
27.tq: Start with the sure Article–provision pairs and eliminate codes containing a misplaced constitutional subject.
xs: **74(2)** – advice **not inquired into** by any court (a-iii); **77(1)** – executive action **in the President's name** (b-ii).
**77(2)** – **authentication** of orders (c-i); **77(3)** – rules for **transaction and allocation of business** (d-iv) — so option **(1) a–iii, b–ii, c–i, d–iv** is correct.
xa: Art 77(3) rules: **Allocation of Business Rules, 1961** and **Transaction of Business Rules, 1961**.
**Art 74(1):** CoM headed by the PM to **aid and advise** the President.
**Art 78:** PM's duty to **communicate** all CoM decisions to the President.

27.s: Which of the following is NOT a duty of the Prime Minister under Article 78?
o: Furnishing information relating to administration when called for by the President
Submitting for the consideration of the Council any matter decided by an individual Minister when the President requires it
Communicating to the President decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to administration and legislative proposals
Administering the oath of office and secrecy to all Union Ministers
27.x: Options A, B and C are duties of the Prime Minister under Article 78 (communicating Council decisions, furnishing information, and placing a minister's individual decision before the Council when the President requires). Administering the oaths of office and secrecy to Union Ministers is done by the President, not the PM.
27.tq: Find the one function belonging to the President rather than the Prime Minister.
xs: **Administering the oath** to Union Ministers is NOT a PM duty under Art 78 — the **President** administers it — so option **(4)** is correct.

**Art 78** duties: **communicate all decisions** of the CoM and legislative proposals; **furnish information** called for; submit a minister's sole decision to the **CoM** if the President requires — options (1)-(3).
xa: **Art 77(1):** all executive action is **expressed in the President's name**.
**Art 74(2):** ministerial advice is **not inquired into** by any court.
The PM's own oath is also administered by the **President**.

27.s: During a National Emergency, the President of India
o: acquires unrestricted discretion to disregard the advice of the Council of Ministers
continues to be bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers
becomes the real executive in place of the Prime Minister
may dismiss the entire Council without following constitutional advice
27.x: A National Emergency does not confer discretionary power on the President to disregard the binding advice of the Council of Ministers. The parliamentary executive relationship continues.
27.tq: Guard against the emergency-powers trap by checking whether the constitutional advice requirement has been altered.
xs: During a **National Emergency** the President **continues to be bound** by the CoM's advice — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ The President does **not** acquire **discretionary powers** in an emergency — a PYQ trap; options (1), (3), (4) assume such powers.
xa: **Art 74(1):** advice is binding **after one reconsideration**.
**Art 74(2):** advice is **not inquired into** by any court.
PM = **de facto** head of government; President = **de jure** head of State.

27.s:
Arrange the following provisions in the order of their appearance in the Constitution:
A. Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
B. Prime Minister's duties to communicate information to the President
C. All executive action expressed in the President's name
D. Collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha
27.x: The provisions occur in the order Article 74(1), Article 75(3), Article 77(1) and Article 78: advice, collective responsibility, executive expression and Prime Ministerial duties.
27.tq: Use the Article numbers as the sequence: 74, 75, 77 and 78.
xs: Order: **A** (aid and advise, **Art 74(1)**) → **D** (collective responsibility, **Art 75**) → **C** (President's name, **Art 77(1)**) → **B** (PM's duties, **Art 78**) — so option **(1) A, D, C, B** is correct.
**Art 75** covers appointment, pleasure, **collective responsibility**, oath, the 6-month rule and salaries.
xa: **Art 74(2):** advice **not inquired into** by any court.
**Art 77(3):** **Allocation of Business** and **Transaction of Business Rules, 1961**.
"All work of the GoI is done in the name of the President" = **Art 77**.

27.s: Article 77(1) of the Constitution provides that all executive action of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the
27.x: Article 77(1) requires all executive action of the Government of India to be expressed in the name of the President.
27.tq: Match the constitutional article with the authority in whose name executive action is expressed.
xs: Under **Art 77(1)**, all executive action of the GoI is **expressed in the name of the President** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **PM** heads the CoM that advises (**Art 74(1)**), but action is never in the name of the PM, Parliament or the CoM.
xa: **Art 77(2):** **authentication** of orders as per rules.
**Art 77(3):** rules for **convenient transaction** and **allocation of business**.
