30.x: Statement 1 is correct: about 815 members. Statement 2 is wrong: the ratio would rise from 2.2:1 to 3.3:1, not fall. Statement 3 is correct: the ministerial cap would rise from 81 to 122 (or 133 per another source). Hence 1 and 3 only.
30.tq: A bigger Lok Sabha raises the LS:RS ratio (2.2 -> 3.3) and dilutes the Rajya Sabha.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: LS strength would rise by **50%** to **~815**.
Statement 2 wrong: the LS-RS ratio would **rise** from **2.2:1 to 3.3:1**, not fall.
Statement 3 correct: the **15%** ministerial cap would rise from **81 to 122** (another source: **81 to 133**).
xa: The **84th Amendment (2001)** froze LS seat allocation on the **1971 census** till the first census **after 2026**.
The **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026** sought a maximum of **850** seats.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the proposed expansion of the Lok Sabha:
1. Southern States have expressed apprehension that their relative share would decline.
2. Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan are expected to gain relatively from such an expansion.
3. The debate is linked to the lifting of the freeze based on the 1971 Census.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: All three statements are correct. The proposed expansion has generated concern in southern States because the relative representation of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan may increase after the 1971-based freeze is lifted.
30.tq: Test the regional comparison and the constitutional background together.
xs: All three statements, **1, 2 and 3**, are correct — option **(4)**.
**Southern States** would lose share relative to **UP, Bihar and Rajasthan**.
The debate is tied to lifting the **1971** freeze.
xa: **Tamil Nadu** Assembly resolved to freeze the LS at **543** and keep the **2.2:1** ratio.
Law Commission's **170th Report (1999)** proposed **25%** more seats via a party list.

30.s: The Law Commission's 170th Report, submitted in 1999, proposed which of the following alternatives in the context of parliamentary representation?
o: A 50 per cent reduction in Rajya Sabha seats
A 25 per cent increase in seats through a party-list system
Direct election of the President by the people
Abolition of reserved seats in the Lok Sabha
30.x: The Law Commission's 170th Report of 1999 proposed increasing representation by 25 per cent through a party-list system.
30.tq: Link the institutional proposal with the report number and year.
xs: The Law Commission's **170th Report (1999)** proposed **25%** more seats via a **party list** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was an alternative in the LS expansion debate; it did not seek RS cuts, direct presidential elections or abolition of reserved seats.
xa: The current proposal: raise LS strength by **50% (to ~815)**.
The LS-RS ratio would go from **2.2:1 to 3.3:1**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026:
1. It was introduced along with the Delimitation Bill, 2026.
2. It sought to raise the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850.
3. The proposed 850 seats comprised 815 for the States and 35 for the Union Territories.
4. It was passed by the Lok Sabha with the required special majority.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Bill was defeated in the Lok Sabha and therefore did not secure the required special majority.
30.tq: Identify the single false statement by checking the legislative outcome.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1-3: introduced with the **Delimitation Bill, 2026**; LS maximum **550 to 850**; **815** for states, **35** for UTs.
Statement 4 wrong: it was **defeated in the Lok Sabha** — **298 for, 230 against** of **528** present.
xa: It also sought to **fast-track women's reservation**.
It fell short of the **Art. 368** special majority.

30.s: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, was defeated because it failed to secure the special majority required under
30.x: A constitutional amendment Bill must satisfy the special-majority requirement under Article 368; the 2026 Bill fell short of it.
30.tq: Use the article-number association for constitutional amendment procedure.
xs: The Bill failed to secure the special majority under **Article 368** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Vote: **298 for, 230 against** of **528** present.
**Art. 94(c)** concerns removal of the Speaker; **Art. 356** is President's Rule.
xa: Parliament amends the Constitution under **Art. 368** but cannot alter the **basic structure**.
For **constitutional amendment bills** there is **no joint sitting**.

30.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the resolution adopted by the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly in the debate on Lok Sabha delimitation?
o: It proposed equal representation for every State in both Houses.
It supported increasing the Lok Sabha to 850 seats and a 3.3:1 ratio.
It sought to freeze the Lok Sabha at 543 seats and retain the 2.2:1 Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha ratio.
It sought to reduce the Lok Sabha to 525 seats and abolish the Rajya Sabha.
30.x: The Tamil Nadu Assembly resolved to retain the Lok Sabha at 543 seats and preserve the approximate 2.2:1 Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha ratio.
30.tq: Use the precise figures to distinguish the State Assembly's position from the expansion proposal.
xs: The **Tamil Nadu** Assembly resolved to **freeze the Lok Sabha at 543** and keep the **2.2:1** LS:RS ratio — so option **(3)** is correct.
It opposed, not supported, the **850**-seat, **3.3:1** plan.
xa: Southern States fear losing share to **UP, Bihar and Rajasthan**.
Present LS strength: **543** (**524** States + **19** UTs).

30.s: Which one of the following Bills was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee during the 2026 Monsoon Session?
30.x: The FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee during the session.
30.tq: Identify the Bill by linking it with the parliamentary committee action.
xs: The **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026** was sent to a **JPC** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026** was **defeated** in the LS, not referred.
xa: Monsoon Session **2026**: from **20 July**, adjourned sine die **13 Aug**.
Productivity: Lok Sabha **19%**, Rajya Sabha **39%**; **12 Bills** passed.

30.s: On 11 March 2026, the Lok Sabha rejected by voice vote a resolution seeking removal of the Speaker under
30.x: The resolution seeking removal of Speaker Om Birla was moved under Article 94(c) and was rejected by voice vote on 11 March 2026.
30.tq: Apply the article-number trap by distinguishing the Speaker's removal provision from neighbouring parliamentary provisions.
xs: The resolution to remove Speaker **Om Birla** was under **Article 94(c)** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was rejected by **voice vote** on **11 Mar 2026**.
**Art. 100** = quorum; **Art. 105** = privileges.
xa: The **Speaker** presides over a **joint sitting** and certifies **Money Bills**.
The **Lok Sabha** elects the **Speaker and Deputy Speaker**.

30.s:
Which of the following proposals has been discussed in relation to limiting the use of party whips in Parliament?
1. Party whips should be limited to confidence votes.
2. Party whips should be limited to money bills.
3. Party whips should be abolished in all legislative business.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: The proposals discussed were to limit party whips to confidence votes and money bills. A general abolition of whips in all legislative business was not stated.
30.tq: Reject the extreme extension of a limited reform proposal.
xs: Proposals **1 and 2** — limit whips to **confidence votes** and **money bills** — option **(3)**.
The notes record no proposal to **abolish** whips in all business.
xa: Concern: **declining sittings and productivity**.
Monsoon Session **2026**: LS productivity **19%**.

30.s: The Andhra State Act of 1953 and the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act of 2014 were enacted under which Article of the Constitution?
30.x: Both the creation of Andhra State in 1953 and the reorganisation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014 were carried out under Article 3, which concerns the formation and alteration of States.
30.tq: Use the common constitutional provision rather than the different years of enactment.
xs: **Andhra State (1953)** and the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014** were both made under **Article 3** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Art. 3** covers forming new states and altering areas, boundaries, names; the bill needs the **President's recommendation**.
xa: The **2014** Act amended the **Fourth Schedule**: undivided AP's **18** RS seats = **AP 11 + Telangana 7**.
AP has **25 LS** and **11 RS** seats; Assembly **175**.

31.s: Which Article provides for the election of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
31.x: Article 93 provides that the House of the People shall choose two members to be Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
31.tq: Match the constitutional article with the office it creates.
xs: **Article 93**: the LS elects the **Speaker and Deputy Speaker** from its members — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Art. 89** is about the RS **Chairman and Deputy Chairman**; **Art. 100** = quorum / casting vote; **Art. 85** = sessions.
xa: **Art. 94**: Speaker resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**; removal by a **majority of all the then members** after **14 days'** notice.
The **Deputy Speaker** is elected **after the Speaker**.

31.s: The salary and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha are charged on the:
31.x: The salaries and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 97.
31.tq: Use the constitutional funding source rather than a general parliamentary budget description.
xs: The Speaker's salary is **charged on the Consolidated Fund** of India (**Art 97**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
Being charged, it is not voted upon — the Public Account and Contingency Fund are wrong.
xa: On **dissolution**, the Speaker continues till immediately before the **first meeting of the new LS**.
The **Speaker Pro Tem** is the senior-most member, sworn in by the **President**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Speaker of the Lok Sabha under Article 94:
1. The Speaker vacates office on ceasing to be a member of the Lok Sabha.
2. The Speaker resigns by writing to the President.
3. The Speaker can be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members, after 14 days' notice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker. Statement 3 is correct: removal needs an effective majority and 14 days' notice. Hence 1 and 3 only.
31.tq: Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker and vice versa; Deputy Chairman resigns to the Chairman.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: the Speaker **vacates office on ceasing to be a member** (**Art 94**).
Statement 2 wrong: the Speaker **resigns to the Deputy Speaker**, not the President.
Statement 3 correct: removal by a **majority of all the then members** (effective majority) after **14 days'** notice.
xa: ⚠ Speaker → resigns to Deputy Speaker; Deputy Speaker → to Speaker; Deputy Chairman → to Chairman.
Removal motions against **Mavalankar (1954)**, **Hukum Singh (1966)**, **Jakhar (1987)** all **failed**.

31.s: While a resolution for the removal of the Speaker is under consideration, which one of the following is correct?
o: The Speaker cannot speak or vote under any circumstance
The Speaker’s membership of the House automatically terminates
The Speaker cannot preside, but may speak and take part in the proceedings and vote in the first instance, not in the event of a tie
The Speaker may preside but cannot vote
31.x: Article 96 prevents the Speaker from presiding while the removal resolution is under consideration. The Speaker may speak, participate and vote in the first instance, but cannot exercise a casting vote in case of a tie.
31.tq: Separate the restriction on presiding from the retained rights to participate and vote.
xs: While his removal is pending, the Speaker **cannot preside**, but may **speak, take part** and **vote in the first instance**, not on a tie — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is **Art 96**; his membership does not end.
xa: ⚠ The **RS Chairman**, in the same situation, **cannot vote** at all but may speak.
The **casting vote** (on a tie) is under **Art 100(1)**.

31.s: Which of the following pairs of removal motions against Lok Sabha Speakers is correctly matched?
31.x: Removal motions against G. V. Mavalankar in 1954, Hukum Singh in 1966 and Balram Jakhar in 1987 failed. The motion concerning Om Birla was listed for debate in 2026, not 1987.
31.tq: Pair each office-holder with the correct year and reject swapped dates.
xs: **G.V. Mavalankar — 1954** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Hukum Singh** faced his motion in **1966**, **Balram Jakhar** in **1987** — all failed.
**Om Birla**'s motion was signed by **118** MPs and listed for debate on **9 Mar 2026**.
xa: ⚠ **1954 – 1966 – 1987** = Mavalankar – Hukum Singh – Jakhar.
The LS rejected the Om Birla resolution by **voice vote**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Speaker when the Lok Sabha is dissolved:
1. The Speaker continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha.
2. The outgoing Speaker presides over the new House as Speaker Pro Tem and conducts the election of the new Speaker.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Speaker does not vacate office on dissolution. Statement 2 is wrong: the Speaker Pro Tem is the senior-most member, sworn in by the President, not the outgoing Speaker. Hence 1 only.
31.tq: Speaker Pro Tem = senior-most member, sworn in by the President.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)** (1 only).
Statement 1 correct: the Speaker **continues till immediately before the first meeting of the new LS**.
Statement 2 wrong: the **Speaker Pro Tem** is the **senior-most member**, sworn in by the **President**, not the outgoing Speaker.
xa: The Pro Tem Speaker **presides and conducts the new Speaker's election**.
The Speaker's salary is charged on the **Consolidated Fund** (**Art 97**).

31.s: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha exercises a casting vote:
o: Whenever the Council of Ministers advises the Speaker to do so
On every bill passed by the House
Only during a joint sitting of Parliament
Only when there is an equality of votes
31.x: Under Article 100(1), the Speaker normally does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote when the votes are equally divided.
31.tq: Distinguish the ordinary vote from the casting vote used only to break a tie.
xs: The Speaker has a **casting vote** **only in case of a tie** (equality of votes) — so option **(4)** is correct.
This is **Art 100(1)**; it is not on advice, not on every bill, and not only at joint sittings.
xa: ⚠ Quorum = **100(3)**; casting vote = **100(1)**.
The **RS Chairman** also has a **casting vote only**.

31.s: Who has the final authority to decide whether a bill is a Money Bill?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
31.x: Article 110(3) gives the Speaker of the Lok Sabha the final authority to decide whether a bill is a Money Bill.
31.tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ test to identify the constitutionally designated authority.
xs: The **Speaker of the Lok Sabha** has the **final say** on whether a bill is a **Money Bill** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This is under **Art 110(3)**.
xa: He presides over a **joint sitting** (**Art 108**; **Art 118(4)**).
His rulings are protected by **Art 122**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the powers of the Speaker:
1. The Speaker decides cases under the Tenth Schedule, subject to judicial review.
2. The Speaker recognises the Leader of the Opposition subject to the applicable requirement regarding the strength of the party.
3. The Speaker appoints chairmen of parliamentary committees.
4. Rulings of the Speaker are protected by Article 122.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: All four statements are correct. The Speaker’s decisions under the Tenth Schedule remain subject to judicial review, and the Speaker also performs the listed recognition, committee and ruling-related functions.
31.tq: Use a multi-function statement set and verify each power independently.
xs: All four statements, **1, 2, 3 and 4**, are correct — option **(4)**.
He decides **Tenth Schedule** cases, subject to judicial review (**Kihoto Hollohan, 1992**).
He recognises the **Leader of the Opposition**, **appoints committee chairmen**, and his rulings are protected by **Art 122**.
xa: LoP recognition needs at least **one-tenth** of the House's strength.
The LoP became statutory under the **1977 Act**.

31.s: The party seeking recognition of the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha is required, according to the Speaker’s direction, to have at least:
31.x: Recognition of the Leader of the Opposition requires the party to have at least one-tenth of the strength of the House, according to the Speaker’s direction. The office has statutory status since the 1977 Act.
31.tq: Distinguish the one-tenth threshold from other parliamentary fractions.
xs: The party needs at least **one-tenth of the House's strength** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This comes from the **Speaker's direction**; the LoP is **statutory since the 1977 Act**.
xa: Quorum is also **one-tenth** of total members (**Art 100(3)**).
The Speaker also decides **Tenth Schedule** cases.

31.s: A joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament under Article 108 is presided over by the
o: senior-most member of the Rajya Sabha
31.x: Under Article 118(4), the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting (the Deputy Speaker in his absence). The President summons the joint sitting but does not preside. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (the Vice-President) does not preside over it, and there is no role for the senior-most Rajya Sabha member.
31.tq: President summons a joint sitting; the Speaker presides (Art. 118(4)).
xs: A **joint sitting** is presided over by the **Speaker of the Lok Sabha** — so option **(3)** is correct.
If the Speaker is absent, the **Deputy Speaker** presides — not the RS Chairman.
xa: The Speaker also certifies **Money Bills** (**Art 110(3)**).
The **RS Chairman** is the **Vice-President**, ex officio (**Art 64, 89**).

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha:
1. The Deputy Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha after the election of the Speaker.
2. The Deputy Speaker resigns by addressing the resignation to the Speaker.
3. The Deputy Speaker presides over a joint sitting when the Speaker is absent.
4. The Deputy Speaker is subordinate to the Speaker in exercising the office’s constitutional functions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Deputy Speaker is not subordinate to the Speaker while exercising the office’s functions, so statement 4 is false.
31.tq: Spot the reversed institutional relationship in the final statement.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: elected **by the LS after the Speaker**; statement 2: **resigns to the Speaker**.
Statement 3: presides over a **joint sitting** if the Speaker is absent.
Statement 4 wrong: he is **not subordinate to the Speaker**.
xa: By convention he is from the **Opposition**.
He becomes **chairman of any committee** he is appointed to.

31.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Panel of Chairpersons of the Lok Sabha is correct?
o: It is nominated by the Deputy Speaker and can preside even when the Speaker’s office is vacant
It is nominated by the President and may contain up to twenty members
It is nominated by the Speaker and may contain up to ten members
It is elected by the Rajya Sabha and contains exactly ten members
31.x: The Speaker nominates a Panel of Chairpersons consisting of up to ten members. A panel member may preside in the absence of both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, but not when the Speaker’s office is vacant.
31.tq: Check both the nominating authority and the numerical ceiling.
xs: The **Panel of Chairpersons** is **nominated by the Speaker**, **up to 10** members — so option **(3)** is correct.
A member cannot preside when the **Speaker's office is vacant**.
xa: A panel member presides in the **absence of both** Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
RS equivalent: **Panel of Vice-Chairpersons**, nominated by the **Chairman**.

31.s: A member of the Panel of Chairpersons may preside over the Lok Sabha when:
o: The President directs the panel member to preside over a joint sitting
The Speaker’s office is vacant, irrespective of the presence of the Deputy Speaker
The Lok Sabha has been dissolved and no new Speaker has been elected
Both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are absent, but the Speaker’s office is not vacant
31.x: A panel member may preside in the absence of both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker. The panel member cannot preside when the office of Speaker is vacant.
31.tq: Read the condition cumulatively: absence of both officers is different from vacancy of the office.
xs: A panel member presides when **both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are absent**, but the **Speaker's office is not vacant** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Not when the Speaker's office is **vacant**.
xa: The panel has **up to 10** members, nominated by the **Speaker**.
At a **joint sitting**, the **Deputy Speaker** presides if the Speaker is absent.

31.s: Which of the following statements regarding vacancies of Deputy Speaker offices is correct?
o: The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post was filled in June 2019, while the office was vacant in eight State Assemblies in 2025.
The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since 2014, and the office was vacant in ten State Assemblies.
The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since June 2019, and the office was vacant in eight State Assemblies in 2026.
The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since June 2021, and the office was vacant in six State Assemblies.
31.x: The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since June 2019. The office was reported vacant in eight State Assemblies, with Jharkhand’s vacancy lasting 21 years.
31.tq: Match the vacancy count and starting date without swapping the two time references.
xs: The **LS Deputy Speaker** post has been **vacant since June 2019**, and the State office was vacant in **8 State Assemblies** (**2026**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Jharkhand**'s vacancy has lasted **21 years** (as of **Jun 2026**).
xa: State office is under **Art 178**.
The post stayed empty through the **17th and 18th** Lok Sabhas.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the conventional relationship between the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Opposition?
o: The Deputy Speaker is appointed by the President on the advice of the Opposition
The Deputy Speaker can belong only to a party represented in the Rajya Sabha
The Deputy Speaker is conventionally chosen from the Opposition, though this is not a constitutional requirement
The Deputy Speaker must always be nominated by the ruling party
31.x: The Deputy Speaker is conventionally chosen from the Opposition. This is a parliamentary convention and not an express constitutional requirement.
31.tq: Distinguish a political convention from a mandatory constitutional qualification.
xs: By **convention**, the Deputy Speaker is from the **Opposition** — not a constitutional requirement — so option **(3)** is correct.
He is elected by the **LS** (**Art 93**), not appointed by the President or nominated by the ruling party.
xa: He is **not subordinate** to the Speaker.
The post has been **vacant since June 2019**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha:
1. The Deputy Chairman is elected by the Rajya Sabha from among its members.
2. The Deputy Chairman resigns by writing to the President.
3. The Deputy Chairman can be removed by an effective majority after 14 days' notice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: Statement 1 is correct (Art. 89(2)). Statement 2 is wrong: the Deputy Chairman resigns to the Chairman. Statement 3 is correct: removal needs an effective majority with 14 days' notice. Hence 1 and 3 only.
31.tq: Deputy Chairman resigns to the Chairman.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **elected from RS members** (**Art 89(2), 90**).
Statement 2 wrong: he **resigns to the Chairman**.
Statement 3 correct: removal by **effective majority** with **14 days'** notice.
xa: **Harivansh**'s term as Deputy Chairman ended **9 Apr 2026**.
When the VP acts as President, the **Deputy Chairman** presides (**Art 91**).

31.s: Who was the first Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
31.x: S. Radhakrishnan was the first Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and held the office from 1952 to 1962.
31.tq: Separate the first office-holder from the present office-holders and deputy office-holders.
xs: **S. Radhakrishnan** was the **first Chairman** of the RS (**1952-62**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Harivansh** was **Deputy Chairman**, never Chairman.
xa: ⚠ **S. Radhakrishnan** = first Chairman; **C.P. Radhakrishnan** = present Chairman.
The **Vice-President** is **ex officio Chairman** (**Art 64, 89**).

31.s: In the vacancy of the office of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the power of the Deputy Chairman to decide on a judge-removal motion under Article 91 was upheld by the Supreme Court in January 2026 in the:
31.x: In January 2026, the Supreme Court upheld, in the Justice Varma case, the Deputy Chairman’s power under Article 91 to decide on a judge-removal motion when the Chairman’s office was vacant.
31.tq: Match the recent judicial ruling with the precise constitutional power and case name.
xs: The **SC (Jan 2026)** upheld the Deputy Chairman's **Art 91** power in the **Justice Varma case** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It covered deciding a **judge-removal motion** while the **Chairman's office was vacant**.
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** is about **Tenth Schedule** review; Mavalankar and Hukum Singh were Speakers facing removal motions.
xa: **Harivansh**'s term as Deputy Chairman ended **9 Apr 2026**.
Under **Art 91** the Deputy Chairman also presides when the VP acts as President.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha:
1. The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
2. While a resolution for his removal is under consideration, he cannot preside but may speak, and he cannot vote.
3. When the Vice-President acts as President, the Deputy Chairman performs the duties of the Chairman.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Vice-President is ex officio Chairman (Arts. 64 and 89). Statement 2 is correct: unlike the Speaker, who can vote in the first instance during his removal proceedings, the Chairman cannot vote at all while his removal is pending, though he may speak. Statement 3 is correct: under Article 91 the Deputy Chairman presides when the Chairman's office is vacant or the Vice-President is acting as President. Hence all three.
31.tq: Speaker under removal: can vote (first instance). Chairman under removal: cannot vote at all.
xs: All three statements, **1, 2 and 3**, are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: the **VP** is **ex officio Chairman** (**Art 64, 89**).
Statement 2: while his removal is pending, he **cannot preside** and **cannot vote**, but may speak.
Statement 3: when the VP acts as President, the **Deputy Chairman** presides (**Art 91**).
xa: ⚠ The **Speaker** in that situation **can vote** in the first instance.
The Chairman is removed **only when removed as VP**.

31.s: As per the position in 2026, which one of the following is correct regarding the presiding officers of the Rajya Sabha?
o: Harivansh is the Chairman and C.P. Radhakrishnan the Deputy Chairman
C.P. Radhakrishnan is the Chairman, and Harivansh's term as Deputy Chairman ended on 9 April 2026
S. Radhakrishnan is the Chairman and Harivansh the Deputy Chairman
C.P. Radhakrishnan is the Deputy Chairman, and the office of Chairman is vacant
31.x: C.P. Radhakrishnan, as Vice-President, is the present ex officio Chairman, and Harivansh's term as Deputy Chairman ended on 9 April 2026. Harivansh was never Chairman, S. Radhakrishnan was the first Chairman (1952-62), and the Chairman's office is not described as vacant.
31.tq: First Chairman: S. Radhakrishnan; present Chairman: C.P. Radhakrishnan.
xs: **C.P. Radhakrishnan** is the **present Chairman**, and **Harivansh**'s term as **Deputy Chairman** ended on **9 Apr 2026** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**S. Radhakrishnan** was the **first** Chairman (**1952-62**), not the present one.
xa: The Chairman has a **casting vote only**.
RS has a **Panel of Vice-Chairpersons** nominated by the Chairman.

31.s: With reference to Article 98 of the Constitution, which one of the following is correct?
o: The President appoints all secretarial staff directly and Parliament has no power to regulate recruitment by law.
The Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha must have identical secretarial establishments without any common posts.
Each House has separate secretarial staff, although posts common to both Houses may be created.
The executive government alone regulates recruitment to the secretariats of both Houses in all circumstances.
31.x: Article 98 establishes separate secretarial staff for each House while permitting the creation of posts common to both Houses.
31.tq: Use the constitutional general rule and its permitted exception to eliminate statements using exclusive powers.
xs: Under **Art 98**, each House has **separate secretarial staff**, though **posts common to both Houses** may be created — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Parliament may regulate recruitment by law**; the executive does not control it.
xa: Head: **Secretary-General**, appointed by the **presiding officer**, rank = **Cabinet Secretary**.
The Secretariat is **independent of the executive**.

31.s: Until Parliament makes a law regulating recruitment and conditions of service of the secretarial staff of the Houses, rules may be made by the President after consultation with the:
o: Chief Justice of India and Attorney-General of India
Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha and Secretary-General of the Rajya Sabha
Prime Minister and Union Home Minister
Speaker of the Lok Sabha and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
31.x: In the absence of a law by Parliament, the President may make rules after consulting the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
31.tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ method to distinguish the constitutional consultees from parliamentary officials and ministers.
xs: Until Parliament legislates, the **President** makes rules **after consulting the Speaker/Chairman** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Not the CJI, the Secretaries-General or the PM.
xa: **Art 98** provides each House a **separate secretarial staff**.
Each Secretariat is headed by a **Secretary-General**.

31.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the Secretary-General of a House of Parliament is correct?
1. Each House has a Secretary-General as its head of secretarial staff.
2. The Secretary-General is appointed by the presiding officer of the concerned House.
3. The office holds rank equal to that of the Cabinet Secretary.
4. The secretariat is independent of the executive.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
31.x: The secretariat of each House is headed by its Secretary-General, appointed by the concerned presiding officer. The Secretary-General has the rank of Cabinet Secretary, and the parliamentary secretariat is independent of the executive.
31.tq: Test office, appointing authority, rank and institutional independence as separate elements of one constitutional arrangement.
xs: All four statements, **1, 2, 3 and 4**, are correct — option **(4)**.
The **Secretary-General** heads each House's staff, is **appointed by the presiding officer**, and ranks with the **Cabinet Secretary**.
The Secretariat is **independent of the executive**.
xa: **Posts common to both Houses** may be created (**Art 98**).
Recruitment: Parliament may regulate **by law**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the sessions of Parliament:
1. The President summons each House.
2. The six-month interval is counted from the last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next.
3. The Constitution expressly names the Budget, Monsoon and Winter Sessions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The President summons each House, and the six-month rule is calculated from the last sitting to the first sitting. Budget, Monsoon and Winter Sessions are conventional names, not sessions expressly named in the Constitution.
31.tq: Separate constitutional requirements from parliamentary conventions.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **President summons** each House (**Art 85**).
Statement 2 correct: the gap is counted from the **last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next** (**APPSC G2 2017**).
Statement 3 wrong: the **three sessions** exist **by convention**.
xa: Hence at least **two sessions a year**.
States follow the same six-month rule under **Art 174**.

31.s: The period between prorogation of Parliament and the commencement of its next session is known as:
31.x: The period from prorogation to the next session is called a recess. It is different from adjournment, which interrupts a sitting within a session.
31.tq: Discriminate between a break within a session and the interval between two sessions.
xs: The period from **prorogation to the next session** is a **recess** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Adjournment sine die** ends a sitting; **dissolution** ends the life of the LS.
xa: **Session** = first sitting → prorogation/dissolution.
**Prorogation** is ordered by the **President** (**Governor** in States).

31.s: A quorum in either House of Parliament is ordinarily:
o: One-half of the total membership, including the presiding officer
One-tenth of the total membership, including the presiding officer
One-fourth of the elected membership, excluding nominated members
One-twentieth of the total membership, excluding the presiding officer
31.x: Under Article 100(3), the quorum is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House, including the presiding officer.
31.tq: Check both the fraction and whether the presiding officer is included.
xs: Quorum is **one-tenth of total members, including the presiding officer** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The provision is **Art 100(3)**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes list it as **Art 100(1)**, but **100(1)** actually carries the **casting vote**.
State Assemblies averaged only **24 sittings** in **2025** (**Odisha 43**, **Nagaland 7**).

31.s:
Under Article 86 of the Constitution of India, the President may
1. Address either House of Parliament separately or both Houses together.
2. Require the attendance of members for the purpose of the address.
3. Send messages to either House with respect to a pending Bill.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Article 86 empowers the President to address either House or both Houses together, require members' attendance and send messages to either House regarding pending Bills.
31.tq: Test the exact scope of Article 86 by separating the President’s powers of addressing, requiring attendance and sending messages.
xs: All three statements, **1, 2 and 3**, are correct — option **(4)**.
Under **Art 86**, the President may **address either House or both**, **require attendance**, and **send messages**.
xa: **Art 87**: **special address** at the **first session after each general election** and the **first session of each year**.
The address is debated on a **Motion of Thanks**.

31.s:
The special address delivered by the President under Article 87 is made at which of the following occasions?
1. The first session after each general election to the Lok Sabha.
2. The first session of Parliament in each year.
3. Every session immediately after prorogation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Article 87 provides for the President’s special address at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year. It is not required after every prorogation.
31.tq: Identify the two constitutionally specified occasions and reject the overbroad time-based statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Art 87**: special address at the **first session after each general election** and the **first session of each year**.
Statement 3 wrong: it is not given after every prorogation.
xa: It **outlines government policy**, debated on a **Motion of Thanks**.
**Art 86** covers addresses **at any time** and **messages**.

31.s: The address of the President outlining the policies of the Government is debated in Parliament through a:
31.x: The President’s address outlining Government policy is debated through a Motion of Thanks in Parliament.
31.tq: Match the constitutional address with the parliamentary motion that follows it.
xs: The President's address is debated through a **Motion of Thanks** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The address **outlines government policy**.
xa: The **special address** is under **Art 87**.
The **Budget** session (**Feb-May**) is the longest.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the summoning of Parliament:
1. The President may summon the two Houses separately.
2. The Constitution requires both Houses to be summoned together on every occasion.
3. Each House must meet within six months of its previous sitting.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The President need not summon both Houses together, and the maximum interval between sessions is six months. Statement 2 is false.
31.tq: Identify the statement that reverses the constitutional rule on separate summoning.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **President summons each House**; they need not be summoned together.
Statement 2 wrong: the Constitution does not require summoning them together.
Statement 3 correct: the gap between sessions is **not more than 6 months** (**Art 85**).
xa: The gap runs from the **last sitting** of one session to the **first sitting** of the next.
States: same rule under **Art 174**.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the usual parliamentary sessions and their periods?
o: Budget—April to July; Monsoon—September to November; Winter—January to February
Budget—February to May; Monsoon—July to August/September; Winter—November to December
Budget—January to March; Monsoon—May to June; Winter—September to October
Budget—March to June; Monsoon—August to October; Winter—December to January
31.x: The usual sessions are the Budget Session from February to May, the Monsoon Session from July to August/September, and the Winter Session from November to December.
31.tq: Match each session with its conventional time period.
xs: **Budget — February to May**, **Monsoon — July to September**, **Winter — November to December** — option **(2)**.
These three sessions exist **by convention**, not in the Constitution.
xa: The **Budget** session is the **longest**.
Only **2** oral answers were recorded in the LS in the **Monsoon Session 2026**.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly describes adjournment sine die?
o: Termination of the life of the House without fixing a date for reassembly
Suspension of a sitting by the President until the next session
Termination of a session by the Governor without affecting pending notices
Termination of a sitting by the presiding officer without fixing a date for the next sitting
31.x: Adjournment sine die terminates a sitting without fixing a date for the next sitting. It does not terminate the House or the session, and pending bills remain alive.
31.tq: Separate the presiding officer’s power over a sitting from the President’s power over a session.
xs: **Adjournment sine die** ends a **sitting** by the **presiding officer**, **no date fixed** for the next — so option **(4)** is correct.
It does not end the life of the House, is not ordered by the President or Governor, and has **no effect** on bills.
xa: Pending bills **continue** into the next session (**APPSC 2025**).
⚠ Adjournment / sine die = presiding officer; prorogation / dissolution = **President**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding prorogation:
1. It is ordered by the President in respect of Parliament.
2. It terminates a session.
3. Bills pending before Parliament lapse on prorogation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The President prorogues Parliament and prorogation terminates the session. Bills do not lapse on prorogation, although pending notices generally lapse except notices to introduce bills.
31.tq: Test the effect of prorogation separately from the effect of dissolution.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: **prorogation** is by the **President** and ends the **session**.
Statement 3 wrong: **bills do not lapse** on prorogation; only pending notices lapse, except notices to introduce bills.
xa: On **dissolution**, many bills **lapse**.
In States, prorogation is by the **Governor**.

31.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Adjournment sine die — causes bills to lapse
Adjournment — terminates the life of the House
Prorogation — terminates a sitting for a few hours
Dissolution — terminates the life of the Lok Sabha
31.x: Dissolution terminates the life of the Lok Sabha. Adjournment and adjournment sine die affect sittings, while prorogation terminates a session; none of these causes bills to lapse merely by adjournment or prorogation.
31.tq: Use the ‘ends’ column to reject reversed effects.
xs: **Dissolution — terminates the life of the Lok Sabha** is correct — option **(4)**.
**Adjournment sine die** has **no effect** on bills; **adjournment** ends a **sitting**; **prorogation** ends the **session**.
xa: Dissolution is by the **President**, for the **LS only**.
On dissolution **many bills lapse**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The office of Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha has remained vacant throughout the 17th Lok Sabha.
2. The office of Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha has remained vacant through the 18th Lok Sabha.
3. The Deputy Speaker’s post has remained continuously occupied in both these Lok Sabhas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The Deputy Speaker’s post remained vacant through both the 17th and 18th Lok Sabhas. Therefore, statement 3 is false.
31.tq: Use a present-affairs comparison across two successive Lok Sabhas and reject the directly reversed statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
The **Deputy Speaker's post** stayed **empty through the 17th and 18th** Lok Sabhas.
Statement 3 wrong: the post was not occupied.
xa: It has been **vacant since June 2019**.
State office (**Art 178**) vacant in **8 State Assemblies**.

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Office-holder)
 a. Speaker of the first Andhra Pradesh Assembly
 b. Deputy Speaker of the first Andhra Pradesh Assembly
 c. Chairman of the first Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council

List-II (Person)
 i. Madapati Hanumantha Rao
 ii. Kalluri Subbarao
 iii. Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao

Codes:
 a  b  c
1. iii  ii  i
2. ii   iii i
3. iii  i   ii
4. i    ii  iii
31.x: Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was the Speaker, Kalluri Subbarao was the Deputy Speaker, and Madapati Hanumantha Rao was the first Council Chairman in the first Andhra Pradesh Assembly of 1956.
31.tq: Start from the sure office-holder pair and complete the matching after distinguishing the Assembly offices from the Council office.
xs: **a–iii, b–ii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
First AP Assembly (**1956**): Speaker **Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao**; Deputy Speaker **Kalluri Subbarao**; first Council Chairman **Madapati Hanumantha Rao**.
xa: ⚠ The LS Speaker resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**; State presiding offices are under **Art 178**.
**Jharkhand** has had no Deputy Speaker for **21 years**.

31.s: During the Monsoon Session of 2026, the Lok Sabha recorded how many oral answers, according to the cited assessment of legislative scrutiny?
31.x: Only two oral answers were recorded in the Lok Sabha during the Monsoon Session of 2026, a point cited in criticism concerning low scrutiny.
31.tq: Test a precise session-wise figure rather than relying on a general impression about parliamentary scrutiny.
xs: Only **two** oral answers (**2**) were recorded in the LS in the **Monsoon Session 2026** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is cited as evidence of **low scrutiny**.
xa: State Assemblies averaged only **24 sittings** in **2025**.
The **Deputy Speaker's post** stayed empty through the **17th and 18th** Lok Sabhas.

32.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the recognised tools of parliamentary control over the executive?
o: Judicial review by the Supreme Court
32.x: Judicial review is a constitutional function of the judiciary, not a parliamentary device listed among the tools of legislative control over the executive.
32.tq: Separate parliamentary control devices from mechanisms belonging to another constitutional organ.
xs: **Judicial review by the Supreme Court** is NOT a tool of parliamentary control — so option **(4)** is correct.
The recognised tools include **Question Hour**, **Zero Hour**, **half-an-hour discussion**, short-duration discussion, **calling attention**, adjournment, censure and no-confidence motions.
**Budget approval** and the **Motion of Thanks** are also listed tools, so options (1), (2) and (3) are all genuine devices.
xa: The **committee system** is also a tool: Government Assurances, Petitions, Subordinate Legislation, **PAC** and **Estimates**.
⚠ Order of Indian firsts: **1953** short-duration discussion – **1954** calling attention – **1962** Zero Hour.
**States** use the same devices plus estimates and public accounts committees.

32.s: Which one of the following correctly compares the devices used by Parliament and State Legislatures for controlling the executive?
o: State Legislatures cannot use Question Hour or motions
Parliament alone uses these devices; State Legislatures use only debates
State Legislatures use the same devices, along with estimates and public accounts committees
State Legislatures use only the no-confidence motion
32.x: State Legislatures use the same parliamentary devices for executive control and also use estimates and public accounts committees.
32.tq: Test the Union–State comparison by identifying the correct extension rather than an exclusive claim.
xs: **State Legislatures use the same devices**, along with **estimates and public accounts committees** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Hence options saying States cannot use Question Hour, use only debates, or use only the no-confidence motion are all wrong.
xa: The Union tools: Question Hour, Zero Hour, half-an-hour and short-duration discussions, and **calling attention**, **adjournment**, **censure** and **no-confidence** motions.
Committees: **Government Assurances**, **Petitions**, **Subordinate Legislation**, **PAC**, **Estimates**; plus **Budget approval** and the **Motion of Thanks**.
The **AP Legislature** uses the same devices — e.g., the AP Legislative Council was adjourned amid a Question Hour row on the **Tirumala laddu** issue (**Feb 2026**).

32.s: Question Hour in the Lok Sabha is generally held during:
o: The first hour of every sitting
Only the first sitting of each week
The hour immediately before the day's adjournment
The last hour of every sitting
32.x: Question Hour is held during the first hour of every sitting of the Lok Sabha, when Ministers answer questions.
32.tq: Test the standard time slot without confusing it with the different Rajya Sabha Zero Hour sequence.
xs: Question Hour is held during **the first hour of every sitting** in the Lok Sabha — so option **(1)** is correct.
In it ministers answer searching questions, and it draws the **maximum attendance** of members.
xa: It is the **most effective vigil** on the executive — the day-to-day method of control.
**Starred** questions = **oral** answer, supplementaries allowed, **green** paper; **unstarred** = **written**, no supplementaries, **white** paper.
**Zero Hour** in the Lok Sabha starts **immediately after Question Hour**.
Question Hour ran only **60%** of its scheduled time — a noted criticism.

32.s:
Which of the following correctly matches the type of question with its answer and supplementary-question position?
1. Starred question — Oral answer — Supplementaries allowed
2. Unstarred question — Written answer — Supplementaries not allowed
3. Short-notice question — Oral answer — Supplementaries allowed
4. Question to a private member — Oral or written answer
Which of the above are correctly matched?
32.x: All four matches are correct. Starred and short-notice questions receive oral answers with supplementaries allowed; unstarred questions receive written answers without supplementaries; a question to a private member may receive an oral or written answer.
32.tq: Check each row independently, especially the answer mode and supplementary-question rule.
xs: All four pairs are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**Starred** = **oral**, supplementaries allowed; **unstarred** = **written**, supplementaries not allowed.
**Short-notice** = **oral**, supplementaries allowed; a question **to a private member** (on his bill/resolution) = **oral or written**.
xa: Paper colours: starred **green**, unstarred **white**, short-notice **light pink**, private member **yellow**.
Short-notice question: notice **less than 10 days**, on a matter of **urgent public importance**.
Ordinary questions need at least **15 clear days'** notice.

32.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Question to a private member — Blue paper
32.x: A question addressed to a private member is printed on yellow paper, not blue paper. Starred, unstarred and short-notice questions are associated with green, white and light pink paper respectively.
32.tq: Use the comparison table to locate the single altered colour designation.
xs: **Question to a private member — Blue paper** is wrongly matched — so option **(4)** is correct; it is printed on **yellow** paper.
The other pairs are right: short-notice = **light pink**, starred = **green**, unstarred = **white**.
xa: ⚠ Starred = **oral + green**; unstarred = **written + white**.
A question to a private member is on **his bill/resolution** and may get an **oral or written** answer.
Short-notice questions allow **supplementaries** and get an **oral** answer.

32.s: A short-notice question differs from an ordinary question in that it may be admitted when notice is given:
o: Only on the day of the sitting
At least 15 clear days in advance
32.x: A short-notice question is one for which notice is given less than 10 days in advance. Ordinary questions require at least 15 clear days' notice.
32.tq: Discriminate between the two notice thresholds instead of treating all questions alike.
xs: A short-notice question may be admitted on notice of **less than 10 days** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**At least 15 clear days'** notice is for **ordinary** questions, so option (2) is wrong.
xa: A short-notice question must be on a matter of **urgent public importance** and gets an **oral answer**.
It is printed on **light pink** paper; supplementaries are allowed.
**Zero Hour** matters need **no prior notice** of the kind a question needs — only same-day intimation to the Presiding Officer.

32.s: Which of the following is considered the most effective method of day-to-day vigilance over the executive?
32.x: Question Hour is regarded as the most effective method of day-to-day vigilance over the executive because Ministers are required to answer questions.
32.tq: Match the parliamentary device with its principal accountability function.
xs: **Question Hour** is the most effective method of **day-to-day** vigil on the executive — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is held in the **first hour** of every sitting, when ministers answer searching questions.
**Motion of Thanks** and **Budget approval** are also tools, but not the day-to-day vigil; **yielding the floor** is just a member giving way to another member or the Chair.
xa: ⚠ The **no-confidence motion** is the **most powerful weapon** of executive accountability (APPSC-G2 2025) — do not confuse with Question Hour.
Starred questions get **oral** answers; unstarred get **written** answers.
Question Hour ran only **60%** of its scheduled time in recent criticism.

32.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the status of Zero Hour in the Indian Parliament?
o: It is a device borrowed from the British Parliament
It is mentioned in the Rules of Procedure of both Houses
It is an informal parliamentary innovation and is not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure
It is expressly mentioned in the Constitution
32.x: Zero Hour is an informal Indian innovation. It is not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure and has been in use since 1962; it was not borrowed from another country.
32.tq: Distinguish a formal constitutional or rule-based device from an informal parliamentary practice.
xs: Zero Hour is an **informal** device **not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is an **Indian innovation**, not borrowed from any other country, so option (1) is wrong; it is in neither the Rules nor the Constitution.
xa: In use since **1962**.
In the **Lok Sabha** it starts **immediately after Question Hour**; in the **Rajya Sabha** it precedes Question Hour.
Ministers are **not bound to reply** to Zero Hour matters.
⚠ Indian innovations: short-duration discussion **1953**, calling attention **1954**, Zero Hour **1962**.

32.s: With reference to Zero Hour in the Rajya Sabha, which of the following statements is correct?
o: It follows Question Hour and has a fixed duration of one hour
It is held only after the day's regular agenda is completed
It is not permitted in the Rajya Sabha
It precedes Question Hour, during which urgent public matters may be raised
32.x: In the Rajya Sabha, urgent matters of public importance are raised during the first hour, before Question Hour.
32.tq: Separate the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha arrangements instead of applying the Lok Sabha sequence to both Houses.
xs: In the Rajya Sabha, Zero Hour **precedes Question Hour**, when **urgent public matters** are raised in the first hour — so option **(4)** is correct.
Zero Hour has **no fixed duration** in the rules, so option (1) is wrong.
xa: In the **Lok Sabha**, Zero Hour starts **immediately after Question Hour** and lasts until regular business is taken up.
Zero Hour is **not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure**; in use since **1962**.
Members only **intimate the Presiding Officer** the same day; he decides whom to allow.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Zero Hour:
1. It has no fixed duration prescribed in the Rules.
2. It continues until the regular business of the day is taken up in the Lok Sabha.
3. A member must give the same prior notice as is required for an ordinary question.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Zero Hour has no fixed duration in the Rules and in the Lok Sabha lasts until the day's regular agenda is taken up. Members do not give the prior notice required for an ordinary question; they intimate the Presiding Officer on the same day.
32.tq: Test the distinction between same-day intimation for Zero Hour and formal prior notice for questions.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — Zero Hour has **no fixed duration** in the rules.
Statement 2: correct — in the Lok Sabha it lasts **until regular business is taken up**.
Statement 3: wrong — Zero Hour is **without the prior notice** a question needs; members only intimate the Presiding Officer the **same day**.
xa: Zero Hour is an **Indian innovation** in use since **1962**, not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure.
Ministers are **not bound to reply**.
Follow-up: the **Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs** sends extracts of the Chair's directions to the ministry concerned for action.

32.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of matters raised during Zero Hour?
o: The Presiding Officer decides which members may be allowed to raise them
Members may raise them without the prior notice required for a question
Ministers are constitutionally bound to give an immediate reply
They concern urgent matters of public importance
32.x: Ministers are not bound to reply to matters raised during Zero Hour. The other features correctly describe the procedure.
32.tq: Find the single statement that reverses a procedural limitation.
xs: **Ministers constitutionally bound to give an immediate reply** is NOT a feature — so option **(3)** is correct; ministers are **not bound to reply** in Zero Hour.
The rest are true: members raise matters **without prior notice**, and the **Presiding Officer decides** whom to allow.
xa: Zero Hour starts **immediately after Question Hour** in the Lok Sabha.
It is informal and **not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure**; in use since **1962**.
Chair's directions / assurances → **Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs** forwards them to the ministry concerned.

32.s: In the Lok Sabha, the time immediately following the Question Hour, during which members raise matters of urgent public importance without the prior notice required for questions, is known as
32.x: Zero Hour begins immediately after Question Hour in the Lok Sabha; members raise matters with only same-day intimation to the Presiding Officer, not the notice a question needs. Calling Attention, half-an-hour and short-duration discussions are formal devices under the Rules that require prior notice.
32.tq: After Question Hour + no prior notice + not in the Rules = Zero Hour (since 1962).
xs: The time right after Question Hour when matters are raised without prior notice is **Zero Hour** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Calling attention** seeks an authoritative statement from a minister; **half-an-hour discussion** is for factual elucidation; **short-duration discussion** is under **Rule 193** with no vote.
xa: Exam angle: this exact stem appeared in **APPSC-GS 2025** and **G2 2023, 2025**.
Zero Hour is an **Indian innovation** (**1962**), not in the Rules of Procedure.
Ministers are **not bound to reply**; the Presiding Officer decides whom to allow.

32.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

1. Rule 377, Lok Sabha — Matters not raisable under any other device
2. Special Mentions, Rajya Sabha — Equivalent device to Rule 377 matters
3. Rule 193, Lok Sabha — Short-duration discussion without voting
4. Rule 184, Lok Sabha — Discussion followed by voting

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: All four pairs are correct. Rule 377 and Special Mentions serve corresponding purposes in the two Houses, while Rules 193 and 184 distinguish discussions without and with voting respectively.
32.tq: Start with rule-number pairs and then confirm the presence or absence of voting.
xs: All four pairs are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**Rule 377 (LS)** = matters not raisable under any other device; the Rajya Sabha equivalent is **Special Mentions** (Rule **180A-E**).
**Rule 193** = short-duration discussion, **no voting**; **Rule 184** = discussion followed by a **vote**.
xa: **Rule 198 (LS)** = no-confidence motion.
Privilege motion = **Rule 222 (LS)**, **Rule 187 (RS)**.
Short-duration discussion: max **2 hours**; Indian innovation (**1953**).

32.s:
Arrange the following parliamentary discussion devices in chronological order of their introduction or institutional association:
A. Calling Attention
B. Short-duration discussion
C. Zero Hour

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: Short-duration discussion is an Indian innovation of 1953, Calling Attention dates from 1954, and Zero Hour is associated with 1962. Therefore, the correct order is B, A, C.
32.tq: Place the dated devices first and compare the closely spaced years 1953, 1954 and 1962.
xs: The order is **B, A, C** — option **(2)**.
**Short-duration discussion** **1953** → **Calling attention** **1954** → **Zero Hour** **1962**.
xa: All three are **Indian innovations**; Zero Hour was not borrowed from any other country.
Short-duration discussion is under **Rule 193**, max **2 hours**, no voting.
Calling attention is **in the Rules of Procedure**; Zero Hour is **not**.

32.s:
A Short-duration Discussion in the Lok Sabha has which of the following features?
1. It is limited to a maximum of two hours.
2. It is an Indian innovation of 1953.
3. It necessarily ends with a formal vote.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because a short-duration discussion does not involve voting.
32.tq: Identify the duration and origin while rejecting the false voting consequence.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — maximum **2 hours**.
Statement 2: correct — an **Indian innovation** of **1953**.
Statement 3: wrong — under **Rule 193** there is **no voting**.
xa: ⚠ **Rule 184** = discussion followed by a vote.
**Half-an-hour discussion**: matter sufficiently debated needing factual elucidation; no formal motion or vote.
Next Indian innovations: calling attention **1954**, Zero Hour **1962**.

32.s: A half-an-hour discussion is intended for:
o: A matter that can be raised only through a No-confidence Motion
A demand for grant requiring reduction by Rs 100
A matter already sufficiently debated but requiring factual elucidation
A breach of privilege requiring immediate suspension of the House
32.x: A half-an-hour discussion is held on a matter that has been sufficiently debated but requires further factual elucidation. It involves no formal motion or vote.
32.tq: Apply the purpose of the device to a scenario requiring clarification rather than a fresh decision.
xs: A half-an-hour discussion is for **a matter sufficiently debated but needing factual elucidation** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It has **no formal motion or vote**.
Reducing a demand by **Rs 100** is a **token cut**; a breach of privilege goes by a **privilege motion** — so options (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: **Short-duration discussion** (Rule **193**): max **2 hours**, no vote, Indian innovation of **1953**.
**Rule 184** discussion ends in a vote.
**Rule 377 (LS)** covers matters not raisable under any other device.

32.s: An Adjournment Motion in Parliament can be admitted only when it concerns:
o: A demand for grant requiring reduction by one rupee
Any matter raised without prior notice
A matter of definite and urgent public importance
32.x: An Adjournment Motion sets aside the normal business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.
32.tq: Match the motion with its defining procedural condition rather than with a related device.
xs: An Adjournment Motion concerns **a definite matter of urgent public importance** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It sets aside the House business to discuss that matter.
Reducing a demand to **Re 1** is a **policy cut**; matters raised without prior notice belong to **Zero Hour**.
xa: It is moved **only in the Lok Sabha** with **50 members'** support.
It carries an **element of censure**; debate lasts at least **2 h 30 min**.
⚠ Adjournment and no-confidence are both **Lok Sabha only** and both need **50 members**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about an Adjournment Motion:
1. It can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
2. It requires the support of 50 members.
3. It has an element of censure.
4. Its debate lasts at least two hours and thirty minutes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All four statements are correct. An Adjournment Motion is a Lok Sabha device, requires 50 members' support, carries an element of censure and involves debate of at least two hours and thirty minutes.
32.tq: Test the House, numerical requirement, character and duration together.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **Lok Sabha only**. Statement 2: **50 members'** support.
Statement 3: it has an **element of censure**. Statement 4: debate lasts at least **2 h 30 min**.
xa: It sets aside House business for a **definite matter of urgent public importance**.
⚠ The **no-confidence motion** is also Lok Sabha only with **50 members**.
**Calling attention**, by contrast, is used in both Houses and seeks an **authoritative statement** from a minister.

32.s: Which one of the following motions is available in both Houses and seeks an authoritative statement from a Minister?
32.x: A Calling Attention Motion is available in both Houses and seeks an authoritative statement from the concerned Minister.
32.tq: Use the combination of House availability and procedural purpose to identify the motion.
xs: The **Calling Attention Motion** is used in both Houses and seeks an **authoritative statement** from a minister — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Adjournment** and **no-confidence** motions are **Lok Sabha only**; **cut motions** are on demands for grants in the Lok Sabha.
xa: Calling attention is an **Indian innovation** since **1954**, included in the **Rules of Procedure**.
It draws a minister's attention to a matter of **urgent public importance**.
**Privilege motions** are also in both Houses — **Rule 222 (LS)**, **Rule 187 (RS)**.

32.s: The Calling Attention procedure is significant because it is:
o: An Indian innovation introduced in 1962 but not included in the Rules
An Indian innovation introduced in 1954 and included in the Rules of Procedure
32.x: Calling Attention is an Indian innovation dating from 1954 and is provided for in the Rules of Procedure.
32.tq: Discriminate between the dates and rule status of Calling Attention and Zero Hour.
xs: Calling attention is **an Indian innovation of 1954 included in the Rules of Procedure** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is not British (option 1); **1962** with no place in the Rules describes **Zero Hour** (option 3).
xa: It draws a minister's attention to a matter of **urgent public importance** and seeks an **authoritative statement**.
Used in **both Houses**.
⚠ **1953** short-duration – **1954** calling attention – **1962** Zero Hour.

32.s:
Match the following types of cut motions with their purposes:

List-I (Cut motion)
A. Policy cut
B. Economy cut
C. Token cut

List-II (Purpose or amount)
1. Reduction by a specified amount to effect economy
2. Reduction of the demand to Re 1 to express disapproval of policy
3. Reduction by Rs 100 to ventilate a specific grievance

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
32.x: A policy cut reduces the demand to Re 1, an economy cut reduces it by a specified amount, and a token cut reduces it by Rs 100 to raise a specific grievance.
32.tq: Start from the distinctive numerical values—Re 1 and Rs 100—and then identify the remaining pair.
xs: **Policy cut** = reduce demand to **Re 1** → disapproval of policy.
**Economy cut** = reduce by a **specified amount**; **token cut** = reduce by **Rs 100** → a specific grievance.
xa: Cut motions are moved on **demands for grants** in the **Lok Sabha**.
**Budget approval** is one of the listed tools of parliamentary control.
The **Estimates Committee** suggests economies and efficiency in the estimates.

32.s: A privilege motion, moved when a member feels that a minister or member has committed a breach of privilege, is raised in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha respectively under
32.x: A privilege motion is governed by Rule 222 of the Lok Sabha rules and Rule 187 of the Rajya Sabha rules. Rule 184 (LS) is a discussion followed by a vote, Rule 193 (LS) is a short-duration discussion without a vote, Rule 180A-E (RS) covers Special Mentions, and Rule 198 (LS) is the no-confidence motion.
32.tq: Privilege: LS 222 / RS 187. No-confidence: LS 198.
xs: A privilege motion is under **Rule 222** (LS) and **Rule 187** (RS) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Rule 184** = discussion with vote; **Rule 193** = short-duration discussion; **Rule 180A-E** = Special Mentions (RS); **Rule 198** = no-confidence motion.
xa: A privilege motion concerns a **breach of privilege** by a minister or member and is available in **both Houses**.
A privilege notice was given in the Rajya Sabha against the **Union Education Minister** (**May 2026**).
Committee of Privileges: **15** members (LS, by the Speaker); **10** (RS, by the Chairman).

32.s:
With reference to a no-confidence motion, consider the following statements:
1. It is expressly mentioned in the Constitution.
2. Its constitutional basis is connected with Article 75(3).
3. It may be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
4. It requires the support of 50 members for leave to be granted.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: A no-confidence motion is not expressly mentioned in the Constitution. It flows from Article 75(3), is moved only in the Lok Sabha, and requires the support of 50 members for leave.
32.tq: Trap the incorrect constitutional-status statement while checking House, support and Article details separately.
xs: Statements **2, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: wrong — it is **not mentioned in the Constitution**.
Statement 2: correct — it flows from **Article 75(3)**, collective responsibility to the **Lok Sabha**.
Statements 3 and 4: correct — **only in the Lok Sabha**, with **50 members** for leave.
xa: Moved under **Rule 198**; **no reasons need be stated**.
If passed, the whole **Council of Ministers must resign**.
First instance: against **Nehru** (**1963**) by **J.B. Kripalani**.

32.s: A no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha is moved under which Rule of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business?
32.x: A no-confidence motion is moved under Rule 198 of the Rules of Procedure of the Lok Sabha.
32.tq: Test precise rule-number recall using nearby numerical distractors.
xs: A no-confidence motion is moved under **Rule 198** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Rule 184** is a discussion followed by a vote.
xa: Basis: **Article 75(3)** — collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha; not in the Constitution itself.
Needs **50 members**; **no reasons** need be stated.
⚠ Privilege = **Rule 222**; short-duration discussion = **Rule 193**.

32.s: Which one of the following statements about a no-confidence motion is correct?
o: Reasons for moving it must necessarily be stated
It can be moved in either House of Parliament
It can be moved only by the Leader of the Opposition
32.x: The Speaker exercises discretion in admitting or rejecting a no-confidence motion. Reasons need not be stated, and the motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
32.tq: Apply the 'who would do this job?' test to distinguish the Speaker's procedural role from political roles.
xs: **The Speaker decides its admissibility** — he has **discretion to admit or reject** it — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
**No reasons need be stated** (option 1 wrong); it is moved **only in the Lok Sabha** (option 2 wrong).
Leave needs the support of **50 members**, not just the Leader of the Opposition.
xa: ⚠ Trap: the Speaker does **not resign or dissolve** the House.
It is the **most powerful weapon** of executive accountability (APPSC-G2 2025).
⚠ "Reasons must be stated" = **censure motion**.

32.s: If a no-confidence motion is passed in the Lok Sabha, what is the constitutional consequence?
o: The Lok Sabha is automatically dissolved
The concerned Minister must resign, while the Council continues
Only the Prime Minister must resign
The entire Council of Ministers must resign
32.x: The motion tests the collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha. If passed, the whole Council of Ministers must resign.
32.tq: Connect the procedural outcome with the constitutional principle of collective responsibility.
xs: If passed, **the entire Council of Ministers must resign** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It enforces **collective responsibility** under **Article 75(3)**; the Lok Sabha is not dissolved.
xa: A **censure motion**, if passed, does **not** bind the ministers to resign.
The no-confidence motion is moved under **Rule 198**, only in the Lok Sabha.
Andhra State: **Prakasam ministry** fell by one vote (**69 for, 68 against**) in Nov **1954**.

32.s: The first no-confidence motion against the Union Council of Ministers was moved against Jawaharlal Nehru in 1963 by:
32.x: The first no-confidence motion against Jawaharlal Nehru was moved in 1963 by J.B. Kripalani.
32.tq: Link the event, year and mover rather than relying on the event alone.
xs: The first no-confidence motion, against **Nehru** in **1963**, was moved by **J.B. Kripalani** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Gouthu Latchanna** moved the motion against the **Prakasam** ministry in **Andhra State** (Nov **1954**).
xa: The Andhra motion was carried **69 for, 68 against**; the ministry fell after **13 months**.
President's Rule followed: **16 Nov 1954 - 27 Mar 1955**.
No-confidence is moved under **Rule 198** with **50 members'** support.

32.s: Which of the following correctly describes the no-confidence motion moved against the Andhra State ministry in November 1954?
o: It was moved by Gouthu Latchanna and carried by 69 votes to 68
It was moved by Gouthu Latchanna and defeated by 68 votes to 69
It was moved by J.B. Kripalani and defeated by 69 votes to 68
It resulted in the continuation of the Prakasam ministry for five years
32.x: Gouthu Latchanna's motion in November 1954 was carried by 69 votes to 68. The Prakasam ministry consequently fell after 13 months.
32.tq: Use the vote margin and mover together to avoid swapping a closely related historical instance.
xs: It was moved by **Gouthu Latchanna** and **carried by 69 votes to 68** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **Prakasam** ministry fell by one vote after **13 months**, so option (4) is wrong; **J.B. Kripalani** moved the first one against Nehru (**1963**).
xa: President's Rule in Andhra State: **16 Nov 1954 - 27 Mar 1955**.
A passed no-confidence motion forces the whole **Council of Ministers** to resign.
Constitutional basis: **Article 75(3)** — collective responsibility.

32.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A Censure Motion may be directed against a Minister, a group of Ministers or the whole Council of Ministers.
2. A No-confidence Motion is directed against the entire Council of Ministers.
3. Passing a Censure Motion compels the Council of Ministers to resign.
4. Passing a No-confidence Motion requires the Council of Ministers to resign.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is false because passing a Censure Motion does not compel resignation, whereas passing a No-confidence Motion does.
32.tq: Find the single reversed consequence in a comparison table.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — censure may target the **Council of Ministers, a minister or a group**.
Statement 2: correct — no-confidence targets the **entire Council of Ministers**.
Statement 3: wrong — after censure ministers are **not bound to resign**; Statement 4: correct — after no-confidence they **must resign**.
xa: Censure **must state reasons**; no-confidence needs **no reasons**.
Censure seeks **disapproval of a policy**.
No-confidence: **only in Lok Sabha**, **50 members**, **Rule 198**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The no-confidence motion is regarded as the most powerful weapon for enforcing the accountability of the executive.
2. A censure motion must state the reasons for its adoption in the Lok Sabha.
3. A no-confidence motion must state the grounds on which it is based.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: the no-confidence motion is the most powerful weapon of executive accountability, while Question Hour is the most effective day-to-day vigil. Statement 2 is correct: a censure motion must state its reasons. Statement 3 is wrong: a no-confidence motion need not state any reasons. Hence 1 and 2 only.
32.tq: Reasons must be stated = censure; no reasons needed = no-confidence.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — no-confidence is the **most powerful weapon** of executive accountability (APPSC-G2 2025).
Statement 2: correct — a censure motion **must state reasons**.
Statement 3: wrong — a no-confidence motion needs **no reasons**.
xa: ⚠ **Question Hour** = most effective **day-to-day** vigil; no-confidence = most powerful weapon.
The **Speaker** has discretion to admit or reject a no-confidence motion.
Censure can be against a **minister or a group**; no-confidence only the **entire** Council.

32.s:
With reference to resolutions in Parliament, consider the following statements:
1. A resolution is a self-contained proposal.
2. Every resolution is a substantive motion.
3. A mover may withdraw a resolution at any time without the leave of the House.
4. A resolution must be put to vote.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: A resolution is a self-contained proposal and always takes the form of a substantive motion. It must be put to vote, but its mover cannot withdraw it without the leave of the House.
32.tq: Test the procedural exception by identifying the statement that reverses the withdrawal rule.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 2: correct — a resolution is a **self-contained proposal**, **always a substantive motion**.
Statement 3: wrong — the mover **cannot withdraw without leave of the House**; Statement 4: correct — it **must be put to vote**.
xa: Same subject barred for **one year**.
**Private member's** resolutions are taken up on **alternate Fridays**, afternoon.
Types: **private member's**, **government** (e.g., approving treaties), **statutory**.

32.s: A resolution on the same subject as an earlier resolution is generally barred from being moved for what period?
32.x: A resolution on the same subject is barred for one year.
32.tq: Use the precise time-period distinction in procedural rules.
xs: A resolution on the same subject is barred for **one year** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Six months, two years or the rest of the session are not what the notes give; the bar is **one year**.
xa: A resolution is **always a substantive motion** and must be **put to vote**.
The mover cannot withdraw it **without leave of the House**.
Private member's resolutions: **alternate Fridays**, afternoon.

32.s: Private Members’ Resolutions in Parliament are generally taken up on:
o: The last sitting day of every month
32.x: Private Members’ Resolutions are taken up on alternate Fridays during the afternoon.
32.tq: Match the device with its distinctive day-and-time arrangement.
xs: Private members' resolutions are taken up on **alternate Fridays in the afternoon** — so option **(3)** is correct.
