They are not a Monday, Wednesday or month-end item; the slot is **alternate Fridays**.
xa: A **government resolution** is moved by a minister, e.g., approving **treaties**.
A **statutory resolution** is moved under a constitutional/statutory provision.
A resolution is a **self-contained proposal**; same subject barred for **one year**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding types of resolutions in Parliament:
1. A Government resolution is moved by a minister, for example to approve a treaty.
2. A resolution moved under a constitutional or statutory provision is called a statutory resolution.
3. Unlike a private member's resolution, a Government resolution need not be put to vote.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct as per the types of resolutions. Statement 3 is wrong: every resolution is a substantive motion and must be put to vote. So '1 and 2 only' is right; options including 3 are wrong.
32.tq: Every resolution = substantive motion = must be voted; types differ only in who moves it and under what power.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — a **government resolution** is moved by a minister (e.g., approving **treaties**).
Statement 2: correct — one under a constitutional/statutory provision is a **statutory** resolution.
Statement 3: wrong — every resolution is a **substantive motion** and **must be put to vote**.
xa: Private member's resolutions: **alternate Fridays**, afternoon.
The mover cannot withdraw a resolution **without leave of the House**.
Same subject barred for **one year**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A point of order is raised when proceedings depart from the Rules or the Constitution.
2. A point of order is itself subject to a regular debate in the House.
3. The Presiding Officer rules on a point of order.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. A point of order is not subject to regular debate; the Presiding Officer rules on it.
32.tq: Use the procedural consequence to reject the statement that adds an impermissible debate.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — raised when proceedings **depart from rules/Constitution**.
Statement 2: wrong — a point of order has **no debate**; Statement 3: correct — the **Presiding Officer rules** on it.
xa: **Yielding the floor**: member speaking gives way to another member or the Chair.
**Simple closure**: "matter sufficiently discussed; be put to vote".
**Rule 377 (LS)** matters are those that are **not points of order** ("special mention").

32.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Simple closure — Only important clauses are debated
Closure by compartments — All pending clauses are voted on when time ends
Kangaroo closure — Only important clauses are debated and the others are taken as passed
Guillotine — Matter is declared sufficiently discussed and put to vote
32.x: C is correct: under kangaroo closure only the important clauses are debated and the rest are taken as passed. A is wrong because simple closure means the matter is declared sufficiently discussed and put to vote; B is wrong because putting all pending clauses to vote when time ends is the guillotine; D is wrong because it describes simple closure, not the guillotine.
32.tq: Discriminate among similar closure terms by matching each device with its exact operation.
xs: **Kangaroo closure — only important clauses debated, others taken as passed** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Simple closure** = matter sufficiently discussed, put to vote; **closure by compartments** = clauses grouped into parts, debated and voted part by part.
Voting all pending clauses when time ends is the **guillotine**, not simple closure.
xa: ⚠ Kangaroo = only important clauses debated; guillotine = **undiscussed** clauses voted when allotted time ends.
**Point of order**: raised when proceedings depart from rules; no debate.
Whips: **one-line** informative, **two-line** attendance, **three-line** strict voting.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding parliamentary closure devices:
1. Under closure by compartments, clauses are grouped into parts and debated and voted upon part by part.
2. Under the guillotine, only the important clauses are debated and the remaining clauses are taken as passed.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: closure by compartments groups clauses into parts, with debate and vote part by part. Statement 2 is wrong: that describes kangaroo closure; under the guillotine all pending clauses are put to vote when the allotted time ends, even undiscussed ones. Hence 1 only; options 2, 'Both' and 'Neither' fail.
32.tq: Guillotine = time runs out, everything voted; Kangaroo = jump over unimportant clauses.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — **closure by compartments** groups clauses into parts, with debate and vote **part by part**.
Statement 2: wrong — that is **kangaroo closure**; the **guillotine** puts all pending clauses to vote when allotted time ends.
xa: **Simple closure**: "matter sufficiently discussed; be put to vote".
**Yielding the floor**: speaking member gives way to another member or the Chair.
**Point of order**: Presiding Officer rules; no debate.

32.s: When a member who is speaking gives way to another member or to the Chair, the procedure is known as:
32.x: Yielding the floor occurs when the member speaking gives way to another member or to the Chair.
32.tq: Match the ordinary procedural action with its precise parliamentary term.
xs: A member giving way to another member or the Chair is **yielding the floor** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Simple closure** ends debate and puts the matter to vote; **point of order** is raised when proceedings depart from rules; **calling attention** seeks a minister's statement.
xa: **Kangaroo closure**: only important clauses debated, others taken as passed.
**Guillotine**: all pending clauses put to vote when time ends.
**Three-line whip** = strict voting direction.

32.s: In the context of parliamentary functioning, the term “guillotine” is associated with
o: The rejection of all delegated legislation by Parliament
The closure of discussion and voting on demands without completing detailed debate
The removal of the Speaker by the President
The automatic dissolution of the Rajya Sabha after a general election
32.x: The guillotine refers to curtailing discussion and putting demands to vote without completing detailed debate, and is cited as an issue affecting parliamentary debate quality.
32.tq: Identify the parliamentary procedure by connecting the term with its effect on debate time.
xs: The guillotine is **closure of discussion and voting without completing detailed debate** — so option **(2)** is correct.
When the allotted time ends, **all pending clauses** are put to vote, **even undiscussed ones**.
xa: ⚠ **Kangaroo closure** = only important clauses debated; the rest taken as passed.
**Closure by compartments** = debate and vote part by part.
Criticism: 17th Lok Sabha sent only **16%** of Bills to committees vs **71%** in the 15th.

32.s: The office of Whip in the Indian parliamentary system derives its authority primarily from:
o: The Rules of Procedure of Parliament
A specific provision of the Constitution
32.x: The office of Whip is not mentioned in the Constitution, the Rules of the House or any parliamentary statute. It is based on conventions of parliamentary government.
32.tq: Distinguish a conventional office from a constitutional, statutory or rule-based office.
xs: The Whip rests on **parliamentary conventions** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is **not mentioned in the Constitution, the Rules of the House or any statute** — so options (2), (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: ⚠ Only the convention statement was valid in **APPSC-G1 2024**.
Defying the whip on a vote can attract **Tenth Schedule** disqualification.
Whips: **one-line** informative, **two-line** attendance, **three-line** strict voting direction.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding a party Whip:
1. Each political party appoints a Whip or Chief Whip.
2. The Whip seeks to ensure attendance and voting according to the party line.
3. Defiance of a Whip can attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All three statements are correct. A party Whip enforces party discipline regarding attendance and voting, and defiance in relevant circumstances may attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
32.tq: Check whether all statements describe connected functions and consequences of party discipline.
xs: All three statements are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
Each party appoints a **whip/chief whip** to ensure **attendance and voting per party line**.
Defying the whip on a vote can attract **Tenth Schedule** disqualification.
xa: The Whip rests on **conventions** — not in the Constitution, Rules or any statute.
The **Minister of Parliamentary Affairs** keeps close contact with chief whips of both Houses.
**Three-line** whip = strict voting direction.

32.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the types of Whip:

List-I (Type)
A. One-line Whip
B. Two-line Whip
C. Three-line Whip

List-II (Purpose)
1. Strict voting direction
2. Informative communication
3. Direction to attend the House

Select the correct code:
32.x: A one-line Whip is informative, a two-line Whip directs members to attend, and a three-line Whip gives a strict voting direction.
32.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes with swapped functions.
xs: **One-line** whip = informative; **two-line** = attendance; **three-line** = strict voting direction.
xa: Defying the whip on a vote can attract **Tenth Schedule** disqualification.
The office of Whip rests on **conventions** of parliamentary government.
Each party appoints a **whip / chief whip**.

32.s: Which Union Minister maintains close contact with the Chief Whips of political parties in both Houses of Parliament?
o: Minister of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
32.x: The Minister of Parliamentary Affairs keeps close contact with the Chief Whips of parties in both Houses.
32.tq: Use the functional association between parliamentary coordination and the concerned ministry.
xs: The **Minister of Parliamentary Affairs** keeps close contact with the chief whips — so option **(3)** is correct.
This liaison covers the chief whips of parties in **both Houses**.
xa: The same ministry sends extracts of the Chair's **Zero Hour** directions/assurances to the ministry concerned for action.
Whips ensure **attendance and voting** per party line.
Defiance can bring **Tenth Schedule** disqualification.

32.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the composition of the Committee of Privileges?
o: Lok Sabha—10 members nominated by the Chairman; Rajya Sabha—15 members nominated by the Speaker
Lok Sabha—15 members nominated by the Speaker; Rajya Sabha—10 members nominated by the Chairman
Both Houses—15 members elected by the respective Houses
Both Houses—10 members nominated by the President
32.x: The Lok Sabha Committee of Privileges has 15 members nominated by the Speaker, while the Rajya Sabha Committee has 10 members nominated by the Chairman.
32.tq: Check both membership and nominating authority; the two Houses are deliberately reversed in distractors.
xs: LS: **15 members nominated by the Speaker**; RS: **10 members nominated by the Chairman** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) swaps the numbers and nominating authorities.
xa: DRSCs: **24** (16 LS + 8 RS); **31 members = 21 LS + 10 RS**; set up in **1993**.
**Ethics Committee**: RS **4 March 1997**; LS **16 May 2000**.
⚠ DRSC **31 = 21 + 10**; SC/ST Welfare **30 = 20 + 10**, no minister as member.

32.s:
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is the ex-officio Chairperson of which of the following committees?
1. Business Advisory Committee
2. Rules Committee
3. General Purposes Committee

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: The Speaker is ex-officio Chairperson of the Business Advisory Committee, the Rules Committee and the General Purposes Committee.
32.tq: Identify the common constitutional-office relationship across the listed committees.
xs: The Speaker chairs all three — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
He is **ex-officio chair** of the **Business Advisory Committee**, the **Rules Committee** and the **General Purposes Committee**.
xa: **Standing committees** are permanent (e.g., Business Advisory, Petitions, Privileges, Rules); **ad hoc** ones end when the task is done.
Committee of Privileges (LS): **15** members nominated by the **Speaker**.
**Committee on Petitions** = **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament (APPSC-GS 2025).

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Department-related Standing Committees (DRSCs):
1. They were set up in 1993.
2. There are 24 DRSCs: 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha.
3. Each DRSC has 31 members with a quorum of 15.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: DRSCs were set up in 1993 and number 24 (16 LS + 8 RS). Statement 3 is wrong: each has 31 members (21 LS + 10 RS) but the quorum is 11, not 15. So '1 and 2 only'; options with 3 are wrong.
32.tq: DRSC numbers: 24 = 16 + 8; 31 = 21 + 10; quorum 11.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — DRSCs were set up in **1993**.
Statement 2: correct — **24 DRSCs** = **16 under Lok Sabha + 8 under Rajya Sabha**.
Statement 3: wrong — each has **31 members** (21 LS + 10 RS), but the quorum is **11**, not 15.
xa: Chairs are appointed by the **Speaker** (LS committees) and the **Chairman** (RS committees).
⚠ DRSC **31 = 21 + 10**; SC/ST Welfare Committee **30 = 20 + 10**.
DRSCs are among Parliament's **"watchdogs"** over the executive.

32.s: Who appoints the Chairpersons of Department-related Standing Committees?
o: The Prime Minister for Lok Sabha committees and the Vice-President for Rajya Sabha committees
The respective ministers heading the departments concerned
The Speaker for Lok Sabha committees and the Chairman for Rajya Sabha committees
32.x: The Speaker appoints the Chairpersons of Lok Sabha DRSCs, while the Chairman appoints the Chairpersons of Rajya Sabha DRSCs.
32.tq: Apply the authority-to-House distinction instead of attributing all appointments to one presiding officer.
xs: DRSC chairs are appointed by **the Speaker for Lok Sabha committees and the Chairman for Rajya Sabha committees** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Not the Prime Minister, ministers or the President — options (1), (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: **24** DRSCs: **16** under Lok Sabha, **8** under Rajya Sabha; set up in **1993**.
Each DRSC: **31 members = 21 LS + 10 RS**; quorum **11**.
The Speaker is **ex-officio chair** of the Business Advisory, Rules and General Purposes Committees.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about ad hoc committees:
1. Inquiry committees may be set up by a motion or by the Speaker or Chairman.
2. A Committee on MPLADS is an example of an inquiry committee.
3. Ad hoc committees continue permanently after completing their assigned task.
4. Select and Joint Committees on Bills are included among ad hoc committees.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Inquiry committees may be created by a motion or by the Speaker or Chairman; the Committee on MPLADS is an example. Select and Joint Committees on Bills are also ad hoc, and such committees end when their task is completed.
32.tq: Identify the false permanence statement and retain the statements describing formation and termination.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 2: correct — **inquiry committees** are set up by a motion or by the **Speaker/Chairman**, e.g., the **Committee on MPLADS**.
Statement 3: wrong — ad hoc committees **end when the task is done**.
Statement 4: correct — **Select / Joint Committees on Bills** are ad hoc.
xa: Another inquiry-type ad hoc example: the **Railway Convention Committee**.
**Standing committees** are permanent: Business Advisory, Petitions, Privileges, Rules.
Select = one House; Joint = **both Houses**, formed on a motion adopted in the House.

32.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a Select Committee from a Joint Committee on a Bill?
o: A Select Committee has members from one House, whereas a Joint Committee has members from both Houses.
A Select Committee is permanent, whereas a Joint Committee is temporary.
A Select Committee is appointed by the President, whereas a Joint Committee is appointed by the Speaker alone.
A Select Committee examines financial accounts, whereas a Joint Committee examines only petitions.
32.x: A Select Committee consists of members of one House. A Joint Committee consists of members of both Houses and is formed on a motion adopted in the House.
32.tq: Discriminate between the two bill committees by their House composition.
xs: A **Select Committee has members from one House**, a **Joint Committee from both Houses** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Both are **ad hoc** committees on Bills, so option (2) is wrong.
xa: A Joint Committee is formed on a **motion adopted in the House**.
Ad hoc committees **end when the task is done**; standing committees are permanent.
Inquiry committees (e.g., **MPLADS**, **Railway Convention Committee**) are the other ad hoc type.

32.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of permanent Standing Committees?
o: Committee on MPLADS, Railway Convention Committee and Joint Committee on a Bill
Committee on MPLADS, Select Committee and Joint Committee on a Bill
Select Committee, Joint Committee and Committee on Public Undertakings
Business Advisory Committee, Committee on Petitions, Committee of Privileges and Committee on Rules
32.x: Business Advisory, Petitions, Privileges and Rules are examples of permanent Standing Committees. Inquiry committees and Select or Joint Committees on Bills are ad hoc and end after completing their tasks.
32.tq: Separate permanent standing bodies from task-specific ad hoc committees.
xs: **Business Advisory, Petitions, Privileges and Rules** committees are all permanent standing committees — so option **(4)** is correct.
**MPLADS** and **Railway Convention** committees are ad hoc inquiry committees; **Select/Joint** Committees on Bills are ad hoc too.
xa: Ad hoc committees **end when the task is done**.
The Speaker chairs the **Business Advisory**, **Rules** and **General Purposes** Committees ex officio.
Committee of Privileges: LS **15** members (Speaker), RS **10** members (Chairman).

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the Public Accounts Committee:
1. It consists of 22 members, comprising 15 members from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha.
2. Its members are elected annually by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.
3. A minister can be a member of the Committee.
4. Its Chairperson is appointed by the Speaker.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: The Public Accounts Committee has 15 Lok Sabha and 7 Rajya Sabha members, elected annually by proportional representation through the single transferable vote. Ministers cannot be members, and the Chairperson is appointed by the Speaker.
32.tq: Split the composition, election and eligibility statements before choosing the coded combination.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — **22** = **15 LS + 7 RS**. Statement 2: correct — elected annually by **PR-STV**.
Statement 3: wrong — **no minister** can be a member.
Statement 4: correct — the chair is **appointed by the Speaker**.
xa: Chair from the **Opposition since 1967**.
It examines **CAG audit reports**; its recommendations are **not binding**.
PAC for **2026-27** held its first meeting under **K.C. Venugopal**.

32.s: Since 1967, the Chairperson of the Public Accounts Committee has generally been appointed from:
o: The ruling party in the Lok Sabha
32.x: Since 1967, the Chairperson of the Public Accounts Committee has been appointed from the Opposition.
32.tq: Remember the institutional convention rather than confusing it with the Estimates Committee convention.
xs: Since **1967**, the PAC chair has come from **the Opposition** — so option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ It is the **Estimates Committee** chair who is invariably from the **ruling party** — so option (2) is wrong.
xa: PAC: **22** members = 15 LS + **7 RS**; **1-year** term; no minister.
Set up in **1921** under the **Government of India Act, 1919**.
PAC for **2026-27** met first under **K.C. Venugopal**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Public Accounts Committee (PAC):
1. It checks whether money was spent within the scope of the demand.
2. Its recommendations are binding on the executive.
3. It examines the execution of policy and not policy as such.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: the PAC checks spending 'within the scope of the demand'. Statement 3 is correct: it examines execution, not policy. Statement 2 is wrong: PAC recommendations are not binding. Hence 1 and 3 only; every other option includes statement 2.
32.tq: PAC = post-facto, advisory, execution-only.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — it checks money spent **"within the scope of the demand"**.
Statement 2: wrong — its recommendations are **not binding**.
Statement 3: correct — it examines **execution, not policy**.
xa: It examines **CAG audit reports** and points out **waste, loss, nugatory expenditure**.
Chair from the **Opposition since 1967**.
PAC and Estimates Committee are quoted for **financial discipline and accountability**.

32.s: The present form of the Estimates Committee was established in 1950 on the recommendation of:
32.x: The present form of the Estimates Committee originated in 1950 on the recommendation of John Mathai.
32.tq: Discriminate between the persons associated with different committees and reform areas.
xs: The Estimates Committee took its present form in **1950** on the recommendation of **John Mathai** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Krishna Menon**'s committee led to the **CPU** (**1964**); **Ashok Dalwai** is linked to doubling farmers' income.
xa: The Estimates Committee originated in **1921**.
**30** members, all from **Lok Sabha**; chair invariably from the **ruling party**.
Nicknamed the **"Continuous economy committee"**.

32.s:
The Estimates Committee is correctly associated with which of the following functions?
1. Suggesting economies and administrative efficiency.
2. Suggesting alternative policies.
3. Examining the form of estimates.
4. Auditing CAG reports on public sector undertakings as its principal function.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: The Estimates Committee suggests economies, efficiency, administrative reforms, alternative policies and improvements in the form of estimates. Auditing CAG reports on public sector undertakings is associated with the Committee on Public Undertakings, not its principal function.
32.tq: Separate prospective examination of estimates from retrospective audit of public undertakings.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
The Estimates Committee suggests **economies, efficiency, administrative reform** and **alternative policies**, and examines the **form of the estimates**.
Statement 4: wrong — CAG reports on PSUs are examined by the **Committee on Public Undertakings**.
xa: It has **30** members, all from the **Lok Sabha**; no minister.
Present form in **1950** on **John Mathai**'s recommendation.
⚠ "Which committee has no Rajya Sabha member" = **Estimates**.

32.s: The Committee on Public Undertakings was created in 1964 on the recommendation of the:
32.x: The Committee on Public Undertakings was created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee.
32.tq: Link the committee’s origin year with the correct recommending body.
xs: The CPU was created in **1964** on the **Krishna Menon Committee**'s recommendation — so option **(2)** is correct.
**John Mathai** shaped the **Estimates Committee** (**1950**); the **2nd ARC** dealt with ethics and e-governance; **Ashok Dalwai** with farmers' income.
xa: CPU: **22** = 15 LS + 7 RS; chair appointed by the Speaker.
It examines reports/accounts of **PSUs** and **CAG reports** on them.
It checks **sound business principles** and **prudent commercial practices**.

32.s: Which one of the following parliamentary financial committees consists only of members of the Lok Sabha, with no member from the Rajya Sabha?
32.x: The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha, elected annually by proportional representation. The Public Accounts Committee and the Committee on Public Undertakings each have 22 members (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha), and every DRSC has 21 Lok Sabha and 10 Rajya Sabha members.
32.tq: Estimates = 30, all Lok Sabha. PAC and CPU = 22 (15 + 7).
xs: The **Estimates Committee** has no Rajya Sabha member — so option **(3)** is correct.
It has **30** members, all from the **Lok Sabha**.
**PAC** and **CPU** each have **22** (15 LS + 7 RS); each **DRSC** has 21 LS + 10 RS.
xa: It is the **only committee** with no Rajya Sabha members.
Its chair is invariably from the **ruling party**.
Nickname: **"Continuous economy committee"**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the Public Accounts Committee:
1. It was first set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919.
2. It examines the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General.
3. Its Chairperson is invariably drawn from the ruling party.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: the PAC was set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919. Statement 2 is correct: it examines the CAG's audit reports. Statement 3 is wrong: since 1967 the PAC Chairperson has been from the Opposition; it is the Estimates Committee chair who is invariably from the ruling party. Hence 1 and 2 only.
32.tq: PAC chair = Opposition (since 1967); Estimates chair = ruling party.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — set up in **1921** under the **Government of India Act, 1919**.
Statement 2: correct — it examines **CAG audit reports**.
Statement 3: wrong — its chair has been from the **Opposition since 1967**.
xa: ⚠ PAC chair = **Opposition**; Estimates chair = **ruling party**.
Its recommendations are **not binding**; it examines execution, not policy.
**22** members = 15 LS + **7 RS**.

32.s: Which committee is described as the “Continuous economy committee”?
32.x: The Estimates Committee is known as the “Continuous economy committee.”
32.tq: Match the nickname with the committee concerned with economies and efficiency.
xs: The **Estimates Committee** is the "Continuous economy committee" — so option **(2)** is correct.
It suggests **economies, efficiency, administrative reform** and alternative policies.
xa: **30** members, all from the **Lok Sabha**.
Present form in **1950** on **John Mathai**'s recommendation.
⚠ The **Committee on Petitions** is the **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament.

32.s:
The term “watchdogs over the executive” is associated with which of the following groups of committees?
1. Public Accounts Committee
2. Estimates Committee
3. Committee on Public Undertakings
4. Department-related Standing Committees
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: The Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings, Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Committee on Government Assurances and Department-related Standing Committees are described as watchdogs over the executive.
32.tq: Recognise the inclusive option when all listed oversight committees perform executive scrutiny.
xs: All four are called Parliament's **"watchdogs"** over the executive — option **(4)**.
The watchdog list: **PAC**, **Estimates**, **CPU**, **Subordinate Legislation**, **Government Assurances** and **DRSCs**.
xa: **Committee on Subordinate Legislation**: checks rule-making (delegated) powers.
**Committee on Government Assurances**: tracks ministers' promises till implemented.
**Committee on Petitions** = **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament.

32.s: Which committee tracks assurances and promises made by ministers until they are implemented?
o: Committee on Papers Laid on the Table
32.x: The Committee on Government Assurances tracks assurances and promises made by ministers until implementation.
32.tq: Match the committee’s name with its specific monitoring role.
xs: The **Committee on Government Assurances** tracks ministers' assurances till implemented — so option **(3)** is correct.
**CPU** examines PSUs; **Papers Laid on the Table** checks ministers' papers; **Petitions** examines petitions on bills.
xa: It is one of Parliament's **"watchdogs"** over the executive.
**Subordinate Legislation** committee checks delegated rule-making powers.
Zero Hour assurances are forwarded by the **Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs** to the ministry concerned.

32.s: The Committee on Papers Laid on the Table primarily checks whether:
o: The estimates contain alternative taxation policies
Public sector undertakings follow commercial principles
Papers laid by ministers, other than statutory orders, comply with the relevant requirements
32.x: The Committee on Papers Laid on the Table checks papers laid by ministers, other than statutory orders, for compliance.
32.tq: Distinguish documentary scrutiny from assurance-tracking and financial scrutiny.
xs: It checks **papers laid by ministers, other than statutory orders**, for compliance — so option **(3)** is correct.
Commercial principles of PSUs = **CPU**; ministers' assurances = **Government Assurances** committee.
xa: **Committee on Subordinate Legislation**: whether rule-making (delegated) powers are properly exercised.
**Committee on Petitions** = **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament.
**Estimates Committee** = **"Continuous economy committee"**.

32.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes is correct?
o: No minister can be a member of the Committee.
The Committee consists only of nominated members.
Only Rajya Sabha ministers are excluded from membership.
A minister may be a member if nominated by the Speaker.
32.x: No minister can be a member of the Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
32.tq: Test the membership restriction directly, using the ministerial eligibility trap.
xs: **No minister can be a member** of the Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs — so option **(1)** is correct.
The bar is total: no exception for Rajya Sabha ministers or for Speaker's nomination, so options (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: It has **30 members** = **20 from Lok Sabha + 10 from Rajya Sabha**.
**Committee on Empowerment of Women**: both Houses, constituted **29 April 1997**.
**PAC** and **Estimates Committee** also bar ministers.

32.s: Which parliamentary committee is described as the 'Ombudsman' of Parliament, examining petitions on bills and on matters of general public interest?
32.x: The Committee on Petitions examines petitions on bills and matters of public interest and is called Parliament's 'Ombudsman'. The Committee on Government Assurances tracks ministers' promises, the Committee on Subordinate Legislation checks the exercise of delegated rule-making powers, and the Committee of Privileges examines breaches of privilege.
32.tq: Ombudsman = Petitions; continuous economy = Estimates.
xs: The **Committee on Petitions** is the **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
**Government Assurances** tracks ministers' promises; **Subordinate Legislation** checks delegated rule-making.
xa: It is a **standing** (permanent) committee.
**Estimates Committee** = "Continuous economy committee".
Committee of Privileges: LS **15** (Speaker), RS **10** (Chairman).

32.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Kasturirangan — Education and the 5+3+3+4 structure
2. Urjit Patel — Inflation targeting at 4% with a tolerance band of plus or minus 2%
3. Nachiket Mor — Monetary policy framework
4. Shanta Kumar — Decentralised procurement and DBT for food
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
32.x: Kasturirangan is linked with education and the 5+3+3+4 structure, Urjit Patel with inflation targeting at 4% plus or minus 2%, and Shanta Kumar with FCI/PDS reform including decentralised procurement and DBT for food. Nachiket Mor is associated with financial inclusion, not monetary policy.
32.tq: Detect the deliberately swapped reform area in the third pair.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Kasturirangan** = education, **NEP 2020**, **5+3+3+4**; **Urjit Patel** = inflation targeting (**4% +/- 2%**).
**Shanta Kumar** = FCI/PDS reform, **DBT for food**, **decentralised procurement**.
The notes list **Urjit Patel**, not Nachiket Mor, for monetary policy — so pair 3 fails.
xa: **2nd ARC**: code of ethics, **Right to Public Services**, e-governance.
**Ashok Dalwai**: doubling farmers' income — value addition, land leasing.

32.s: The reform area associated with the Ashok Dalwai Committee includes:
o: DBT for food and decentralised procurement under the PDS
Value addition and land leasing in the context of doubling farmers’ income
Inflation targeting and monetary policy independence
32.x: Ashok Dalwai’s reform area concerns doubling farmers’ income, including value addition and land leasing.
32.tq: Identify the policy package that belongs to the specified reform objective.
xs: **Ashok Dalwai** = **value addition and land leasing** for **doubling farmers' income** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**5+3+3+4** = Kasturirangan; **DBT for food** = Shanta Kumar; **inflation targeting** = Urjit Patel.
xa: **2nd ARC**: code of ethics, Right to Public Services, e-governance.
Kasturirangan's area is linked to **NEP 2020**.
Urjit Patel: inflation target **4% +/- 2%**.

32.s: Which body's recommendations are associated with a code of ethics, the Right to Public Services and e-governance?
32.x: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2nd ARC) is linked with a code of ethics, the Right to Public Services and e-governance. Shanta Kumar dealt with FCI/PDS, Ashok Dalwai with farmers' income and Kasturirangan with education.
32.tq: ARC = Administration: ethics, services, e-gov.
xs: Code of ethics, **Right to Public Services** and **e-governance** = the **Second Administrative Reforms Commission** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Shanta Kumar** = FCI/PDS; **Ashok Dalwai** = farmers' income; **Kasturirangan** = education.
xa: Shanta Kumar: **DBT for food**, decentralised procurement.
Kasturirangan: **NEP 2020**, **5+3+3+4**.
Urjit Patel: inflation targeting (**4% +/- 2%**).

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the removal of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha under Article 94(c):
1. The resolution requires a majority of all the then members of the House.
2. A notice of fourteen days is required.
3. The notice must be supported by at least fifty members.
4. The procedure is governed by Rules 200–203 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Lok Sabha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All four statements are correct. Article 94(c), the fourteen-day notice requirement, support of fifty members and Lok Sabha Rules 200–203 govern the removal procedure.
32.tq: Check each procedural requirement separately, especially the constitutional provision, notice period, numerical support and relevant Rules.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Removal under **Art. 94(c)** = **majority of all members** + **14 days' notice** + **50 members'** support.
The procedure is in **LS Rules 200-203**.
xa: A resolution against Speaker **Om Birla** was **dismissed by voice vote** (**Mar 2026**).
The Speaker has **discretion to admit or reject** a no-confidence motion.
⚠ A no-confidence motion (vs the government) also needs **50 members**, under **Rule 198**.

32.s: In the 17th Lok Sabha, what proportion of Bills were referred to parliamentary committees?
32.x: Only 16% of Bills in the 17th Lok Sabha were referred to committees; the corresponding figure for the 15th Lok Sabha was 71%.
32.tq: Separate the figures belonging to the 17th and 15th Lok Sabhas instead of selecting the larger comparison value.
xs: Only **16%** of Bills went to committees in the 17th Lok Sabha — so option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ **71%** was the 15th Lok Sabha's figure.
xa: Question Hour ran only **60%** of its scheduled time.
UK comparison: every Bill examined by committees of both Houses; India: **under one-fifth** referred.
Ad hoc **Select / Joint Committees on Bills** examine Bills referred to them.

32.s: Question Hour in Parliament functioned for what proportion of its scheduled time, according to the cited assessment?
32.x: Question Hour ran for only 60% of its scheduled time in the cited assessment.
32.tq: Distinguish the Question Hour utilisation figure from the committee attendance and Bill-referral percentages.
xs: Question Hour ran only **60%** of its scheduled time — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ **71%** was the share of Bills sent to committees in the 15th Lok Sabha.
xa: 17th Lok Sabha: only **16%** of Bills went to committees.
Question Hour is the **first hour** of every sitting and the most effective **day-to-day** vigil.
Fewer than **one-fifth** of Bills are referred to committees in India vs all in the UK.

32.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly is correct?
o: Biometric attendance was introduced only for members of Parliament from the Budget Session of 2026.
Biometric attendance for MLAs was introduced from the Budget Session of 2026.
Biometric attendance for MLAs was introduced from the Monsoon Session of 2025.
Biometric attendance was introduced for MLAs from the Winter Session of 2026.
32.x: Andhra Pradesh introduced biometric attendance for MLAs from its Budget Session in 2026.
32.tq: Use precise state-level identification by checking the institution, year and legislative session together.
xs: **Biometric attendance for MLAs** came from the **Budget Session 2026** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is for **MLAs**, not MPs, and from the Budget Session, not Monsoon or Winter.
xa: The **AP Legislature** uses the same devices as Parliament.
The **AP Legislative Council** was adjourned amid a row on the **Tirumala laddu** issue (**Feb 2026**).
Andhra State: **Prakasam** ministry fell by one vote (**69 for, 68 against**) in Nov **1954**.

33.s: A Government Bill in Parliament ordinarily requires what period of notice before introduction, whereas a Private Member's Bill requires what period?
33.x: A Government Bill requires seven days' notice, while a Private Member's Bill requires one month's notice before introduction.
33.tq: Compare the two notice periods directly and watch for their reversal in the options.
xs: A Government Bill needs **7 days'** notice and a Private Member's Bill **1 month's** notice — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses the two; **14 days** is the Rajya Sabha's limit for returning a Money Bill, not a notice period.
xa: A Government Bill is introduced by a **minister**; a Private Member's Bill by any MP who is **not a minister**.
Rejection of a Government Bill signals **loss of confidence**; defeat of a private bill does not affect the government.
Only **14** private members' bills have become law, the last in **1970**.

33.s: Who normally drafts a Government Bill and who drafts a Private Member's Bill?
o: The Government Bill is drafted by the Rajya Sabha Secretariat, while the Private Member's Bill is drafted by the President
The Government Bill is drafted by the department with the Law Ministry, while the Private Member's Bill is drafted by the member
Both are drafted by the concerned Member of Parliament
Both are drafted by the Election Commission
33.x: A Government Bill is drafted by the concerned department in association with the Law Ministry. A Private Member's Bill is drafted by the member introducing it.
33.tq: Use the drafting agency as the decisive distinction between Government and Private Member's Bills.
xs: A Government Bill is drafted by **the department with the Law Ministry**; a Private Member's Bill **by the member** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Neither the Secretariat, the President nor the Election Commission drafts Bills, so the other options are wrong.
xa: Notice: Government Bill **7 days**; Private Member's Bill **1 month**.
The LS **Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions** classifies them and allots time.
Defeat of a Private Member's Bill has **no bearing** on the government.

33.s: Which one of the following functions is performed by the Lok Sabha's Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions?
o: It recommends the President's assent to Money Bills
It decides whether a Government Bill should be returned by the President
It appoints Ministers of the Union
It examines Private Members' constitutional amendment Bills before their introduction
33.x: The Lok Sabha committee examines constitutional amendment Bills introduced by Private Members before their introduction, besides classifying Bills and allotting time.
33.tq: Test the committee's specific procedural role rather than its general legislative association.
xs: The committee **examines constitutional amendment bills by private members before introduction** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It also **classifies** private members' bills and **allots time** to them.
xa: The **Rajya Sabha** has no such committee — its **Business Advisory Committee** allots time.
Only **14** private members' bills have become law, the last in **1970**.
A Private Member's Bill needs **1 month's** notice and is drafted by the member.

33.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Private Members' Bills:
1. A Private Member's Bill is introduced by an MP who is not a Minister.
2. Its defeat necessarily amounts to a loss of confidence in the government.
3. In the Lok Sabha, time for such Bills is allotted by the Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: defeat of a Private Member's Bill has no bearing on the government's continuation in office.
33.tq: Reject the political-consequence trap and retain the proposer and time-allocation statements.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — introduced by any MP who is **not a minister**.
Statement 2: wrong — its defeat has **no bearing** on the government; it is a Government Bill's rejection that signals loss of confidence.
Statement 3: correct — the LS **Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions** allots time.
xa: In the **Rajya Sabha**, the **Business Advisory Committee** allots time.
Notice for a Private Member's Bill: **1 month**.
Only **14** have become law, the last in **1970**.

33.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Rajya Sabha's procedure for Private Members' Bills is correct?
o: No body can allot time for such Bills in the Rajya Sabha
The Rajya Sabha's Business Advisory Committee allots time for Private Members' Bills
The Rajya Sabha has a Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions identical to the Lok Sabha committee
The President allots time for such Bills in the Rajya Sabha
33.x: The Rajya Sabha has no separate Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions for this purpose; its Business Advisory Committee allots the time.
33.tq: Distinguish the Lok Sabha committee from the Rajya Sabha's Business Advisory Committee.
xs: In the Rajya Sabha, the **Business Advisory Committee** allots time for Private Members' Bills — so option **(2)** is correct.
The RS **has no** Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions, so option (3) is wrong.
xa: The LS committee classifies such bills, allots time and examines private members' **constitutional amendment bills** before introduction.
Private Member's Bill: **1 month's** notice, drafted by the member.
Only **14** private members' bills became law; last in **1970**.

33.s: How many Private Members' Bills have become law, and in which year was the last such Bill enacted?
33.x: Only 14 Private Members' Bills have become law, and the last such enactment was in 1970.
33.tq: Pair the count with the year; do not treat the numerical figure and date as separate clues.
xs: Only **14** Private Members' Bills have become law, the last in **1970** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The other number-year pairs do not match the notes' record of **14** laws.
xa: A Private Member's Bill is introduced by any MP who is **not a minister**, with **1 month's** notice.
Its defeat does **not affect** the government.
The LS **Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions** classifies them and allots time.

33.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. First Reading — Publication in the Gazette
2. Second Reading — Committee stage and clause-by-clause consideration
3. Third Reading — Acceptance or rejection of the Bill as a whole
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
33.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. The Second Reading includes general discussion, committee consideration and clause-by-clause voting, while the Third Reading concerns the Bill as a whole.
33.tq: Use the stage-wise table structure to verify each pair independently.
xs: All three pairs are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
**First reading**: leave to introduce, title and objectives, published in the **Gazette**.
**Second reading**: general discussion → **committee stage** → **clause-by-clause** voting; **Third reading**: bill accepted or rejected **as a whole**.
xa: Three readings take place in **each House** (APPSC-GS 2018).
At the third reading **no amendments of substance** are allowed.
The second House may pass, amend, reject, or keep the bill for **6 months**.

33.s: After an ordinary Bill is passed by one House, the other House may:
o: Return it only to the President
Pass it, amend it, reject it, or keep it pending for six months
Certify it as a Money Bill
33.x: The second House may pass, amend or reject an ordinary Bill, or keep it pending for six months, potentially creating a deadlock.
33.tq: Choose the option that lists the complete range of legislative responses rather than an exclusive power.
xs: The second House may **pass, amend, reject, or keep it pending for six months** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Only the **Speaker certifies** Money Bills, so option (3) is wrong.
xa: A deadlock leads to a **joint sitting** (**Art. 108**).
Joint sitting ground: not passed for **more than six months**, excluding prorogation/adjournment over **4 consecutive days**.
An ordinary bill may be introduced in **either House**.

33.s: The absence of a constitutionally prescribed time limit for the President to act on an ordinary Bill makes possible what is commonly known as:
33.x: Since no fixed time limit is prescribed for presidential action, the President may keep an ordinary Bill pending indefinitely, a situation known as a pocket veto.
33.tq: Link the procedural omission—the absence of a time limit—with its established constitutional term.
xs: With **no time limit** fixed for the President, a **"pocket veto"** is possible — so option **(2)** is correct.
Under **Art. 111** the President may give assent, withhold assent or **return** a non-money bill for reconsideration.
xa: If re-passed, with or without amendment, the President **must assent**.
A **Money Bill** cannot be returned for reconsideration.
⚠ The Governor's options are under **Art. 200**; the President's on reserved state bills under **Art. 201**.

33.s:
Arrange the following stages of an ordinary Bill in the correct chronological order:
A. Consideration by the second House
B. First Reading in the originating House
C. Presidential action
D. Second and Third Readings in the originating House
33.x: The Bill is first introduced in the originating House, undergoes its Second and Third Readings, is transmitted to the second House, and then reaches the President.
33.tq: Fix the first and final stages, then place the two parliamentary House stages between them.
xs: The order is **B, D, A, C** — option **(1)**.
**First reading** in the originating House → **second and third readings** there → the **second House** goes through the same stages → **President's assent** (**Art. 111**).
xa: First reading includes publication in the **Gazette**.
Second reading has the **committee stage** and **clause-by-clause** voting.
A deadlock between the Houses leads to a **joint sitting**.

33.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Absolute veto — Indian President has no such power
Suspensive veto — Indian President may return a non-money Bill, but must assent if it is repassed
Pocket veto — Bill must be decided within ten days
Qualified veto — Indian President may override Parliament by a two-thirds majority
33.x: A suspensive veto permits return of a non-money Bill; if Parliament repasses it, with or without amendment, the President must assent. The Constitution does not prescribe a time limit for the pocket veto, and qualified veto is not held by the Indian President.
33.tq: Separate the four veto types by their effect and by whether the Indian President possesses them.
xs: **Suspensive veto** — the President may **return a non-money bill**, but **must assent** if it is re-passed — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (3) is wrong: **no time limit** is fixed, which is why a **pocket veto** is possible.
xa: Art. 111 options: **give assent, withhold assent, return for reconsideration**.
Re-passage may be **with or without amendment**.
A **Money Bill** cannot be returned by the President.

33.s: Which one of the following is included within the scope of a Money Bill under Article 110(1) of the Constitution?
o: Fees for licences issued by local authorities
Taxes imposed by a municipality for local purposes
Imposition of fines by a criminal court
Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax
33.x: A Money Bill may deal with the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of a tax. Fines, licence fees and local taxes are not, by themselves, matters of a Money Bill.
33.tq: Identify the exact constitutional subject instead of selecting nearby revenue-related terms.
xs: **Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax** is an **Art. 110(1)** matter — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Fines/penalties**, **fees for licences**, and **taxes by local bodies for local purposes** are not money-bill matters — options (1), (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: Other Art. 110(1) matters: **borrowing by GoI**; custody of the **Consolidated/Contingency Fund**.
Also: appropriation from the **CFI** and declaring expenditure **charged**.
A Money Bill deals **only** with Art. 110(1) matters.

33.s:
Consider the following statements regarding a Money Bill:
1. It may deal with the custody of money in the Public Account of India.
2. It may provide for the receipt of money into, or the audit of, the Consolidated Fund of India.
3. It may deal with matters incidental to the matters specified in Article 110(1).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: All three statements describe matters covered by Article 110(1), including Public Account custody, receipt or audit of Consolidated Fund money, and incidental matters.
33.tq: Check each statement against the constitutional list and use the comprehensive option only when every item fits.
xs: All three are Art. 110(1) matters — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
Art. 110(1) covers **receipt/custody/audit** of **CFI or Public Account** money.
It also covers **incidental matters**.
xa: Also: taxes, **borrowing by GoI**, custody of the **Consolidated/Contingency Fund**.
Not money bills: **fines/penalties**, **licence fees**, local-body taxes for local purposes.
The **Speaker certifies** a Money Bill under **Art. 110(3)**; decision **final**.

33.s: A Bill containing provisions exclusively relating to the matters specified in Article 110(1) can be introduced in Parliament only when which one of the following conditions is satisfied?
o: It is introduced in the Lok Sabha by a private member after prior approval of the Rajya Sabha
It is introduced in the Lok Sabha by a minister on the recommendation of the President
It is introduced in either House by any member with the consent of the Speaker
It is introduced in the Rajya Sabha by a minister on the recommendation of the President
33.x: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, only by a minister, and only on the President's recommendation.
33.tq: Split the conditions by asking who introduces, where it is introduced and whose recommendation is required.
xs: A Money Bill is introduced **only in the Lok Sabha**, only by a **minister**, only on the **President's recommendation** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2019).
Private members, the Rajya Sabha and "either House" are all excluded — options (1), (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: The **Speaker certifies** it (**Art. 110(3)**); decision is **final**.
The Rajya Sabha must return it within **14 days** (**Art. 109**).
**No joint sitting** on a Money Bill.

33.s:
With reference to the Speaker's certificate on a Money Bill, consider the following statements:
1. The decision of the Speaker under Article 110(3) is final.
2. The certificate is endorsed on the Bill when it is sent to the Rajya Sabha.
3. The certificate is also endorsed when the Bill is presented to the President.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: The Speaker's decision is final under Article 110(3), and the certificate is endorsed on the Bill sent to the Rajya Sabha and presented to the President.
33.tq: Track the certificate through both constitutional transmission stages rather than limiting it to introduction.
xs: All three statements are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
**Art. 110(3)**: the **Speaker certifies**; the decision is **final**.
The certificate is endorsed when sent to the **Rajya Sabha** (**Art. 109**) and to the **President** (**Art. 111**).
xa: The Rajya Sabha must return it within **14 days**, with or without recommendations.
The President may assent or withhold but **cannot return** it.
The **Finance Bill** is usually certified a Money Bill.

33.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the role of the Rajya Sabha on a Money Bill:
1. It must return the Bill within 14 days, with or without recommendations.
2. The Lok Sabha is bound to accept the recommendations of the Rajya Sabha.
3. If the Bill is not returned within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses.
4. A deadlock over a Money Bill can be resolved through a joint sitting.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct (Art. 109: return within 14 days; otherwise deemed passed). Statement 2 is wrong: the Lok Sabha may accept or reject the recommendations. Statement 4 is wrong: there is no joint sitting for a Money Bill. Hence '1 and 3 only'; the other options include 2 or 4.
33.tq: Money Bill in RS: 14 days, recommend only, LS free to ignore, no joint sitting.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — RS returns it within **14 days** (**Art. 109**). Statement 3: correct — if not returned, **deemed passed**.
Statement 2: wrong — the LS **may accept or reject** RS recommendations.
Statement 4: wrong — there is **no joint sitting** for a Money Bill.
xa: The AP Legislative Council too can only recommend on money bills within **14 days**.
Monsoon Session 2026: the RS **returned several money bills** to the Lok Sabha.
Joint sittings are barred for **Money Bills** and **constitutional amendment bills**.

33.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the President's action on a Money Bill is correct?
o: The President may assent to it or withhold assent, but cannot return it for reconsideration.
The President must refer it to the Supreme Court before giving assent.
The President may return it to Parliament for reconsideration once.
The President has no constitutional role after the Speaker certifies it.
33.x: Under Article 111, a Money Bill cannot be returned by the President for reconsideration. The President may assent to it or withhold assent; in practice, assent follows the prior recommendation for introduction.
33.tq: Test the important exception that distinguishes Money Bills from ordinary Bills at the assent stage.
xs: The President may **assent or withhold assent**, but **cannot return** a Money Bill — so option **(1)** is correct (**Art. 111**).
In practice he **assents**, since it is introduced on his recommendation.
xa: ⚠ Some notes say he "**cannot withhold**" a Money Bill.
For non-money bills the President can **return for reconsideration**; must assent if re-passed.
Financial Bills I and II **can** be returned.

33.s: Which case upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill, while the Money-Bill issue was subsequently referred to a larger bench in another case?
33.x: The Aadhaar Act was upheld as a Money Bill in K.S. Puttaswamy (2018). The Money-Bill question was later referred to a seven-judge bench in Rojer Mathew (2019).
33.tq: Anchor the judicial developments by matching the case names with their years and sequence.
xs: **K.S. Puttaswamy (2018)** upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill; **Rojer Mathew (2019)** referred the question to a larger bench — so option **(1)** is correct.
Options (2) and (3) swap the years.
xa: Rojer Mathew referred it to a **7-judge** bench.
The **Speaker's** certificate on a Money Bill is **final** under **Art. 110(3)**.
A Money Bill deals **only** with **Art. 110(1)** matters.

33.s:
With reference to Financial Bill-I under Article 117(1), consider the following statements:
1. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha.
2. It requires the President's recommendation at the stage of introduction.
3. The Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments to it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Rajya Sabha may amend or reject a Financial Bill-I; its powers are not restricted to making recommendations.
33.tq: Trap the transfer of the Rajya Sabha's limited Money Bill power to Financial Bill-I.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — FB-I is introduced **only in the LS**.
Statement 2: correct — the President's recommendation is needed **at introduction**.
Statement 3: wrong — the RS can **amend or reject** FB-I.
xa: FB-I contains Art. 110 matters **partially, plus other matters**; no Speaker's certificate.
A **joint sitting** is allowed for FB-I.
Amendments **reducing/abolishing** a tax need no recommendation; those **increasing** a tax do.

33.s: Which one of the following correctly describes a Financial Bill-II under Article 117(3)?
o: It can be introduced in either House and requires the President's recommendation at the consideration stage
It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha by a Minister
It contains exclusively matters specified in Article 110
It cannot be amended or rejected by the Rajya Sabha
33.x: A Financial Bill-II may be introduced in either House, by a Minister or a private member, but the President's recommendation is required when it is taken into consideration. The Rajya Sabha may amend or reject it.
33.tq: Separate Financial Bill-II from both the Lok Sabha-only rule and the Money Bill rule.
xs: FB-II can be introduced in **either House** and needs the President's recommendation at the **consideration** stage — so option **(1)** is correct.
It contains **no** Art. 110 matters — only **expenditure from the CFI** — and the RS can **amend or reject** it.
xa: FB-II may be introduced by a **minister or a private member**.
It is governed by **Art. 117(3)**.
⚠ Trap: some notes say all financial bills start in LS only → **FB-II can start in either House**.

33.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Money Bill — Joint sitting not permitted
33.x: A Financial Bill-I does not require the Speaker's certificate. A Money Bill requires that certificate; joint sitting is permitted for Financial Bills-I and II but not for a Money Bill.
33.tq: Check the certification column separately from the House of introduction and joint-sitting columns.
xs: **Financial Bill-I — Speaker's certificate required** is wrongly matched — so option **(3)** is correct; FB-I needs **no** certificate.
The rest are right: a Money Bill needs the certificate and has **no joint sitting**; FB-II allows a joint sitting.
xa: FB-I: **only LS**, minister only, President's recommendation **at introduction**.
The President **can return** FB-I and FB-II but not a Money Bill.
Every money bill is a financial bill, but **not every financial bill** a money bill.

33.s:
Arrange the following Bills in the order of the extent of matters under Article 110 covered by them, beginning with the widest coverage:
A. Financial Bill-II
B. Money Bill
C. Financial Bill-I

Select the correct sequence.
33.x: A Money Bill deals exclusively with Article 110 matters; a Financial Bill-I contains such matters partly along with other matters; a Financial Bill-II contains none of the Article 110 matters.
33.tq: Order the Bills by comparing the extent of Article 110 content rather than their financial character alone.
xs: The order is **B, C, A** — option **(1)**.
**Money Bill** = Art. 110 matters **exclusively**; **FB-I** = **partially**, plus other matters; **FB-II** = **not at all**.
xa: FB-II deals only with **expenditure from the CFI** (**Art. 117(3)**).
Only the Money Bill needs the **Speaker's certificate**.
Joint sitting: barred for Money Bills, **allowed** for FB-I and FB-II.

33.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill.
2. Every Financial Bill is a Money Bill.
3. A Finance Bill gives effect to the tax proposals of the Budget.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because every financial bill is not a Money Bill; the categories are not identical.
33.tq: Watch for the reversed inclusion trap in the paired expressions 'every Money Bill' and 'every Financial Bill'.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — every money bill is a financial bill.
Statement 2: wrong — **not every financial bill** is a money bill.
Statement 3: correct — the **Finance Bill** gives effect to the Budget's **tax proposals**.
xa: The Finance Bill is **usually certified a Money Bill**.
⚠ Trap: some notes reverse the definitions.

33.s: A proposed amendment to a Financial Bill-I seeks to abolish an existing tax. Is the President's recommendation required for such an amendment?
o: No, because Financial Bills-I never require recommendation
Yes, because every amendment to a tax requires recommendation
No, an amendment reducing or abolishing a tax does not require such recommendation
Yes, but only when the Bill is pending in the Rajya Sabha
33.x: An amendment reducing or abolishing a tax does not require the President's recommendation. An amendment increasing a tax requires such recommendation.
33.tq: Distinguish the direction of the tax change; reducing or abolishing tax is treated differently from increasing it.
xs: No — an amendment **reducing or abolishing** a tax needs **no** President's recommendation — so option **(3)** is correct.
An amendment **increasing** a tax **does** need it — so option (1) "never" and option (2) "every amendment" are wrong.
xa: FB-I itself needs the President's recommendation **at introduction** and starts **only in LS**.
The RS can **amend or reject** FB-I.
FB-I can go to a **joint sitting**.

33.s: Which one of the following statements correctly compares the President's power to return the Bills?
o: The President cannot return any financial legislation
The President can return only a Financial Bill-II
The President cannot return a Money Bill but can return Financial Bills-I and II
The President can return a Money Bill but cannot return either Financial Bill
33.x: A Money Bill cannot be returned by the President for reconsideration, whereas Financial Bills-I and II can be returned.
33.tq: Compare the President's return power across the three categories instead of assuming all financial Bills follow the Money Bill rule.
xs: The President **cannot return a Money Bill** but **can return Financial Bills I and II** — so option **(3)** is correct.
So options (1), (2) and (4) are wrong: FB-I and FB-II both **can** be returned; a Money Bill **cannot**.
xa: On a Money Bill he may **assent or withhold** (**Art. 111**).
Joint sitting: **not allowed** for Money Bills; **allowed** for FB-I and FB-II.
If a returned bill is re-passed, the President **must assent**.

33.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 117(3) — Financial Bill-II at the consideration stage
Article 3 — Formation of new States or alteration of their areas, boundaries or names
Article 274 — Bills relating exclusively to expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India
33.x: Article 274 concerns Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested. Bills involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India require recommendation under Article 117(3).
33.tq: Use the Article-subject match and reject the swapped Article 274 description.
xs: **Article 274 — expenditure from the CFI** is wrongly matched — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 274** covers bills affecting **taxation in which states are interested**; CFI expenditure bills fall under **Art. 117(3)**.
The others are right: **Art. 3** = new states/boundaries/names; **Art. 117(1)** = FB-I.
xa: Art. 3 bills need the President's prior recommendation and may start in **either House**.
**Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026** (to "Keralam") was under **Art. 3**.
Money Bills and **FB-I** cannot originate in the Rajya Sabha.

33.s: A Bill involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India is proposed for consideration. At what stage is the President's recommendation required under Article 117(3)?
o: No recommendation is required at any stage
Before the Bill is taken into consideration
Only before its introduction in the Rajya Sabha
Only after the Bill has been passed by both Houses
33.x: For a Financial Bill-II involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, the President's recommendation is required before the Bill is taken into consideration.
33.tq: Focus on the stage specified—consideration—not merely on the fact that the Bill concerns public expenditure.
xs: Under **Art. 117(3)** the recommendation is needed **before the bill is taken into consideration** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is not needed at introduction, so FB-II can start in **either House**.
xa: FB-II can be moved by a **minister or private member**.
RS can **amend or reject** it; **joint sitting** allowed.
**Art. 117(1)** bills need the recommendation **at introduction**.

33.s: Which one of the following statements regarding State legislation is correct?
o: Such a Bill can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha
Such a Bill requires the Speaker's certificate as a Money Bill
A Bill restricting inter-State trade may be introduced in a State Legislature without any prior sanction
A Bill restricting inter-State trade requires the President's previous sanction before introduction in a State Legislature
33.x: A State Bill restricting inter-State trade cannot be introduced without the President's previous sanction.
33.tq: Apply the prior-sanction rule at the State level and distinguish it from parliamentary Money Bill certification.
xs: A state bill **restricting inter-state trade** needs the **President's previous sanction** before introduction — so option **(4)** is correct.
So option (3), "without any prior sanction", is wrong.
xa: **Art. 274**: bills affecting taxation in which states are interested need the President's recommendation.
**Art. 3**: bills on new states or boundaries/names also need it.
Governor's options under **Art. 200**: assent, withhold, return non-Money Bill, reserve.

33.s: A Bill affecting taxation in which States are interested can be introduced in Parliament only with
o: the prior recommendation of the President
the approval of every State Legislature
the recommendation of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
the prior consent of the GST Council alone
33.x: A Bill affecting taxation in which States are interested requires the President's prior recommendation before introduction.
33.tq: Ask who gives the required constitutional recommendation and avoid substituting a related authority.
xs: A bill affecting taxation in which states are interested needs **the prior recommendation of the President** — so option **(1)** is correct (**Art. 274**).
Not the Speaker or state legislatures — options (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: **Art. 3** bills (new states, names) also need the President's prior recommendation.
**Art. 117(3)** bills need it before **consideration**.
A state bill restricting **inter-state trade** needs the President's **previous sanction**.

33.s: A deadlock arising because the two Houses finally disagree on amendments to an ordinary Bill is dealt with through the mechanism provided in:
33.x: Article 108 provides for a joint sitting to resolve specified deadlocks between the two Houses over an ordinary Bill.
33.tq: Match the deadlock mechanism with the correct constitutional article, distinguishing it from Articles 109–111.
xs: A deadlock is resolved by a joint sitting under **Article 108** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Art. 109** = RS returning Money Bills in **14 days**; **Art. 110** = Money Bill definition; **Art. 111** = President's assent.
xa: Grounds: the other House **rejects** the bill, the Houses **finally disagree on amendments**, or it is not passed for **more than six months**.
The joint sitting is **summoned by the President**.

33.s:
Which of the following situations can constitute a deadlock warranting consideration of a joint sitting under Article 108?
1. The other House rejects the Bill.
2. The Houses finally disagree on amendments.
3. The other House does not pass the Bill for more than six months, excluding specified periods of prorogation or adjournment.
Select the correct answer using the code below.
33.x: All three situations are grounds for a joint sitting. In calculating the six-month period, periods of prorogation and adjournment over four consecutive days are excluded.
33.tq: Test all three constitutional grounds together, including the qualifying exclusion in the time condition.
xs: All three are grounds — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
The other House **rejects** the bill; the Houses **finally disagree on amendments**; or it is not passed for **more than six months**.
In the six months, prorogation/adjournment over **4 consecutive days** is excluded.
xa: The President "**notifies his intention**" → neither House proceeds with the bill.
Decision by **simple majority of members present and voting** of both Houses together.
Quorum: **one-tenth** of total members.

33.s: If the President does not summon a joint sitting after a deadlock under Article 108, the Bill:
o: Automatically becomes law after six months
Is deemed to have been rejected by the Rajya Sabha only
Must be referred to the Supreme Court
33.x: If the President does not summon the joint sitting, the Bill comes to an end. It does not automatically become law or receive judicial certification.
33.tq: Apply the consequence of non-summoning instead of assuming that a deadlocked Bill remains permanently pending.
xs: If the President does not summon it, the bill **comes to an end** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2017).
It does not become law automatically — option (1) is wrong.
xa: The joint sitting is **summoned by the President**.
Presided by the **Speaker** → Deputy Speaker → **Deputy Chairman of RS**.
A joint sitting **cannot be summoned** for a bill that has already lapsed.

33.s: A decision at a joint sitting is taken by:
o: A unanimous vote of the presiding officers of both Houses
A simple majority of members present and voting in both Houses together
A special majority of the total membership of both Houses
A two-thirds majority of members present and voting in each House separately
33.x: The Bill is decided by a simple majority of the members of both Houses present and voting together at the joint sitting.
33.tq: Distinguish the voting threshold and the combined body voting from special-majority procedures.
xs: Decided by a **simple majority of members present and voting** of both Houses together — so option **(2)** is correct.
No two-thirds or special majority, and the Houses do not vote separately.
xa: Quorum: **one-tenth** of total members.
⚠ The **VP/Chairman does not preside**; the Speaker does.
**Money bills** and **constitutional amendment bills** are excluded.

33.s: Which one of the following sets contains only the categories of Bills excluded from a joint sitting?
o: Private Members' Bills and Government Bills
Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills
33.x: Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills cannot be referred to a joint sitting. Financial Bills of types I and II can go to a joint sitting.
33.tq: Identify the two express exclusions and avoid treating every financial measure as excluded.
xs: **Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills** are excluded from a joint sitting — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Financial bills (I) and (II)** and ordinary bills can go to a joint sitting.
xa: Joint sitting is under **Art. 108**.
Decision by **simple majority** of members present and voting.

33.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with a joint sitting of Parliament?
1. 1961 — Dowry Prohibition Bill
2. 1978 — Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill
3. 2002 — Prevention of Terrorism Bill
Select the correct answer using the code below.
33.x: All three pairs are correct. These are the three occasions on which a joint sitting of Parliament was held: 1961, 1978 and 2002 respectively.
33.tq: Verify each year–Bill pair independently, using the distinctive chronological list as the anchor.
xs: All three pairs are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
**1961** Dowry Prohibition Bill; **1978** Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill; **2002** Prevention of Terrorism Bill (POTA).
xa: ⚠ **1961 – 1978 – 2002** = Dowry – Banking Service Commission – POTA.
The joint sitting is **presided by the Speaker**.
Grounds: rejection, final disagreement on amendments, or delay of **more than six months**.

33.s: At a joint sitting of the two Houses under Article 108, if both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha are absent, who presides?
o: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Vice-President)
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
The senior-most member of the Lok Sabha
33.x: The order is: Speaker, then Deputy Speaker, then the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and failing all three, a member chosen by those present. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (the Vice-President) does not preside over a joint sitting, the President only summons it, and there is no rule for the senior-most Lok Sabha member.
33.tq: Joint sitting chair: Speaker > Deputy Speaker > RS Deputy Chairman; never the VP/Chairman.
xs: With the Speaker and Deputy Speaker absent, the **Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** presides — so option **(2)** is correct.
Order: **Speaker** → **Deputy Speaker** → **Deputy Chairman of RS** → a member chosen by those present.
⚠ The **VP/Chairman does not preside**; the President only **summons** it.
xa: Decision: **simple majority** of members present and voting.
Quorum: **one-tenth** of total members.
The President "notifies his intention"; neither House then proceeds with the bill.

33.s: A Bill passed by the Rajya Sabha is pending before the Lok Sabha when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. What is the position of the Bill?
o: It becomes law after the dissolution
It is automatically referred to a joint sitting
33.x: A Bill passed by the Rajya Sabha and pending in the Lok Sabha lapses when the Lok Sabha is dissolved.
33.tq: Apply the rule that a Bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses irrespective of which House passed it first.
xs: A bill **passed by RS, pending in LS** **lapses** on dissolution — so option **(3)** is correct.
Bills pending in the LS — originated there or sent by the RS — lapse.
xa: A bill **passed by LS, pending in RS** also lapses.
A bill pending in RS **not yet passed by LS** does **not** lapse.
The Rajya Sabha is **never dissolved**.

33.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding a joint sitting and dissolution of the Lok Sabha?
o: A joint sitting can be summoned even after the Bill has lapsed
A joint sitting cannot be summoned for a Bill that has already lapsed
Every Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha is automatically sent to a joint sitting
A lapsed Bill must be placed before a joint sitting in the next session
33.x: A joint sitting cannot be summoned for a Bill that has already lapsed. Dissolution may terminate the Bill before the deadlock-resolution procedure can operate.
33.tq: Distinguish the existence of a Bill from the procedural stage required for a joint sitting.
xs: A joint sitting **cannot be summoned for a bill that has already lapsed** — so option **(2)** is correct.
So options (1) and (4) are wrong.
xa: But a bill for which the President has **notified a joint sitting before dissolution** does not lapse.
Bills passed by both Houses pending **assent** do not lapse.
⚠ "Passed by LS but not yet taken up in RS does not lapse" is **false** (APPSC-G1 2024).

33.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the effect of parliamentary proceedings:

List-I (Event)
a. Adjournment or adjournment sine die
b. Prorogation
c. Dissolution of the Lok Sabha

List-II (Effect)
i. All pending business before the Lok Sabha lapses
 ii. Pending notices generally lapse, except notices for introducing Bills
 iii. Bills do not lapse and may be taken up in the next session

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
33.x: Adjournment or adjournment sine die does not cause Bills to lapse; prorogation causes pending notices to lapse except notices for introducing Bills; dissolution causes all pending business before the Lok Sabha to lapse.
33.tq: Start from the sure pair that adjournment does not terminate Bills, then match prorogation and dissolution.
xs: **a–iii, b–ii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
**Adjournment / sine die**: bills **do not lapse** — taken up next session (APPSC-GS 2025).
**Prorogation**: pending notices lapse, **except notices for introducing bills**; **dissolution**: all pending before the LS lapse.
xa: Bills do **not lapse** on prorogation either.
The **Rajya Sabha** is never dissolved.
A bill pending in RS **not yet passed by LS** survives dissolution.

33.s:
With reference to dissolution of the Lok Sabha, which of the following bills does NOT lapse?
1. A bill pending in the Rajya Sabha which has not been passed by the Lok Sabha
2. A bill passed by both Houses and awaiting the President’s assent
3. A bill returned by the President for reconsideration
4. A bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha
