33.x: Bills pending in the Rajya Sabha and not passed by the Lok Sabha, bills passed by both Houses awaiting assent, and bills returned for reconsideration do not lapse. A bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses.
33.tq: Classify each bill by its stage at the time of Lok Sabha dissolution.
xs: Bills **1, 2 and 3** do not lapse — option **(1)**.
Pending in RS **not yet passed by LS**; passed by both Houses pending **assent**; **returned by the President** for reconsideration — none lapse.
Item 4 — **passed by LS, pending in RS** — **lapses**.
xa: A bill with a joint sitting **notified before dissolution** also survives.
⚠ APPSC-G1 2024 treated "passed by LS but not yet taken up in RS does not lapse" as **false**.
A bill passed by RS, pending in LS lapses.

33.s: A joint sitting of Parliament has already been notified before the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. What is the position of the bill concerned?
o: It does not lapse merely because of dissolution
It must be returned to the Rajya Sabha for fresh introduction
It becomes a Money Bill automatically
33.x: A bill for which a joint sitting has been notified before dissolution does not lapse merely on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
33.tq: Look for the specific exception to the general rule that dissolution causes bills to lapse.
xs: It **does not lapse** merely because of dissolution — so option **(2)** is correct.
The President had **notified a joint sitting before dissolution**.
xa: A joint sitting **cannot** be summoned for a bill that has already lapsed.
Bills passed by both Houses pending **assent** also do not lapse.
The joint sitting would be presided over by the **Speaker**.

33.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024:
1. It relates to simultaneous elections.
2. It proposes a new Article 82A.
3. It had already been enacted after receiving the required two-thirds majority in both Houses.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: The Bill relates to simultaneous elections and proposes Article 82A. It remained before the Joint Parliamentary Committee and had not been enacted after securing the required majority.
33.tq: Use the status trap: a Bill referred to a committee must not be treated as an enacted law.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: correct — the **129th Amendment** Bill, 2024 is **ONOE** and adds new **Art. 82A**.
Statement 3: wrong — it is **still before the JPC**; opposition argues the government lacks a **two-thirds majority** (Aug 2026).
xa: Constitutional amendment bills are **excluded from joint sittings**.
Monsoon Session 2026: **12 Bills** passed; **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026** referred to a JPC.

33.s: The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council, in relation to a Money Bill, can
o: refer it to a joint sitting within fourteen days
amend it finally within fourteen days
33.x: The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council can only make recommendations on a Money Bill within fourteen days. It cannot reject or amend the Bill finally.
33.tq: Apply the special limitation on the Upper House of a State Legislature to a Money Bill.
xs: The AP Legislative Council can only **make recommendations within 14 days** on a money bill — so option **(1)** is correct.
It cannot reject, amend finally or seek a joint sitting.
xa: The Rajya Sabha's position is the same: return within **14 days** (**Art. 109**); LS may accept or reject.
**Andhra State Bill**: introduced **10 Aug 1953**; assent **14 Sep 1953**.
There is **no joint sitting** for Money Bills.

33.s: The Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 is associated constitutionally with
33.x: The alteration of the name of a State is dealt with under Article 3. The Bill was passed by the Rajya Sabha during the Monsoon Session of 2026.
33.tq: Match the territorial-change subject with the relevant constitutional Article.
xs: The **Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026** falls under **Article 3** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Art. 82A** is from the **129th Amendment** (ONOE) Bill.
xa: It renames Kerala to **"Keralam"** and was passed by the **Rajya Sabha**.
Art. 3 bills need the **President's prior recommendation** and may start in **either House**.
**NCDC (Amendment) Bill, 2026** was also passed by the RS.

33.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Governor's power under Article 200:
1. The Governor may assent to a Bill passed by the State Legislature.
2. The Governor may withhold assent to a Bill.
3. The Governor may reserve a Bill for the consideration of the President.
4. The Governor may return a Money Bill for reconsideration.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct options under Article 200. Statement 4 is false because a Money Bill cannot be returned for reconsideration by the Governor.
33.tq: Split the options by checking the constitutional exception relating to Money Bills.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Art. 200** options: **assent**, **withhold**, **return non-Money Bill**, **reserve** for the President.
Statement 4: wrong — only a **non-Money Bill** can be returned.
xa: The President's options on reserved bills are under **Art. 201**.
The SC's "**deemed assent**" and fixed timelines for Governors (Tamil Nadu Governor judgment, **April 2025**).
A **five-judge** advisory opinion (Nov **2025**) held courts **cannot fix** such timelines or declare deemed assent.

33.s:
With reference to timelines for assent to State Bills, consider the following statements:
1. In the Tamil Nadu Governor case (April 2025), the Supreme Court laid down fixed timelines for Governors and applied 'deemed assent'.
2. In November 2025, a five-judge Bench, giving its advisory opinion on a Presidential Reference, held that courts cannot fix such timelines or declare deemed assent.
3. The November 2025 opinion upheld the deemed assent granted in the Tamil Nadu case.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statement 1 is correct: the April 2025 Tamil Nadu Governor judgment introduced fixed timelines and deemed assent. Statement 2 is correct: the five-judge Bench's advisory opinion on the Presidential Reference (November 2025) held that courts cannot fix such timelines or declare deemed assent. Statement 3 is wrong: that opinion is contrary to deemed assent, not an endorsement of it. Hence 1 and 2 only.
33.tq: Apr 2025 TN case: deemed assent + timelines; Nov 2025 Presidential Reference opinion: courts cannot do either.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — the **Tamil Nadu Governor judgment** (**April 2025**) set fixed timelines and applied **"deemed assent"**.
Statement 2: correct — a **five-judge Bench's advisory opinion** on the **Presidential Reference** (Nov **2025**) held courts **cannot fix** such timelines or declare deemed assent.
Statement 3: wrong — that opinion went **against** deemed assent, not in support of it.
xa: ⚠ APPCA dates the Tamil Nadu judgment to **2023**; the notes give **April 2025**.
Governor's options under **Art. 200**: assent, withhold, **return non-Money Bill**, reserve.
The President's options on reserved bills are under **Art. 201**.

34.s: The expression ‘Annual Financial Statement’ occurring in the Constitution refers to the:
o: Annual estimate of receipts and expenditure under Article 112
34.x: The Annual Financial Statement under Article 112 is the constitutional expression for the Budget. It contains the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government for the financial year.
34.tq: Distinguish the constitutional term from the commonly used word ‘Budget’.
xs: The **Annual Financial Statement** is the estimate of **receipts and expenditure** under **Article 112** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is the constitutional name for the **Budget** (APPSC-GS 2018, 2023); the Appropriation Bill is under **Art. 114**, a separate stage.
xa: ⚠ The word **"budget" is not used** in the Constitution.
The **President** causes it to be laid before **both Houses**; the **Finance Minister** presents it in the Lok Sabha.
It covers **three funds** and has two parts: **Revenue Budget** + **Capital Budget**.

34.s: The financial year to which the Annual Financial Statement relates extends from:
34.x: The financial year in India runs from 1 April to 31 March.
34.tq: Use the numerical-date clue to identify the correct financial-year cycle.
xs: The financial year runs **1 April - 31 March** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The AFS (**Article 112**) estimates receipts and expenditure for this year.
xa: The **Budget Circular** starts the process in **September**.
Union Budget 2026-27 was presented on **1 Feb 2026**.
Since the **1 Feb** budget (**2017**), a vote on account is usually needed only in **interim-budget** years.

34.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the word ‘Budget’ is correct?
o: The word does not occur in the Constitution of India.
The word is expressly used in Article 112 of the Constitution.
The word occurs only in the Seventh Schedule.
The word is defined in Article 114 of the Constitution.
34.x: The Constitution uses the expression ‘Annual Financial Statement’, not the word ‘Budget’.
34.tq: Test the distinction between a popular administrative term and the exact constitutional expression.
xs: The word **"budget" does not occur** in the Constitution — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Article 112** uses **"Annual Financial Statement"**; **Art. 114** is about the Appropriation Bill — so options (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: "Budget" comes from the French **"bougette"** — "little bag".
The budget is prepared by the **Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs**.
First Union budget: **26 Nov 1947**, by **R.K. Shanmukham Chetty**.

34.s: Who causes the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before both Houses of Parliament?
o: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
34.x: The President causes the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before both Houses of Parliament.
34.tq: Apply the ‘who would perform this constitutional function?’ method.
xs: **The President** causes the AFS to be laid before **both Houses** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **Finance Minister** only presents it in the Lok Sabha; the Speaker and Chairman do not lay it.
xa: Union Budget **2023-24** was presented by **Nirmala Sitharaman** (APPSC-GS 2023).
The AFS is under **Article 112**.
The **Contingency Fund of India** is also at the **President's** disposal.

34.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Budget process begins with the issue of the Budget Circular.
2. The Budget Circular is generally issued in September.
3. The Halwa ceremony marks the printing of the Budget documents.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
34.x: The process begins with the Budget Circular, generally issued in September, and printing is traditionally marked by the Halwa ceremony.
34.tq: Combine procedural facts and select the coded option containing all correct statements.
xs: All three statements are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
The **Budget Circular** starts the process, in **September**.
The **Halwa ceremony** marks printing, at **North Block**.
xa: "Budget" comes from **"bougette"** (French, "little bag").
Prepared by the **Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs**, Ministry of Finance.
First Union budget: **26 Nov 1947** (APPSC-GS 2018).

34.s:
Consider the following statements about the Union Budget:
1. It covers the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund and Public Account.
2. It is presented in Revenue Budget and Capital Budget parts.
3. The Finance Bill and the Budget are constitutionally identical documents.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
34.x: The Budget covers the three public funds and is presented in Revenue and Capital parts. The Finance Bill is a separate legal instrument giving effect to tax proposals, so statement 3 is false.
34.tq: Use a reversed-meaning trap to distinguish the Budget from the Finance Bill.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — the Budget covers **three funds**: Consolidated, Contingency and Public Account.
Statement 2: correct — two parts: **Revenue Budget** + **Capital Budget**.
Statement 3: wrong — the Budget is the **Annual Financial Statement** (**Art. 112**); the Finance Bill is a separate bill.
xa: Withdrawal from the CFI needs an **appropriation law** (**Art. 114(3)**).
The **CAG** audits all three funds of the Union and states.
The word **"budget"** is not used in the Constitution.

34.s: The Union Budget is prepared by the Budget Division of the
o: Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance
Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance
34.x: The Budget is prepared by the Budget Division in the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance.
34.tq: Apply the “which department does this job?” authority-identification method.
xs: The budget is prepared by the **Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs**, Ministry of Finance — so option **(2)** is correct.
Not the Departments of Expenditure or Revenue, nor Parliamentary Affairs.

34.s: The first Union Budget of independent India was presented by R. K. Shanmukham Chetty on
34.x: R. K. Shanmukham Chetty presented the first Union Budget of independent India on 26 November 1947.
34.tq: Use the date-person association rather than confusing the first Budget with later Budget-calendar changes.
xs: The first Union budget was presented on **26 November 1947** by **R.K. Shanmukham Chetty** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2018).
**1 February** became budget day only from **2017**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: The Budget = **Annual Financial Statement** under **Article 112**.
Union Budget 2023-24: **Nirmala Sitharaman** (APPSC-GS 2023).
Union Budget 2026-27: **1 Feb 2026**.

34.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Consolidated Fund of India:
1. It includes all revenues received by the Union Government.
2. It includes loans raised by the Union Government, including Treasury Bills and internal or external loans.
3. It includes repayments of loans received by the Union Government.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
34.x: All three statements are correct. The Consolidated Fund comprises Union revenues, loans raised through specified sources and loan repayments received by the Union.
34.tq: Check whether each statement covers a separate component of the same constitutional fund.
xs: All three are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
The **Consolidated Fund of India** (**Art. 266(1)**) holds **all revenues**, **all loans raised** (T-bills, internal/external) and **loan repayments**.
Withdrawal needs an **appropriation law** (**Art. 114(3)**).
xa: **Public Account** (**266(2)**): PF, small savings, deposits, remittances; no appropriation needed.
**Contingency Fund** (**Art. 267**): unforeseen expenditure, at the **President's** disposal.
States have their own Consolidated Fund under **Art. 266(1)** too.

34.s:
Which of the following is correctly matched with the Public Account of India?
1. Provident funds — amounts held by the government in a fiduciary capacity
2. Small savings — amounts credited to the Public Account
3. Deposits and remittances — transactions included in the Public Account
4. Withdrawal — requires an appropriation law in every case
34.x: Provident funds, small savings, deposits and remittances are credited to the Public Account. Withdrawal from it does not require appropriation in the same manner as withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund, making statement 4 incorrect.
34.tq: Find the statement that reverses the constitutional rule applicable to the Public Account.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
The **Public Account** holds **PF**, **small savings**, **deposits** and **remittances**; the government acts as **banker/trustee**.
Pair 4 is wrong: Public Account withdrawals need **no appropriation**.
xa: Public Account is under **Art. 266(2)** — ⚠ some notes wrongly put it under 266(1).
The **Consolidated Fund** needs an appropriation law (**Art. 114(3)**).
The **CAG** audits all three funds.

34.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Contingency Fund of India:
1. It is provided for under Article 267 and was established by the Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950.
2. It is held by the Finance Secretary in the Department of Expenditure.
3. It is at the disposal of the President for unforeseen expenditure pending approval by Parliament; advances made from it are recouped later.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
34.x: Statement 1 is correct: Art. 267 and the 1950 Act. Statement 3 is correct: the Fund is at the President's disposal for unforeseen expenditure, and executive advances are recouped later. Statement 2 is wrong: it is held by the Finance Secretary in the Department of Economic Affairs, not the Department of Expenditure. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
34.tq: Contingency Fund: Art. 267, 1950 Act, President's disposal, Finance Secretary (DEA).
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1: correct — **Art. 267** and the **Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950**.
Statement 2: wrong — it is held by the **Finance Secretary (DEA)**, the Department of Economic Affairs.
Statement 3: correct — at the **President's** disposal for unforeseen expenditure; executive advances are **recouped later**.
xa: Corpus: **₹30,000 crore** from FY **2021-22**.
Earlier ₹**500 crore** from **2005**, raised from ₹**50 crore**.
A **state** Contingency Fund is set up by state law (**Art. 267(2)**), at the **Governor's** disposal.

34.s: What is the corpus of the Contingency Fund of India stated for the financial year 2021-22 onwards?
34.x: The corpus of the Contingency Fund of India was raised to ₹30,000 crore from the financial year 2021-22.
34.tq: Distinguish the present corpus from the earlier corpus and from larger budgetary figures.
xs: The Contingency Fund corpus is **₹30,000 crore** from FY **2021-22** — so option **(2)** is correct.
₹**500 crore** was the earlier corpus (from **2005**); ⚠ ₹**1 lakh crore** is the proposed **Economic Stabilisation Fund**.
xa: Before 2005 it was ₹**50 crore** (some notes say ₹**5 crore**).
It is held by the **Finance Secretary (DEA)** and is at the **President's** disposal.
Established by the **Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950** under **Art. 267(1)**.

34.s: Which one of the following statements regarding audit of government funds is correct?
o: The CAG audits all three funds of the Union and the States.
The CAG audits the Consolidated and Public Accounts but not Contingency Funds.
The Finance Secretary audits all three funds and reports to the CAG.
The CAG audits only the Consolidated Fund of India.
34.x: The Comptroller and Auditor General audits the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund and Public Account of both the Union and the States.
34.tq: Watch for the exclusion of one fund and identify the constitutional audit authority.
xs: **The CAG audits all three funds of the Union and the States** — so option **(1)** is correct.
So options limiting the CAG to one or two funds, or giving audit to the Finance Secretary, are wrong.
xa: The three funds: **Consolidated** (**266(1)**), **Public Account** (**266(2)**), **Contingency** (**267**).
The Finance Secretary (DEA) only **holds** the Contingency Fund.
An **excess grant** needs **PAC** approval first.

34.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding constitutional funds.
List-I (Fund)
 a. Consolidated Fund
 b. Public Account
 c. Contingency Fund
List-II (Article)
 i. Article 267
 ii. Article 266(2)
 iii. Article 266(1)

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
34.x: The Consolidated Fund is covered by Article 266(1), the Public Account by Article 266(2), and the Contingency Fund by Article 267.
34.tq: Start from the sure constitutional article and eliminate codes with a misplaced fund.
xs: **a–iii, b–ii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
**Consolidated Fund** = **Art. 266(1)**; **Public Account** = **Art. 266(2)**; **Contingency Fund** = **Art. 267**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes put the Public Account under **266(1)**.
State Contingency Fund = **Art. 267(2)**, created by state law.
Withdrawal from the CFI needs an appropriation law (**Art. 114(3)**).

34.s: Which of the following correctly describes withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India or a State?
o: It is governed by the rules of the Public Account
It requires only the recommendation of the Finance Commission
It requires an appropriation law under Article 114(3)
It can be made by executive order without legislative authority
34.x: Withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund requires an appropriation law, with Article 114(3) applying to the Union appropriation process.
34.tq: Distinguish legislative appropriation from executive access to public funds.
xs: Withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund needs an **appropriation law** under **Art. 114(3)** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Public Account rules need no appropriation; the executive cannot withdraw by order — options (1) and (4) are wrong.
xa: The Appropriation Bill covers **grants voted by Lok Sabha + charged expenditure**.
The **Contingency Fund** allows executive advances, **recouped later**.
The CFI holds all revenues, all loans raised and loan repayments.

34.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Public Account — Withdrawal only after appropriation under Article 114(3)
Contingency Fund — Advances by the executive, recouped later
Public Account — Government acts as trustee
Consolidated Fund — Withdrawal only by appropriation law
34.x: The Public Account does not require Parliamentary authorisation for withdrawal. The appropriation requirement under Article 114(3) relates to withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund.
34.tq: Find the fund whose withdrawal rule has been deliberately swapped with another fund.
xs: **Public Account — withdrawal only after appropriation** is wrong — so option **(1)** is correct; the Public Account needs **no appropriation**.
The others are right: Contingency Fund = **executive advances recouped later**; Public Account = govt as **trustee**; Consolidated Fund = **appropriation law**.
xa: Public Account holds **PF, small savings, deposits, remittances**.
Contingency Fund corpus: **₹30,000 crore** from **2021-22**.
The **CAG** audits all three funds.

34.s: A policy cut motion is intended to express:
o: Approval of additional expenditure on a new service
Approval of the policy behind a Demand for Grant
A demand for expenditure from the Contingency Fund
Disapproval of the policy behind a Demand for Grant
34.x: A policy cut proposes to reduce the demand to Re 1, thereby expressing disapproval of the policy underlying the demand.
34.tq: Link the form of reduction with the political purpose of the motion.
xs: A policy cut expresses **disapproval of the policy** behind the demand — so option **(4)** is correct.
It reduces the demand to **Re 1**.
xa: **Economy cut**: reduce by a specified amount → economy in expenditure.
**Token cut**: reduce by **Rs 100** → ventilate a specific grievance.
⚠ **Re 1** = policy cut; **Rs 100** = token cut.

34.s: Under an economy cut motion, the Demand for Grant is:
34.x: An economy cut seeks a reduction by a specified amount to suggest economy in expenditure.
34.tq: Separate the three cut motions by their precise reduction amounts.
xs: An economy cut reduces the demand **by a specified amount** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Rs 100** = token cut; **Re 1** = policy cut — options (1) and (3) are wrong.
xa: Its purpose is **economy in expenditure**.
Cut motions are moved only in the **Lok Sabha** during voting on demands.
A passed cut motion signals **loss of confidence**.

34.s:
Consider the following statements about cut motions:
1. They are moved only in the Lok Sabha.
2. They are moved during voting on Demands for Grants.
3. Passage of a cut motion indicates loss of confidence in the Council of Ministers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
34.x: Cut motions are moved only in the Lok Sabha during voting on Demands for Grants. If passed, they indicate that the government has lost the confidence of the House.
34.tq: Combine the location, stage and political consequence of a cut motion.
xs: All three statements are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
Cut motions are moved only in the **Lok Sabha** during **voting on demands**.
A passed cut motion signals **loss of confidence**.
xa: **Policy cut** = **Re 1**; **token cut** = **Rs 100**; **economy cut** = a specified amount.
Supplementary, additional and excess grants are under **Art. 115**.
A **token grant** (re-appropriation) must also be voted by the LS.

34.s: The Appropriation Bill is introduced under Article:
34.x: Article 114 deals with Appropriation Bills.
34.tq: Link the named Bill with its exact constitutional article.
xs: The Appropriation Bill is under **Article 114** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Art. 112** = AFS; **Art. 115** = supplementary, additional, excess grants.
xa: **Art. 114(3)**: no money withdrawn from the CFI except under appropriation by law.
It carries an **automatic repeal clause**.
⚠ APPSC-G1 2024: statements **I and IV** were valid.

34.s: An Appropriation Bill includes:
o: Voted grants of the Lok Sabha and charged expenditure, subject to the amount in the Annual Financial Statement
Expenditure from the Public Account alone
34.x: The Appropriation Bill covers grants voted by the Lok Sabha as well as charged expenditure, and the amount cannot exceed that authorised in the Annual Financial Statement.
34.tq: Combine the two components of an appropriation instead of treating it as voted expenditure alone.
xs: It covers **grants voted by Lok Sabha + charged expenditure**, not exceeding the AFS amount — so option **(1)** is correct.
So "only voted" and "only charged" are both wrong; the **Public Account** needs no appropriation.
xa: No amendment may **vary the amount or alter the destination** of a voted grant, or vary charged expenditure.
It carries an **automatic repeal clause**.
It is under **Art. 114**.

34.s: Article 114(3) provides that money shall not be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under:
o: A resolution of the Rajya Sabha
A recommendation of the Public Accounts Committee
An executive order of the Finance Minister
34.x: Article 114(3) requires an appropriation made by law before money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India.
34.tq: Identify the legally necessary authority rather than an advisory or executive substitute.
xs: **Art. 114(3)**: no withdrawal from the CFI except under **an appropriation made by law** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Not a Rajya Sabha resolution, a PAC recommendation or an executive order.
xa: The **Public Account** needs no appropriation.
The **Contingency Fund** allows advances, **recouped later**.
**Vote on account** (**Art. 116**) gives an advance till the **Appropriation Act**.

34.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Appropriation Bill under Article 114:
1. No amendment may be proposed that would vary the amount or alter the destination of any grant voted by the Lok Sabha.
2. An amendment may vary the amount of expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
3. The Bill carries an automatic repeal clause.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
34.x: Statement 1 is correct: no amendment may vary the amount or alter the destination of a voted grant. Statement 2 is wrong: charged expenditure also cannot be varied by amendment. Statement 3 is correct: the Appropriation Bill carries an automatic repeal clause. Hence 1 and 3 only.
34.tq: Appropriation Bill: no change to amount/destination of voted grants or to charged expenditure; repeals itself automatically.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — no amendment may **vary the amount or alter the destination** of a voted grant.
Statement 2: wrong — **charged expenditure** cannot be varied either.
Statement 3: correct — it has an **automatic repeal clause**.
xa: ⚠ APPSC-G1 2024 key: statements **I and IV** valid.
It covers voted grants + charged expenditure, within the **AFS** amount.
**Art. 114(3)** bars withdrawal from the CFI without appropriation by law.

34.s:
Consider the following statements regarding a vote on account:
1. It is made under Article 116 as an advance for part of the year, generally about two months, until the Appropriation Act is passed.
2. Since the Budget was advanced to 1 February (2017), it is needed in every regular Budget year.
3. In election years it may cover three to five months.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
34.x: Statement 1 is correct: Art. 116, about two months (one-sixth), till the Appropriation Act. Statement 3 is correct: 3-5 months in election years. Statement 2 is wrong: since the 1 February Budget, a vote on account is usually needed only in interim-Budget years. Hence '1 and 3 only'; other options include 2.
34.tq: Vote on account = Art. 116, ~2 months, now mainly an interim-Budget (election-year) device.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1: correct — **Art. 116**, about **two months** (one-sixth), till the **Appropriation Act**.
Statement 2: wrong — since the **1 Feb** budget (**2017**), it is usually needed only in **interim-budget** years.
Statement 3: correct — **3-5 months** in election years.
xa: **Vote of credit** (Art. 116): unexpected demand of indefinite magnitude.
**Exceptional grant** (Art. 116): not part of the current service of any year.
⚠ **115** = supplementary, additional, excess; **116** = vote on account, credit, exceptional.

34.s: An exceptional grant is one which:
o: Provides an advance for the first two months of the year
Is not part of the current service of any year
Is sanctioned after expenditure has exceeded the grant
Meets a new service not included in the Budget
34.x: An exceptional grant is made for a purpose that is not part of the current service of any financial year.
34.tq: Separate the exact meanings of exceptional, additional and excess grants.
xs: An exceptional grant is **not part of the current service of any year** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Advance for **two months** = vote on account; spending beyond the grant = **excess grant**; new service = **additional grant**.
xa: It is under **Art. 116**.
**Vote of credit** (Art. 116): unexpected demand of **indefinite magnitude/character**.
**Supplementary grant** (**Art. 115**): sanctioned amount insufficient.

34.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Grant)
A. Supplementary grant
B. Additional grant
C. Excess grant
D. Vote of credit

List-II (Purpose)
1. Expenditure exceeds the amount already granted
2. New service not included in the Budget
3. Sanctioned amount is insufficient
4. Unexpected demand of indefinite magnitude or character

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
34.x: A supplementary grant meets an insufficiency; an additional grant covers a new service; an excess grant relates to expenditure beyond the amount granted; and a vote of credit meets an unexpected indefinite demand.
34.tq: Start from the sure pair and match each grant with its distinctive purpose.
xs: **Supplementary** = amount insufficient; **additional** = new service not in the budget.
**Excess** = spent more than granted; **vote of credit** = unexpected demand of indefinite magnitude/character.
xa: ⚠ **115** = supplementary, additional, excess; **116** = vote on account, vote of credit, exceptional.
Excess grants need **PAC** approval first.
The LS approved the **second batch of Supplementary Demands for Grants (2025-26)**.

34.s: An excess grant becomes relevant when:
o: The expenditure is not part of the current service of any year
A new service is proposed in the current Budget
The sanctioned amount is insufficient before expenditure is incurred
Expenditure has exceeded the amount originally granted and prior approval of the Public Accounts Committee is required
34.x: An excess grant is required when expenditure has exceeded the amount granted. It requires prior scrutiny and approval by the Public Accounts Committee.
34.tq: Distinguish an excess already incurred from a supplementary requirement anticipated during the year.
xs: An excess grant is for spending **more than granted**, needing **PAC approval first** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Not current service = **exceptional**; new service = **additional**; insufficient amount = **supplementary**.
xa: It falls under **Art. 115**.
The **PAC** examines **CAG** audit reports.
**Token grant** (re-appropriation) must also be voted by the LS.

34.s: A token grant is associated with:
o: An emergency demand of indefinite magnitude
A fresh withdrawal from the Public Account without parliamentary approval
A reduction of a Demand for Grant to Re 1
Re-appropriation and approval by the Lok Sabha
34.x: A token grant relates to re-appropriation and must also be voted by the Lok Sabha.
34.tq: Distinguish the budgetary token grant from the token cut motion.
xs: A token grant is for **re-appropriation** and must be **voted by the Lok Sabha** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Reducing a demand to **Re 1** is a **policy cut**; indefinite demand = **vote of credit**.
xa: ⚠ A **token cut** (cut motion) reduces a demand by **Rs 100** — not the same as a token grant.
**Excess grant** needs PAC approval first.
The **Public Account** needs no appropriation at all.

34.s: In the Union Budget 2026-27, the Finance Minister proposed an Economic Stabilisation Fund to cushion the economy against global shocks and supply-chain disruptions. What is its proposed size?
34.x: The proposed Economic Stabilisation Fund is Rs 1 lakh crore. Rs 30,000 crore is the corpus of the Contingency Fund of India from 2021-22, a figure easily confused with it; Rs 50,000 crore and Rs 2 lakh crore are not stated for this Fund.
34.tq: Economic Stabilisation Fund = Rs 1 lakh crore; Contingency Fund of India = Rs 30,000 crore.
xs: The Economic Stabilisation Fund is **₹1 lakh crore** — so option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ **₹30,000 crore** is the Contingency Fund corpus from **2021-22**.
xa: It is meant for **global shocks** and **supply-chain disruptions**.
Proposed in Union Budget 2026-27 (**1 Feb 2026**).
The LS approved the **second batch of Supplementary Demands for Grants (2025-26)** under **Art. 115**.

35.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the financial committees of Parliament:
1. Members of these committees are elected annually by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.
2. The term of the members is one year.
3. Ministers are eligible to serve as members of these committees.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
35.x: Members are elected annually by proportional representation through the single transferable vote and hold office for one year. Ministers are ineligible to serve on these committees.
35.tq: Identify the true procedural statements and reject the eligibility trap.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — members are elected annually by **proportional representation (STV)**.
Statement 2: correct — the term is **1 year**.
Statement 3: wrong — **ministers are ineligible**.
xa: Financial committees: **Estimates**, **PAC**, **COPU**.
Their role: keep **"an unremitting vigil"** over expenditure and performance.
Their control is **after** expenditure; the budget's is **before** — complementary.

35.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the composition of the Estimates Committee?
o: 30 members, all elected from the Lok Sabha
22 members, including 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
22 members, all elected from the Lok Sabha
30 members, including 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
35.x: The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all of whom are drawn from the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha has no representation in it.
35.tq: Use the composition figures to distinguish the three financial committees.
xs: The Estimates Committee has **30 members, all from the Lok Sabha** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**22** (15 LS + 7 RS) is the **PAC/COPU**; **30** (20 LS + 10 RS) is the **SC/ST Welfare** Committee.
xa: It is the **largest** financial committee, with **no** Rajya Sabha member.
Its chairman is appointed by the Speaker and is **invariably from the ruling party**.
⚠ **31** (21 + 10) = each DRSC; **30** (20 + 10) = SC/ST Welfare; **30** all-LS = Estimates.

35.s: The chairperson of the Estimates Committee is appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and is invariably from which political grouping?
o: A party represented only in the Rajya Sabha
35.x: The Speaker appoints the chairperson of the Estimates Committee, who is invariably a member of the ruling party.
35.tq: Distinguish the convention for the Estimates Committee from the Opposition-chairman convention of the PAC.
xs: The Estimates Committee chairman is **invariably from the ruling party** — so option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ The **PAC** chairman is from the **Opposition** (since **1967**), so option (4) is wrong.
xa: The chairman is **appointed by the Speaker**.
**30** members, all from the Lok Sabha.
Nicknamed the **"Continuous economy committee"**.

35.s:
Consider the following statements about parliamentary financial control:
1. The budget exercises control before expenditure takes place.
2. The financial committees exercise control after expenditure has taken place.
3. Parliamentary financial committees replace the budgetary process entirely.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
35.x: The budget provides control before expenditure, while the financial committees examine expenditure and performance after the event. They complement, rather than replace, the budgetary process.
35.tq: Track the time sequence of control and reject the extreme replacement claim.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — the **budget** controls **before** expenditure.
Statement 2: correct — financial committees control **after** expenditure.
Statement 3: wrong — the two are **complementary**; committees do not replace the budget.
xa: The committees keep **"an unremitting vigil"** over expenditure and performance.
Criticism: the PAC is a **post-mortem** check.
Frequent **guillotine** weakens financial control.

35.s: The Public Accounts Committee originated in 1921 under the:
35.x: The Public Accounts Committee originated in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919.
35.tq: Use the year–enactment pair to avoid confusion among the constitutional reform Acts.
xs: The PAC began in **1921** under the **Government of India Act, 1919** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The other Acts (1935, 1909, 1892) are not the PAC's origin as per the notes.
xa: The **Estimates Committee** also traces to **1921** (Standing Financial Committee); present form **1950**.
**COPU**: **1964**, Krishna Menon Committee.
**DRSCs**: **1993** (**17** committees), on the Rules Committee's recommendation.

35.s: The Estimates Committee of Parliament took its present form in 1950 on the recommendation of:
35.x: The Estimates Committee traces to the Standing Financial Committee of 1921 but took its present form in 1950 on John Mathai's recommendation. Krishna Menon is linked to COPU (1964); Ambedkar and Mavalankar are distractors.
35.tq: Estimates = 1950, John Mathai; COPU = 1964, Krishna Menon.
xs: The Estimates Committee took its present form in **1950** on **John Mathai's** recommendation — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Krishna Menon** is linked to **COPU** (**1964**).
xa: It traces to **1921** (Standing Financial Committee).
⚠ **1950** = John Mathai; **1964** = Krishna Menon Committee; **1993** = Rules Committee.
Its chairman is invariably from the **ruling party**.

35.s: The Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) was set up in 1964 on the recommendation of the:
35.x: COPU was created in 1964 on the Krishna Menon Committee's recommendation. John Mathai is linked to the Estimates Committee (1950); Sarkaria dealt with Centre-State relations; the Rules Committee recommended DRSCs (1993).
35.tq: COPU 1964 = Krishna Menon.
xs: COPU was set up in **1964** on the **Krishna Menon Committee** recommendation — so option **(2)** is correct.
**John Mathai** = Estimates (**1950**); the **Rules Committee** = DRSCs (**1993**).
xa: COPU: **22** members (15 LS + 7 RS).
Its chairman comes from **LS members**, appointed by the Speaker.
COPU is one of Parliament's **watchdog** committees.

35.s: The Public Accounts Committee consists of:
o: 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha
31 members: 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
22 members, all from the Lok Sabha
35.x: The PAC has 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha (as associate members). 30 all-LS is the Estimates Committee; 31 (21+10) is a DRSC; the PAC does include Rajya Sabha members.
35.tq: PAC and COPU = 22 (15+7); Estimates = 30, all LS.
xs: The PAC has **22 members: 15 LS + 7 RS** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**30** all-LS = Estimates; **31** (21 + 10) = each DRSC.
xa: RS members are **associate** members.
Chairman: **Opposition member since 1967** (convention).
Members elected annually by **STV**, for **1 year**; ministers ineligible.

35.s: The Public Accounts Committee primarily scrutinises which combination of documents?
o: Election expenditure statements, census reports and Finance Commission reports
Appropriation Bills, Money Bills and constitutional amendment Bills
Annual reports of political parties and reports of the Union Public Service Commission
Appropriation Accounts, Finance Accounts and reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General
35.x: The Public Accounts Committee examines the Appropriation Accounts, Finance Accounts and audit reports submitted by the Comptroller and Auditor-General.
35.tq: Use the document-based function to separate PAC work from legislative scrutiny.
xs: The PAC scrutinises **appropriation accounts, finance accounts** and **CAG audit reports** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Bills, election statements and party reports are not its work.
xa: It checks money spent **"within the scope of the demand"**.
It flags **waste, extravagance, loss, nugatory expenditure**.
It reports to the **Lok Sabha (Speaker)**.

35.s: In examining government expenditure, the Public Accounts Committee checks whether money was spent:
o: Within the scope of the demand for grant
Only after approval by the Supreme Court
35.x: The PAC checks whether expenditure remained within the scope of the demand for grant approved by Parliament.
35.tq: Apply the committee’s audit function to a spending situation.
xs: The PAC checks money spent **within the scope of the demand** — so option **(1)** is correct.
No court approval, supplementary-only or PSU-only rule applies — the other options are wrong.
xa: It scrutinises **appropriation accounts**, **finance accounts** and **CAG audit reports**.
It tests **efficiency, economy and propriety**, not only legality.
Its recommendations are **not binding**.

35.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Public Accounts Committee:
1. It may take up certain matters on its own.
2. Its recommendations are binding on the government.
3. It tests efficiency, economy and propriety, not merely legality.
4. It can examine the formulation of the policy itself, not merely its execution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
35.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the PAC may take up matters on its own and tests efficiency, economy and propriety. Statement 2 is wrong: its recommendations are not binding. Statement 4 is wrong: it cannot examine policy, only its execution. Hence '1 and 3 only'; the other options include 2 or 4.
35.tq: PAC limits: not binding, no policy review.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — it **may take up matters on its own**.
Statement 2: wrong — its recommendations are **not binding**.
Statement 3: correct — it tests **efficiency, economy and propriety**; Statement 4: wrong — it **cannot examine policy**, only its execution.
xa: It reports to the **Lok Sabha (Speaker)**.
Criticism: a **post-mortem** check.
It is the **"Watchdog"** on departmental expenditure (APPSC-G2 2017).

35.s:
Assertion (A): The chairperson of the Public Accounts Committee is generally selected from the Opposition.
Reason (R): The selection of an Opposition member as chairperson is a constitutional rule applicable in every case.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
35.x: A is true: the PAC chairman has been an Opposition member since 1967. R is false: this is a convention, not a constitutional or statutory rule applicable in every case. Hence 'A is true but R is false'.
35.tq: Separate a parliamentary convention from a binding constitutional requirement.
xs: **A is true but R is false** — option **(3)**.
A: true — the PAC chairman has been an **Opposition member since 1967**.
R: false — this is by **convention, not rule** (APPSC-G2 2017).
xa: The chairman is appointed by the **Speaker**.
PAC chairman for **2026-27**: **K.C. Venugopal**.
⚠ Estimates chairman = **ruling party**.

35.s: Who is the Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee for 2026-27?
35.x: K.C. Venugopal, an Opposition member, chairs the PAC for 2026-27, in line with the convention of an Opposition chairman. Jairam Ramesh is linked to a privilege notice; Om Birla is the Speaker; Dharmendra Pradhan is the Education Minister.
35.tq: PAC chair = Opposition by convention; 2026-27 K.C. Venugopal.
xs: The PAC chairman for **2026-27** is **K.C. Venugopal** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Jairam Ramesh** gave a privilege notice; **Dharmendra Pradhan** is the Education Minister.
xa: The PAC chairman is from the **Opposition** by **convention** since **1967**.
Average MP attendance at **16** DRSCs and the PAC was only **53%** since the September reconstitution.
The PAC reports to the **Lok Sabha (Speaker)**.

35.s:
Consider the following statements about Departmentally Related Standing Committees:
1. They were introduced in 1993 with 17 committees.
2. Their number became 24 from 2004.
3. Their establishment was based on the recommendation of the Rules Committee.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
35.x: All three statements are correct: DRSCs began in 1993 with 17 committees, expanded to 24 from 2004, and were introduced on the recommendation of the Rules Committee.
35.tq: Combine the origin year, numerical expansion and recommending body in one verification set.
xs: All three statements are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
DRSCs began in **1993** with **17** committees, on the **Rules Committee** recommendation.
They number **24** since **2004**.
xa: **16 under LS, 8 under RS**.
Each has **31 members: 21 LS + 10 RS**; quorum **11**.
They scrutinise **demands for grants**, bills, annual reports and long-term policy.

35.s: Each Departmentally Related Standing Committee consists of:
o: 25 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
31 members: 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members: 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
35.x: Each DRSC has 31 members, comprising 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.
35.tq: Distinguish the DRSC composition from the 30-member SC/ST Welfare Committee.
xs: Each DRSC has **31 members: 21 LS + 10 RS** — so option **(2)** is correct.
xa: Quorum: **11**.
Ministers are **ineligible**.
**24** DRSCs: **16 under LS, 8 under RS**.

35.s:
Which of the following statements regarding Departmentally Related Standing Committees is correct?
1. There are 24 DRSCs.
2. Sixteen are under the Lok Sabha and eight are under the Rajya Sabha.
3. Their quorum is 11.
4. Ministers are eligible to serve on them.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
35.x: There are 24 DRSCs, with 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha; their quorum is 11. Ministers are ineligible, so statement 4 is false.
35.tq: Use the ministerial-eligibility statement as the decisive false element.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
**24** DRSCs = **16 under LS, 8 under RS**; quorum **11**.
Statement 4: wrong — **ministers are ineligible**.
xa: Each has **31 members** (21 LS + 10 RS).
Set up in **1993** with **17** committees; **24** since **2004**.
DRSCs belong to the parliamentary **watchdog group**.

35.s:
The Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinise which of the following?
1. Demands for grants
2. Bills referred to them
3. Annual reports of ministries
4. Long-term policy of the ministries
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
35.x: DRSCs scrutinise demands for grants, referred Bills, annual reports and the long-term policy of the ministries under their jurisdiction.
35.tq: Recognise the full range of DRSC scrutiny rather than limiting it to grants.
xs: All four are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
DRSCs scrutinise **demands for grants**, **bills referred**, **annual reports** and **long-term policy** of their ministries.
xa: **24** DRSCs, each with **31** members.
Origin: **1993**, Rules Committee recommendation.
Low attendance: only **53%** since the September reconstitution.

35.s: Which committee considers petitions relating to Bills and matters of public interest?
35.x: The Committee on Petitions examines petitions relating to Bills and matters of public interest.
35.tq: Match the petition-related function with the exact committee name.
xs: The **Committee on Petitions** considers petitions on bills and public-interest matters — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Government Assurances** tracks ministers' promises; **Privileges** handles privilege questions; **Business Advisory** allots time.
xa: It is the **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament (APPSC-GS 2025).
Strength: **LS 15, RS 10**.
⚠ "Ombudsman" = Petitions; "Watchdog" = PAC; "Continuous economy" = Estimates.

35.s: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation is concerned with:
o: Checking the exercise of delegated rule-making power
35.x: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation checks how delegated rule-making powers are exercised.
35.tq: Distinguish delegated legislation from assurances, ethics and business scheduling.
xs: It **checks the exercise of delegated rule-making** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Assurances = **Government Assurances**; time allotment = **Business Advisory**; members' conduct = **Ethics**.
xa: Strength: **LS 15, RS 15**.
It is in the parliamentary **watchdog group**.
Also among standing committees: **Papers Laid on the Table**, **Rules Committee**.

35.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Committee on Government Assurances — Exercises delegated rule-making power
Business Advisory Committee — Allots time for government and other business
Committee of Privileges — Examines members’ conduct
Ethics Committee — Considers questions of privilege
35.x: The Business Advisory Committee allots time for government and other business. Questions of privilege belong to the Committee of Privileges, members’ conduct to the Ethics Committee, and delegated rule-making to the Committee on Subordinate Legislation.
35.tq: Find the only correctly assigned function among neighbouring standing committees.
xs: **Business Advisory Committee — allots time for government and other business** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Government Assurances** tracks assurances; **Privileges** handles privilege questions; **Ethics** handles members' conduct.
xa: The Business Advisory Committee: **LS 15**, **Speaker chairs**.
Ethics: **RS 4 Mar 1997**; **LS 16 May 2000**.
Subordinate Legislation checks **delegated rule-making**.

35.s: Which of the following committees is chaired by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
35.x: The Speaker chairs the Lok Sabha Business Advisory Committee, which allots time for government and other business.
35.tq: Use the authority–function relationship to identify the committee chaired by the Speaker.
xs: The Speaker chairs the **Business Advisory Committee** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It allots time for **government and other business**.
xa: It has **15** members in the Lok Sabha.
Privileges: **LS 15** members, **nominated by the Speaker**.
**Petitions** = "Ombudsman"; **Subordinate Legislation** = delegated rule-making.

35.s: The Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes consists of:
o: 31 members: 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members: 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 15 from the Rajya Sabha
35.x: The Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs has 30 members, comprising 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.
35.tq: Compare the committee’s 20–10 composition with the similar 21–10 DRSC figure.
xs: The SC/ST Welfare Committee has **30 members: 20 LS + 10 RS** — so option **(2)** is correct.
xa: A **minister is ineligible**.
It examines reports of the **National Commissions for SCs and STs**.
⚠ **30** all-LS = Estimates — same number, different make-up.

35.s:
Consider the following statements about the Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs:
1. A Minister may serve as a member of the committee.
2. It examines the working of welfare programmes for SCs and STs in Union ministries and bodies.
3. It examines reports of the National Commissions for SCs and STs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
35.x: The committee examines welfare programmes and the reports of the National Commissions. Ministers are ineligible to serve on it, making statement 1 incorrect.
35.tq: Apply the common ministerial-ineligibility rule while retaining the committee’s substantive functions.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: wrong — a **minister is ineligible**.
Statements 2 and 3: correct — it examines **welfare programmes** for SCs/STs in Union ministries and the **National Commissions' reports**.
xa: It also examines implementation of **constitutional safeguards**.
Strength: **30** = **20 LS + 10 RS**.
It is a **standing** committee.

35.s: With reference to the Committee of Privileges, which one of the following is correct?
o: Lok Sabha committee has 15 members nominated by the Speaker; Rajya Sabha committee has 10 members
Both Houses have committees of 22 members elected by proportional representation
Lok Sabha committee has 10 members; Rajya Sabha committee has 15 members
It is a joint committee of 31 members from both Houses
35.x: The Lok Sabha Committee of Privileges has 15 members nominated by the Speaker and the Rajya Sabha committee has 10. The 22-member elected pattern belongs to PAC/COPU, option C reverses the two figures, and 31 members is the size of a DRSC.
35.tq: Privileges: LS 15 (Speaker nominates), RS 10.
xs: Privileges: **LS 15, nominated by the Speaker**; **RS 10** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**22** elected by PR = PAC/COPU; **31** = a DRSC; option (3) reverses the figures.
xa: It handles **questions of privilege** referred by the House/Chair.
Source for RS figure: **APPCA Jun 2026**.
**Jairam Ramesh**'s privilege notice against **Dharmendra Pradhan** was over remarks on a standing committee.

35.s: Ethics Committees were constituted in the two Houses of Parliament in which order?
o: Lok Sabha in 1997, Rajya Sabha in 2000
Rajya Sabha on 4 March 1997, Lok Sabha on 16 May 2000
Both Houses on the same day in 2000
Rajya Sabha in 2000, Lok Sabha in 2004
35.x: The Rajya Sabha set up its Ethics Committee first, on 4 March 1997; the Lok Sabha followed on 16 May 2000. The other options reverse or misstate the dates.
35.tq: Ethics: RS first (1997), LS later (2000).
xs: Ethics Committees: **Rajya Sabha on 4 March 1997**, **Lok Sabha on 16 May 2000** — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ **RS first**, LS later — option (1) reverses it.
xa: The Ethics Committee deals with **members' conduct**.
Source: **IYB 2026**.
⚠ Privileges (not Ethics) handles **questions of privilege**.

35.s: Which of the following committees exist only in the Lok Sabha?
o: Committee on Petitions and Committee of Privileges
Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions and Committee on Absence of Members
Rules Committee and Committee on Papers Laid on the Table
Committee on Subordinate Legislation and Committee on Government Assurances
35.x: The Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions and the Committee on Absence of Members are Lok Sabha-only. Petitions, Privileges, Rules, Papers Laid, Subordinate Legislation and Government Assurances committees exist in both Houses.
35.tq: LS-only: Private Members' Bills; Absence of Members.
xs: **Private Members' Bills and Resolutions** and **Absence of Members** are **LS-only** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Petitions, Privileges, Subordinate Legislation and Government Assurances exist in **both Houses** (separate LS and RS strengths).
xa: Also standing: **Papers Laid on the Table**, **Rules Committee**.
Petitions: **LS 15, RS 10**; Government Assurances: **LS 15, RS 10**.
Subordinate Legislation: **LS 15, RS 15**.

35.s: Ad hoc committees of Parliament are broadly of which two kinds?
o: Inquiry committees for a subject, and Select or Joint Committees on Bills
35.x: The two broad kinds are inquiry committees set up for a particular subject and Select or Joint Committees constituted to examine Bills.
35.tq: Classify the two categories before considering specific examples.
xs: Ad hoc committees are **inquiry committees** and **Select/Joint Committees on Bills** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Both **cease once they report**.
xa: Inquiry examples: **MPLADS**, **Security in Parliament Complex**, **Railway Convention**.
**Select Committee** = one House; **Joint Committee** = both Houses.
Financial standing committees: **Estimates, PAC, COPU**.

35.s: A Bill is referred to a Select Committee or a Joint Committee by:
o: A direction of the Comptroller and Auditor-General
An order of the President without parliamentary motion
A resolution of the Supreme Court
35.x: Referral of a Bill to a Select Committee or Joint Committee takes place through a motion in the House.
35.tq: Ask which parliamentary authority can initiate the referral.
xs: A bill is referred **by motion in the House** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Select Committee** = one House; **Joint Committee** = both Houses.
xa: JPC examples: **Bofors** (**1987**), **2G spectrum** (**2011**).
Currently before JPCs: **129th Amendment** (ONOE), **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026**.
Ad hoc committees **cease once they report**.

35.s:
Arrange the following Joint Parliamentary Committee investigations in chronological order:
A. 2G spectrum
B. Bofors
C. Ketan Parekh
D. Harshad Mehta securities scam
E. Soft-drink pesticides
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
35.x: The investigations occurred in the order Bofors (1987), Harshad Mehta securities scam (1992), Ketan Parekh (2001), soft-drink pesticides (2003) and 2G spectrum (2011).
35.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the three middle investigations by year.
xs: The order is **B, D, C, E, A** — option **(1)**.
**Bofors 1987** → **Harshad Mehta 1992** → **Ketan Parekh 2001** → **soft-drink pesticides 2003** → **2G 2011**.
xa: JPCs are **Joint Committees** — members of **both Houses**.
Currently before JPCs: ONOE (**129th Amendment**) Bill, **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026**, **Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhisthan Bill, 2025**.
Ad hoc committees **cease once they report**.

35.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Bills currently before Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs):
1. The Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 relating to One Nation, One Election is before a JPC.
2. The FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 is before a JPC.
3. The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhisthan Bill, 2025 is before a Select Committee of the Rajya Sabha alone, not a JPC.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
35.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the 129th Amendment (ONOE) Bill and the FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 are before JPCs. Statement 3 is wrong: the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhisthan Bill, 2025 is also before a JPC (a joint committee of both Houses), not a single-House Select Committee. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
35.tq: Current JPC trio: ONOE (129th CAB), FCRA 2026, Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhisthan 2025.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: correct — the **129th Amendment (ONOE)** Bill and the **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026** are before JPCs.
Statement 3: wrong — the **Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhisthan Bill, 2025** is also **before a JPC**.
xa: A JPC = members of **both Houses**; a Select Committee = **one House**.
Past JPCs: **Bofors 1987**, **Harshad Mehta 1992**, **2G 2011**.
Referral is **by motion in the House**.

35.s: Which committee is popularly described as the ‘Ombudsman’ of Parliament?
35.x: The Committee on Petitions is popularly described as the Ombudsman of Parliament because it considers petitions on bills and matters of public interest.
35.tq: Match the distinctive nickname with the committee’s grievance-related function.
xs: The **Committee on Petitions** is the **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025).
**Government Assurances** tracks promises; **Privileges** handles privilege; **Ethics** handles conduct.
xa: It examines petitions on **bills** and **public-interest** matters.
⚠ "Watchdog" = **PAC**; "Continuous economy" = **Estimates**.
Strength: **LS 15, RS 10**.

35.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

Committee — Characterisation
1. Public Accounts Committee — Watchdog on departmental expenditure and irregularities
2. Estimates Committee — Suggests economies and alternative policies
3. Committee on Petitions — Examines only public accounts

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
35.x: The PAC is described as a watchdog on departmental expenditure and irregularities, and the Estimates Committee suggests economies and alternative policies. The Committee on Petitions deals with petitions on bills and public-interest matters, not only public accounts.
35.tq: Locate the single function mismatch in a set of closely related committee descriptions.
xs: Pairs **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
PAC = **"Watchdog"** on departmental expenditure and irregularities (APPSC-G2 2017); Estimates = suggests **economies and alternative policies**.
Pair 3 is wrong — Petitions handles **petitions on bills and public-interest matters**.
xa: Estimates Committee: **financial control reforms** (APPSC-G1 2018).
Petitions = **"Ombudsman"**.
Estimates = **"Continuous economy committee"**.

35.s: Which of the following groups consists of committees regarded as part of the parliamentary watchdog group?
o: Subordinate Legislation, Government Assurances, Estimates, PAC, COPU and DRSCs
Committee on Petitions, Supreme Court, PAC and Finance Commission
Rules Committee, Election Commission, Estimates and CAG
Finance Commission, UPSC, Election Commission, PAC and COPU
35.x: The watchdog group comprises the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Committee on Government Assurances, Estimates Committee, PAC, COPU and Departmentally Related Standing Committees.
35.tq: Check the complete group and exclude constitutional bodies that are not parliamentary committees.
xs: The watchdog group is **Subordinate Legislation, Government Assurances, Estimates, PAC, COPU and DRSCs** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **Supreme Court**, **Finance Commission**, **Election Commission**, **UPSC** and **CAG** are not parliamentary committees.
xa: ⚠ The PAC alone is often called the **"Watchdog"**.
Petitions = **"Ombudsman"**.
These committees keep an **"unremitting vigil"** on the executive's spending.

35.s: Which parliamentary committee is described as a 'continuous economy committee'?
35.x: The Estimates Committee is called a 'continuous economy committee' because it suggests economies and alternative policies. The PAC is the 'watchdog' on expenditure; the Petitions Committee is the 'Ombudsman'; the Business Advisory Committee allots time.
35.tq: Estimates = economy; PAC = watchdog; Petitions = Ombudsman.
xs: The **Estimates Committee** is the **"Continuous economy committee"** — so option **(3)** is correct.
PAC = **"Watchdog"**; Petitions = **"Ombudsman"**; Business Advisory = **allots time**.
xa: It suggests **economies and alternative policies**.
**30** members, all LS; chairman from the **ruling party**.
Present form in **1950** (John Mathai).

35.s: The privilege notice issued by Jairam Ramesh concerned remarks made by which Union Minister about a standing committee?
35.x: Jairam Ramesh issued a privilege notice against Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over remarks concerning a standing committee.
35.tq: Match the privilege notice with the person against whom it was issued.
xs: Jairam Ramesh's privilege notice was against Education Minister **Dharmendra Pradhan** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**John Mathai** and **Krishna Menon** are linked to committee origins; **K.C. Venugopal** chairs the PAC (**2026-27**).
xa: The remarks concerned a **standing committee**.
Privileges Committee: **LS 15** (Speaker nominates), **RS 10**.
MPs' average attendance at DRSCs and PAC: only **53%**.

35.s: Which of the following best describes a criticism of the Public Accounts Committee?
o: It replaces the budget and prevents all unauthorised expenditure in advance.
It is a post-mortem check, and frequent use of the guillotine can weaken financial control.
It can examine only the legality of expenditure and never its propriety.
It is a pre-expenditure approving authority whose recommendations automatically bind the government.
35.x: The PAC is criticised as a post-mortem mechanism because it examines expenditure after it occurs; frequent guillotine of demands can further weaken financial control. Its recommendations are not binding.
35.tq: Contrast post-expenditure scrutiny with pre-expenditure budgetary control and reject absolute claims.
xs: The PAC is a **post-mortem** check, and frequent **guillotine** weakens financial control — so option **(2)** is correct.
It does not replace the budget; it tests **propriety**, not only legality; its advice is **not binding** — options (1), (3), (4) are wrong.
xa: Financial committees control **after** expenditure; the budget **before**.
The PAC **cannot examine policy**, only its execution.
It may take up matters **on its own**.

35.s:
Consider the following statements about parliamentary committee functioning in 2026:
1. The average attendance in the 16 Departmentally Related Standing Committees and the Public Accounts Committee was 53%.
2. Five meetings were postponed for lack of quorum.
3. The Public Accounts Committee held no meeting during 2026–27.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
35.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: average attendance at the 16 DRSCs and the PAC was only 53% since the September reconstitution, and five meetings were postponed for lack of quorum. Statement 3 is the trap: there is no basis for saying the PAC held no meeting; it is one of the committees whose (low) attendance was measured. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
35.tq: Find the false statement by checking the numerical attendance figure, the quorum-related postponements and the existence of the PAC meeting.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — average attendance at **16** DRSCs and the PAC was only **53%** since the September reconstitution.
Statement 2: correct — **five meetings** were postponed for lack of quorum.
Statement 3: wrong — nothing says the PAC held no meeting; it was among the committees measured.
xa: DRSC quorum is **11**.
PAC for **2026-27** is chaired by **K.C. Venugopal**.
Criticism: PAC advice **not binding**.

36.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 105 protects freedom of speech in Parliament.
2. Article 194 protects freedom of speech in State Legislatures.
3. Privileges other than those specified in law are fully codified in a single parliamentary statute.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: Articles 105 and 194 provide the respective speech protections. Parliamentary privileges have not been comprehensively codified in a single statute and also rest on conventions, rules, statutes and judicial rulings.
36.tq: Spot the absolute claim that converts uncodified privileges into a single statutory code.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Art. 105** gives freedom of speech and immunity in **Parliament**.
Statement 2 correct: **Art. 194** gives the same protection in **State Legislatures**.
Statement 3 wrong: privileges "as defined by law" have **never been codified**; they rest on **conventions**, rules, statutes and judicial rulings.
xa: The conventions originally came from **House of Commons** practice.
**Art. 122** (Parliament) / **Art. 212** (states): courts cannot question proceedings for **procedural irregularity**.
Punishments for breach: **admonition**, **reprimand**, **imprisonment**, **suspension/expulsion**.

36.s: The immunity connected with freedom of speech under Articles 105 and 194 includes protection for
o: all statements made by a member outside the House
anything said or any vote given in the House, subject to constitutional provisions
every statement made during an election campaign
criminal acts committed anywhere by a member
36.x: The privilege covers anything said or any vote given in the respective House. It does not create general immunity for statements or criminal conduct outside legislative proceedings.
36.tq: Apply the territorial and functional limits of legislative privilege to a practical situation.
xs: The immunity covers **anything said or any vote given in the House** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 105** (Parliament) and **Art. 194** (states) give freedom of speech and immunity for what is **said or voted** in the House.
The protection is tied to House proceedings, not to statements outside the House, campaign speeches or crimes elsewhere.
xa: **Sita Soren (2024)**: privilege gives **no immunity for bribery** to speak or vote.
Other privileges "as defined by law" have **never been codified**.
⚠ **Art. 105/194** = privileges; **Art. 122/212** = courts barred on **procedural irregularity**.

36.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Article)
A. Article 105
B. Article 122
C. Article 194
D. Article 212

List-II (Subject)
I. Courts not to inquire into proceedings of a State Legislature on grounds of procedural irregularity
II. Privileges of Parliament
III. Courts not to inquire into proceedings of Parliament on grounds of procedural irregularity
IV. Privileges of State Legislatures

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
36.x: Article 105 concerns Parliament's privileges, Article 122 concerns parliamentary proceedings, Article 194 concerns State Legislature privileges and Article 212 concerns State Legislature proceedings.
36.tq: Start with the sure privilege pairs and then distinguish Articles 122 and 212 by the House concerned.
xs: Correct code: **A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 105** = privileges of **Parliament**; **Art. 194** = privileges of **State Legislatures**.
**Art. 122** = courts cannot question **Parliament's** proceedings for **procedural irregularity**; **Art. 212** = the same for **State Legislatures**.
xa: Pairing trick: Parliament articles **105/122**, state articles **194/212**.
Privilege notices: **LS Rule 222** / **RS Rule 187**, usually after **Question Hour**.
**Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: privilege decisions reviewable only for **gross illegality or unconstitutionality**.

36.s: In Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court held that legislative privilege
o: gives no immunity for bribery connected with speaking or voting
gives complete immunity for accepting a bribe to speak or vote
applies only to proceedings of State Legislatures
overrides the power of courts to investigate corruption
36.x: The seven-judge Bench held that privilege does not protect bribery to speak or vote, thereby overruling the contrary position in P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
36.tq: Use the later larger-Bench decision to identify the overruling of an earlier precedent.
xs: **Sita Soren (2024)** held privilege **gives no immunity for bribery** connected with speaking or voting — option **(1)**.
A **7-judge Bench** gave the ruling and **overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**, which had allowed such immunity.
So option (2) states the overruled position; the ruling is not limited to State Legislatures.
xa: **Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: privilege decisions reviewable only for **gross illegality or unconstitutionality**.
Privilege source: **Art. 105** (Parliament) and **Art. 194** (states).
⚠ **P.V. Narasimha Rao** = **1998** (overruled); **Sita Soren** = **2024**.

36.s: In Raja Ram Pal (2007), the Supreme Court held that decisions of a House in matters of privilege are:
o: Reviewable only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality
Reviewable on every ground of procedural irregularity
Subject to approval by the President
36.x: Raja Ram Pal (2007) held that privilege decisions can be reviewed, but only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality. They are not wholly immune; mere procedural irregularity is protected by Art. 122/212; the President has no approving role.
36.tq: Raja Ram Pal 2007 = limited review of privilege decisions.
xs: **Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: privilege decisions are **reviewable only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality** — option **(2)**.
So they are not wholly immune (option 1 wrong).
Mere **procedural irregularity** is shielded by **Art. 122/212**, so option (3) is wrong; the President has no approving role.
xa: **Sita Soren (2024)**: **7-judge Bench**, **no immunity for bribery** to speak or vote.
Final say on a privilege notice lies with the **House**, after the **Privileges Committee** recommends.
Punishments: **admonition**, **reprimand**, **imprisonment**, **suspension/expulsion**.

36.s: A Member of Parliament wishing to allege breach of privilege or contempt by a minister, another member or an outsider generally raises the matter under
o: Lok Sabha Rule 187 or Rajya Sabha Rule 222
Lok Sabha Rule 222 or Rajya Sabha Rule 187
36.x: Privilege notices are raised under Rule 222 in the Lok Sabha and Rule 187 in the Rajya Sabha, usually after Question Hour.
36.tq: Test the paired procedural rules while guarding against a deliberate reversal of the two Houses.
xs: A privilege notice is raised under **Lok Sabha Rule 222 / Rajya Sabha Rule 187** — option **(3)**.
It is usually raised **after Question Hour**; any MP can allege breach by a **minister, member or outsider**.
Option (1) swaps the rules; **Arts 103/192** deal with other disqualifications; **Para 6** of the Tenth Schedule is about defection.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Rule 222 = LS**, **Rule 187 = RS**.
Presiding Officer grants/denies consent → House decides or refers to **Privileges Committee**.
**RS Privileges Committee**: **10** members, usually chaired by the **Deputy Chairman**.

36.s:
Consider the following statements about a privilege notice:
1. The Presiding Officer may grant or deny consent.
2. The matter may be left to the decision of the House or referred to the Committee of Privileges.
3. The Committee of Privileges finally imposes punishment without any decision by the House.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: The Presiding Officer controls consent and may refer the matter to the committee. The committee examines and recommends action, but the House takes the final decision.
36.tq: Trace the institutional sequence and identify the statement that gives final authority to the committee instead of the House.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **Presiding Officer grants or denies consent**.
Statement 2 correct: he **lets the House decide** or refers it to the **Privileges Committee**.
Statement 3 wrong: the committee examines witnesses and **recommends**; the **House decides**.
xa: Notice is raised under **LS Rule 222 / RS Rule 187**, usually after **Question Hour**.
**RS committee**: **10** members, usually chaired by the **Deputy Chairman**.
**Contempt** is wider than breach: any act **obstructing the House** or its members.

36.s: Which of the following best distinguishes contempt of the House from breach of privilege?
o: Contempt is wider and includes any act obstructing the House or its members in their functions
Contempt is narrower and concerns only members of the House
Breach of privilege applies only to ministers, whereas contempt applies only to outsiders
There is no distinction between the two expressions
36.x: Contempt has a wider scope and includes acts that obstruct the House or its members in the discharge of their functions. A breach concerns infringement of a specific privilege.
36.tq: Discriminate between the broader concept and the specific infringement instead of treating the terms as identical.
xs: **Contempt is wider** — any act **obstructing the House or its members in their functions** — option **(1)**.
So contempt is not narrower (option 2), and the two terms are distinct (option 4 wrong).
A privilege notice can allege breach or contempt by a **minister, member or outsider**, so option (3)'s split is wrong.
xa: Punishments: **admonition**, **reprimand**, **imprisonment**, **suspension/expulsion**.
**Maharashtra**: the **Legislative Council's Privileges Committee** summoned **Kunal Kamra** on a breach notice.
Privileges rest on **conventions**, rules, statutes and judicial rulings — **never codified**.

36.s: Which of the following is NOT a recognised punishment for breach of privilege or contempt of the House?
36.x: The recognised punishments include admonition, reprimand, imprisonment, suspension and expulsion. Dissolution of the Supreme Court is not a parliamentary punishment.
36.tq: Find the institutionally impossible punishment while retaining the listed parliamentary sanctions.
xs: **Dissolution of the Supreme Court** is not a privilege punishment — option **(2)**.
Recognised punishments: **admonition**, **reprimand**, **imprisonment** and **suspension/expulsion**.
So options (1), (3) and (4) are all valid punishments.
xa: The **House decides** the punishment after the **Privileges Committee** recommends.
**Contempt** = any act **obstructing the House** or members in their functions.
**Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: such decisions reviewable only for **gross illegality or unconstitutionality**.

36.s: The Committee of Privileges of the Rajya Sabha consists of:
o: 10 members usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman
22 members chaired by the Leader of the Opposition
31 members chaired by a member of the ruling party
36.x: The Rajya Sabha Privileges Committee has 10 members and is usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman. Fifteen members is the Lok Sabha committee's strength; 22 and 31 are PAC/COPU and DRSC sizes.
36.tq: RS Privileges = 10, Deputy Chairman.
xs: The **Rajya Sabha** Privileges Committee has **10 members**, **usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman** — option **(2)**.
It examines witnesses and **recommends**; the **House decides**.
xa: ⚠ **Rule 222 = LS**, **Rule 187 = RS** for privilege notices.
