The Presiding Officer may let the House decide or refer the matter to the **Privileges Committee**.
**Maharashtra Legislative Council's** committee summoned **Kunal Kamra**.

36.s: The Privileges Committee of which body summoned comedian Kunal Kamra on a breach of privilege notice?
36.x: The Maharashtra Legislative Council's Privileges Committee summoned Kunal Kamra on a breach notice. The matter did not arise in either House of Parliament or in Delhi.
36.tq: Kunal Kamra = Maharashtra Legislative Council.
xs: The **Maharashtra Legislative Council's** Privileges Committee summoned **Kunal Kamra** — option **(3)**.
He was summoned on a **breach of privilege notice**; not by either House of Parliament or Delhi.
xa: State legislature privileges flow from **Art. 194**; Parliament's from **Art. 105**.
**Contempt** is wider than breach — any act **obstructing the House**.
Punishments: **admonition**, **reprimand**, **imprisonment**, **suspension/expulsion**.

36.s: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 amended which of the following Articles in connection with vacation of seats and disqualification?
36.x: The 52nd Amendment amended Articles 101, 102, 190 and 191 concerning vacation of seats and disqualification.
36.tq: Match the amendment with its actual constitutional provisions rather than with nearby provisions on ministerial limits.
xs: The **52nd Amendment, 1985** amended **Articles 101, 102, 190 and 191** on vacation of seats and disqualification — option **(2)**.
**Arts 75(1B), 164(1B), 361B** came with the **91st Amendment, 2003**; **Arts 105/194** are privilege articles.
xa: The 52nd Amendment inserted the **Tenth Schedule** (APPSC-GS **2019**).
It was the **first constitutional mention of political parties**.
**91st Amendment (2003)** deleted the **split** exception and capped ministries at **15%**.

36.s: The principal objective of the anti-defection law is to
o: curb defections induced by the lure of office and promote stable governments
abolish political parties from the legislative process
transfer legislative control from parties to the Election Commission
36.x: The law was intended to curb horse-trading and defections for office, thereby promoting party discipline and stable governments.
36.tq: Identify the purpose from the cause-effect relationship rather than from the constitutional location of the law.
xs: The law aims to **curb defections induced by the lure of office** and ensure **stable governments** — option **(2)**.
It also targets **horse-trading** and secures **party discipline**.
xa: Background: defections toppled governments in the **1960s-70s** ("**Aaya Ram Gaya Ram**", Haryana **1967**).
**Y.B. Chavan Committee (1967-69)** studied defections; Bills of **1973 and 1978** lapsed.
Enacted by the **52nd Amendment, 1985** (**Tenth Schedule**).
Criticism: muzzles **dissent** without stopping **mass defections**.

36.s: The expression “Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram”, associated with frequent defections, became prominent in the political context of
36.x: The expression became associated with rampant defections in Haryana in 1967, a phenomenon that contributed to the enactment of the anti-defection law.
36.tq: Link the famous expression with its precise State and year instead of the year of the 52nd Amendment.
xs: "**Aaya Ram Gaya Ram**" is linked to **Haryana in 1967** — option **(2)**.
Defections toppled governments in the **1960s-70s**, leading to the anti-defection law.
xa: **Y.B. Chavan Committee on Defections (1967-69)** studied the problem.
Anti-defection Bills of **1973 and 1978** lapsed.
AP link: **Nadendla Bhaskara Rao's** defection toppled **NTR's** government in **1984** — fed the demand for the **1985** law.
⚠ **1974** = **35th Amendment** (Sikkim schedule), not a defection episode.

36.s:
With reference to the history of the Tenth Schedule, consider the following statements:
1. The 35th Amendment Act, 1974 used a Tenth Schedule in connection with Sikkim’s association with India.
2. The Tenth Schedule associated with Sikkim was omitted by the 36th Amendment Act, 1975.
3. The present anti-defection provisions were contained in that original Sikkim-related Tenth Schedule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: The 35th Amendment introduced a different Tenth Schedule concerning Sikkim, and the 36th Amendment omitted it. It was not the present anti-defection Schedule.
36.tq: Discriminate between two similarly numbered Schedules by comparing their subject and amendment history.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **35th Amendment (1974)** used a "Tenth Schedule" for **Sikkim's association**.
Statement 2 correct: the **36th Amendment (1975)** deleted that old schedule.
Statement 3 wrong: the anti-defection Tenth Schedule came with the **52nd Amendment (1985)** — a different schedule.
xa: ⚠ Trap: Sikkim schedule = **35th**, **1974**; anti-defection schedule = **52nd**, **1985**.
The 52nd Amendment also amended **Arts. 101, 102, 190, 191**.
**91st Amendment (2003)** tightened the law.

36.s: Which constitutional amendment first gave political parties constitutional recognition through the Tenth Schedule?
36.x: The 52nd Amendment Act, 1985 inserted the Tenth Schedule and mentioned political parties in the Constitution for the first time, thereby giving them constitutional recognition.
36.tq: Separate the first constitutional recognition from the later amendment that tightened the law.
xs: The **52nd Amendment Act, 1985** first gave political parties constitutional mention — option **(2)**.
It inserted the **Tenth Schedule** and mentioned **political parties for the first time**.
The **91st Amendment (2003)** only tightened the law later.
xa: It also amended **Arts. 101, 102, 190, 191** (vacation of seats, disqualification).
Tenth Schedule question appeared in **APPSC-GS 2019**.
⚠ Do not confuse with the **35th Amendment (1974)** Sikkim "Tenth Schedule".

36.s:
With reference to the applicability of the anti-defection law, consider the following statements:
1. Members of State Legislative Councils are covered by the law.
2. Independent members are covered by the law.
3. Nominated members are outside the scope of the law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: Members of both Houses of Parliament and both Houses of State Legislatures, including MLCs, are covered. Independents and nominated members are also covered; therefore, statement 3 is false.
36.tq: Combine a specific applicability fact with a reversed exclusion to identify the false statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: members of **both Houses of State Legislatures**, so **Legislative Council** members too, are covered.
Statement 2 correct: **independents** are disqualified if they **join any party** after election.
Statement 3 wrong: **nominated members** are covered — disqualified if they join a party **after 6 months**.
xa: The law operates on the **"legislature party"**.
Party member: disqualified for **voluntarily giving up membership** or defying the **whip** (not condoned within **15 days**).
⚠ Nominated member joining within **6 months** is allowed.

36.s: Which committee examined the problem of defections during the period 1967–1969, before the enactment of the Tenth Schedule?
36.x: The Y.B. Chavan Committee on Defections studied the problem during 1967–1969.
36.tq: Identify the committee from its specific period and subject.
xs: The **Y.B. Chavan Committee on Defections (1967-69)** studied the problem — option **(4)**.
**Dinesh Goswami** was **1990**, **Law Commission's 170th Report** **1999** and **NCRWC** **2002** — all after the law.
xa: Anti-defection Bills of **1973 and 1978** lapsed.
Context: "**Aaya Ram Gaya Ram**", Haryana **1967**.
⚠ **170th** Report = Law Commission (1999); **NCRWC** = 2002; **Dinesh Goswami** = 1990.

36.s: Which of the following statements regarding anti-defection legislation before 1985 is correct?
o: The Bills introduced in 1973 and 1978 lapsed.
The Bills introduced in 1973 and 1978 were enacted as ordinary laws.
The Bills introduced in 1973 and 1978 became constitutional amendments.
The Bills introduced in 1973 and 1978 were referred to the Election Commission and withdrawn.
36.x: The anti-defection Bills introduced in 1973 and 1978 lapsed and did not become law.
36.tq: Use the dates as a numerical pair and distinguish lapse from enactment.
xs: The anti-defection **Bills of 1973 and 1978 lapsed** — option **(1)**.
The law came only with the **52nd Amendment, 1985**, inserting the **Tenth Schedule**.
xa: **Y.B. Chavan Committee (1967-69)** studied defections earlier.
Context: "**Aaya Ram Gaya Ram**" (Haryana **1967**).
**NTR's** government toppled by **Nadendla Bhaskara Rao** (**1984**) fed the demand for the **1985** law.

36.s: A member elected as an independent becomes liable for disqualification under the Tenth Schedule if the member
o: votes against the Government on a money bill
joins a political party before election
joins a political party after election
36.x: An independent member is disqualified if he or she joins any political party after election.
36.tq: Apply the member-category rule specifically to an independent legislator.
xs: An independent is disqualified if he **joins a political party after election** — option **(3)**.
Joining before election is no defection; whip-based grounds apply to **party members**.
xa: Nominated member: disqualified if he joins a party **after 6 months** of taking his seat.
Party member: **voluntarily gives up membership** or defies the **whip** (not condoned within **15 days**).
Whip clause = **Para 2(1)(b)**.

36.s: A member belonging to a political party may be disqualified when the member votes or abstains contrary to the party whip without permission and the party does not condone the action within
36.x: Voting or abstaining against the party direction without permission attracts disqualification unless the party condones the conduct within 15 days.
36.tq: Recall the exact condonation period and avoid substituting a general legislative time limit.
xs: The party must **condone** the vote/abstention within **15 days**, or the member is disqualified — option **(2)**.
The ground: **votes or abstains against the whip** without permission.
The whip clause is **Para 2(1)(b)**.
xa: Other party-member ground: **voluntarily giving up membership**, even without resigning.
**Subhash Desai (2023)**: the **political party**, not the legislature party, appoints the whip.
Reform: limit whips to **confidence votes and Money Bills** (Dinesh Goswami **1990**, Law Commission **1999**).

36.s: Which one of the following is NOT a ground of disqualification under the Tenth Schedule?
o: A party member votes against the whip with permission from the party.
A party member voluntarily gives up party membership, even without formally resigning.
A nominated member joins a political party after six months of taking the seat.
An independent member joins a political party after election.
36.x: Voting against the whip with permission is not a ground of disqualification. The other three situations are specified grounds under the Tenth Schedule.
36.tq: Find the exception by checking whether the required permission or time condition defeats disqualification.
xs: Voting against the whip **with permission from the party** is not a ground — option **(1)**.
Disqualification needs a vote/abstention **without permission**, not condoned within **15 days**.
Options (2), (3) and (4) are listed grounds: **voluntarily giving up membership**, nominated member joining **after 6 months**, independent **joining a party**.
xa: **Ravi S. Naik (1994)**: giving up membership can be **inferred from conduct**.
**G. Viswanathan (1996)**: an **expelled** member still belongs to his party.
Whip clause = **Para 2(1)(b)**.

36.s: The expression “voluntarily giving up membership” under the Tenth Schedule was explained in Ravi S. Naik v. Union of India to mean that:
o: It applies only when a member votes against the party whip.
It can be inferred from conduct, such as publicly supporting a rival party.
It can arise only after a written resignation is accepted.
It is identical to formal resignation from the political party.
36.x: Ravi S. Naik held that voluntarily giving up membership is not the same as resigning; it may be inferred from conduct, including publicly backing a rival party.
36.tq: Distinguish formal resignation from conduct-based inference.
xs: **Ravi S. Naik (1994)**: giving up membership **can be inferred from conduct**, e.g. **publicly backing a rival party** — option **(2)**.
It is **not the same as resigning**, so options (3) and (4) are wrong; whip-defiance is a separate ground.
xa: **G. Viswanathan (1996)**: an **expelled** member who **joins another party** has voluntarily given up membership.
Whip ground: vote/abstain against the whip, not condoned within **15 days**.
Dinesh Goswami (**1990**) wanted disqualification only for giving up membership or whip defiance on **confidence** motions.

36.s:
Consider the following statements with reference to G. Viswanathan v. Speaker, Tamil Nadu:
1. Expulsion from a political party does not by itself mean that the member ceases to belong to that party for the purposes of the Tenth Schedule.
2. An expelled member who joins another political party may be treated as having voluntarily given up membership.
3. Expulsion automatically protects a member from disqualification for joining another party.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: An expelled member continues to be regarded as belonging to the original party for the Tenth Schedule. Joining another party may amount to voluntarily giving up membership; hence statement 3 is false.
36.tq: Test the distinction between expulsion and cessation of party membership.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **G. Viswanathan (1996)** — an **expelled** member **still belongs** to his party.
Statement 2 correct: if he **joins another party**, he has **voluntarily given up membership**.
Statement 3 wrong: expulsion gives no shield for joining another party.
xa: **Ravi S. Naik (1994)**: giving up membership is **not the same as resigning**; inferred from **conduct**.
**Subhash Desai (2023)**: **political party** appoints the whip and leader in the House.
⚠ **Kihoto** (1992) = validity + review; **Keisham** (2020) = **three months**.

36.s: Under Para 4 of the Tenth Schedule, protection from disqualification on the ground of merger requires that
o: two-thirds of the legislature party agrees to merge and the original political party also merges
all members of the legislature party join another party
one-half of the legislature party joins another party
the Speaker alone approves the merger
36.x: A valid merger requires two conditions: the original political party must merge with another party, and at least two-thirds of the legislature party must agree to the merger.
36.tq: Apply both cumulative tests for a valid merger instead of relying only on the numerical threshold.
xs: A valid merger needs **two-thirds of the legislature party** to agree **and** the **original political party** to merge — option **(1)**.
These are the **two tests** in **Para 4**.
Two-thirds of legislators cannot by themselves create a "**deemed merger**" (**Subhash Desai**, 2023).
xa: Neither those who merge nor those who stay are disqualified.
⚠ **Merger = two-thirds** (Para 4, in force); **Split = one-third** (Para 3, deleted **2003**).
**June 2019**: **4 of 6 TDP Rajya Sabha MPs** "merged" with BJP under Para 4.
Misuse: Para 4 used as a **defence for mass defection** (AAP, TMC cases, **2026**).

36.s:
Consider the following statements about the merger exception:
1. Members who merge with another party are protected from disqualification.
2. Members who remain with the original party are also protected, provided the merger requirements are satisfied.
3. A one-third split remains an independent exception under the Tenth Schedule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: Both groups are protected when the Para 4 merger conditions are met. The one-third split exception was deleted by the 91st Amendment in 2003.
36.tq: Test the contrast between the merger exception still in force and the deleted split exception.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: those who **merge** are not disqualified.
Statement 2 correct: those who **stay** with the original party are also protected.
Statement 3 wrong: the **one-third split** (Para 3) was **deleted by the 91st Amendment, 2003**.
xa: Per **IYB 2026**, the deletion brought **splits within the purview of disqualification**.
Merger needs the **original political party** to merge **and** two-thirds of the legislature party.
Presiding officers (**Para 5**) may leave their party on election and rejoin later.

36.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 75(1A) — Fifteen per cent limit on the Union Council of Ministers
Para 3 of the Tenth Schedule — Split exception
Para 4 of the Tenth Schedule — Merger exception
Article 105(1)-(2) — Fifteen per cent limit on a State Council of Ministers
36.x: Article 105(1)-(2) concerns freedom of speech and related parliamentary privileges. The 15 per cent limit on a State Council of Ministers is provided under Article 164(1A).
36.tq: Find the wrong authority-provision pairing by separating privilege provisions from ministerial-limit provisions.
xs: **Article 105(1)-(2)** is wrongly paired: it is about **freedom of speech / privileges** — option **(4)**.
The **15%** cap on a **State** Council of Ministers is **Art. 164(1A)**.
The other pairs are correct: **Art. 75(1A)** = Union **15%** cap; **Para 3** = split; **Para 4** = merger.
xa: **Art. 164(1A)** sets a minimum of **12** ministers.
**Arts 75(1B), 164(1B), 361B** bar a disqualified defector from ministerial/remunerative posts.
All came via the **91st Amendment, 2003**.

36.s: Under Article 164(1A), the Council of Ministers in a State cannot exceed 15 per cent of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly, subject to a minimum of
36.x: The State Council of Ministers is capped at 15 per cent of the Assembly strength, but it cannot consist of fewer than 12 ministers.
36.tq: Recall both parts of a compound numerical rule: the percentage ceiling and the statutory minimum.
xs: Minimum is **12 ministers** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 164(1A)** caps a State Council of Ministers at **15%** of Assembly strength, with a minimum of **12**.
xa: **Art. 75(1A)**: Union Council capped at **15%** of Lok Sabha strength.
Both added by the **91st Amendment, 2003**, which also deleted the **split** exception.
**Arts 75(1B), 164(1B), 361B**: defector cannot be a Minister until **re-elected**.

36.s: A person disqualified under the anti-defection provisions is barred from becoming a Minister or holding a remunerative political post until re-elected under
36.x: Articles 75(1B), 164(1B) and 361B impose these restrictions on a disqualified defector until re-election.
36.tq: Match the consequence of disqualification with the specific provisions introduced by the 91st Amendment.
xs: The bar is in **Articles 75(1B), 164(1B) and 361B** — option **(1)**.
A disqualified defector cannot be a **Minister** or hold a **remunerative political post** until **re-elected**.
**Arts 101, 102, 190, 191** were amended by the **52nd** Amendment for vacation of seats; **105/194** are privileges.
xa: These came with the **91st Amendment, 2003**.
Same Amendment: **15%** cap under **Art. 75(1A)** and **Art. 164(1A)**.
**NCRWC (2002)** had urged barring defectors from any **public or remunerative political office**.

36.s:
With reference to disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, consider the following statements:
1. The Speaker or Chairman acts as a tribunal while deciding the question of disqualification.
2. The Election Commission gives an opinion before the Speaker or Chairman decides the matter.
3. The decision is subject to judicial review on limited grounds.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Election Commission does not give an opinion in Tenth Schedule proceedings; that arrangement applies to certain other disqualifications under Articles 103 and 192.
36.tq: Split the options by distinguishing Tenth Schedule proceedings from disqualifications under Articles 103 and 192.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: under **Para 6** the **Speaker/Chairman** decides, acting as a **tribunal**.
Statement 2 wrong: the **Election Commission gives no opinion** (UPSC **2025** PYQ).
Statement 3 correct: decision is **subject to judicial review** after it is made, on limited grounds.
xa: ⚠ Contrast: **other** disqualifications (**Arts 103 and 192**) → President/Governor decides on the **EC's opinion**.
Review grounds: **mala fides**, **perversity**, violation of **natural justice** or constitutional mandate.
**Keisham (2020)**: decide within **three months**.

36.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992):
1. The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Tenth Schedule.
2. It struck down Paragraph 7 of the Schedule.
3. It held that the Tenth Schedule violates the basic structure because it restricts legislators' freedom of speech.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Constitution Bench held that the law did not violate legislators' freedom of speech or the basic structure.
36.tq: Find the statement that reverses the court's conclusion on constitutional validity and basic structure.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** **upheld the validity** of the Tenth Schedule.
Statement 2 correct: it **struck down Para 7**.
Statement 3 wrong: the Court found **no violation** of legislators' free speech or the **basic structure**.
xa: Para 7 fell as it was **not ratified by States** under **Art. 368(2)**; ruling on it was **3:2**.
Decided by a **Constitution Bench**.
Speaker's decision reviewable only **after** it is made.

36.s: Why was Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule struck down in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu?
o: It barred judicial review without the required ratification by the States under Article 368(2)
It transferred disqualification powers to the Election Commission
It permitted nominated members to vote in all elections
It abolished the office of the Speaker
36.x: Paragraph 7 attempted to oust the jurisdiction of courts. Its provisions were held invalid because the amendment had not been ratified by the States as required under Article 368(2).
36.tq: Match the constitutional defect with the provision that attempted to exclude court jurisdiction.
xs: **Para 7** barred courts but was **not ratified by the States under Art. 368(2)** — option **(1)**.
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** struck it down; the ruling on Para 7 was **3:2**.
EC has no role under the Tenth Schedule; the Speaker remains the deciding authority (**Para 6**).
xa: The Tenth Schedule itself was **upheld as valid**.
Decision now **subject to judicial review**, but only **after** the decision.
⚠ **Kihoto** (1992) = validity + review; **Keisham** (2020) = **three months**; **Subhash Desai** (2023) = whip.

36.s: Judicial review of a decision of the Speaker or Chairman under the Tenth Schedule is generally available
o: under no circumstances, because the decision is final
before the decision is made, on every question of fact
only after the decision, and on limited grounds such as mala fides or perversity
only when the Election Commission grants permission
36.x: Kihoto Hollohan preserved judicial review after the decision, but limited it to grounds such as mala fides, perversity, violation of natural justice and constitutional mandate.
36.tq: Reject the absolute-finality trap and identify both the timing and limited grounds of review.
xs: Review is available **only after the decision**, on limited grounds like **mala fides or perversity** — option **(3)**.
Other grounds: violation of **natural justice** or of a **constitutional mandate**.
**Para 7**, which barred courts, was **struck down** in **Kihoto Hollohan**, so option (1) is wrong; the EC has no role.
xa: Deciding authority: **Speaker/Chairman** acting as a **tribunal** (**Para 6**).
No time limit in the Schedule; **Keisham (2020)** set **three months**.
**Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: privilege decisions reviewable only for **gross illegality or unconstitutionality**.

36.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the time limit for deciding a disqualification petition under the Tenth Schedule?
o: The Tenth Schedule prescribes three months
The Tenth Schedule prescribes no specific time limit
The Tenth Schedule prescribes three weeks
The Tenth Schedule prescribes six months
36.x: The Tenth Schedule itself prescribes no time limit for the Speaker or Chairman. In Keisham Meghachandra Singh, the Supreme Court urged that the Speaker should decide within three months.
36.tq: Separate the statutory position from the judicially suggested time period.
xs: The **Tenth Schedule prescribes no specific time limit** for the Speaker — option **(2)**.
The **three months** comes from **Keisham Meghachandra Singh (Jan 2020)**, not the Schedule.
**Three weeks** was the SC's **final** deadline for the **Telangana Speaker** (Feb **2026**).
xa: Speakers are seen as partisan because they **do not resign from their party**.
AP example of delay: **23 YSRCP MLAs** (2014-19), petitions **never decided**.
Newer proposal: **fixed constitutional timelines** for Speakers (Jul **2026**).

36.s: In Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur, the Supreme Court indicated that disqualification petitions should ordinarily be decided within:
36.x: The Supreme Court indicated that the Speaker should decide disqualification petitions within three months, except in extraordinary circumstances.
36.tq: Recall the specific judicially indicated time period.
xs: **Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020)**: decide within **three months** — option **(2)**.
Exception: **extraordinary cases**.
xa: The Court also asked **Parliament** to consider a **permanent independent tribunal** instead of the Speaker.
The Schedule itself prescribes **no time limit**.
⚠ **Keisham** = time; **Kihoto** = review; **Subhash Desai** = party over legislature party.

36.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the decision in Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur:
1. The three-month period is subject to exceptions in extraordinary cases.
2. The Supreme Court asked Parliament to consider replacing the Speaker with a permanent independent tribunal.
3. The judgment permanently transferred all Tenth Schedule decisions to the Election Commission.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: The Court recognised extraordinary exceptions to the three-month period and suggested consideration of a permanent independent tribunal. It did not transfer all such decisions to the Election Commission.
36.tq: Reject the statement that converts a recommendation into an immediate institutional transfer.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **three months**, except in **extraordinary cases**.
Statement 2 correct: asked **Parliament** to consider a **permanent independent tribunal**.
Statement 3 wrong: the Speaker remains the authority; the EC gives **no opinion** under the Tenth Schedule.
xa: Case date: **Jan 2020**, Speaker of **Manipur**.
**Dinesh Goswami (1990)** and the **EC** had urged decisions by the **President or Governor** on EC advice.
**Telangana**: SC gave a **final 3 weeks** with a **contempt** warning (Feb **2026**).

36.s: Which of the following developments is associated with the later litigation concerning the Telangana Speaker?
o: The petitions were dismissed because the Tenth Schedule does not apply to State Legislatures.
The Supreme Court issued a time-bound direction and later allowed three weeks for deciding the last two of ten BRS petitions, with a warning of contempt.
The Election Commission decided all ten petitions without reference to the Speaker.
The Supreme Court abolished the office of the Speaker as the deciding authority.
36.x: The Supreme Court issued a time-bound direction in the Telangana matter and later gave three weeks for the last two of ten BRS petitions, warning of contempt.
36.tq: Select the option containing the precise sequence of judicial actions.
xs: SC gave a **time-bound direction**, then a **final 3 weeks** for the **last 2 of 10 BRS MLAs**, warning of **contempt** — option **(2)**.
**Seven** petitions were rejected in **Dec 2025**; the warning came in **Feb 2026**.
The law does cover State Legislatures; the Speaker, not the EC, decides.
xa: The **10 BRS MLAs** had moved to **Congress**.
**Keisham (2020)**: **three months** limit.
AP precedent: **23 YSRCP MLAs** (2014-19), petitions **never decided**.

36.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Case)
A. Ravi S. Naik v. Union of India
B. G. Viswanathan v. Speaker, Tamil Nadu
C. Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra

List-II (Holding)
I. Political party appoints the whip and the leader in the House
II. Expelled member continues to belong to the party for Tenth Schedule purposes
III. Voluntarily giving up membership may be inferred from conduct

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
36.x: Ravi S. Naik concerned inference from conduct; G. Viswanathan concerned the status of an expelled member; Subhash Desai concerned the party’s authority over the whip and House leader.
36.tq: Start from the sure case-holding pair and eliminate incompatible combinations.
xs: Correct code: **A–III, B–II, C–I** — option **(1)**.
**Ravi S. Naik (1994)**: giving up membership **inferred from conduct**.
**G. Viswanathan (1996)**: **expelled** member still belongs to the party.
**Subhash Desai (2023)**: **political party** appoints the **whip and leader** in the House.
xa: **Kihoto Hollohan (1992)**: Tenth Schedule valid; **Para 7** struck down.
**Keisham (2020)**: decide within **three months**.
**Sita Soren (2024)**: **no immunity for bribery**.

36.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the distinction between a political party and a legislature party:
1. The legislature party cannot be conflated with the political party.
2. Two-thirds of legislators can by themselves create a deemed merger of the original political party.
3. The political party has a role in appointing the whip under the principle laid down in Subhash Desai.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: The legislature party is distinct from the political party, and the political party appoints the whip. Two-thirds of legislators cannot by themselves create a deemed merger of the original party.
36.tq: Spot the overbroad claim that treats a numerical legislative group as the whole political party.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **legislature party cannot be conflated with the political party** (**Subhash Desai**, 2023).
Statement 2 wrong: two-thirds of legislators **cannot** by themselves create a **deemed merger**.
Statement 3 correct: the **political party** appoints the **whip** and leader in the House.
xa: Context: the **Shiv Sena** case, May **2023**.
**SC Bench (Jul 2026)** — **Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe** — sought the Centre's reply on "deemed merger" under **Para 4**.
**AIADMK** Palaniswami camp cited the ruling (May **2026**) to claim the whip.

36.s: The Palaniswami camp of the AIADMK cited the Subhash Desai ruling in May 2026 in relation to control over the:
36.x: The Palaniswami camp cited the ruling to claim control of the whip under Paragraph 2(1)(b).
36.tq: Link the contemporary application to the precise constitutional provision mentioned.
xs: The Palaniswami camp claimed control of the **whip under Para 2(1)(b)** — option **(2)**.
It relied on **Subhash Desai (2023)**: the **political party** appoints the whip.
xa: Para **2(1)(b)** is the whip clause: vote/abstain against it, not condoned within **15 days** → disqualified.
Legislature party **cannot be conflated** with the political party.
Valid merger needs two-thirds of the legislature party **of the original party**.

36.s:
With reference to the Karnataka defection case of 2019, consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court upheld the disqualification of 17 rebel MLAs.
2. The Speaker could permanently bar the disqualified members from contesting elections.
3. The Court held that the Speaker could not bar them from contesting until the end of the term.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: The Court upheld the disqualification of 17 rebel MLAs but held that the Speaker could not prevent them from contesting until the end of the legislative term. Permanent disqualification from contesting was not authorised.
36.tq: Separate the upheld disqualification from the rejected additional penalty.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: SC **upheld the disqualification of 17 rebel MLAs**.
Statement 2 wrong and statement 3 correct: the Speaker **cannot bar them from contesting** until end of term.
xa: **Karnataka 2019** is also an example of the **resignation route**.
**Telangana**: SC gave the Speaker a **final 3 weeks** (Feb **2026**).
Speaker decisions reviewable for **mala fides**, **perversity**, violation of **natural justice**.

36.s: “Resort politics” in the context of anti-defection and floor tests refers to:
o: Sending legislators abroad for parliamentary training
Dissolving the legislature before a confidence motion
Sequestering legislators before a floor test to prevent poaching
Suspending legislators who abstain from voting
36.x: Resort politics involves keeping legislators together or sequestered before a floor test to prevent rival parties from poaching them.
36.tq: Decode the political practice from its purpose rather than from its literal name.
xs: Resort politics = **sequestering legislators before a floor test** to stop **poaching** — option **(3)**.
It is one of the **ways around the law**, along with the **resignation route** and **merger misuse**.
xa: **Resignation route**: MLAs **resign** to cut the majority mark (Karnataka **2019**, MP **2020**).
**Merger misuse**: Para 4 **two-thirds** rule as a defence for mass defection.
**AAP**: **7 of 10** Rajya Sabha MPs claimed a "merger" with the BJP (Apr **2026**).

36.s: Which one of the following best describes the resignation route used to avoid disqualification proceedings?
o: Members secure prior permission from the Election Commission before changing parties.
Members remain in the House but abstain from every vote until the next election.
Members resign, reduce the majority mark, and later re-contest on the new party's ticket.
Members are automatically merged into the new party without resigning.
36.x: In the resignation route, MLAs resign instead of defecting, thereby reducing the majority mark without being disqualified, and may later re-contest on the new party’s ticket.
36.tq: Follow the sequence of action, immediate consequence and later political outcome.
xs: MLAs **resign**, **cutting the majority mark**, then **re-contest on the new party's ticket** — option **(3)**.
Resigning avoids **disqualification**, since they never defect while members.
No EC permission exists; merger needs **two-thirds** under **Para 4**, not automatic.
xa: Examples: **Karnataka 2019**, **MP 2020**.
**Karnataka 2019**: SC upheld disqualification of **17** rebel MLAs.
**Resort politics**: legislators **sequestered** before a floor test.

36.s: The resignation route described in connection with anti-defection politics was illustrated by developments in:
o: Madhya Pradesh in 2014 and Karnataka in 2016
Karnataka in 2019 and Madhya Pradesh in 2020
Telangana in 2019 and Andhra Pradesh in 2020
Tamil Nadu in 2021 and Maharashtra in 2022
36.x: Karnataka 2019 and Madhya Pradesh 2020 were cited as examples of the resignation route.
36.tq: Use the paired years and States as a precise factual combination.
xs: **Karnataka in 2019** and **Madhya Pradesh in 2020** — option **(2)**.
In both, MLAs **resigned** instead of defecting, cutting the majority mark.
xa: In Karnataka, SC upheld disqualification of **17 rebel MLAs** but let them contest.
AP **2014-19**: **23 YSRCP MLAs** moved to TDP — Speaker-delay example, not resignation.
Telangana **2024-26**: another Speaker-delay example.

36.s: Which of the following is a reason for concern regarding delay by Speakers in deciding disqualification petitions?
o: The Election Commission prevents Speakers from deciding petitions.
Speakers are appointed for life and cannot be removed.
The Constitution prescribes a mandatory seven-day period for every petition.
There is no fixed time limit and Speakers continue to belong to political parties.
36.x: The concern arises from the absence of a fixed time limit and the partisan context in which Speakers, who do not resign from their parties, decide petitions.
36.tq: Identify the institutional weakness by separating the actual reason from absolute claims.
xs: **No fixed time limit**, and Speakers **continue to belong to political parties** — option **(4)**.
Indian Speakers **do not resign from their party**, so are seen as partisan.
The Schedule prescribes **no time limit**; no seven-day rule exists, and the EC plays no role.
xa: Examples: **AP 2014-19** (**23 YSRCP MLAs**, petitions undecided); **Telangana 2024-26**.
**Keisham (2020)**: **three months**; asked Parliament to consider an **independent tribunal**.
Newer proposal: **fixed constitutional timelines** (Jul **2026**).

36.s: The two-thirds rule under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule has been criticised because it may be used to:
o: Transfer disqualification powers to Governors automatically
Make every independent member a nominated member
Prevent all mergers between political parties
36.x: The Paragraph 4 two-thirds rule has been used as a defence for mass defection and has therefore attracted criticism.
36.tq: Test the practical consequence of a formal exception.
xs: The **Para 4 two-thirds rule** is criticised as a **defence for mass defection** — option **(3)**.
Under **Para 4**, if **two-thirds** of the legislature party agree to merge, neither those who merge nor those who stay are disqualified.
It does not prevent mergers (option 4 wrong); disqualification is decided by the **Speaker/Chairman**, not Governors.
xa: **AAP**: **7 of 10** Rajya Sabha MPs claimed a "merger" with the BJP (Apr **2026**).
**TMC**: **20** Lok Sabha MPs told Speaker **Om Birla** they would merge with the **NPCI**.
**Subhash Desai (2023)**: two-thirds of legislators **cannot by themselves** create a "deemed merger".
**Law Commission's 170th Report (1999)** wanted the **split and merger exceptions deleted**.

36.s: Which of the following pairs of events was cited in relation to alleged misuse of the merger exception?
o: Seven TMC MPs joining the BJP in April 2026; twenty AAP MPs joining the NPCI in June 2026
Seven BJP Rajya Sabha MPs joining the AAP in April 2026; twenty NPCI MPs joining the TMC in June 2026
Seven AAP Lok Sabha MPs joining the BJP in June 2026; twenty TMC MLAs joining the NPCI in April 2026
Seven AAP Rajya Sabha MPs joining the BJP in April 2026; twenty TMC MPs joining the NPCI in June 2026
36.x: The examples cited were seven AAP Rajya Sabha MPs joining the BJP in April 2026 and twenty TMC MPs joining the NPCI in June 2026.
36.tq: Match the numbers, Houses or groups, and months without reversing the direction of movement.
xs: **7 AAP Rajya Sabha MPs** joined the **BJP** (Apr **2026**) and **20 TMC MPs** the **NPCI** (Jun **2026**) — option **(4)**.
The **7 of 10** AAP MPs included **Raghav Chadha**.
The **20 TMC Lok Sabha MPs** were **two-thirds** of the party, and told Speaker **Om Birla**.
The other options swap the parties, Houses or months.
xa: NPCI = **Nationalist Citizens Party of India**; another source calls it "**National People's Congress of India**".
These show **merger misuse** — Para 4 used as a defence for mass defection.
**SC Bench (Jul 2026)** said shortcomings are **"matters for Parliament"**.

36.s: In July 2026, the Bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe, while hearing the challenge to Paragraph 4, stated that shortcomings in the provision were:
o: Outside the jurisdiction of every constitutional authority
Matters for the Election Commission alone
36.x: The Bench sought the Centre’s reply but observed that any shortcomings in Paragraph 4 were matters for Parliament.
36.tq: Distinguish a judicial observation about legislative remedy from a transfer of jurisdiction.
xs: The Bench said any shortcomings are **"matters for Parliament"** — option **(1)**.
**Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe** sought the **Centre's reply** on a plea against "**deemed merger**" under **Para 4**.
xa: **Subhash Desai (2023)**: two-thirds of legislators cannot by themselves create a **deemed merger**.
Para 4 has **two tests**: the **original political party** must merge and **two-thirds** of the legislature party must agree.
Timeline: Telangana contempt warning (Feb **2026**) → AAP and TMC "merger" cases (Apr-Jul **2026**).

36.s: The Supreme Court’s proceedings concerning the alleged mergers of AAP and TMC legislators in 2026 primarily related to which provision of the anti-defection law?
36.x: The proceedings concerned the claim of a ‘deemed merger’ under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule.
36.tq: Identify the precise paragraph instead of relying on the general subject of defection.
xs: The AAP and TMC cases concern a "**deemed merger**" under **Paragraph 4** — option **(3)**.
**Para 4** is the **merger** exception (**two-thirds** of the legislature party).
**Para 2(1)(b)** is the whip clause; **Para 3** was the **split** exception, deleted in **2003**.
xa: ⚠ **Merger = two-thirds** (Para 4); **Split = one-third** (Para 3, deleted).
**Para 5**: presiding officers may leave their party; **Para 6**: Speaker/Chairman decides; **Para 7**: struck down.
**June 2019**: **4 of 6 TDP** Rajya Sabha MPs "merged" with BJP under Para 4.

36.s: Which one of the following statements about political defections in Andhra Pradesh is correct?
o: All 23 MLAs were disqualified by the Election Commission
The disqualification petitions concerning 23 YSRCP MLAs who moved to the TDP between 2014 and 2019 were never decided
The Supreme Court decided the petitions before the end of 2014
The 23 YSRCP MLAs who moved to the TDP between 2014 and 2019 were disqualified immediately
36.x: The petitions were never decided, making the episode a standard example of delay by the Speaker in anti-defection proceedings.
36.tq: Test the institutional authority and the outcome rather than assuming that a petition automatically results in disqualification.
xs: The petitions on **23 YSRCP MLAs** who moved to the **TDP** (**2014-19**) were **never decided** — option **(2)**.
It is the **standard AP example of Speaker delay**.
The Speaker, not the EC, decides, so there was no EC disqualification or immediate disqualification.
xa: Speakers are partisan as they **do not resign from their party**; the Schedule sets **no time limit**.
**Keisham (2020)**: decide within **three months**.
Other example: **Telangana 2024-26** (**10 BRS MLAs** to Congress).

36.s: What was the constitutional significance of the June 2019 event involving four of the six TDP Rajya Sabha MPs?
o: They were disqualified by the Rajya Sabha Chairman for voting against the party
They were nominated to the Rajya Sabha by the President
They merged with the BJP under Paragraph 4, and the Rajya Sabha Chairman accepted the merger
They formed an independent party without invoking the Tenth Schedule
36.x: In June 2019, four of the six TDP Rajya Sabha MPs were treated as having merged with the BJP under Paragraph 4, and the Rajya Sabha Chairman accepted the merger.
36.tq: Identify the relevant Tenth Schedule provision and distinguish a merger from disqualification.
xs: **4 of 6 TDP Rajya Sabha MPs** "merged" with the **BJP** under **Para 4**; the **RS Chairman accepted** it — option **(3)**.
In the Rajya Sabha the **Chairman** decides Tenth Schedule questions (**Para 6**).
They were not disqualified, nor nominated; Para 4 is the Tenth Schedule merger exception.
xa: Para 4 needs **two-thirds** of the legislature party to agree.
AP **1984**: **Nadendla Bhaskara Rao** toppled **NTR's** government.
AP **2014-19**: **23 YSRCP MLAs** moved to TDP; petitions never decided.

36.s: The 1984 defection episode involving Nadendla Bhaskara Rao resulted in
o: the immediate abolition of the Tenth Schedule
the fall of N.T. Rama Rao's government, followed by NTR's restoration after a month, strengthening the demand for the 1985 law
the dissolution of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council for three years
the merger of the Telugu Desam Party with the Congress
36.x: Nadendla Bhaskara Rao's defection toppled N.T. Rama Rao's government in 1984. NTR was restored after a month, and the episode contributed to the demand that led to the 1985 anti-defection law.
36.tq: Link the immediate political consequence with the later constitutional response without reversing the sequence.
xs: **NTR's** government fell; **NTR was restored after a month**, feeding demand for the **1985** law — option **(2)**.
The defection was by **Nadendla Bhaskara Rao** in **1984**.
The Tenth Schedule came in **1985**, so it could not have been abolished in 1984.
xa: The 1985 law = **52nd Amendment**, inserting the **Tenth Schedule**.
Earlier: "**Aaya Ram Gaya Ram**" (Haryana **1967**); **Y.B. Chavan Committee (1967-69)**.
AP **June 2019**: **4 of 6 TDP** RS MPs merged with BJP.

36.s:
Match List-I (Body) with List-II (Recommendation on the anti-defection law):
List-I
A. Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990)
B. Law Commission, 170th Report (1999)
C. NCRWC (2002)
D. Election Commission

List-II
I. Delete the split and merger exceptions and treat pre-poll alliances as parties
II. Bar defectors from any public or remunerative political office for the rest of the term and treat the defector's vote as invalid
III. Decisions to be made by the President or Governor on the EC's binding advice
IV. Disqualify only for voluntarily giving up membership or voting against the whip on a confidence or no-confidence motion

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
36.x: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III: Goswami (1990) would disqualify only for voluntarily giving up membership or defying the whip on confidence/no-confidence motions; the Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) would delete the split and merger exceptions and treat pre-poll alliances as parties; NCRWC (2002) would bar defectors from public or remunerative political office for the rest of the term and treat their votes as invalid; the EC wanted the President/Governor to decide on its binding advice. Option B swaps B and C; options C and D misplace Goswami and the EC.
36.tq: Anchor two: Law Commission = delete split/merger + pre-poll alliances; NCRWC = defector's vote invalid. The rest falls in place.
xs: Correct code: **A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III** — option **(1)**.
**Dinesh Goswami (1990)**: disqualify only for **giving up membership** or defying the whip on a **confidence/no-confidence** motion.
**Law Commission 170th Report (1999)**: **delete split and merger exceptions**; **pre-poll alliances** as parties.
**NCRWC (2002)**: bar defectors from **public or remunerative political office**; **defector's vote invalid**.
**Election Commission**: **President or Governor** to decide on the **EC's binding advice**.
xa: Goswami also wanted the **President or Governor** to decide on the **EC's advice**.
⚠ **170th** Report = Law Commission (**1999**); **NCRWC** = **2002**; **Dinesh Goswami** = **1990**.
**Manish Tewari's Bill (2010)**: limit the law to **confidence and money votes**.

36.s: Which of the following is a newer proposal concerning the functioning of the anti-defection law?
o: Fixed constitutional timelines for Speakers and creation of an independent tribunal
Removal of the whip from confidence motions
Transfer of all legislative powers to the Election Commission
36.x: Newer proposals include fixed constitutional timelines for Speakers and an independent tribunal, the latter having been suggested for consideration by the Supreme Court in 2020.
36.tq: Select the option that combines the two reform proposals without changing their institutional character.
xs: Newer proposals: **fixed constitutional timelines** for Speakers and an **independent tribunal** — option **(2)**.
Timelines were proposed in Jul **2026**; the **independent tribunal** was suggested by the **SC** in **2020** (**Keisham**).
xa: **Keisham (2020)**: decide within **three months**.
Reform: limit whips to **confidence votes and Money Bills**.
**Telangana**: SC gave a **final 3 weeks** with a **contempt** warning (Feb **2026**).

36.s: The proposal to limit the operation of the whip and disqualification under the anti-defection law primarily to confidence and money votes seeks to ensure that legislators may:
o: Vote against every money bill without party discipline
Avoid all party whips during the entire legislative term
Dissent even on a confidence motion without consequences
Dissent freely on matters that do not threaten the government's survival
36.x: The proposal would retain party discipline for votes threatening government survival, such as confidence, no-confidence and money bills, while allowing dissent on other matters.
36.tq: Apply the reform principle to distinguish survival votes from ordinary legislative votes.
xs: Legislators could **dissent freely on votes that do not threaten the government's survival** — option **(4)**.
The whip would apply only to **confidence and no-confidence motions and money bills**.
So discipline stays on confidence and money votes — options (1), (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: Backers: **Dinesh Goswami (1990)** and **Law Commission (1999)**.
**Manish Tewari's private member's Bill (2010)** proposed the same.
Criticism it answers: the law **muzzles dissent** without stopping mass defections.

36.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Dinesh Goswami supported limiting the whip to votes connected with government survival.
2. The Law Commission’s 170th Report supported limiting the whip to votes that threaten the government.
3. Manish Tewari’s private member’s Bill of 2010 proposed such a limitation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: All three statements are correct. The proposal was associated with Dinesh Goswami in 1990, the Law Commission in 1999, and Manish Tewari’s private member’s Bill in 2010.
36.tq: Use the chronological cluster of supporters and proposals; all three statements are supported.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **Dinesh Goswami (1990)** backed limiting the whip to votes threatening the government.
Statement 2: the **Law Commission (1999)**, **170th Report**, backed it too.
Statement 3: **Manish Tewari's private member's Bill (2010)** proposed limiting the law to **confidence and money votes**.
xa: Such votes = **confidence and no-confidence motions and money bills**.
Law Commission also wanted to **delete split and merger exceptions**.
**NCRWC (2002)**: defector's vote **treated as invalid**.

36.s:
Arrange the following reform proposals in chronological order:
A. Law Commission’s 170th Report
B. Dinesh Goswami Committee recommendation
C. Manish Tewari’s private member’s Bill
D. Supreme Court suggestion to consider an independent tribunal
36.x: The sequence is Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999), Manish Tewari’s Bill (2010), and the Supreme Court’s independent-tribunal suggestion (2020).
36.tq: Fix the earliest and latest items first, then place the intermediate proposals by year.
xs: Correct order: **B, A, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**Dinesh Goswami** (**1990**) → **Law Commission 170th Report** (**1999**) → **Manish Tewari's Bill** (**2010**) → **SC independent tribunal** (**2020**).
xa: **NCRWC** came in **2002**, between the Law Commission and Tewari.
**Fixed constitutional timelines** for Speakers is a newer proposal (Jul **2026**).
The tribunal idea came in **Keisham Meghachandra Singh** (Jan **2020**).

36.s: Which one of the following is a major criticism of the anti-defection law mentioned in the context of Indian parliamentary practice?
o: It stifles intra-party dissent and legislators’ free expression without necessarily stopping mass defections.
It has abolished the Speaker’s authority over the House.
It prevents all coalition governments from being formed.
It applies exclusively to nominated Members of Parliament.
36.x: Critics argue that the law suppresses intra-party dissent and free expression, while failing to prevent mass defections effectively. The other statements do not describe the criticism.
36.tq: Find the option that captures both sides of the criticism rather than an absolute consequence.
xs: The law **stifles intra-party dissent and free expression** without stopping **mass defections** — option **(1)**.
The Speaker still decides disqualification (**Para 6**); the law covers party, independent and nominated members, not only nominated.
xa: Critics say the law has been left "**impotent**".
**Speaker not neutral**: Indian Speakers **do not resign from their party**.
Reform: limit whips to **confidence votes and Money Bills**.

36.s: Which one of the following best describes the broad judicial-legislative relationship in the development of India’s anti-defection law since 2003?
o: Parliament has shaped the law substantially more than the courts.
The courts have shaped the law more than Parliament has.
The Election Commission has exclusively shaped the law.
Neither Parliament nor the courts have influenced its development.
36.x: Since 2003, the courts have shaped the working and interpretation of the anti-defection law more extensively than Parliament has through judicial decisions.
36.tq: Use the comparative institutional claim rather than confusing the institutions involved.
xs: Since **2003**, **courts have shaped the law more than Parliament** — option **(2)**.
Three pillars: **Kihoto** (review), **Keisham** (time), **Subhash Desai** (party over legislature party).
xa: The last parliamentary change was the **91st Amendment, 2003**.
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** upheld the Schedule but **struck down Para 7**.
**SC Bench (Jul 2026)** said shortcomings are **"matters for Parliament"**.

36.s: A contempt warning issued in February 2026 in Telangana was mentioned in connection with which broad constitutional issue?
o: Privileges of the Rajya Sabha Chairman
36.x: The Telangana contempt warning was cited in the broader context of current anti-defection and legislative-conduct controversies.
36.tq: Link the current event to the correct constitutional controversy without overextending its subject.
xs: The Telangana contempt warning concerns **anti-defection** — option **(3)**.
SC gave the **Telangana Speaker** a **final 3 weeks** to decide the last 2 of **10 BRS MLAs** who moved to Congress, warning of **contempt** (Feb **2026**).
xa: Earlier the SC set a **time-bound direction** (**2025**); **seven** petitions were rejected in Dec **2025**.
Timeline next: AAP and **20 TMC MPs** "merger" cases (Apr-Jul **2026**).
**Keisham (2020)**: **three months** limit.

36.s:
With reference to the Supreme Court proceedings concerning a ‘deemed merger’ under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule, consider the following statements:
1. Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe sought the response of the Centre.
2. The plea concerned a deemed merger by a legislature party.
3. The Court indicated that shortcomings in the legal provision were matters for Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: All three statements are correct. The Bench sought the Centre’s reply on the Paragraph 4 plea and observed that deficiencies in the law were for Parliament to address.
36.tq: Check the bench, the legal issue and the institution responsible for legislative correction.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe** sought the **Centre's reply**.
Statement 2: the plea was against a "**deemed merger**" by a **legislature party** under **Para 4**.
Statement 3: the Bench said shortcomings are **"matters for Parliament"** (Jul **2026**).
xa: **Subhash Desai (2023)**: legislature party **cannot be conflated** with the political party.
Para 4's **two tests**: original party merges + **two-thirds** of the legislature party agree.
Cases: **AAP** (**7 of 10** RS MPs) and **TMC** (**20** LS MPs).

36.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The anti-defection law has been criticised for muzzling dissent.
2. One criticism is that it may restrain intra-party dissent without effectively preventing mass defections.
3. The law has been described by critics as having become ‘impotent’.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: All three statements reflect criticisms of the working of the anti-defection law, especially its effect on internal dissent and its perceived inability to prevent mass defections.
36.tq: Recognise that several differently worded criticisms may all be valid when no absolute claim is made.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: the law **muzzles legislators' free expression and dissent**.
Statement 2: it **stifles intra-party dissent without stopping mass defections**.
Statement 3: critics say it has been left "**impotent**".
xa: **Speaker not neutral**: Indian Speakers **do not resign from their party**.
Reform: whips only for **confidence votes and Money Bills**.
Examples of mass defection: **AAP** and **TMC** "mergers" (**2026**).

36.s: Why has the neutrality of the Speaker in anti-defection proceedings been questioned in India?
o: Indian Speakers generally do not resign from their political parties after assuming office.
The Speaker is appointed by the Supreme Court and cannot be removed.
The Speaker has no role in deciding disqualification petitions.
The Speaker is not a member of any political party after election.
36.x: The Speaker’s neutrality has been questioned because Indian Speakers generally continue to remain associated with their political parties instead of resigning from them.
36.tq: Apply the institutional-neutrality principle to the office-holder’s political affiliation.
xs: Indian Speakers **do not resign from their party** — option **(1)**.
So they are seen as **partisan**; with **no time limit**, petitions can be delayed.
The Speaker decides disqualification (**Para 6**) as a **tribunal**, so options (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: AP example: **23 YSRCP MLAs** (**2014-19**), petitions never decided.
**Keisham (2020)**: **three months**; consider an **independent tribunal**.
**Para 5**: presiding officers **may** leave their party on election and rejoin later.

36.s: A proposal to reform the anti-defection law suggests that party whips should generally be limited to which matters?
o: All legislative debates and private members’ business
36.x: The reform proposal is to limit the operation of whips mainly to confidence votes and Money Bills, thereby allowing greater legislative dissent on other matters.
36.tq: Separate the proposed limited use of the whip from its wider present criticism.
xs: Whips limited to **confidence votes and Money Bills** — option **(2)**.
These are votes that **threaten the government's survival**; on others legislators are free to dissent.
xa: Backers: **Dinesh Goswami (1990)** and **Law Commission (1999)**.
**Manish Tewari's Bill (2010)** proposed the same limit.
Whip clause today: **Para 2(1)(b)**; not condoned within **15 days** → disqualified.

36.s: The first constitutional mention of political parties in India was made through which Constitutional Amendment?
36.x: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1985 introduced the anti-defection provisions and constituted the first constitutional mention of political parties.
36.tq: Use the first-versus-later constitutional reference distinction.
xs: The **52nd Amendment Act, 1985** first mentioned political parties — option **(2)**.
It inserted the **Tenth Schedule** and amended **Arts. 101, 102, 190, 191**.
xa: The **91st Amendment (2003)** tightened it: **split** exception deleted, **15%** ministry cap.
⚠ **35th Amendment (1974)** had a different "Tenth Schedule" for **Sikkim**, deleted by the **36th** (**1975**).
Tenth Schedule asked in **APPSC-GS 2019**.

36.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Kihoto Hollohan — Judicial review under the anti-defection law
Keisham Meghachandra Singh — Recognition of national parties
Subhash Desai — Abolition of the office of the Speaker
Kihoto Hollohan — Limitation of whips to Money Bills
36.x: Kihoto Hollohan is associated with judicial review of decisions under the anti-defection law. The other pairings assign unrelated issues to the cases.
36.tq: Match each landmark case with its distinctive legal contribution.
xs: **Kihoto Hollohan — judicial review** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Kihoto (1992)** upheld the Schedule, **struck down Para 7**, and allowed review **after** the decision.
**Keisham** = **three months** time limit; **Subhash Desai** = **political party appoints the whip**.
xa: Review grounds: **mala fides**, **perversity**, violation of **natural justice** or constitutional mandate.
Para 7 fell for want of **State ratification** under **Art. 368(2)**; ruling was **3:2**.
Whips limited to Money Bills is a **reform proposal**, not a judgment.

36.s: In Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020), the Supreme Court urged that the Speaker should ordinarily decide a disqualification petition within
36.x: The Supreme Court urged the Speaker to decide within three months and asked Parliament to consider establishing an independent tribunal for such matters.
36.tq: Use the exact judicially suggested period rather than the different periods associated with other cases.
xs: **Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020)**: decide within **three months** — option **(4)**.
Exception: **extraordinary cases**; the Schedule itself has **no time limit**.
**Three weeks** was the Telangana deadline (Feb **2026**).
xa: Asked **Parliament** to consider a **permanent independent tribunal**.
Case: Speaker of **Manipur**, Jan **2020**.
⚠ **Kihoto** = review; **Keisham** = time; **Subhash Desai** = party.

36.s: With reference to the Subhash Desai judgment, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It removed judicial review of the Speaker’s decision.
It gave primacy to the political party over the legislature party.
It treated the legislature party as superior to the political party in matters of defection.
It restricted the anti-defection law to Money Bills.
36.x: The Subhash Desai judgment is associated with the principle that the political party, rather than merely its legislature party, has primacy in matters relevant to defection.
36.tq: Discriminate between the political party and the legislature party, a key confusable pair.
xs: **Subhash Desai (2023)** gave **primacy to the political party over the legislature party** — option **(2)**.
The **political party**, not the legislature party, **appoints the whip and the leader** in the House.
So option (3) is the reverse; judicial review comes from **Kihoto**, not this case.
xa: The **Shiv Sena** case (May **2023**), from **Maharashtra**.
Two-thirds of legislators **cannot** create a "**deemed merger**" by themselves.
**AIADMK** Palaniswami camp cited it for the whip under **Para 2(1)(b)** (May **2026**).

37.s: The average number of sitting days per year declined from approximately how many in the First Lok Sabha to approximately how many in the Seventeenth Lok Sabha (2019–24)?
37.x: The average sittings declined from about 135 days per year in the First Lok Sabha to about 55 days per year in the Seventeenth Lok Sabha.
37.tq: Use the paired historical figures and eliminate reversed or rounded alternatives.
xs: Sittings fell from about **135 days/year** (**1st Lok Sabha**) to about **55** (**17th Lok Sabha, 2019-24**) — option **(2)**.
That is a decline of well over half across the Lok Sabhas.
xa: Lok Sabha now sits **60-70 days a year** vs **150+** sittings of the **UK House of Commons**.
**Art. 85(1)** only bars a gap of more than **six months** between sessions; **no minimum** sitting days.
**NCRWC (2000-02)** proposed a minimum of **120** days (LS) and **100** (RS).

37.s:
With reference to the present sitting pattern of the Lok Sabha, consider the following statements:
1. The Lok Sabha generally sits for around 60–70 days a year.
2. The UK House of Commons has more than 150 sittings a year.
3. The Lok Sabha sits for more days than the UK House of Commons.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
37.x: The Lok Sabha sits around 60–70 days annually, whereas the UK House of Commons has more than 150 sittings. Statement 3 reverses this comparison.
37.tq: Check the direction of the comparison before evaluating the statements.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the Lok Sabha sits **60-70 days a year**.
Statement 2 correct: the **UK House of Commons** has **150+** sittings.
Statement 3 wrong: it reverses the comparison — the Lok Sabha sits far less.
xa: Trend: **135** days/year (**1st LS**) → about **55** (**17th LS**).
Proposal: a **fixed parliamentary calendar**.

37.s: Article 85(1) of the Constitution provides that:
o: The Rajya Sabha must sit for at least 100 days every year
There cannot be a gap of more than six months between two sessions of Parliament
The Lok Sabha must hold three sessions every year
Parliament must sit for at least 120 days every year
37.x: Article 85(1) bars a gap of more than six months between sessions but prescribes no minimum number of sitting days.
37.tq: Distinguish a constitutional maximum gap from a minimum sitting requirement.
xs: **Art. 85(1)** bars a **gap of more than six months** between sessions — option **(2)**.
It sets **no minimum** sitting days, so options (1), (3) and (4) are wrong.
The **120 / 100** figures are **NCRWC** proposals, not constitutional rules.
xa: ⚠ **Art. 85(1)** = Parliament's six-month gap; **Art. 174** = States' **6**-month gap.
State Assemblies met on average **24 days** (PRS **2025**), many only to satisfy **Art. 174**.
**Art. 123** = Ordinances.

37.s: During the Monsoon Session of 2026, which of the following correctly describes the productivity of the two Houses?
o: Lok Sabha 25 per cent and Rajya Sabha 16 per cent
Lok Sabha 19 per cent and Rajya Sabha 39 per cent
Lok Sabha 60 per cent and Rajya Sabha 53 per cent
Lok Sabha 39 per cent and Rajya Sabha 19 per cent
37.x: PRS data placed Lok Sabha productivity at 19 per cent and Rajya Sabha productivity at 39 per cent during the Monsoon Session of 2026.
37.tq: Read the House-wise figures without reversing the pair.
xs: Monsoon Session **2026**: **Lok Sabha 19%**, **Rajya Sabha 39%** — option **(2)**.
LS productivity was **among the lowest in 22 years** (PRS).
Option (4) swaps the Houses; **25%/16%** are Bill-referral shares of the **16th/17th** LS.
xa: Question Hour ran **1%** (LS) and **12%** (RS) of scheduled time.
Estimated loss: **₹175 crore**; **12** Bills passed, only one debated in detail.

37.s: In the Seventeenth Lok Sabha, Question Hour ran for approximately what proportion of its scheduled time?
37.x: During the Seventeenth Lok Sabha, Question Hour ran for only 60 per cent of its scheduled time.
37.tq: Distinguish the long-term Lok Sabha figure from the much lower Monsoon Session 2026 figure.
xs: In the **17th Lok Sabha**, Question Hour ran only **60 per cent** of scheduled time — option **(3)**.
So about two-fifths of the hour meant for **questions to ministers** was lost to disruption or adjournment.
xa: ⚠ **60%** is also the share of Bills referred to committees in the **14th LS**.
Monsoon **2026**: Question Hour ran **1%** (LS), **12%** (RS); only **2** (LS) and **16** (RS) questions answered orally.
Proposal: **strengthen Question Hour** and protect opposition debate time.

37.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding suspension-related rules in the Lok Sabha.

List-I (Rule)
a. Rule 373
b. Rule 374
c. Rule 374A

List-II (Effect)
i. Automatic suspension for five sittings or the rest of the session for grave disorder
ii. Member directed to withdraw for the day
iii. Suspension by a House motion up to the remainder of the session

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
37.x: Rule 373 concerns withdrawal for the day, Rule 374 concerns suspension by House motion up to the remainder of the session, and Rule 374A provides automatic suspension for grave disorder.
37.tq: Start from the sure rule-effect pair and eliminate codes that reverse the suspension procedures.
xs: Correct code: **a–ii, b–iii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
**Rule 373**: Speaker orders member to **withdraw for the day**.
**Rule 374**: named member **suspended by House motion**, up to remainder of session.
**Rule 374A**: **automatic suspension** for **5 sittings** or rest of session for **grave disorder**.
xa: Rajya Sabha: **Rule 255** = withdrawal for the day (Chairman); **Rule 256** = suspension by House motion.
⚠ **373 / 255** = withdraw for the day; **374 / 256** = House motion; **374A** = automatic.

37.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Rajya Sabha Rule 255 — suspension by House motion for the remainder of the session
Lok Sabha Rule 373 — withdrawal for the day ordered by the Speaker
Lok Sabha Rule 374 — suspension by House motion
Rajya Sabha Rule 256 — suspension by House motion, not beyond the remainder of the session
37.x: Rule 255 of the Rajya Sabha authorises the Chairman to direct withdrawal for the day. Suspension by House motion is dealt with under Rule 256.
37.tq: Find the swapped Rajya Sabha rule and effect.
xs: **RS Rule 255** is wrongly matched: it is the **Chairman directing withdrawal for the day** — option **(1)**.
Suspension by House motion in the Rajya Sabha is **Rule 256**, not beyond the remainder of the session.
Pairs (2), (3) and (4) are correct: **Rule 373**, **Rule 374**, **Rule 256**.
xa: **Rule 374A** (LS): automatic suspension for **5 sittings** for grave disorder.
⚠ **373 / 255** = for the day; **374 / 256** = by House motion.

37.s:
Consider the following statements about the Monsoon Session of 2026:
1. Question Hour ran for only 1% of its scheduled time in the Lok Sabha and 12% in the Rajya Sabha.
2. The estimated loss from disruptions was about Rs 175 crore.
3. All 12 Bills passed were debated in detail.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
37.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Question Hour ran 1% (LS) and 12% (RS) of scheduled time, and the estimated loss was Rs 175 crore. Statement 3 is wrong: of the 12 Bills passed, only one (the Public Examination Amendment Bill) was debated in detail. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
37.tq: Monsoon 2026: QH 1%/12%, Rs 175 crore, 12 Bills, one debated.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: Question Hour ran **1%** (LS) and **12%** (RS) of scheduled time.
Statement 2 correct: estimated loss **₹175 crore**.
Statement 3 wrong: of **12** Bills passed, **only one** was debated in detail — the **Public Examination Amendment Bill**.
xa: That Bill is the **anti-paper-leak** law.
Productivity: **LS 19%**, **RS 39%**.
Questions answered orally: **2** (LS), **16** (RS).

37.s:
Consider the following statements about legislation in the Seventeenth Lok Sabha:
1. Less than one-fifth of Bills went to committees.
2. Fifty-eight per cent of Bills were passed within two weeks of introduction.
3. Thirty-five per cent of Bills were debated for less than one hour.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
37.x: All three statements are correct: less than one-fifth went to committees, 58 per cent were passed within two weeks, and 35 per cent received less than one hour of debate.
37.tq: When all three independently stated figures align, do not reject the comprehensive option merely because it is broad.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: only **16%** of Bills were referred in the **17th LS** — less than a fifth.
Statement 2: **58%** were passed within **two weeks** of introduction (PRS, Jun **2026**).
Statement 3: **35%** were debated for **less than one hour**.
xa: UK: **every Bill** is examined by committees of both Houses.
Proposal: **mandatory committee scrutiny** before passage.

37.s: Which one of the following correctly compares the committee scrutiny of Bills in India and the United Kingdom?
o: In India less than one-fifth of Bills go to committees, whereas in the UK every Bill is examined by committees of both Houses.
In India every Bill is examined by committees of both Houses, whereas in the UK less than one-fifth is examined.
Only the Rajya Sabha in India and only the House of Commons in the UK examine Bills through committees.
Neither country refers Bills to committees before passage.
37.x: Less than one-fifth of Indian Bills go to committees, while every Bill in the UK is examined by committees of both Houses.
37.tq: Test both sides of the comparison instead of focusing on only one country.
xs: India: **less than a fifth** of Bills go to committees; UK: **every Bill** examined by committees of **both Houses** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses the two countries.
xa: **17th LS** referred only **16%** of Bills; the **15th** referred **71%**.
Systematic **DRSC** system only from **1993**.
Average attendance at DRSC meetings: **53%** (Digital Sansad).

37.s: The systematic system of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees was introduced in India in:
37.x: The systematic committee system, including Department-related Standing Committees, began in 1993.
37.tq: Distinguish the institutional starting year from later reform proposals.
xs: The systematic **DRSC** committee system began in **1993** — option **(3)**.
Before that India had no **systematic** committee scrutiny of departments; even now **less than a fifth** of Bills go to committees.
xa: **1977** = **LoP Salary and Allowances Act**; **1967** = PAC chaired by Opposition.
Average attendance at **DRSC** meetings: **53%**.
Referral share fell to **16%** in the **17th LS**.

37.s: Heavy reliance on ordinances and delegated legislation is associated with:
o: Declining legislative engagement and reduced parliamentary scrutiny
Increased legislative engagement and longer committee scrutiny
The abolition of the Rajya Sabha’s legislative role
The compulsory referral of every Bill to a committee
37.x: The increased use of ordinances under Article 123 and delegated legislation has grown as legislative engagement has fallen.
37.tq: Link the stated cause and effect rather than treating ordinance-making as an isolated power.
xs: Heavy use of ordinances and delegated legislation goes with **declining legislative engagement** and **weak scrutiny** — option **(1)**.
Ordinances are under **Art. 123**; delegated legislation grows as legislative engagement falls.
xa: Proposals: define "**immediate necessity**" by law; courts test urgency per **Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)**.
**Publish reasons** for each ordinance.
**Money Bill route** (Art. **110**) is another bypass — e.g. **Aadhaar Act, 2016**.

37.s: Which of the following was NOT among the proposals concerning the use of ordinances?
o: Judicial examination of urgency in light of Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)
Making every ordinance permanent without legislative approval
37.x: The proposals were to define immediate necessity, permit courts to test urgency, and publish reasons for ordinances. Permanent operation without legislative approval was not proposed.
37.tq: Identify the extreme proposal that goes beyond the stated reform measures.
xs: **Making every ordinance permanent without legislative approval** was not proposed — option **(2)**.
Real proposals: define "**immediate necessity**" by law, test urgency per **Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)**, **publish reasons**.
xa: Ordinances = **Art. 123**.
Ordinances and delegated legislation grow as **legislative engagement falls**.
Other bypass: **Money Bill route** under **Art. 110**.

37.s: The principal constitutional concern regarding the use of the Money Bill route is that it:
o: Requires the approval of every State Legislature
Can bypass the Rajya Sabha for measures that may not strictly fall within Article 110
Can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha
Prevents the Lok Sabha from considering financial legislation
37.x: The Money Bill route may bypass the Rajya Sabha for laws whose provisions may not strictly fit within Article 110. The Aadhaar Act, 2016, is cited as an example.
37.tq: Identify the institutional consequence of the classification rather than the subject of the Bill.
xs: The Money Bill route can **bypass the Rajya Sabha** for laws that may not strictly fit **Art. 110** — option **(2)**.
Example: **Aadhaar Act, 2016**.
xa: Notes: the **RS only returned it**.
Other bypass: heavy use of **ordinances (Art. 123)**.
Criticism of weak control: **executive dominance**, **guillotine**, delegated legislation.

37.s: In which Lok Sabha was the highest share of Bills referred to parliamentary committees?
37.x: The 15th Lok Sabha referred 71% of Bills to committees, against 60% in the 14th, 25% in the 16th and only 16% in the 17th.
37.tq: Referral: 60 → 71 → 25 → 16 per cent (14th to 17th).
xs: The **15th Lok Sabha** referred the highest share — **71%** — option **(2)**.
xa: ⚠ **60%** = Bills referred (**14th**) and Question Hour run (**17th**).
**17th LS**: **58%** of Bills passed within **two weeks**; **35%** debated under **one hour**.
UK: every Bill examined by committees of both Houses.

37.s: A party must generally have at least what proportion of the strength of the Lok Sabha to have its leader recognised as the Leader of the Opposition?
37.x: The Speaker recognises the Leader of the Opposition when the party has at least one-tenth of the House’s strength, equivalent to 55 members in the Lok Sabha.
37.tq: Distinguish the one-tenth recognition threshold from larger parliamentary thresholds.
xs: The party needs at least **one-tenth** of the House's strength — option **(3)**.
That is quorum-size: **55** in the Lok Sabha; recognition is by the **Speaker**.
xa: Statutory status: **Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977**.
Opposition tools: **Question Hour**, **motions**, **committees**.
**PAC** chaired by the Opposition since **1967**.

37.s: The statutory status of the Leader of the Opposition is provided under the:
o: Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977
37.x: The Leader of the Opposition has statutory status under the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977.
37.tq: Match the office with the statute specifically dealing with its salary and allowances.
xs: The LoP's statutory status comes from the **Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977** — option **(1)**.
The other Acts named do not give the LoP statutory status in the notes.
xa: Recognised by the **Speaker** if the party has **one-tenth** of the House (**55** in LS).
**PAC** chaired by the Opposition since **1967**.
Monsoon **2026**: united opposition pushed the **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026** to a **JPC**.

37.s:
