xs: The AIJS debate is **uniform merit-based recruitment** versus **State and High Court control** and **local-language needs** — option **(1)** is correct.
Lok Adalats, Governors and military tribunals are unrelated to the AIJS.
xa: AIJS is enabled by **Art. 312** (**42nd Amendment**) but **not yet created**.
Other judicial officers are recruited under **Art. 234** after consulting the **SPSC and HC**.
**National Judicial Academy**: **Bhopal**.

44.s: Lok Adalats derive their statutory basis primarily from the:
44.x: Lok Adalats are established under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
44.tq: Match the institution with its specific parent statute.
xs: Lok Adalats rest on the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** — option **(4)** is correct.
The **Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008** is for Gram Nyayalayas; the **1971** Act is contempt; the **1968** Act is judges' inquiry.
xa: A Lok Adalat award is **deemed a civil court decree**, final, **no appeal**.
First Lok Adalat camp: **Gujarat, 1982** (some notes say Delhi **1985**).
**CGIT-cum-Labour Courts** also hold Lok Adalats.

44.s: The Gram Nyayalayas Act was enacted in:
44.x: Gram Nyayalayas are established under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008.
44.tq: Separate the year of the Gram Nyayalayas statute from the year in which it came into force.
xs: The **Gram Nyayalayas Act** was enacted in **2008** — option **(3)** is correct.
It came into force on **2 Oct 2009**.
**1987** is the **Legal Services Authorities Act** (Lok Adalats).
xa: A Gram Nyayalaya is presided by a **Nyayadhikari** (**JMFC** rank) — a **mobile court** at intermediate panchayat level.
Gram Nyayalayas get **₹50 crore** under the court-infrastructure scheme.
⚠ **1987** = Lok Adalat Act; **2008** = Gram Nyayalayas Act; **1982** = first Lok Adalat camp.

44.s: Which of the following correctly describes a Gram Nyayalaya?
o: It is presided over by a Nyayadhikari of JMFC rank and functions as a mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level
It is presided over by a High Court Judge and hears only constitutional cases
It is a permanent bench of the Supreme Court in every village
It is presided over by the District Magistrate and hears only revenue disputes
44.x: A Gram Nyayalaya is presided over by a Nyayadhikari of Judicial Magistrate First Class rank and functions as a mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level.
44.tq: Identify the institution through its presiding officer, level and mobile character.
xs: A Gram Nyayalaya is presided by a **Nyayadhikari of JMFC rank** and is a **mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level** — option **(1)** is correct.
It is not an HC/SC bench and not run by the District Magistrate.
xa: Act: **Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008** (in force **2 Oct 2009**).
First mobile court: **Punhana (Haryana), 2007**.
Funding: **₹50 crore** within the **₹5,357 crore** court-infrastructure outlay.

44.s: The first mobile court in India was established at Punhana in:
44.x: The first mobile court was established at Punhana in Haryana in 2007.
44.tq: Combine the place, State and year instead of selecting a familiar judicial institution.
xs: The first mobile court was at **Punhana**, **Haryana in 2007** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Gujarat 1982** is the first **Lok Adalat** camp; **Delhi 1985** an alternative Lok Adalat date; **Bhopal** hosts the **National Judicial Academy**.
xa: Gram Nyayalayas also function as **mobile courts**.
**Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Lok Adalats:
1. An award of a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court.
2. An appeal against a Lok Adalat award lies to the High Court.
3. The first Lok Adalat camp was held in Gujarat in 1982.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: a Lok Adalat award is deemed a civil court decree, and the first camp was held in Gujarat in 1982. Statement 2 is wrong: the award is final and no appeal lies against it. So '1 and 3 only'.
44.tq: Lok Adalat award = civil decree, final, no appeal.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the award is **deemed a civil court decree**.
Statement 2 wrong: the award is **final**, with **no appeal**.
Statement 3 correct: first Lok Adalat camp — **Gujarat, 1982**.
xa: Basis: **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.
Some notes say the first camp was in **Delhi 1985**.
**CGIT-cum-Labour Courts** also hold Lok Adalats.

44.s: More than how many cases are pending in the lower courts?
44.x: More than four crore cases are pending in the lower courts.
44.tq: Retain the approximate magnitude rather than confusing crore-based figures.
xs: More than **4 crore** cases are pending in lower courts — option **(2) Four crore** is correct.
An APPSC **2022** PYQ put total pendency at over **4.7 crore**, about **87%** in subordinate courts.
xa: Reform tools: **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)** and the **National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG)**.
**Kerala**: first **fully paperless district court**.
The **Department of Justice** portal tracks district vacancies monthly.

44.s: Which institution tracks vacancies in the district judiciary on a monthly basis?
44.x: The Department of Justice web portal tracks vacancies in the district judiciary every month.
44.tq: Identify the responsible administrative portal rather than a judicial body with a similar function.
xs: The **Department of Justice web portal** tracks district judiciary vacancies monthly — option **(2)** is correct.
The Law Commission, NJAC and NALSA are not named for this in the notes.
xa: HC sanctioned strength (**18 Sep 2025**): **1,122**, of which **804** filled.
SC: **2** vacancies in May **2026** + **3** more retirements due in **2026**.
Court infrastructure scheme is monitored on the **Nyaya Vikas Portal**.

44.s: Which of the following correctly describes e-Courts Phase III?
o: It is limited to Gram Nyayalayas and excludes district courts.
It is a scheme for appointing judges to the Supreme Court.
It covers only the period 2014–2019 and replaces all High Courts.
It covers the period 2023–2027 and functions alongside the National Judicial Data Grid as a reform tool.
44.x: e-Courts Phase III covers 2023–2027 and, together with the National Judicial Data Grid, is intended to improve judicial administration and access to case information.
44.tq: Combine the duration of a programme with its institutional purpose.
xs: **e-Courts Phase III** covers **2023-27** and works alongside the **National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG)** as a reform tool — option **(4)** is correct.
It is a **digitisation** tool — not limited to Gram Nyayalayas, not an appointment scheme, and it replaces no court.
xa: **Kerala** has the first **fully paperless district court**.
**Fast-track courts** handle paper-leak cases under the **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024**.
Court infrastructure is monitored on the **Nyaya Vikas Portal**.

44.s: Which State has the first fully paperless district court?
44.x: Kerala has the first fully paperless district court.
44.tq: Use the distinctive achievement-state association.
xs: **Kerala** has the first **fully paperless district court** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is part of the **digitisation** push with **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)** and the **NJDG**.
xa: More than **4 crore cases** are pending in lower courts.
The **Department of Justice** web portal tracks district vacancies monthly.
Infrastructure scheme outlay: **₹5,357 crore** for **2021-26**.

44.s: Fast-track courts were cited as a reform tool particularly for cases relating to:
o: Constitutional amendment disputes under the Basic Structure doctrine
Appointment of members of the Finance Commission
Paper leaks under the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024
44.x: Fast-track courts may be used for paper-leak cases under the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.
44.tq: Connect a reform mechanism with the specific category of cases for which it was cited.
xs: Fast-track courts were cited for **paper leaks** under the **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024** — option **(4)** is correct (TH **31 Jul 2026**).
Criticism: fast-track courts add **speed without adding judges**.
xa: Other reform tools: **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)** + **NJDG**.
Gram Nyayalayas get **₹50 crore** under the court-infrastructure scheme.
Pendency: over **4.7 crore** cases, about **87%** in subordinate courts (APPSC **2022** PYQ).

44.s:
Consider the following statements about the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for court infrastructure:
1. Funding is normally shared 60:40 between the Centre and the States.
2. North-Eastern and Himalayan States get 90:10 funding.
3. Union Territories get 75 per cent central funding.
4. The scheme is monitored through the Nyaya Vikas Portal.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the normal ratio is 60:40, and 90:10 for NE and Himalayan States. Statement 3 is wrong: UTs get 100 per cent funding. Statement 4 is correct: the scheme is monitored on the Nyaya Vikas Portal. So option A misses statement 4, and options C and D include the wrong statement 3.
44.tq: 60:40 normal, 90:10 NE/Himalayan, 100% UTs; monitored on Nyaya Vikas.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct — option **(2) 1, 2 and 4 only**.
Statement 1 correct: normal sharing is **60:40**.
Statement 2 correct: **NE & Himalayan states** get **90:10**.
Statement 3 wrong: **UTs** get **100%**, not 75 per cent; Statement 4 correct: monitored on the **Nyaya Vikas Portal**.
xa: It is a **Centrally Sponsored Scheme**.
Outlay: **₹5,357 crore** for **2021-26**, incl. **₹50 crore** for **Gram Nyayalayas**.
Digitisation runs through **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional basis of judicial review:
1. The expression ‘judicial review’ is expressly defined in the Constitution.
2. The power flows from several constitutional provisions.
3. It is regarded as part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: The term ‘judicial review’ is not used in the Constitution, but the power flows from several Articles and is part of the basic structure.
44.tq: Distinguish an express constitutional label from a power inferred from several provisions.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 wrong: the term "**judicial review**" is **not used** in the Constitution.
Statement 2 correct: the power **flows from several Articles** (e.g. **13, 32, 226**).
Statement 3 correct: it is **part of the basic structure** (**Kesavananda 1973**; **L. Chandra Kumar 1997**).
xa: Meaning: courts test laws and executive orders against the Constitution and declare them **ultra vires / void**.
Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + Fundamental Rights.
Theory: **supremacy of the Constitution / limited government**.

44.s: Judicial review in India is based on which combination of constitutional features?
o: Collective responsibility, adult suffrage and emergency powers
A written Constitution, federalism and Fundamental Rights
An unwritten constitution, unitary government and parliamentary privilege
44.x: Judicial review follows from India’s written Constitution, federal structure and protection of Fundamental Rights.
44.tq: Select the combination of structural features that supports the power under examination.
xs: Judicial review rests on **a written Constitution, federalism and Fundamental Rights** — option **(2)** is correct.
Courts act as **umpire** of the Centre-State division and guardian of a **written, supreme Constitution**.
The other combinations (DPSPs, conventions, unwritten constitution) are not the basis in the notes.
xa: It is a **symbol of federal government** (APPSC key).
**Britain** has no review of Acts of Parliament (**parliamentary sovereignty**).
Origin: **USA** — **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.

44.s: The Indian system of judicial review is described as blending
o: American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary sovereignty
French administrative supremacy with British federalism
Canadian judicial restraint with Australian parliamentary sovereignty
British judicial supremacy with American parliamentary sovereignty
44.x: India combines the American idea of judicial supremacy with the British tradition of parliamentary sovereignty.
44.tq: Match each constitutional characteristic with its correct comparative source.
xs: India blends **American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary sovereignty** — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses the two sources — the usual trap.
France, Canada and Australia are not the sources of the blend.
xa: Theory behind review: **supremacy of the Constitution / limited government**.
Review is **narrower than the USA**: "**procedure established by law**" vs "**due process of law**".
**Canada** and **Australia** do have judicial review (written constitutions).

44.s: The Supreme Court’s recognition of judicial review as part of the basic structure is associated particularly with
o: Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and L. Chandra Kumar, 1997
44.x: The basic-structure status of judicial review is associated with Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and was reaffirmed in the context of judicial review of tribunals in L. Chandra Kumar, 1997. Golaknath and Sajjan Singh predate the basic-structure doctrine (Minerva Mills, 1980, later reaffirmed it).
44.tq: Match the constitutional doctrine with its landmark cases and years.
xs: Judicial review as **basic structure** is tied to **Kesavananda Bharati, 1973** and **L. Chandra Kumar, 1997** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Hussainara Khatoon (1979)** = first PIL (speedy trial); **Vishaka (1997)** = workplace harassment guidelines.
**S.P. Gupta (1981)** = locus standi; **M.C. Mehta** = environment cases.
xa: **Kesavananda (1973)** also laid down the **Basic Structure** doctrine itself.
**Madras Bar Association (2025)** struck down re-enacted tribunal conditions of the **Tribunals Reforms Act 2021**.
Amendments overcoming judgments remain subject to the **basic structure**.

44.s: The constitutional theory underlying judicial review in India is principally the theory of:
o: Supremacy of the Constitution and limited government
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
44.x: Judicial review rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the idea of limited government. India combines elements of American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary supremacy, while Parliament remains subject to the Constitution.
44.tq: Reject absolute formulations and identify the constitutional limitation underlying review.
xs: The theory behind judicial review is **supremacy of the Constitution and limited government** — option **(3)** is correct.
Not unlimited judicial supremacy, absolute parliamentary sovereignty, or executive supremacy.
India's model is a **synthesis** of **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
xa: ⚠ Judicial review = symbol of **federal government** (APPSC key); theory = **supremacy of the Constitution**.
Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + FRs.
SC (**17 May 2026**): **majoritarianism cannot override constitutionalism**.

44.s: The power of a constitutional court to examine laws and executive orders and declare them ultra vires or void is known as
44.x: Judicial review is the power of courts to test the constitutional validity of laws and executive actions and invalidate those that are ultra vires.
44.tq: Distinguish the formal power of constitutional scrutiny from activism and restraint.
xs: Testing laws and executive orders and declaring them **ultra vires / void** is **judicial review** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Judicial activism** = wider intervention shaping public policy; **judicial restraint** = its **antithesis**.
xa: The term "judicial review" is **not used** in the Constitution.
Three grounds: **violation of FRs**, **lack of legislative competence**, **contravention of the Constitution / Basic Structure**.
Origin: **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.

44.s: The doctrine of judicial review was formally established in the United States through which case?
o: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
44.x: Marbury v. Madison (1803), decided under Chief Justice John Marshall, is regarded as the landmark case establishing judicial review in the United States.
44.tq: Use the landmark-case and year combination to identify the doctrine’s formal origin.
xs: Judicial review was established in the USA through **Marbury v. Madison** (**1803**, CJ **John Marshall**) — option **(3)** is correct.
**Olga Tellis** = right to livelihood; **Kesavananda** = Basic Structure; **Puttaswamy** = privacy (**2017**) — all Indian cases.
xa: Its roots go back to **Sir Edward Coke's** resistance to **King James I** (17th-century England).
**Arthur Schlesinger Jr.** coined "**judicial activism**" in **1947**.
**Britain** has no review over Acts of Parliament.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Judicial review exists in countries having written constitutions such as Canada and Australia.
2. The United Kingdom permits judicial review of Acts of Parliament in the same manner as the United States.
3. Parliamentary sovereignty is a characteristic of the British constitutional system.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Judicial review exists in countries such as Canada and Australia. The United Kingdom does not permit courts to invalidate Acts of Parliament in the same manner because of parliamentary sovereignty.
44.tq: Find the reversed comparison between written-constitution systems and British parliamentary sovereignty.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Canada** and **Australia**, with written constitutions, have judicial review.
Statement 2 wrong: **Britain** has **no review over Acts of Parliament**.
Statement 3 correct: Britain rests on **parliamentary sovereignty**.
xa: Origin: **USA**, **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.
India blends **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
Roots: **Sir Edward Coke** vs **King James I**.

44.s: Judicial review in India is regarded as a symbol of which of the following?
44.x: Judicial review is a symbol of federal government: courts act as umpire of the Centre-State division under a written, supreme Constitution. Parliamentary, unitary and presidential forms do not by themselves require such an umpire.
44.tq: Judicial review = symbol of federalism; theory = supremacy of the Constitution.
xs: Judicial review is a symbol of **federal government** (APPSC key) — option **(2)** is correct.
Courts act as **umpire of the Centre-State division** under a **written, supreme Constitution**.
Parliamentary, unitary or presidential forms do not by themselves need such an umpire.
xa: Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + Fundamental Rights.
Theory: **supremacy of the Constitution / limited government**.
**Art. 131**: SC original jurisdiction in **Centre-State** disputes.

44.s: Article 226 differs from Article 32 principally because the High Courts may issue writs under Article 226 for
o: Fundamental Rights and any other purpose
44.x: The writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 extends to enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose, making it wider in scope than Article 32.
44.tq: Compare the scope of two similar writ jurisdictions by identifying the additional phrase.
xs: HCs may issue writs under **Art. 226** for **Fundamental Rights and any other purpose** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 32** is for **FRs** only; so Art. 226 is **wider than Art. 32**.
Presidential references are **Art. 143**; federal disputes **Art. 131**.
xa: **Art. 32** = "**heart and soul**" (**Ambedkar**).
SC and HC writs (**32 / 226**) are protectors and guarantors of FRs.
PIL may be filed under **Art. 32** or **Art. 226**.

44.s: What was the effect of the 42nd and 43rd Constitutional Amendments on the judicial review power of High Courts?
o: The 42nd Amendment restored the power and the 43rd abolished it
The 42nd Amendment barred review of Central laws by High Courts and the 43rd restored that power
Both Amendments abolished judicial review by High Courts
The 42nd Amendment transferred the power to State Legislatures and the 43rd returned it to Parliament
44.x: The 42nd Amendment, 1976, restricted High Courts from reviewing Central laws; the 43rd Amendment, 1977, restored that power.
44.tq: Track the reversal by pairing each Amendment with its distinct effect.
xs: The **42nd Amendment** (**1976**) **barred HCs from reviewing central laws**; the **43rd** (**1977**) **restored** the power — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses them; neither moved the power to legislatures.
xa: ⚠ **42nd** barred → **43rd** restored; **38th** barred → **44th** reversed.
**38th Amendment (1975)** made satisfaction under **Arts. 123, 213, 352** non-justiciable.
**1st Amendment (1951)** followed **land-reform and reservation** rulings.

44.s:
Match List-I (Article) with List-II (Basis of judicial review):
List-I
a. Article 131
b. Article 136
c. Article 143
d. Article 227
List-II
i. High Court superintendence over subordinate courts
ii. Advisory jurisdiction on a Presidential reference
iii. Special Leave to appeal
iv. Supreme Court original jurisdiction in Centre-State disputes
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
44.x: Article 131 is the SC's original jurisdiction in Centre-State disputes (iv); Article 136 is Special Leave (iii); Article 143 is advisory jurisdiction on Presidential reference (ii); Article 227 is HC superintendence over subordinate courts (i). Option B swaps 131 and 136; option C swaps 136 and 143; option D gets only 136 right and mismatches 131, 143 and 227.
44.tq: 131 original, 136 special leave, 143 advisory, 227 superintendence.
xs: Correct match: **a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i** — option **(1)** is correct.
**131** = SC original jurisdiction in **Centre-State disputes**; **136** = **Special Leave**.
**143** = **advisory** on Presidential reference; **227** = **HC superintendence** over subordinate courts.
xa: **Art. 137** = SC **reviews its own judgments**.
**Art. 139A** (**44th Amendment 1978**) = SC may **transfer cases to itself**.
**Art. 141** = SC law binding on all courts.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 245 makes legislative power subject to the Constitution.
2. Article 246(3) gives the States exclusive power over matters in the State List, subject to the Constitution.
3. Articles 251 and 254 deal with repugnancy between certain laws.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All three statements are correct. Articles 245 and 246 govern legislative competence, while Articles 251 and 254 address inconsistency or repugnancy between laws.
44.tq: Test several related Articles as a constitutional-competence cluster.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Art. 245** makes legislative power **subject to the Constitution**.
Statement 2: **Art. 246(3)** gives States exclusive power over the **State List**.
Statement 3: **Arts. 251, 254** deal with **repugnancy** — state law void to the extent of inconsistency.
xa: **Lack of legislative competence** is one of the **three grounds** of review.
**Art. 13**: laws inconsistent with FRs are **void**.
**Art. 372(1)**: review of **pre-Constitution laws**.

44.s: Article 372(1) is relevant to judicial review because it concerns
o: the appointment of High Court judges
the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
44.x: Article 372(1) provides the constitutional basis for continuing pre-Constitution laws subject to their consistency with the Constitution and judicial review.
44.tq: Identify the historical category of laws linked to the Article.
xs: **Art. 372(1)** concerns **the review of pre-Constitution laws** — option **(1)** is correct.
HC appointments = **Art. 217**; advisory = **Art. 143**.
xa: **Art. 13** also voids pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with FRs.
**Arts. 251, 254**: **repugnancy**.
APPSC **2023** matched **137**-review, **226**-HC writs, **13**-void laws, **32**-SC writs.

44.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised ground of judicial review in India?
o: Contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure
Disagreement with the policy preference of the majority party
44.x: The recognised grounds include violation of Fundamental Rights, lack of legislative competence and contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure. Mere disagreement with political policy is not by itself a ground.
44.tq: Exclude a political preference that is not a constitutional ground of review.
xs: **Disagreement with the majority party's policy** is NOT a ground of review — option **(2)** is the answer.
The three grounds: **violation of FRs**, **lack of legislative competence**, **contravention of constitutional provisions / Basic Structure**.
xa: Courts **avoid policy/political questions**.
**State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977)**: SC declined a political question → **restraint**.
Writs are **discretionary** — refused where an effective alternative remedy exists.

44.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
A. Article 13
B. Article 32
C. Article 137
D. Article 226

List-II (Subject)
1. Review of its own judgments by the Supreme Court
2. High Court writ jurisdiction
3. Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights to be void
4. Supreme Court writ jurisdiction for restoration of Fundamental Rights

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
44.x: Article 13 concerns laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights; Article 32 provides Supreme Court writs; Article 137 permits Supreme Court review; and Article 226 concerns High Court writs for Fundamental Rights and other purposes.
44.tq: Start from the sure Article–subject pairs and test the remaining combinations.
xs: Correct match: **A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2** — option **(1)** is correct.
**13** = laws inconsistent with FRs **void**; **32** = **SC writs** for FRs.
**137** = SC **reviews its own judgments**; **226** = **HC writs**.
xa: This matches the **APPSC-G2 2023** PYQ.
⚠ **137** = review; **136** = Special Leave; **13** = void laws.
**Art. 226** covers FRs "**and any other purpose**".

44.s: Article 139A, inserted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, deals with the power of the Supreme Court to:
o: issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
44.x: Article 139A empowers the Supreme Court to transfer certain cases to itself. It was inserted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
44.tq: Link the Article number with the distinctive procedural power it confers.
xs: **Art. 139A** (**44th Amendment 1978**) lets the SC **transfer cases to itself** — option **(4)** is correct.
Writs = **Art. 32**; HC appointments = **Art. 217**.
xa: The **44th Amendment** also reversed the **38th Amendment**'s non-justiciability bar.
**Art. 137**: review of its own judgments.
**Art. 141**: SC law binding on all courts.

44.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of the 38th and 44th Constitutional Amendments on the satisfaction of the President or Governor?
o: The 38th Amendment made specified satisfactions non-justiciable, while the 44th Amendment reversed that position.
The 38th Amendment introduced judicial review and the 44th Amendment abolished it.
Both Amendments permanently excluded judicial review of all executive satisfaction.
The 38th Amendment applied only to Governors and the 44th Amendment only to the President.
44.x: The 38th Amendment (1975) made the satisfaction under Articles 123, 213 and 352 non-justiciable; the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed that position.
44.tq: Track the before-and-after constitutional change instead of treating the two amendments as identical.
xs: The **38th Amendment** made specified satisfactions **non-justiciable**; the **44th** reversed it — option **(1)** is correct.
The 38th (**1975**) covered satisfaction under **Arts. 123, 213, 352**; the 44th came in **1978**.
It applied to **both** President and Governor.
xa: Still reviewable on **mala fides or irrelevant grounds** — e.g. President's Rule in **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
⚠ **42nd** barred → **43rd** restored; **38th** barred → **44th** reversed.
**Art. 361**: President/Governor **not answerable** to courts; **no mandamus**.

44.s: The decisions taken by the President or Governor may be subjected to judicial review when they are challenged on grounds such as:
o: The personal popularity of the office-holder
Mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds
The absence of legislative approval for every executive act
44.x: Although constitutional protection applies to the office-holder in the manner specified by Article 361, the decisions themselves may be reviewed on grounds such as mala fides or irrelevant considerations. The review of President’s Rule in S.R. Bommai illustrates this principle.
44.tq: Distinguish reviewable grounds of invalidity from mere political disagreement.
xs: Decisions can be reviewed for **mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds** — option **(3)** is correct.
Example: President's Rule reviewed in **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
Popularity or mere policy disagreement are not grounds.
xa: **Art. 361**: the **President/Governor** personally are **not answerable** to courts.
**Art. 74(2)** / **163(3)**: ministerial advice **cannot be inquired into**.
**44th Amendment (1978)** reversed the **38th**'s non-justiciability bar.

44.s:
With reference to judicial review in India and the United States, consider the following statements:
1. Article 21 of the Indian Constitution uses the expression ‘procedure established by law’.
2. The United States Constitution is associated with the expression ‘due process of law’.
3. The Indian scope of judicial review is generally narrower than the United States scope in this respect.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All three statements are correct. Indian review under ‘procedure established by law’ traditionally focuses on legal validity and procedure, while American due process includes procedural and substantive fairness.
44.tq: Compare the exact constitutional phrases before judging the broader legal consequence.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Art. 21** uses "**procedure established by law**" (validity + procedure).
Statement 2: the US uses "**due process of law**" (procedural + substantive fairness).
Statement 3: Indian review is therefore **narrower than the USA**.
xa: The US Supreme Court is called a "**third chamber**".
Courts in India **avoid political questions**.
Writs are **discretionary**.

44.s: The description of the United States Supreme Court as a ‘third chamber’ primarily indicates its extensive role in
o: Reviewing and shaping governmental policy through constitutional adjudication
44.x: The expression reflects the extensive policy impact of the United States Supreme Court’s constitutional review and interpretation.
44.tq: Interpret the institutional metaphor rather than treating it as a literal constitutional body.
xs: "**Third chamber**" points to the US Court **reviewing and shaping governmental policy** through constitutional adjudication — option **(2)** is correct.
It flows from US "**due process of law**" review (procedural + **substantive** fairness).
The US Court does not run elections, appoint governors or prepare budgets.
xa: Indian review under "**procedure established by law**" is **narrower**.
Judicial activism also **began and developed in the USA** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).

44.s:
Consider the following statements about the limits of judicial review in India:
1. Courts generally avoid deciding purely political or policy questions.
2. Delimitation decisions are wholly beyond judicial review, even if capricious.
3. Writs, being discretionary, may be refused where an effective alternative remedy exists.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Statement 1 is correct: courts avoid policy and political questions. Statement 2 is wrong: delimitation review is limited but possible if the decision is capricious (Kishorchandra Chhanganlal Rathod, 2024). Statement 3 is correct: writs are discretionary and may be refused where an effective alternative remedy exists. So '1 only' misses statement 3, and options C and D include statement 2.
44.tq: 'Limited but possible' beats 'wholly beyond review'.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: courts **avoid policy/political questions**.
Statement 2 wrong: delimitation review is **limited but possible if capricious** (**Kishorchandra Chhanganlal Rathod, 2024**).
Statement 3 correct: writs are **discretionary**, refused where an **effective alternative remedy** exists.
xa: **State of Rajasthan (1977)**: SC declined a political question.
Review is **narrower than the USA** under **Art. 21**.
**Aravali Golf Club (2007)**: judges told not to encroach on other branches.

44.s:
Match the following Articles with their effect on judicial review:
a. Article 74(2)
b. Article 163(3)
c. Article 361
i. President and Governor not answerable to any court for exercise of their powers
ii. Advice of Ministers to the Governor cannot be inquired into by any court
iii. Advice of Ministers to the President cannot be inquired into by any court
44.x: Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring into ministerial advice to the President (iii); Article 163(3) is the same bar for advice to the Governor (ii); Article 361 makes the President and Governor not answerable to courts, so no mandamus lies against them (i). The other codes swap these pairs.
44.tq: 74(2) President's advice, 163(3) Governor's advice, 361 personal immunity.
xs: Correct match: **a-iii, b-ii, c-i** — option **(1)** is correct.
**74(2)**: ministers' advice to the **President** cannot be inquired into.
**163(3)**: same bar for advice to the **Governor**; **361**: President/Governor **not answerable** to courts.
xa: **No mandamus** lies against the President/Governor (TH, **29 Jan 2026**).
Their decisions may still be reviewed for **mala fides** — **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.

44.s: When a legislature responds to a judicial judgment, which of the following is constitutionally permissible?
o: Overruling the Constitution through an ordinary statute
Removing the basis of the judgment through an amendment to law, including retrospectively where valid, or amending the Constitution subject to the basic structure
Directing the judiciary to reconsider every concluded case through an executive order
Simply declaring the judgment void without changing the legal basis
44.x: The legislature cannot simply overrule a judgment. It may remove the legal basis through a valid amendment, including a retrospective validating Act where appropriate, or amend the Constitution subject to the basic structure doctrine.
44.tq: Distinguish changing the legal basis of a judgment from directly nullifying judicial power.
xs: The legislature may **remove the basis of the judgment** by amending the law (retrospectively if valid) or **amend the Constitution subject to the basic structure** — option **(2)** is correct.
It **cannot simply overrule** a judgment or declare it void; an executive order cannot reopen cases.
An ordinary statute cannot override the Constitution.
xa: The judicial route: **review petition** under **Art. 137**; **curative petition** as last resort.
Example: **Tribunals Reforms Act 2021** re-enacted struck-down conditions → struck down again in **Madras Bar Association (2025)**.

44.s: The First Amendment to the Constitution in 1951 was associated with the legislative response to early rulings concerning:
o: Emergency powers and preventive detention only
44.x: The First Amendment, enacted in 1951, followed early judicial rulings relating to land reform and reservation.
44.tq: Link a constitutional amendment with the subjects that prompted it.
xs: The **1st Amendment (1951)** followed early rulings on **land reform and reservation** — option **(4)** is correct.
Example: **Kameshwar Singh** on land reform.
xa: Assent on **18 June 1951**; it created the **Ninth Schedule**.
Its **75 years** were marked in **2026**.
⚠ Later: **42nd** barred HC review of central laws → **43rd** restored.

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021:
1. It re-enacted conditions that had earlier been struck down by the Court.
2. The re-enacted provisions were struck down again in Madras Bar Association in 2025.
3. It replaced the Constitution’s basic structure doctrine with ordinary statutory law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because an ordinary Act cannot replace the basic structure doctrine of the Constitution.
44.tq: Reject the extreme claim that an ordinary statute can alter a constitutional limitation.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **Tribunals Reforms Act 2021** **re-enacted conditions** the Court had struck down.
Statement 2 correct: they were struck down again in **Madras Bar Association (2025)**.
Statement 3 wrong: neither a law nor an amendment may breach the **Basic Structure**.
xa: Core rule: the legislature **cannot simply overrule** a judgment.
Valid route: **remove the basis** of the judgment via a **validating Act**.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**: judicial review is **part of the basic structure**.

44.s:
When a government seeks to overcome the effect of a judicial judgment, which of the following may constitutionally be adopted, subject to the Basic Structure limitation?
1. A constitutional amendment altering the legal basis of the decision
2. A valid ordinary or validating law removing the basis of the judgment
3. A simple executive order declaring the judgment inoperative
4. A review petition under Article 137

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
44.x: A constitutional amendment, a valid law removing the basis of the judgment, and a review petition under Article 137 are available remedies; a curative petition may be the last judicial resort. A simple executive order cannot overrule a court judgment.
44.tq: Separate constitutionally recognised remedies from an executive attempt to overrule the judiciary.
xs: Items 1, 2 and 4 are permissible — option **(2) 1, 2 and 4 only**.
A **constitutional amendment** and a **validating law removing the basis** are valid, subject to the **basic structure**.
A **review petition** under **Art. 137** is available; a **curative petition** is the last resort.
An **executive order** cannot declare a judgment inoperative.
xa: Example of failure: **Tribunals Reforms Act 2021** → **Madras Bar Association (2025)**.
Curative petition was created in **Rupa Ashok Hurra**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements about the origin of judicial activism:
1. Judicial activism began and developed in the USA.
2. The term was coined in 1947 by the American historian Arthur Schlesinger Jr.
3. In India, judicial activism took root in the early 1950s, soon after the Constitution came into force.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Statement 1 is correct: judicial activism (and judicial restraint) developed in the USA. Statement 2 is correct: Arthur Schlesinger Jr. coined the term in 1947. Statement 3 is wrong: in India it took root post-Emergency, in the mid-1970s. So '1 only' misses statement 2, and options C and D include the wrong statement 3.
44.tq: USA origin, Schlesinger 1947, India post-Emergency mid-1970s.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: judicial activism **began and developed in the USA** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
Statement 2 correct: **Arthur Schlesinger Jr.** coined the term in **1947**.
Statement 3 wrong: in India it took root **post-Emergency, mid-1970s**.
xa: Judicial **restraint**, its antithesis, also developed in the USA.
First PIL: **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**.
PIL era: CJI **Y.V. Chandrachud**'s tenure (**1978-85**).

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Judicial review tests laws against the Constitution.
2. Judicial activism involves a wider form of judicial intervention that may shape public policy.
3. Judicial overreach refers to judicial intervention that remains entirely within the executive domain.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect because judicial overreach occurs when courts enter the executive or legislative domain, thereby straining separation of powers.
44.tq: Find the statement that reverses the meaning of a closely related concept.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: judicial review **tests laws against the Constitution**.
Statement 2 correct: activism is **wider intervention shaping public policy**.
Statement 3 wrong: **overreach** is courts **entering the executive or legislative domain**, straining **separation of powers**.
xa: **Upendra Baxi**: ideal = **judicial prudence** — fill the vacuum, don't replace institutions.
Overreach concerns: "**judicial adventurism**", weak enforcement of PIL orders.

44.s:
With reference to judicial review and judicial activism, consider the following statements:
1. Judicial review is generally interpretative and legalistic.
2. Judicial activism is generally creative, proactive and reform-oriented.
3. In judicial review, the judge’s role is to declare what the law is while following the framers’ original intent.
4. Judicial activism may require the legislature or executive to perform duties.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All four statements correctly describe the distinction between judicial review or restraint and judicial activism.
44.tq: Confirm each row of a comparison before selecting the inclusive option.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Review/restraint: **interpretative, legalistic**; judge **declares what the law is**, following **framers' original intent**.
Activism: **creative, proactive, reform-oriented**; forces legislature/executive to **perform duties**.
xa: Review asks "**Is the law valid?**"; activism asks "**Is the law just and adequate for today?**"
Instruments: **suo motu cognisance**, **continuing mandamus**, **guidelines**, **Art. 142**.

44.s:
Arrange the following stages in the development of judicial activism in India in chronological order:
A. Recognition of privacy as a fundamental right in Puttaswamy
B. Expansion of Article 21 through livelihood, education, health and environmental rights
C. Emergence of activism after the Emergency
D. Governance and accountability cases involving matters such as 2G and coal blocks
44.x: The sequence is: post-Emergency activism in the mid-1970s, expansion of Article 21 from 1979 to the 1980s, governance cases from the 1990s onward, and Puttaswamy in 2017.
44.tq: Fix the landmark year of Puttaswamy first and then arrange the earlier stages.
xs: Correct order: **C, B, D, A** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Mid-1970s** post-Emergency → **1979 to 1980s** Art. 21 expansion → **1990s** governance cases (**2G**, **coal blocks**) → **2017** **Puttaswamy**.
xa: Mid-1970s: **Krishna Iyer** and **Bhagwati** opened access.
1990s cases also include the **CVC case**, **Jharkhand Assembly** case and the **Affidavit case**.
First PIL: **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**.

44.s: Which one of the following is NOT associated with the expansion of Article 21 during the 1979–1980s stage of judicial activism?
o: Constitutional recognition of privacy as a fundamental right in Puttaswamy
44.x: Privacy was recognised as a fundamental right in Puttaswamy in 2017. The earlier stage involved expansion of Article 21 to livelihood, education, health and a clean environment.
44.tq: Separate the 1979–1980s Article 21 developments from the later 2017 privacy ruling.
xs: **Privacy in Puttaswamy** is NOT part of the 1979-1980s stage — option **(3)** is the answer; it came in **2017**.
The 1979-1980s stage expanded **Art. 21** to **livelihood** (**Olga Tellis**), **education**, **health** and **clean environment**.
xa: Olga Tellis: right to livelihood for **pavement dwellers** (**1985**).
The same stage saw **PIL/SAL** emerge.
**1990s onward**: governance cases — **2G**, **coal block cancellation**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Judicial dynamism is another expression used for judicial activism.
2. Judicial activism is generally regarded as the antithesis of judicial restraint.
3. Judicial activism and judicial restraint necessarily require identical judicial approaches.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Judicial dynamism is another term for judicial activism, and activism is contrasted with judicial restraint. The two approaches do not require identical judicial methods.
44.tq: Reject the absolute equivalence between two contrasting judicial approaches.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: activism is **also called judicial dynamism**.
Statement 2 correct: **judicial restraint** is the **antithesis** of activism.
Statement 3 wrong: the two are **opposite** approaches.
xa: Restraint cases: **Aravali Golf Club (2007)** + **State of Rajasthan (1977)**.
Activism cases: **Vishaka**, **Olga Tellis**, **M.C. Mehta**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the development of Public Interest Litigation in India:
1. It grew out of judicial activism.
2. It was an outcome of judicial restraint.
3. It democratised access to courts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: PIL developed through judicial activism and helped democratise access to courts. It was not an outcome of judicial restraint.
44.tq: Reject the reversed conceptual pair and retain the two positively stated consequences.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: PIL (= **SAL**) is an **outcome of judicial activism**.
Statement 2 wrong: it is **not** an outcome of judicial restraint.
Statement 3 correct: PIL **democratised access** to courts.
xa: Negatives: **overburdened courts**, increasing **misuse**.
**Locus standi** was relaxed — any public-spirited citizen can move court.
First PIL: **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**.

44.s: Who filed the first Public Interest Litigation case, Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, in 1979?
44.x: Kapila Hingorani filed Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, the first major PIL case, concerning the rights of undertrial prisoners.
44.tq: Match the landmark case with the person who initiated it.
xs: **Kapila Hingorani** filed **Hussainara Khatoon** (**1979**) — option **(2)** is correct; she is the "**Mother of PILs**".
**P.N. Bhagwati** was a **pioneer** judge of PIL; **O. Chinnappa Reddy** and **D.A. Desai** laid the base of activism — none filed the case.
xa: The case secured undertrials' right to **speedy trial**.
⚠ "Mother of PILs" = **Hingorani** (petitioner); pioneers = **Bhagwati** + **Krishna Iyer** (judges).
Bhagwati became CJI in **1985**.

44.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Hussainara Khatoon case — disclosure of candidates’ assets and education
44.x: The disclosure of candidates’ assets and education was dealt with in the affidavit case. Hussainara Khatoon concerned speedy trial for undertrial prisoners.
44.tq: Find the swapped subject associated with a landmark case.
xs: **Hussainara Khatoon — disclosure of candidates' assets** is NOT correctly matched — option **(4)** is the answer.
Hussainara Khatoon (**1979**) secured undertrials' right to **speedy trial**; asset disclosure came from the **Affidavit case**.
**Vishaka** = workplace harassment; **S.P. Gupta** = locus standi; **M.C. Mehta** = environment.
xa: **Vishaka guidelines (1997)** came before the **POSH Act 2013**.
M.C. Mehta directives were criticised as **policy-making**.

44.s: The expression ‘epistolary jurisdiction’ in the context of PIL refers to the practice of treating which of the following as petitions?
o: Only affidavits filed by government departments
Police charge sheets and audit reports
44.x: Under epistolary jurisdiction, courts treated letters and postcards as writ petitions and also acted on newspaper reports indicating violations of rights.
44.tq: Identify the exact forms of informal communication accepted by courts.
xs: **Epistolary jurisdiction** treats **letters, postcards and newspaper reports** as petitions — option **(3)** is correct.
It goes with relaxed **locus standi** — any public-spirited citizen can move court for others.
xa: A downside: a **flood of letter petitions** is listed among overreach concerns.
PIL = **Social Action Litigation (SAL)**.
PIL definition (APPSC **2019**): action for **public or general interest**.

44.s:
With reference to Public Interest Litigation, consider the following statements:
1. It may be filed under Article 32 before the Supreme Court.
2. It may be filed under Article 226 before a High Court.
3. It can be initiated only by the person whose fundamental right has been directly violated.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: PIL may be filed under Articles 32 and 226. The third statement is false because locus standi is relaxed and a public-spirited citizen may approach the court for others.
44.tq: Separate the constitutional remedies from the deliberately narrow description of standing.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
PIL may be filed under **Art. 32 (SC)** or **Art. 226 (HC)**.
Statement 3 wrong: **locus standi** is relaxed — a **public-spirited citizen** can file for those who cannot.
xa: **S.P. Gupta (1981)** dealt with **locus standi**.
**Epistolary jurisdiction**: letters and postcards treated as petitions.
PIL = **SAL**, an outcome of **judicial activism**.

44.s: Which of the following judges, apart from Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati, helped lay the foundation for judicial activism?
o: O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai
44.x: Justices O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai are identified as having laid the base of judicial activism along with the better-known PIL pioneers.
44.tq: Distinguish judicial contributors from cases and litigants.
xs: **O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai** laid the base of activism — option **(1)** is correct.
**Kapila Hingorani** was a petitioner; **M.C. Mehta**, **Hussainara Khatoon**, **S.P. Gupta** and **Vishaka** are case names.
xa: PIL pioneers: Justices **P.N. Bhagwati** and **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.
**Y.V. Chandrachud**: PIL era was his tenure (**1978-85**).
**Upendra Baxi**: ideal = **judicial prudence**.

44.s: Which of the following is a major negative consequence associated with the increasing misuse of Public Interest Litigation?
o: Removal of locus standi from constitutional law
Transfer of all cases to Lok Adalats
44.x: Although PIL democratised access to courts, its misuse has also contributed to the overburdening of courts.
44.tq: Balance the stated positive and negative consequences instead of choosing an extreme institutional effect.
xs: PIL misuse has led to **overburdening of courts** — option **(1)** is correct.
Misuse stems from **publicity, political or personal motives**.
Locus standi was **relaxed**, not removed; judicial review and courts were not abolished.
xa: Positive: PIL **democratised access** to courts.
"**Revisiting PIL jurisdiction**" — misuse, overreach, weak enforcement (LENSD, **2 May 2026**).
Other concerns: **delays in other cases**, weak enforcement of PIL orders.

44.s: Public Interest Litigation in India is also known as—
44.x: PIL is also called Social Action Litigation (SAL); it is an outcome of judicial activism, not restraint. Class-action arbitration is a different private remedy, and 'epistolary' describes the letter-petition jurisdiction, not the name of PIL.
44.tq: PIL = SAL; via Art 32/226; relaxed locus standi.
xs: PIL is also called **Social Action Litigation (SAL)** (APPSC-G2 **2023**) — option **(2)** is correct.
SAL is an outcome of **judicial activism**, not judicial restraint.
"**Epistolary**" describes letter-petition jurisdiction, not PIL's name.
xa: PIL definition (APPSC **2019**): legal action for **public or general interest**.
First PIL: **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**, filed by **Kapila Hingorani**.
Filed under **Art. 32** or **Art. 226**.

44.s: Which one of the following is NOT an evolution genuinely attributed to the Supreme Court?
o: Exemptions to Fundamental Rights expressly written in Articles 31A to 31C and Article 33
44.x: Exemptions and restrictions relating to Fundamental Rights in Articles 31A–31C and 33 are constitutional provisions, not judicial evolutions created by the Supreme Court.
44.tq: Distinguish a court-created doctrine from provisions expressly embedded in the Constitution.
xs: **Exemptions to Fundamental Rights** in **Arts. 31A-31C and 33** are written in the Constitution itself, not evolved by the Supreme Court — option **(3)**.
**Basic Structure** was evolved in **Kesavananda (1973)**; **continuing mandamus** and **expansion of Art. 21** are also genuine SC evolutions.
This exact point was asked in **APPSC 2017**.
xa: Other genuine SC evolutions: **PIL** and **removal of handcuffs** (prisoners' dignity).
**Continuing mandamus**: the case is kept open to **monitor compliance**.
Art. 21 expansion covered **livelihood (Olga Tellis)**, education, health and clean environment.

44.s: The Basic Structure doctrine was evolved by the Supreme Court in
44.x: The Basic Structure doctrine was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala in 1973.
44.tq: Link the doctrine to its landmark case and year rather than to a later activism remedy.
xs: The **Basic Structure** doctrine was evolved in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — option **(4)**.
**Vishaka (1997)** gave workplace harassment guidelines; **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)** was the first PIL on **speedy trial**.
xa: Kesavananda also held judicial review to be **part of the basic structure**; **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** reaffirmed it.
Neither a constitutional amendment nor a validating law may breach the **Basic Structure**.
**2017**: privacy declared a fundamental right in **Puttaswamy**.

44.s: The judicial direction removing handcuffs from prisoners primarily reflects the expansion of
44.x: Removal of unnecessary handcuffing is associated with protection of prisoners’ dignity and the broader human-rights dimension of judicial activism.
44.tq: Identify the constitutional value protected by the remedy instead of the physical measure itself.
xs: **Removal of handcuffs** is an SC evolution protecting **prisoners' dignity** and human rights — option **(2)**.
It belongs to the line of judicial activism that expanded **Art. 21**.
xa: Other genuine SC evolutions: **Basic Structure** (**Kesavananda 1973**), **PIL**, **continuing mandamus**.
**Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**: undertrials' right to **speedy trial** — first PIL, a prisoners' case.
⚠ "Exemptions to Fundamental Rights" (**Arts. 31A-31C, 33**) are written in the Constitution, **not** an SC doctrine.

44.s:
Consider the following statements about instruments of judicial activism:
1. Under continuing mandamus, the court keeps a case open to monitor compliance.
2. Suo motu cognisance means the court acts on its own; it is advised only in exceptional cases of constitutional importance.
3. Expert committees are panels appointed by Parliament to review court judgments.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Statement 1 is correct: continuing mandamus keeps the case open to monitor compliance. Statement 2 is correct: suo motu means the court acts on its own, advised only in exceptional cases of constitutional importance. Statement 3 is wrong: expert committees are court-appointed panels that inform and monitor the court's directions. So '1 only' misses statement 2, and options C and D include statement 3.
44.tq: Expert committees are appointed by the court, not by Parliament.
xs: Statement 1 correct: under **continuing mandamus** the case is kept open to **monitor compliance**.
Statement 2 correct: **suo motu** = court acts on its own; advised only in **exceptional cases** of constitutional importance.
Statement 3 wrong: **expert committees** are **court-appointed** panels that inform and monitor directions, not Parliament's — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **Guidelines** fill a legislative vacuum — **Vishaka (1997)** before the **POSH Act 2013**.
**Art. 142 "complete justice"**: interim remedy for legislative delay; resolves deadlocks between branches.
Judicial activism is also called **judicial dynamism**; its antithesis is **judicial restraint**.

44.s: The Vishaka Guidelines were issued by the Supreme Court primarily to
o: fill a legislative vacuum relating to workplace sexual harassment
abolish the writ jurisdiction of High Courts
44.x: The Vishaka Guidelines of 1997 addressed workplace sexual harassment in the absence of legislation and operated until the POSH Act, 2013.
44.tq: Identify the subject of the guidelines and distinguish them from other activism cases.
xs: **Vishaka Guidelines (1997)** filled a **legislative vacuum** on **workplace sexual harassment** — option **(1)**.
They operated until Parliament passed the **POSH Act 2013**.
xa: Guidelines are one of the **instruments of activism**, along with suo motu cognisance and **continuing mandamus**.
**Coal block cancellation** and **2G** belong to the 1990s-onward governance stage of activism.
⚠ Activism cases = **Vishaka**, **Olga Tellis**, **M.C. Mehta**; restraint cases = **Aravali Golf Club (2007)**, **State of Rajasthan (1977)**.

44.s: Article 142 of the Constitution is relevant to judicial activism because it enables the Supreme Court to
o: make laws for every subject in the Union List
remove elected State governments without constitutional procedure
do complete justice and provide interim remedies where legislative delay creates difficulty
44.x: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice, including interim remedies in situations involving legislative delay and institutional deadlock.
44.tq: Identify the constitutional power from its precise function rather than from an exaggerated legislative claim.
xs: **Art. 142** lets the SC do **"complete justice"** — an interim remedy where **legislative delay** creates difficulty — option **(4)**.
It also resolves **deadlocks between branches**; it does not let the Court make laws, remove governments or appoint MPs.
xa: Concern: "complete justice" is **undefined** and may **bypass democratic scrutiny**.
Other instruments: **suo motu cognisance**, **continuing mandamus**, **guidelines**, court-appointed **expert committees**.
**Upendra Baxi**: courts must fill the vacuum, not replace democratic institutions; ideal = **judicial prudence**.

44.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Hussainara Khatoon — Speedy trial for undertrials and first PIL
Olga Tellis — Workplace sexual harassment guidelines
Prakash Singh — Right to livelihood of pavement dwellers
44.x: Hussainara Khatoon (1979) is associated with speedy trial for undertrials and is regarded as the first PIL. Olga Tellis concerned livelihood, Vishaka workplace harassment and Prakash Singh police reforms.
44.tq: Start with the sure case-outcome pair and eliminate swapped judicial remedies.
xs: **Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979)** was the **first PIL** — undertrials' right to **speedy trial** — option **(1)**.
**Olga Tellis** = right to **livelihood** (pavement dwellers); **Vishaka** = **workplace harassment** guidelines.
xa: The prisoners' case was filed on behalf of others by **Kapila Hingorani**, the "**Mother of PILs**".
⚠ Pioneers of PIL (judges) = **P.N. Bhagwati** + **V.R. Krishna Iyer**; Hingorani was the petitioner.
The PIL era = CJI **Y.V. Chandrachud**'s tenure (**1978-85**).

44.s: The decision in Olga Tellis is primarily associated with the proposition that
o: workplace harassment guidelines are constitutionally mandatory
the right to livelihood is included within Article 21
police officers must have fixed tenure
44.x: Olga Tellis (1985) recognised the right to livelihood of pavement dwellers as part of the protection afforded by Article 21.
44.tq: Match the case with its specific Article 21 expansion.
xs: **Olga Tellis (1985)** brought the **right to livelihood** of pavement dwellers within **Art. 21** — option **(2)**.
Workplace harassment guidelines = **Vishaka (1997)**; privacy as a fundamental right = **Puttaswamy (2017)**.
xa: Stage **1979 to 1980s**: PIL/SAL era; Art. 21 expanded to livelihood, **education**, **health**, **clean environment**.
**S.P. Gupta (1981)**: **locus standi** relaxed.
**M.C. Mehta** cases (1980s onward): wide environmental directives.

44.s: The M. C. Mehta cases are significant for
o: wide-ranging environmental directions, although some directions were criticised as policy-making
creating the first State Security Commission
44.x: The M. C. Mehta cases from the 1980s onward produced extensive environmental directions and also generated debate about judicial policy-making.
44.tq: Retain both the substantive outcome and the criticism attached to the case group.
xs: The **M.C. Mehta** cases (1980s onward) gave **wide environmental directions**, criticised as **policy-making** — option **(3)**.
**Basic Structure** came from **Kesavananda (1973)**; privacy from **Puttaswamy (2017)**.
xa: Under PIL misuse concerns, the notes list **policy directives in M.C. Mehta** cases.
⚠ M.C. Mehta = **activism**; restraint = **Aravali Golf Club (2007)** and **State of Rajasthan (1977)**.
**Overreach**: courts entering the executive or legislative domain strains **separation of powers**.

44.s: Which of the following is NOT commonly identified as a concern associated with judicial activism?
o: Weak enforcement of orders passed in public interest litigation
Reduction of delays in all other pending cases as an automatic consequence
44.x: Judicial activism has been associated with concerns such as violation of separation of powers, courts doing executive work, weak enforcement of PIL orders, letter petitions and delays in other cases. Reduction of all other delays is not such a concern.
44.tq: Locate the option that does not fit the established list of concerns.
xs: **Reduction of delays** in other cases is not a concern — activism actually causes **delays in other cases** — option **(2)**.
Listed concerns: violation of **separation of powers**, **courts doing executive work**, **weak enforcement** of PIL orders, flood of letter petitions.
xa: Critics also call it "**judicial adventurism**".
**PIL misuse**: publicity, political or personal motives.
**Art. 142** worry: undefined "**complete justice**" bypasses democratic scrutiny.

44.s: Which of the following may constitute misuse of Public Interest Litigation?
o: Seeking relief for a genuinely disadvantaged group
Enforcing a constitutional right of a vulnerable class
Requesting judicial protection against an unlawful public action
Filing petitions solely for publicity or political motives
44.x: PIL may be misused for publicity or political or personal motives. Genuine protection of disadvantaged groups is the intended purpose of PIL.
44.tq: Apply the purpose of PIL to distinguish genuine public interest from private or political motives.
xs: Filing PIL for **publicity or political motives** is **misuse** — option **(4)**.
Helping disadvantaged or vulnerable groups is the very purpose of PIL: those who **cannot** move court themselves.
xa: PIL **positives**: **democratised access** to courts; **negatives**: overburdened courts, increasingly **misused**.
**Locus standi** relaxed → any **public-spirited citizen** can move court for those who cannot.
PIL is filed under **Art. 32 (SC)** or **Art. 226 (HC)**.

44.s: The concern relating to Article 142 in the context of judicial activism arises mainly because of which combination?
o: Its undefined expression ‘complete justice’ and the possibility of bypassing democratic scrutiny
Its complete prohibition of judicial remedies and legislative review
Its exclusive application to criminal appeals and election disputes
Its transfer of all executive powers to the Supreme Court
44.x: The broad and undefined expression ‘complete justice’ under Article 142 is viewed as capable of bypassing democratic scrutiny when used expansively.
44.tq: Link a constitutional provision with the specific institutional concern attached to it.
xs: The worry about **Art. 142** is its **undefined "complete justice"** and that it **bypasses democratic scrutiny** — option **(1)**.
Art. 142 is an instrument of activism: interim remedy for **legislative delay** and resolving deadlocks between branches.
xa: Other concerns of activism: **separation of powers**, weak enforcement of PIL orders, "**judicial adventurism**".
LENSD (**27 May 2026**) carried the Art. 142 debate.
**Upendra Baxi**'s ideal = **judicial prudence**.

44.s: According to Upendra Baxi’s view, the proper role of courts in a democratic system is to:
o: Exercise executive power whenever a PIL is filed
Avoid intervention even where constitutional rights are violated
Replace democratic institutions whenever they act slowly
Fill a constitutional or institutional vacuum without replacing democratic institutions
44.x: Upendra Baxi argued that courts should fill a vacuum rather than replace democratic institutions. Judicial prudence represents the ideal approach.
44.tq: Identify the middle position between judicial passivity and judicial substitution.
xs: **Upendra Baxi**: courts must **fill the vacuum**, **not replace democratic institutions** — option **(4)**.
His ideal for the judiciary is **judicial prudence**.
xa: **Overreach** = courts entering the executive or legislative domain, straining **separation of powers**.
Restraint: **Aravali Golf Club (2007)** told judges not to encroach on legislative and executive functions.
Pioneers of PIL: Justices **P.N. Bhagwati** and **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.

44.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (2007) : SC told judges not to encroach on legislative and executive functions
2. State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) : SC declined to decide a political question
3. M.C. Mehta cases : example of judicial restraint
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
44.x: Pair 1 is correct: in Aravali Golf Club (2007) the SC told judges not to encroach on legislative and executive functions. Pair 2 is correct: in State of Rajasthan (1977) the SC declined a political question, showing restraint. Pair 3 is wrong: the M.C. Mehta cases are cited for policy directives, a concern of activism, not restraint. So '1 only' misses pair 2, and options C and D include pair 3.
44.tq: Restraint cases: Chander Hass 2007 and State of Rajasthan 1977; M.C. Mehta = activism.
xs: Pair 1 correct: **Aravali Golf Club (2007)** — judges not to **encroach** on legislative and executive functions.
Pair 2 correct: **State of Rajasthan (1977)** — SC declined a **political question** (restraint).
Pair 3 wrong: **M.C. Mehta** cases are **activism** (environmental policy directives) — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **Judicial restraint** is the **antithesis** of activism; it also developed in the **USA**.
Restraint = interpretative: "Is the law valid?"; activism = "Is the law just and adequate for today?"
Courts avoid **political questions**, but delimitation is reviewable if capricious (**Kishorchandra Chhanganlal Rathod, 2024**).

44.s: In March 2026, the Supreme Court’s action concerning an NCERT chapter on judicial delay and corruption was criticised by opponents as:
o: Delegated legislation by the Election Commission
A violation of Article 32 by Parliament
44.x: The Supreme Court’s ban on the NCERT chapter was criticised as censorship under Article 19. The criticism formed part of the debate on judicial overreach.
44.tq: Identify the constitutional criticism associated with a contemporary judicial action.
xs: Critics called the SC's **Mar 2026** ban on an NCERT chapter on judicial delay and corruption **censorship under Art. 19** — option **(2)**.
It is cited as a **debate example** of judicial overreach.
xa: **Overreach** strains **separation of powers**.
**Art. 142** worries: undefined "complete justice", bypassing **democratic scrutiny**.
**Upendra Baxi**: courts fill the vacuum but must not replace democratic institutions.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh shifted to Hyderabad with the formation of Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956.
2. The Andhra State High Court was originally established at Amaravati.
3. Before 1954, the Andhra districts were within the jurisdiction of the Madras High Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: the Andhra State High Court was established at Guntur.
44.tq: Find the wrong location statement by separating the 1954 Guntur stage from the later Amaravati stage.
xs: Statement 1 correct: the HC moved to **Hyderabad** with the formation of AP from **1 Nov 1956**.
Statement 2 wrong: the Andhra State High Court was set up at **Guntur** (**5 July 1954**), not Amaravati.
Statement 3 correct: before 1954 the **Madras HC (1862)** covered the Andhra districts — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: First CJ of the Andhra State HC: **Koka Subba Rao**.
Journey: Guntur (**1954**) → Hyderabad (**1956**) → common HC (**2014**) → **Amaravati** (**2019**).
Separate AP HC at Amaravati from **1 Jan 2019** — India's **25th** High Court.

44.s: Which of the following correctly describes the judicial arrangement after the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh on 2 June 2014 and before 1 January 2019?
o: Separate High Courts functioned at Amaravati and Hyderabad respectively.
A Common High Court functioned at Vijayawada.
Andhra Pradesh and Telangana shared a Common High Court at Hyderabad.
Both States continued under the Madras High Court.
44.x: From 2014 until the establishment of the separate Andhra Pradesh High Court, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana shared a Common High Court at Hyderabad.
44.tq: Distinguish the interim common-court arrangement from the later separate High Courts.
xs: From **2 June 2014** to **1 Jan 2019**, AP and Telangana shared a **common High Court at Hyderabad** — option **(3)**.
It was provided by **Sec. 30** of the **AP Reorganisation Act 2014**; separate AP HC (**Sec. 31**) came only in 2019 at **Amaravati**.
xa: After 2019 the **Telangana** High Court stayed at **Hyderabad**.
First (acting) CJ of the new AP HC: **C. Praveen Kumar**, took charge at **Vijayawada** (temporary premises).
⚠ **Sec. 30** = common HC; **Sec. 31** = separate AP HC; **Sec. 32** = judges.

44.s: Under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, which section provided for a separate High Court for Andhra Pradesh, with its principal seat to be notified by the President?
44.x: Section 31 provided for the separate High Court of Andhra Pradesh and stated that its principal seat would be notified by the President.
44.tq: Use the exact statutory provision rather than confusing the separate court with its judges or the common court.
xs: **Section 31** of the AP Reorganisation Act 2014 provided a **separate High Court for AP**, principal seat notified by the **President** — option **(3)**.
**Sec. 30** = common HC; **Sec. 32** = judges of the AP HC.
xa: PYQ: **APPSC-GS 2022** key 31-b, 30-c, 32-a.
The separate AP HC began functioning at **Amaravati** from **1 Jan 2019**.
New HCs are created by a **Parliament law** and brought into being by **Presidential notification**.

44.s: Which of the following statements about the first leadership of the new Andhra Pradesh High Court is correct?
o: Justice C. Praveen Kumar took charge as the first acting Chief Justice, while Justice J.K. Maheshwari became the first regular Chief Justice.
Justice Lisa Gill became the first Chief Justice when the court was established in 1954.
Justice Koka Subba Rao became the first Chief Justice of the new court in 2019.
Justice J.K. Maheshwari took charge as the first acting Chief Justice and Justice C. Praveen Kumar became the first regular Chief Justice.
44.x: Justice C. Praveen Kumar took charge as the first acting Chief Justice on 1 January 2019, and Justice J.K. Maheshwari became the first regular Chief Justice in October 2019.
44.tq: Separate acting office from regular office and match each person with the correct stage.
xs: **C. Praveen Kumar** was the **first (acting) CJ** (took charge **1 Jan 2019**); **J.K. Maheshwari** the **first regular CJ** (**Oct 2019**) — option **(1)**.
**Koka Subba Rao** was first CJ of the Andhra State HC at **Guntur (1954)**; **Lisa Gill** was recommended in **Feb 2026**.
xa: **Lisa Gill** is the **first woman** to head the AP HC.
Praveen Kumar took charge at **Vijayawada** (temporary premises).
Exam angle: date **1 Jan 2019**, seat **Amaravati**, first CJ "in Vijayawada".

44.s:
Consider the following statements about the separate High Court of Andhra Pradesh:
1. It began functioning at Amaravati from 1 January 2019.
2. Its creation took the number of High Courts in India from 24 to 25.
3. After bifurcation, the Telangana High Court also shifted to Amaravati.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Statement 1 is correct: the separate AP High Court began functioning at Amaravati on 1 January 2019. Statement 2 is correct: the count went from 24 to 25, making AP's the 25th High Court. Statement 3 is wrong: the Telangana High Court stayed at Hyderabad. So '1 only' misses statement 2, and the options with statement 3 are wrong.
44.tq: Remember the pair: AP HC to Amaravati on 1 Jan 2019 as the 25th HC; Telangana HC stays at Hyderabad.
xs: Statement 1 correct: separate AP HC at **Amaravati** from **1 Jan 2019**.
Statement 2 correct: HC count went from **24 to 25**; AP's is the **25th** High Court.
Statement 3 wrong: the **Telangana** HC stayed at **Hyderabad** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: India has **25 High Courts**; **AP (1 Jan 2019)** is the newest.
Oldest: **Calcutta** (**2 July 1862**); Madras HC also 1862.
AP Reorganisation Act: **Sec. 30** common HC, **Sec. 31** separate AP HC, **Sec. 32** judges.

44.s:
Match the following sections of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 with their provisions:
a. Section 30
b. Section 31
c. Section 32
i. Judges of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh
ii. Common High Court for Telangana and Andhra Pradesh
iii. Separate High Court for Andhra Pradesh
44.x: Section 30 provided the common High Court at Hyderabad (ii), Section 31 the separate High Court of AP with its seat notified by the President (iii), and Section 32 the judges of the AP High Court (i). The other codes swap these sections.
44.tq: 30 common, 31 separate AP HC, 32 its judges (APPSC 2022 PYQ).
xs: **Sec. 30** = **common HC** (ii); **Sec. 31** = **separate AP HC** (iii); **Sec. 32** = **judges** of AP HC (i) — **a-ii, b-iii, c-i**, option **(1)**.
Sec. 31's principal seat was to be **notified by the President**.
xa: PYQ: **APPSC-GS 2022** asked this match.
Common HC at **Hyderabad**, 2014-2018; separate AP HC from **1 Jan 2019** at **Amaravati**.
First regular CJ: **J.K. Maheshwari** (**Oct 2019**).

44.s: The Andhra State High Court, set up on 5 July 1954, was located at—
44.x: The Andhra State High Court was established at Guntur on 5 July 1954 with Koka Subba Rao as its first Chief Justice. Kurnool was the seat of the Andhra State Assembly, Hyderabad became the HC seat from 1 November 1956, and Amaravati only from 1 January 2019.
44.tq: HC journey: Guntur 1954, Hyderabad 1956, common HC 2014, Amaravati 2019.
xs: The Andhra State High Court was set up at **Guntur** on **5 July 1954** — option **(3)**.
**Hyderabad** became the seat from **1 Nov 1956**; **Amaravati** only from **1 Jan 2019**.
xa: First Chief Justice: **Koka Subba Rao**.
Before 1954 the **Madras HC (1862)** covered the Andhra districts.
Between **2014** and 2019 AP and Telangana shared a **common HC** at Hyderabad.

44.s:
Which of the following are recognised significance and criticisms of judicial activism?
1. It democratises access to justice.
2. It can force executive accountability.
3. It may blur the separation of powers.
4. It has no effect on the workload of courts.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
44.x: Judicial activism has democratised access to justice and promoted executive accountability, but it can also blur separation of powers and contribute to overburdened courts. Statement 4 is incorrect.
44.tq: Accept the two positive functions and reject the absolute claim that activism has no workload consequences.
xs: Statements 1, 2 correct: activism **democratised access to justice** and **forced executive accountability**.
Statement 3 correct: it may **blur separation of powers**.
Statement 4 wrong: it **overburdens courts** — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Pendency: over **4.7 crore** cases, about **87%** in subordinate courts (as of May 2022).
Other concerns: weak enforcement of PIL orders, **flood of letter petitions**, "**judicial adventurism**".
PIL negatives: overburdened courts; increasingly **misused**.

44.s: As of May 2022, approximately what proportion of the more than 4.7 crore pending cases was reported to be in subordinate courts?
44.x: More than 4.7 crore cases were pending, with approximately 87% reported to be in subordinate courts.
44.tq: Use the magnitude and percentage together to identify the correct pendency figure.
xs: About **87%** of the **4.7 crore** pending cases were in **subordinate courts** (May 2022) — option **(1)**.
This was an **APPSC 2022 PYQ** figure.
xa: **Lower courts** have more than **4 crore** cases pending.
Reform tools: **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)** + **National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG)**.
**Kerala**: first **fully paperless district court**.

44.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the significance of fast-track courts in the judicial-debate context?
o: They may add speed without adding judges, leaving structural capacity concerns unresolved.
They necessarily reduce pendency by appointing more judges.
They transfer all constitutional cases to the executive.
They eliminate the need for subordinate courts.
44.x: A criticism of fast-track courts is that they may increase the speed of disposal without increasing the number of judges, thereby not fully addressing structural capacity problems.
44.tq: Distinguish procedural acceleration from an increase in judicial capacity.
xs: **Fast-track courts** add **speed without adding judges** — structural capacity stays unresolved — option **(1)**.
They are used e.g. for paper-leak cases under the **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024**.
xa: Pendency: over **4.7 crore** cases, about **87%** in subordinate courts.
HC sanctioned strength **1,122**, of which **804** filled (18 Sep 2025).
Court infrastructure scheme: **₹5,357 crore** for **2021-26**, monitored on the **Nyaya Vikas Portal**.

44.s: Which one of the following recent developments is correctly matched?
o: Lisa Gill — first woman Chief Justice of the Andhra Pradesh High Court, recommended in February 2026
Pakistan’s 27th Amendment — creation of the Ninth Schedule in India
First Amendment of India — establishment of Pakistan’s Federal Constitutional Court
