50.s: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between Articles 285 and 289?
o: Article 285 concerns exemption of Union property from State tax, while Article 289 concerns exemption of State property from Union tax, subject to taxation of commercial activity.
Article 285 concerns State borrowing and Article 289 concerns Union borrowing.
Both Articles exclusively exempt State property from Union taxation.
Both Articles deal only with the distribution of divisible taxes.
50.x: Article 285 addresses the exemption of Union property from State taxation. Article 289 addresses the exemption of State property from Union taxation, with commercial activity being taxable as specified.
50.tq: Use the direction of taxation—Union property versus State property—to avoid a reversed comparison.
xs: **Art. 285**: **Union property** exempt from **state taxes**; **Art. 289**: **state property** exempt from **Union taxes** (commercial activity taxable) — option **(1)**.
This is **mutual exemption**; borrowing is **Arts. 292-293**.
xa: Exception: the Centre can tax a state's **commercial operations** and **state-owned companies**.
**Art. 276**: state tax on professions — ceiling **₹2,500**.
Financial relations = **Arts. 268-293**.

50.s: A dispute between the Union and a State concerning a legal right may be instituted in the Supreme Court under its original jurisdiction. The relevant Article is:
50.x: Article 131 confers original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court in disputes involving legal rights between the Union and one or more States or between States.
50.tq: Match the intergovernmental dispute mechanism with the Article conferring original jurisdiction.
xs: **Article 131**: SC **original** jurisdiction — Union-State disputes go by **original suit** — option **(4)**.
Example: **State of Kerala v UoI (2024)** on the **Net Borrowing Ceiling**.
xa: ⚠ Matters referred to the **Finance Commission** are **excluded** from Art. 131.
**Net Borrowing Ceiling** is imposed via **Art. 293(3)**.
A state indebted to the Centre **needs the Centre's consent** to borrow.

50.s: Which of the following statements regarding fiscal matters and Article 131 is correct?
o: Every matter referred to the Finance Commission must be decided by the Supreme Court under Article 131.
Matters referred to the Finance Commission are excluded from the scope of Article 131.
Article 131 applies only to disputes between private persons and States.
Article 131 abolishes the advisory role of the Finance Commission.
50.x: Matters referred to the Finance Commission are excluded from the scope of Article 131. Article 131 concerns original suits involving qualifying legal-right disputes between the Union and States or among States.
50.tq: Reject the overbroad statement by distinguishing a constitutional reference to the Finance Commission from an original suit.
xs: **Matters referred to the FC** are **excluded** from **Art. 131** — option **(2)**.
Art. 131 is an **original suit** in the SC (e.g. **Kerala 2024**).
xa: **Art. 280** = Finance Commission; **281** = its recommendations.
**16th FC (2026-31)** retained **41%**; the Centre **accepted** its devolution recommendations.
**Kerala v UoI (2024)** challenged the **Net Borrowing Ceiling**.

50.s: Financial relations between the Union and the States are principally dealt with in which Part and range of Articles?
50.x: Part XII is titled Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits, and the financial-relations provisions stated here are Articles 268 to 293.
50.tq: Separate the Part number from the broader syllabus range and identify the exact constitutional framework.
xs: Financial relations = **Part XII**, **Arts. 268-293** — option **(1)**.
Within it: **268-281** distribution of revenues, **280** Finance Commission, **292-293** borrowing.
xa: **Art. 265**: no tax except by **authority of law**.
**Arts. 266/267**: **Consolidated Funds, Public Accounts / Contingency Fund**.
Taxing entries: **Union List 15**; **State List 20**.

50.s: Which of the following receipts is credited to the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 266?
o: All Union revenues, loans raised and loan repayments received
Only grants received by local bodies
Only tax revenue collected by the Union
Only money held in trust for States
50.x: The Consolidated Fund of India receives all revenues of the Union, loans raised by it and loan repayments received by it.
50.tq: Test the complete constitutional list rather than the narrower phrase tax revenue.
xs: The **Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 266)** receives **all Union revenues, loans raised and loan repayments received** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 267** is the **Contingency Fund**.
xa: **Art. 292**: Union borrows on the security of the **CFI**, within limits fixed by **Parliament by law**.
**Statutory grants (Art. 275)** are **charged on the CFI**.
**Art. 293(1)**: a state borrows on the security of **its Consolidated Fund**.

50.s: Which of the following is a power of the Union during a Financial Emergency under Article 360?
o: To transfer all State taxes permanently to local bodies
To suspend the Constitution of every State
To direct States on financial propriety and require certain Money and Financial Bills to be reserved for the President
50.x: During a Financial Emergency, the Centre may issue directions to States regarding financial propriety and require Money and Financial Bills to be reserved for the President.
50.tq: Identify the actual financial direction powers while rejecting extreme constitutional consequences.
xs: **Art. 360**: the Centre can **direct states on financial propriety** and require **Money and Financial Bills** reserved for the **President** — option **(3)**.
It does not suspend state constitutions or abolish legislatures.
xa: ⚠ **Art. 354** = **National Emergency** power to modify distribution of revenues.
Art. 354's effect lasts until the **end of the financial year** in which the emergency ends.
**Art. 293(3)**: indebted states need the **Centre's consent** to borrow.

50.s: During a National Emergency, the President can modify the constitutional distribution of revenues between the Union and the States under which Article, with effect lasting until the end of the financial year in which the emergency ends?
50.x: Article 354 lets the President modify the distribution of revenues during a National Emergency, until the end of the financial year in which the emergency ceases. Article 360 is Financial Emergency, Article 280 the Finance Commission and Article 293 State borrowing.
50.tq: 354 = revenue sharing in National Emergency; 360 = Financial Emergency.
xs: **Article 354**: in a **National Emergency** the President can **modify distribution of revenues** till the end of that **financial year** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 360** = Financial Emergency; **280** = Finance Commission; **293** = state borrowing.
xa: Art. 360: directions on **financial propriety** + **Money and Financial Bills** reserved for the President.
**Arts. 268-281**: distribution of revenues.
Disputes: **Art. 131** original suit; FC matters **excluded**.

50.s: Under Article 268 of the Constitution, which one of the following arrangements is correct?
o: Levied by the States and collected jointly by the Union and the States
Levied and collected by the States but appropriated by the Union
Levied by the Union and collected and appropriated by the States
Levied, collected and appropriated exclusively by the Union
50.x: Article 268 covers duties levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States. Stamp duties on specified instruments are examples.
50.tq: Identify the authority responsible for levy, collection and appropriation separately.
xs: **Art. 268**: **levied by the Union**, **collected and appropriated by the states** — option **(3)**.
Example: **stamp duties** on bills of exchange, cheques, promissory notes, insurance policies, share transfers.
xa: ⚠ **269** = Union collects, **assigned to states**; **271** surcharges = **Centre only**.
Excise on **medicinal/toilet preparations** under 268 ended with GST.
**268A** (service tax, **88th Amendment, 2003**) was **omitted by the 101st Amendment, 2016**.

50.s: Which one of the following is NOT an example of a duty covered under Article 268?
o: Stamp duty on bills of exchange
50.x: Income tax forms part of the divisible pool under Article 270. Article 268 includes stamp duties on bills of exchange, cheques, insurance policies and share transfers.
50.tq: Find the item belonging to the neighbouring constitutional provision rather than Article 268.
xs: **Income tax** is in the divisible pool under **Art. 270**, not Art. 268 — option **(2)**.
**Art. 268** covers **stamp duties** on **insurance policies**, **cheques**, **bills of exchange**.
xa: Art. 268: Union levies, **states collect and appropriate**.
Art. 270 pool also includes **corporation tax**, **CGST**, Centre's share of **IGST**.
Net proceeds are certified by the **CAG**.

50.s: Taxes levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States are dealt with under which Article?
50.x: Article 269 deals with taxes levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States, including taxes on inter-State sale or consignment of goods.
50.tq: Use the levy-collection-distribution distinction to identify the Article.
xs: **Article 269**: taxes **levied and collected by the Union** but **assigned to the states** — option **(3)**.
This was the **PYQ 2018** (APPSC-GS 2018) answer.
xa: Examples: taxes on **inter-state sale/purchase of goods** (not newspapers) and on **consignment**.
⚠ **268** = Union levies, **states collect**; **270** = **shared**; **271** = **Centre only**.
Pre-2000 Art. 269 taxes (estate duty, railway fares, newspapers) were folded into the **Art. 270** pool by the **80th CAA**.

50.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 269 deals with taxes on inter-State sale or purchase of goods, other than newspapers.
2. Article 269 includes taxes on consignment of goods.
3. Such taxes are collected by the States and appropriated by them.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
50.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Under Article 269, the Union levies and collects these taxes and assigns them to the States; they are not collected and appropriated directly by the States.
50.tq: Separate the constitutional authority collecting a tax from the authority ultimately receiving it.
xs: Statements 1, 2 correct: **Art. 269** covers **inter-state sale/purchase** of goods (**not newspapers**) and **consignment**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **Union collects**; proceeds are **assigned to states** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: ⚠ Collected and appropriated by states = **Art. 268** (stamp duties).
**Art. 269A**: **IGST** on inter-state supplies.
**Art. 271** surcharges: **exclusively for the Union**.

50.s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
o: Article 269 — Surcharge exclusively for the Union
Article 270 — Stamp duties collected and appropriated by States
50.x: Article 269A concerns IGST on inter-State supplies. Article 268 covers specified stamp duties, Article 269 covers assigned taxes, and Article 271 covers surcharges.
50.tq: Discriminate among closely placed Articles by matching each Article with its distinctive tax arrangement.
xs: **Art. 269A** — **IGST**, i.e. **GST on inter-state supplies** — option **(3)**.
**268** = **stamp duties** collected by states; **269** = taxes **assigned** to states; surcharges for the Union = **271**.
xa: 269A revenue goes to the **destination state**.
269A was inserted by the **101st Amendment, 2016**.
IGST is shared as Parliament provides on **GST Council** advice.

50.s: Service tax was associated with Article 268A before that Article was omitted by which Constitutional Amendment?
50.x: Article 268A was introduced for service tax by the 88th Amendment in 2003 and was omitted by the 101st Amendment in 2016 with the introduction of GST.
50.tq: Pair the provision with the amendment that removed it, not the amendment that introduced it.
xs: **Art. 268A** (service tax) was **omitted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016** — option **(3)**.
It had been added by the **88th Amendment, 2003**; service tax was replaced by **GST**.
xa: 101st Amendment inserted **246A, 269A, 279A**.
**80th CAA, 2000** omitted **Art. 272**.
GST from **1 July 2017**.

50.s:
Consider the following statements about the 80th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000:
1. It gave effect to the Tenth Finance Commission's 'Alternative Scheme of Devolution', making all central taxes shareable.
2. It was made effective from 1 April 2000.
3. It omitted Article 272, which dealt with sharing of Union excise duties.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
50.x: Statement 1 is correct: the 80th Amendment enacted the 10th FC's Alternative Scheme of Devolution, under which states share gross proceeds of all Union taxes. Statement 2 is wrong: though enacted in 2000, it was effective from 1 April 1996. Statement 3 is correct: Article 272 (shared Union excise duties) was omitted by it. So A, B and D all include the wrong statement 2.
50.tq: 80th CAA: enacted 2000 but effective 1 April 1996 - the classic date trap.
xs: Statement 1 correct: the **80th CAA** enacted the **10th FC's "Alternative Scheme of Devolution"** — all central taxes shareable.
Statement 2 wrong: it was effective from **1 April 1996**.
Statement 3 correct: it **omitted Art. 272** (Union excise sharing) — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: Share: IYB = **26%** of gross Union taxes; APP = **29%** (26% + 3% in lieu of additional excise duties).
It folded old **Art. 269** taxes into the **Art. 270** pool.
**Corporation tax** shared since the **80th Amendment**.

50.s: Which one of the following was NOT folded into the Article 270 pool by the 80th Constitutional Amendment?
o: Taxes on stock-exchange transactions other than stamp duty
50.x: Pre-2000 taxes on stock-exchange transactions, estate duty, railway fares and newspapers were folded into the Article 270 pool. Surcharges remain exclusively for the Union under Article 271.
50.tq: Identify the item expressly excluded from the divisible pool.
xs: **Surcharges** were not folded in — they stay **exclusively for the Union** under **Art. 271** — option **(1)**.
The **80th CAA** folded pre-2000 Art. 269 taxes — **stock-exchange transactions**, **estate duty**, **railway fares**, newspapers — into the **Art. 270** pool.
xa: PYQ trap: surcharges under Art. 271 are **not shared** with states (APPSC-G1 2024).
Art. 270 excludes **268, 269, 269A** taxes, **surcharges** and **cesses**.
Non-shareable cesses ~**18%** of Centre's gross tax revenue.

50.s: A State claims a share in a surcharge levied on a tax covered by Article 270. Which constitutional position is applicable?
o: The surcharge is collected and appropriated by the State concerned.
The surcharge is automatically divided between the Union and the States.
The surcharge is exclusively retained by the Union.
The surcharge is distributed only on the recommendation of the GST Council.
50.x: Article 271 permits surcharges on taxes under Articles 269 and 270 for Union purposes; such surcharges are exclusively retained by the Union and are not shared with the States.
50.tq: Apply the exception for surcharges to a practical intergovernmental revenue claim.
xs: Surcharges under **Art. 271** are **exclusively retained by the Union** — option **(3)**.
Saying they are shared with states is the false statement (**APPSC-G1 2024**).
xa: Art. 271 surcharges are on **Art. 269/270** taxes.
Non-shareable **cesses and surcharges** cut effective devolution to near **31-32%** vs the **41%** award.
Art. 270 pool is shared on **FC** recommendation.

50.s: Corporation tax is shared with the States under the arrangement mentioned from which Constitutional Amendment?
50.x: Corporation tax is levied and collected by the Union and has been shared with the States since the 80th Constitutional Amendment.
50.tq: Test the amendment number associated with a specific tax-sharing change.
xs: **Corporation tax** is shared with states since the **80th Amendment** — option **(2)**.
It is a **Union** tax, never levied by states (UPPSC 2008).
xa: 80th CAA effective **1 April 1996**; enacted the **10th FC's** scheme.
**Customs duty** too is now in the divisible pool (**Art. 270**).
Net proceeds certified by the **CAG**.

50.s: The proceeds of IGST on inter-State supply are apportioned between the Centre and the States on the advice of the:
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
50.x: Article 269A provides for apportionment of IGST on inter-State supply between the Centre and the States on the advice of the GST Council.
50.tq: Identify the constitutional body associated with the specific tax-distribution mechanism.
xs: **IGST** proceeds are shared as Parliament provides on **GST Council** advice (**Art. 269A**) — option **(1)**.
Revenue goes to the **destination state**.
xa: **GST Council** = **Art. 279A**; chaired by the **Union Finance Minister**.
Art. 270 pool includes the **Centre's share of IGST**.
GST components: **CGST, SGST, IGST, UTGST**.

50.s: Which of the following correctly describes the taxes covered by Article 270?
o: All Union List taxes without any exceptions
Union List taxes shared through the Finance Commission, excluding specified taxes, surcharges and cesses
Only customs duties and Union excise duties
All State List taxes collected by the Union
50.x: Article 270 covers Union List taxes shared as recommended by the Finance Commission, but excludes Articles 268, 269 and 269A taxes, Article 271 surcharges and cesses.
50.tq: Watch for the extreme word “all” and test the constitutional exclusions from the divisible pool.
xs: **Art. 270** = Union taxes shared on **FC** recommendation, **excluding 268, 269, 269A** taxes, **surcharges and cesses** — option **(2)**.
Examples: **income tax**, **corporation tax**, **CGST**, Centre's share of **IGST**.
xa: States' share: **41%** of the divisible pool (**15th FC**; retained by **16th FC**).
**Customs duty** is now in the divisible pool.
Net proceeds certified by the **CAG**.

50.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the authority that levies it?
50.x: Excise on liquor is a State tax. Customs duty is levied by the Union, agricultural income tax by the States, and entertainment tax is largely subsumed in GST except for local bodies.
50.tq: Use the “who levies the tax?” test to distinguish Union and State revenue sources.
xs: **Excise on liquor** is levied by the **states** — option **(3)**.
**Customs** is a **Union** tax; **agricultural income tax** is **states** only; **entertainment tax** is a state tax largely subsumed in GST.
xa: Excise on liquor = UPPSC 2014; agricultural income tax = **UPPSC 2009**.
**Customs** is not a state tax revenue (**JPSC 2013**).
**Land revenue** is a **state** tax.

50.s: Who certifies the net proceeds relevant to the divisible pool?
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
50.x: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India certifies the net proceeds used in determining the divisible pool.
50.tq: Use the institutional-responsibility approach: identify who certifies rather than who recommends devolution.
xs: **Net proceeds** are certified by the **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)** — option **(4)**.
The FC recommends the sharing; the CAG certifies the proceeds.
xa: Divisible pool = **Art. 270** taxes.
**CAG's State Finances 2023-24** report is in current relevance.

50.s: What percentage of the divisible pool was recommended as the States’ share for 2021–26 and retained for 2026–31?
50.x: The States’ share was fixed at 41% of the divisible pool for 2021–26 by the Fifteenth Finance Commission and retained by the Sixteenth Finance Commission for 2026–31.
50.tq: Distinguish the headline percentage share from the lower effective share of gross tax revenue.
xs: States' share = **41%** of the divisible pool — **15th FC (2021-26)**, retained by **16th FC (2026-31)** — option **(3)**.
⚠ **42%** was the **14th FC**'s share.
xa: **14th FC**: "**compositional shift**" — more **unconditional (untied)** transfers (APPSC-G1 2017).
Tax devolution **₹12.87 lakh crore** in **2024-25**.
Non-shareable cesses cut effective devolution near **31-32%**.

50.s: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 inserted which set of provisions in connection with GST?
50.x: The 101st Amendment inserted Articles 246A, 269A and 279A for the GST framework and the GST Council.
50.tq: Recall the distinctive cluster of GST-related Articles.
xs: The **101st Amendment, 2016** inserted **Articles 246A, 269A and 279A** — option **(2)**.
**246A** = concurrent GST law; **269A** = **IGST**; **279A** = **GST Council**.
xa: It **omitted 268A** (service tax).
It amended Arts **248-250**, **268-271**, **286**, **366**, **368** + Sixth/Seventh Schedules.
GST from **1 July 2017**.

50.s: Goods and Services Tax (GST) was introduced in India with effect from which date?
50.x: GST came into effect on 1 July 2017 pursuant to the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.
50.tq: Use the precise implementation date rather than the year of constitutional amendment.
xs: GST came into effect on **1 July 2017** — option **(2)**.
It followed the **101st CAA, 2016**.
xa: GST is **destination-based** and subsumed ~**17** taxes.
"**GST 2.0**": effective **September 2025**.
Compensation cess guaranteed revenue for **5 years (2017-22)**.

50.s:
Consider the following statements about the Goods and Services Tax (GST):
1. It is a destination-based tax.
2. It subsumed about 17 earlier taxes.
3. It has only three components - CGST, SGST and IGST - and no separate Union Territory GST.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
50.x: Statement 1 is correct: GST is destination-based. Statement 2 is correct: it subsumed about 17 taxes. Statement 3 is wrong: GST has four components - CGST, SGST, IGST and UTGST. So B, C and D wrongly include statement 3.
50.tq: Remember four GSTs: Central, State, Integrated, Union Territory.
xs: Statements 1, 2 correct: GST is **destination-based** and subsumed ~**17** taxes.
Statement 3 wrong: GST also has **UTGST** — components are **CGST, SGST, IGST, UTGST** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: GST from **1 July 2017** (**101st CAA**).
**IGST** revenue goes to the **destination state** (**Art. 269A**).
**Art. 246A**: **only Parliament** legislates on inter-state supply.

50.s: Why can neither the Union nor the States alone carry a decision in the GST Council?
o: Because the Union Finance Minister does not vote in the Council
Because the States have a veto over all GST matters
Because the Council requires unanimous approval in every matter
Because the Centre has one-third and the States together have two-thirds of the weighted votes, while three-fourths is required
50.x: A GST Council decision needs three-fourths of the weighted votes. The Centre holds only one-third and all States together only two-thirds, so neither side can reach three-fourths alone; options A-C misstate the voting rules.
50.tq: Apply the voting weights and threshold instead of recalling either figure in isolation.
xs: **Centre one-third**, **states together two-thirds**; decisions need **three-fourths** of weighted votes — option **(4)**.
So **neither side** can carry a decision alone.
xa: ⚠ **1/3 – 2/3 – 3/4** = **Centre – states – majority needed**.
Chair: **Union Finance Minister**.
**Mohit Minerals (2022)**: recommendations **not binding**.

50.s: Under Article 246A, which legislative arrangement applies to GST?
o: Parliament and State Legislatures can both make GST laws, but only Parliament can legislate on inter-State supplies
Only Parliament can make laws on all GST matters
Parliament can legislate only on intra-State supplies
Only State Legislatures can make laws on GST within their territories
50.x: Article 246A gives concurrent GST legislative power to Parliament and State Legislatures, while Parliament alone legislates on inter-State supplies.
50.tq: Test the exception within a concurrent legislative power.
xs: **Art. 246A**: **Parliament + state legislatures** both make GST law; **only Parliament** for **inter-state supplies** — option **(1)**.
It was inserted by the **101st Amendment, 2016**.
xa: **Art. 269A**: **IGST** on inter-state supplies.
**Art. 279A**: **GST Council**.
**AP HC (May 2026)**: Central and state GST authorities must decide who proceeds — **no dual action**.

50.s: The revenue from Integrated GST on inter-State supplies is intended to go to which State?
o: The State where the goods were manufactured
The State where the supplier is registered
The State selected by the GST Council annually
50.x: Article 269A concerns IGST, with the revenue going to the destination State in accordance with the destination-based character of GST.
50.tq: Link the tax type with the destination-based principle and avoid the origin-state trap.
xs: **IGST** revenue goes to the **destination state** — option **(2)**.
GST is **destination-based** (**Art. 269A**).
xa: IGST is shared as Parliament provides on **GST Council** advice.
Centre's share of **IGST** is in the **Art. 270** pool.
**Art. 246A**: only Parliament legislates on **inter-state supply**.

50.s: Compensation Cess under the GST system was primarily imposed on which category of goods?
50.x: Compensation Cess on luxury and sin goods was used to fund compensation to States for GST-related revenue loss.
50.tq: Use the purpose-and-base combination rather than confusing cess with a general GST levy.
xs: **Compensation cess** was imposed on **luxury/"sin" goods** — option **(4)**.
It funded **states' compensation** promised by the **101st Amendment**.
xa: It guaranteed revenue for **5 years (2017-22)**.
Kerala lists "**cessation of GST compensation**" as a fiscal stress.
Luxury/sin goods kept **existing rates** + compensation cess.

50.s: In a situation where both Central and State GST authorities investigate the same entity, what direction was given by the Andhra Pradesh High Court in May 2026?
o: The authorities must decide among themselves which authority will proceed, without dual action
The investigation must be transferred to the GST Council
The State authority must always withdraw the investigation
50.x: The Andhra Pradesh High Court held that the Central and State GST authorities must decide who proceeds, so that there is no dual action against the same entity.
50.tq: Test the practical consequence of overlapping authority through a short factual scenario.
xs: **AP HC (May 2026)**: Central and state GST authorities must **decide who proceeds** — **no dual action** — option **(1)**.
It arose where both investigated the **same entity**.
xa: **Art. 246A**: **Parliament + state legislatures** both make GST law.
**GST Council** = **Art. 279A**.
**GST 2.0**: effective **September 2025**.

50.s: Which of the following is a criticism concerning State fiscal autonomy under the GST regime?
o: States obtained exclusive control over IGST
States acquired independent powers over all indirect taxes
States surrendered independent indirect-tax powers and concerns were raised about weighted voting
The Union surrendered its power to legislate on inter-State supplies
50.x: The GST framework has been criticised because States surrendered independent indirect-tax powers and because of concerns regarding the weighted voting structure.
50.tq: Identify the precise federalism concern instead of accepting an exaggerated transfer of powers.
xs: States **surrendered independent indirect-tax powers**, and **weighted voting** is questioned — option **(3)**.
Critics say the **Centre effectively holds a veto**.
xa: Votes: **Centre 1/3**, **states 2/3**; decisions need **3/4**.
**Mohit Minerals (2022)**: Council recommendations **not binding**, only persuasive.
Compensation ended after **five years**.

50.s: The Supreme Court's decision in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) held that the recommendations of the GST Council are:
o: Binding only when supported by a unanimous vote
Binding on Parliament and State Legislatures in every matter
Persuasive and not binding on Parliament and State Legislatures
50.x: The Court held that GST Council recommendations have persuasive value but are not binding on Parliament or State Legislatures.
50.tq: Distinguish persuasive constitutional coordination from binding legislative authority.
xs: **Mohit Minerals (2022)**: GST Council recommendations are **not binding**, only **persuasive** — option **(3)**.
They bind neither **Parliament** nor **state legislatures**.
xa: GST Council: **Art. 279A**; chair **Union Finance Minister**.
Members: Union **MoS (Finance)** + **State Finance Ministers**.
Decisions need **3/4 of weighted votes**.

50.s: The GST 2.0 framework referred to in the Economic Survey 2025-26 became effective from:
50.x: GST 2.0 became effective in September 2025.
50.tq: Distinguish the effective date from the year of the Economic Survey.
xs: "**GST 2.0**" became effective in **September 2025** — option **(2)**.
GST itself began on **1 July 2017**.
xa: GST subsumed ~**17** taxes; destination-based.
**AP HC (May 2026)**: **no dual action** by Central and state GST authorities.

50.s: Which of the following correctly describes the composition of the GST Council?
o: The Union Home Minister, State Home Ministers and the RBI Governor
The Finance Commission Chairman and the Chief Secretaries of all States
The Union Finance Minister, the Union Minister of State for Finance and the State Finance Ministers
The Prime Minister, Union Finance Minister and Chief Ministers of all States
50.x: The GST Council comprises the Union Finance Minister as Chairperson, the Union Minister of State in charge of Finance and the State Finance Ministers.
50.tq: Distinguish the Council’s composition from other federal bodies.
xs: GST Council = **Union Finance Minister** (chair), Union **MoS (Finance)** and **State Finance Ministers** — option **(3)**.
It is set up under **Art. 279A**.
xa: Votes: **Centre one-third**, **all states together two-thirds**.
Decisions need **three-fourths** of weighted votes.
**Mohit Minerals (2022)**: recommendations **not binding**.

50.s:
Assertion (A): The Centre is considered by critics to have an effective veto in the GST Council.
Reason (R): The Centre has one-third of the weighted votes, while a decision requires a three-fourths majority.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
50.x: Both statements are true, and the Centre’s one-third vote share combined with the three-fourths threshold enables it to block a decision without support from other members.
50.tq: Connect a voting threshold with its practical federal consequence.
xs: **A** true: critics say the **Centre effectively holds a veto**.
**R** true: Centre has **one-third** of votes and decisions need **three-fourths** — so it can block alone; R is the **correct explanation**, option **(1)**.
xa: States together hold **two-thirds**.
⚠ **1/3 – 2/3 – 3/4** = **Centre – states – majority needed**.
States also **surrendered independent indirect-tax powers**.

50.s: The compensation cess under GST was guaranteed to compensate States’ revenue loss for which period?
50.x: GST compensation cess guaranteed States’ revenue for five years from 2017 to 2022.
50.tq: Use the duration and start-end years together to avoid a shifted-period trap.
xs: Compensation cess guaranteed states' revenue for **5 years (2017-22)** — option **(2)**.
Compensation was promised by the **101st Amendment**.
xa: It was levied on **luxury/"sin" goods**.
It **ended after five years**; Kerala cites its cessation as fiscal stress (**11 May 2026**).
GST from **1 July 2017**.

50.s: Under which Article of the Constitution are statutory grants-in-aid to needy States, including grants for the welfare of Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Areas, provided?
50.x: Statutory grants-in-aid are provided under Article 275 on the recommendation of the Finance Commission. They include grants for needy States and for the welfare of Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Areas.
50.tq: Distinguish the specific Article governing statutory grants from the nearby Article on discretionary grants.
xs: **Article 275** provides **statutory grants** for needy states, **ST welfare** and **Scheduled Areas** — option **(1)**.
They are given on the **Finance Commission's** advice and **charged on the CFI**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **not** on **NITI Aayog's** advice (PYQ 2019; APPSC-GS 2019).
**Art. 282** = **discretionary** grants for **any public purpose**.
Other grants: in lieu of **export duty on jute** to Assam, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha.

50.s:
Consider the following statements regarding grants-in-aid:
1. Statutory grants under Article 275 are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
2. Discretionary grants under Article 282 may be made for any public purpose.
3. Statutory grants are made on the recommendation of NITI Aayog.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
50.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: statutory grants under Article 275 are made on the recommendation of the Finance Commission, not NITI Aayog.
50.tq: Find the wrong recommending authority by separating the constitutional body from the advisory policy institution.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **Art. 275** statutory grants are **charged on the CFI**.
Statement 2 correct: **Art. 282** discretionary grants are for **any public purpose**.
Statement 3 wrong: statutory grants come on the **Finance Commission's** advice, **not NITI Aayog** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: **NITI Aayog has no financial powers**.
Discretionary grants were earlier via the **Planning Commission**; now **Union ministries**.
Art. 275 grants meet **state-specific needs** formulas cannot capture.

50.s: With reference to discretionary grants under Article 282, which of the following statements is correct?
o: They are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
They are intended exclusively for Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Areas.
They can be made only on the recommendation of the Finance Commission.
They may be made for any public purpose and were historically administered through the Planning Commission.
50.x: Article 282 permits discretionary grants for any public purpose. Historically, the larger part of such Central grants was associated with the Planning Commission; they are not charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
50.tq: Discriminate discretionary grants by their broad purpose and non-charged character.
xs: **Art. 282** grants are for **any public purpose**, historically via the **Planning Commission** — option **(4)**.
They are **not** charged on the CFI and not on FC advice; **ST/Scheduled Area** grants are **Art. 275**.
xa: Historically discretionary grants were the **larger** share of Central grants.
Now given by **Union ministries**; the **Planning Commission was abolished (2015)**.
**Gadgil formula (1969)** distributed **Central Plan assistance** among states.

50.s: Grants in lieu of export duty on jute have been associated with which group of States?
o: Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh
Assam, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha
Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand
50.x: The special grants in lieu of export duty on jute are associated with Assam, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha.
50.tq: Recall the complete geographical list rather than selecting a group based on general regional similarity.
xs: Grants in lieu of **export duty on jute** go to **Assam, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They are listed among the **other grants** in the grants-in-aid scheme, beside the **statutory grants** of **Art. 275**.
xa: **Statutory grants (Art. 275)** are given on the **Finance Commission's** advice and are **charged on the Consolidated Fund of India**.
**Discretionary grants (Art. 282)** can be made for **any public purpose**; earlier recommended by the **Planning Commission**, now by Union ministries.
⚠ Statutory grants are NOT made on **NITI Aayog's** advice (**APPSC-GS 2019** trap).
Art. 275 also covers grants for **ST welfare** and **Scheduled Areas**.

50.s: A shift in the composition of transfers from grants-in-aid to tax devolution generally results in:
o: A reduction in unconditional transfers to States
An increase in unconditional or untied transfers to States
An increase in the Central parameters attached to every transfer
50.x: Tax devolution is formula-based and generally untied. Therefore, shifting from grants to tax devolution increases the share of unconditional transfers available to States.
50.tq: Apply the distinction between untied tax devolution and conditional grants to identify the consequence of a compositional shift.
xs: Shifting transfers from grants to **tax devolution** causes **an increase in unconditional or untied transfers to States** — option **(3)** is correct.
Tax devolution is **formula-based and untied**, whereas **CSS** grants carry **central parameters** and **matching shares**.
The **14th FC's "compositional shift"** raised devolution and cut grants — the **APPSC-G1 2017** answer was "increases the share of unconditional transfers".
xa: **14th FC** set the states' share at **42%**; the **15th FC** at **41%** (2021-26).
The **16th FC** (2026-31) retained **41%**, and the Centre **accepted** its devolution recommendations.
Tax devolution was **₹12.87 lakh crore** in **2024-25** (BE ₹12.47 lakh crore).

50.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Tax devolution is generally formula-based and untied.
2. Centrally Sponsored Scheme grants may contain Central parameters and matching-share requirements.
3. A rise in tax devolution necessarily eliminates all grants to States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
50.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because an increase in tax devolution does not eliminate all forms of grants to States.
50.tq: Reject the absolute statement while retaining the two precise distinctions between devolution and scheme grants.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: tax devolution is **formula-based and untied**.
Statement 2 is correct: **Centrally Sponsored Scheme** grants carry **central parameters** and **matching shares**.
Statement 3 is wrong: transfers still include **FC grants**, **CSS** and other grants alongside devolution.
xa: The **14th FC's "compositional shift"** raised devolution and cut grants → larger **untied** transfers.
States' share: **41%** of the divisible pool (**15th FC**, retained by the **16th FC**).
**Statutory grants** flow under **Art. 275** on the Finance Commission's advice; discretionary grants under **Art. 282**.

50.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the vertical share of the divisible pool recommended by the Fifteenth Finance Commission?
50.x: The Fifteenth Finance Commission recommended a 41 percent share of the divisible pool for the States. The 42 percent figure relates to the Fourteenth Finance Commission.
50.tq: Separate the closely spaced percentages associated with successive Finance Commissions.
xs: The **15th Finance Commission** (2021-26) fixed the states' vertical share at **41 percent** — option **(2)** is correct.
**42%** was the **14th FC's** figure; the **16th FC** (2026-31) retained **41%**.
**32%** is near the **effective** devolution (**31-32%**) once non-shareable cesses are excluded — not the award.
xa: Non-shareable cesses are about **18%** of the Centre's gross tax revenue.
The **10th FC** gave the "**Alternative Scheme of Devolution**", enacted by the **80th CAA, 2000**.
Under that scheme the states' share was **29%** = **26%** + **3%** in lieu of additional excise duties.
**Art. 280** creates the Finance Commission; **Art. 281** deals with its recommendations.

50.s: The Gadgil formula was introduced in 1969 for the distribution of Central Plan assistance during the:
50.x: The Gadgil formula, associated with D. R. Gadgil, was introduced in 1969 during the Fourth Five Year Plan for distributing Central Plan assistance among States.
50.tq: Link the formula to its year and Plan period rather than to the later Gadgil–Mukherjee formula.
xs: The **Gadgil formula** (**1969**) distributed Central Plan assistance in the **Fourth Five Year Plan** — option **(2)** is correct.
It was devised by **D.R. Gadgil**; the **Eighth Plan** saw the later **Gadgil-Mukherjee** formula, not the original.
xa: Gadgil weights: **population 60**, per-capita income **10**, tax effort **10**, ongoing irrigation/power **10**, special problems **10**.
**Gadgil-Mukherjee** weights: population **60%**, per capita income **25%**, fiscal management **7.5%**, special problems **7.5%**.
⚠ Sources differ on Gadgil-Mukherjee: **1991** with population **55** vs **1990** with population **60%**.
**APPSC-G2 2017** answer: Gadgil formula = "**devolution of funds**".

50.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Gadgil formula — distribution of Central Plan assistance among States
Gadgil formula — appointment of the Finance Commission
Gadgil formula — determination of profession-tax ceilings
Gadgil formula — settlement of inter-State legal disputes
50.x: The Gadgil formula was used for the devolution or distribution of Central Plan assistance among States. It was not related to constitutional taxation limits, Finance Commission appointments or judicial disputes.
50.tq: Identify the policy domain associated with the formula and reject unrelated constitutional functions.
xs: The **Gadgil formula** was used for the **distribution of Central Plan assistance among States** — option **(1)** is correct.
The profession-tax ceiling is fixed by **Art. 276(2)**; inter-state disputes go to the Supreme Court under **Art. 131**; the Finance Commission is set up under **Art. 280** — none involve Gadgil.
xa: Introduced in **1969** for the **Fourth Five Year Plan**, by **D.R. Gadgil**.
**APPSC-G2 2017** keyed the Gadgil formula as "**devolution of funds**".
It lost relevance when the **Planning Commission was abolished (2015)** and Plan grants ended.
**NITI Aayog has no financial powers**.

50.s: Special category States traditionally received Central Plan assistance on which terms?
o: 100 percent grant without any loan component
50.x: Special category States had the first charge on Central Plan assistance and received it on the favourable terms of 90 percent grant and 10 percent loan.
50.tq: Recall the grant–loan ratio and reject the more familiar but incorrect rounded alternatives.
xs: Special category States got the first charge on central plan assistance on **90 percent grant and 10 percent loan** — option **(4)** is correct.
The **90 : 10** grant-loan ratio was their favourable term; none of the other ratios applied.
xa: Parameters (**NDC**): **hilly/difficult terrain**, low population density or sizeable **tribal population**, **strategic border location**.
Also: **economic and infrastructural backwardness** and **non-viable state finances**.
**AP angle:** post-**2014** demand for **special category status**.

50.s: Which of the following was NOT a parameter traditionally associated with special category status?
o: Strategic location along an international border
High per-capita income and commercially viable State finances
Low population density or a sizeable tribal population
50.x: Special category parameters included difficult terrain, low population density or sizeable tribal population, strategic border location, economic and infrastructural backwardness, and non-viable State finances. High per-capita income and commercially viable finances were not such parameters.
50.tq: Find the reversed economic condition among otherwise recognised special-category characteristics.
xs: **High per-capita income and commercially viable State finances** was NOT a parameter — option **(3)** is the answer.
The NDC parameters were the opposite: **economic and infrastructural backwardness** and **non-viable state finances**.
**Strategic border location**, **hilly/difficult terrain** and **low population density or sizeable tribal population** were genuine parameters.
xa: Special category States had the first charge on central plan assistance on **90% grant : 10% loan**.
Andhra Pradesh has demanded **special category status** since **2014**.
The Plan-grant system ended with the **Planning Commission's abolition (2015)**.

50.s:
Assertion (A): The Gadgil and Gadgil–Mukherjee formulas lost their earlier role in intergovernmental transfers.
Reason (R): The Planning Commission was abolished and Plan grants ended.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
50.x: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the abolition of the Planning Commission together with the ending of Plan grants explains why the formulas lost their earlier role.
50.tq: Test whether the institutional change stated in the Reason directly explains the policy consequence in the Assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
A is true: the **Gadgil** and **Gadgil-Mukherjee** formulas distributed **Central Plan assistance** and lost relevance.
R is true and explains A: the **Planning Commission was abolished (2015)**, **Plan grants ended**, and transfers shifted to **Finance Commission devolution**.
xa: **Gadgil formula**: **1969**, **Fourth Plan**; Gadgil-Mukherjee from the **Eighth Plan**.
**NITI Aayog has no financial powers** — it did not inherit the Plan-grant role.
The Planning Commission was **extra-constitutional** and once gave the larger part of Central grants under **Art. 282**.

50.s: Under Article 292, the Union Government may borrow:
o: On the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, within limits fixed by Parliament by law
Only on the security of State Consolidated Funds
Only from foreign sources without parliamentary limits
Without reference to any law made by Parliament
50.x: Article 292 authorises Union borrowing on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, subject to limits fixed by Parliament by law.
50.tq: Identify the borrowing authority, security and statutory limit together.
xs: **Art. 292**: the Union borrows **on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, within limits fixed by Parliament by law** — option **(1)** is correct.
State Consolidated Funds secure **state** borrowing under **Art. 293(1)**, not Union borrowing.
Union borrowing is never free of **Parliament's** law-fixed limits, so options 3 and 4 fail.
xa: **Art. 293(1):** a state borrows **only within India**, on its own Consolidated Fund.
**Art. 293(2):** the **Union can lend to states** or guarantee their loans (**APPSC-G2 2025**).
**Art. 266:** the **Consolidated Fund of India** receives all Union revenues, loans raised and loan repayments.

50.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 293(1):
1. A State may borrow only within India.
2. State borrowing is secured on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
3. A State may raise direct foreign loans under Article 293(1).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
50.x: A State may borrow only within India on the security of its Consolidated Fund. Article 293(1) does not permit the State to raise direct loans abroad.
50.tq: Reject the extreme extension of a State's borrowing power beyond the constitutional limitation.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: under **Art. 293(1)** a state borrows **only within India**.
Statement 2 is correct: the loan is on the security of the state's **Consolidated Fund**.
Statement 3 is wrong: a state **cannot raise loans abroad** — no direct foreign loans.
xa: **Art. 293(3):** a state indebted to the Centre **needs the Centre's consent** for a new loan; consent may carry conditions.
The **Net Borrowing Ceiling** is imposed via **Art. 293(3)** and counts **off-budget borrowings**.
**SDLs** (State bonds, **5-30 years**) are auctioned by the **RBI via eKuber**.

50.s: Which of the following correctly describes Article 293(2)?
o: The Supreme Court fixes the borrowing limit of every State.
The State may guarantee loans of the Union without limitation.
Parliament may dissolve a State that defaults on a loan.
The Union may lend to States or guarantee their loans.
50.x: Article 293(2) empowers the Union to make loans to States and to give guarantees in respect of loans raised by States.
50.tq: Ask which authority holds the specific lending or guarantee power.
xs: **Art. 293(2)**: **the Union may lend to States or guarantee their loans** — option **(4)** is correct.
The borrowing limit is fixed by **GoI** (the **Net Borrowing Ceiling**), not the Supreme Court; nothing in Art. 293 lets Parliament dissolve a state.
xa: This clause was asked in **APPSC-G2 2025**.
**Art. 292:** the Union borrows on the security of the **Consolidated Fund of India**.
**Art. 293(3):** while a central loan/guarantee is outstanding, a state needs the **Centre's consent** for a new loan.

50.s: A State has an outstanding loan or guarantee from the Union and proposes to raise a fresh loan. Under Article 293(3), which requirement applies?
o: Consent of the Union is required, and conditions may be attached to that consent.
Only the approval of the Reserve Bank of India is constitutionally required.
Consent of the State Finance Commission is sufficient.
No consent is required if the loan is raised within India.
50.x: When a Union loan or guarantee remains outstanding, the State requires the consent of the Union to raise a further loan; the consent may be subject to conditions.
50.tq: Apply the prior-debt condition to determine which authority's consent is necessary.
xs: Under **Art. 293(3)** the **consent of the Union is required**, and **conditions may be attached** — option **(1)** is correct.
It applies when any **central loan or guarantee is outstanding** — even for loans raised within India, so option 4 is wrong.
**GoI** fixes the market-borrowing limit, not the RBI or a State Finance Commission.
xa: The **Net Borrowing Ceiling** is imposed via Art. 293(3) and **counts off-budget borrowings**.
**State of Kerala v UoI (2024)** challenged it by an original suit under **Art. 131**.
The **16th FC** caps state fiscal deficit at **3% of GSDP** and calls for ending off-budget borrowing.

50.s: State Development Loans are best described as:
o: Foreign currency loans issued directly by the Union Government
State bonds generally having maturities of 5 to 30 years and auctioned by the RBI through eKuber
Short-term grants distributed by the Finance Commission
Loans issued only by private commercial banks without an auction
50.x: State Development Loans are State bonds with maturities of 5–30 years and are auctioned by the Reserve Bank of India through eKuber.
50.tq: Combine the instrument, maturity range and issuing mechanism in one identification question.
xs: **SDLs** are **State bonds** of **5-30 years**, **auctioned by the RBI through eKuber** — option **(2)** is correct.
They are state, not Union, borrowings — states borrow **only within India** under **Art. 293(1)**, so foreign-currency Union loans are wrong.
xa: Nine states raised **₹20,461 crore** through SDLs (**18 Jun 2026**).
SDLs are about **35% of TN's revenue receipts** (2024-25 RE).

50.s: The additional borrowing permission above the normal ceiling for power-sector reforms was stated as:
50.x: An additional borrowing allowance of 0.5 per cent of GSDP was permitted above the normal ceiling for power-sector reforms, including again in 2025–26.
50.tq: Test the exact percentage attached to a conditional borrowing relaxation.
xs: States got extra borrowing room of **0.5% of GSDP** for **power-sector reforms** — option **(3)** is correct.
It ran from **2021-22 to 2025-26**, again in 2025-26, about **₹1,71,612 crore**.
xa: Extra borrowing is also allowed for **NPS/UPS contributions**: **Rs. 62,778 Cr** for all States (2024-25).
**GoI** fixes the market-borrowing limit — the **Net Borrowing Ceiling** under **Art. 293(3)**.
The **16th FC** caps state fiscal deficit at **3% of GSDP**.

50.s: Which one of the following is associated with the recommendations of the Sixteenth Finance Commission regarding State finances?
o: A fiscal deficit ceiling of 3% of GDP for the Union alone
A fiscal deficit ceiling of 5% of GSDP and expansion of off-budget borrowing
A fiscal deficit ceiling of 3% of GSDP and ending off-budget borrowing
A prohibition on all State borrowing from domestic sources
50.x: The Sixteenth Finance Commission caps the State fiscal deficit at 3% of GSDP and calls for ending off-budget borrowing.
50.tq: Match the numerical ceiling with the correct level of government and fiscal practice.
xs: The **16th FC** caps the state fiscal deficit at **3% of GSDP** and calls for **ending off-budget borrowing** — option **(3)** is correct.
It concerns **State** finances, not the Union alone; it seeks to end, not expand, off-budget borrowing.
xa: The **16th FC** (**2026-31**) retained the states' share at **41%**; the Centre **accepted** its devolution recommendations.
The **Net Borrowing Ceiling** already **counts off-budget borrowings**.
AP's memorandum to the 16th FC sought extra weight for **capital-city and infrastructure costs** after bifurcation (**Feb 2026**).

50.s: Kerala v. Union of India (2024) concerned a suit under Article 131 challenging—
o: The appointment of the Governor under Article 156
The distribution of river waters under Article 262
The Net Borrowing Ceiling imposed under Article 293(3)
The validity of GST under Article 279A
50.x: Kerala's 2024 suit under Article 131 challenged the Net Borrowing Ceiling imposed under Article 293(3).
50.tq: Match the case, constitutional jurisdiction and disputed fiscal provision.
xs: **Kerala v UoI (2024)** was an original suit under **Art. 131** against the **Net Borrowing Ceiling imposed under Article 293(3)** — option **(3)** is correct.
The NBC is fixed by **GoI**, counts **off-budget borrowings**, and limits a state's market borrowing.
xa: **Art. 131** suits exclude matters **referred to the Finance Commission**.
**Art. 293(3):** a state indebted to the Centre needs the **Centre's consent** for a new loan.
Kerala also lists "**cessation of GST compensation**" as a fiscal stress (**11 May 2026**).

50.s:
With reference to the Sixteenth Finance Commission, consider the following statements:
1. It retained the vertical share of States in the divisible pool at 41%.
2. The Union Government accepted this recommendation in Budget 2026–27.
3. The vertical share refers to the distribution of the divisible pool among individual States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
50.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Vertical devolution concerns the Centre–State share, whereas distribution among individual States is inter se devolution, making statement 3 incorrect.
50.tq: Separate vertical devolution from inter se distribution before eliminating the reversed definition.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: the **16th FC** (2026-31) **retained 41%** of the divisible pool for states.
Statement 2: the Centre **accepted** its devolution recommendations.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **vertical share** is the Centre-States split of the **divisible pool**, not the split among individual states.
xa: Non-shareable cesses (~**18%** of gross tax revenue) cut effective devolution to about **31-32%**.
The **16th FC** caps state fiscal deficit at **3% of GSDP**.

50.s: The 2024 “Chalo Delhi” protest by southern States was primarily associated with opposition to
o: the replacement of grants by cesses
the abolition of State Development Loans
conditionality attached to Centrally Sponsored Schemes only
50.x: The protest concerned the perceived adverse effect of population-heavy or population-based criteria on the devolution share of southern States.
50.tq: Identify the policy issue represented by the protest instead of confusing it with other fiscal criticisms.
xs: The **2024 "Chalo Delhi"** protest by southern states was against **population-based criteria in devolution** — option **(3)** is correct.
Southern states objected to **population-heavy** devolution criteria.
xa: Gadgil-type formulas weighted **population** at **60%**.
Other debates: **vertical fiscal imbalance**, **CSS conditionality**, and **non-shareable cesses**.
AP's memorandum to the **16th FC** sought extra weight for **capital-city and infrastructure costs** (**Feb 2026**).

50.s: Which one of the following is NOT identified as a criticism or debate concerning Centre–State fiscal relations?
o: Conditionality attached to Centrally Sponsored Schemes
50.x: Vertical fiscal imbalance, non-shareable cesses and CSS conditionality are identified criticisms. Abolition of the Finance Commission is not identified as such an issue.
50.tq: Find the option that introduces an unrelated institutional claim rather than a stated fiscal criticism.
xs: **Abolition of the Finance Commission** is NOT among the listed debates — option **(1)** is the answer.
The listed criticisms are **vertical fiscal imbalance**, **CSS conditionality**, and **non-shareable cesses**.
The Finance Commission still functions: the **16th FC** covers **2026-31**.
xa: Non-shareable cesses are ~**18%** of gross tax revenue → effective devolution near **31-32%** vs the **41%** award.
Southern states' **2024 "Chalo Delhi"** protest opposed **population-based** devolution criteria.
The **CAG's State Finances 2023-24** report is a current reference.

50.s: The post-2014 demand specifically associated with Andhra Pradesh in the context of Centre–State relations is for
o: separate representation in the Finance Commission
transfer of all Union taxes to the State
50.x: Andhra Pradesh has continued its post-2014 demand for special category status.
50.tq: Identify the State-specific demand without extending it into an absolute fiscal claim.
xs: Andhra Pradesh's post-**2014** demand is for **special category status** — option **(2)** is correct.
Special category states got central plan assistance on **90% grant : 10% loan**.
xa: Parameters: **hilly terrain**, low population density/**tribal population**, **strategic border location**, **backwardness**, **non-viable finances**.
AP's memorandum to the **16th FC** sought extra weight for **capital-city and infrastructure costs** after bifurcation (**Feb 2026**).
**AP net borrowings** were **Rs. 60,485.40 Cr** in 2024-25.

50.s:
Consider the following statements regarding non-shareable cesses and effective devolution:
1. About 18% of the Centre’s gross tax revenue is estimated to be in non-shareable cesses.
2. Non-shareable cesses reduce the effective amount available for tax devolution to States.
3. Effective devolution is thereby estimated to remain near 31–32%, despite a 41% award.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
50.x: All three statements are correct. Non-shareable cesses, estimated at about 18% of gross tax revenue, reduce the effective devolution to around 31–32%, below the 41% award share.
50.tq: Connect the quantitative figure with its fiscal consequence instead of treating the awarded share as the effective share.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: non-shareable cesses are ~**18%** of the Centre's gross tax revenue.
Statement 2: cesses are excluded from the divisible pool, cutting what is shared under **Art. 270**.
Statement 3: effective devolution is near **31-32%** vs the **41%** award.
xa: The **Art. 270** pool covers all Union taxes **except** Arts 268, 269, 269A, **surcharges and cesses**.
**Art. 271 surcharges** are **exclusively for the Union** — a false "shared with states" statement was set in **APPSC-G1 2024**.
**Net proceeds** are certified by the **CAG**.

51.s: Which of the following correctly describes the subject matter of Part XI of the Constitution?
o: Elections and special provisions for certain classes
Emergency provisions and amendment of the Constitution
Legislative and administrative relations between the Union and the States
Financial relations and trade within India
51.x: Part XI contains legislative relations in Articles 245–255 and administrative relations in Articles 256–263 between the Union and the States.
51.tq: Part-number and subject matching using the adjacent Part XII as a distractor.
xs: Part XI deals with **legislative and administrative relations** between the Union and the States — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Legislative relations** run from **Arts 245-255**; **administrative relations** from **Arts 256-263**.
**Financial relations** (option 4) belong to **Part XII**, not Part XI.
xa: **Part XII** covers **financial relations** in **Arts 268-293**.
UKPSC 2024 keyed **Part XI** as the Part on Centre-State legislative and administrative relations.
Shaping factors of Centre-State relations: **constitutional provisions, conventions, judicial interpretation** and **mechanisms for dialogue** (UPPSC 2009: all four).

51.s: Part XII of the Constitution primarily deals with—
o: Emergency relations between the Union and the States
Financial relations between the Union and the States
Administrative relations between the Union and the States
51.x: Part XII deals with financial relations, including Articles 268 to 293.
51.tq: Direct Part-subject recall with a Part XI subject as the principal trap.
xs: Part XII primarily deals with **financial relations** between the Union and the States — so option **(2)** is correct.
It spans **Arts 268-293**.
**Administrative relations** (option 3) sit in **Part XI** (**Arts 256-263**), along with legislative relations.
xa: **Part XI** = legislative (**Arts 245-255**) + administrative (**Arts 256-263**) relations.
During a National Emergency, the President can **reduce or cancel** financial transfers under **Art 354**.
⚠ Fiscal friction: cesses and surcharges are excluded, so the divisible pool is only about **81%** of gross tax revenue.

51.s: Which one of the following is a unitary feature of the Indian Constitution?
o: A constitutional prohibition on Union directions to States
Separate and independent judicial systems for the Union and each State
Dual citizenship for Union and State citizens
All India Services serving both the Union and the States
51.x: All India Services are a unitary feature because they provide a common administrative structure serving both the Union and the States. India has single citizenship and an integrated judiciary.
51.tq: Identify the one genuine unitary feature among reversed or non-existent federal features.
xs: **All India Services** serving both the Union and the States are a **unitary feature** — so option **(4)** is correct.
India has **single citizenship**, not dual citizenship (option 3).
India has an **integrated judiciary**, not separate Union and State judicial systems (option 2).
The Union can in fact give **directions** to States (e.g. **Art 353** in an emergency; defying them counts as a breakdown under **Art 365**), so option 1 is wrong.
xa: Unitary features listed together: **single citizenship**, **integrated judiciary**, **AIS**, **emergency powers**.
**AIS** is also an area of friction because of **central control of officers**.
Planning process and party politics also shape Centre-State relations (**UKPSC 2002**).

51.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of Article 353 during a National Emergency?
o: State Governments are suspended and Parliament directly administers all States.
The Supreme Court assumes the executive functions of the States.
The Governor alone exercises all executive power of the State.
The Centre may give directions to a State on any matter, but State Governments are not suspended.
51.x: Article 353 enlarges the executive authority of the Union, enabling it to direct a State on any matter. It does not suspend State Governments.
51.tq: Separate the expanded Union power from the false claim that State Governments are abolished.
xs: Under **Art 353**, the Centre can **direct a State on "any" matter**, but **State Governments are not suspended** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Option 1 is wrong: Art 353 enlarges Union executive power; it does not suspend State governments or hand them to Parliament.
This is the **executive** effect of a National Emergency.
xa: ⚠ **250 – 353 – 354** = **legislative – executive – financial** effects of a National Emergency.
**Art 250**: Parliament can legislate on **any State List subject**; such laws lapse **6 months** after the emergency ends.
**Art 354**: the President can **reduce or cancel** transfers until the end of that financial year.

51.s: Under Article 354, what may the President do during a National Emergency?
o: Transfer all State taxes to the Consolidated Fund of India
Suspend the distribution of all taxes without placing the order before Parliament
Reduce or cancel certain transfers to States until the end of the financial year
51.x: Article 354 permits the President to modify or reduce financial transfers during the Emergency, generally until the end of the financial year. The order is required to be laid before Parliament.
51.tq: Direct financial-effect question testing the exact scope of Article 354.
xs: Under **Art 354**, the President may **reduce or cancel transfers** to States **until the end of that financial year** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The orders must be **laid before Parliament**, so option 2 ("without placing before Parliament") is wrong.
Art 354 is the **financial** effect of a National Emergency.
xa: ⚠ **250 – 353 – 354** = **legislative – executive – financial**.
**Art 353**: Centre can direct a State on **"any" matter**; State governments are **not suspended**.
Part XII (**Arts 268-293**) governs financial relations in normal times.

51.s: Which of the following best characterises the federal structure of India during a National Emergency?
o: It becomes more strongly federal because State powers are constitutionally protected.
It remains completely unaffected in legislative, executive and financial spheres.
It becomes confederal, with States acquiring international personality.
It becomes quasi-unitary, with increased powers for the Union.
51.x: A National Emergency strengthens the Union and makes the constitutional system operate in a unitary or quasi-unitary manner.
51.tq: Use the overall constitutional effect rather than one isolated emergency provision.
xs: During a National Emergency the Constitution becomes **unitary rather than federal**, i.e. **quasi-unitary** with increased Union powers — so option **(4)** is correct.
All three spheres change: **legislative (Art 250)**, **executive (Art 353)** and **financial (Art 354)** — so option 2 is wrong.
xa: Parliament can legislate on **any State List subject** (**Art 250**); such laws lapse **6 months** after the emergency.
The **Lok Sabha term** can be extended by **1 year at a time**.
Other unitary features: **single citizenship**, **integrated judiciary**, **AIS**, **emergency powers**.

51.s: During the operation of a National Emergency, the term of the Lok Sabha may be extended by Parliament by—
o: Five years at a time, with the approval of the Supreme Court
Six months at a time, without any limit
One year at a time, subject to constitutional conditions
Two years at a time, permanently
51.x: The term of the Lok Sabha may be extended by Parliament for one year at a time during a National Emergency, subject to the constitutional limitation concerning the period after the Emergency ends.
51.tq: Test the exact duration and avoid confusing it with the duration of the Emergency itself.
xs: During a National Emergency, the **Lok Sabha term** may be extended by **one year at a time** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Options 1, 2 and 4 give periods (**five years**, **six months**, **two years**) the notes do not provide for.
xa: **Six months** is the lapse period for Parliament's State-List laws after the emergency ends (**Art 250**) — ⚠ don't confuse it with the term extension.
During the emergency the Constitution becomes **unitary rather than federal**.
**Art 353** — Centre directs States on **"any" matter**; **Art 354** — President can **reduce or cancel** transfers.

51.s: Article 355 imposes on the Union the duty to—
o: Appoint all State ministers during political instability.
Permit States to maintain independent armed forces.
Ensure that every State follows the same social and economic policy.
Protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and ensure constitutional governance.
51.x: Article 355 requires the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to ensure that the government of each State is carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
51.tq: Direct duty-and-function question using neighbouring but constitutionally unsupported powers as distractors.
xs: **Art 355** obliges the Union to **protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance** and ensure **governance per the Constitution** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The other options (appointing State ministers, State armed forces, uniform policy) are not part of Art 355.
xa: The Art 355 duty is the **justification for Art 356** (President's Rule).
**Art 365**: a State **defying Union directions** counts as a breakdown of constitutional machinery.
Asked in **UPSC 2003** and **UPPSC 2001**.

51.s: The constitutional justification most directly associated with the imposition of President's Rule under Article 356 is the Union's duty under—
51.x: The duty imposed on the Union by Article 355 to protect States and ensure constitutional government provides the constitutional basis connected with Article 356 action.
51.tq: Discriminate between the Union's protective duty and unrelated constitutional provisions.
xs: President's Rule under **Art 356** is justified by the Union's duty under **Article 355** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Art 355**: protect every State against **external aggression and internal disturbance** and ensure governance per the Constitution.
xa: **Art 365**: defying Union directions counts as a **breakdown** (a ground linked to Art 356).
**Art 356** has been used **over 125 times**, often against **opposition governments**.
⚠ **250 – 353 – 354** are the emergency Articles (legislative – executive – financial), not Art 356.

51.s: Laws made by Parliament on State List matters under Article 250 cease to have effect:
o: One year after the Emergency ends
Only after repeal by every State Legislature
Six months after the Emergency ends
51.x: Such laws do not become void immediately; they cease to have effect six months after the National Emergency ends.
51.tq: Distinguish the post-emergency sunset period from immediate expiry.
xs: Laws made by Parliament on State List subjects under **Art 250** lapse **6 months after the emergency ends** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They do not lapse **immediately**, nor need repeal by State Legislatures.
xa: **Art 250** = legislative effect; **353** = executive; **354** = financial.
⚠ **One year at a time** is the Lok Sabha term extension during emergency, not the lapse period.
During an emergency the Constitution becomes **unitary rather than federal**.

51.s: The Governor's office frequently becomes an area of Centre-State friction because the Governor—
o: Is elected directly by the people of the State for a fixed term
Is appointed by the Chief Minister and removable by the Assembly
Is a permanent member of the Union Cabinet
Holds office during the pleasure of the President, under Article 156
51.x: The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President under Article 156. Disputes also arise over assent to Bills and addresses to the Legislative Assembly.
51.tq: Who-controls-the-office question testing appointment and tenure authority.
xs: The Governor **holds office at the President's pleasure** under **Art 156** — so option **(4)** is correct.
This makes the office a tool of the Centre, and disputes follow over **assent** to Bills and the **Assembly address**.
xa: Recent cases: **delays on bills** in **TN and Kerala** (**23 Mar 2026**).
**Addresses to the Assembly skipped** (**26 Jan 2026**).
Other friction areas: **Art 356** misuse, **fiscal** devolution, **AIS / river waters**, **CBI** consent.

51.s: Which of the following has been identified as a recurring area of friction concerning Governors?
o: Appointment of judges to the Supreme Court by State Legislatures
Allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha by municipal bodies
Delay in assenting to Bills and issues relating to the address of the Assembly
Determination of the Union Budget by the Governor
51.x: Delays in assent to Bills and disputes regarding the Governor's address to the Legislative Assembly are recurring Centre-State friction points.
51.tq: Direct issue-identification question focused on the Governor's constitutional role.
xs: **Delay in assent to Bills** and disputes over the **Assembly address** are recurring Governor friction points — so option **(3)** is correct.
The Governor holds office at the **President's pleasure** (**Art 156**), which fuels these disputes.
xa: Bills delayed in **TN and Kerala** (**23 Mar 2026**).
Addresses to the Assembly **skipped** (**26 Jan 2026**).
TN's **Kurian Joseph Committee** (Part I, **16 Feb 2026**) calls for a **"structural reset"** of federalism.

51.s: President's Rule under Article 356 has been used in India—
o: Exactly 100 times, exclusively with State consent
Only once, in a Union Territory
Fewer than 25 times and only during wartime
More than 125 times, often against governments led by opposition parties
51.x: Article 356 has been used over 125 times, and its frequent use against opposition governments has been a major source of Centre-State friction.
51.tq: Use the approximate historical frequency and the associated political pattern together.
xs: **Art 356** has been used **over 125 times**, often **against opposition governments** — so option **(4)** is correct.
This frequent use is a major area of Centre-State friction.
xa: The constitutional justification for Art 356 is the Union's duty under **Art 355**.
**Art 365**: defying Union directions counts as a **breakdown**.
Other friction areas: **Governor** (Art 156), **fiscal** (divisible pool ~**81%**), **CBI** consent, **Art 262** river disputes.

51.s: Why does the exclusion of cesses and surcharges from the divisible pool create friction between the Union and the States?
o: Because cesses and surcharges are constitutionally collected by States.
Because the divisible pool is limited to about 81% of gross tax revenue.
Because States receive the entire gross tax revenue directly.
Because the divisible pool consists only of non-tax revenue.
51.x: Cesses and surcharges are excluded from the divisible pool, leaving the pool at approximately 81% of gross tax revenue and reducing the shareable base for States.
51.tq: Link the fiscal mechanism to its federal consequence rather than choosing an absolute claim.
xs: Because **cesses and surcharges are excluded**, the **divisible pool is limited to about 81% of gross tax revenue** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This shrinks the base shared with States, a key **fiscal** friction point.
xa: States now demand **50%** devolution (**3 Feb 2026**).
**GST compensation** ended in **June 2022**.
Borrowing limits led to litigation — **Kerala v.** the Union.

51.s:
Match the following areas of Centre-State friction with the relevant constitutional or statutory reference:
List-I
 a. Inter-State river-water disputes
 b. Consent for CBI investigation
 c. Governor's tenure
List-II
 i. Section 6 of the DSPE Act
 ii. Article 156
 iii. Article 262
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
51.x: Article 262 concerns inter-State river-water disputes, Section 6 of the DSPE Act concerns State consent for CBI investigation, and Article 156 concerns the Governor's office.
51.tq: Start from the statutory CBI reference and complete the constitutional pairings.
xs: Correct matching: **a-iii, b-i, c-ii** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**River-water disputes** → **Art 262**; **CBI consent** → **Sec 6 of the DSPE Act**; **Governor's tenure** → **Art 156** (President's pleasure).
xa: Several States have **withdrawn CBI consent** (APPCA 2026).
**Art 356** has been used **over 125 times**, often against opposition governments.
Fiscal friction: divisible pool only about **81%** of gross tax revenue.

51.s:
With reference to the Central Bureau of Investigation, consider the following statements:
1. State consent is required under Section 6 of the DSPE Act.
2. Several States have withdrawn the consent previously granted.
3. The CBI can investigate in every State without any State-related legal limitation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
51.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The requirement of State consent means that the CBI does not have an unlimited, State-independent power to investigate in every State.
51.tq: Reject the absolute claim in statement 3 by applying the consent requirement.
xs: **Statements 1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the CBI needs **State consent** under **Sec 6 of the DSPE Act**.
Statement 2 is correct: **several States have withdrawn** that consent.
Statement 3 is wrong: the consent requirement is exactly a **State-related legal limitation** on the CBI.
xa: Other friction areas: **Governor** (**Art 156**), **Art 356**, **AIS**, **Art 262** river-water disputes.
Fiscal friction: divisible pool about **81%** of gross tax revenue as **cesses and surcharges** are excluded.

51.s: Which one of the following statements regarding GST compensation is correct?
o: GST compensation is constitutionally guaranteed indefinitely without a time limit.
The compensation began only after the 16th Finance Commission.
The compensation promised to States ended in June 2022.
GST compensation was abolished before the GST regime commenced.
51.x: The compensation arrangement promised to States under the GST framework ended in June 2022.
51.tq: Test the precise end date of a well-known fiscal arrangement.
xs: **GST compensation** promised to States **ended in June 2022** — so option **(3)** is correct.
So it was not indefinite (option 1); its end is itself a recent friction issue.
xa: States demand **50%** devolution (**3 Feb 2026**).
**Borrowing** limits: **Kerala v.** the Union.
Divisible pool is only about **81%** of gross tax revenue because **cesses and surcharges** are excluded.

51.s: If Special Category Status had been extended to Andhra Pradesh in the stated form, it would have implied what level of central funding for Centrally Sponsored Schemes?
51.x: The proposed Special Category Status would have meant 90% central funding for Centrally Sponsored Schemes.
51.tq: Direct percentage recall using progressively higher funding shares as distractors.
xs: **SCS** would have meant **90%** central funding for **Centrally Sponsored Schemes** — so option **(4)** is correct.
SCS was promised in Parliament by PM **Manmohan Singh** but **not written into APRA 2014**.
xa: AP got **special packages** instead of SCS.
Opposition says ~**₹5 lakh crore** of APRA promises are unmet — **Kadapa steel plant**, **Dugarajapatnam port**, metro rail.
**Polavaram** is a **national project** under **Sec 90 of APRA 2014**, **100%** Centre-funded.
