51.s: Which of the following is included among the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act-related assurances claimed by the opposition to remain unmet?
o: Kadapa steel plant, Dugarajapatnam port and metro rail
Visakhapatnam airport, Kurnool dam and inland waterways
Amaravati High Court, Sriharikota port and a national university only
Polavaram barrage, Hyderabad metro and a new Parliament building
51.x: The cited unmet assurances include the Kadapa steel plant, Dugarajapatnam port and metro rail, and were valued at about ₹5 lakh crore by the opposition.
51.tq: Use the cluster of named assurances and reject substitutions from nearby infrastructure projects.
xs: The unmet APRA assurances cited are the **Kadapa steel plant**, **Dugarajapatnam port** and **metro rail** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The opposition values the unmet promises at about **₹5 lakh crore**.
xa: **SCS** was promised by PM **Manmohan Singh** but **not written into APRA 2014**; it would mean **90%** CSS funding.
**Polavaram**: national project under **Sec 90 of APRA 2014**.
**SCS + APRA promises** are AP's main federal grievances.

51.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Polavaram project:
1. It was declared a national project under Section 89 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014.
2. As a national project, it is 100% funded by the Centre.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
51.x: Statement 1 is wrong: Polavaram is a national project under Section 90 of APRA 2014, not Section 89 (a common trap). Statement 2 is correct: it is 100% Centre-funded. Hence A, C and D are incorrect.
51.tq: Polavaram = Section 90, APRA 2014, 100% central funding.
xs: Only **statement 2** is correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: Polavaram is a **national project** under **Sec 90** of APRA 2014, **not Sec 89**.
Statement 2 is correct: as a national project it is **100% Centre-funded**.
xa: ⚠ **Trap:** some notes wrongly cite **Sec 89** or the **LARR Act**.
Total sanctioned: **₹12,157 crore**; **89%** complete; to be dedicated by **March 2027**.
Budget 2026-27: **₹3,320 crore** for storage up to **41.15 m** vs demand for full **45.72 m**.

51.s: Which of the following correctly describes the latest stated position regarding Polavaram funding and progress?
o: ₹12,157 crore has been sanctioned in total; the project was 89% complete and targeted for dedication by March 2027.
₹3,320 crore has been sanctioned in total; the project was 41.15% complete and targeted for dedication by June 2026.
₹45,720 crore has been sanctioned in total; the project was 100% complete and dedicated in 2024.
₹5 lakh crore has been sanctioned in total; the project was 50% complete and targeted for dedication by March 2028.
51.x: The stated figures are total sanctions of ₹12,157 crore, 89% completion and a target for dedication by March 2027.
51.tq: Combine three numerical facts and reject options that swap an allocation figure for the total sanction.
xs: **₹12,157 crore** sanctioned in total, **89% complete**, to be dedicated by **March 2027** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**₹3,320 crore** (option 2) is the **Budget 2026-27** allocation, not the total; **41.15** is a storage height in metres, not a percentage.
**₹5 lakh crore** (option 4) is the opposition's estimate of unmet APRA promises.
xa: Budget 2026-27 funds storage up to **41.15 m** vs the demand for the full **45.72 m**.
Polavaram is a **national project** under **Sec 90 of APRA 2014**, **100%** Centre-funded.
⚠ Not **Sec 89** or the LARR Act.

51.s: Regarding Special Category Status (SCS) for Andhra Pradesh, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: SCS was written into the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 but never notified
SCS was promised in Parliament by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh but was not written into the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014
SCS was granted to Andhra Pradesh by the 14th Finance Commission
SCS was promised by Prime Minister Narendra Modi through Section 90 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014
51.x: Prime Minister Manmohan Singh promised SCS in Parliament, but the promise was not written into APRA 2014, and AP got special packages instead. It was never part of the Act. The 14th Finance Commission dropped the special/general category distinction rather than granting SCS. Section 90 of APRA concerns Polavaram as a national project, not SCS.
51.tq: SCS: promised on the floor, missing from the Act.
xs: **SCS** was promised in Parliament by PM **Manmohan Singh** but was **not written into APRA 2014** — so option **(2)** is correct.
So option 1 (written into the Act) is wrong; AP got **special packages** instead.
**Sec 90 of APRA 2014** concerns **Polavaram** as a national project, not SCS — option 4 is wrong.
xa: SCS would have meant **90%** central funding for CSS.
Unmet APRA assurances (~**₹5 lakh crore**): **Kadapa steel plant**, **Dugarajapatnam port**, metro rail.
**SCS + APRA** promises are AP's main federal grievances; **Polavaram** is the flagship central commitment.

51.s: Which committee has been associated with the call for a “structural reset” of federalism?
o: Kurian Joseph Committee of Tamil Nadu
51.x: The Tamil Nadu Kurian Joseph Committee was associated with the call for a structural reset of federalism.
51.tq: Direct committee-identification question using familiar Centre-State committees as distractors.
xs: Tamil Nadu's **Kurian Joseph Committee** calls for a **"structural reset"** of federalism — so option **(4)** is correct.
Its **Part I** report came on **16 Feb 2026**.
xa: Recent friction: Governors delaying bills in **TN and Kerala** (**23 Mar 2026**).
States demand **50%** devolution (**3 Feb 2026**).
**GST compensation** ended in **June 2022**.

51.s: Which of the following best captures the Andhra Pradesh-specific federal grievances identified in relation to Centre-State relations?
o: Only the appointment of municipal commissioners and the creation of new districts
Special Category Status and Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act assurances, with Polavaram as a flagship central commitment
Exclusive control over the Union List and abolition of the Finance Commission
Withdrawal from the GST Council and establishment of an independent currency
51.x: For Andhra Pradesh, the principal federal grievances are the demand for Special Category Status and implementation of assurances under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act. Polavaram represents a major central commitment.
51.tq: Synthesize the State-specific issues without extending them into constitutionally impossible demands.
xs: AP's federal grievances are **SCS** and **APRA assurances**, with **Polavaram** as the **flagship central commitment** — so option **(2)** is correct.
SCS was promised by PM **Manmohan Singh** but **not written into APRA 2014**.
xa: Unmet APRA promises (~**₹5 lakh crore**): **Kadapa steel plant**, **Dugarajapatnam port**, metro rail.
**Polavaram**: national project under **Sec 90 of APRA 2014**; **89%** complete; dedication by **March 2027**.
SCS would mean **90%** central funding for CSS.

52.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with its source?
o: Emergency provisions — Government of India Act, 1935; ordinance power — Government of India Act, 1935
Emergency provisions — Weimar Constitution; ordinance power — Government of India Act, 1919
Suspension of Fundamental Rights — Government of India Act, 1935; emergency provisions — Weimar Constitution
Emergency provisions — Charter Act, 1833; ordinance power — Weimar Constitution
52.x: The emergency provisions and the ordinance power under Articles 123 and 213 are both regarded as relics of the Government of India Act, 1935. The Weimar Constitution is associated with suspension of Fundamental Rights during an emergency.
52.tq: Separate the common source of two constitutional features from the distinct German source of another feature.
xs: Both the **emergency provisions** and the **ordinance power** come from the **Government of India Act, 1935** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The ordinance power (**Arts 123/213**) is also a **1935 Act relic**, so options pairing it with the 1919 Act or other sources are wrong.
xa: Three emergencies: **National (Art. 352)**, **President's Rule (Art. 356)**, **Financial (Art. 360)**.
⚠ Approval windows: **1 month – 2 months – 6 months** = **352 – 360 – 356**.
**Art. 355** (Union's duty to protect states) is the basis for **Art. 356**.

52.s: Which constitutional amendment substituted the expression “internal disturbance” with “armed rebellion” as a ground for National Emergency under Article 352?
52.x: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 replaced “internal disturbance” with “armed rebellion” in Article 352.
52.tq: Discriminate between closely numbered Constitutional Amendments and their specific changes.
xs: The **44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978** replaced "**internal disturbance**" with "**armed rebellion**" in Art. 352 — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **38th CAA (1975)** made satisfaction non-justiciable; the **39th** shielded PM/Speaker election disputes; the **42nd (1976)** raised terms to **6 years**.
xa: The 44th CAA also made **written Cabinet advice** mandatory — **Art. 352(3)**.
It barred **Art. 358** for **armed rebellion**, and stopped **Art. 359** from touching **Arts. 20 and 21**.
⚠ The **1975** emergency was declared on "**internal disturbance**" — the ground before the 44th CAA.

52.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the written advice required for proclamation of National Emergency:
1. The advice must be given by the Union Cabinet.
2. The requirement was inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act.
3. The requirement is contained in Article 352(3).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
52.x: All three statements are correct. Article 352(3), inserted through the 44th Amendment, makes written advice of the Union Cabinet mandatory.
52.tq: Use the constitutional sub-clause and amendment together to verify all statements.
xs: **All three statements** are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
Statement 1: the advice must be **written advice of the Union Cabinet**.
Statement 2: it was inserted by the **44th CAA** (**1978**).
Statement 3: it sits in **Art. 352(3)**.
xa: ⚠ **Trap:** some UPSC notes wrongly say "new **Article 352A**".
Approval by both Houses within **1 month** by **special majority**.
Notice by **1/10 of Lok Sabha members** → special sitting within **14 days** to consider disapproval.

52.s:
Consider the following statements regarding parliamentary approval of a National Emergency:
1. The proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month.
2. The approval requires only a simple majority in each House.
3. Once approved, it continues for six months and can be extended indefinitely with approval every six months.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
52.x: Statement 1 is correct: both Houses must approve within one month. Statement 2 is wrong: approval needs a special majority (simple majority within two months applies to a Financial Emergency). Statement 3 is correct: it then runs six months and can be extended indefinitely, six months at a time. So A omits 3, and C and D wrongly include 2.
52.tq: National = 1 month + special majority; Financial = 2 months + simple majority.
xs: **Statements 1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: both Houses must approve within **1 month**.
Statement 2 is wrong: approval needs a **special majority**; **simple majority** within **2 months** is for a **Financial Emergency**.
Statement 3 is correct: it runs **6 months**, extendable **indefinitely** with approval every 6 months.
xa: President's Rule: **6 months** per approval, maximum **3 years**.
Financial Emergency has **no maximum period** — continues till revoked.

52.s:
Consider the following statements regarding revocation of a National Emergency:
1. The President must revoke it only if the Lok Sabha disapproves it by a special majority.
2. If one-tenth of the members of the Lok Sabha give notice, a special sitting must be held within 14 days to consider disapproval.
3. The President may revoke it at any time.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
52.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the President must revoke it if the Lok Sabha disapproves it by a simple majority. Statement 2 is correct: notice by 1/10 of Lok Sabha members requires a special sitting within 14 days. Statement 3 is correct: the President may revoke it at any time. So A and D wrongly include 1, and C omits 2.
52.tq: Approval is hard (special majority), revocation is easy (simple majority of Lok Sabha).
xs: **Statements 2 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: the President must revoke if the **Lok Sabha** disapproves by a **simple majority**, not special majority.
Statement 2 is correct: notice by **1/10 of Lok Sabha members** → special sitting within **14 days**.
Statement 3 is correct: the President may revoke it **any time**.
xa: President's Rule too can be revoked by the President **at any time**, with **no parliamentary approval** needed.
Approval of a National Emergency: both Houses within **1 month** by **special majority**.

52.s:
Consider the following statements regarding judicial review of a proclamation under Article 352:
1. The 38th Constitutional Amendment made the President’s satisfaction non-justiciable.
2. The bar on judicial review was subsequently reversed.
3. In Minerva Mills, the Supreme Court held that the proclamation could be reviewed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
52.x: The 38th Amendment attempted to make the satisfaction non-justiciable; this position was later reversed, and Minerva Mills affirmed that the proclamation is reviewable.
52.tq: Arrange the legal development as an amendment, reversal and judicial ruling.
xs: **All three statements** are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
Statement 1: the **38th CAA (1975)** made the President's satisfaction **non-justiciable**.
Statement 2: that bar was **later reversed**.
Statement 3: **Minerva Mills (1980)** held the proclamation **reviewable**.
xa: **S.R. Bommai (1994)**: a proclamation under **Art. 356** is subject to **judicial review** (mala fide or irrelevant grounds).
**ADM Jabalpur (1976)** held even the right to life unenforceable; rejected in **Puttaswamy (2017)**.
**Rameshwar Prasad (2006)** struck down the **Bihar Assembly** dissolution.

52.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (National Emergency)
A. First proclamation
B. Second proclamation
C. Third proclamation

List-II (Year or date)
I. 25 June 1975
II. 1962
III. 1971

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
52.x: The first National Emergency was proclaimed in 1962, the second in 1971, and the third on 25 June 1975.
52.tq: Start with the sure chronological pair and then eliminate the remaining codes.
xs: Correct match: **A–II, B–III, C–I** — so option **(1)** is correct.
1st emergency **1962** (**Chinese aggression**); 2nd **1971** (**Indo-Pak war**); 3rd **25 June 1975** ("**internal disturbance**").
xa: The 1975 emergency was proclaimed by President **Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed**.
**25 June** is observed as "**Samvidhan Hatya Diwas**".
The **44th CAA, 1978** later replaced "internal disturbance" with "**armed rebellion**".

52.s: Which event immediately preceded the proclamation of the National Emergency in June 1975 and formed an important background to it?
o: The Allahabad High Court voided Indira Gandhi’s 1971 election.
The Lok Sabha passed a resolution of no confidence against the Union Cabinet.
The Supreme Court struck down the 42nd Amendment.
The Election Commission postponed the general election indefinitely.
52.x: The Allahabad High Court judgment voiding Indira Gandhi’s 1971 election formed the immediate political background to the 1975 Emergency.
52.tq: Link a constitutional event to its immediate triggering political development.
xs: The trigger was the **Allahabad HC voiding Indira Gandhi's 1971 election** (**Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
The emergency followed on **25 June 1975** on the ground of "**internal disturbance**".
xa: The **39th CAA** then put the **PM's and Speaker's election disputes** beyond courts.
The **42nd CAA (1976)** — the "**mini-constitution**" — raised Lok Sabha/Assembly terms to **6 years**.
**ADM Jabalpur (1976)** held even the right to life unenforceable.

52.s: The 39th Constitutional Amendment Act, enacted during the Emergency period, placed which disputes beyond the jurisdiction of courts?
o: Disputes relating to elections of the President and Vice-President only
All disputes concerning State Legislative Assemblies
Election disputes concerning the Prime Minister and the Speaker
Disputes relating to the proclamation of Financial Emergency
52.x: The 39th Amendment placed election disputes concerning the Prime Minister and the Speaker beyond the courts.
52.tq: Match the amendment with the particular constitutional office affected, not a neighbouring office.
xs: The **39th CAA** put **election disputes of the PM and the Speaker** beyond courts — so option **(3)** is correct.
It followed the **Allahabad HC** voiding **Indira Gandhi's 1971 election**.
xa: **38th CAA (1975)**: made satisfaction **non-justiciable** (later reversed).
**42nd CAA (1976)**: "mini-constitution"; terms raised to **6 years**.
**44th CAA, 1978**: "internal disturbance" → "**armed rebellion**"; written Cabinet advice.

52.s: Which of the following was a consequence of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976?
o: The term of the Lok Sabha was reduced to four years.
The terms of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies were raised to six years.
The President’s power to proclaim Emergency was abolished.
The Rajya Sabha was made subject to dissolution every five years.
52.x: The 42nd Amendment, popularly called the “mini-Constitution,” raised the terms of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies to six years.
52.tq: Identify the specific institutional change associated with the “mini-Constitution.”
xs: The **42nd CAA (1976)** raised the **terms of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies to six years** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is called the "**mini-constitution**".
xa: **38th CAA (1975)**: satisfaction **non-justiciable**; **39th**: PM and Speaker election disputes beyond courts.
**44th CAA, 1978**: ground changed to "**armed rebellion**"; **Arts. 20 and 21** protected from **Art. 359**.
During an emergency, terms can be extended **1 year at a time**, not beyond **6 months** after it ends.

52.s: Since 2025, 25 June is observed as:
52.x: 25 June is observed as “Samvidhan Hatya Diwas” in remembrance of the proclamation of the 1975 Emergency.
52.tq: Test the exact official commemorative expression rather than a near-synonym.
xs: **25 June** is observed as "**Samvidhan Hatya Diwas**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
It marks the emergency proclaimed on **25 June 1975** on the ground of "**internal disturbance**".
xa: It was proclaimed by President **Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed**.
Earlier emergencies: **1962** (Chinese aggression) and **1971** (Indo-Pak war).
Background: **Allahabad HC** voided Indira Gandhi's **1971** election.

52.s: Which of the following statements about the 1975 National Emergency is correct?
o: It was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 by President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed on the ground of internal disturbance.
It was proclaimed by Parliament after the 44th Amendment on the ground of internal disturbance.
It was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 by the President on the ground of external aggression.
It was proclaimed on 26 January 1975 by the Union Cabinet on the ground of armed rebellion.
52.x: President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed the Emergency on 25 June 1975 on the ground of internal disturbance.
52.tq: Combine the date, constitutional ground and constitutional authority in one precise recall question.
xs: It was proclaimed on **25 June 1975** by President **Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed** on the ground of **internal disturbance** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was not on "external aggression" (that was **1971**) and predates the **44th CAA, 1978**, which brought in "**armed rebellion**".
xa: The **1st** emergency was in **1962** (**Chinese aggression**).
**25 June** is now "**Samvidhan Hatya Diwas**".
After the 44th CAA, **written advice of the Union Cabinet** is mandatory (**Art. 352(3)**).

52.s: A National Emergency under Article 352 may be proclaimed when there is an imminent danger of war, external aggression or armed rebellion. Such a proclamation may extend to:
o: The whole or any part of India
Any State only, but not the Union Territories
The whole of India and neighbouring countries
52.x: Article 352 permits a National Emergency to be proclaimed for the whole of India or for any part of India when the prescribed imminent danger exists.
52.tq: Test the scope of a constitutional power by separating “whole” from “whole or part.”
xs: A National Emergency can cover the **whole or a part of India** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It can be declared even on **imminent danger** of war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
xa: Grounds after the **44th CAA, 1978**: "internal disturbance" replaced by "**armed rebellion**".
Approval: both Houses within **1 month** by **special majority**.
⚠ A **Financial Emergency** too can cover **India or any part** of it.

52.s: Which constitutional change was introduced by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 in relation to Articles 20 and 21 during a National Emergency?
o: It made both Articles 20 and 21 unenforceable during every Emergency
It transferred the power under Article 359 from the President to the Supreme Court
It removed Article 21 from the list of Fundamental Rights
It ensured that an order under Article 359 could not suspend the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21
52.x: The 44th Amendment inserted the protection that the right to move courts for enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended by an order under Article 359, even during a National Emergency.
52.tq: Identify the amendment’s protective effect and reject the reversal that makes Articles 20 and 21 unenforceable.
xs: The **44th CAA** ensured an **Art. 359** order **cannot suspend** enforcement of **Arts. 20 and 21** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Art. 359 works through a **Presidential order**, which can **never** touch Arts. 20 and 21.
xa: ⚠ LENS Jul **2026** MCQ: "Arts 20 and 21 can be suspended under Art. 359" is **wrong**.
⚠ **358** = **Art. 19**, automatic; **359** = Presidential order, never Arts. 20 and 21.
The 44th CAA also barred Art. 358 when the ground is **armed rebellion**.

52.s: Which judgment overruled the approach of ADM Jabalpur concerning the right to life and personal liberty?
o: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
52.x: The K.S. Puttaswamy judgment of 2017 overruled the approach taken in ADM Jabalpur concerning the suspension of Article 21 protections.
52.tq: Distinguish the later corrective privacy judgment from the earlier Article 21 cases.
xs: **ADM Jabalpur (1976)** was rejected in **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)** — so option **(1)** is correct.
ADM Jabalpur had held even the **right to life** unenforceable during the emergency; it is now effectively overruled.
xa: The **44th CAA** ensures **Art. 359** can never suspend **Arts. 20 and 21**.
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: emergency proclamation **reviewable**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: **9-judge bench**, landmark on **Art. 356**.

52.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 358:
1. It suspends Article 19 automatically during a qualifying National Emergency.
2. It applies when the Emergency is proclaimed on the ground of armed rebellion.
3. After the Forty-fourth Amendment, only laws related to the Emergency receive the relevant protection.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
52.x: Article 358 operates automatically for an Emergency based on war or external aggression, not armed rebellion. The Forty-fourth Amendment also limited protection to laws related to the Emergency.
52.tq: Use the amendment-based exception to detect the false emergency ground.
xs: **Statements 1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **Art. 358** suspends **Art. 19 automatically**.
Statement 2 is wrong: it applies only for **war/external aggression**, **not armed rebellion** (**44th CAA**).
Statement 3 is correct: after the 44th CAA, **only laws related to the Emergency** are protected.
xa: **Lasting protection**: acts done under Art. 358 cannot be challenged even after the emergency.
⚠ **359** needs a **Presidential order** and can never suspend **Arts. 20 and 21**.

52.s: During a National Emergency, the President may modify the distribution of revenues between the Union and the States. Such modification may continue until:
o: The date on which the Emergency is proclaimed
The end of the financial year in which the Emergency ends
Six months after Parliament approves the Emergency
52.x: The President may modify revenue distribution during the Emergency, and the modification can continue until the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ends.
52.tq: Focus on the precise terminal time attached to a financial consequence.
xs: The President can modify revenue distribution **till the end of the financial year in which the emergency ends** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is the **financial** effect of a National Emergency.
xa: Executive effect: the Centre can direct states on **any matter**.
Terms of the Lok Sabha and Assemblies extendable **1 year at a time**, not beyond **6 months** after it ends.
⚠ Don't confuse with a **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)**, which has never been declared.

52.s:
Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes Articles 358 and 359?
1. Article 358 concerns automatic suspension of Article 19 in specified emergencies.
2. Article 359 concerns suspension of the enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights by Presidential order.
3. Articles 20 and 21 may be suspended under Article 359.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
52.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 359 cannot suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of Articles 20 and 21; therefore statement 3 is false.
52.tq: Discriminate between automatic suspension and suspension by Presidential order.
xs: **Statements 1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **Art. 358** suspends **Art. 19 automatically** (war/external aggression).
Statement 2 is correct: **Art. 359** suspends enforcement of specified FRs by **Presidential order**.
Statement 3 is wrong: Art. 359 can **never** suspend **Arts. 20 and 21** (44th CAA).
xa: ⚠ LENS Jul **2026** MCQ keyed "Arts 20 and 21 can be suspended under Art. 359" as **wrong**.
Art. 358 does **not** apply when the ground is **armed rebellion**.

52.s: Which one of the following correctly states the legal effect of acts done during the operation of Article 358?
o: They are void as soon as the Emergency is proclaimed.
They may always be challenged after the Emergency ends.
They require ratification by every State Legislature after the Emergency.
They cannot be challenged even after the Emergency ends, subject to the constitutional conditions governing Article 358.
52.x: Acts done under the protection of Article 358 cannot be challenged even after the Emergency ends, provided they fall within the scope of that protection.
52.tq: Apply the temporal effect of constitutional immunity beyond the Emergency period.
xs: Acts done under **Art. 358** **cannot be challenged even after the emergency ends** — so option **(4)** is correct.
This is the **lasting protection** of Art. 358, now limited to **laws related to the Emergency** (**44th CAA**).
xa: Art. 358 suspends **Art. 19 automatically**, only for **war/external aggression**.
**Art. 359** needs a Presidential order; never **Arts. 20 and 21**.

52.s: While a proclamation of National Emergency is in operation, the term of the Lok Sabha may be extended by law:
o: By one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the Emergency ceases to operate
By six months at a time, but not beyond one year after the Emergency ceases to operate
By one year at a time, without any limit after the Emergency ends
By two years in total, with the approval of the Supreme Court
52.x: Parliament may extend the term of the Lok Sabha (and of State Assemblies) by law for one year at a time during a National Emergency, but the extension cannot continue beyond six months after the Emergency ceases. The six-month unit, the absence of any limit and Supreme Court approval are all incorrect.
52.tq: 1 year at a time; 6 months after it ends.
xs: Terms extendable by law **one year at a time**, **not beyond six months** after the emergency ends — so option **(1)** is correct.
The unit is **1 year**, not six months, and the six-month outer limit rules out "without any limit".
xa: The **42nd CAA (1976)** had raised Lok Sabha/Assembly terms to **6 years**.
Financial effect: revenue distribution modified **till the end of the financial year** in which the emergency ends.
Executive effect: Centre can direct states on **any matter**.

52.s:
Under Article 356, the President may be satisfied that the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution:
1. On the report of the Governor
2. Otherwise than on the report of the Governor
3. Only after obtaining the consent of the State Legislature
Which of the statements given above are correct?
52.x: The President may act on the Governor’s report or otherwise. The consent of the State Legislature is not a precondition for imposing President’s Rule.
52.tq: Separate the constitutional alternatives from an invented mandatory condition.
xs: **Statements 1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
The President acts on the **Governor's report or otherwise** — both 1 and 2 hold.
Statement 3 is wrong: **State Legislature's consent** is not required.
xa: Art. 356 is also deemed under **Art. 365** (non-compliance with Union directions).
Basis: **Art. 355** — the Union's duty to ensure constitutional governance in states.
Approval: **6 months** per approval; maximum **3 years**.

52.s: Failure by a State to comply with directions given by the Union may be treated as a ground for President’s Rule under:
52.x: Article 365 provides that failure to comply with, or give effect to, Union directions can justify the conclusion that the State government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
52.tq: Use the article-number distinction among emergency provisions.
xs: **Article 365** deems non-compliance with **Union directions** a ground for President's Rule — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 355** is the Union's duty to protect states (basis for 356); **Art. 360** is Financial Emergency; **Art. 352** is National Emergency.
xa: President's Rule can come on the **Governor's report or otherwise**.
⚠ **1 month – 2 months – 6 months** = **352 – 360 – 356** approval windows.

52.s: Who can revoke a Proclamation of President’s Rule?
o: The President, at any time, without parliamentary approval
The Governor, with the approval of the State Legislature
The Prime Minister, by an executive order
Parliament alone by a special majority
52.x: The President may revoke President’s Rule at any time, and parliamentary approval is not required for revocation.
52.tq: Ask who would perform the constitutional act rather than who approved it.
xs: President's Rule can be revoked **by the President at any time**, **without parliamentary approval** — so option **(1)** is correct.
No role for the Governor, PM or a special majority of Parliament in revocation.
xa: National Emergency: President may revoke any time and **must** revoke if the **Lok Sabha** disapproves by simple majority.
President's Rule: **6 months** per approval, maximum **3 years**.
Beyond **1 year** only if a **National Emergency** is in operation **AND** the **Election Commission** certifies.

52.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Organ)
a. Executive
b. Legislature
c. Judiciary

List-II (Effect of President’s Rule)
i. High Court powers remain untouched
ii. Parliament legislates for the State
iii. Governor administers on behalf of the President

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
52.x: The Governor administers the State on behalf of the President, Parliament legislates for the State, and the High Court remains unaffected.
52.tq: Start from the sure pair linking the High Court with its unchanged status.
xs: Correct match: **a–iii, b–ii, c–i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Executive: **Council of Ministers dismissed**; **Governor administers** on the President's behalf.
Legislature: Assembly **suspended or dissolved**; **Parliament legislates** (or delegates to the President).
Judiciary: **High Court untouched**.
xa: **Ambedkar** hoped Art. 356 would remain a "**dead letter**".
**Manipur**: PR imposed **Feb 2025**; second extension till **Feb 2026**.

52.s: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar expressed the hope that Article 356 would remain a:
52.x: Ambedkar hoped that the emergency provision under Article 356 would remain a “dead letter” and be used only in exceptional circumstances.
52.tq: Recall the exact phrase associated with a constitutional provision.
xs: **Ambedkar** hoped Art. 356 would remain a "**dead letter**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
In practice it has been among the **most controversial provisions** (PYQ **2025**), with partisan Governor reports.
xa: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** subjected it to **judicial review**.
**First PR in India**: **Punjab, 1951**.
⚠ Art. 356 is also deemed under **Art. 365**.

52.s: Which case is associated with the striking down of the dissolution of the Bihar Legislative Assembly on partisan grounds in 2006?
o: K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
S. R. Bommai v. Union of India
Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
52.x: In Rameshwar Prasad (2006), the Supreme Court struck down the dissolution of the Bihar Assembly on partisan grounds.
52.tq: Use the case-name and judicial action as a paired identification test.
xs: **Rameshwar Prasad (2006)** struck down the **Bihar Assembly dissolution** on partisan grounds — so option **(4)** is correct.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** is the 9-judge Art. 356 landmark; **ADM Jabalpur (1976)** is on the right to life; **Puttaswamy (2017)** rejected ADM Jabalpur.
xa: Bommai: no **arbitrary dissolution**; Assembly may only be **suspended** until Parliament approves.
Bommai: **floor test** is the only test of majority.

52.s: Parliament approved the second extension of President’s Rule in Manipur up to:
52.x: The second extension of President’s Rule in Manipur was approved up to February 2026.
52.tq: Track the end point of an extension rather than the date of original imposition.
xs: Parliament approved the **second extension** of Manipur's PR **till February 2026** (in **Aug 2025**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
PR was imposed in Manipur in **Feb 2025**.
xa: President's Rule needs approval every **6 months**; maximum **3 years**.
Beyond **1 year** only if a **National Emergency** is in operation **AND** the **Election Commission** certifies elections cannot be held.

52.s: President's Rule under Article 356 can be continued beyond one year only if:
o: A National Emergency is in operation or the Election Commission certifies that elections cannot be held
The Governor recommends it and the State Legislature consents
A National Emergency is in operation and the Election Commission certifies that elections cannot be held
Parliament approves it by a special majority every three months
52.x: Beyond one year, President's Rule needs both conditions together: a National Emergency in operation AND an Election Commission certificate that elections cannot be held. The 'or' version is the common trap. Governor's recommendation or state consent are not conditions, and approval is every six months (maximum three years), not every three months by special majority.
52.tq: Beyond 1 year: Emergency AND EC certificate - both.
xs: Beyond **1 year**, PR continues only if a **National Emergency is in operation and the Election Commission certifies** elections cannot be held — so option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ Both conditions are needed — option 1's "**or**" is the trap.
Approval is every **6 months** (maximum **3 years**), not every three months by special majority.
xa: ONOE critique: deferred state polls could prolong PR, clashing with **Art. 356(5)** (**9 Mar 2026**).
PR can be revoked by the President **at any time**.

52.s: The decision in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India was delivered by a Bench comprising:
52.x: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India was decided by a nine-judge Constitution Bench.
52.tq: Test a precise judicial composition figure using nearby Constitution Bench sizes as distractors.
xs: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** was decided by a **9-judge bench** (nine judges) — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is the landmark case on **Art. 356**.
xa: Principles: **judicial review** of proclamation; **floor test**; Assembly only **suspended** until Parliament approves; court can **restore** a government.
**Secularism + federalism** are basic features.

52.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the principles laid down in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India:
1. A proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review.
2. The Governor’s opinion is the conclusive test of majority in the Assembly.
3. The floor test in the Assembly is the proper test of majority.
4. A court can restore a dismissed State government in an appropriate case.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
52.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. The Governor’s opinion is not conclusive; majority must ordinarily be tested on the floor of the Assembly.
52.tq: Reject the wrong-authority trap by distinguishing the Governor’s assessment from the Assembly floor test.
xs: **Statements 1, 3 and 4** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the proclamation is **subject to judicial review**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **Governor's opinion** is not the test; statement 3 — the **floor test** — is.
Statement 4 is correct: a court can **restore** a dismissed government.
xa: Bommai: **9-judge bench**, **1994**.
**Secularism** and **federalism** are basic features; a state government acting against secularism can be dismissed.

52.s: Under the principles laid down in S.R. Bommai, a proclamation under Article 356 may be invalidated by a court when it is based on:
o: A mere change in the ruling party at the Union level
Any political disagreement between the State and Union Governments
The failure of a State Legislature to pass an ordinary Bill
52.x: The proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, particularly where it is mala fide or founded on irrelevant grounds.
52.tq: Apply the judicial-review principle to distinguish constitutionally relevant grounds from political disagreement.
xs: A proclamation can be struck down if based on **mala fide or irrelevant grounds** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Bommai made the Art. 356 proclamation **subject to judicial review**.
xa: Earlier, **Minerva Mills (1980)** held emergency proclamations **reviewable**.
**Floor test** in the Assembly is the only test of majority.
**Rameshwar Prasad (2006)** struck down the **Bihar** dissolution on partisan grounds.

52.s: Which one of the following statements regarding dissolution of a State Legislative Assembly under Article 356 is NOT correct?
o: A court may restore a dismissed government in an appropriate case.
The Assembly may initially be kept under suspension until parliamentary approval.
The Assembly must invariably be dissolved immediately after the proclamation.
52.x: Immediate and automatic dissolution is not required. The Assembly may remain suspended until Parliament approves, and arbitrary dissolution is impermissible.
52.tq: Find the absolute statement that contradicts the Bommai safeguards.
xs: The NOT correct statement is that the **Assembly must invariably be dissolved immediately** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Under Bommai the Assembly may only be **suspended until Parliament approves**; **no arbitrary dissolution**.
A court can **restore** a dismissed government — options 1, 2 and 3 are all correct statements.
xa: **Floor test** decides majority, not the Governor's opinion.
**Rameshwar Prasad (2006)** applied this to strike down the **Bihar Assembly** dissolution.

52.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched in the context of S.R. Bommai v. Union of India?
o: Secularism — an ordinary statutory principle only
Federalism — not a feature of the Constitution
Secularism and federalism — basic features of the Constitution
Governor’s opinion — conclusive proof of majority
52.x: The judgment recognised secularism and federalism as basic features of the Constitution. It also held that a State government acting against secularism may be dismissed, subject to constitutional and judicial safeguards.
52.tq: Pair constitutional doctrines with their status and eliminate the reversed descriptions.
xs: Bommai held **secularism and federalism** to be **basic features** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The Governor's opinion is not proof of majority — the **floor test** is (option 4 wrong).
xa: A state government acting **against secularism** can be dismissed.
Bommai: **9-judge bench**, **1994**.
Proclamation under 356 is subject to **judicial review**.

52.s: The first and longest spell of President’s Rule in Andhra Pradesh extended from:
52.x: The first and longest spell in Andhra Pradesh began on 18 January 1973 and ended on 10 December 1973.
52.tq: Match both endpoints of a constitutional time period, not merely its starting year.
xs: The first and longest AP spell ran from **18 January 1973 to 10 December 1973** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It followed the **Jai Andhra** agitation and ended when **Jalagam Vengala Rao** became CM.
**1 March – 8 June 2014** (option 4) was the **second** spell.
xa: **First PR in AP**: **January 1973** (PYQ **2019/2021**).
The 1973 spell ended after the **Six-Point Formula**, validated by the **32nd CAA, 1973** (**Art. 371D**).
**First PR in India**: **Punjab, 1951**.

52.s: The first spell of President’s Rule in Andhra Pradesh ended when:
o: Jalagam Vengala Rao became Chief Minister
Kiran Kumar Reddy resigned as Chief Minister
N. T. Rama Rao became Chief Minister
52.x: The first spell ended on 10 December 1973 when Jalagam Vengala Rao became Chief Minister.
52.tq: Avoid the wrong-person-with-the-event trap by matching the event to its actual political figure.
xs: The first spell ended when **Jalagam Vengala Rao became Chief Minister** (**10 Dec 1973**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Kiran Kumar Reddy's** resignation (option 2) triggered the **2014** spell; **Telangana** was formed **2 June 2014**.
xa: The 1973 spell followed the **Jai Andhra** agitation.
It ended after the **Six-Point Formula**, validated by the **32nd CAA, 1973** (Art. 371D).
⚠ **Trap:** not the 33rd CAA — that concerns **resignation of legislators**.

52.s: The first instance of President’s Rule in India occurred in:
52.x: Punjab witnessed the first imposition of President’s Rule in India in 1951.
52.tq: Combine the correct State and year to defeat swapped-location options.
xs: The first President's Rule in India was in **Punjab, 1951** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Andhra Pradesh** had its first spell only in **January 1973**, so option 4 is wrong.
xa: **First PR in AP**: **January 1973** (PYQ **2019/2021**), after the **Jai Andhra** agitation.
**Ambedkar** hoped Art. 356 would remain a "**dead letter**".
Art. 356 is among the **most controversial provisions** (PYQ **2025**).

52.s: The second spell of President's Rule in Andhra Pradesh (1 March to 8 June 2014) followed:
o: The resignation of Chief Minister Kiran Kumar Reddy over bifurcation
The death of a sitting Chief Minister
A Supreme Court order dissolving the Assembly
52.x: The 2014 spell followed Chief Minister Kiran Kumar Reddy's resignation over the bifurcation of the State; Telangana was formed on 2 June 2014. The Jai Andhra agitation led to the first spell in 1973. Neither a Chief Minister's death nor a Supreme Court order caused the 2014 spell.
52.tq: 1973 = Jai Andhra; 2014 = bifurcation resignation.
xs: The 2014 spell followed CM **Kiran Kumar Reddy's resignation over bifurcation** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Jai Andhra** agitation (option 1) led to the **1973** spell.
xa: **Telangana** was formed on **2 June 2014**; the spell ran **1 Mar 2014 - 8 Jun 2014**.
First and longest AP spell: **18 Jan 1973 - 10 Dec 1973**.

52.s: In December 2020, the Andhra Pradesh High Court raised the question of whether it could record a breakdown of the constitutional machinery in the State. This concerned which Article?
52.x: A breakdown of constitutional machinery in a State is the ground for President's Rule under Article 356, which the AP High Court referred to in December 2020 (PYQ 2021). Article 352 is National Emergency, Article 360 Financial Emergency, and Article 365 deems non-compliance with Union directions a breakdown but is not the President's Rule provision itself.
52.tq: Breakdown of state machinery = 356.
xs: A breakdown of constitutional machinery is the ground for **Article 356** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **AP High Court (Dec 2020)** asked whether it could record such a breakdown (PYQ **2021**).
**Art. 352** = National Emergency; **Art. 360** = Financial Emergency; **Art. 365** deems non-compliance a breakdown but is not the PR provision.
xa: PR is on the **Governor's report or otherwise**.
**First PR in AP**: **January 1973**.

52.s: Under Article 360, a Financial Emergency may be proclaimed when the financial stability or credit of:
o: India alone is threatened, but not any part of India
Only the banking system of a State is threatened
India or any part of its territory is threatened
Any part of India alone is threatened, but not India as a whole
52.x: Article 360 applies where the financial stability or credit of India or any part of its territory is threatened.
52.tq: Test the constitutional wording “India or any part thereof” without narrowing the scope.
xs: Art. 360 applies when the **financial stability or credit of India or any part** is threatened — so option **(3)** is correct.
It covers both India as a whole and **any part**, so options 1 and 4 are wrong.
xa: Approval within **2 months** by **simple majority**; **no maximum period**.
Effects: cut salaries incl. **SC and HC judges**; State **Money/Financial Bills reserved**.
**Never declared** so far.

52.s: Which one of the following correctly states the parliamentary approval requirement for a Financial Emergency?
o: Approval within one month by special majority
Approval within six months by special majority
Approval within two months by simple majority
Approval within three months by absolute majority
52.x: A proclamation of Financial Emergency must be approved by Parliament within two months by a simple majority.
52.tq: Separate Article 360’s two-month simple-majority rule from Article 352’s one-month special-majority rule.
xs: A Financial Emergency needs approval **within two months by simple majority** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**1 month, special majority** (option 1) is for a **National Emergency**.
xa: It continues with **no maximum period**, till revoked.
Grounds: **financial stability or credit** of India or any part threatened.

52.s:
Consider the following statements about a Financial Emergency:
1. The Constitution prescribes no maximum period for its continuance.
2. It continues until revoked.
3. It has been proclaimed several times in India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
52.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. A Financial Emergency has never been declared in India, so statement 3 is false.
52.tq: Use the exception in the final statement to distinguish constitutional possibility from actual practice.
xs: **Statements 1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statements 1 and 2: there is **no maximum period**; it continues **till revoked**.
Statement 3 is wrong: a Financial Emergency has **never been declared**.
xa: Approval within **2 months** by **simple majority**.
Effects: **canons of financial propriety**; salary cuts incl. **SC and HC judges**.

52.s: Which of the following is NOT a consequence that may follow the proclamation of a Financial Emergency?
o: Automatic dissolution of all State Legislative Assemblies
Reservation of State Money Bills and Financial Bills for the President’s consideration
Directions regarding canons of financial propriety
Reduction of salaries of government servants, including judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts
52.x: Article 360 does not provide for automatic dissolution of State Legislative Assemblies. It permits directions on financial propriety, salary reductions and reservation of specified State Bills for the President.
52.tq: Find the consequence borrowed from Article 356 rather than Article 360.
xs: **Automatic dissolution of State Assemblies** is NOT an effect of a Financial Emergency — so option **(1)** is correct.
Its real effects: directions on **canons of financial propriety**, salary cuts including **SC and HC judges**, and **State Money/Financial Bills reserved** for the President.
xa: It has **never been declared**.
**No maximum period** — continues till revoked.

52.s: The criticism that deferred State elections could prolong President’s Rule is particularly connected with a possible conflict involving:
52.x: Article 356(5) allows President's Rule to continue beyond one year only if a National Emergency is in operation and the Election Commission certifies that elections cannot be held. Deferring State polls under ONOE could prolong President's Rule and clash with this limit.
52.tq: Identify the relevant Article by connecting the policy scenario with the specific constitutional limitation.
xs: The ONOE critique is that deferred polls could prolong PR, clashing with **Article 356(5)** (**9 Mar 2026**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
Art. 356(5) allows PR beyond **1 year** only if a **National Emergency** is on **AND** the **Election Commission** certifies.
**Art. 352(3)** is about written Cabinet advice for a National Emergency.
xa: ⚠ **Trap:** both conditions needed — some notes say "or".
Maximum PR: **3 years**.

52.s: Which one of the following is widely regarded as one of the most controversial provisions of the Indian Constitution?
52.x: Article 356, dealing with failure of constitutional machinery in a State and President’s Rule, is among the most controversial provisions of the Constitution.
52.tq: Use the exact constitutional provision associated with the stated controversy.
xs: **Article 356** is among the **most controversial** provisions (PYQ **2025**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
Criticism: **partisan Governor reports** and use **against opposition**.
xa: **Ambedkar** hoped it would remain a "**dead letter**".
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** made it subject to **judicial review** and the **floor test**.
**Rameshwar Prasad (2006)** struck down a partisan **Bihar** dissolution.

52.s: The 1973 spell of President’s Rule in Andhra Pradesh ended after the implementation of the:
52.x: The 1973 spell of President's Rule in Andhra Pradesh (following the Jai Andhra agitation) ended after the Six-Point Formula, which was validated by the 32nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1973 inserting Article 371D.
52.tq: Match a State-specific constitutional episode with the regional political settlement that ended it.
xs: The 1973 spell ended after the **Six-Point Formula** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The formula was validated by the **32nd CAA, 1973** (**Art. 371D**).
xa: ⚠ **Trap:** CDX says "**33rd**" — the 33rd CAA concerns **resignation of legislators**.
The spell ran **18 Jan 1973 - 10 Dec 1973** after the **Jai Andhra** agitation.
It ended when **Jalagam Vengala Rao** became CM.

52.s: The Six-Point Formula relating to the 1973 Andhra Pradesh episode was validated through the:
52.x: The Six-Point Formula was validated by the 32nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1973, which inserted Article 371D. The 33rd Amendment concerned resignation of legislators.
52.tq: Distinguish the closely numbered 32nd and 33rd Amendments by their subject matter.
xs: The **Six-Point Formula** was validated by the **32nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1973** (**Art. 371D**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ The **33rd CAA** (option 2) concerns **resignation of legislators**, not the Six-Point Formula.
xa: The **1973** AP spell of President's Rule ended after the Six-Point Formula.
That spell ran **18 Jan 1973 - 10 Dec 1973**, after the **Jai Andhra** agitation; it ended when **Jalagam Vengala Rao** became CM.
AP's 2nd spell: **1 Mar 2014 - 8 Jun 2014**, after CM **Kiran Kumar Reddy** resigned over bifurcation.

53.s: Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council primarily to
o: investigate and discuss subjects of common interest between the Union and States or among States
audit the accounts of State Governments
53.x: Article 263 contemplates an Inter-State Council for investigating and discussing subjects of common interest between the Union and States or among States, and for making recommendations on such matters.
53.tq: Focus on the exact constitutional functions instead of assigning judicial or executive powers to the Council.
xs: Under **Art. 263**, the **President** may set up an ISC to **investigate and discuss subjects of common interest** and coordinate policy — so option **(1)** is correct.
Adjudication of disputes is not its role; river disputes go under **Art. 262**.
xa: ⚠ **Art. 262** = river water disputes; **Art. 263** = Inter-State Council; **Art. 131** = original jurisdiction (excludes water disputes).
The ISC was set up in **1990** under Art 263 (APPSC-G1 **2017** key).
Its **Chairman** is the **Prime Minister**; its Standing Committee is chaired by the **Union Home Minister**.

53.s: Which one of the following best describes the nature of the Inter-State Council?
o: A judicial body whose awards are enforceable like Supreme Court judgments
An extra-constitutional body created only by executive resolution
A recommendatory body whose decisions are legally binding on all States
A recommendatory body concerned with consultation on inter-governmental matters
53.x: The Inter-State Council is a constitutional, recommendatory body established under Article 263. It is not a judicial body and is not created merely by an executive resolution.
53.tq: Separate constitutional status from statutory and extra-constitutional status, and distinguish recommendation from binding adjudication.
xs: The ISC is a **recommendatory** body for consultation on inter-governmental matters — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is not judicial (option 1); its decisions are **not binding** (option 3); it is set up under **Art. 263** of the Constitution (option 2 wrong).
xa: Questions are decided by **consensus**; the **Chairman's view** on consensus is final.
Its secretariat is the **Inter-State Council Secretariat** (**MHA**).
Set up in **1990** on the **Sarkaria** recommendation.

53.s:
Consider the following statements about the Inter-State Council:
1. It is chaired by the Prime Minister.
2. Its Standing Committee is chaired by the Union Home Minister.
3. Questions before it are decided by a simple majority vote of the members present.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
53.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Prime Minister is the Chairman of the Council. Statement 2 is correct: the Union Home Minister chairs its Standing Committee. Statement 3 is wrong: questions are decided by consensus, and the Chairman's view on whether consensus exists is final. Hence '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses statement 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' wrongly include statement 3.
53.tq: PM chairs the Council, Home Minister chairs the Standing Committee; decisions by consensus, not voting.
xs: **Statements 1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the **Prime Minister** chairs the ISC.
Statement 2 is correct: the **Union Home Minister** chairs its **Standing Committee**.
Statement 3 is wrong: questions are decided by **consensus**, and the Chairman's view on consensus is final.
xa: ⚠ Zonal Council vice-chairman = a **CM by annual rotation**.
Members include **6 Union Cabinet ministers** nominated by the PM.

53.s:
Which of the following councils has also been set up by the President under Article 263?
1. Central Council of Health
2. Central Council of Local Self-Government
3. Transport Development Council
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
53.x: The Central Council of Health, Central Council of Local Self-Government and Transport Development Council are all stated to have been set up under Article 263.
53.tq: Recognise the less familiar bodies associated with the same constitutional Article.
xs: **All three** were set up under **Art. 263** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The notes list the **Central Council of Health**, **Central Council of Local Self-Government** and **Transport Development Council** as other Art. 263 councils.
xa: The **Inter-State Council** itself was set up under Art 263 in **1990**.
**Sarkaria** proposed renaming the NDC the **National Economic and Development Council** with constitutional status under Art 263.

53.s:
Which of the following bodies had supported the idea of an institutional mechanism for Centre-State coordination before the establishment of the Inter-State Council?
1. Administrative Reforms Commission
2. Rajamannar Committee
3. Sarkaria Commission
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: The Administrative Reforms Commission during 1966–69 and the Rajamannar Committee in 1969 were earlier advocates, while the Sarkaria Commission later recommended the Inter-State Council that was set up in 1990.
53.tq: Track the chronology of successive commissions instead of treating only the final recommending commission as an advocate.
xs: **All three** backed such a body — so option **(4)** is correct.
**ARC (1966-69)** and the **Rajamannar Committee (1969)** were earlier backers.
**Sarkaria** wanted a permanent "**Inter-Governmental Council**" (RPSC **2023** key).
xa: The ISC was finally set up in **1990** under **Art 263**.
Sarkaria also proposed the **National Economic and Development Council** under Art 263.

53.s:
Consider the following statements about the Sarkaria Commission's proposals on Centre-State coordination:
1. It wanted a permanent body called the 'Inter-Governmental Council'.
2. It proposed renaming the National Development Council as the National Economic and Development Council with constitutional status under Article 280.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
53.x: Statement 1 is correct: Sarkaria wanted a permanent 'Inter-Governmental Council'. Statement 2 is wrong: the renamed National Economic and Development Council was to get constitutional status under Article 263, not Article 280 (which deals with the Finance Commission). So '1 only'; '2 only' and 'Both' wrongly accept statement 2, and 'Neither' wrongly rejects statement 1.
53.tq: Both Sarkaria proposals hang on Article 263; Article 280 is the Finance Commission.
xs: Only **statement 1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: Sarkaria wanted a permanent "**Inter-Governmental Council**".
Statement 2 is wrong: the **National Economic and Development Council** was to get status under **Art 263**, not Art 280.
xa: The **ISC** was set up in **1990** under Art 263.
Earlier backers: **ARC (1966-69)** and **Rajamannar Committee (1969)**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the composition of the Inter-State Council:
1. The Chief Ministers of States are members.
2. The Administrators of Union Territories without legislatures are members.
3. Six Union Cabinet Ministers nominated by the Prime Minister are members.
4. Governors of all States are permanent members.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: Chief Ministers, Administrators of UTs without legislatures and six Union Cabinet Ministers nominated by the Prime Minister are included. Governors are included in relation to States under President's Rule, not as permanent members of all States.
53.tq: Watch for the overbroad membership statement using “all States”.
xs: **Statements 1, 2 and 3** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Members: **CMs of all states** (and UTs with assemblies), **Administrators of UTs without assemblies**, and **6 Union Cabinet ministers** nominated by the PM.
Statement 4 is wrong: only **Governors of states under PR** are members, not all Governors permanently.
xa: **Chairman**: **Prime Minister**.
**Standing Committee**: chaired by the **Union Home Minister**.

53.s: The Inter-State Council under Article 263 was actually set up in which year, and on whose recommendation?
o: 1969, on the recommendation of the Rajamannar Committee
1966, on the recommendation of the Administrative Reforms Commission
1990, on the recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission
2007, on the recommendation of the Punchhi Commission
53.x: The Inter-State Council was established in 1990 under Article 263 following the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation. The ARC (1966) and the Rajamannar Committee (1969) had earlier supported such a body, but it was not set up on their advice. The Punchhi Commission came later.
53.tq: ISC = 1990, Sarkaria, PM in the chair.
xs: The ISC was set up in **1990** on the **Sarkaria Commission's** recommendation — so option **(3)** is correct.
**ARC (1966-69)** and **Rajamannar Committee (1969)** had backed it earlier but it was not set up on their advice.
xa: Set up under **Art 263** (APPSC-G1 **2017** key).
Sarkaria's term was a permanent "**Inter-Governmental Council**".
It is **recommendatory**, deciding by **consensus**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements about the Zonal Councils:
1. The Chief Ministers act as Vice-Chairmen by annual rotation.
2. Their recommendations are legally binding on the participating States.
3. They are deliberative and advisory bodies.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: Chief Ministers serve as Vice-Chairmen by annual rotation, and the Councils are deliberative and advisory. Their recommendations are not binding.
53.tq: Reject the statement that converts an advisory recommendation into a binding direction.
xs: **Statements 1 and 3** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: CMs are **vice-chairman by annual rotation**.
Statement 2 is wrong: recommendations are **not binding**.
Statement 3 is correct: Zonal Councils are **deliberative and advisory**.
xa: Members also include **2 other ministers** per state and UT Administrators/LGs.
Criticism: they are only **recommendatory** and need **more resources**.

53.s: Which one of the following States is included in the Southern Zonal Council according to the current composition?
53.x: The Southern Zonal Council includes Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, Telangana and Puducherry.
53.tq: Use regional grouping to distinguish Southern members from Central, Eastern and Northern members.
xs: **Telangana** is a member of the **Southern Zonal Council** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Southern members: **AP, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, Telangana, Puducherry**.
**Chhattisgarh** is in the **Central** Council and **Rajasthan** in the **Northern** Council.
xa: ⚠ APP's list omits Telangana; **IYB 2026** and LENS include it.
The **31st Southern Zonal Council** met on **20 Aug 2026** at **Mamallapuram** (TN), chaired by **Amit Shah**.

53.s: Which of the following issues was urged for early settlement at the 31st Southern Zonal Council meeting?
o: Expansion of the Northern Freight Corridor
53.x: Amit Shah urged the early settlement of southern water disputes and river-linking at the meeting.
53.tq: Link the policy issue to the subject-specific function of a regional coordination council.
xs: **Amit Shah** urged early settlement of **southern water disputes and river-linking** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **31st SZC** met on **20 Aug 2026** at **Mamallapuram** (TN).
xa: AP CM **N. Chandrababu Naidu** attended.
Telangana planned to seek **national status** for **Kaleshwaram** and **Palamuru-Rangareddy** at the SZC.
Zonal Councils are **deliberative and advisory**.

53.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Zonal Council)
a. Northern
b. Central
c. Eastern
 d. Western

List-II (Members)
i. Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha
ii. Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
iii. Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh
iv. Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Delhi, Chandigarh, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
53.x: The Northern Council has the listed northern States, Delhi and UTs; the Central Council has Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh; the Eastern and Western combinations correspond to i and ii respectively.
53.tq: Start with the sure regional pair and then eliminate codes that disturb the geographical grouping.
xs: Correct code: **a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Northern**: Haryana, HP, Punjab, Rajasthan, Delhi + **Chandigarh, J&K, Ladakh**.
**Central**: **Chhattisgarh, MP, Uttarakhand, UP** — only option 1 has a-iv and b-iii.
xa: **Southern**: **AP, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, Telangana, Puducherry** (IYB 2026).
CMs are **vice-chairman by annual rotation**; councils are **deliberative and advisory**.

53.s: Which Article guarantees freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India?
53.x: Article 301 declares freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India, subject to the provisions that follow.
53.tq: Match the article number with its central principle before considering exceptions.
xs: **Article 301** guarantees **freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse** throughout India — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Art 302** lets Parliament restrict it in **public interest**; **Art 304** covers state restrictions; **Art 307** provides an authority.
xa: **Art 303**: no **preference/discrimination** by Union or states.
**Art 305**: saving of existing laws and **state monopolies**.
**Art 306** (Part B states) is **repealed**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Articles 301 to 307:
1. Parliament may impose restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse in the public interest under Article 302.
2. Article 303 deals with preference or discrimination by the Union or States.
3. Article 305 saves existing laws and State monopolies.
4. Article 306 continues to operate as the principal provision governing Part B States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Article 306, relating to Part B States, has been repealed and is no longer an operative principal provision.
53.tq: Use the repealed-provision trap to distinguish Article 306 from operative provisions.
xs: **Statements 1, 2 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
1: **Art 302** — Parliament may restrict in **public interest**; 2: **Art 303** — no **preference/discrimination**; 3: **Art 305** — saves **existing laws, state monopolies**.
Statement 4 is wrong: **Art 306** (Part B states) is **repealed**.
xa: **Art 304(b)**: a State bill needs the **President's previous sanction**.
**Art 307**: authority for Arts 301-304, e.g. an **Inter-State Commerce Commission**.

53.s: A State Legislature proposes a bill imposing restrictions on trade, commerce or intercourse with other States under Article 304(b). What constitutional requirement applies before the bill is introduced?
o: Previous consent of the Supreme Court
53.x: A bill imposing reasonable restrictions in the public interest under Article 304(b) requires the previous sanction of the President before its introduction in the State Legislature.
53.tq: Ask which constitutional authority must act first in a State trade-restriction scenario.
xs: A bill under **Art 304(b)** needs the **President's previous sanction** — so option **(3)** is correct.
PYQ **2018**: a bill restricting goods from other states needs the **President's** previous sanction.
xa: **Art 301**: freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse.
**Art 302**: Parliament may restrict in **public interest**.
**Art 307**: authority such as an **Inter-State Commerce Commission**.

53.s: Article 307 contemplates the establishment of an authority for carrying out the purposes of Articles 301 to 304. Which of the following is an example mentioned in this context?
53.x: An Inter-State Commerce Commission is an example of the authority contemplated under Article 307 for carrying out the purposes of Articles 301 to 304.
53.tq: Distinguish the trade-and-commerce authority from broader Centre-State coordination bodies.
xs: The example under **Art 307** is an **Inter-State Commerce Commission** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Art 307 provides an authority for carrying out **Arts 301-304**.
The **Inter-State Council Secretariat** (option 1) serves the ISC under **Art 263**.
xa: **Art 304(b)** bills need the **President's previous sanction**.
**Art 306** (Part B states) is **repealed**.

53.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Tribunal)
 a. Godavari Tribunal
 b. First Krishna Tribunal
 c. Second Krishna Tribunal
 d. Vansadhara Tribunal

List-II (Year)
 i. 2004
 ii. 1969
 iii. 2010
 iv. 1969

Which of the following is the correct code?
53.x: Godavari Tribunal 1969 (a-ii), First Krishna Tribunal 1969 (b-iv), Second Krishna Tribunal 2004 (c-i) and Vansadhara Tribunal 2010 (d-iii), so the code is A. B wrongly gives the Second Krishna Tribunal 2010 and Vansadhara 2004.
53.tq: Start from the sure pair and distinguish the two tribunals constituted in 1969.
xs: Correct code: **a–ii, b–iv, c–i, d–iii** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Godavari 1969**, **KWDT-I 1969**, **KWDT-II 2004**, **Vansadhara 2010**.
xa: ⚠ Tribunals involving AP: **Godavari**, **Krishna-II**, **Vansadhara** (with Odisha).
Other tribunals: **Narmada 1969**, **Ravi-Beas 1986**, **Cauvery 1990**, **Mahadayi 2010**.
Tribunals are set up under the **ISRWD Act, 1956**.

53.s: Which of the following pairs of inter-State water dispute tribunal and States is NOT correctly matched?
o: Second Krishna — Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh
First Krishna — Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh
Godavari — Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha
53.x: The Vansadhara Tribunal involves Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, not Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
53.tq: Find the wrong State in the tribunal composition rather than relying only on the tribunal name.
xs: **Vansadhara — Odisha and Chhattisgarh** is wrong: Vansadhara involves **Odisha and AP** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Krishna-II**: Maharashtra, Karnataka, AP; **Godavari**: Maharashtra, Karnataka, AP, MP, Odisha — both correct.
xa: Vansadhara Tribunal: **2010**; Krishna-II: **2004**; Godavari: **1969**.
**Mahadayi (2010)**: Goa, Karnataka, Maharashtra.

53.s: Which of the following water dispute tribunals was constituted in 1990?
53.x: The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal was constituted in 1990. The Narmada Tribunal dates to 1969, Ravi-Beas to 1986 and Mahadayi to 2010.
53.tq: Use the year as the discriminator among closely related tribunals.
xs: The **Cauvery Tribunal** was set up in **1990** — so option **(3)** is correct.
xa: Cauvery states: **Karnataka, Kerala, TN, Puducherry**.
⚠ **1990** is also the year the **Inter-State Council** was set up.

53.s: Which one of the following States is NOT a party to any of the Godavari, Krishna or Vansadhara tribunals listed below?
53.x: Andhra Pradesh is party to all three listed tribunals; Maharashtra is involved in the Godavari and Krishna disputes, and Odisha in the Godavari and Vansadhara disputes. Chhattisgarh is not listed in these tribunal compositions.
53.tq: Group the States by tribunal membership and identify the outsider.
xs: **Chhattisgarh** is not a party to the Godavari, Krishna or Vansadhara tribunals — so option **(2)** is correct.
**AP** is party to all three; **Maharashtra** to Godavari and Krishna; **Odisha** to Godavari and Vansadhara.
xa: Godavari states: **Maharashtra, Karnataka, AP, MP, Odisha**.
**Krishna tribunals**: **KWDT-I** (1969) + **KWDT-II** (2004).
Chhattisgarh sits in the **Central Zonal Council**.

53.s:
Consider the following pairs of water disputes tribunal and party States:
1. Narmada Tribunal — Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra
2. Ravi-Beas Tribunal — Punjab and Haryana
3. Mahadayi Tribunal — Goa, Kerala and Tamil Nadu
4. Cauvery Tribunal — Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
53.x: Pairs 1, 2 and 4 are correct as per the tribunal table. Pair 3 is wrong: the Mahadayi Tribunal (2010) involves Goa, Karnataka and Maharashtra. So '1, 2 and 4 only'; '1 and 2 only' leaves out the correct Cauvery pair, and the options including 3 are wrong.
53.tq: Mahadayi = Goa + Karnataka + Maharashtra (west-coast river); Cauvery = Karnataka, Kerala, TN, Puducherry.
xs: **Pairs 1, 2 and 4** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
1: **Narmada** — Rajasthan, Gujarat, MP, Maharashtra; 2: **Ravi-Beas** — Punjab, Haryana; 4: **Cauvery** — Karnataka, Kerala, TN, Puducherry.
Pair 3 is wrong: **Mahadayi** involves **Goa, Karnataka, Maharashtra**.
xa: Years: Narmada **1969**, Ravi-Beas **1986**, Cauvery **1990**, Mahadayi **2010**.
⚠ **Mullaperiyar** dam (**1895**, Periyar) is in Kerala but run by TN under a lease.

53.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 262 of the Constitution:
1. Parliament may exclude the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and all other courts in respect of inter-State river water disputes.
2. The original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131 includes all inter-State river water disputes.
3. The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 provides for the constitution of tribunals.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Article 262(2) permits Parliament to bar the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other courts, and Article 131 does not cover inter-State water disputes.
53.tq: Split the options by checking the constitutional exception to Article 131.
xs: **Statements 1 and 3** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **Art. 262(2)** lets Parliament bar the **Supreme Court and all other courts**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **Art. 131** original jurisdiction **excludes water disputes**.
Statement 3 is correct: the **ISRWD Act, 1956** provides for tribunals.
xa: **River Boards Act 1956**: **no board** ever set up.
⚠ **Art. 262** = river disputes; **Art. 263** = Inter-State Council.

53.s: The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act and the River Boards Act were enacted in which year?
53.x: Both the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act and the River Boards Act were enacted in 1956.
53.tq: Test the exact year against nearby constitutional and legislative dates.
xs: Both the **ISRWD Act** and the **River Boards Act** date from **1956** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Both are laws under **Art. 262**.
xa: Under **Sec. 3** of the ISRWD Act, a State complains to the **Centre**.
**No board** has ever been set up under the River Boards Act.
**KRMB + GRMB** came instead under the **AP Reorganisation Act 2014**.

53.s: Which Article empowers Parliament to provide for the adjudication of disputes relating to the use, distribution or control of waters of an inter-State river or river valley?
53.x: Article 262 empowers Parliament to provide for adjudication of inter-State river-water disputes.
53.tq: Distinguish the adjacent inter-State provisions by their subject matter.
xs: **Article 262** empowers Parliament to provide for **adjudication of inter-state river disputes** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Art. 263** is the **Inter-State Council**, not water adjudication.
xa: **Art. 262(2)**: may bar the **SC and all courts**.
**Art. 131** original jurisdiction **excludes** water disputes.
Laws under Art. 262: **ISRWD Act, 1956** and **River Boards Act 1956**.

53.s: Under Section 3 of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, a State having a river-water dispute complains to the:
53.x: Section 3 of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 provides for a State to make a complaint to the Central Government regarding an inter-State river-water dispute.
53.tq: Apply the “who receives the complaint?” test before identifying the adjudicatory body.
xs: Under **Section 3** of the ISRWD Act, a State complains to the **Central Government** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The Supreme Court can be barred under **Art. 262(2)**, so a State does not go to it directly.
xa: In **Aug 2026**, Telangana planned to raise **Karnataka's unauthorised Krishna projects** under **Section 3**.
The ISRWD Act provides for **tribunals**.

53.s: Which one of the following statements about the two 1956 laws is correct?
o: The River Boards Act created tribunals, while the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act created permanent river boards.
The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act provides for tribunals, whereas no board has ever been set up under the River Boards Act.
The River Boards Act repealed Article 262 and transferred water to the Union List.
Both laws provide only for advisory councils and neither concerns adjudication.
53.x: The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 provides for tribunals. Although the River Boards Act, 1956 provides a statutory framework for river boards, no board has ever been set up under it.
53.tq: Compare the institutional purpose and practical outcome of the two similarly dated Acts.
xs: The **ISRWD Act** provides for **tribunals**, whereas **no board** has ever been set up under the **River Boards Act** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Both are **1956** laws under **Art. 262**; neither repealed Art. 262.
xa: **KRMB** and **GRMB** were set up under the **AP Reorganisation Act 2014**, with an **Apex Council**.
A State complains to the Centre under **Sec. 3** of the ISRWD Act.

53.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Krishna and Godavari water institutions involving Andhra Pradesh and Telangana:
1. The KRMB and GRMB were set up under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.
2. An Apex Council is part of this institutional framework.
3. The Second Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (KWDT-II) was constituted in 1969.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
53.x: Statement 1 is correct: KRMB and GRMB come from the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014. Statement 2 is correct: the boards work with an Apex Council. Statement 3 is wrong: KWDT-I was set up in 1969, KWDT-II in 2004. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses the Apex Council, and options with 3 are wrong.
53.tq: KWDT-I 1969, KWDT-II 2004; boards + Apex Council from the 2014 Reorganisation Act.
xs: **Statements 1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
1: **KRMB + GRMB** were set up under the **AP Reorganisation Act 2014**; 2: an **Apex Council** is part of the framework.
Statement 3 is wrong: **KWDT-I** was **1969**; **KWDT-II** was **2004**.
xa: AP-Telangana disputes: control of boards, **Rayalaseema Lift**, hydel generation.
**Jan 2026**: first **CWC-chaired** inter-state committee meeting.
