74.s: Which one of the following is NOT a constitutional body?
74.x: The NHRC is a statutory body set up under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993; calling it constitutional is a common trap. The NCSC (Art 338), NCST (Art 338A) and NCBC (Art 338B, constitutional since 2018) are the only constitutional commissions in this group.
74.tq: Constitutional = 338, 338A, 338B only; NHRC is statutory.
xs: The **National Human Rights Commission** is NOT a constitutional body — option **(4)**.
It is **statutory**, under the **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993**.
The **NCSC** (**Art. 338**), **NCST** (**Art. 338A**) and **NCBC** (**Art. 338B**) are the only constitutional commissions.
xa: ⚠ "**NHRC is constitutional**" is a stock trap (list-matching question, G2 **2023**).
The NCBC is constitutional only since **2018** (**102nd Amendment**); earlier statutory under the **NCBC Act 1993**.
Other statutory commissions: **NCW** (1990 Act), **NCM** (1992 Act), **NCPCR** (2005 Act).

74.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Adoption of the Paris Principles
B. Promulgation of the Ordinance preceding the PHRA
C. Establishment of the NHRC
D. Endorsement of the Paris Principles by the UN General Assembly
74.x: The Paris Principles were adopted in October 1991, the Ordinance was promulgated on 28 September 1993, the NHRC was established on 12 October 1993, and UNGA endorsement followed on 20 December 1993.
74.tq: Fix the first and last events before arranging the close 1993 dates.
xs: The order is **A, B, C, D** — option **(1)**.
A: the **Paris Principles** came from Paris in **Oct 1991**.
B: the **Ordinance** preceding the PHRA was issued on **28 Sep 1993**.
C: the **NHRC** was set up on **12 Oct 1993**; D: the **UNGA endorsed** the Paris Principles on **20 Dec 1993**.
xa: The NHRC **conforms to the Paris Principles**.
The NHRC's legal basis is the **Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA) 1993**; SHRCs come under the same Act.
The **UDHR** was adopted in **1948**; **10 Dec** is Human Rights Day.

74.s:
Consider the following statements regarding State Human Rights Commissions:
1. State Human Rights Commissions are established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
2. The Centre may assign human-rights functions relating to Union Territories to State Human Rights Commissions.
3. Human-rights functions in Delhi remain with the National Human Rights Commission.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
74.x: All three statements are correct. SHRCs are governed by the PHRA, the Centre can assign them certain UT functions, but Delhi remains with the NHRC.
74.tq: Test the general rule and the Delhi-specific exception together.
xs: All three statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: SHRCs are set up under the **PHRA 1993**.
Statement 2: the **2019 amendment** lets the Centre give **UT** human-rights functions to SHRCs.
Statement 3: **Delhi** stays with the **NHRC**.
xa: SHRC jurisdiction covers only **State List and Concurrent List** subjects.
⚠ SHRC members are **appointed by the Governor** but **removed only by the President**.
After **2019**, an SHRC chair may be a former **Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court**.

74.s:
With reference to the National Human Rights Commission after the 2019 amendment, consider the following statements:
1. Its Chairperson may be a former Chief Justice of India or a former Supreme Court judge.
2. It has three human-rights members, of whom at least one must be a woman.
3. The term of office is three years or until the age of 70 years, whichever is earlier.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
74.x: All three statements reflect the post-2019 position. Earlier, only a former CJI could chair the NHRC, there were two human-rights members and the term was five years.
74.tq: Test amendment-based changes by contrasting the current rule with the earlier arrangement.
xs: All three statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: after the **PHR (Amendment) Act 2019** the chair may be a former **CJI or a Judge of the Supreme Court**.
Statement 2: there are **3 human-rights members, at least one woman**.
Statement 3: the term is **three years** or age **70**, with reappointment allowed.
xa: Before 2019: chair only an **ex-CJI**, **2** human-rights members, term **five years** or age 70.
Removal is by the **President** after an **SC inquiry** for misbehaviour or incapacity.
The 2019 amendment added the **NCBC**, **NCPCR** chairs and the **Chief Commissioner for PwD** as deemed members.

74.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the selection committee for appointment to the NHRC:
1. The Prime Minister is its Chairperson.
2. The Union Home Minister is a member.
3. The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is a member.
4. The Chief Justice of India is its Chairperson.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
74.x: The Prime Minister chairs the six-member committee, which includes the Union Home Minister and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Chief Justice of India is not its Chairperson.
74.tq: Separate the recommending committee from the appointing authority and identify the wrongly assigned role.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **PM** chairs the selection committee.
Statements 2 and 3 correct: the **Union Home Minister** and the **Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman** are members.
Statement 4 wrong: the **CJI** is not on the committee; the President appoints on the committee's recommendation.
xa: Other members: the **Lok Sabha Speaker** and the **Leaders of Opposition in both Houses**.
The NHRC is appointed by the **President**; the **NCW** and **NCM** by the **Central Government**.
For an **SHRC**, the **Governor** appoints on a committee of the **CM**, Speaker, Home Minister and Leader of Opposition.

74.s:
Which of the following were added as deemed (ex officio) members of the NHRC by the 2019 amendment?
1. Chairperson of the National Commission for Backward Classes
2. Chairperson of the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights
3. Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities
4. Chairperson of the National Commission for Women
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
74.x: The 2019 amendment added the chairpersons of the NCBC and the NCPCR, and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, as deemed members. The NCW chairperson was already a deemed member before 2019, along with the NCM, NCSC and NCST chairpersons, so item 4 was not an addition. Answer: 1, 2 and 3 only.
74.tq: 2019 added NCBC, NCPCR and CC-PwD; NCW, NCM, NCSC and NCST were already deemed members.
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3** were the **2019** additions — option **(1)**.
The **2019 amendment** added the chairpersons of the **NCBC** and the **NCPCR** and the **Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities**.
Item 4 wrong: the **NCW** chairperson was already a deemed member before 2019, with the **NCM, NCSC and NCST** chairs.
xa: Post-2019 NHRC: Chair + **3** members + deemed members; **3 years** or **70**.
The chair may now be a former **CJI or a Judge of the Supreme Court**.
At least **one** of the human-rights members must be a **woman**.

74.s: Which one of the following is a power exercised by the NHRC while conducting an inquiry?
o: Power to amend the law under which the inquiry is conducted
Power to impose a binding monetary penalty on the Union Government
Powers of a civil court for summoning witnesses and calling for documents
Power to punish every witness for contempt without judicial process
74.x: During inquiries, the NHRC has the powers of a civil court, including summoning witnesses, calling for documents and receiving evidence on affidavit. It cannot itself amend legislation or impose a binding monetary penalty on the government.
74.tq: Ask which authority has the procedural power rather than the final coercive power.
xs: The NHRC has the **powers of a civil court** in inquiries — **summoning witnesses** and **calling for documents** — option **(3)**.
It can also receive **evidence on affidavit**.
It cannot compel anyone: its **recommendations are not binding**, so a binding penalty or amending law is beyond it.
xa: The government **must respond** to NHRC recommendations.
**Time bar**: it **cannot inquire after one year** from the alleged violation.
Its role over the **armed forces** is limited.

74.s:
Consider the following statements about the recommendations of the NHRC:
1. They are binding on the government.
2. The government is required to respond to them.
3. The Commission cannot compel implementation of its recommendations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
74.x: NHRC recommendations are not binding. However, the government must respond, and the Commission cannot compel their implementation.
74.tq: Separate the duty to respond from the power to compel implementation.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 wrong: NHRC recommendations are **not binding**.
Statements 2 and 3 correct: the **government must respond**, but the Commission **cannot compel** implementation.
xa: In inquiries the NHRC has the powers of a **civil court**.
Example: notices to the AP **DGP** and **Chief Secretary** on the Sai Krishna **custodial death** (**28 Jun 2026**), citing **Art. 21**.
It cannot inquire into a matter **after one year** of the incident.

74.s: A complaint alleging a human-rights violation committed eighteen months ago is ordinarily outside the jurisdiction of the NHRC because the Commission
o: cannot inquire into an incident after one year from its occurrence
has jurisdiction only over incidents occurring outside India
can inquire only after a criminal conviction
can inquire only into incidents committed by private persons
74.x: The NHRC cannot inquire into a complaint after one year from the date of the alleged violation.
74.tq: Apply the statutory time-bar rule to a factual situation.
xs: The NHRC **cannot inquire into an incident after one year** from its occurrence — option **(1)**.
An incident eighteen months old is past this **one-year time bar**.
The other options (only foreign incidents, only after conviction, only private persons) are not limits the notes give.
xa: In inquiries the NHRC has **civil court** powers: summon witnesses, call for documents.
Recommendations are **not binding**; the government must respond.
Limited role over the **armed forces**.

74.s:
Consider the following statements about international human-rights documents:
1. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948.
2. The ICCPR and ICESCR were adopted in 1966.
3. CEDAW was adopted in 1979.
4. The Convention against Torture was adopted in 1984.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
74.x: All four statements are correct: the UDHR dates to 1948, the ICCPR and ICESCR to 1966, CEDAW to 1979 and the Convention against Torture to 1984.
74.tq: Arrange a compact list of dates without allowing one familiar year to distort the others.
xs: All four statements **1, 2, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(4)**.
**CEDAW** — **1979**; **Convention against Torture** — **1984**.
xa: The **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child** dates from **1989**; India acceded in **1992**.
**10 Dec** is **Human Rights Day**, marking the UDHR.
The **Paris Principles** (Oct **1991**) were endorsed by the UNGA on **20 Dec 1993**.

74.s: Human Rights Day is observed on 10 December in commemoration of the adoption of the
o: Convention on the Rights of the Child
International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
74.x: Human Rights Day is observed on 10 December to commemorate the adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948.
74.tq: Link the commemorative date to the correct international instrument.
xs: Human Rights Day (**10 December**) marks the adoption of the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** — option **(2)**.
The **UDHR** was adopted in **1948**.
The **CRC** is of **1989**, the **ICESCR** of **1966** and the **Convention against Torture** of **1984**.
xa: **ICCPR and ICESCR** — both **1966**; **CEDAW** — **1979**.
India acceded to the CRC in **1992**; the **NCPCR** checks laws against the **UNCRC**.
The NHRC conforms to the **Paris Principles** (Oct **1991**).

74.s: Under the 2019 amendment relating to State Human Rights Commissions, the Chairperson of a State Human Rights Commission may be:
o: A former Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court
Only a serving Chief Justice of India
74.x: After the 2019 amendment, the Chairperson may be a former Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court.
74.tq: Watch the qualifying words ‘former’ and ‘High Court’ in eligibility questions.
xs: After the **2019** amendment an SHRC chair may be a **former Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court** — option **(2)**.
Earlier only a former **Chief Justice** of a High Court could chair it.
The parallel change for the **NHRC**: former **CJI or a Judge of the Supreme Court**.
xa: SHRC members are appointed by the **Governor** and removed only by the **President**.
The selection committee: **CM**, Speaker, Home Minister, Leader of Opposition (+ Council Chairman and LoP where a Council exists).
SHRCs take only **State List and Concurrent List** matters.

74.s: A proposal to allow Chairpersons of State Human Rights Commissions to act as State Information Commissioners would principally arise in States having:
o: A large number of pending RTI appeals
74.x: The issue was raised in the context of States having few appeals under the Right to Information framework.
74.tq: Apply the factual trigger to the administrative situation described in the question.
xs: The idea arose for States with **very few RTI appeals** — option **(2)**.
The **Supreme Court** asked whether SHRC chairs could act as **State Information Commissions** in such States (**11 Feb 2026**).
The question was about using existing **SHRCs**, so options about States with many appeals or no SHRC do not fit.
xa: SHRCs are created under the **PHRA 1993**.
An SHRC chair, after **2019**, is a former **Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court**.
SHRC: **appointed by the Governor**, **removed by the President**.

74.s: A State Human Rights Commission may inquire into a matter only when it relates to
o: Any matter regardless of its legislative list
The State List or the Concurrent List and is not already before the NHRC or another statutory commission
Only matters already decided by a court
74.x: The jurisdiction of an SHRC extends to matters in the State List and Concurrent List, but it cannot inquire into a matter already pending before the NHRC or another statutory commission.
74.tq: Apply both jurisdictional limits: legislative list and prior institutional consideration.
xs: An SHRC may inquire only into **State List or Concurrent List** matters **not already before the NHRC or another statutory commission** — option **(2)**.
So the **Union List** alone or "any matter" are wrong.
It also will not take a case already pending elsewhere.
xa: SHRCs are set up under the **PHRA 1993**.
The **2019 amendment** lets the Centre give **UT** functions to SHRCs; **Delhi** stays with the NHRC.
⚠ SHRC: **appointed by the Governor**, **removed by the President**.

74.s: The Chairperson and members of a State Human Rights Commission are appointed by ______ but can be removed only by ______.
74.x: The Governor appoints SHRC members on the recommendation of a committee of the Chief Minister, Speaker, Home Minister and Leader of Opposition (plus the Council Chairman and its LoP where a Council exists). Only the President can remove them. A reverses the two roles. The Chief Minister chairs the committee but does not appoint, and the State Legislature has no power to remove.
74.tq: SHRC: Governor appoints, President removes (like SPSC).
xs: SHRC members are appointed by **the Governor** but removed only by **the President** — option **(2)**.
The Governor acts on a committee of the **CM**, **Speaker**, **Home Minister** and **Leader of Opposition**.
The CM only sits on the committee; the **State Legislature** has no removal role.
xa: Where a Council exists, the **Council Chairman** and its **LoP** join the committee.
For the **NHRC**, the **President** appoints on a committee chaired by the **PM**.
After **2019** the SHRC chair is a former **Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court**.

74.s:
The National Commission for Women was constituted in:

a. January 1990
b. January 1992
c. January 1993
d. January 1995
74.x: The National Commission for Women was constituted in January 1992 under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990.
74.tq: Distinguish the year of the parent Act from the year in which the body was set up.
xs: The **NCW** was constituted in **January 1992** — option **(4)**.
It is a **statutory body** under the **NCW Act, 1990** (G2-GS **2019** key).
**January 1990** confuses the Act's year with the constitution date.
xa: First NCW chairperson: **Jayanti Patnaik** (**1992**); present: **Vijaya Rahatkar**.
⚠ **Rekha Sharma** was the chairperson in July **2023** (G2-GS 2023 key).
The NCW is one of the **WCD Ministry's** three statutory bodies, with **NCPCR** and **CARA**.

74.s:
The National Commission for Women consists of:

a. A Chairperson, three Members and a Member-Secretary
b. A Chairperson, five Members and a Member-Secretary
c. A Chairperson, seven Members and a Secretary-General
d. Five Members and a Secretary appointed by Parliament
o: A Chairperson, seven Members and a Secretary-General
A Chairperson, three Members and a Member-Secretary
Five Members and a Secretary appointed by Parliament
A Chairperson, five Members and a Member-Secretary
74.x: The NCW comprises one Chairperson, five Members and one Member-Secretary. All are nominated by the Central Government.
74.tq: Use the exact composition and do not confuse nomination with election or parliamentary appointment.
xs: The NCW has a **Chairperson, five Members and a Member-Secretary** — option **(4)**.
Among the 5 members, at least **1 SC and 1 ST**.
All are **nominated by the Central Government**, not appointed by Parliament.
xa: NCW term: **3 years**; removal by the **Centre**.
The **NCM** has a Chair, Vice-Chair and **5 members** (**7** in all).
The NCW is a **statutory body** under the **NCW Act, 1990**.

74.s:
Who nominates the Chairperson, Members and Member-Secretary of the National Commission for Women?

a. The President of India
b. The Parliament
c. The Central Government
d. The Supreme Court of India
74.x: The Chairperson, five Members and Member-Secretary of the NCW are nominated by the Central Government.
74.tq: Apply the “who would do this job?” method to distinguish nomination from constitutional appointment.
xs: The NCW's chair, members and Member-Secretary are nominated by **the Central Government** — option **(3)**.
⚠ The **NHRC** is appointed by the **President**; the **NCW** and **NCM** by the **Central Government**.
Neither **Parliament** nor the **Supreme Court** nominates them.
xa: NCW: Chairperson + **5 members** (at least 1 SC and 1 ST) + Member-Secretary.
NCW term **3 years**; removal by the Centre.
NCM members are also appointed by the **Central Government, not the President**.

74.s:
Which one of the following is NOT a function of the National Commission for Women?

a. Suggesting amendments to laws affecting women
b. Taking suo motu notice where women’s rights are denied
c. Commissioning special studies on discrimination and atrocities against women
d. Enforcing criminal sentences imposed by courts
o: Suggesting amendments to laws affecting women
Taking suo motu notice where women’s rights are denied
Commissioning special studies on discrimination and atrocities against women
Enforcing criminal sentences imposed by courts
74.x: The NCW may review laws, suggest amendments, take suo motu notice and commission special studies. It does not enforce criminal sentences imposed by courts.
74.tq: Reject the option that converts a recommendatory statutory function into a coercive judicial power.
xs: **Enforcing criminal sentences imposed by courts** is NOT an NCW function — option **(4)**.
**Section 10** of the NCW Act, 1990 lists functions such as reviewing laws and **suggesting amendments**.
It also takes **suo motu notice** of rights denied and commissions **special studies** on discrimination and atrocities.
xa: It reviews constitutional and **legal safeguards** for women and advises on policy.
The **Central Government must consult the NCW** on all major policy matters affecting women.
**Jan Sunwai**: the NCW's public hearings of women's grievances.

74.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Commission for Women:

1. The Central Government must consult it on all major policy matters affecting women.
2. It may appoint committees for particular purposes.
3. It may co-opt persons from outside the Commission.
4. It has no power to regulate its own procedure.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
74.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The NCW may regulate its own procedure, so statement 4 is false.
74.tq: Spot the negative statement that reverses an expressly stated procedural power.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: the **Central Government must consult the NCW** on all major policy matters affecting women.
Statements 2 and 3: it may **appoint committees** and **co-opt outsiders**.
Statement 4 wrong: the NCW **regulates its own procedure**.
xa: NCW functions are listed in **Section 10** of the NCW Act, 1990.
It handles **complaints** and takes **suo motu notice**; commissions **special studies**.
It holds **Jan Sunwai** public hearings.

74.s:
In the context of women’s rights, a ‘Jan Sunwai’ refers to:

a. A closed-door meeting of judges
b. A public hearing of women’s grievances
c. An annual financial audit of women’s commissions
d. A legislative session on gender budgeting
o: A public hearing of women’s grievances
A legislative session on gender budgeting
An annual financial audit of women’s commissions
74.x: Jan Sunwai refers to public hearings conducted to hear and address women’s grievances.
74.tq: Test the exact meaning of a programme term rather than its broad policy context.
xs: A **Jan Sunwai** is a **public hearing of women's grievances** — option **(1)**.
It is an NCW tool for grievance redressal.
AP example: the **AP Mahila Commission** held a five-day Jan Sunwai in five zones, **9-13 March 2026**, on NCW directions.
xa: The AP zones included **Nellore**, **Guntur**, **Vijayawada** and **Rajamahendravaram**.
AP Mahila Commission chairperson: **Rayapati Sailaja**.
The NCW takes **complaints and suo motu notice** under **Section 10** of its Act.

74.s: The NCPCR is a statutory body established under the
o: Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
74.x: The NCPCR was established under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, although it monitors the implementation of several other child-related laws.
74.tq: Match the institution with its constituting statute rather than a law it monitors.
xs: The NCPCR is a statutory body under the **Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005** — option **(2)**.
It was set up in **2007**.
The **JJ Act 2015**, **POCSO Act 2012** and **RTE Act 2009** are Acts it monitors, not its parent Act.
xa: **SCPCRs** also come under the **CPCR Act 2005**.
The NCPCR checks laws against the **UNCRC**; India acceded in **1992**.
It is one of the **WCD Ministry's** statutory bodies with **NCW** and **CARA**.

74.s: The NCPCR’s mandate includes examining whether laws and policies are in conformity with the
o: Paris Agreement and the Constitution alone
Convention against Torture and the Geneva Conventions
Constitution of India and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights alone
74.x: The NCPCR keeps laws and policies in line with the Constitution and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. India acceded to the UNCRC in 1992.
74.tq: Identify the paired domestic and international foundations of the child-rights mandate.
xs: The NCPCR keeps laws and policies in line with the **Constitution** and the **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child** — option **(3)**.
The **CRC** dates from **1989**; India acceded in **1992**.
The **Convention against Torture** (**1984**) and **ICCPR** (**1966**) are not its benchmark.
xa: The NCPCR monitors the **RTE**, **POCSO** and **JJ** Acts.
It was set up in **2007** under the **CPCR Act, 2005**.
**POCSO monitoring** is shared with the State Commissions (**SCPCRs**).

74.s: India acceded to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child in
74.x: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted in 1989, and India acceded to it in 1992.
74.tq: Distinguish the year of adoption of an international convention from India’s accession year.
xs: India acceded to the **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child** in **1992** — option **(3)**.
⚠ **1989** is the year of the **CRC** itself, not India's accession.
The NCPCR checks Indian laws against the **UNCRC**.
xa: **CEDAW** — **1979**; **Convention against Torture** — **1984**.
Child-rights Acts: **RTE 2009**, **POCSO 2012**, **JJ 2015**.

74.s: The Right to Education provision monitored by the NCPCR concerning 25 per cent free seats is found in Section
74.x: Section 12(1)(c) of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 concerns the 25 per cent reservation of seats for children in specified private unaided schools.
74.tq: Match the precise statutory section with the policy obligation it contains.
xs: The **25% free seats** provision of the RTE Act is **Sec 12(1)(c)** — option **(3)**.
The **Supreme Court's** RTE ruling on it was in the news in **2026**.
The **RTE Act** (**2009**) is among the Acts the **NCPCR** monitors.
xa: The NCPCR also monitors the **POCSO Act 2012** and **JJ Act 2015**.
The NCPCR was set up in **2007** under the **CPCR Act, 2005**.
India acceded to the **UNCRC** in **1992**.

74.s:
Consider the following statements regarding State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights:
1. They function under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005.
2. They exist as State counterparts alongside the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights.
3. They oversee child-rights directions such as those relating to menstrual hygiene in schools.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
74.x: All three statements are correct. SCPCRs operate under the CPCR Act, 2005, alongside the NCPCR, and address child-rights directions including school menstrual-hygiene measures.
74.tq: Combine the parent statute, institutional relationship and functional example before selecting the code.
xs: All three statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(4)**.
Statements 1 and 2: **SCPCRs** come under the **CPCR Act 2005**, alongside the **NCPCR**.
Statement 3: both oversee child-rights directions, e.g. the **SC's menstrual-hygiene ruling** for schools (**Feb 2026**).
xa: **POCSO monitoring** is shared by the NCPCR and SCPCRs.
The NCPCR was set up in **2007**.
It checks laws against the **Constitution** and **UNCRC**.

74.s:
Which of the following enactments are monitored by the NCPCR?
1. Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
2. Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
3. Juvenile Justice Act, 2015
4. National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
74.x: The NCPCR monitors the RTE Act, 2009, the POCSO Act, 2012 and the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015. The National Commission for Minorities Act is not part of this child-rights monitoring mandate.
74.tq: Remove the unrelated statute from a cluster of child-rights laws.
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3** are monitored by the NCPCR — option **(1)**.
These are the **RTE Act 2009**, **POCSO Act 2012** and **JJ Act 2015**.
The **NCM Act, 1992** created the **National Commission for Minorities**; it is not a child-rights law.
xa: The NCPCR itself rests on the **CPCR Act, 2005** (set up **2007**).
The RTE's **25% free seats** rule is **Sec 12(1)(c)**.
**SCPCRs** share POCSO monitoring.

74.s: The number of communities notified as minorities by the Government of India is
74.x: Six communities are notified as minorities: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Parsis, with Jains added on 27 January 2014 as the latest notified minority.
74.tq: Count the notified communities and avoid omitting the later-listed Jain community.
xs: **Six** communities are notified minorities — option **(1)**.
They are **Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis** and **Jains**.
**Jains** were the latest, notified on **27 Jan 2014**.
xa: **15** States have State Minorities Commissions, including **AP**.
The statutory **NCM** came under the **NCM Act, 1992** (set up **1993**).
NCM: **5 including the chair** must be from minorities; term **3 years**.

74.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched regarding the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis?

a. Act lapsed — 1998
b. Change to non-statutory status — 2004
c. Ministry — Women and Child Development
d. Governing Act currently in force — NCSK Act, 1993
o: Governing Act currently in force — NCSK Act, 1993
74.x: The NCSK Act, 1993 lapsed in 2004, after which the NCSK continued as a non-statutory body under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. The Act is not currently in force as its governing basis.
74.tq: Separate the original statutory status from the present non-statutory status.
xs: **Change to non-statutory status — 2004** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
The **NCSK Act 1993** **lapsed in 2004**, so it is not in force and did not lapse in 1998.
Since then the NCSK is a **non-statutory body under MoSJE**, not the WCD Ministry.
xa: Its tenure is extended by **government resolution**.
Jan **2022**: extended **three years** to **31 March 2025**; next to **31 March 2028**.
⚠ UPSC notes still call it a "statutory body".

74.s:
In January 2022, the Union Cabinet extended the tenure of the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis for:

a. One year beyond 31 March 2022
b. Two years beyond 31 March 2022
c. Three years beyond 31 March 2022
d. Five years beyond 31 March 2022
74.x: In January 2022, the Union Cabinet extended the NCSK for three years beyond 31 March 2022, taking the tenure up to 31 March 2025.
74.tq: Match the extension period with its terminal date rather than relying on the Act’s original year.
xs: In **January 2022** the Cabinet extended the NCSK for **three years beyond 31 March 2022** — option **(2)**.
That took it to **31 March 2025** (APPSC **2021** PYQ).
The next extension: **3 more years, to 31 March 2028**.
xa: The NCSK Act **1993** lapsed in **2004**; the body continues by resolution.
It monitors the **Manual Scavengers Act, 2013**.
A **missed-call grievance line** for sanitation workers was launched on NCSK's foundation day, **23 August** (**2026**).

74.s:
The tenure of the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis was subsequently extended up to:

a. 31 March 2026
b. 31 March 2027
c. 31 March 2028
d. 31 December 2028
74.x: After the extension up to 31 March 2025, the NCSK received a further three-year extension up to 31 March 2028.
74.tq: Track successive tenure extensions chronologically and identify the final date.
xs: The NCSK tenure was next extended to **31 March 2028** — option **(1)**.
The earlier extension (Jan **2022**) ran **three years** to **31 March 2025**.
The later one added **3 more years**.
xa: The NCSK is a **non-statutory body under MoSJE** since **2004**.
Present Vice-Chairperson: **Hardeep Singh Gill**.
Related scheme: **NAMASTE** (**2022**; **NSKFDC**).

74.s:
Which of the following functions is associated with the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis?

a. Monitoring the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers Act, 2013 and reporting to the Government
b. Conducting the census of all urban households
c. Appointing municipal commissioners in every State
d. Issuing constitutional amendments concerning sanitation
o: Appointing municipal commissioners in every State
Conducting the census of all urban households
Monitoring the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers Act, 2013 and reporting to the Government
74.x: The NCSK monitors implementation of the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers Act, 2013 and reports to the Government.
74.tq: Identify the option that states a monitoring and reporting responsibility rather than an unrelated executive power.
xs: The NCSK monitors the **Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers Act, 2013** and **reports to the Government** — option **(3)**.
The other options (census, appointing municipal commissioners, constitutional amendments) are not its mandate.
It continues as a **non-statutory body under MoSJE**.
xa: Foundation day **23 August**: a **missed-call grievance line** for sanitation workers was launched (**2026**).
**NAMASTE** (**2022**) is linked to the **NSKFDC**.
Tenure runs to **31 March 2028**.

74.s:
Which one of the following is correctly matched?

a. NAMASTE — 2022; associated with NSKFDC
b. Jan Sunwai — appointment of NCSK Vice-Chairperson
c. NCSK Act — constitutional provision under Article 338A
d. Article 350B — National Commission for Safai Karamcharis
o: Jan Sunwai — appointment of NCSK Vice-Chairperson
NCSK Act — constitutional provision under Article 338A
Article 350B — National Commission for Safai Karamcharis
74.x: NAMASTE is associated with the NSKFDC and dates from 2022. Jan Sunwai concerns public hearings of women’s grievances, Article 338A concerns the NCST, and Article 350B concerns linguistic minorities.
74.tq: Use nearby institutional facts to catch swapped bodies, Articles and programmes.
xs: **NAMASTE — 2022; associated with NSKFDC** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Jan Sunwai** means public hearings of women's grievances, not an NCSK appointment.
**Art. 338A** is the **NCST** provision; the NCSK is not a constitutional body.
xa: The NCSK came under the **NCSK Act 1993**, which **lapsed in 2004**.
NCSK present Vice-Chairperson: **Hardeep Singh Gill**.
It monitors the **Manual Scavengers Act, 2013**.

74.s: Which one of the following persons was identified as the Chairman of the Andhra Pradesh State Commission for Scheduled Castes during the review of welfare schemes in SPSR Nellore?
74.x: K.S. Jawahar was identified as the Chairman of the Andhra Pradesh State Commission for Scheduled Castes while reviewing SC/ST welfare schemes in SPSR Nellore.
74.tq: Keep State-level office-holders separate from chairpersons of the corresponding national commissions.
xs: **K.S. Jawahar** is Chairman of the **AP State SC Commission** — option **(2)**.
He reviewed SC/ST schemes in **SPSR Nellore** and took **196 petitions** (**28 Aug 2026**).
**Bhagwan Lal Sahni** was the first NCBC chair, **Suraj Bhan** the first separate NCSC chair, and **Harjit Singh Grewal** heads the NCM.
xa: The AP State Commission for SCs and STs rests on the **AP State Commission for SCs and STs Act, 2003**, **reconstituted in 2016**.
State commissions are created by **State laws**; reports go to the **Governor**.
⚠ **Art 338(9)** and **338A(10)** do not create State commissions; they make the Union and States **consult** the national commission.

74.s: The Andhra Pradesh State Human Rights Commission functions from:
74.x: The Andhra Pradesh State Human Rights Commission works from Kurnool.
74.tq: Use location discrimination among major Andhra Pradesh cities.
xs: The **AP State Human Rights Commission** works from **Kurnool** — option **(3)**.
It is an SHRC under the **PHRA 1993**.
Its members are appointed by the **Governor** and removed only by the **President**.
xa: The **AP Commission for Backward Classes** rests on the **AP Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993** and is a permanent body.
The NHRC sought reports from the AP DGP, Chief Secretary and **AP SHRC** on **Gade Sai Krishna's** custodial death (**28 Jun 2026**).
SHRCs take only **State List and Concurrent List** matters.

74.s: The Andhra Pradesh State Human Rights Commission was established under the:
74.x: The Andhra Pradesh State Human Rights Commission is a State Human Rights Commission established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
74.tq: Distinguish the exact parent statute from similarly worded but nonexistent Acts.
xs: The **AP State Human Rights Commission** was set up under the **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993** — option **(4)**.
All SHRCs rest on the **PHRA 1993**, the same Act as the NHRC.
There is no separate "NHRC Act" or AP Human Rights Act in the notes.
xa: The AP SHRC works from **Kurnool**.
After **2019**, an SHRC chair is a former **Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court**.
The **2019 amendment** lets the Centre give **UT** functions to SHRCs.

74.s: Who is the Chairperson of the Andhra Pradesh State Commission for Women according to the 2026 information?
74.x: Rayapati Sailaja is the Chairperson of the Andhra Pradesh State Commission for Women.
74.tq: Separate a State Commission appointment from the Chairpersons of the National Commission for Women.
xs: **Rayapati Sailaja** chairs the **AP State Commission for Women** (Mahila Commission) — option **(4)**.
**Vijaya Rahatkar** is the present **NCW** chairperson; **Rekha Sharma** was NCW chair in **2023**; **Jayanti Patnaik** was the first NCW chair.
State Commissions for Women come under **State Acts**.

75.s: The India Against Corruption movement was led by
75.x: India Against Corruption was led by Anna Hazare and was central to the 2011 civil society campaign for the Jan Lokpal Bill.
75.tq: Distinguish the movement’s leader from members of the later drafting committee.
xs: **India Against Corruption (IAC)** was led by **Anna Hazare** — option **(1)**.
It began in **2011** and pushed the civil-society **Jan Lokpal Bill**.
**Shanti Bhushan** and **Prashant Bhushan** sat on the civil-society side of the drafting panel; **Pranab Mukherjee** chaired it for the Government.
xa: Fasts: **Jantar Mantar (April 2011)** and **Ramlila Maidan (August 2011)**.
Civil-society members also included **Arvind Kejriwal** and **Justice N. Santosh Hegde**.
The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Bill was passed in **December 2013**.

75.s: Anna Hazare’s fasts that intensified pressure for the Jan Lokpal Bill were held at
o: Jantar Mantar in April 2011 and Ramlila Maidan in August 2011
Ramlila Maidan in April 2011 and Jantar Mantar in August 2011
Jantar Mantar in August 2011 and Ramlila Maidan in December 2011
Rajghat in April 2011 and Jantar Mantar in August 2011
75.x: The fasts were held at Jantar Mantar in April 2011 and at Ramlila Maidan in August 2011.
75.tq: Pair each venue with its correct month and reject the reversed sequence.
xs: The fasts were at **Jantar Mantar in April 2011** and **Ramlila Maidan in August 2011** — option **(1)**.
They pushed the civil-society **Jan Lokpal Bill**.
They were part of the **India Against Corruption** movement led by **Anna Hazare**.
xa: A **Joint Drafting Committee** was formed in **April 2011**: chair **Pranab Mukherjee**, co-chair **Shanti Bhushan**.
The Lokpal Bill 2011 was introduced in the Lok Sabha in **August 2011**.
It was passed by the Lok Sabha on **27 December 2011**.

75.s:
With reference to the Joint Drafting Committee formed in April 2011, consider the following statements:
1. Pranab Mukherjee was the chairperson on the Government side.
2. Shanti Bhushan was the co-chairperson from the civil society side.
3. Anna Hazare, Prashant Bhushan, Arvind Kejriwal and Justice N. Santosh Hegde represented civil society.
4. P. Chidambaram, Veerappa Moily, Kapil Sibal and Salman Khurshid were on the Government side.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: All four statements correctly identify the chairpersons and members of the Government and civil society sides of the April 2011 Joint Drafting Committee.
75.tq: Classify every name by side and office before choosing the complete combination.
xs: All four statements **1, 2, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(4)**.
Government side: **Pranab Mukherjee** (chair), **P. Chidambaram**, **Veerappa Moily**, **Kapil Sibal**, **Salman Khurshid**.
Civil society: **Shanti Bhushan** (co-chair), **Anna Hazare**, **Prashant Bhushan**, **Arvind Kejriwal**, **Justice N. Santosh Hegde**.
xa: ⚠ Drafting panel: chair **Pranab Mukherjee**; co-chair **Shanti Bhushan**.
**Justice N. Santosh Hegde** later gave the Karnataka Lokayukta's **Bellary** mining report (**2011**).
The committee was formed in **April 2011**, the month of the **Jantar Mantar** fast.

75.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the dates associated with the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013?
o: Assent was given on 1 January 2014 and the Act came into force on 16 January 2014.
Assent was given on 16 January 2014 and the Act came into force on 1 January 2014.
Both assent and commencement took place on 1 January 2014.
Both assent and commencement took place on 16 January 2014.
75.x: The President gave assent on 1 January 2014, while the Act came into force on 16 January 2014.
75.tq: Discriminate between two closely related dates by matching each date with its legal event.
xs: **Assent** came on **1 January 2014** and the Act **came into force** on **16 January 2014** — option **(1)**.
⚠ TH (**23 Mar 2026**) wrongly gives 1 January 2014 as commencement — that is the assent date.
**16 January 2014** is the APPSC key (APPSC **2019**, G2 **2025**).
xa: Parliament passed it on **17 December 2013** (Rajya Sabha) and **18 December 2013** (Lok Sabha).
The Lokpal actually began functioning on **27 March 2019**.
The Lokpal is a **statutory body**, not constitutional.

75.s: The Lokpal actually began functioning on:
75.x: Although the Act came into force in 2014, the Lokpal began functioning on 27 March 2019 after its Chairperson and members were appointed.
75.tq: Distinguish commencement of an Act from the date on which an institution began functioning.
xs: The Lokpal actually began functioning on **27 March 2019** — option **(2)**.
This was after the chairperson and members were appointed.
**16 January 2014** is commencement, **1 January 2014** assent and **17 December 2013** Rajya Sabha passage.
xa: First Lokpal: **Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose**, appointed **17 March 2019** (UPSC notes: **19** March).
Criticism: the **2013** Act → first Lokpal only in **2019** shows delay.
Second chair: **Justice A.M. Khanwilkar** since **10 March 2024**.

75.s:
Consider the following statements about the Lokpal:
1. It is a statutory body.
2. It is a constitutional body created directly by the Constitution.
3. Its composition may include a Chairperson and up to eight members.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Lokpal is established by statute and is not a constitutional body.
75.tq: Use the statutory-versus-constitutional distinction and test the numerical composition separately.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1: the Lokpal is a **statutory body**.
Statement 2 wrong: it is **not constitutional**.
Statement 3: it has a **Chairperson + not more than 8 members**.
xa: **50%** of members are **judicial**; at least **50%** from **SC, ST, OBC, minorities and women**.
CDI suggests **constitutional status** and a **model Lokayukta Act**.
The Act came into force on **16 January 2014**.

75.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the declaration of assets under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas law:
1. The original law required declaration of assets and liabilities of the public servant, spouse and dependent children.
2. The declaration was required within 30 days of entering office.
3. The 2016 amendment prescribed the form and manner of declaration directly in the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The 2016 amendment provided that the form and manner would be prescribed by the Central Government; it did not place the prescription in the Constitution.
75.tq: Reject the wrong-authority trap in statement 3 and retain the two precise statutory details.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: the original Act required **assets and liabilities of self, spouse and dependent children**.
Statement 2: the declaration was due within **30 days** of entering office.
Statement 3 wrong: the **2016 amendment** left the **form and manner** to be **prescribed by the Central Government**, not the Constitution.
xa: The **2016** amendment filled "a small gap" in the Act (UPSC Governance).
The **2013** Act also amended the **DSPE Act** (CBI Director's committee; a **Directorate of Prosecution**).
The Lokpal is a **statutory body**.

75.s: Which of the following persons is NOT a member of the Selection Committee for appointment of the Lokpal?
o: Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge nominated by the Chief Justice of India
75.x: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is not a member of the Lokpal Selection Committee. The committee includes the Prime Minister, Lok Sabha Speaker, Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, the CJI or nominee, and an eminent jurist.
75.tq: Use the membership trap involving the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
xs: The **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** is NOT on the Lokpal Selection Committee — option **(3)**.
Members: **PM (chair)**, **Lok Sabha Speaker**, **Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha**, **CJI or an SC judge he nominates**, and an **eminent jurist**.
This trap was the UKPSC **2025** key.
xa: The **President** appoints on the Selection Committee's recommendation.
The eminent jurist is nominated by the President on the recommendation of the other members.
A **Search Committee** of at least **seven** prepares the panel.

75.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Selection Committee of the Lokpal:
1. The Prime Minister is its Chairperson.
2. The Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha is a member.
3. One eminent jurist is nominated by the President on the recommendation of the other members.
4. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is its ex officio member.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is not a member of the Selection Committee.
75.tq: Identify the incorrect member by comparing the two presiding officers of Parliament.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: the **PM** chairs; statement 2: the **Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha** is a member.
Statement 3: one **eminent jurist** is nominated by the **President** on the other members' recommendation.
Statement 4 wrong: the **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is NOT a member**.
xa: Others: **Speaker of the Lok Sabha**; **CJI** or an SC judge nominated by the CJI.
A **Search Committee** of at least **seven** persons prepares the panel.
At least **half** of the Search Committee must be from SC, ST, OBC, minorities and women.

75.s:
With reference to the Search Committee constituted for the Lokpal, consider the following statements:
1. It is set up by the Selection Committee.
2. It prepares a panel for consideration.
3. It must have at least seven persons.
4. At least half of its members must be from SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities and women.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: All four statements are correct. The Search Committee is constituted by the Selection Committee, prepares a panel, has at least seven persons and must satisfy the specified representation requirement.
75.tq: Check each component of a statutory committee’s constitution and functions.
xs: All four statements **1, 2, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(4)**.
The **Search Committee** is set up by the **Selection Committee** to prepare a **panel**.
It has at least **seven** persons, at least **half** from **SC, ST, OBC, minorities and women**.
xa: The Selection Committee is chaired by the **PM**.
The **President** makes the appointment.
The Lokpal bench itself must be at least **50%** from these groups.

75.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Lokpal is correct?
o: The Lokpal may inquire into a complaint filed at any time after the alleged offence.
A Chairperson or member of the Lokpal may simultaneously be an MP or MLA.
The Act applies only to public servants posted within India.
A Chairperson or member of the Lokpal cannot be an MP or MLA.
75.x: A Chairperson or member of the Lokpal cannot be a Member of Parliament or a Member of a Legislative Assembly. The Act also covers public servants outside India and bars complaints filed after seven years from the alleged offence.
75.tq: Reject the option that reverses an eligibility restriction while checking related jurisdictional limits.
xs: A Lokpal Chairperson or member **cannot be an MP or MLA** — option **(4)**.
Option 1 wrong: complaints made **after seven years** from the alleged offence are barred.
Option 3 wrong: the Act covers public servants **in and outside India** (UKPSC **2025** key).
xa: Term: **5 years or age 70**, whichever earlier; **no reappointment**.
Chairperson eligibility: former **CJI**, an **SC judge**, or an eminent person with **25 years'** experience.
Exclusion for MPs: nothing said or any vote **in Parliament**.

75.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the composition of the Lokpal:
1. The Chairperson may be a former Chief Justice of India or a former Supreme Court judge.
2. An eminent person with 25 years' experience in specified fields may be eligible to be Chairperson.
3. The Chairperson must necessarily be a serving judge of the Supreme Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: A former Chief Justice of India, former Supreme Court judge, or an eminent person with 25 years' relevant experience may qualify. The Chairperson need not be a serving Supreme Court judge.
75.tq: Identify the false restrictive qualification created by the word 'necessarily'.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: a former **CJI** or an **SC judge** can be Chairperson.
Statement 2: so can an eminent person with **25 years'** experience in anti-corruption policy, public administration, vigilance, finance, law or management.
Statement 3 wrong: a **serving** SC judge is not required; the chair may be "sitting or former".
xa: Members: up to **8**, **50%** judicial (former SC judges or former HC Chief Justices).
Bar: cannot be an **MP or MLA**.
Present chair: **Justice A.M. Khanwilkar**, a retired SC judge.

75.s: The term of office of the Chairperson or a member of the Lokpal is
o: six years irrespective of age, with one reappointment
eight years or until attaining 70 years of age, whichever is later
five years or until attaining 65 years of age, whichever is later, with reappointment permitted
five years or until attaining 70 years of age, whichever is earlier, with no reappointment
75.x: The term is five years or until the age of 70, whichever is earlier, and reappointment is not permitted. A member may become Chairperson within the total five-year period.
75.tq: Watch the reversed comparison words 'earlier' and 'later' and the reappointment trap.
xs: The term is **five years or age 70**, whichever is **earlier**, with **no reappointment** — option **(4)**.
A member may become Chairperson within a **5-year** total.
The other options' terms do not match the Act.
xa: Bar: a Chairperson or member **cannot be an MP or MLA**.
The **Rajasthan** Lokayukta's tenure was cut from **8** years to **5** years (APPSC G1 **2018** key).
AP's new Lokayukta has a **5-year term** (**20 Aug 2026**).

75.s:
With reference to the Lokpal, consider the following statements:
1. The Chairperson may have not more than eight members.
2. At least half of the members are required to be judicial members.
3. A member can be reappointed after completing the first term.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: The Chairperson is assisted by not more than eight members, and at least 50% of the members must be judicial. Reappointment is not permitted.
75.tq: Combine composition rules with a negative tenure condition to eliminate the false statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **not more than 8 members**.
Statement 2: **50%** of members are **judicial**.
Statement 3 wrong: there is **no reappointment**.
xa: At least **50%** must also be from **SC, ST, OBC, minorities and women** — the two 50% rules apply together.
Present bench: **6 members** against a sanctioned **8** (Jun **2026**).
Term: **5 years or age 70**.

75.s: Which of the following correctly describes the composition of the Lokpal?
o: A Chairperson and up to eight members, with 50% judicial members and at least 50% representation from SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities and women
Only a serving Chief Justice of India and four Governors
A Chairperson and exactly eight non-judicial members, all appointed by Parliament
A Chairperson and two Vigilance Commissioners without any representational requirement
75.x: The Lokpal consists of a Chairperson and up to eight members. Half the members are judicial, and at least half must be from SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities and women.
75.tq: Use composition, judicial share and representational requirements together to identify the correct body.
xs: The Lokpal is a **Chairperson and up to eight members**, with **50% judicial** and at least **50%** from **SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities and women** — option **(1)**.
Judicial members are former **SC judges** or former **HC Chief Justices**.
Members are appointed by the **President**, not Parliament.
xa: The **Selection Committee** is chaired by the **PM**.
Judicial members now: Justices **Lingappa Narayana Swamy**, **Sanjay Yadav**, **Ritu Raj Awasthi**.
Non-judicial: **Sushil Chandra** (ex-CEC), **Pankaj Kumar**, **Ajay Tirkey**.

75.s: The Chairperson and members of the Lokpal are appointed by
75.x: They are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a Selection Committee. The Prime Minister only chairs that committee; the CJI (or nominee) is merely a member; Parliament has no appointing role.
75.tq: Lokpal: President appoints, PM-led Selection Committee recommends.
xs: Lokpal members are appointed by **the President** — option **(2)**.
He acts on the recommendation of a **Selection Committee**.
The **PM** only chairs the committee and the **CJI** (or nominee) is a member; Parliament has no role.
xa: Committee: **PM**, **Lok Sabha Speaker**, **LoP in Lok Sabha**, **CJI** or nominee, **eminent jurist**.
⚠ The **Rajya Sabha Chairman** is not a member.
⚠ State **Lokayuktas** are appointed by the **Governor**.

75.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with the jurisdiction of the Lokpal?
o: Central officials of Groups A, B, C and D — Group C and D complaints are referred to the CVC
Members of Parliament — all speeches and votes in Parliament are subject to inquiry
NGOs — covered only when they receive foreign contribution below ₹10 lakh
Indian public servants abroad — excluded because jurisdiction ends outside India
75.x: The Lokpal’s jurisdiction covers central officials of Groups A, B, C and D, while complaints against Group C and D officials are sent to the CVC, which reports back to the Lokpal. Parliamentary speeches and votes are excluded, NGOs are covered above the stated threshold, and public servants outside India are included.
75.tq: Separate closely related jurisdictional exceptions and administrative routes.
xs: **Central officials of Groups A, B, C and D** are covered, with **Group C and D** complaints going to the **CVC** — option **(1)**.
The CVC reports back to the Lokpal.
Option 2 wrong: anything said or any vote **in Parliament** is excluded; option 3 wrong: NGOs are covered above **₹10 lakh**; option 4 wrong: servants **outside India** are covered.
xa: The **PM** is covered with safeguards.
Bodies set up by an **Act of Parliament** or funded by government are covered.
Criticism: Group C/D in practice left to the **CVC**.

75.s: Which of the following categories of organisations comes within the Lokpal’s jurisdiction when the stated condition is fulfilled?
o: Only organisations receiving domestic donations above ₹10 lakh
Only constitutional bodies receiving no government funding
Every private company, irrespective of funding
NGOs, trusts and societies receiving foreign contributions above ₹10 lakh
75.x: NGOs, trusts and societies receiving foreign contributions above ₹10 lakh come within the stated jurisdiction of the Lokpal.
75.tq: Focus on both the organisation category and the exact monetary threshold.
xs: **NGOs, trusts and societies** receiving **foreign contribution above ₹10 lakh** (FCRA) are covered — option **(4)**.
The test is **foreign** contribution, not domestic donations.
Bodies set up by an **Act of Parliament** or **funded by government** are also covered.
xa: Central officials of **Groups A, B, C and D** are covered.
**Union Ministers** and **MPs** are covered.
Public servants **in and outside India** are covered.

75.s:
The jurisdiction of the Lokpal over the Prime Minister is subject to which of the following exclusions?
1. International relations
2. Security
3. Public order
4. Atomic energy and space
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
75.x: The Prime Minister’s excluded areas include international relations, external and internal security, public order, atomic energy and space. Therefore, all four listed categories are covered by the exclusions.
75.tq: Group several statutory exceptions together and check whether any listed category falls outside them.
xs: All four **1, 2, 3 and 4** are exclusions for the PM — option **(3)**.
The excluded areas: **international relations**, **external and internal security**, **public order**, **atomic energy and space**.
Outside these the PM is covered, with safeguards.
xa: An inquiry against the PM needs the **full bench** and a **two-thirds** majority.
It is held **in camera**.
Complaints are barred **after seven years**.

75.s: An allegation against the Prime Minister relates to a matter not covered by the statutory exclusions. Which condition is required for an inquiry by the Lokpal?
o: Approval by the Union Cabinet through an open hearing
Prior approval of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha alone
Approval by the full Bench with at least a two-thirds majority, with the proceedings held in camera
Approval by a simple majority of any two members, in public proceedings
75.x: An inquiry against the Prime Minister requires approval of the full Bench by at least a two-thirds majority, and the inquiry is held in camera.
75.tq: Apply the special procedural safeguards to a concrete jurisdictional situation.
xs: An inquiry against the PM needs the **full Bench** with at least a **two-thirds majority**, held **in camera** — option **(3)**.
Neither the **Cabinet** nor the **Rajya Sabha Chairman** has a role.
A simple majority or public proceedings would not satisfy the safeguard.
xa: Excluded subjects: **international relations**, **security**, **public order**, **atomic energy and space**.
Lokpal: Chairperson + up to **8** members.
The Lokpal has **civil court** powers: summon persons, requisition records.

75.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the jurisdiction of the Lokpal:
1. It extends to Union Ministers and Members of Parliament.
2. It covers anything said or any vote given by an MP in Parliament.
3. It applies to Indian public servants both within and outside India.
4. It covers bodies established by an Act of Parliament or funded by the government.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Statement 2 is false because anything said or any vote given by an MP in Parliament is outside the Lokpal’s jurisdiction.
75.tq: Use the parliamentary speech-and-vote exception to reject an otherwise broad jurisdiction statement.
xs: Statements **1, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **Union Ministers** and **MPs** are covered.
Statement 2 wrong: anything said or any **vote in Parliament** is excluded.
Statements 3 and 4: public servants **in and outside India**, and bodies under an **Act of Parliament** or **government-funded**, are covered.
xa: NGOs with **foreign contribution above ₹10 lakh** are covered.
⚠ UPSC **2025** key marks the "not posted abroad" statement wrong.
Groups **A, B, C and D** officials are covered.

75.s: A complaint is made seven years after the alleged offence. Under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the Lokpal:
o: can inquire only if the complaint concerns a Union Minister
cannot inquire into it after the statutory seven-year period
can inquire only after approval of the Rajya Sabha Chairman
must inquire into it because there is no limitation period
75.x: The Lokpal cannot inquire into a complaint made after seven years from the alleged offence.
75.tq: Apply the statutory time limit to a filing scenario.
xs: The Lokpal **cannot inquire** into a complaint made **after seven years** from the alleged offence — option **(2)**.
So there is a limitation period; it is not a Union Minister or Rajya Sabha Chairman exception.
The bar is **7 years** from the alleged offence.
xa: Inquiry Wing report after reference: **60 days**.
Preliminary inquiry: **90 days**, plus **90 days** with **reasons in writing**.
Investigation: **6 months**, extendable by **6 months**.

75.s: Section 11 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, requires the establishment of
o: a vigilance wing headed by the CVC and an audit wing headed by the CAG
an inquiry wing headed by a Director of Inquiry and a prosecution wing headed by a Director of Prosecution
a judicial wing headed by the Chief Justice of India and a police wing headed by the CBI Director
a parliamentary wing headed by the Speaker and a prosecution wing headed by the Attorney General
75.x: Section 11 requires an inquiry wing headed by a Director of Inquiry and a prosecution wing headed by a Director of Prosecution.
75.tq: Match each statutory wing with its specifically designated head.
xs: **Section 11** requires an **inquiry wing** headed by a **Director of Inquiry**; a **prosecution wing** is headed by a **Director of Prosecution** — option **(2)**.
The prosecution wing files cases before the **Special Court**.
Both wings were **still being staffed** (parliamentary standing committee, **23 Mar 2026**).
xa: The Inquiry Wing was recently set up with **3 SPs** (general, economic/banking, cyber).
The Lokpal has **superintendence and direction** over the **CBI** in cases it refers.
It can **attach and confiscate** corruptly acquired property.

75.s: The Inquiry Wing of the Lokpal conducts preliminary inquiry into offences under the:
75.x: The Inquiry Wing conducts preliminary inquiries into offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
75.tq: Use the statutory subject of the inquiry rather than the name of the investigating wing alone.
xs: The Inquiry Wing makes preliminary inquiries into offences under the **Prevention of Corruption Act** (PCA) — option **(2)**.
It is headed by a **Director of Inquiry** (**Section 11**).
Its report after a reference is due in **60 days**.
xa: SC **split verdict** on **Section 17A** of the PCA (prior approval before investigation), **22 Jan 2026**.
Justice **K.V. Viswanathan** upheld 17A only with a **binding opinion of the Lokpal/Lokayukta**; Justice **B.V. Nagarathna** held it unconstitutional.
AP's **ACB** investigates **Prevention of Corruption Act** offences.

75.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the powers associated with the Lokpal:
1. The Prosecution Wing files cases before the Special Court.
2. The Lokpal exercises superintendence and direction over the CBI in cases referred by it.
3. The Lokpal may summon persons and requisition records in the manner of a civil court.
4. Property acquired by corrupt means can be attached and confiscated even while prosecution is pending.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: All four statements are correct. The Lokpal’s framework includes prosecution before the Special Court, specified CBI superintendence, civil-court powers and attachment or confiscation of tainted property during pending prosecution.
75.tq: Check each statement against a distinct power before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All four statements **1, 2, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: the **Prosecution Wing** files cases before the **Special Court**; statement 2: **superintendence and direction** over the **CBI** in cases **referred by the Lokpal**.
Statement 3: **civil court** powers to summon persons and requisition records.
Statement 4: it may **attach and confiscate** corrupt property even while prosecution is pending.
xa: It can also direct protection of documents and recommend **transfer/suspension** and disciplinary action.
⚠ The **CVC Act 2003** gives the CVC superintendence over the CBI in PCA cases generally; the Lokpal only in cases it refers.
Criticism: **dependence on the CBI**.

75.s: The report of the Inquiry Wing after a reference is ordinarily required within:
75.x: The Inquiry Wing is required to submit its report within 60 days after a reference.
75.tq: Distinguish the 60-day report period from the separate 90-day preliminary inquiry period.
xs: The Inquiry Wing reports within **60 days** after a reference — option **(2)**.
**90 days** is the preliminary inquiry limit.
Investigation is **6 months**, extendable by **6 months**.
xa: Special Court trial: **1 year**, extendable up to **2 years**.
Complaints are barred after **7 years**.
The Inquiry Wing is headed by a **Director of Inquiry** under **Section 11**.

75.s:
With reference to the preliminary inquiry under the Lokpal framework, consider the following statements:
1. It is ordinarily to be completed within 90 days.
2. It may be extended by a further 90 days.
3. Extension does not require recording reasons in writing.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: A preliminary inquiry ordinarily has a 90-day limit and may be extended by another 90 days. Reasons for the extension must be recorded in writing, making statement 3 false.
75.tq: Spot the negative requirement trap: written reasons are necessary for extension.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: a preliminary inquiry ordinarily takes **90 days**.
Statement 2: a further **90 days** is allowed.
Statement 3 wrong: the extension needs **reasons in writing** (TH **30 Jul 2026**).
xa: Inquiry Wing report: **60 days**.
Investigation: **6 months** + **6 months**.
Trial: **1 year**, extendable up to **2 years**.

75.s: The investigation period under the Lokpal framework is:
o: Six months, extendable by six months
Nine months, extendable by three months
Three months, extendable by three months
One year, extendable by one year
75.x: Investigation is to be completed within six months and may be extended by a further six months.
75.tq: Keep the base period and permissible extension as a matched pair.
xs: Investigation takes **six months**, extendable by **six months** — option **(1)**.
**90 + 90 days** is the preliminary inquiry.
**1 year** extendable up to **2 years** is the Special Court trial.
xa: Inquiry Wing report: **60 days**.
Complaint bar: **after seven years**.
In cases it refers, the Lokpal directs the **CBI**.

75.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: First Lokpal — Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose
Lokpal inquiry and prosecution wings — fully staffed from the commencement of the Act
Group C and D complaints — Central Vigilance Commission
75.x: The Lokpal’s inquiry wing under Section 11 and its prosecution wing were reported as still not fully staffed. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
75.tq: Find the overstated institutional claim containing the false completion detail.
xs: **Inquiry and prosecution wings — fully staffed from the commencement of the Act** is NOT correct — option **(3)**.
A parliamentary standing committee found both **still being staffed**; the **Director of Inquiry** appointment "in process" (**23 Mar 2026**).
The other pairs are right: first Lokpal **Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose**; began work **27 March 2019**; **Group C and D** complaints go to the **CVC**.
xa: Ghose left office on **27 May 2022**; the post was then vacant for about **two years**.
The Inquiry Wing was set up under **Section 11** with **3 SPs**.
Criticism: more than a decade after the Act, staffing is incomplete.

75.s: Under the Lokpal framework, a trial by the Special Court is ordinarily to be completed within
o: six months, extendable by six months
one year, extendable up to two years
75.x: The Special Court trial has a one-year limit extendable up to two years. Six months plus six months is the investigation limit; 90 plus 90 days is the preliminary inquiry; 60 days is the Inquiry Wing's report.
75.tq: 60 days report, 90+90 inquiry, 6+6 months investigation, 1-2 years trial.
xs: A Special Court trial takes **one year**, extendable up to **two years** — option **(2)**.
**Six months + six months** is the investigation limit.
**90 + 90 days** is the preliminary inquiry; **60 days** the Inquiry Wing's report.
xa: The **Prosecution Wing** files cases before the **Special Court**.
It is headed by a **Director of Prosecution**.
The Lokpal can attach property even while **prosecution is pending**.

75.s: Who has been the second Chairperson of the Lokpal since 10 March 2024?
75.x: Justice Ajay Manikrao Khanwilkar, a retired Supreme Court judge, became the second Chairperson of the Lokpal on 10 March 2024.
75.tq: Distinguish the Chairperson from the judicial members of the bench.
xs: **Justice A.M. Khanwilkar** (**Ajay Manikrao Khanwilkar**) has been the second Lokpal chair since **10 March 2024** — option **(4)**.
He is a retired **SC judge**, appointed after a gap of nearly two years (UPPSC **2024** key).
**Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose** was the first; **Ritu Raj Awasthi** and **Lingappa Narayana Swamy** are judicial members.
xa: Ghose was appointed **17 March 2019** and left on **27 May 2022**.
Present bench: **6 members** against a sanctioned **8**.
Non-judicial members: **Sushil Chandra**, **Pankaj Kumar**, **Ajay Tirkey**.

75.s:
Which of the following is correctly matched?

1. Justice Lingappa Narayana Swamy — Judicial member
2. Sushil Chandra — Non-judicial member
3. Pankaj Kumar — Non-judicial member
4. Ajay Tirkey — Judicial member
75.x: Justice Lingappa Narayana Swamy is a judicial member, while Sushil Chandra and Pankaj Kumar are non-judicial members. Ajay Tirkey is also non-judicial, so statement 4 is false.
75.tq: Use the judicial versus non-judicial classification to catch the swapped designation.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Justice Lingappa Narayana Swamy** is a judicial member.
**Sushil Chandra** (former CEC) and **Pankaj Kumar** are non-judicial.
Pair 4 wrong: **Ajay Tirkey** is a **non-judicial** member.
xa: Other judicial members: Justices **Sanjay Yadav** and **Ritu Raj Awasthi**.
The bench has **6 members** against **8** sanctioned (Jun **2026**).
Rule: **50%** of members must be **judicial**.

75.s: Which of the following was the subject of judicial scrutiny in the Mahua Moitra matter?
o: The tender for seven BMW cars
The Lokpal's order of 12 November 2025 sanctioning a chargesheet
The appointment of the Director of Inquiry under Section 11
The appointment of the first Lokpal in March 2019
75.x: The Delhi High Court set aside the Lokpal's 12 November 2025 order sanctioning a chargesheet in the Mahua Moitra matter and held that the law had been 'mutilated'. The Supreme Court agreed to clarify the sanction procedure.
75.tq: Match the case with its specific order and avoid nearby Lokpal controversies.
xs: The matter concerned the Lokpal's **12 November 2025** order **sanctioning a chargesheet** — option **(2)**.
The **Delhi HC** set it aside, saying the Lokpal had "**mutilated**" the law.
The **Supreme Court** agreed to clarify the sanction procedure (**14 Mar 2026**).
xa: The **BMW tender** for **seven** cars (~**₹5 crore**) was cancelled after criticism (**2 Jan 2026**).
Criticism: the Lokpal has **no power of prior sanction**.
The Director of Inquiry appointment was still "in process" (**23 Mar 2026**).

75.s:
Which of the following has been identified as a criticism or practical limitation of the Lokpal?
1. It has no power of prior sanction.
2. Group C and Group D matters are, in practice, left to the Central Vigilance Commission.
3. It is dependent on the Central Bureau of Investigation for inquiries.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: The listed criticisms are the absence of power of prior sanction, practical exclusion of Group C and D matters in favour of the CVC, and dependence on the CBI.
75.tq: Check whether all three statements describe limitations rather than statutory powers.
xs: All three statements **1, 2 and 3** are criticisms — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **no power of prior sanction**.
Statement 2: **Group C/D** matters in practice left to the **CVC**.
Statement 3: **dependence on the CBI**.
xa: Delay: **2013** Act → first Lokpal only in **2019**; then a two-year vacancy (**2022-24**).
Inquiry and prosecution wings still **unstaffed**.
CDI suggests **constitutional status** and a **model Lokayukta Act**.

75.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose left the office of Lokpal.
B. The Lokpal began functioning.
C. Justice A.M. Khanwilkar became Chairperson of the Lokpal.
75.x: The Lokpal began functioning on 27 March 2019, Justice Ghose left office on 27 May 2022, and Justice Khanwilkar became Chairperson on 10 March 2024.
75.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the intervening vacancy event.
xs: The order is **B, A, C** — option **(1)**.
B: the Lokpal began functioning on **27 March 2019**.
A: **Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose** left office on **27 May 2022**.
C: **Justice A.M. Khanwilkar** became chair on **10 March 2024**.
xa: Between Ghose and Khanwilkar the post was vacant for about **two years** under an acting Chairperson.
Ghose was appointed **17 March 2019** (UPSC notes: **19** March).
The Act had come into force on **16 January 2014**.

75.s: Who was appointed the first Lokpal of India in March 2019?
75.x: Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose, a retired Supreme Court judge, became the first Lokpal in March 2019. Khanwilkar is the present (second) Chairperson since 2024; Santosh Hegde was Karnataka Lokayukta; Ritu Raj Awasthi is a judicial member.
75.tq: First Lokpal = P.C. Ghose (2019); second = Khanwilkar (2024).
xs: **Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose**, a retired **Supreme Court judge**, became the first Lokpal in **March 2019** — option **(3)**.
**Justice A.M. Khanwilkar** is the present (second) chair since **2024**.
**Justice N. Santosh Hegde** gave Karnataka's **Bellary** report; **Ritu Raj Awasthi** is a judicial member.
xa: APPSC answer for the first Lokpal's year: **2019** (APPSC **2018** key).
The Lokpal **started work** on **27 Mar 2019**.
Ghose left office on **27 May 2022**.

75.s: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act required every State to establish a Lokayukta within:
o: Six months of the Act’s assent
Two years of the first Lokpal appointment
One year of the commencement of the Act
Five years of the establishment of the Central Vigilance Commission
75.x: Every State was required to set up a Lokayukta within one year of the commencement of the Act.
75.tq: Test the exact time limit and its starting point.
xs: Every State had to set up a Lokayukta within **one year of commencement** of the Act — option **(3)**.
This is **Section 63** of the **2013** Act.
Each State does so by **its own State law**.
xa: By **2013**, **21 States and 1 UT (Delhi)** already had Lokayuktas.
There is **no uniform model**; CDI asks the Centre to encourage a **uniform, robust model**.
The Act came into force on **16 January 2014**.

75.s: Which of the following statements correctly describes the uniformity of Lokayukta institutions in India?
o: All States follow an identical Act and identical jurisdiction.
The Chief Justice of India determines the jurisdiction of every Lokayukta.
Each State establishes the institution under its own Lokayukta Act, resulting in differences in jurisdiction and coverage.
The Union Government appoints all Lokayuktas under one central law.
75.x: Lokayuktas are established under the respective State Acts, and there is no uniformity among States regarding jurisdiction, coverage of the Chief Minister or judicial qualifications.
75.tq: Reject the absolute uniformity claim and apply the federal institutional arrangement.
xs: Each State sets up its Lokayukta under **its own Lokayukta Act**, so jurisdiction and coverage differ — option **(3)**.
There is no uniformity in jurisdiction, **cover of the CM**, or **judicial qualification**.
Lokayuktas are appointed by the **Governor**, not the Union Government.
xa: CDI asks the Centre to encourage a **uniform, robust model**.
The CM is covered in **HP, AP, MP, Gujarat** but excluded in **Maharashtra, UP, Rajasthan, Bihar, Odisha**.
Judicial qualification is required in **UP, HP, AP, Gujarat, Odisha, Karnataka, Assam**.

75.s: Which State was the first in India to establish a Lokayukta?
75.x: Maharashtra was the first State to establish a Lokayukta, in 1971.
75.tq: Separate the first institution from the first law by focusing on the verb ‘establish’.
xs: **Maharashtra** was the first State to set up a Lokayukta, in **1971** — option **(3)**.
⚠ **Odisha** was first to **pass a law** (**1970**), but its institution came only in **1983**.
**Rajasthan's** Act is of **1973** and **Andhra Pradesh's** of **1983**.
xa: This is the BPSC **2021** key.
Maharashtra has a **Lokayukta + Upa-Lokayukta**.
Maharashtra also covers **former** ministers and civil servants.

75.s: Which State was the first to pass a law relating to the Lokayukta?
75.x: Odisha was the first State to pass a Lokayukta law, in 1970. The institution in Odisha came into existence later, in 1983.
75.tq: Distinguish ‘first to pass a law’ from ‘first to establish an institution’.
xs: **Odisha** was the first State to pass a Lokayukta law, in **1970** — option **(1)**.
Its institution came only in **1983**.
⚠ **Maharashtra** set up the first Lokayukta, in **1971**.
xa: In Odisha, officials are designated as "**Lokpal**".
Odisha excludes the **Chief Minister** from the Lokayukta's jurisdiction.

75.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (State)
A. Odisha
B. Maharashtra
C. Madhya Pradesh
D. Karnataka

List-II (Year of Lokayukta Act)
1. 1970
2. 1971
3. 1981
4. 1984

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
75.x: Odisha enacted its law in 1970, Maharashtra in 1971, Madhya Pradesh in 1981 and Karnataka in 1984.
75.tq: Start from the sure early-year pairs and eliminate codes that shift them.
xs: The match is **A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4** — option **(1)**.
**Madhya Pradesh** — **1981**; **Karnataka** — **1984**.
xa: Karnataka has its own **Lokayukta Police** wing.
⚠ **1970** Odisha law ≠ **1971** Maharashtra institution.

75.s: The Lokayukta in a State is generally appointed by the
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
75.x: The Lokayukta is appointed by the Governor under the respective State's Lokayukta Act.
75.tq: Identify the authority legally associated with the appointment.
xs: A State Lokayukta is appointed by the **Governor** — option **(1)**.
He generally consults the **Chief Justice of the High Court** and the **Leader of the Opposition**.
This is the APPSC key.
