122.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: MoSJE ran the survey with AIIMS-NDDTC, and alcohol (14.6%) was most used. Statement 3 is wrong: cannabis (2.8%) came before opioids (2.1%). So '1 and 2 only'.
122.tq: Order: alcohol > cannabis > opioids.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **2019** survey was run by **MoSJE with AIIMS-NDDTC**.
Statement 2 correct: **alcohol** was used most — **14.6%**.
Statement 3 wrong: **cannabis (2.8%)** came before **opioids (2.1%)**.
xa: **Art. 47** asks the State to try to prohibit intoxicating drinks and harmful drugs.
ADSI 2024 drug-overdose deaths: **978** (up **50%**).
**NMBA** — **15 Aug 2020** — **272** districts first, now all.

122.s: India's geographical position in relation to major drug-producing regions is described as lying between the
122.x: India lies between the Golden Crescent and the Golden Triangle, two major drug-producing regions.
122.tq: Distinguish the two similarly named trafficking regions by their exact titles.
xs: India lies between the **Golden Crescent** and the **Golden Triangle** — option **(1)**.
These are the two major drug-producing regions; the other names are distractors.
xa: Drug enforcement: **Police**, **NCB (1986, MHA)**, **Customs**, **DRI**.
**NDPS Act, 1985** — **Sec. 71** treatment centres.
**Anti-drug day**: **26 June**.

122.s: The International Day against Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking is observed on
122.x: 26 June is observed as the anti-drug day.
122.tq: Separate the anti-drug observance date from other programme and launch dates.
xs: The anti-drug day is observed on **26 June** — option **(2)**.
**15 August** (**2020**) is the launch date of **NMBA**; **10 October** (**2022**) is the launch of **Tele-MANAS**.
xa: **NMBA** — MoSJE; implemented by **NISD**; started in **272** districts.
**Nasha Mukt Yuva** campaign (Aug **2026**) — **MoYAS** through **MY Bharat**.
Most-used substance: **alcohol (14.6%)**, then **cannabis (2.8%)**, **opioids (2.1%)**.

122.s:
Consider the following statements about NCRB's ADSI 2024 report:
1. It recorded 1,70,746 suicides.
2. Daily wagers formed about 31% of the suicides.
3. Drug-overdose deaths fell by about 50%.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
122.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: ADSI 2024 recorded 1,70,746 suicides, about 31% of them daily wagers. Statement 3 is wrong: drug-overdose deaths (978) rose by 50%, not fell. So '1 and 2 only'.
122.tq: Daily wagers are the largest group, about 31%.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **NCRB ADSI 2024** recorded **1,70,746** suicides.
Statement 2 correct: **daily wagers** were about **31%**.
Statement 3 wrong: **drug-overdose deaths (978)** **rose** by **50%**.
xa: Other groups: **homemakers 22,113**, **unemployed 14,778**, **students 14,488**.
ADSI 2024 was released in **May 2026**.
AP ran **463** school and **308** college suicide-prevention programmes in **2023-25**.

122.s: As per ADSI 2015, the leading cause of farmer suicides was
122.x: Bankruptcy or indebtedness ranked first among the causes of farmer suicides in ADSI 2015, followed by farming-related issues.
122.tq: Identify the first-ranked cause rather than a related secondary cause.
xs: In **ADSI 2015**, **bankruptcy/indebtedness** ranked first among causes of farmer suicides — option **(1)**.
**Farming-related issues** came second; this was the **APPSC-G1 2017** key.
xa: ADSI 2024: **1,70,746** suicides; **daily wagers** about **31%**.
**Tele-MANAS** helpline — toll-free **14416**.
**Sec. 115**, Mental Healthcare Act **2017**: presumes **severe stress** — no trial or punishment.

122.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Durkheim's type)
 a. Egoistic
 b. Altruistic
 c. Anomic
 d. Fatalistic

List-II (Condition)
 i. Too much regulation
 ii. Too little social integration
 iii. Too much social integration
 iv. Too little regulation

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
122.x: Egoistic suicide is associated with too little integration, altruistic with too much integration, anomic with too little regulation, and fatalistic with too much regulation.
122.tq: Start with the sure conceptual pairs and eliminate codes containing reversed meanings.
xs: The correct match is **a–ii, b–iii, c–iv, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Egoistic** = too little **integration**; **Altruistic** = too much integration.
**Anomic** = too little **regulation** (crisis, sudden change); **Fatalistic** = too much regulation.
xa: The four types come from **Durkheim's** **Le Suicide** (**1897**).
⚠ Integration pair: **Egoistic / Altruistic**; regulation pair: **Anomic / Fatalistic**.
ADSI 2024 recorded **1,70,746** suicides.

122.s:
Consider the following statements about attempted suicide in law:
1. Section 309 IPC made it punishable with imprisonment up to one year and/or fine.
2. In P. Rathinam (1994), Section 309 was upheld as valid.
3. Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 presumes severe stress, so there is no trial or punishment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
122.x: Statement 1 is correct: Sec. 309 provided up to one year and/or fine. Statement 2 is wrong: P. Rathinam (1994) called Sec. 309 invalid. Statement 3 is correct: Sec. 115 presumes severe stress, bars trial and punishment and requires State care. So '1 and 3 only'.
122.tq: Rathinam struck at 309; MHCA Sec. 115 presumes stress.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Sec. 309 IPC** punished attempted suicide with up to **one year** and/or fine.
Statement 2 wrong: **P. Rathinam (1994)** called Sec. 309 **invalid**.
Statement 3 correct: **Sec. 115**, **MHCA 2017**, presumes **severe stress** — no trial or punishment; State must provide care.
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: APP notes give **3 months** for Sec. 309.
**BNS 2023**: no general offence of attempted suicide; **Sec. 226** covers only attempts to **coerce a public servant**.

122.s: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the provision relating to attempt to suicide applies specifically when the attempt is made to
o: End one's life under any circumstance
122.x: The BNS 2023 contains no general offence of attempted suicide; Section 226 covers an attempt made to coerce a public servant.
122.tq: Distinguish a general offence from the specific statutory exception.
xs: **BNS 2023** has no general attempted-suicide offence; **Sec. 226** covers only attempts to **coerce a public servant** — option **(3)**.
So an attempt to end one's life **under any circumstance** is no longer a general offence under the BNS.
xa: Old **Sec. 309 IPC**: up to **one year** and/or fine.
**P. Rathinam (1994)** called Sec. 309 invalid.
**Sec. 115** of the **Mental Healthcare Act 2017** presumes **severe stress**; State must provide care.

122.s: Tele-MANAS is a tele-mental-health helpline launched on 10 October 2022. Its toll-free number is
122.x: Tele-MANAS was launched on 10 October 2022 and can be accessed through the toll-free number 14416.
122.tq: Combine the launch-date and service-number clues without confusing other helplines.
xs: **Tele-MANAS** (launched **10 Oct 2022**) has the toll-free number **14416** — option **(4)**.
It is a **tele-mental-health helpline**.
xa: **Sec. 115**, **MHCA 2017** — presumes severe stress; no trial or punishment for attempted suicide.
ADSI 2024: **1,70,746** suicides; **daily wagers** about **31%**.
AP ran **463** school and **308** college suicide-prevention programmes (**2023-25**).

122.s: Under the Indian Penal Code, which one of the following was an act whose attempt was punishable but whose completed commission could not be punished?
122.x: Section 309 IPC punished attempted suicide, but a completed suicide cannot be punished since the person is dead. Murder, dacoity and kidnapping are punishable whether attempted or completed.
122.tq: Attempt punishable, act not = suicide (Sec. 309 IPC).
xs: **Suicide** is the act whose **attempt** was punishable but whose **completed act** cannot be punished — option **(2)** (MPPSC **1991** key).
**Sec. 309 IPC** punished the attempt with up to **one year** and/or fine.
xa: **P. Rathinam (1994)** called Sec. 309 invalid.
**Sec. 115**, **MHCA 2017**: no trial or punishment; State must provide care.
**BNS 2023**: **Sec. 226** only for attempts to **coerce a public servant**.

122.s: Which State topped the Social Justice Ministry's list of beggars?
122.x: West Bengal topped the Social Justice Ministry's state list of beggars.
122.tq: Test the state-ranking fact directly without confusing it with city-level data.
xs: **West Bengal** tops the Social Justice Ministry's state list of beggars — option **(3)** (BPSC **2017** key).
The figure comes from **state data** on beggars compiled by the **Social Justice Ministry**.
xa: **Indore** — **first beggar-free city** (**2025**).
**SMILE** (MoSJE, **2022**) — rehabilitation of persons engaged in begging.
**SC (2021)** refused to ban begging, calling it a **socio-economic problem**.

122.s: The Bombay Prevention of Begging Act was enacted in
122.x: The Bombay Prevention of Begging Act was enacted in 1959 and became a punitive model copied by many States.
122.tq: Distinguish the year of the statute from nearby social-law enactment years.
xs: The **Bombay Prevention of Begging Act** dates from **1959** — option **(2)**.
It is the **punitive model** many states copied.
xa: **Delhi HC (2018, Harsh Mander)** decriminalised begging in Delhi.
**SC (2021)** refused to ban begging — a **socio-economic problem**.
**SMILE** marks the shift from punitive laws to **rights-based rehabilitation**.

122.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Delhi High Court decriminalised begging in Delhi in 2018.
2. The case was associated with Harsh Mander.
3. In 2021, the Supreme Court banned begging throughout India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
122.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Supreme Court in 2021 refused to ban begging and regarded it as a socio-economic problem.
122.tq: Find the false judicial conclusion by checking the direction of the court's action.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1–2 correct: the **Delhi HC (2018)**, in the **Harsh Mander** case, decriminalised begging in Delhi.
Statement 3 wrong: the **SC (2021)** **refused** to ban begging, calling it a **socio-economic problem**.
xa: Punitive model: **Bombay Prevention of Begging Act, 1959**.
**SMILE** (**2022**) — rehabilitation of persons engaged in begging.
**SMILE-Beggary Survey App** — launched at the **Chandigarh Chintan Shivir** (**24-26 Apr 2026**).

122.s: SMILE, launched by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment in 2022, includes a sub-scheme for
o: Construction of prisons for habitual beggars
Removal of beggars from all urban areas
Comprehensive rehabilitation of persons engaged in begging
122.x: SMILE includes a sub-scheme for comprehensive rehabilitation of persons engaged in begging and shifts towards rights-based rehabilitation.
122.tq: Choose the precise welfare objective rather than a punitive substitute.
xs: **SMILE** (**MoSJE, 2022**) has a sub-scheme for **comprehensive rehabilitation of persons engaged in begging** — option **(4)**.
It marks a shift from **punitive laws** to **rights-based rehabilitation** — not institutionalisation, prisons or removal.
xa: **SMILE-Beggary Survey App** — **Chandigarh Chintan Shivir** (**24-26 Apr 2026**).
**NISD** trains officials, e.g. on **children who beg**.
**Indore** — **first beggar-free city** (**2025**).

122.s: Which city was declared the first beggar-free city in 2025?
122.x: Indore was declared the first beggar-free city in 2025.
122.tq: Separate the city-level distinction from State-level beggar statistics.
xs: **Indore** was declared the **first beggar-free city** (**2025**) — option **(1)**.
It is listed as a **FIRST** under social defence, whose scope includes **beggary**.
xa: **West Bengal** tops the state list of beggars.
**SMILE** (**2022**) — rehabilitation of persons engaged in begging.
**Delhi HC (2018, Harsh Mander)** decriminalised begging in Delhi.

122.s: Which one of the following best describes the changing approach towards social problems such as suicide, drug abuse and beggary?
o: From statutory regulation towards complete absence of regulation
From health and rehabilitation towards punishment alone
From punishment towards health and rehabilitation
122.x: The approach is moving from punishment, including Section 309 and anti-begging laws, towards health and rehabilitation through measures such as MHCA, SMILE and NMBA.
122.tq: Identify the direction of change by comparing the earlier punitive approach with the newer rehabilitative approach.
xs: The approach is shifting **from punishment towards health and rehabilitation** — option **(4)**.
Punishment: **Sec. 309** and **anti-begging laws**; health and rehabilitation: **MHCA**, **SMILE**, **NMBA**.
xa: **P. Rathinam (1994)** called Sec. 309 invalid; **MHCA 2017 Sec. 115** bars trial or punishment.
**SC (2021)** treated begging as a **socio-economic problem**.
**NMBA** (**2020**) is implemented by **NISD** with a focus on campuses.

123.s: Who propounded the concept of the “culture of poverty” in 1959?
123.x: The concept of the “culture of poverty” was propounded by Oscar Lewis in 1959.
123.tq: Test the exact proponent and year together to avoid confusing the concept with later poverty theorists.
xs: The **"culture of poverty"** was propounded by **Oscar Lewis** in **1959** — option **(1)**.
It means **fatalism and poverty** are **passed down generations**.
xa: ⚠ **René Lenoir** (France, **1974**) coined **social exclusion** — do not confuse with Lewis.
**Absolute poverty**: below the **minimum needed to survive**.
**STs** have the highest poverty, then **SCs** — the cause is **discrimination and exclusion**.

123.s: Which of the following best describes the central idea associated with the culture of poverty?
o: Poverty results only from differences in natural resources
Poverty is caused exclusively by temporary unemployment
Fatalism and poverty may be transmitted across generations
123.x: The culture-of-poverty perspective associates poverty with fatalism and patterns that are passed down from one generation to another.
123.tq: Identify the option expressing the intergenerational social transmission of poverty rather than an absolute economic claim.
xs: The culture of poverty holds that **fatalism and poverty are transmitted across generations** — option **(4)**.
The idea is **Oscar Lewis's** (**1959**); it does not blame only resources or temporary unemployment.
xa: **Social exclusion** (coined by **René Lenoir**, **1974**) shuts people out of **facilities, benefits and opportunities**.
Bases of exclusion: **caste, gender, disability, religion, region**.
Social indicators of poverty: **illiteracy**, **malnutrition**, **poor health care**, lack of **safe water and sanitation**.

123.s: Which one of the following is NOT generally treated as a social indicator of poverty?
123.x: Illiteracy, malnutrition, poor health care and lack of safe water and sanitation are the listed social indicators of poverty. Size of the house is not one; UPPSC 2025 keyed it as the NOT-a-social-indicator option.
123.tq: Find the item outside the established social-indicator group.
xs: **Size of the house** is not a social indicator of poverty — option **(3)**; **UPPSC 2025** keyed it as the NOT option.
The social indicators are **illiteracy**, **malnutrition**, **poor health care** and lack of **safe water and sanitation** — so options (1), (2), (4) are indicators.
xa: **Absolute poverty**: below the minimum needed to survive.
**National MPI** standard-of-living indicators include **cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, housing, electricity, assets, bank accounts**.
The MPI has **3 equally weighted dimensions** and **12 indicators**.

123.s: The Y.K. Alagh Committee’s poverty estimation method was based on calorie requirements of
o: 2,700 calories in rural areas and 2,400 calories in urban areas
2,400 calories in rural areas and 2,100 calories in urban areas
2,100 calories in rural areas and 2,400 calories in urban areas
2,200 calories in both rural and urban areas
123.x: The Y.K. Alagh Committee, formed in 1979, used a calorie norm of 2,400 calories for rural areas and 2,100 calories for urban areas. The corresponding expenditure was treated as the poverty line.
123.tq: Use the rural–urban comparison to distinguish the calorie norms.
xs: The **Y.K. Alagh Committee** (**1979**) used **2,400 calories rural** and **2,100 calories urban** — option **(2)**.
The poverty line was the **spending needed** to buy those calories; option (3) reverses the figures.
xa: ⚠ **Alagh** = calories only; **Tendulkar** = dropped the calorie anchor; **Rangarajan** = food plus non-food.
**Lakdawala** (report **1993**) kept the calorie base with **state-specific** lines.
**Tendulkar** (report **2009**) used **MRP** and an urban basket for both sectors.

123.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
123.x: The Y.K. Alagh Committee was associated with the 1979 poverty estimation method. The Lakdawala, Tendulkar and Rangarajan reports are associated with 1993, 2009 and 2014 respectively.
123.tq: Start with the sure year–committee pair and eliminate the shifted dates.
xs: **Y.K. Alagh Committee — 1979** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Lakdawala** report was **1993**, not 1985; **Tendulkar** report **2009** (set up **2005**); **Rangarajan** report **2014** — options (3) and (4) swap the last two.
xa: Alagh: **2,400 rural / 2,100 urban** calories.
Rangarajan (2011-12): **₹32 rural / ₹47 urban a day**.
**Oct 2025**: RBI updated the **Rangarajan** line using **HCES 2022-23**.

123.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Lakdawala methodology:
1. It retained a calorie base.
2. It used state-specific poverty lines.
3. It used CPI-AL for rural areas and CPI-IW for urban areas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
123.x: The Lakdawala methodology retained the calorie base, used state-specific poverty lines, and applied CPI-AL for rural areas and CPI-IW for urban areas.
123.tq: Check each statement against the committee’s method, price indices and regional treatment.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
**Lakdawala** (report **1993**) kept a **calorie base** and drew **state-specific** poverty lines.
It used **CPI-AL** for **rural** and **CPI-IW** for **urban** areas.
xa: Lakdawala estimate for **2004-05**: **27.5%**.
Tendulkar estimate for the same year: **37.2%**.
⚠ **Tendulkar** later **dropped the calorie anchor**.

123.s:
Consider the following poverty estimates:
1. Lakdawala methodology - 27.5% for 2004-05
2. Tendulkar methodology - 37.2% for 2004-05
3. Tendulkar methodology - 29.5% for 2011-12
Which of the above is/are correctly matched?
123.x: Pairs 1 and 2 are correct: for 2004-05 Lakdawala gave 27.5% and Tendulkar 37.2%. Pair 3 is wrong: Tendulkar's 2011-12 figure is 21.9%. So '1 and 2 only'.
xs: Pairs **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Pair 1 correct: **Lakdawala** gave **27.5%** for **2004-05**.
Pair 2 correct: **Tendulkar** gave **37.2%** for **2004-05**.
Pair 3 wrong: Tendulkar's **2011-12** figure is **21.9%**.
xa: On the Tendulkar line poverty fell to **2.3%** in **2023-24** (ES 2025-26).
Tendulkar line is criticised as **too low**.
Rangarajan (2011-12): **₹32 rural / ₹47 urban a day**.

123.s: Which of the following was a significant departure introduced by the Tendulkar Committee methodology?
o: It used only rural consumption baskets for both sectors.
It excluded non-food expenditure from the poverty line.
It restored the calorie anchor as the sole basis of poverty estimation.
It dropped the calorie anchor and included health and education expenditure.
123.x: The Tendulkar Committee (report 2009) dropped the calorie anchor, used the Mixed Reference Period (MRP), applied the urban basket to both sectors and included health and education spending. The other options are wrong: it did not use a rural-only basket, exclude non-food spending or restore the calorie anchor.
123.tq: Identify the methodological change rather than the older calorie-based approach.
xs: **Tendulkar** **dropped the calorie anchor** and **included health and education** spending — option **(4)**.
It used **MRP** and the **urban basket for both** sectors — so a rural-only basket (1) is wrong.
It did not restore the calorie anchor; **Alagh** was the calorie-only method.
xa: **Rangarajan** (**2014**) added **food plus non-food** items (housing, clothing, education, health, transport).
⚠ **₹972/₹1,407** a month are **Rangarajan's**, not Tendulkar's.

123.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Rangarajan poverty-line estimates for 2011–12?
o: ₹32 per day in urban areas and ₹47 per day in rural areas
₹32 per day in rural areas and ₹47 per day in urban areas
₹47 per day in both rural and urban areas
₹27 per day in rural areas and ₹33 per day in urban areas
123.x: The Rangarajan estimates were ₹32 per day for rural areas and ₹47 per day for urban areas, equivalent to ₹972 and ₹1,407 per month respectively.
123.tq: Split the rural–urban figures before considering the monthly equivalents.
xs: **Rangarajan** (2011-12): **₹32 rural** and **₹47 urban** a day — option **(2)**.
That equals **₹972 / ₹1,407 a month**; option (1) reverses rural and urban.
xa: ⚠ Trap: APSES and CDI wrongly give ₹972/₹1,407 as **Tendulkar's** — the **APPSC-GS 2025** key confirms **₹32** as Rangarajan's.
Rangarajan used **food plus non-food** (housing, clothing, education, health, transport).
**Oct 2025**: RBI updated the Rangarajan line with **HCES 2022-23**.

xs: The order is **IRDP (1978-80) → SGSY (1999) → NREGA (2005-06) → DAY-NRLM (2011)** — **B, A, C, D**, option **(1)**.
**SGSY** merged IRDP, so IRDP must come first; **DAY-NRLM** restructured SGSY, so it comes last.

123.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct dates. Statement 3 is wrong: the 100-day guarantee is per rural household, not per adult individual. So '1 and 2 only'.

xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.

123.s: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the original MGNREGA guarantee described here?
o: A legal right to 100 days of unskilled wage work per rural household per year
Payment of unemployment allowance if work is not provided within 15 days
Social audits by the Gram Sabha
Reservation of exactly half of all workdays for women
123.x: The guarantee required that one-third of workers be women, not exactly half. The 100-day legal guarantee, 15-day unemployment allowance and Gram Sabha social audits are features of MGNREGA.
123.tq: Look for the changed proportion in an otherwise familiar list of features.
xs: **Exactly half of workdays for women** is not a feature — option **(4)**; the Act requires **one-third** of workers to be **women**.
The **100-day legal right** per rural household, **unemployment allowance** after **15 days**, and **Gram Sabha social audits** are all features.
xa: **NREGA** in force **2 Feb 2006**; renamed **MGNREGA** on **2 Oct 2009**.

It preceded the national **NREGA** (passed **2005**) by decades.

Assertion (A): The Tendulkar poverty line is criticised in poverty-related debates.
Reason (R): It is considered too low to adequately capture the extent of poverty.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
123.x: Both the assertion and the reason are true. The criticism of the Tendulkar poverty line arises because it is considered too low.

xs: **Both A and R are true** and **R is the correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
The **Tendulkar line** is criticised because it is **considered too low**.

124.s:
Consider the following statements about human rights:
1. They are inherent and inalienable, held simply because one is human.
2. They rest on human dignity and are universal across cultures.
3. They exist only when granted by a national legislature.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
124.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: human rights are inherent and inalienable, rest on human dignity and are universal across cultures. Statement 3 is wrong: they are held because one is human, not because a legislature grants them. So '1 and 2 only' is right; the other options include statement 3.
124.tq: Inherent + inalienable + universal = not a gift of the State.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: human rights are **inherent, inalienable** rights held simply because one is **human**.
Statement 2 correct: they rest on **human dignity** and are **universal** across cultures.
Statement 3 wrong: they are not granted by a legislature — they belong to every person by being human.
xa: Human rights are **indivisible and interdependent** (affirmed by the **Vienna Declaration, 1993**).
Every **Fundamental Right** is a human right, but not every human right is an FR.
**Karel Vasak (1977)** classified them into **three generations**.

124.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Civil-political rights and socio-economic rights are indivisible and interdependent.
2. The Vienna Declaration of 1993 affirmed the indivisibility and interdependence of human rights.
3. Human rights are confined to rights expressly declared Fundamental Rights in the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
124.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because human rights are broader than constitutional Fundamental Rights.
124.tq: Use the constitutional-scope statement as the false comparison against the Vienna principle.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **civil-political** and **socio-economic** rights are **indivisible and interdependent**.
Statement 2 correct: this was affirmed by the **Vienna Declaration, 1993**.
Statement 3 wrong: every FR is a human right, but **not every human right is an FR**.
xa: Example: the **right to vote** is only a **statutory right** (**Sec 62, RP Act**).
**OHCHR** was set up in **1993**, after the **Vienna Conference**.
Human rights rest on **human dignity** and are **universal** across cultures.

124.s: In India, the right to vote is best described as a:
o: Statutory right under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act
124.x: The right to vote is only a statutory right, conferred by Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act. It is not a Fundamental Right (Art. 19 lists freedoms of speech, movement etc.), a Directive Principle (Art. 47 concerns nutrition, health and prohibition) or a Fundamental Duty. This shows that not every human right is a Fundamental Right.
124.tq: Vote = statutory right (Sec. 62 RP Act), not an FR.
xs: The **right to vote** is only a **statutory right** under **Section 62** of the **Representation of the People Act** — option **(2)**.
It is not a Fundamental Right, DPSP or Fundamental Duty — showing that **not every human right is an FR**.
xa: Voting is a **first-generation** (liberty) right in Vasak's scheme, with life, speech and fair trial.
Every **Fundamental Right** is a human right.
Human rights are **inherent and inalienable**, held because one is human.

124.s:
Consider the following statements about the generations of human rights:
1. The three-generation classification was proposed by Karel Vasak in 1977.
2. The three generations are mapped to liberty, equality and fraternity.
3. Third-generation rights are civil and political rights such as free speech and fair trial.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
124.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Karel Vasak (1977) proposed three generations mapped to liberty, equality and fraternity. Statement 3 is wrong: civil and political rights are first-generation; third-generation rights are collective rights such as a healthy environment, development and peace. So '1 and 2 only' is right; the other options include statement 3.
124.tq: Vasak 1977: 1st liberty (civil-political), 2nd equality (socio-economic), 3rd fraternity (collective).
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Karel Vasak (1977)** proposed the **three generations**.
Statement 2 correct: they map to **liberty, equality and fraternity**.
Statement 3 wrong: civil and political rights are **first-generation**; the third is **collective** rights — **healthy environment, development, peace**.
xa: Second generation (equality): **work, education, health**, **eradication of social discrimination**.
Generations **overlap** — e.g. **education** is both second- and third-generation.
⚠ **1st – 2nd – 3rd = liberty – equality – fraternity**.

124.s:
Match the generation of human rights with its principal category.

List-I
 a. First generation
 b. Second generation
 c. Third generation

List-II
 i. Collective rights such as peace and development
 ii. Civil and political rights
 iii. Economic, social and cultural rights

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
124.x: First-generation rights are civil and political; second-generation rights are economic, social and cultural; third-generation rights are collective rights such as peace and development.
124.tq: Start with the familiar civil-political first generation and complete the sequence by category.
xs: The correct match is **a–ii, b–iii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
**First** = **civil and political** rights; **Second** = **economic, social and cultural** rights.
**Third** = **collective rights** such as **peace and development**.
xa: Proposed by **Karel Vasak (1977)**.
⚠ **liberty – equality – fraternity** for the 1st, 2nd and 3rd generations.
Third generation also includes a **healthy environment** (UPSC).

124.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The generations of human rights are mutually exclusive.
2. Education may be classified as both a second-generation and a third-generation right.
3. The first generation primarily comprises civil and political rights.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
124.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false because the generations overlap rather than being mutually exclusive.
124.tq: Spot the absolute claim that conflicts with the overlap among generations.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 wrong: the generations **overlap**; they are not mutually exclusive.
Statement 2 correct: **education** is both a **second-** and a **third-generation** right (UPSC).
Statement 3 correct: the **first generation** comprises **civil and political** rights — life, speech, fair trial, vote.
xa: Second generation includes **eradication of social discrimination** (JPSC **2016**).
Third generation: **healthy environment, development, peace**.
Scheme proposed by **Karel Vasak (1977)**.

124.s: In Karel Vasak's classification of human rights, the eradication of social discrimination falls under which generation?
o: It is not a human right in Vasak's scheme
124.x: Eradication of social discrimination is grouped with work, education and health as a second-generation (equality) right. First-generation rights are civil and political (life, speech, fair trial, vote); third-generation rights are collective (healthy environment, development, peace). It is a recognised human right, so the last option is wrong.
124.tq: 2nd gen = equality = economic, social, cultural rights + ending social discrimination.
xs: **Eradication of social discrimination** is a **second-generation (equality)** right — option **(2)** (JPSC **2016**).
It sits with **work, education and health** among **economic, social and cultural** rights.
**First** generation is civil-political (life, speech, fair trial, vote); **third** is collective (environment, development, peace).
xa: ⚠ **1st – 2nd – 3rd = liberty – equality – fraternity**.
Generations **overlap** — **education** is both second- and third-generation.
Classification by **Karel Vasak (1977)**.

124.s:
Consider the following statements about the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR):
1. It was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948.
2. Its drafting was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt.
3. It contains 40 articles.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
124.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the UDHR was adopted by the UNGA on 10 December 1948 (Human Rights Day) and Eleanor Roosevelt chaired its drafting. Statement 3 is wrong: the UDHR has 30 articles. So '1 and 2 only' is right; every other option includes the false statement 3.
124.tq: UDHR: 10 Dec 1948, Eleanor Roosevelt, 30 articles.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **UNGA** adopted the UDHR on **10 December 1948**.
Statement 2 correct: **Eleanor Roosevelt** chaired its drafting.
Statement 3 wrong: the UDHR has **30 articles**, not 40.
xa: **Human Rights Day**: **10 December**.
The UDHR is **not a treaty** → **not legally binding**.
Its **80th anniversary** falls in **Dec 2028**.

124.s: Which one of the following is NOT specifically included among the rights recognised in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
o: Right to an adequate standard of living
124.x: The listed UDHR rights include dignity, liberty, equality, life, an adequate standard of living and education. A right to universal basic income is not included.
124.tq: Find the entitlement that falls outside the stated UDHR list.
xs: A **right to universal basic income** is not in the UDHR — option **(1)** (JPSC **2023**).
Included: **dignity, liberty and equality**, **life**, an **adequate standard of living** and **education**.
xa: UDHR: **30 articles** covering civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights.
⚠ Privacy is protected by UDHR **Art. 12** and ICCPR **Art. 17**, though a JPSC **2016** key treated it as not UN-listed.
Adopted **10 December 1948**; drafting chaired by **Eleanor Roosevelt**.

124.s:
Consider the following statements about the Universal Declaration of Human Rights:
1. It is a treaty.
2. It is legally binding in the same manner as a ratified international covenant.
3. It covers civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights.
Which of the statements given above is correct?
124.x: Statement 3 is correct because the UDHR covers all five categories of rights listed. Statements 1 and 2 are false: the UDHR is not a treaty and is not legally binding as a treaty.
124.tq: Reject the treaty and legal-bindingness traps while retaining the accurate scope statement.
xs: Only statement **3** is correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 3 correct: the UDHR's **30 articles** cover **civil, political, economic, social and cultural** rights.
Statements 1 and 2 wrong: the UDHR is **not a treaty** and so is **not legally binding**.
xa: Binding covenants came later: **ICCPR** and **ICESCR** (adopted **16 Dec 1966**).
**International Bill of Human Rights** = **UDHR + ICCPR + ICESCR** + optional protocols.
Adopted by the **UNGA** on **10 December 1948**.

124.s: Which of the following statements regarding privacy and international human rights law is correct?
o: Privacy is protected by Article 12 of the UDHR and Article 17 of the ICCPR.
Privacy was included only in the ICESCR and not in the UDHR.
Privacy is protected only by Article 19 of the ICCPR.
Privacy is protected by neither the UDHR nor the ICCPR.
124.x: The UDHR protects privacy under Article 12 and the ICCPR protects it under Article 17.
124.tq: Distinguish the correct privacy provisions from the commonly confused expression-rights provision.
xs: **Privacy** is protected by **UDHR Art. 12** and **ICCPR Art. 17** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 19** of the ICCPR is **expression**, not privacy; the **ICESCR** covers work, social security, health and education.
xa: ⚠ A **JPSC 2016** key treated privacy as not a UN-listed human right — expect this only in badly set questions.
Other ICCPR articles: **life (Art. 6)**, **no torture (Art. 7)**, **fair trial (Art. 14)**.
UDHR does not include a **right to universal basic income** (JPSC **2023**).

124.s: The International Bill of Human Rights comprises:
o: The ICCPR, ICESCR and the Vienna Declaration only
Only the UDHR and the ICCPR
The UDHR, UN Charter and International Court of Justice Statute
The UDHR, ICCPR, ICESCR and the optional protocols
124.x: The International Bill of Human Rights consists of the UDHR, the ICCPR, the ICESCR and the optional protocols.
124.tq: Test the complete composition of a named international instrument group.
xs: The **International Bill of Human Rights** = **UDHR + ICCPR + ICESCR + optional protocols** — option **(4)**.
The **Vienna Declaration** (1993) affirmed indivisibility; it is not part of the Bill.
xa: **ICESCR** in force **3 Jan 1976**; **ICCPR** in force **23 Mar 1976**.
**ICCPR First OP** (**1966**) — individual complaints; **Second OP** (**1989**) — abolition of the death penalty.
**ICESCR OP** (**2008**) — complaints.

124.s: Which of the following rights is associated with the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights?
o: Work, social security, health and education, realised progressively
124.x: The ICESCR covers work, social security, health and education, with these rights realised progressively. The other options refer to ICCPR provisions.
124.tq: Separate the economic-social covenant from the civil-political covenant by its subject matter.
xs: The **ICESCR** covers **work, social security, health and education**, **realised progressively** — option **(1)**.
**Torture (Art. 7)**, **privacy (Art. 17)** and **expression (Art. 19)** belong to the **ICCPR**.
xa: ICESCR adopted **16 Dec 1966**; in force **3 Jan 1976**.
⚠ ICESCR in force **Jan 1976** before ICCPR **Mar 1976**.
**ICESCR OP** (**2008**) provides for complaints.

124.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched with the ICCPR?
124.x: Article 19 of the ICCPR concerns expression. Privacy is protected under Article 17; the other three pairings are correct.
124.tq: Find the swapped article number in the list of ICCPR rights.
xs: **Article 19 — Right to privacy** is wrong — option **(3)**: ICCPR **Art. 19** is **expression**; privacy is **Art. 17**.
The other pairs are right: **Art. 6 life**, **Art. 7 no torture**, **Art. 14 fair trial**.
xa: UDHR protects privacy under **Art. 12**.
ICCPR adopted **16 Dec 1966**; in force **23 Mar 1976**.
India has been a **party to the ICCPR since 1979**.

124.s:
Consider the following statements about optional protocols in the International Bill of Human Rights:
1. The First Optional Protocol to the ICCPR (1966) provides for individual complaints.
2. The Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR (1989) aims at abolition of the death penalty.
3. The Optional Protocol to the ICESCR, providing for complaints, was adopted in 1976.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
124.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the ICCPR First OP (1966) allows individual complaints and the Second OP (1989) concerns abolition of the death penalty. Statement 3 is wrong: the ICESCR OP was adopted in 2008 (1976 is when the covenants entered into force). So '1 and 2 only' is right; the other options include statement 3.
124.tq: OPs: 1966 complaints, 1989 death penalty, 2008 ICESCR complaints.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **ICCPR First OP (1966)** provides for **individual complaints**.
Statement 2 correct: the **Second OP (1989)** aims at **abolition of the death penalty**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **ICESCR OP** was adopted in **2008**; **1976** is when the covenants came into force.
xa: India has **not signed the First Optional Protocol**.
So Indians cannot take complaints to the UN after exhausting domestic remedies.
⚠ ICESCR in force **Jan 1976**, ICCPR **Mar 1976**.

124.s: India's position concerning the ICCPR First Optional Protocol is correctly stated as follows:
o: India signed the First Optional Protocol in 1979 and permits direct UN complaints without domestic remedies.
India has not been a party to the ICCPR since its adoption.
India has been a party to the ICCPR since 1979 but has not signed the First Optional Protocol.
India is party only to the Second Optional Protocol and not to the ICCPR.
124.x: India has been a party to the ICCPR since 1979 but has not signed its First Optional Protocol. Consequently, individuals in India cannot use that protocol's UN complaints procedure after exhausting domestic remedies.
124.tq: Separate membership in the parent covenant from signature of its optional protocol.
xs: India has been a **party to the ICCPR since 1979** but has **not signed the First Optional Protocol** — option **(3)**.
So Indians **cannot take complaints to the UN** after exhausting domestic remedies.
xa: First OP (**1966**) — **individual complaints**; Second OP (**1989**) — **death penalty** abolition.
India has also **not ratified CAT** (signed **1997**).
ICCPR rights: **life (Art. 6)**, **fair trial (Art. 14)**, **privacy (Art. 17)**, **expression (Art. 19)**.

124.s:
Which of the following statements regarding India’s position on selected UN human-rights treaties is correct?
1. CERD was ratified by India in 1968.
2. CEDAW was ratified by India in 1993.
3. India signed CAT in 1997 but has not ratified it.
4. India acceded to CRC in 1992.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
124.x: All four statements are correct: India ratified CERD in 1968 and CEDAW in 1993, signed but did not ratify CAT in 1997, and acceded to CRC in 1992.
124.tq: Track the precise verbs—ratified, signed and acceded—along with their years.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4)**.
**CERD** ratified **1968**; **CEDAW** ratified **1993**.
**CAT** signed **1997**, **not ratified**; **CRC** acceded **1992**.
xa: ⚠ Signed but not ratified: **CAT**, **CPED**; not signed: **CMW**.
Treaty years: **CERD 1965**, **CEDAW 1979**, **CAT 1984**, **CRC 1989**.

124.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. CMW — Migrant workers
2. CRPD — Persons with disabilities
3. CPED — Enforced disappearance
4. CAT — Discrimination against women
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
124.x: CMW concerns migrant workers, CRPD concerns persons with disabilities, and CPED concerns enforced disappearance. CAT concerns torture, not discrimination against women.
124.tq: Find the swapped subject in a treaty–subject list.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
**CMW** — **migrant workers**; **CRPD** — **persons with disabilities**; **CPED** — **enforced disappearance**.
Pair 4 wrong: **CAT** concerns **torture**; discrimination against women is **CEDAW**.
xa: India: **CMW not signed**; **CPED signed 2007, not ratified**.
**CRPD** ratified **2007** → **RPwD Act, 2016**.
**CAT** (**1984**) — India **signed 1997, not ratified**.

124.s: Which one of the following correctly describes India’s position concerning CMW, CRPD and CPED?
o: CMW was ratified in 1990, CRPD was signed in 2007, and CPED was not signed.
CMW was not signed, CRPD was ratified in 2007, and CPED was signed in 2007 but not ratified.
CMW was acceded to in 1992, CRPD was ratified in 1993, and CPED was ratified in 2006.
CMW was signed in 1990, CRPD was not ratified, and CPED was acceded to in 2007.
124.x: India has not signed CMW; it ratified CRPD in 2007; and it signed CPED in 2007 but has not ratified it.
124.tq: Separate the statuses not signed, ratified and signed but not ratified.
xs: **CMW not signed**, **CRPD ratified 2007**, **CPED signed 2007 but not ratified** — option **(2)**.
The other options invent dates: CMW is from **1990** and CPED from **2006**, but India neither signed CMW nor ratified CPED.
xa: ⚠ Signed but not ratified: **CAT** and **CPED**; not signed: **CMW**.
**CRPD** gave rise to the **RPwD Act, 2016** — disabilities raised from **7 to 21**.
**CEDAW** (**1979**) — India **ratified 1993**.

124.s: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 is associated with which treaty and what change in the number of recognised disabilities?
124.x: The CRPD concerns persons with disabilities and gave rise to the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, which raised recognised disabilities from 7 to 21.
124.tq: Link the treaty, implementing legislation and numerical change as one factual chain.
xs: The **RPwD Act, 2016** flows from the **CRPD** and raised recognised disabilities **from 7 to 21** — option **(4)**.
**CPED** is on **enforced disappearance** and **CEDAW** on **discrimination against women**; option (1) reverses the numbers.
xa: CRPD adopted **2006**; India **ratified 2007**.
**CPED** (**2006**) — India **signed 2007, not ratified**.
**CMW** (**1990**, migrant workers) — India **not signed**.

124.s:
Match the following rights with the year or date of their recognition by the UN General Assembly.

a. Right to development
a. 1986
b. Right to water and sanitation
c. Right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment

1. 28 July 2010
2. 28 July 2022
3. 1986

Select the correct combination:
124.x: The Right to Development was recognised in 1986; the Right to Water and Sanitation on 28 July 2010; and the Right to a Clean, Healthy and Sustainable Environment on 28 July 2022.
124.tq: Anchor the two exact July dates first and then match the remaining year.
xs: The correct match is **a–3, b–1, c–2** — option **(1)**.
**Right to development** — Declaration of **1986**; **water and sanitation** — **28 July 2010**.
**Clean, healthy and sustainable environment** — **28 July 2022**, declared a **universal human right**.
xa: These are **third-generation** (collective) rights — **healthy environment, development, peace**.
The environment right appeared in an **APPSC 2021** paper.
⚠ Both water (**2010**) and environment (**2022**) resolutions fall on **28 July**.

124.s: On 28 July 2022, the United Nations General Assembly recognised which of the following as a universal human right?
o: Right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment
124.x: The UN General Assembly recognised the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment as a universal human right on 28 July 2022.
124.tq: Use the precise official formulation rather than a broader environmental phrase.
xs: On **28 July 2022** the UNGA recognised the **right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment** as a **universal human right** — option **(3)**.
A **universal basic income** right is not even in the UDHR (JPSC **2023**).
xa: **Right to water and sanitation** — **28 July 2010**.
**Right to development** — Declaration of **1986**.
Third-generation rights: **healthy environment, development, peace**.

124.s:
Consider the following statements about the UN Human Rights Council:
1. It was formed in 2006, replacing the UN Commission on Human Rights.
2. It is based in Vienna.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
124.x: Statement 1 is correct: the HRC was formed in 2006 as the successor to the UN Commission on Human Rights. Statement 2 is wrong: the HRC is based in Geneva (Vienna is linked to the 1993 conference after which OHCHR was set up). So '1 only' is right; '2 only' and 'Both' wrongly accept Vienna, and 'Neither' wrongly rejects statement 1.
124.tq: HRC = 2006 + Geneva; Vienna = 1993 conference/OHCHR.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **UNHRC** was formed in **2006**, replacing the **UN Commission on Human Rights**.
Statement 2 wrong: it is based in **Geneva**, not Vienna.
xa: **47 members**, elected by the **UNGA** for **3-year terms**; at most **two consecutive terms**.
**Vienna** links to the **1993** conference after which **OHCHR** was set up.
The HRC runs the **Universal Periodic Review** since **2008**.

124.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the UN Human Rights Council:
1. It consists of 47 members.
2. Its members are elected by the UN General Assembly.
3. Members are elected for three-year terms.
4. A member may serve an unlimited number of consecutive terms.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
124.x: The Council has 47 members elected by the UN General Assembly for three-year terms. A member can serve at most two consecutive terms, making statement 4 false.
124.tq: Find the false duration statement by checking the limit on consecutive terms.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
The UNHRC has **47 members**, elected by the **UNGA**, for **3-year terms**.
Statement 4 wrong: a member may serve at most **two consecutive terms**.
xa: A **two-thirds** UNGA vote can **suspend** a member for gross violations.
Seats: **Africa 13**, **Asia-Pacific 13**, Latin America & Caribbean **8**, Western Europe & Others **7**, Eastern Europe **6**.
India was a member for **2019-21** and **2022-24**.

124.s: A member of the UN Human Rights Council may be suspended for gross violations of human rights by:
o: A unanimous decision of the Human Rights Council
A two-thirds vote of the UN General Assembly
A decision of the International Court of Justice
A simple majority vote of the Security Council
124.x: The UN General Assembly may suspend a Council member for gross and systematic violations through a two-thirds vote.
124.tq: Ask which authority exercises the power and what voting threshold applies.
xs: A **two-thirds vote** of the **UN General Assembly** can suspend a member for gross violations — option **(2)**.
Neither the HRC itself, the **ICJ** nor the **Security Council** has this power.
xa: Members are **elected by the UNGA** — **47**, for **3-year terms**.
At most **two consecutive terms**.
⚠ **USA** stopped participating in and funding the UNHRC by presidential memorandum.

124.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the regional distribution of seats in the UN Human Rights Council.

List-I (Region)
a. Africa
b. Asia-Pacific
c. Latin America and the Caribbean
d. Eastern Europe

List-II (Seats)
i. 6
ii. 8
iii. 13
iv. 7

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
124.x: Africa has 13 seats, Asia-Pacific has 13, Latin America and the Caribbean has 8, and Eastern Europe has 6.
124.tq: Start with the repeated 13-seat pair and then verify the remaining regional allocations.
xs: The match is **a–iii, b–iii, c–ii, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Africa 13**, **Asia-Pacific 13**, **Latin America & Caribbean 8**, **Eastern Europe 6**.
xa: **Western Europe & Others**: **7** seats; total **47**.
**APPSC 2018** asked the **Asia-Pacific** seat count (**13**).
Members serve **3-year terms**, at most **two consecutive**.

124.s: India was a member of the UN Human Rights Council during which of the following periods?
124.x: India served on the Council during 2019–21 and again during 2022–24.
124.tq: Use the paired-term chronology to distinguish the two specified Indian memberships.
xs: India was a UNHRC member for **2019-21** and **2022-24** — option **(2)**.
Members serve **3-year terms**, at most **two consecutive terms** — matching India's two back-to-back terms.
xa: The HRC (**2006**) is based in **Geneva**.
Asia-Pacific holds **13** of the **47** seats.
The HRC runs the **UPR** — peer review of every UN member state.

124.s: Which of the following statements correctly describes the Universal Periodic Review (UPR)?
o: It examines only the implementation of economic and social rights.
It is a peer review of the human rights record of every UN member state.
It is a judicial review conducted only for states accused of treaty violations.
It is a review conducted by the International Court of Justice every three years.
124.x: The UPR is a peer review of the human rights record of every UN member state, conducted under the Human Rights Council.
124.tq: Distinguish universal peer review from judicial or treaty-specific review.
xs: The **UPR** is a **peer review** of the human rights record of **every UN member state** — option **(2)**.
It is run by the **HRC** (not the ICJ), in cycles of about **4.5 years** since **2008**; it is not judicial and not limited to economic rights.
xa: The HRC (**2006**) replaced the **UN Commission on Human Rights**.
**Special rapporteurs** = HRC "special procedures" — unpaid independent experts.
**Treaty bodies** = committees of independent experts monitoring each core treaty.

124.s: The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights was set up in 1993 following the:
124.x: The OHCHR was established in 1993 after the Vienna Conference.
124.tq: Match the institution with the conference that preceded its establishment.
xs: **OHCHR** was set up in **1993**, after the **Vienna Conference** — option **(2)**.
The **Vienna Declaration, 1993** affirmed that rights are **indivisible and interdependent**.
xa: ⚠ **1993** = **OHCHR** + **Paris Principles** (UNGA) + **NHRC** (**12 Oct**).
**OHCHR 2026** convened the **Global Alliance for Human Rights** (Imagine-Dialogue-Act).
It looks ahead to the **UDHR's 80th anniversary (Dec 2028)**.

124.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes treaty bodies from special rapporteurs in the UN human rights machinery?
o: Treaty bodies are organs of the General Assembly, whereas special rapporteurs are organs of the Security Council.
Treaty bodies are courts, whereas special rapporteurs are elected representatives of states.
Treaty bodies are committees of independent experts monitoring core treaties, whereas special rapporteurs are unpaid independent experts on a country or theme.
Treaty bodies review only refugee matters, whereas special rapporteurs review only economic rights.
124.x: Treaty bodies are committees of independent experts that monitor core treaties. Special rapporteurs are unpaid independent experts appointed under the Human Rights Council's special procedures to examine a theme or country.
124.tq: Separate the two similar mechanisms by their composition and mandate.
xs: **Treaty bodies** are **committees of independent experts monitoring each core treaty**; **special rapporteurs** are **unpaid independent experts on a theme or a country** — option **(3)**.
Special rapporteurs are the HRC's **"special procedures"** — not state representatives or Security Council organs.
xa: Core treaties: **CERD, CEDAW, CAT, CRC, CMW, CRPD, CPED**.
The **UPR** is a **peer review** run by the HRC.
**GANHRI** accredits NHRIs: **"A"** fully compliant, **"B"** partly compliant.

124.s: In 2026, the Global Alliance for Human Rights convened by the OHCHR used which model?
124.x: The Global Alliance for Human Rights used the Imagine–Dialogue–Act model in preparation for the UDHR's 80th anniversary in December 2028.
124.tq: Test the exact three-part formulation associated with the current initiative.
xs: The **Global Alliance for Human Rights** used an **Imagine–Dialogue–Act** model — option **(4)**.
It was convened by the **OHCHR** in **2026** (**16 Jun 2026**).
xa: It was convened ahead of the **UDHR's 80th anniversary (Dec 2028)**.
**OHCHR** was set up in **1993**, after the **Vienna Conference**.
UDHR adopted **10 December 1948**.

124.s: The 80th anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, ahead of which the OHCHR convened the Global Alliance for Human Rights, falls in:
124.x: The UDHR was adopted in December 1948, so its 80th anniversary falls in December 2028.
124.tq: 1948 + 80 = 2028; Human Rights Day is 10 December.
xs: The **UDHR's 80th anniversary** falls in **December 2028** — option **(2)**.
The UDHR was adopted on **10 December 1948**.
xa: **Human Rights Day**: **10 December**.
**OHCHR** convened the **Global Alliance for Human Rights** (Imagine-Dialogue-Act) ahead of it.
UDHR drafting was chaired by **Eleanor Roosevelt**.

124.s: The Paris Principles relating to national human rights institutions were adopted by the UN General Assembly in:
124.x: The Paris Principles were adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1993.
124.tq: Distinguish the adoption year of the institutional standards from treaty years.
xs: The **Paris Principles** were adopted by the **UNGA** in **1993** — option **(3)**.
**1968** is the start of the **UN Human Rights Prize**; **1977** is Vasak's generations; **2006** the **HRC**.
xa: ⚠ **1993** = OHCHR + Paris Principles + **NHRC (12 Oct)**.
Contents: **broad mandate in law**, **independence**, **pluralist composition**, **adequate resources**, **powers to investigate**.
**GANHRI** accredits NHRIs: **"A"** = fully compliant.

124.s: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the Paris Principles?
o: Exclusive dependence on the executive for investigations
A broad mandate set out in law
124.x: The Paris Principles require independence and autonomy from government and powers to investigate; exclusive dependence on the executive is contrary to these requirements.
124.tq: Find the option that reverses the institutional-independence requirement.
xs: **Exclusive dependence on the executive** is not a feature — option **(2)**.
The Paris Principles demand **independence and autonomy from government** and **powers to investigate**.
**Pluralist composition**, **adequate resources** and a **broad mandate set out in law** are features.
xa: Adopted by the **UNGA** in **1993**.
India's **NHRC** (**12 Oct 1993**) was set up in conformity with them.
**GANHRI**'s **Sub-Committee on Accreditation** grades NHRIs **"A"** or **"B"**.

124.s:
With reference to the National Human Rights Commission of India, consider the following statements:
1. It was set up in conformity with the Paris Principles.
2. It is a statutory body.
3. It is a constitutional body.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
124.x: The NHRC was established in conformity with the Paris Principles and is a statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. It is not a constitutional body.
124.tq: Use the statutory–constitutional distinction as the decisive discriminator.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **NHRC** (**12 Oct 1993**) was set up in conformity with the **Paris Principles**.
Statement 2 correct: it is a **statutory** body under the **Protection of Human Rights Act 1993**.
Statement 3 wrong: it is **not a constitutional** body.
xa: **2019 amendment**: term cut to **3 years**.
Three human-rights members required, **including a woman**.
⚠ **1993** = OHCHR + Paris Principles + NHRC.

124.s:
Consider the following statements about GANHRI accreditation of national human rights institutions:
1. GANHRI accredits them through its Sub-Committee on Accreditation.
2. 'A' status means an institution is only partly compliant with the Paris Principles.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
124.x: Statement 1 is correct: GANHRI accredits NHRIs through its Sub-Committee on Accreditation. Statement 2 is wrong: 'A' means fully compliant; 'B' means partly compliant. So '1 only' is right; '2 only' and 'Both' accept the reversed grades, and 'Neither' rejects a true statement.
124.tq: A = fully compliant, B = partly compliant.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **GANHRI** accredits NHRIs through its **Sub-Committee on Accreditation**.
Statement 2 wrong: **"A"** = **fully compliant**; **"B"** = **partly compliant**.
xa: Compliance is measured against the **Paris Principles** (UNGA **1993**).
Paris Principles demand **independence** and **powers to investigate**.
India's **NHRC** is a **statutory** body.

124.s:
Consider the following statements about Amnesty International:
1. It was founded in 1961 in London.
2. It received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977.
3. It is the New York-based body known for investigative reports.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
124.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Amnesty International was founded in London in 1961, works on prisoners of conscience and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977. Statement 3 is wrong: the New York-based body known for investigative reports is Human Rights Watch. So '1 and 2 only' is right; the other options include statement 3.
124.tq: Amnesty = London 1961, Nobel 1977; HRW = New York.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Amnesty International** was founded in **1961** in **London**.
Statement 2 correct: it won the **Nobel Peace Prize** in **1977**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **New York-based** body known for **investigative reports** is **Human Rights Watch**.
xa: Amnesty focuses on **prisoners of conscience**.
Amnesty called Afghanistan's new police law **"a sweeping assault on human rights"**.
HRW criticised the **Taliban's ban on all protests**.

124.s: The UN Human Rights Prize is given by which body, and normally at what interval?
o: UN General Assembly, usually every five years
UN Security Council, every three years
UN Human Rights Council, every four years
124.x: The UN Human Rights Prize is given by the UN General Assembly, usually once every five years, and has been awarded since 1968.
124.tq: Identify both the awarding authority and the periodicity rather than relying on the name alone.
xs: The **UN Human Rights Prize** is given by the **UN General Assembly**, **usually every five years** — option **(2)**.
It has been awarded since **1968**.
xa: **Human Rights Day**: **10 December**.
**Amnesty International** won the **Nobel Peace Prize** in **1977**.
The **HRC** (**2006**) is based in **Geneva**.

124.s: The criticism that Afghanistan’s new police law constituted “a sweeping assault on human rights” was associated with which organisation?
124.x: Amnesty International described Afghanistan’s new police law as “a sweeping assault on human rights.”
124.tq: Use the organisation–statement association to distinguish similar human-rights bodies.
xs: **Amnesty International** called Afghanistan's new police law **"a sweeping assault on human rights"** — option **(4)** (TH, **28 Aug 2026**).
**Human Rights Watch** criticised the **Taliban's ban on all protests** — the confusable pair.
xa: HRW also criticised Israel's **white-phosphorus** shelling of **Yohmor, Lebanon**.
Amnesty: founded **1961**, **London**; **Nobel Peace Prize 1977**.
HRW is **New York-based**.

124.s: Which of the following statements regarding India’s international human-rights commitments is correct?
o: India has not ratified CAT and has not accepted the ICCPR First Optional Protocol.
India has ratified CAT but has not accepted the ICCPR First Optional Protocol.
India has not signed CAT but has accepted the ICCPR First Optional Protocol.
India has ratified CAT and accepted the ICCPR First Optional Protocol.
124.x: India has not ratified the Convention against Torture and has not accepted the First Optional Protocol to the ICCPR.
124.tq: Distinguish non-ratification of CAT from non-acceptance of the ICCPR Optional Protocol.
xs: India has **not ratified CAT** and has **not accepted the ICCPR First Optional Protocol** — option **(1)**.
India **signed CAT in 1997** but has not ratified it; it is a party to the ICCPR since **1979** without the First OP.
xa: The First OP allows **individual complaints** to the UN.
**CPED** — also **signed 2007, not ratified**.
**Pellet guns** in crowd control were criticised as **inhuman and degrading treatment**.

124.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Magna Carta
B. Event of 1688
C. Declaration of Independence of 1776
D. French Revolution of 1789
124.x: The sequence is Magna Carta (1215), the event of 1688, the Declaration of Independence (1776), and the French Revolution (1789).
124.tq: Fix the earliest date first and then arrange the remaining milestones by year.
xs: The order is **Magna Carta (1215) → 1688 → 1776 → 1789** — **A, B, C, D**, option **(1)**.
The **Magna Carta** is the **first document** of the human rights campaign.
xa: The **UDHR** followed much later — **10 December 1948**.
**Karel Vasak (1977)** later mapped rights to **liberty, equality and fraternity**.
**Vienna Declaration, 1993** — rights are **indivisible and interdependent**.

124.s:
Arrange the following instruments in chronological order:
A. CEDAW
B. Magna Carta
C. Universal Declaration of Human Rights
D. ICCPR
124.x: The chronological order is Magna Carta (1215), UDHR (1948), ICCPR (1966) and CEDAW (1979).
124.tq: Anchor the sequence with the medieval Magna Carta and the latest convention, then place the UN instruments by year.
xs: The order is **Magna Carta (1215) → UDHR (1948) → ICCPR (1966) → CEDAW (1979)** — **B, C, D, A**, option **(1)**.
The **ICCPR** was adopted on **16 Dec 1966**, and **CEDAW** in **1979** — so CEDAW is last.
xa: ICCPR in force **23 Mar 1976**; **ICESCR** in force **3 Jan 1976**.
India ratified **CEDAW** in **1993**.
India has been a **party to the ICCPR since 1979**.

125.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Every Fundamental Right is a human right, but not every human right is a Fundamental Right.
2. The right to vote in India is a Fundamental Right under Part III of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
125.x: Statement 1 is correct: Fundamental Rights are a part of the wider body of human rights. Statement 2 is wrong: the right to vote is only a statutory right, not a Fundamental Right. So '1 only' is right; '2 only' and 'Both' accept the false claim, and 'Neither' rejects a true statement.
125.tq: Right to vote = statutory, not FR.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: every **Fundamental Right** is a **human right**, but not every human right is an FR.
Statement 2 wrong: the **right to vote** is only a **statutory right**, not a Fundamental Right.
xa: The **UDHR** was proclaimed on **10 December 1948** (**Human Rights Day**); it has **30 articles**.
FRs available to **citizens + foreigners alike**: Arts. **14, 20, 21, 23, 25-28**.
UDHR values are also reflected in the **Preamble, DPSPs and Fundamental Duties**.

125.s: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was proclaimed on
125.x: The UDHR was proclaimed on 10 December 1948, which is observed as Human Rights Day.
125.tq: Use the date associated with Human Rights Day as the identifying clue.
xs: The **UDHR** was proclaimed on **10 December 1948** — option **(1)**; the day is **Human Rights Day**.
**16 December 1966** is the date the **ICCPR and ICESCR** were adopted by the UNGA.
xa: The UDHR has **30 articles**.
Its **80th anniversary** falls in **Dec 2028** — the target of the **Global Alliance for Human Rights**.
Under the **PHRA 1993**, "International Covenants" = **ICCPR and ICESCR**.

125.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Article 14 — Article 7 of the UDHR
2. Article 21 — Article 3 of the UDHR
3. Article 32 — Article 8 of the UDHR
4. Article 23 — Article 26 of the UDHR
125.x: Articles 14, 21 and 32 correspond respectively to UDHR Articles 7, 3 and 8. Article 23 corresponds to UDHR Article 4, not Article 26.
125.tq: Start with the sure constitutional-UDHR correspondences and eliminate the swapped pair.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Art. 14** ↔ UDHR **Art. 7**; **Art. 21** ↔ UDHR **Art. 3**; **Art. 32** ↔ UDHR **Art. 8** (effective remedy).
Pair 4 wrong: **Art. 23** parallels UDHR **Art. 4**; UDHR **Art. 26** parallels **Art. 21A** (education).
xa: **Art. 19** freedoms parallel UDHR **Arts. 13, 19, 20, 23**.
**Art. 24** (no child below **14** in hazardous work) parallels UDHR **Arts. 4, 25(2)**.
**Art. 23** also bans **bonded labour**.

125.s: Article 21A of the Constitution, viewed alongside the UDHR, relates to
o: Free and compulsory education for children between six and fourteen years and UDHR Article 26
Equality before law and UDHR Article 7
Prohibition of forced labour and UDHR Article 4
125.x: Article 21A provides free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen years and parallels Article 26 of the UDHR.
125.tq: Pair the age range, constitutional article and international parallel precisely.
xs: **Art. 21A** gives **free, compulsory education** for children **6-14** and parallels **UDHR Art. 26** — option **(1)**.
It was added by the **86th CAA, 2002**.
**Equality before law** is Art. 14 (UDHR Art. 7); **remedies** Art. 32 (UDHR Art. 8); **forced labour** Art. 23 (UDHR Art. 4).
xa: **Art. 21** (life and personal liberty) ↔ UDHR **Art. 3**.
**Art. 24**: no child below **14** in factories, mines, hazardous work.
**Art. 41** (DPSP) covers **work/education/public assistance**.

125.s: Which one of the following Fundamental Rights is available to both citizens and foreigners?
o: Article 30 right of minorities to establish educational institutions
Article 29 protection of language and script of citizens
Article 21 protection of life and personal liberty
125.x: Articles 14, 20, 21, 23 and 25 to 28 are available to citizens and foreigners alike. Article 19 is available only to citizens.
125.tq: Separate citizen-specific freedoms from rights available to every person.
xs: **Art. 21** (life and personal liberty) is available to **citizens and foreigners alike** — option **(4)**.
Arts. **14, 20, 21, 23, 25-28** cover foreigners too; **Arts. 19, 29, 30** are not in that list.
xa: Art. 21 parallels **UDHR Art. 3**.
**Art. 23** bans traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour — also for foreigners.
SC: "a person does not become a **non-person** after going to jail".

125.s:
Which of the following groups reflects principles found in all three of the following: the Preamble, the Directive Principles of State Policy and the Fundamental Duties?
1. Principles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
2. Principles wholly confined to international trade law
3. Human-rights-oriented constitutional values
Which of the statements given above are correct?
125.x: The Preamble, DPSPs and Fundamental Duties reflect UDHR principles and human-rights-oriented constitutional values. They are not based on principles wholly confined to international trade law.
125.tq: Identify the common constitutional theme and reject the unrelated extreme statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
UDHR principles and human-rights values are reflected in the **Preamble, DPSPs and Fundamental Duties** (UPSC **2020**: all three).
Statement 2 wrong: they are not confined to **international trade law**.
xa: DPSPs carry the **social-economic rights of the ICESCR** — **39(a)** livelihood, **39(d)** equal pay, **43** living wage.
FD **51A(e)**: renounce practices derogatory to **women's dignity**.
**Art. 51(c)** (DPSP): foster respect for **international law and treaty obligations**.

125.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the Directive Principle concerned?
1. Article 39(a) — Adequate means of livelihood
2. Article 39(d) — Equal pay for equal work
3. Article 42 — Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
4. Article 43 — Living wage
125.x: Articles 39(a), 39(d), 42 and 43 respectively relate to adequate livelihood, equal pay, humane work conditions with maternity relief, and living wage.
125.tq: Start from the article-number anchors and verify each policy objective.
xs: All four pairs are correct — option **(4)**.
**39(a)** — **livelihood**; **39(d)** — **equal pay**.
**42** — **just and humane conditions + maternity relief**; **43** — **living wage**.
xa: ⚠ **42 = maternity relief**; **43 = living wage**.
**Art. 41** — **work, education, public assistance**.
These DPSPs reflect the **social-economic rights of the ICESCR**.

125.s: The Directive Principles relating to livelihood, equal pay, work, education, public assistance, humane working conditions, maternity relief and living wage chiefly reflect the
o: Institutional principles of the Paris Agreement
Civil and political rights of the ICCPR alone
Social and economic rights of the ICESCR
125.x: These Directive Principles express social and economic rights associated with the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
125.tq: Distinguish social-economic covenant rights from civil-political rights.
xs: These DPSPs reflect the **social and economic rights** of the **ICESCR** — option **(4)**.
Arts. **39(a)**, **39(d)**, **41**, **42**, **43** cover livelihood, equal pay, work/education/public assistance, humane conditions with maternity relief and living wage.
The **ICCPR** covers civil and political rights, which the FRs mirror instead.
xa: ICCPR and ICESCR were adopted by the UNGA on **16 Dec 1966**.
The **PHRA 1993** defines "International Covenants" as **ICCPR and ICESCR**.
⚠ **42** = maternity relief; **43** = living wage.

125.s: Which Fundamental Duty is specifically related to protecting the dignity of women?
125.x: Article 51A(e) requires citizens to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
125.tq: Distinguish the women’s-dignity duty from environmental and education-related duties.
xs: **Article 51A(e)** requires citizens to **renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women** — option **(1)**.
It is a **Fundamental Duty** (FD), one of the places where **UDHR** values are reflected.
xa: UDHR principles are reflected in the **Preamble, DPSPs and Fundamental Duties** (UPSC **2020**).
**Vishaka (1997)** relied on **CEDAW** for workplace harassment guidelines.
**Art. 42** provides **maternity relief**.

125.s:
Match the following Articles of the Constitution with their principal welfare-related mandates.

List-I
(a) Article 41
(b) Article 42
(c) Article 43
(d) Article 47

List-II
(i) Living wage
(ii) Nutrition, public health and prohibition
(iii) Work, education and public assistance
(iv) Humane conditions of work and maternity relief

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
125.x: Article 41 covers work, education and public assistance; Article 42 humane work conditions and maternity relief; Article 43 living wage; and Article 47 nutrition, public health and prohibition.
125.tq: Match each Article with its distinctive welfare mandate.
xs: The match is **a–iii, b–iv, c–i, d–ii** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 41** — **work, education and public assistance**; **Art. 42** — **humane conditions and maternity relief**.
**Art. 43** — **living wage**; **Art. 47** — nutrition, public health and prohibition.
xa: ⚠ **42 = maternity relief**, **43 = living wage** — the commonly swapped pair.
**39(a)** — livelihood; **39(d)** — equal pay.
These carry the **social-economic rights of the ICESCR**.

125.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 73 extends the executive power of the Union.
2. Article 51(c) directs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations.
3. Article 253 permits only the executive and not Parliament to implement international treaties through domestic law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
125.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Article 253 specifically empowers Parliament to legislate for implementing treaties and international agreements.
125.tq: Identify the wrong authority in the treaty-implementation statement and separate executive power from legislative power.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Art. 73** extends the **Union executive power**.
Statement 2 correct: **Art. 51(c)** (DPSP) directs the State to foster respect for **international law and treaty obligations**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Art. 253** lets **Parliament** legislate for any part of India to **implement treaties**.
xa: ⚠ **253 = treaty laws**.
**Guruvayur Devaswom (2003)**: courts may rely on **international conventions**.
**Vishaka (1997)** relied on **CEDAW**.

125.s: The Vishaka guidelines on workplace sexual harassment were framed by relying substantially on:
o: The First Optional Protocol to the ICCPR
125.x: In Vishaka (1997), the Supreme Court relied on the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) to frame workplace-harassment guidelines.
125.tq: Match the landmark Indian case with the specific international convention it used.
xs: **Vishaka (1997)** relied on **CEDAW** to frame **workplace harassment** guidelines — option **(4)**.
The **UNCRC** relates to children (**NCPCR**); the **ICCPR First OP** is an individual-complaint mechanism India has not signed.
xa: ⚠ **1997** = **Vishaka** (CEDAW) and **D.K. Basu** (arrest safeguards).
**Guruvayur Devaswom (2003)**: PIL principles let courts rely on international conventions.
**Art. 253**: Parliament may legislate to implement treaties.

125.s: Which of the following statements regarding international conventions and Indian courts is correct?
o: Guruvayur Devaswom held that international conventions can never be considered by Indian courts.
Article 51(c) automatically gives every international convention the force of a constitutional amendment.
Vishaka (1997) relied exclusively on the ICCPR and not on CEDAW.
The principles of public interest litigation enabled courts to rely on international conventions in Guruvayur Devaswom (2003).
125.x: The principles associated with public interest litigation enabled courts to rely on international conventions in Guruvayur Devaswom (2003). The other statements overstate or misidentify the legal effect and applicable convention.
125.tq: Choose the precise judicial use of international conventions rather than an absolute claim about their legal status.
xs: In **Guruvayur Devaswom (2003)**, **PIL principles** let courts **rely on international conventions** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) reverses that holding; **Vishaka** relied on **CEDAW**, not the ICCPR.
**Art. 51(c)** only directs the State to **foster respect** for international law — it gives treaties no constitutional force.
xa: **Art. 253**: **Parliament** legislates to implement treaties.
**D.K. Basu (1997)** — arrest safeguards.
India is a party to the **ICCPR since 1979**.

125.s: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR), set up in 2007, works in line with which international instrument?
125.x: The NCPCR was set up in 2007 and works in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC).
125.tq: Link the national child-rights institution with the correct international child-rights instrument.
xs: The **NCPCR** (set up **2007**) works in line with the **UNCRC** — option **(2)**.
India **acceded to the UNCRC in 1992**.
xa: **CEDAW** — relied on in **Vishaka (1997)**.
India has **not signed the ICCPR First Optional Protocol**.
**Art. 24**: no child below **14** in factories, mines, hazardous work.

125.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the dates associated with the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993?
125.x: The Ordinance was issued on 28 September 1993, while the NHRC was constituted on 12 October 1993.
125.tq: Separate closely related dates by placing the event against its proper sequence.
xs: **Ordinance: 28 Sept 1993**; **NHRC constituted: 12 October 1993** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) swaps the two; **20 Dec 1993** is the **UNGA endorsement** of the Paris Principles.
xa: The Act is deemed in force from **28 September 1993**.
⚠ Ordinance/in force **28 Sept**; NHRC **12 Oct 1993**.
Objective: **NHRC + SHRCs + Human Rights Courts**.

125.s: The National Human Rights Commission was constituted in conformity with the Paris Principles, which were adopted in Paris in
125.x: The Paris Principles were adopted in Paris in October 1991. They were endorsed by the UN General Assembly on 20 December 1993.
125.tq: Distinguish adoption of an international standard from its later UN endorsement.
xs: The **Paris Principles** were adopted in **Paris** in **October 1991** — option **(1)**.
The **UNGA** endorsed them on **20 Dec 1993**; September 1993 is the PHRA Ordinance date.
xa: The **NHRC** (**12 October 1993**) was set up in conformity with them.
**16 Dec 1966** — adoption of the **ICCPR and ICESCR**.
**NHRC advice is non-binding** — a criticism.
