135.x: The B.P. Mandal Commission was established in 1979 by the Janata Government headed by Morarji Desai.
135.tq: Avoid the common trap of confusing the government that appointed a commission with the government that implemented its recommendations.
xs: The Mandal Commission was set up in **1979** by the **Janata Government** of **Morarji Desai** — option **(1)**.
The **Nehru** Government set up the first commission (**Kalelkar**, **1953**).
The **V.P. Singh** Government **implemented** Mandal in **1990** — it did not set it up.
xa: Mandal reported in **1980**; OBCs = **52%** of population.
It used **11 indicators** and recommended **27%** for OBCs.
**27%** of central civil posts were reserved in **1993** (UPSC, IYB).

135.s: The Mandal Commission recommended reservation of what percentage of posts for Other Backward Classes?
135.x: The Mandal Commission recommended 27 per cent reservation for OBCs. Its estimate that OBCs constituted 52 per cent of the population was a population figure, not the recommended quota.
135.tq: Distinguish the recommended reservation percentage from the estimated share of the population.
xs: Mandal recommended **27 per cent** reservation for OBCs — option **(3)**.
⚠ **52%** was its estimate of the **OBC population**, not the quota.
**10%** is the **EWS** quota (**103rd**).
xa: Implemented by **V.P. Singh** in **1990**; central civil posts reserved in **1993**.
The **CEI Act, 2006** also gave **27% OBC** seats in central institutions.
⚠ **27%** = Mandal quota = CEI seats (**2006**).

135.s: Which of the following correctly describes the implementation of the Mandal Commission recommendations?
o: They were implemented by the V.P. Singh Government in 1990, and 27 per cent of Central civil posts were reserved in 1993.
They were implemented by the V.P. Singh Government in 1993, and posts were reserved in 1995.
They were implemented by the Morarji Desai Government in 1979, and posts were reserved in 1980.
They were implemented by the Nehru Government in 1955, and posts were reserved in 1990.
135.x: The V.P. Singh Government implemented the Mandal recommendations in 1990, and 27 per cent of Central civil posts were reserved for OBCs in 1993.
135.tq: Track the sequence of appointment, report, political implementation and operational reservation.
xs: Mandal was implemented by the **V.P. Singh Government in 1990**, and **27%** of central civil posts reserved in **1993** — option **(1)**.
**Morarji Desai** (**1979**) only set the commission up; it reported in **1980**.
**1955** is the **Kalelkar** report year under the Nehru era — not Mandal.
xa: Creamy layer criteria: **DoPT Office Memorandum of Sept 1993**, based on **Justice R.N. Prasad** committee.
Creamy-layer income limit: **₹1 lakh (1993)** → **₹8 lakh (2017)**.
Mandal Commission = reservation in **government employment** (APPSC **2019** key).

135.s: The Mandal Commission used how many indicators covering social, educational and economic factors?
135.x: The Mandal Commission used 11 indicators covering social, educational and economic dimensions of backwardness.
135.tq: Recall the exact quantitative detail attached to the commission's methodology.
xs: The Mandal Commission used **11 indicators** — social, educational and economic — option **(3)**.
**27** is its recommended OBC quota, not the number of indicators.
xa: Mandal: set up **1979**, report **1980**, OBCs **52%** of population.
Kalelkar's criteria: low caste status, lack of education, poor representation in govt service, trade and industry.
⚠ Mandal = Second commission (**B.P. Mandal**); Kalelkar = First (**1953**).

135.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the two early Backward Classes Commissions is correct?
o: The Kaka Kalelkar Commission listed about 2,399 castes, whereas the Mandal Commission estimated OBCs at 52 per cent of the population.
The Kaka Kalelkar Commission was appointed in 1979 and the Mandal Commission in 1953.
Both commissions were appointed by the V.P. Singh Government.
Both commissions recommended 27 per cent reservation and were fully implemented.
135.x: The Kaka Kalelkar Commission's report listed about 2,399 castes, while the Mandal Commission estimated OBCs at 52 per cent of the population. The two commissions differed in date, government and outcome.
135.tq: Compare corresponding rows of the two commission profiles rather than memorising isolated names.
xs: **Kalelkar** listed about **2,399 castes**; **Mandal** estimated OBCs at **52 per cent** of the population — option **(1)**.
Kalelkar was appointed in **1953** and Mandal in **1979** — option (2) swaps them.
Kalelkar was set up by **Nehru**'s Govt and Mandal by **Morarji Desai**'s; only Mandal led to **27%**, and Kalelkar was **not implemented**.
xa: ⚠ APP says Kalelkar listed "nearly **3,000** castes".
Mandal used **11 indicators**; Kalelkar reported in **1955**, Mandal in **1980**.
**Rohini Commission** later sub-categorised about **3,000** Central-list OBC castes.

135.s: Which commission is associated with recommending reservation for backward classes in government employment, leading to the 27 per cent OBC quota?
135.x: The B.P. Mandal Commission (1979) is the commission on reservation in government employment (APPSC 2019, GS 2019); it recommended 27 per cent for OBCs. Kalelkar's report (1955) was not implemented; Rohini deals with OBC sub-categorisation; R.N. Prasad framed creamy-layer criteria.
135.tq: Govt employment reservation commission = Mandal.
xs: The **B.P. Mandal Commission** recommended reservation in **government employment**, leading to the **27%** OBC quota — option **(2)**.
**Kalelkar** (report **1955**) was **not implemented**.
**Rohini** deals with OBC **sub-categorisation**; **R.N. Prasad** framed **creamy-layer** criteria.
xa: GS **2019** / APPSC **2019** key: "commission on reservation in government employment" = **Mandal**.
Implemented by **V.P. Singh** in **1990**; central posts reserved in **1993**.
**Oversight Committee (M. Veerappa Moily, 2006)** raised total seats so general-category seats did not shrink.

135.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Indra Sawhney judgment:
1. Caste may be the main criterion for determining backwardness.
2. Total reservation should ordinarily not exceed 50 per cent.
3. The creamy layer among OBCs should be excluded.
4. Reservation for OBCs was extended to promotions as a general rule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Indra Sawhney accepted caste as a possible main criterion, prescribed the general 50 per cent ceiling and excluded the creamy layer. It confined reservation to initial appointments and did not extend it to promotions as a general rule.
135.tq: Locate the single reversal in the statement dealing with promotion.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **caste can be the main criterion** of backwardness (overruled **Balaji**).
Statement 2: total reservation **not above 50%** except in extraordinary cases. Statement 3: the **creamy layer** is excluded from OBCs.
Statement 4 is wrong: reservation was confined to **initial appointment**, not promotion.
xa: The **77th (1995)** answered it with **Art. 16(4A)** — promotion reservation for SCs/STs.
Indra Sawhney directed a **permanent statutory body** → the **NCBC**.
**Carry-forward** allowed within the **50%** ceiling, applied year by year.

135.s: Which one of the following statements correctly reflects the ruling in Indra Sawhney regarding carry-forward vacancies?
o: Carry-forward is allowed, but it must operate within the 50 per cent ceiling on a year-by-year basis.
Carry-forward is prohibited in every situation.
Carry-forward applies only to EWS vacancies.
Carry-forward is unlimited and is calculated only once in a decade.
135.x: Indra Sawhney permitted carry-forward of vacancies, subject to the 50 per cent ceiling being applied year by year.
135.tq: Combine the carry-forward rule with the year-by-year ceiling rather than treating either as absolute.
xs: **Carry-forward** is allowed but must stay **within the 50% ceiling**, applied **year by year** — option **(1)**.
Indra Sawhney fixed total reservation **not above 50%** except in extraordinary cases.
It is not limited to EWS; EWS (**103rd**) came much later.
xa: The **81st (2000)** made unfilled **backlog vacancies** a separate class, outside the **50%** ceiling (**Art. 16(4B)**).
**Janhit Abhiyan**: the **50% cap** applies to backward-class quotas.
The **76th (1994)** put Tamil Nadu's **69%** law in the **Ninth Schedule**.

135.s: The permanent statutory body for backward-class lists directed by the Supreme Court in Indra Sawhney subsequently became the:
135.x: The permanent statutory body directed for backward-class lists subsequently became the National Commission for Backward Classes.
135.tq: Match the judicially directed institutional role with the body that performs it.
xs: The permanent statutory body directed in **Indra Sawhney** became the **National Commission for Backward Classes** — option **(4)**.
The statutory **NCBC Act 1993** was **repealed** in **2018**; the NCBC is now constitutional under **Art. 338B** (**102nd**).
xa: **NCBC role**: examines **inclusion/exclusion** requests for OBC lists.
Present NCBC is the **8th**; **Niranjan Jyoti** appointed Chairperson (2026).
Before 2018, **Art. 338(10)** sent BC complaints to the **SC commission**.

135.s: Which amendment-clause pair is correctly matched?
135.x: The First Amendment, 1951 inserted Article 15(4). Article 16(4A) was inserted by the 77th Amendment, Article 16(4B) by the 81st, Article 15(5) by the 93rd and Article 16(6) by the 103rd Amendment.
135.tq: Start with the sure amendment-clause pair and eliminate the swapped clauses.
xs: **First Amendment — Article 15(4)** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Art. 15(4)** was added to overcome **Champakam Dorairajan**.
xa: **81st (2000)** = **Art. 16(4B)** backlog vacancies.
**85th (2001)** = **consequential seniority**, nullifying the "catch-up" rule.

135.s: Article 16(4A), relating to reservation in promotion for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, was inserted by the
135.x: The 77th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1995 inserted Article 16(4A) to provide reservation in promotion for SCs and STs, in response to the Indra Sawhney judgment.
135.tq: Use the article-number and amendment-number association to distinguish closely related reservation amendments.
xs: **Art. 16(4A)** (promotion reservation for SCs/STs) was inserted by the **77th Amendment (1995)** — option **(1)**.
It answered **Indra Sawhney**, which confined reservation to initial appointment.
**76th** = TN's **69%** law in the **Ninth Schedule**; **81st** = backlog; **85th** = consequential seniority.
xa: **82nd (2000)**: proviso to **Art. 335** — relaxed qualifying marks for SCs/STs in promotion.
⚠ APPSC G2 **2024** keyed relaxation to the "**89th**" — wrong; it is the **82nd**.
**81st (2000)**: **Art. 16(4B)** — backlog vacancies outside the **50%** ceiling.

135.s: The 85th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001 provided for
o: identification of SEBCs by the States
consequential seniority in promotion and nullified the catch-up rule
reservation in private unaided educational institutions including minority institutions
135.x: The 85th Amendment provided consequential seniority along with promotion and nullified the catch-up rule.
135.tq: Use a distinctive legal consequence to identify the correct amendment.
xs: The **85th (2001)** gave **consequential seniority** with promotion and nullified the **catch-up** rule — option **(2)**.
States' power to identify SEBCs = **105th (2021)**; private unaided institutions = **93rd**, which **excluded** minority institutions; **10% EWS** = **103rd**.
xa: **77th (1995)**: **Art. 16(4A)** promotion reservation.
**81st (2000)**: **Art. 16(4B)** backlog vacancies.
**82nd (2000)**: relaxed qualifying marks in promotion (proviso to **Art. 335**).

135.s:
With reference to the 93rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2005, consider the following statements:
1. It inserted Article 15(5).
2. It enabled reservation in educational institutions, including private unaided institutions.
3. Minority educational institutions were excluded from its scope.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: The 93rd Amendment inserted Article 15(5) and enabled reservation in educational institutions, including private unaided institutions, while excluding minority institutions.
135.tq: Test the main provision together with its important constitutional exception.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: the **93rd (2005)** inserted **Art. 15(5)**.
Statement 2: reservation in educational institutions incl. **private aided or unaided**.
Statement 3: **minority institutions excluded**.
xa: It overcame **P.A. Inamdar (2005)**.
It is the base for the **CEI Act, 2006** — **27% OBC** seats, in force **Jan 2007**.
GS **2007** key: the CEI Act rests on the **93rd Amendment**.

135.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: 103rd Amendment — Constitutional status to the NCBC
135.x: The 102nd Amendment Act, 2018 gave constitutional status to the NCBC through Article 338B and inserted Article 342A. Article 15(5) belongs to the 93rd Amendment, EWS reservation to the 103rd, and restoration of States' power to the 105th.
135.tq: Trap article and amendment swaps by matching each amendment with its exact constitutional change.
xs: **102nd Amendment — Articles 338B and 342A** — option **(3)**.
**102nd (2018)** made the **NCBC** constitutional (**Art. 338B**) and inserted **342A** and **366(26C)**.
Wrong pairs: **Art. 15(5)** = **93rd**; **10% EWS** = **103rd**; NCBC status ≠ 103rd.
xa: **105th (2021)** restored **States' power** to identify SEBCs → answer to **Jaishri Patil**.
102nd = **123rd Bill**; 105th = **127th Bill**.

135.s: Which of the following correctly represents the amendment and the corresponding Constitutional Amendment Bill?
135.x: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted from the 124th Constitutional Amendment Bill. The 102nd and 105th Amendments corresponded to the 123rd and 127th Bills respectively.
135.tq: Distinguish the enacted amendment number from the preceding bill number.
xs: **103rd Amendment — 124th Amendment Bill** — option **(4)** (APPSC G1 **2019** key).
**102nd** = **123rd Bill**; **105th** = **127th Bill** — so options (1)–(3) are mismatched.
xa: **103rd (2019)**: **10% EWS**, in force **January 2019**; inserted **Art. 15(6) and 16(6)**.
Upheld in **Janhit Abhiyan (7 Nov 2022)** by **3:2**, a **five-judge** bench.
Dissent: CJI **U.U. Lalit** and Justice **S. Ravindra Bhat**.

135.s: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct?
o: The 82nd Amendment concerns relaxation of qualifying standards in promotion for SCs and STs.
The 81st Amendment deals with unfilled backlog vacancies.
The 89th Amendment introduced the relaxation of qualifying marks under Article 335.
The 77th Amendment deals with reservation in promotion for SCs and STs.
135.x: The 89th Amendment did not introduce the relaxation of qualifying marks; that change was made by the 82nd Amendment Act, 2000. The 89th Amendment is associated with the bifurcation of the SC/ST Commission.
135.tq: Find the wrong amendment-provision association among closely related reservation amendments.
xs: The NOT-correct statement is that the **89th Amendment introduced relaxation of qualifying marks** — option **(3)**.
Relaxation (proviso to **Art. 335**) came by the **82nd (2000)**; the **89th** split the **SC/ST Commission**.
Other statements are correct: **81st** = backlog vacancies; **77th** = promotion reservation for SCs/STs.
xa: ⚠ APPSC G2 **2024** keyed relaxation to the "**89th**" — WRONG.
**85th (2001)**: consequential seniority.
**76th (1994)**: TN **69%** law in the **Ninth Schedule**.

135.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.
List-I (Constitutional Amendment)
 a. 77th Amendment
 b. 81st Amendment
 c. 82nd Amendment
 d. 85th Amendment
List-II (Provision)
 i. Consequential seniority in promotion
 ii. Backlog vacancies as a separate class
 iii. Reservation in promotion under Article 16(4A)
 iv. Relaxation in qualifying marks for promotion
135.x: The 77th Amendment inserted Article 16(4A), the 81st dealt with backlog vacancies, the 82nd inserted the proviso to Article 335, and the 85th provided consequential seniority.
135.tq: Start from the sure amendment-purpose pair and eliminate codes with a misplaced provision.
xs: Correct code: **a–iii, b–ii, c–iv, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**77th** → **Art. 16(4A)** promotion; **81st** → **backlog vacancies** as a separate class.
**82nd** → **relaxation in qualifying marks** (**Art. 335**); **85th** → **consequential seniority**.
xa: The **85th (2001)** nullified the "**catch-up**" rule.
**77th (1995)** answered **Indra Sawhney**.
**81st**: backlog vacancies sit outside the **50%** ceiling.

135.s: The 76th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1994 is associated with which one of the following?
o: Inserting Article 16(4A) for reservation in promotion
Placing Tamil Nadu's 69 per cent reservation law in the Ninth Schedule
Giving constitutional status to the NCBC
135.x: The 76th Amendment (1994) placed Tamil Nadu's 69 per cent reservation law in the Ninth Schedule. Article 16(4A) came through the 77th (1995), consequential seniority through the 85th (2001), and constitutional status of the NCBC through the 102nd (2018).
135.tq: 76th = TN 69% in Ninth Schedule; 77th = 16(4A).
xs: The **76th (1994)** put **Tamil Nadu's 69%** reservation law in the **Ninth Schedule** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 16(4A)** = **77th (1995)**; consequential seniority = **85th (2001)**; NCBC status = **102nd (2018)**.
xa: Indra Sawhney: total reservation **not above 50%** except in extraordinary cases.
SC reserved verdict on TN's BC (Muslim) quota for converts (8 Aug 2026).
**103rd (2019)**: **10% EWS** — over and above existing reservation.

135.s: Which clause was added to the Constitution to overcome the judgment in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan?
135.x: Article 15(4) was inserted by the First Amendment, 1951 to overcome Champakam Dorairajan. Article 16(4) was in the original Constitution; Article 15(5) came by the 93rd Amendment (2005) and Article 16(4B) by the 81st (2000).
135.tq: Champakam Dorairajan -> 1st Amendment -> 15(4).
xs: **Article 15(4)** was added to overcome **Champakam Dorairajan** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 15(5)** = **93rd** (to overcome **P.A. Inamdar**); **Art. 16(4B)** = **81st** (backlog).
xa: Exam angle: "which article was added to overcome Champakam Dorairajan" → **15(4)**.
**Art. 16(4A)**: promotion reservation (**77th**).

135.s: The Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006, providing 27 per cent OBC reservation, came into force in:
135.x: Although enacted in 2006, the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act came into force in 2007.
135.tq: Separate the enactment year from the commencement year.
xs: The **CEI (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006** came into force in **Jan 2007** — option **(3)**.
It gives **27% OBC** seats in central institutions; based on **Art. 15(5)** (**93rd, 2005**).
**2006** is the enactment year, **2005** the 93rd Amendment year — not the commencement.
xa: GS **2007** key: **93rd Amendment** underlies the CEI Act.
**Oversight Committee (M. Veerappa Moily, 2006)** expanded seats (about **54%**, phased).

135.s: Which one of the following was the principal objective of the Oversight Committee headed by M. Veerappa Moily in 2006?
o: To prepare the Central List of Scheduled Tribes
To implement OBC reservation by expanding seats so that general-category seats did not shrink
To identify the creamy layer among SCs and STs
To abolish reservation in Central educational institutions
135.x: The Oversight Committee headed by M. Veerappa Moily planned implementation through expansion of seats, thereby protecting the existing number of general-category seats.
135.tq: Use the committee’s stated implementation purpose rather than its year alone.
xs: The **Moily Oversight Committee (2006)** aimed to implement OBC reservation by **expanding seats** so **general-category seats did not shrink** — option **(2)**.
It proposed raising total seats by about **54%**, **phased**.
Creamy layer among SCs/STs is a later debate (CJI **Gavai**, **Nov 2025**), not Moily's task.
xa: The **CEI Act, 2006** gave **27% OBC** seats, in force **Jan 2007**.
**Rohini Commission** handles **sub-categorisation** of OBCs.

135.s: The 93rd Constitutional Amendment (2005), which inserted Article 15(5) enabling reservation in admissions including private institutions, was enacted to overcome which judgment?
135.x: Article 15(5) was inserted by the 93rd Amendment to overcome P.A. Inamdar (2005), which had barred quotas in private unaided institutions; it excludes minority institutions and is the basis of the CEI Act, 2006. Indra Sawhney concerns Mandal, M. Nagaraj promotion reservation, Janhit Abhiyan EWS.
135.tq: 93rd -> 15(5) -> overcame P.A. Inamdar -> CEI Act 2006.
xs: The **93rd (2005)** inserting **Art. 15(5)** overcame **P.A. Inamdar (2005)** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 15(5)** covers admissions incl. **private aided or unaided** institutions, **excluding minority institutions**.
**Indra Sawhney** concerns the Mandal quota; **Janhit Abhiyan (2022)** upheld **EWS**.
xa: Art. 15(5) is the base for the **CEI Act, 2006**.
**Jaishri Patil** → answered by the **105th (2021)**.
**Champakam Dorairajan** → answered by **Art. 15(4)**.

135.s: The criteria for identifying the creamy layer among OBCs were framed through which of the following instruments and period?
o: The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, based on the Kalelkar Commission
The Ministry of Social Justice notification of 2004, based on the Justice G. Rohini Commission
The DoPT Office Memorandum of September 1993, based on the Justice R.N. Prasad Expert Committee
The DoPT Office Memorandum of 2017, based on the Mandal Commission
135.x: The creamy-layer criteria were framed through the DoPT Office Memorandum of September 1993, based on the Justice R.N. Prasad Expert Committee.
135.tq: Identify the correct instrument, year and associated committee together.
xs: Creamy-layer criteria came through the **DoPT Office Memorandum of Sept 1993**, based on the **Justice R.N. Prasad Expert Committee** — option **(3)**.
**2017** is when the income limit rose to **₹8 lakh**, not when criteria were framed.
**Rohini** = sub-categorisation; **102nd** = NCBC constitutional status.
xa: Status exclusions: children of **constitutional post-holders**, **Class-I officers**, parents both **Class-II**.
The creamy layer itself originated in **Indra Sawhney**.

135.s: The income ceiling for determining the OBC creamy layer, after the 2017 revision and described as still current, is
135.x: The income ceiling was revised to ₹8 lakh per annum in 2017 and is stated to remain current.
135.tq: Distinguish the latest threshold from earlier figures in the revision sequence.
xs: The OBC creamy-layer ceiling since **2017** is **₹8 lakh per annum** — option **(1)**.
Earlier limits: **4.5 lakh (2008)**, **6 lakh (2013)** — now outdated.
xa: ⚠ **₹8 lakh** = OBC creamy-layer limit = **EWS** income ceiling.
**AP** aligned its State/public-sector definitions with the central threshold.

135.s: Which of the following statements regarding the application of the central creamy-layer threshold in Andhra Pradesh is correct?
o: Andhra Pradesh applies the threshold only to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
Andhra Pradesh has rejected the central threshold for all public-sector definitions.
Andhra Pradesh has fixed a separate threshold of ₹6 lakh for public-sector definitions.
Andhra Pradesh has aligned its State and public-sector definitions with the central threshold.
135.x: Andhra Pradesh aligned its State and public-sector definitions with the central creamy-layer threshold of ₹8 lakh.
135.tq: Test the State-level application of a central numerical standard.
xs: **AP has aligned its State and public-sector definitions with the central threshold** — option **(4)**.
The central threshold is **₹8 lakh** a year (**2017**), not a separate **₹6 lakh** (the **2013** limit).
xa: Creamy layer was introduced by **Indra Sawhney** to exclude socially advanced OBCs.
**EWS** criteria: income **below ₹8 lakh**, **5 acres** farm land, **1,000 sq ft** flat.

135.s:
With reference to Union of India v. Rohith Nathan, consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court held that parental salary alone cannot place a candidate in the creamy layer.
2. The Court ordered the creation of supernumerary posts.
3. In August 2026, the Centre sought clarification concerning 958 CSE-2025 candidates.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: The 11 March 2026 verdict held that parental salary alone cannot determine creamy-layer status and ordered supernumerary posts. In August 2026, the Centre sought clarification regarding 958 CSE-2025 candidates.
135.tq: Combine the judicial holding, consequential direction and subsequent administrative development.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Rohith Nathan (11 March 2026)** — **parental salary alone** cannot place a candidate in the creamy layer.
Statement 2: the Court ordered **supernumerary posts**.
Statement 3: in **Aug 2026** the Centre sought clarification on **958** CSE-**2025** candidates.
xa: The SC is likely to set up a **special Bench** on it.
Creamy-layer limit: **₹8 lakh** (**2017**), via **DoPT OM** framework of **Sept 1993**.
Status exclusions include **Class-I officers** and parents both **Class-II**.

135.s: Who supported the introduction of a creamy-layer principle for Scheduled Castes in the debate mentioned in the context of 2025?
o: The Chief Justice of India, B.R. Gavai
The Chairman of the Kalelkar Commission
The Union Minister of Social Justice
135.x: Chief Justice of India B.R. Gavai supported the idea of applying a creamy-layer principle to Scheduled Castes.
135.tq: Match the public position with the correct constitutional functionary.
xs: CJI **B.R. Gavai** backed a creamy layer for **SCs** (**Nov 2025**) — option **(1)**.
The **Union government opposed** it (**Aug 2026**), saying SC/ST status flows from **Arts. 341/342**.
xa: The OBC creamy layer originated in **Indra Sawhney**.
**Rohith Nathan (2026)**: parental salary alone does not decide creamy layer.
**Niranjan Jyoti** is the **NCBC Chairperson** (2026).

135.s: The Union Government opposed applying the creamy-layer principle to SCs and STs on the ground that their status flows from
135.x: In August 2026, the Union Government opposed the proposal, stating that SC/ST status flows from Articles 341 and 342.
135.tq: Discriminate between closely related constitutional provisions concerning reservations and community identification.
xs: The Union opposed SC/ST creamy layer because their status flows from **Articles 341 and 342** — option **(1)**.
**Arts. 338B and 342A** relate to the **NCBC** and **SEBC** lists (**102nd**), not SCs/STs.
**Arts. 15 and 16** are the reservation-enabling clauses.
xa: CJI **B.R. Gavai** had backed SC creamy layer (**Nov 2025**).
OBC creamy-layer income limit: **₹8 lakh** (**2017**).
**Art. 16(4A)** (**77th**) gives promotion reservation to SCs/STs.

135.s: The creamy-layer principle for OBCs, which excludes socially advanced sections from reservation benefits, was introduced through the decision in
o: Union of India v. Rohith Nathan
State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
135.x: The creamy-layer principle for excluding socially advanced OBCs was introduced through the Indra Sawhney decision.
135.tq: Use the landmark-case association rather than the later constitutional amendment association.
xs: The OBC creamy layer was introduced by **Indra Sawhney** — option **(3)**.
**Rohith Nathan (2026)** only clarified that **parental salary alone** cannot decide creamy layer.
**Champakam Dorairajan** led to **Art. 15(4)**; **Jaishri Patil** to the **105th**.
xa: Criteria: **DoPT OM Sept 1993** (**R.N. Prasad** committee).
Income limit now **₹8 lakh** (**2017**).
Indra Sawhney also fixed the **50%** ceiling.

135.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the categories associated with the OBC creamy layer under the Indra Sawhney framework?
o: All children of persons belonging to OBC communities, irrespective of social or economic status
Children whose parents are both Class-II officers
135.x: The framework identifies specified socially advanced categories, including children of Class-I officers and parents who are both Class-II officers. It does not exclude all OBC children irrespective of their circumstances.
135.tq: Reject the sweeping option that converts specified exclusions into a universal exclusion.
xs: NOT a creamy-layer category: **all children of OBC persons irrespective of social or economic status** — option **(2)**.
The creamy layer excludes only **socially advanced** OBCs — specified status groups and high earners.
Included: children of **constitutional post-holders**, **Class-I officers**, and parents **both Class-II**.
xa: Also excluded: senior govt and **armed-forces** officers, **property owners/large landowners**.
Income limit: **₹8 lakh a year** (**2017**).
Origin: **Indra Sawhney**; criteria via **DoPT OM Sept 1993**.

135.s: Justice G. Rohini Commission was constituted in 2017 primarily for
o: identifying the first list of OBCs under Article 340
determining the constitutional validity of EWS reservation
preparing the list of Scheduled Tribes
135.x: The Justice G. Rohini Commission was constituted in 2017 to examine the sub-categorisation of OBCs.
135.tq: Match the commission's name and year with its specific mandate.
xs: The **Justice G. Rohini Commission** (Oct **2017**) was for **sub-categorisation of OBCs** — option **(1)**.
It was to sub-categorise about **3,000** Central-list OBC castes.
**Art. 340** commissions were **Kalelkar** and **Mandal**; **EWS** validity was decided in **Janhit Abhiyan**.
xa: It got **14 extensions**; report to the President **31 July 2023**.
Finding: **~97%** of benefits taken by **25%** of sub-castes.
Proposal: **3-4** sub-groups.

135.s: Which of the following findings was associated with the Justice G. Rohini Commission?
o: About 97% of OBC benefits were taken by 25% of the sub-castes, while about 1,000 communities had zero representation.
The Commission found that only 100 Central-list OBC communities required sub-categorisation.
About 25% of benefits went to 97% of the sub-castes, while no community lacked representation.
All Central-list OBC castes received an equal share of benefits.
135.x: The Commission found that approximately 97% of benefits had been taken by 25% of the sub-castes, while around 1,000 communities had zero representation.
135.tq: Watch for reversed percentages and population groups in a comparison-based finding.
xs: Rohini finding: **~97%** of benefits taken by **25% of sub-castes**; **~1,000** communities with **zero representation** — option **(1)**.
Option (3) reverses the figures.
xa: Task: sub-categorise about **3,000** Central-list OBC castes into **3-4** sub-groups.
Report submitted **31 July 2023**; not yet public.
Set up **Oct 2017**; **14 extensions**.

135.s: The Justice G. Rohini Commission is associated with a proposal to divide the Central-list OBCs into
135.x: The proposal associated with the Commission envisaged three to four sub-groups among the Central-list OBCs.
135.tq: Distinguish the proposed range from nearby numerical alternatives.
xs: Rohini proposed **three or four sub-groups** (**3-4**) — option **(4)**.
Basis: **~97%** of benefits taken by **25%** of sub-castes.
xa: About **3,000** Central-list OBC castes covered.
Around **1,000** communities had **zero representation**.
Report to the President on **31 July 2023**.

135.s: The Justice G. Rohini Commission on sub-categorisation of OBCs submitted its report to the President on:
135.x: The Commission, set up in October 2017 and given 14 extensions, submitted its report to the President on 31 July 2023 (some sources say October 2023); the report is not yet public. October 2017 is when it was set up; the other dates are distractors.
135.tq: Rohini: set up Oct 2017, report 31 July 2023.
xs: The **Rohini Commission** submitted its report on **31 July 2023** — option **(1)**.
**1 October 2017** is close to when it was **set up** (**Oct 2017**), not the report date.
xa: ⚠ UPSC notes say **October 2023**; the report is **not yet public**.
It had **14 extensions**.
Proposal: **3-4** sub-groups.

135.s: Article 342A, as introduced by the 102nd Constitutional Amendment, initially provided that Socially and Educationally Backward Classes were notified by the
135.x: Article 342A provided for the President to notify the Socially and Educationally Backward Classes. The 105th Amendment subsequently restored the States' power to identify SEBCs.
135.tq: Keep the constitutional notifier distinct from the Commission that advises on backward classes.
xs: Keyed answer: the **President** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 342A** (**102nd**, **2018**) created **SEBC lists** at the Union level, which is why States lost the power.
The **105th (2021)** then **restored States' power** to identify and list SEBCs (after **Jaishri Patil**).
xa: Under **Art. 340**, too, it is the **President** who appoints the backward classes commission.
102nd also gave **NCBC** status under **Art. 338B** and added **Art. 366(26C)**.
105th = **127th Bill**.

135.s: Which expression correctly expands SEBC in the context of Articles 342A and the 105th Amendment?
135.x: SEBC means Socially and Educationally Backward Classes. The expression 'Socially and Economically Backward Classes' is not the constitutional expansion used here.
135.tq: Test the exact official phrase rather than a familiar but altered expansion.
xs: SEBC = **Socially and Educationally Backward Classes** — option **(1)**.
⚠ IYB's "**Socially and Economically**" is WRONG.
xa: **Art. 366(26C)** defines SEBCs by reference to **Art. 342A**.
**105th (2021)** restored **States' power** to list SEBCs.
**Art. 15(5)** covers **SEBCs, SCs, STs** in admissions.

135.s: The 102nd Constitutional Amendment added Article 366(26C), which defines Socially and Educationally Backward Classes by reference to
135.x: Article 366(26C), added by the 102nd Amendment, defines SEBCs by reference to Article 342A.
135.tq: Distinguish the defining provision from the related provisions on reservation, commissions and promotion.
xs: **Art. 366(26C)** defines SEBCs by reference to **Article 342A** — option **(1)**.
Both were added by the **102nd Amendment (2018)**, which also gave the **NCBC** status under **Art. 338B**.
**Art. 15(4)** answered **Champakam Dorairajan**; **Art. 338(10)** was the pre-2018 SC-commission clause; **Art. 16(4A)** is promotion (**77th**).
xa: **Art. 342A** = **SEBC lists**; the **105th (2021)** restored **States' power** to list SEBCs.
SEBC = **Socially and Educationally** Backward Classes — ⚠ not "Socially and Economically".
102nd = **123rd Bill**; 105th = **127th Bill**.

135.s: The National Commission for Backward Classes examines requests relating principally to:
o: Appointment of judges to the Supreme Court
Inclusion in or exclusion from backward-class lists
135.x: The NCBC examines requests for inclusion in or exclusion from the lists of backward classes and advises on such matters.
135.tq: Ask which constitutional body would handle the specific administrative request.
xs: The **NCBC** examines **inclusion in or exclusion from** backward-class lists — option **(3)**.
It is constitutional under **Art. 338B** (**102nd, 2018**); the statutory **NCBC Act 1993** was **repealed** in 2018.
xa: **Indra Sawhney** directed a **permanent statutory body** for OBC lists → the NCBC.
The present NCBC is the **8th**; **Niranjan Jyoti** appointed Chairperson (2026).
Before 2018, **Art. 338(10)** sent BC complaints to the **SC commission**.

135.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 102nd Constitutional Amendment from the 105th Constitutional Amendment?
o: The 102nd introduced EWS reservation, while the 105th abolished Article 342A.
The 102nd created constitutional status for the NCBC and inserted Article 342A, while the 105th restored States’ power to identify and list SEBCs.
The 102nd restored State power over SEBC lists, while the 105th created the NCBC.
The 102nd created the first Backward Classes Commission, while the 105th repealed the NCBC Act, 1993.
135.x: The 102nd Amendment Act, 2018 inserted Articles 338B and 342A and gave constitutional status to the NCBC. The 105th Amendment Act, 2021 restored the power of States to identify and list SEBCs.
135.tq: Separate the institutional change made by the 102nd Amendment from the federal-list change made by the 105th.
xs: **102nd** gave the **NCBC** constitutional status and inserted **Art. 342A**; the **105th** **restored States' power** to identify and list SEBCs — option **(2)**.
EWS came through the **103rd (2019)**, not the 102nd; the first BC commission was **Kalelkar (1953)** under **Art. 340**.
The 105th answered **Jaishri Patil**; it did not create the NCBC.
xa: The statutory **NCBC Act 1993** was **repealed** in **2018**.

135.s: Niranjan Jyoti was appointed as the Chairperson of the
135.x: Niranjan Jyoti was appointed Chairperson of the National Commission for Backward Classes.
135.tq: Match the named person with the correct commission rather than a similarly related body.
xs: **Niranjan Jyoti** was appointed Chairperson of the **National Commission for Backward Classes** (2026) — option **(3)**.
The **Rohini Commission** (Oct **2017**) handles OBC sub-categorisation; the first BC commission was **Kalelkar (1953)**.
xa: NCBC is constitutional under **Art. 338B** (**102nd**); present NCBC is the **8th**.
NCBC role: examines **inclusion/exclusion** requests.
Statutory **NCBC Act 1993** repealed in **2018**.

135.s:
With reference to the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, consider the following statements:
1. It inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6).
2. It provides 10 percent reservation for EWS persons not covered by SC, ST or OBC quotas.
3. It was introduced in Parliament as the 124th Constitutional Amendment Bill.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: All three statements are correct. The 103rd Amendment inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6), introduced EWS reservation of 10 percent outside the existing SC, ST and OBC quotas, and originated as the 124th Constitutional Amendment Bill.
135.tq: Use the all-inclusive option only when every constitutional detail is consistent.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: the **103rd (2019)** inserted **Art. 15(6) and 16(6)**.
Statement 2: **10%** for **EWS** not covered by **SC/ST/OBC** quotas.
Statement 3: it was the **124th Amendment Bill** (APPSC G1 **2019** key).
xa: In force **January 2019**; upheld in **Janhit Abhiyan (7 Nov 2022)** by **3:2**.
EWS is **over and above** existing reservation.
States: enabling, **not mandatory**.

135.s:
With reference to the 103rd Constitutional Amendment, consider the following statements:
1. It enables reservation of up to 10 per cent for EWS.
2. The reservation is outside the existing SC, ST and OBC quotas.
3. The provision makes it mandatory for every State to provide EWS reservation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The EWS reservation is enabling rather than mandatory for the States, so statement 3 is incorrect.
135.tq: Watch for the false absolute claim that an enabling constitutional provision is mandatory for every State.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **up to 10%** for **EWS**. Statement 2: **over and above** / in addition to SC/ST/OBC quotas.
Statement 3 is wrong: for States it is **enabling, not mandatory**.
xa: EWS criteria: income **below ₹8 lakh**, **5 acres** farm land, **1,000 sq ft** flat.
Applies to jobs and education, incl. **private** central institutions.
⚠ **₹8 lakh** = OBC creamy-layer limit (**2017**) = EWS ceiling.

135.s:
The constitutional provisions relating to EWS reservation are applicable to which of the following institutions or sectors?
1. Central educational institutions
2. Private educational institutions
3. Posts under the Central Government
4. State Governments on a compulsory basis
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
135.x: The 103rd Amendment provides EWS reservation in central educational institutions, including private institutions, and in posts. Its implementation is not mandatory for State Governments.
135.tq: Identify the statement that overstates the constitutional obligation by using a compulsory application to States.
xs: EWS applies to **central educational institutions**, **private** institutions and **central posts** — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 4 is wrong: for **States** it is **enabling, not mandatory**.
xa: EWS is for those **not covered** by SC/ST/OBC quotas.
Upheld in **Janhit Abhiyan** by a **five-judge** bench (**3:2**).

135.s: For determining EWS eligibility, which one of the following combinations correctly represents the income and asset criteria stated for the purpose?
o: Annual family income below ₹5 lakh, land below 2 acres and flat below 800 sq ft
Annual family income below ₹8 lakh, agricultural land below 10 acres and flat below 1,000 sq ft
Annual family income below ₹8 lakh, agricultural land below 5 acres and flat below 1,000 sq ft
Annual family income below ₹10 lakh, agricultural land below 5 acres and flat below 1,500 sq ft
135.x: The stated EWS criteria include annual family income below ₹8 lakh, agricultural land below 5 acres and a flat below 1,000 square feet.
135.tq: Match the numerical threshold with the associated land and dwelling limits.
xs: EWS criteria: family income **below ₹8 lakh**, farm land below **5 acres**, flat below **1,000 sq ft** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) has the wrong land limit; options (1) and (4) have wrong income figures.
xa: ⚠ **₹8 lakh** is also the **OBC creamy-layer** limit since **2017**.
EWS: **10%**, over and above existing reservation.
Creamy-layer ladder: **₹1 lakh (1993)** → **₹8 lakh (2017)**.

135.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the decision in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India:
1. The 103rd Constitutional Amendment was upheld by a 3:2 majority.
2. Chief Justice U.U. Lalit dissented.
3. Justice S. Ravindra Bhat dissented.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: The EWS amendment was upheld by a 3:2 majority, while Chief Justice U.U. Lalit and Justice S. Ravindra Bhat were among the dissenting judges.
135.tq: Check the judicial split first, then verify both named dissenting judges.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Janhit Abhiyan (7 Nov 2022)** upheld the **103rd** **3:2**, a **five-judge** bench.
Statements 2 and 3: dissent by CJI **U.U. Lalit** and Justice **S. Ravindra Bhat**.
xa: It held the **50% cap** applies to backward-class quotas.
The 103rd inserted **Art. 15(6) and 16(6)** — **10% EWS**.
103rd = **124th Amendment Bill**.

135.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the 50 per cent ceiling referred to in the context of reservation from EWS reservation?
o: The ceiling applies to backward-class reservations, whereas EWS reservation was provided additionally under Articles 15(6) and 16(6).
The ceiling applies only to reservations in promotions.
The ceiling applies exclusively to EWS reservation.
The ceiling was abolished by the 103rd Amendment.
135.x: The 50 per cent ceiling discussed in this context relates to backward-class reservations. EWS reservation was introduced additionally through Articles 15(6) and 16(6).
135.tq: Separate the general reservation ceiling from the constitutional source of EWS reservation.
xs: The **50%** ceiling applies to **backward-class** reservations; EWS was added **additionally** under **Articles 15(6) and 16(6)** — option **(1)**.
**Janhit Abhiyan (2022)**: the **50% cap** applies to backward-class quotas.
The ceiling comes from **Indra Sawhney** and was not abolished; it is not limited to promotions.
xa: EWS is **over and above** / in addition to existing reservation.
Indra Sawhney: **carry-forward** allowed within **50%**, year by year.
**81st (2000)**: backlog vacancies sit outside the **50%** ceiling.

135.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched in relation to the Andhra Pradesh BC groups?
o: BC-E — aboriginal tribes and nomadic groups
135.x: BC-D consists of other classes. BC-B comprises vocational or occupational groups, BC-C comprises SC converts to Christianity, and BC-E comprises socially and educationally backward Muslims.
135.tq: Use the group-composition pairs to detect swapped categories.
xs: **BC-D — other classes** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**BC-B** = **vocational/occupational** groups; **BC-C** = **SC converts to Christianity**.
**BC-E** = socially and educationally backward **Muslims**; aboriginal tribes and nomadic groups = **BC-A**.
xa: **BC-E** was added by the **2007** AP Act.
The **Anantharaman Commission** framed the **A-D** grouping.

135.s: The combined quota shares of BC-A, BC-B, BC-C, BC-D and BC-E in Andhra Pradesh amount to:
135.x: The shares are 7 per cent, 10 per cent, 1 per cent, 7 per cent and 4 per cent respectively, totalling 29 per cent.
135.tq: Add the category-wise figures rather than confusing them with the local-body quota.
xs: AP BC shares total **29 per cent** — option **(3)**.
**34%** is the **local-body** BC quota (rural); **27%** is the central OBC quota.
xa: **BC-E** (**4%**) is for backward **Muslims**, added in **2007**.
Anantharaman's original quota was **25%**.
BC residential schools (**2024-25**) still admit by **BC-A to BC-E** groups.

135.s: The Sukhdev case concerning backward-class reservation in Andhra Pradesh resulted in which of the following conclusions?
o: Caste alone could not be the basis, and 112 classes were identified using poverty, residence and occupation.
All reservation for backward classes was unconstitutional.
Caste alone could be the basis for identifying backward classes.
Reservation could be based only on residence.
135.x: The High Court held in the Sukhdev case that caste alone could not be the basis; consequently, 112 classes were listed using poverty, residence and occupation as considerations.
135.tq: Link the judicial principle with the resulting classification exercise.
xs: **Sukhdev case (HC)**: **caste alone** cannot be the basis → **112** classes listed on **poverty, residence and occupation** — option **(1)**.
It did not strike down all BC reservation, nor rest on residence alone.
xa: After **1956**: separate BC lists for **Andhra (86 castes)** and **Telangana**.
**1963 GO**: **25%** medical seats for **139** castes.
⚠ Contrast: **Indra Sawhney** held caste **can** be the main criterion.

135.s: Which commission was the first Andhra Pradesh Backward Classes Commission and framed the A-D grouping along with a 25 per cent quota?
135.x: The Anantharaman Commission was the first Andhra Pradesh Backward Classes Commission; its report was submitted in 1970 and it framed the A-D grouping and a 25 per cent quota.
135.tq: Identify the commission from its distinctive first-commission and grouping role.
xs: The **Anantharaman Commission** was the first AP BC Commission (report **1970**), framing **A-D** grouping and a **25%** quota — option **(1)**.
**Mandal** was national (**1979**); **Muralidhara Rao** took charge **27 Jan 1982**; **Manjunatha (2016)** was on **Kapus**.
xa: **Muralidhara Rao** reviewed BC reservation and examined inclusion of minorities.
**BC-E** added later by the **2007** Act.
National first commission: **Kalelkar (1953)**.

135.s: The BC-E category in Andhra Pradesh was added through which measure and in which year?
135.x: BC-E was added by the Andhra Pradesh Act of 2007. Earlier lists commonly included only BC-A to BC-D.
135.tq: Match the category’s introduction with the specific legal instrument and year.
xs: **BC-E** was added by the **2007 Andhra Pradesh Act** — option **(1)**.
⚠ CDX lists only **BC-A to BC-D**.
**1984** = NTR's **20%** local-body BC quota; **2010** = AP HC struck the 2007 Act down; **2019** = EWS.
xa: BC-E share: **4%**, for socially and educationally backward **Muslims**.
Earlier **5%** quotas (**2004 and 2005**) were struck down by the **AP High Court**.
The **Supreme Court** let the 2007 quota continue by **interim order** pending a **Constitution Bench**.

135.s: What was the effect of the Supreme Court’s interim order concerning the 4 per cent reservation for backward Muslim groups in Andhra Pradesh?
o: It permanently approved the quota without further judicial examination.
It allowed the quota to continue pending consideration by a Constitution Bench.
It converted the quota into an EWS reservation.
It abolished the quota immediately after the High Court judgment.
135.x: Although the Andhra Pradesh High Court struck down the 2007 Act in 2010, the Supreme Court permitted the 4 per cent quota to continue by an interim order pending a Constitution Bench.
135.tq: Distinguish an interim continuation from final constitutional approval.
xs: The SC's interim order **allowed the quota to continue pending a Constitution Bench** — option **(2)**.
The **AP HC** had struck down the **2007 Act (4%, BC-E)** in **2010**.
It was neither a final approval nor a conversion into EWS.
xa: Earlier **5%** quotas of **2004 and 2005** were struck down by the AP HC.
G2 **2011** answer (Muslim quota State): **Andhra Pradesh**.
BC-E Muslim quota remains a **live issue** in AP.

135.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the Kapu reservation proposal is correct?
1. The Justice Manjunatha Commission was constituted in 2016.
2. A 2017 Bill proposed 5 per cent reservation for Kapus as BC-F.
3. The proposal was approved by the Centre.
4. In 2019, Kapus received 5 per cent reservation within the 10 per cent EWS quota, which was later withdrawn by the succeeding government.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The Centre never approved the 2017 BC-F proposal, so statement 3 is false.
135.tq: Find the wrong authority-action statement among otherwise connected facts.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **Justice Manjunatha Commission (2016)**. Statement 2: the **2017 Bill** gave Kapus **5%** as **BC-F**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it was **never approved by the Centre**.
Statement 4: in **2019** Kapus got **5%** within the **10% EWS** quota; withdrawn by the next government.
xa: Kapu demand and **BC-E** Muslim quota are AP's **live issues**.
AP BC shares: **A 7%, B 10%, C 1%, D 7%, E 4%**.
EWS: enabling, **not mandatory** for States.

135.s:
Consider the following statements regarding reservation for BCs in Andhra Pradesh local bodies:
1. NTR introduced a 20 per cent BC quota in 1984.
2. The quota was raised to 34 per cent for polls held in 1995, 2001, 2006 and 2013.
3. It was subsequently reduced to 24.15 per cent under Government Orders 176, 559 and 560.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: All three statements are correct: the quota began at 20 per cent in 1984, rose to 34 per cent for the specified elections, and was later reduced to 24.15 per cent under the cited Government Orders.
135.tq: Track the changing percentage chronologically and retain the order-specific details.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **NTR** introduced **20%** BC quota in **1984**.
Statement 3: cut to **24.15%** under GOs **176, 559, 560**.
xa: The earlier **34%** was struck down for breaching the overall ceiling.
Current: **34% rural** + **33.33% urban** (19 Aug 2026).
**G.O. Rt. No. 1065** governs ULB polls.

135.s: According to the stated current arrangement for Andhra Pradesh local bodies, the BC quota is:
o: 34 per cent in rural and 33.33 per cent in urban local bodies
29 per cent in rural and 34 per cent in urban local bodies
33.33 per cent in rural and 34 per cent in urban local bodies
24.15 per cent in rural and 20 per cent in urban local bodies
135.x: The stated arrangement provides 34 per cent reservation in rural local bodies and 33.33 per cent in urban local bodies.
135.tq: Compare the rural and urban figures without reversing their order.
xs: Current AP local-body BC quota: **34% in rural** and **33.33% in urban** — option **(1)**.
**24.15%** was the reduced figure under GOs **176, 559, 560**; **20%** was NTR's **1984** quota.
xa: **G.O. Rt. No. 1065 (19 Aug 2026)** for ULB polls under the **AP Municipal Corporations Act 1994** + **Municipalities Act 1965**.
SC **triple test**: dedicated commission, local-body-wise proportion, total within **50%**.
⚠ **29%** = AP BC share in jobs/education, not local bodies.

135.s:
The Supreme Court’s triple test for OBC reservation in local bodies requires:
1. A dedicated commission to examine backwardness.
2. Determination of the reservation proportion local-body-wise.
3. Keeping the total reservation within the 50 per cent ceiling.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: All three requirements form the triple test: a dedicated commission, local-body-wise proportional determination, and compliance with the overall 50 per cent ceiling.
135.tq: Recognise a judicial test as a cumulative set of mandatory conditions.
xs: All three are part of the **triple test** — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Dedicated commission** + **local-body-wise proportion** + total **within 50%**.
xa: AP's earlier **34%** was struck down for breaching the overall ceiling.
Current AP: **34% rural**, **33.33% urban**.
**Indra Sawhney**: **50%** ceiling except in extraordinary cases.

135.s: The earlier 34 per cent reservation for BCs in Andhra Pradesh local bodies was struck down primarily because it:
o: Was introduced through a Constitutional Amendment
Was confined to urban local bodies only
135.x: The earlier 34 per cent local-body reservation was struck down for breaching the overall reservation ceiling.
135.tq: Identify the constitutional limitation triggered by the percentage claimed.
xs: The earlier **34%** was struck down because it **breached the overall reservation ceiling** — option **(3)**.
The SC triple test requires total reservation **within 50%**.
xa: The quota was then cut to **24.15%** (GOs **176, 559, 560**).
NTR started with **20%** in **1984**.

135.s: Which of the following issues has been identified as a criticism or debate concerning reservation in central services?
o: Approximately 40–50% of reserved central posts lie vacant.
All reserved central posts are filled before unreserved posts.
Reserved posts are filled exclusively through State-level commissions.
No reservation is available in central services.
135.x: A criticism noted in the reservation debate is that approximately 40–50% of reserved central posts remain vacant.
135.tq: Select the stated range while rejecting absolute claims about reservation administration.
xs: Criticism: **40-50%** of **reserved central posts lie vacant** — option **(1)**.
So reserved posts are not all filled first; reservation in central posts exists (**27%** OBC from **1993**).
xa: Other debates: no **BC sub-quota** inside **women's reservation**.
**Census 2027** caste enumeration may be used to reassess quotas.
**81st (2000)** lets **backlog vacancies** carry forward as a separate class.

135.s: The 2027 Census has been discussed as potentially useful for
o: determining the composition of the NCBC by direct election
reassessing reservation quotas using caste enumeration
135.x: The 2027 Census, with caste enumeration, may be used to reassess reservation quotas.
135.tq: Link the proposed data exercise to its stated policy application without extending its purpose.
xs: The **2027 Census** with **caste enumeration** may be used for **reassessing reservation quotas** — option **(4)**.
**Arts. 341/342** remain the basis of SC/ST status — the Census does not replace them.
xa: **Telangana Assembly** asked for a **BC/OBC column in Census 2027** (12 Sep 2026).
**Rohini** found **~97%** of benefits with **25%** of OBC sub-castes.
**40-50%** of reserved central posts lie vacant.

135.s: Which of the following represents a reservation-related issue specifically associated with Andhra Pradesh?
o: The creation of the constitutional NCBC by the State Legislature
The replacement of the Central List by a district-wise list
BC-E Muslim quota and the Kapu demand
The demand to abolish all BC-A to BC-E groups
135.x: BC-E Muslim quota and the Kapu demand are identified as live reservation issues in Andhra Pradesh.
135.tq: Separate State-specific reservation issues from national constitutional developments.
xs: AP's live issues: the **BC-E Muslim quota** and the **Kapu demand** — option **(3)**.
The NCBC is constitutional through the **102nd** — no State Legislature created it.
xa: BC-E (**4%**) came by the **2007** Act; the SC let it continue pending a **Constitution Bench**.
Kapus: **Manjunatha Commission (2016)** → **2017 Bill** for **5%** as **BC-F**.
BC residential schools (**2024-25**) still admit by **BC-A to BC-E** groups.

135.s: Which of the following developments relates to the reservation debate in 2026?
o: The Telangana Assembly asked the Centre to include a BC/OBC column in Census 2027.
The Supreme Court directed that no caste enumeration could be considered in Census 2027.
The Union Government abolished the BC/OBC category in the Census.
The Telangana Assembly asked the Centre to remove caste-related questions from Census 2027.
135.x: On 12 September 2026, the Telangana Assembly asked the Centre to add a BC/OBC column in Census 2027.
135.tq: Identify the specific institutional demand and distinguish it from an opposite or absolute claim.
xs: The **Telangana Assembly** asked the Centre to add a **BC/OBC column in Census 2027** (12 Sep 2026) — option **(1)**.
It asked to add, not remove, caste-related data.
xa: Census 2027 caste enumeration may be used to **reassess quotas**.
SC reserved verdict on **TN's BC (Muslim)** quota for converts (8 Aug 2026).
Union opposed **SC/ST creamy layer** (**Aug 2026**).

135.s: Which one of the following is correctly associated with the current debate on reservation for women?
o: Women's reservation has replaced all OBC reservation in central posts.
The NCBC has constitutional authority to impose a BC sub-quota in every State.
A BC sub-quota exists inside women's reservation throughout India.
There is no BC sub-quota inside women's reservation, which has been raised as a criticism.
135.x: The absence of a BC sub-quota within women's reservation has been identified as a criticism and debate.
135.tq: Watch for the reversal between an identified criticism and a claim that the arrangement already exists.
xs: There is **no BC sub-quota inside women's reservation** — a criticism — option **(4)**.
So option (3) is the reverse of the fact; women's reservation has not replaced OBC quotas.
xa: Other debates: **40-50%** of reserved central posts lie vacant.
**Census 2027** caste enumeration may be used to reassess quotas.
The NCBC's role is to examine **inclusion/exclusion** requests, not impose sub-quotas.

136.s: Which of the following correctly represents the procedure for inclusion of a community as a Scheduled Tribe?
o: State proposal → Registrar General of India → NCST → Union Cabinet → Parliament amends the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950
NCST proposal → State Cabinet → President directly amends the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950
State proposal → Parliament → Registrar General of India → Supreme Court
Registrar General of India → State proposal → Union Cabinet → NCST
136.x: The stated sequence is proposal by the State, examination by the Registrar General of India and NCST, consideration by the Union Cabinet, and amendment by Parliament under Article 342(2).
136.tq: Follow the institutional sequence from initiation to the final constitutional amendment authority.
xs: Procedure: **State proposal → Registrar General of India → NCST → Union Cabinet → Parliament** amends the **Constitution (ST) Order 1950** — option **(1)**.
Parliament acts under **Art. 342(2)**; the President does not amend the list directly, and the Supreme Court has no role in it.
The **State** starts the process — the RGI comes second, not first.
xa: **Art. 366(25)** defines Scheduled Tribes.
ST status is **religiously neutral** (RPSC **2010** key).
**NCST** functions from **19 Feb 2004** under **Art. 338A** (**89th Amendment 2003**).

136.s: Under which provision is Parliament empowered to amend the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950 for the purpose of modifying the list of Scheduled Tribes?
136.x: Article 342(2) provides for Parliament to include or exclude groups from the list of Scheduled Tribes by law.
136.tq: Distinguish the procedural provision for amendment from the definitional provision in Article 366(25).
xs: Parliament amends the **Constitution (ST) Order 1950** under **Article 342(2)** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 366(25)** only **defines** STs; **Art. 340** is the backward classes commission; **Art. 16(4A)** is promotion reservation.
xa: Sequence: State → **Registrar General of India** → **NCST** → Cabinet → Parliament.
ST status is **religiously neutral**.
**NCST** created under **Art. 338A** by the **89th Amendment 2003**.

136.s: The term 'Scheduled Tribes' is defined in which provision of the Constitution of India?
136.x: Article 366(25) defines Scheduled Tribes. Article 342(2) lets Parliament modify the ST list, Article 338A creates the NCST, and Article 244(1) applies the Fifth Schedule to Scheduled Areas.
136.tq: Definition = 366(25); list change by Parliament = 342(2).
xs: Scheduled Tribes are defined in **Article 366(25)** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 342(2)**: Parliament modifies the **ST list**; **Art. 338A**: the **NCST**.
xa: ST inclusion: State → **Registrar General of India** → NCST → Cabinet → Parliament.
The **Fifth Schedule** and **Art. 244** protect Scheduled Areas (cited in the **Parasnath Hills** debate).
ST status is **religiously neutral** (RPSC **2010**).

136.s: With regard to the religion of a member of a Scheduled Tribe, which statement is correct?
o: ST status is lost on conversion to any non-Hindu religion
ST status is available only to Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists
ST status is available only to followers of tribal animist faiths
136.x: ST status is religiously neutral (RPSC 2010 key): it does not depend on the religion professed. The other options import the religion test that applies to Scheduled Castes or invent one.
136.tq: SC status is tied to religion; ST status is not.
xs: ST status is **religiously neutral** — option **(3)** (RPSC **2010** key).
So it is not lost on conversion and is not limited to Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists or animists.
xa: STs are defined in **Art. 366(25)**; the list is changed under **Art. 342(2)**.
In AP, STs = **27.39 lakh (5.53%)** in **34** communities.
AP Scheduled Areas cover **10.15%** of the State.

136.s: In tribal usage, the term ‘Diku’ refers to:
o: An outsider-exploiter such as a moneylender, trader, landlord or contractor
136.x: Diku denotes an outsider-exploiter, including a moneylender, trader, landlord or contractor.
136.tq: Distinguish the exact social meaning of a culturally specific term.
xs: **Diku** = an **outsider-exploiter** — **moneylender, trader, landlord or contractor** — option **(4)**.
**Birsa's Ulgulan** targeted British land-grabbing and the **dikus**.
xa: **Abua Raj** = aim of Birsa's **Ulgulan**; **Dharti Aaba** = title of **Birsa Munda**.
**Nistar** = a **community right** under the FRA (with grazing, fishing).
**Marang Buru** = **Parasnath Hills** as revered by **Santhals**.

136.s: Which one of the following combinations correctly identifies major causes and consequences of tribal indebtedness and land alienation?
o: Tribal indebtedness was caused exclusively by modern schools
Restrictive forest laws expanded tribal access to traditional habitats
Revenue farmers eliminated all non-tribal control over tribal land
Colonial moneylenders and revenue farmers contributed to indebtedness and land alienation
136.x: Colonial moneylenders and revenue farmers contributed to indebtedness and land alienation. Restrictive forest laws, on the contrary, cut tribals off from their habitats.
136.tq: Identify the historically correct cause-and-effect relationship.
xs: **Colonial moneylenders and revenue farmers** caused **indebtedness and land alienation** — option **(4)**.
**Restrictive forest laws** did the opposite of option (2): they **cut tribals off from habitat**.
xa: **Displacement**: STs about **9%** of population but **over 50%** of the displaced.
Other problems: **low literacy**, language barriers, **malnutrition**, **forced labour**.
AP's **Regulation 1/70** presumes land belongs to tribals and bans transfers even between non-tribals.

136.s:
Consider the following statements about the problems faced by Scheduled Tribes:
1. Restrictive forest laws cut many tribals off from their habitat.
2. Low literacy and language barriers are among the problems faced by them.
3. Malnutrition, forced labour and displacement are also identified as tribal problems.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
136.x: All three statements correctly identify problems associated with tribal communities: loss of habitat, educational and linguistic disadvantages, malnutrition, forced labour and displacement.
136.tq: Use the all-inclusive option when each listed problem is supported.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **restrictive forest laws** cut tribals off from habitat.
Statement 2: **low literacy** and **language barriers**.
Statement 3: **malnutrition**, **forced labour** and **displacement**.
xa: Colonial **moneylenders + revenue farmers** → indebtedness and **land alienation**.
STs about **9%** of population but **over 50%** of people displaced.
**Forest Conservation Rules 2022** dropped the forest-dwellers' consent clause.

136.s: Scheduled Tribes constitute about 9% of the population but account for over what proportion of people displaced by development projects?
136.x: Scheduled Tribes constitute about 9 per cent of the population but account for over 50 per cent of people displaced by development projects.
136.tq: Test a population-share versus displacement-share comparison.
xs: STs are about **9%** of the population but **over 50%** of those displaced by development projects — option **(3)**.
**Displacement** by development projects is listed among the key tribal problems — a core debate of development vs consent.
xa: AP: **Koya** and **Kondh** oppose **Polavaram** — land rights, poor compensation, displacement without rehabilitation.
**RFCTLARR 2013**: acquisition in **Scheduled Areas** only as a **last resort**, with **Gram Sabha** consent.
RFCTLARR consent: **80% (private)**, **70% (PPP)** affected families.

136.s: The Forest Conservation Rules, 2022 became a subject of dispute between the NCST and the Environment Ministry because they:
o: Added a compulsory tribal veto over every forest diversion
Dropped the forest-dwellers’ consent clause before forest diversion
Prohibited all development projects in forest areas
Transferred all forests to Gram Sabhas
136.x: The 2022 Rules dropped the consent clause of forest-dwellers before forest diversion, leading to a dispute between the NCST and the Environment Ministry.
136.tq: Identify the precise legal change behind an institutional dispute.
xs: The **Forest Conservation Rules 2022** **dropped the forest-dwellers' consent clause** before forest diversion — option **(2)**.
This set the **NCST** against the **Environment Ministry**.
xa: MoEFCC guidelines had barred diversion until FRA processes (esp. **Gram Sabha consent**) were complete.
MoTA letter (**31 Aug 2026**): FRA has **"no provision"** for Gram Sabha consent for **Stage-II** clearance.
**Niyamgiri (2013)**: **Dongria Kondh** gram sabhas rejected bauxite mining → project cancelled.

136.s: Birsa Munda’s Ulgulan was directed against:
o: Only forest conservation by tribal institutions
The Panchsheel principles of tribal development
136.x: Birsa’s Ulgulan was aimed at British land-grabbing and the exploitative dikus.
136.tq: Match the movement with its principal targets.
xs: Birsa's **Ulgulan** was against **British land-grabbing and the dikus** — option **(4)**.
Its issues: **land-grabbing**, **forced labour**; aim **Abua Raj**.
xa: Dates: **1899-1900**; led to the **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908**.
Birsa = **Dharti Aaba**; died in **Ranchi jail** (**1900**).
**15 November** (birth anniversary) is marked by the Union.

136.s: The Santhal Hul of 1855–56 was primarily directed against which combination of groups?
o: Forest officials, contractors and military officers
Rajas, autonomous councils and Gram Sabhas
136.x: The Santhal Hul was directed against zamindars, moneylenders, referred to as dikus, and the police.
136.tq: Directly link the revolt with its principal targets.
xs: The **Santhal Hul (1855-56)** was against **zamindars, moneylenders (dikus) and police** — option **(3)**.
It was led by **Sidhu and Kanhu**.
xa: **Rampa rebellion (1922-24)**: **Alluri Sitarama Raju**, against forest curbs on **podu** and forced labour.
**Srikakulam Girijan (1967-70)**: land alienation, moneylenders; turned **Naxalite**.
**Santhals** revere **Parasnath Hills** as **Marang Buru**.

136.s:
Match List-I (Tribal revolt) with List-II (Leader):
List-I
a. Santhal Hul (1855-56)
b. Birsa's Ulgulan (1899-1900)
c. Rampa rebellion (1922-24)
d. Srikakulam Girijan movement (1967-70)
List-II
i. Alluri Sitarama Raju
ii. Sidhu and Kanhu
iii. Vempatapu Satyanarayana and Adibhatla Kailasam
iv. Birsa Munda (Dharti Aaba)
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
136.x: Santhal Hul was led by Sidhu and Kanhu (a-ii); Birsa's Ulgulan by Birsa Munda, Dharti Aaba (b-iv); the Rampa rebellion by Alluri Sitarama Raju (c-i); the Srikakulam Girijan movement by Vempatapu Satyanarayana and Adibhatla Kailasam (d-iii). Option B swaps Santhal Hul and Ulgulan, option C swaps Rampa and Srikakulam, option D swaps Santhal Hul and Rampa.
136.tq: Anchor the two AP revolts first: Rampa = Alluri, Srikakulam = Vempatapu-Kailasam.
xs: Correct code: **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — option **(1)**.
**Santhal Hul** → **Sidhu and Kanhu**; **Ulgulan** → **Birsa Munda (Dharti Aaba)**.
**Rampa** → **Alluri Sitarama Raju**; **Srikakulam Girijan** → **Vempatapu Satyanarayana and Adibhatla Kailasam**.
xa: Rampa was in the **Godavari agency** against curbs on **podu**.
Ulgulan led to the **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908**.

136.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Birsa Munda’s Ulgulan:
1. It took place during 1899–1900.
2. It was associated with land-grabbing and forced labour.
3. Its objective included the establishment of Abua Raj.
4. It directly led to the enactment of the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
136.x: All four statements are correct. Birsa’s Ulgulan occurred in 1899–1900, opposed land-grabbing and forced labour, sought Abua Raj, and led to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908.
136.tq: Check the date, issue, objective and legislative consequence separately.
xs: All four are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Statements 1–2: **Ulgulan (1899-1900)** against **land-grabbing and forced labour**.
Statement 3: aim **Abua Raj**. Statement 4: led to the **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908**.
xa: Birsa = **Dharti Aaba**; died in **Ranchi jail** (**1900**).
**15 November** marked by the Union.
**Diku** = outsider-exploiter (moneylender, trader, landlord, contractor).

136.s: Birsa Munda is also known by which title?
136.x: Birsa Munda is popularly known as Dharti Aaba.
136.tq: Test the exact title rather than the broader movement association.
xs: Birsa Munda's title is **Dharti Aaba** — option **(2)**.
He led the **Ulgulan** against British land-grabbing and the **dikus**.
xa: His **Ulgulan (1899-1900)** aimed at **Abua Raj**.
It led to the **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908**.
The Union marks his birth anniversary on **15 November**.

136.s:
Arrange the following tribal movements in chronological order:
A. Srikakulam Girijan movement
B. Santhal Hul
C. Rampa rebellion
D. Birsa’s Ulgulan
136.x: The correct sequence is Santhal Hul (1855–56), Birsa’s Ulgulan (1899–1900), Rampa rebellion (1922–24), and Srikakulam Girijan movement (1967–70).
136.tq: Place the events by their stated year ranges before checking the sequence options.
xs: Order: **Santhal Hul → Birsa's Ulgulan → Rampa → Srikakulam Girijan** = **B, D, C, A** — option **(1)**.
xa: Leaders: **Sidhu, Kanhu**; **Birsa Munda**; **Alluri Sitarama Raju**; **Vempatapu Satyanarayana, Adibhatla Kailasam**.
Srikakulam Girijan movement turned **Naxalite**.
Ulgulan → **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908**.

136.s: Which one of the following was NOT an issue associated with the Rampa rebellion?
o: Opposition to land-grabbing by zamindars as the principal recorded issue
Restrictions affecting tribal communities in the Agency area
Forced labour in the Godavari Agency
136.x: The Rampa rebellion (1922-24, Alluri Sitarama Raju) was a revolt against forest-law curbs on podu cultivation and forced labour in the Godavari Agency, so A, C and D are its issues. Zamindars were the target of the Santhal Hul, and land-grabbing was the issue of Birsa's Ulgulan, so B is the odd one out.
136.tq: Find the issue belonging to another revolt rather than the named movement.
xs: NOT a Rampa issue: **opposition to land-grabbing by zamindars** — option **(2)**.
**Rampa (1922-24)**, led by **Alluri Sitarama Raju**, was against forest-law curbs on **podu** and **forced labour** in the **Godavari agency**.
**Zamindars** were the target of the **Santhal Hul**; **land-grabbing** was Birsa's issue.
xa: **Srikakulam Girijan (1967-70)**: land alienation, moneylenders, forest officials.
**Santhal Hul (1855-56)**: zamindars, moneylenders, police.
Ulgulan (**1899-1900**): land-grabbing, forced labour; aim **Abua Raj**.

136.s:
According to T. K. Oommen, modern tribal movements seek which of the following objectives?
1. Political autonomy
2. Recognition of identity
3. Control over resources
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
136.x: T. K. Oommen identified political autonomy, identity recognition and control over resources as objectives of modern tribal movements.
136.tq: Treat a three-part conceptual formulation as a complete list.
xs: All three — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**T.K. Oommen**: modern tribal movements seek **political autonomy, identity recognition and control over resources**.
xa: Approaches: **isolation** (early **Elwin**), **assimilation** (**Ghurye**, **N.K. Bose**), **integration** (**Nehru**).
Birsa's Ulgulan aimed at **Abua Raj**.
⚠ Elwin = early **isolation**, later **integration** with Nehru.

136.s:
Consider the following statements about Birsa Munda:
1. He died in Ranchi jail in 1900.
2. His birth anniversary, 15 November, is marked by the Union Government.
3. His Ulgulan aimed at establishing Abua Raj.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
136.x: All three are correct: Birsa died in Ranchi jail in 1900, his birth anniversary on 15 November is marked by the Union, and his Ulgulan (1899-1900) sought Abua Raj. Options A, B and C each leave out a correct statement.
136.tq: Birsa: Ulgulan 1899-1900, died 1900 in Ranchi jail, 15 Nov birth anniversary.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: Birsa died in **Ranchi jail** (**1900**). Statement 2: **15 November** is marked by the Union.
Statement 3: Ulgulan's aim was **Abua Raj**.
xa: Title: **Dharti Aaba**.
Ulgulan → **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908**.
**Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan** (**Sept 2024**) bears his title.

136.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I: Approach
 a. Isolation
 b. Assimilation
 c. Integration

List-II: Associated idea or proponent
 i. Development while retaining tribal identity
 ii. Tribes treated as ‘backward Hindus’ and absorbed
 iii. Tribes kept apart to protect their culture

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
136.x: Isolation seeks to keep tribes apart for cultural protection; assimilation seeks their absorption as ‘backward Hindus’; integration combines development with retention of identity.
136.tq: Start from the clear idea-pair and complete the remaining matches.
xs: Correct code: **a–iii, b–ii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
**Isolation**: keep tribes **apart** to protect culture; **Assimilation**: tribes as "**backward Hindus**" to be absorbed.
**Integration**: **develop while keeping identity**.
xa: Proponents: isolation — early **Verrier Elwin**; assimilation — **G.S. Ghurye**, **N.K. Bose**; integration — **Nehru** (with Elwin).
Nehru's **Panchsheel** came from his foreword to Elwin's **A Philosophy for NEFA**.
⚠ Elwin = early isolation, later integration.

136.s: Who is associated with the isolation approach to tribal development, described in terms such as ‘museum’ or ‘national park’?
136.x: The isolation approach is associated with early Verrier Elwin and sought to keep tribes apart to protect their culture.
136.tq: Match the distinctive metaphor with its proponent.
xs: The **isolation** ("museum"/national-park) approach = **early Verrier Elwin** — option **(3)**.
**Ghurye** and **N.K. Bose** = assimilation; **Nehru** = integration.
xa: ⚠ Elwin moved from **isolation** to **integration** with Nehru.
Elwin wrote **A Philosophy for NEFA**; Nehru's foreword = source of Panchsheel.
CDX credits **Elwin** with formulating Panchsheel under Nehru's influence.

136.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the assimilation approach and its proponents?
o: It keeps tribes completely separate; it was proposed only by Nehru
It regards tribes as ‘backward Hindus’ to be absorbed; G.S. Ghurye and N.K. Bose are associated with it
It develops tribes while preserving identity; it was proposed only by Elwin
It rejects all cultural contact; it was formulated by Birsa Munda
136.x: Assimilation views tribes as ‘backward Hindus’ to be absorbed and is associated with G.S. Ghurye and N.K. Bose, including Bose’s Hindu method of tribal absorption.
136.tq: Combine the approach, its defining idea and its proponents.
xs: **Assimilation** treats tribes as "**backward Hindus**" to be absorbed — **G.S. Ghurye** and **N.K. Bose** — option **(2)**.
N.K. Bose spoke of the **Hindu method of tribal absorption**.
Keeping tribes separate = **isolation** (early **Elwin**); developing with identity = **integration** (**Nehru**).
xa: **T.K. Oommen**: tribal movements seek autonomy, identity, resource control.
Panchsheel's first principle: develop **along their own genius**.
Source: Nehru's foreword to **A Philosophy for NEFA**.

136.s: Which of the following is the correct first principle of Nehru’s Panchsheel for tribal development?
o: Measure success exclusively by money spent
Separate tribal people permanently from all institutions
Impose uniform administration on all tribal areas
Develop tribal communities along their own genius
136.x: The first principle is to develop tribal people along their own genius, respecting their distinct capacities and culture.
136.tq: Recall the exact wording of a foundational principle.
xs: Panchsheel principle 1: develop tribals **along their own genius** — option **(4)**.
